review_text: We visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage during our trip in Sri Lanka, and overall it was a memorable experience. Seeing the elephants up close was very special, especially watching them walk and spend time near the river. It is a good place for travelers who want to learn more about elephants and capture some beautiful moments. The location is nice, and the experience can be enjoyable for families, couples, and anyone interested in wildlife. However, it can get quite crowded at certain times, and I think the visitor information and overall organization could be improved a little more. Overall, it was a worthwhile stop during our journey. I would recommend visiting if you are traveling nearby and want to see elephants in a unique setting.

We volunteered here for 4 days and had the best time. We spend a couple of hours in the morning cleaning the stalls and refreshing the elephants food supplies (50kg per elephant), then helped out with the public elephant feeding. A couple of hours off over the middle of the day and then spent time bathing the elephants at the river from 2-4pm before following them back up the street and settling them for the night. We saw some reviews complaining that the elephants were chained- yes some are - the males particularly when they are in musk - wanting to mate and overnight. We understood the rationale for this - to protect themselves and each other at night - they all had their own stalls with plenty of food, but we did see neighbours trying to steal food from each other. Also when they are in musk they are more unpredictable. These are huge animals and so on occasions the public do need to be protected from potential risks. We only saw amazing care and attention given to the elephants from the staff, yes there is some shouting ….. think trying to get a load of teenagers off the playing field. The mahouts do carry long sticks with a hook - an ankush, again this is to guide the elephants - they hook the hook over the elephants ears to direct them. We never saw them being ill treated with the ankush. The public can pay to bath the elephants and we did this as part of our volunteering - the elephants did seem to enjoy this and were so relaxed during the experience. Most of these elephants are working elephants who have been rescued and are used to direction and work. We never saw any riding of the elephants by the public at all. We were very impressed with how clean everything was behind the scenes and how the staff really cared for the elephants. We saw the vets in action as well as the mahouts caring for their particular elephants. Everyone does need to remember that these are enormous animals and it is a privilege to see them close up, but it isn’t in the wild and it isn’t a zoo. The animals here are well cared for, have spaces to roam around and head down to the river each day where they freely wander and play in the water. We also saw some complaints about the cost of visiting, especially as a foreigner.  When we were there there were 65 elephants, needing circa 50kg of food each day and with over 200 staff working there. All these costs occur 255 days a year irrespective of the visitor numbers. Consider how much you would have to pay for such an amazing experience in your home countries. We felt the price was very fair.

We are a family of four: two adults and two teens. My husband and I had visited Pinnewala about 16years ago. We had very fond memories of the place and were keen to return. I wish we hadn't. We visited after having experienced a safari drive at Minneriya National Park. Pinnewala has changed significantly.  We arrived late afternoon and headed straight to the river to see the elephants bathe. There must have been about 20 elephants in the river. The staff in green t-shirts advised you to stand in specific spots to pose with the elephants. They are clearly trained to command: lots of trunks came up and we were encouraged to buy small bags of guavas to feed them. The staff took my phone and snapped LOTS of photos of us, as well as another person's child. The elephants were restrained back by the river by a male with a long stick and a metal prod at the top. They were pushed back about 2-3times in the 20mins we were there. There was also a staff member directing a huge hose of cooling river water across the elephants backs. As soon as the staff gave my phone back, he demanded a tip. Then he kept asking for tips for his colleagues, before telling me that I should tip more. We took our time to head back to the park. The entire area becomes like a ghost town as soon as the elephants have walked through. We entered the park, which had jurassic park/ empty zoo vibes. Lots of lovely green fields and trees....... .....And all of the elephants that we saw were all chained. About 20 of them. Most kept in individual pens-styled areas. They had grass in front of them to eat. But we saw a young elephant who just wouldn't eat, and instead kept shaking its head, rocking on its legs. Another female looked as though she was straining forwards against the chain on her back foot.  A (chained) bull was also shaking his head. We don't know what happened to the elephants who came to the river to bathe (as we didn't follow them back). Instead, we just saw lots who are chained up. Im not sure if any of them have the opportunity to roam around the gorgeous, lush fields that we saw. We noted that the Orphanage has a breeding programme. As my husband wryly pointed out, this helps ensure a positive amount of 'stock' to keep the venue going. Signposts proudly state that there are about 40females and just under 30 male elephants. We probably stayed less than an hour in the park. After all, how long can you just look at chained elephants who are quietly eating long grass that's put in front of them. All in all, not what we remember from Pinnewala all those years ago. If you want an ethical experience, seeing elephants roaming freely, then do your research. Sri Lanka has a lot of parks that will offer you a wonderful glimpse into their natural habitat and lives.

Pinnawala is a village in Sri Lanka, renowned for its Elephant Orphanage. Established in 1975, this unique institution serves as a sanctuary for orphaned, injured, and abandoned elephants, offering them care and protection. Situated on a former coconut plantation along the Maha Oya River, Pinnawala provides a spacious environment for these majestic creatures. What began with just a handful of elephants has grown into the largest herd in captivity in the world. Visitors have the opportunity to witness the daily lives of these gentle giants, including their feeding times, where baby elephants are bottle-fed, and their refreshing baths in the river, a spectacle of playful interaction. While primarily a conservation center, Pinnawala has also become a significant tourist attraction, drawing both locals and international visitors eager to get up close with elephants. The income generated from tourism helps sustain the orphanage's operations and the well-being of its residents. The success of Pinnawala's captive breeding program has also contributed to its growth, with numerous births occurring within the sanctuary. These elephants, often orphaned due to human-wildlife conflict or natural incidents, find a safe haven here. Although not a completely natural habitat, Pinnawala strives to offer a life of care and security for these rescued animals, many of whom would not survive in the wild on their own.

If I could give zero stars I would. Upon first glance, this place looked amazing. Walking up to see the elephants roaming was breathtakingly beautiful, & feeding them fruit was something I’d always dreamed about. But the happiness was short lived when I seen one being walked by a keeper with a big chain around his foot and draped over his neck. Along with the keeper holding a long stick with a sharp point on the end. I asked the guide why are there chains, to which he replied it’s because they’re newly rescued and need to go through a two month training programme to be able to integrate with the other elephants. Reading reviews of Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage, it is clear that opinions are deeply divided. Many visitors express concerns about elephants being chained or guided forcefully, while others criticize the very existence of an institution where elephants interact with humans. However, these critiques often lack an understanding of the difficult realities faced in Sri Lanka’s human-elephant coexistence. Yes, some elephants are sometimes chained—but is the alternative better? Some of these elephants are aggressive due to past trauma, and without restraints, they could pose serious danger to both humans and other elephants. Is the alternative to euthanize every elephant that becomes difficult to manage? When we visited Pinnawala, we made a conscious effort to see beyond the surface. We witnessed elephants bathing in the river, enjoying their meals, and interacting with caretakers who, for the most part, demonstrated genuine care and expertise. The orphanage is home to elephants that have been orphaned, injured in train accidents, or displaced due to conflicts with farmers. Without a facility like this, many of these elephants would not survive. Sri Lanka’s Buddhist culture places a strong emphasis on protecting life, which is why injured and disabled elephants are not euthanized as would have been in Europe. Instead, they are given a chance at life—sometimes with visible scars or disabilities that might make visitors uncomfortable, but which are a testament to the efforts made to save them. Pinnawala is government-run, and its existence plays a vital role in Sri Lanka’s broader conservation challenges. Hundreds of elephants die every year due to human-wildlife conflict, particularly through train accidents and electric fences near farmlands. Investing in facilities like Pinnawala helps not only the elephants but also the people who live alongside them by promoting education and sustainable solutions. Pinnawala has veterinarians that travel the country and help elephants in, an outside the orphanage. This can be assistance with landmine or train accidents in the country side of Sri Lanka. Without visitors there is no economy for this. Is Pinnawala perfect? No. Ethical concerns surrounding elephant tourism should always be addressed, and improvements should be encouraged where needed. But dismissing a place like this entirely ignores the complex reality of conservation in a developing country. The truth is, without tourism, there would be little economic incentive for local communities to protect elephants, and their habitats would suffer as a result. Our visit left us with a greater appreciation for the delicate balance between conservation, cultural traditions, and economic survival. Pinnawala is not a flawless sanctuary, but it is an important part of Sri Lanka’s elephant conservation efforts—one that deserves a more nuanced conversation rather than black-and-white judgment. Visit, spend some money, choose the activities that you feel are ethical and help them  become even better at helping these huge, amazing animals.

As a dedicated institute for elephant conservation, we do concern ourselves with elephants’ physiological phenomena at the premises, and managing" musth" elephants in the facility is one of the great challenges for us. Usually about once every year, adult bull elephants go through a change in their behavior known as musth. Musth is caused by increased levels of the male hormone, testosterone. Bulls in musth are much more aggressive than usual, and other bulls usually keep away from them. At this period it is essential to have them chained up for a few days for their safety, and it is true that when they sometimes meet two bull elephants in this state, they fight violently, and such fights result in severe injury or even death. It severely undermined the purpose of conserving elephants in the facility. At this period we are facilitating all the requirements for him in a large shed with confined mobility, and our goal is their comfort. Bulls in musth are much more aggressive than usual and other bulls usually keep away from them. At this period it is essential to be chained up for a few days for their safety and it is true that when sometimes meet two bull elephants in this state, they fight violently and such fights result in severe injury or even death. Dear visitor, A fantastic day from Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage! We thank you for sharing your feedback with us. We are disappointed to read your comment since you are not well aware of our elephant management system at PEO. Firstly, we would like to explain the point you have mentioned in your review of us. Chaining is an important part of managing elephants in Asian countries and it is the simplest and safest tool to confine these large and potentially dangerous animals to a specific area. Because they are more difficult to control in a captive environment, it is essential to usage of chains to control them to some extent. Especially in a captive environment where elephants and humans share, the same space we should concern about elephants’ safety and visitor’s safety too. In this facility, there are certain aggressive and boisterous bull elephants and we are compelled to chain them up for the above reasons. But, we assure you that all the females in the facility are not chained up all the time of the day and they can roam around morning to late evening in the premises. Secondly, it is need to be aware of the other reasons for chaining up some of the bull elephants in the facility. Hence your photo shows one of our tuskers who is experiencing its musth at the premises. As a dedicated institute for elephant conservation, we are concerned with elephants’ physiological phenomena at the premises, and managing musth elephants in the facility is one of our great challenges. Usually about once every year adult bull elephants go through a change in their behavior known as musths. Musts are caused by increased levels of the male hormone, testosterone. Bulls in musth are much more aggressive than usual and other bulls usually keep away from them. During this period it is essential to be chained up for a few days for their safety and it is true that when sometimes meet two bull elephants in this state, they fight violently and such fights result in severe injury or even death. It severely undermined the purpose of conserving elephants in the facility. During this period we facilitated them with all the requirements in large sheds with confined mobility and our goal is their comfort. However, we are constantly respectful of your constructive feedback and we are happily informed that PEO has already taken many steps to minimize the usage of chains for male aggressive elephants and muths elephants in the facility. Please visit us again and be aware of the novel condition of the Orphanage. Thank you. From PEO Team

The elephant sanctuary in Sri Lanka's pinnawala town is a major sanctuary for orphaned and injured elephants. The road to the orphanage is perhaps one of the most scenic drive you may come across in Sri Lanka. The star attraction of the sanctuary was an elephant which has given birth to twins, a rarity. We were also able to see a few elephants in search of a mate. Away from the orphanage across the road the elephants were given a cool bath in the river. There are also a number of souvenir shops near the elephant bathing ghat. The parking space is spacious and the western style toilets were clean and well maintained. There is also an ATM near the entrance where the newly arrived foreign tourists can convert their home currency into Sri Lankan rupees. A fun place for kids to see elephants of all ages at close proximity. The entry fee is nominal and the place well maintained. We could not locate a restaurant in the premises. We could also see a number of birds in the surroundings. A good place to visit with the kids for a picnic. Recommended.

I first visited  Pinnawala 20 years ago and I was enthralled  by the way the elephants were cared for. It was joyous. I was able to spend precious time  close to the elephants that I adore.  Fast forward to 2022 when a couple of months ago we took two of our  grandchildren to relive the experience from 20 years ago. Only one word can describe it...horrendous.  Elephant welfare has been overtaken by unscrupulous keepers out to make as much money from visitors as they can. Because I was obviously carrying our money in my bag I was separated from my family by the keepers who aggressively tried to obtain R5000 from me. Every picture that you took they wanted paying for. Needless to say after a lot of shouting by me to my family and eventually joining them,  they reluctantly backed off. We then saw them hounding a young female backpacker for money. After we went to rescue her she told us she feigned not being able to understand them to thankfully not part with any money. By late afternoon the keepers went home and the orphanage was left to the mahoots to feed and care for the elephants. 3 large tuskers were chained up and exhibiting shocking distress the whole time we were there. To be fair and with just us left in the park, watching the elephants being fed was a wonderful experience. It is such a shame that the elephants, who we believe to be living in an orphanage where you expect care and kindness to be uppermost, are living in nothing more than a money making theme park. Research, and find many other orphanages in Sri Lanka, that do exactly what it says on the tin.

Dear visitor, A fantastic day from Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage ! Thank you very much for visiting Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage and taking time to write us. Further, obviously you did not observe our daily routine trips and their social & family activities in the free roaming area and bathing area. When we focus on your first point, elephants are definitely secured over night at PEO. Elephants are not pets, weight 3-4 tones & are not as peaceful as they often seem to be. The Orphanage is situated in an in habituated area with traffic. This is not a jungle. If even one elephant brakes out, human and his own life are ultimately in danger. However, Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage already has paid its main attention to keep them free in the future, even at night under various difficult circumstances. Also in our daily activity programe, the elephants are definitely well provided with high quality checked food in their places depending on their weight under the veterinary recommendation. We pay attention to their health everyday and maintain their body balance by eating and daily exercising. Especially, they have a large yard to walk and participate in trekking or other activities. As well as, most of our elephants chained were males and were directed to us from the Judiciary of Sri Lanka as they have captured illegally from the wild. We are compelled to use chains on them, as they are court productions and are very boisterous in behavior. However, the calm and cool animals are kept apart without chains. The Tusker is under musth period,   and it is necessary to keep him in a large shed providing all the requirements with confined mobility. Furthermore, as you said in your review, PEO does not sell elephants to many first and second world zoos. In Sri Lanka, animals are exported to foreign countries in accordance with international convections (e.g. CITIES) only during diplomatic grants and animal exchange programs. This process is approved by the Hon. President of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka with the approval of the Minister in charge of the subject. I hope you understand our efforts to keep up the elephants in the facility and please visit us again to see the improvements we are undertaken to set them chain free in three large enclosures already constructed in the Orphanage. Have a nice day! From, PEO  Team.

We ventured to this Orphanage on a ship's shore ex ... it's about a 2 - 2.5 hour drive from the port on a coach. I think if you can get here with a local guide you would be better off as you can spend as much or as little time as you like at the orphanage, whereas on a ship's tour the time is shorter. This orphanage is a government run orphanage and at least paying guests are aware of this when they enter and hopefully all money raised goes towards the elephant's upkeep and setting them free back into the jungle. I found all the public areas where we went and the enclosures we saw were very clean and tidy. Take Sri Lankan money with you - although you can use CC at the Orphanage shop and other shops in the town, generally speaking they don't take cash unless it's Sri Lankan money. There is an opportunity to feed the elephants by hand in one areas of the orphanage however Rupees are required - no USD or other currency and definitely no CC there !!  Luckily our guide exchanged some USD for Rupees but the fruit was gone very quickly. Yes there were a few elephants chained up in another enclosure but of the three enclosures we saw, this was the only one where they were chained.  The reason we were given for this was because they are wild animals... let's face it ... if they are males and are maturing, they could get annoyed about something and cause injuries to other elephants if not their handlers and / or the public if they crashed through the fence. Indeed at the elephant feeding area I saw one elephant get grumpy with another one for muscling in on the food I was feeding it - the elephant turned around and head butted the second elephant in its side to show it's displeasure at eating its food. The third area where we saw elephants at this Orphanage, the elephants were roaming free in a large treed area ... I wondered if this was the first stage of getting them used to fending for themselves before setting them free in the jungle. We had lunch included in our ship's shore excursion at a hotel by the river and luckily for us, they had quite a few elephants bathing there - a lovely thing to see. IMO, this excursion is not suitable for mobility impaired people because the terrain to get to the elephant enclosures is not paved and the surface is uneven.  There's also a few steps to negotiate within the elephant orphanage area.  Also, the "road" to the hotel where we went for lunch was not paved either.

As a dedicated institute for elephant conservation, we do concern elephant’s physiological phenomena at the premises and managing musth elephants in the facility is one of the great challenge of us. Usually about once every year adult bull elephants go through a change in their behavior known as musths. Musts is caused by increased levels of the male hormone, testosterone. Bulls in musth are much more aggressive than usual and other bulls usually keep away from them. At this period it is essential to be chained them up for few days for their own safety and it is truth that when sometime meet two bull elephants at this state, they fight violently and such fights result in severe injury or even death. It is severely undermined the purpose of conserving elephants in the facility. At this period we are facilitated them with all the requirements in  large sheds with confined mobility and our goal is their comfort . However, we are constantly respected to your constructive feedback and we are happily informed that PEO has already taken many steps to minimize the usage of chains for male aggressive elephants and muths elephants in the facility. I had read up about Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage before I visited Sri Lanka and from what I'd read, I was honestly considering skipping the visit due to claims of animal abuse and unnecessary confinement. But as it turned out, I was part of a group and because the group wanted to go, I had little option but to tag along. What I saw there truly horrified me. 1. Elephant calves were confined in a circular pen and their legs tied with metal chains that left little room for manoeuvre or free movement. 2. There was a tusker displaying a classic case of depressive symptoms - head swaying incessantly and bobbing up and down. Like the calves, he was also tied with a short metal chain in a small shed. 3. A herd of elephants we saw there was so scared of the keeper that as soon as he entered the enclosure with his bull-hook, the terrified elephants literally fled away from him. The keeper was careful not to display any aggressive behaviour in front of the tourists but it was obvious from how scared the elephants were, that terrible things go on behind the scenes. 4. While there, we saw a keeper repeatedly strike a pregnant elephant with a huge pole that had a metal spike at its end. He poked and struck her hard despite the presence of tourists there. I cannot imagine what must be going on once tourist hours are over. We then headed off to the river adjacent to the orphanage where they take the elephants for a bath - hoping that at least there, the elephants must be free. But they were not. Even here, the elephants were tied with short chains while tourists threw fruit at them. I would've compared Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage to a zoo but most zoos treat their animals better than this 'orphanage' does. Pinnawala is not a place I would ever visit again. My money isn't going into a place that has made a business out of abusing animals that should've been returned to the wild. Plus, they breed elephants in confinement at Pinnawala. Real orphanages don't typically do that. Instead, I would strongly recommend visiting the Elephant Transit Home near Udawalawe National Park. I haven't been there but from what I've heard, they are much more responsible in caring for orphaned elephants. Plus they return the elephants to the wild once they are old enough - unlike Pinnawala.

Dear Andrea B A fantastic day from Pinnawala Elephant Orphange! Thank you very much for your feedback and taking time to write us. We do not know the person who guided and recommended this place to you. Indeed, this is an Elephant Orphanage under the Department of National Zoological Gardens in Sri Lanka and our primary purpose is protecting orphaned elephants who were stranded in the wild. Accordingly, we conserve these orphaned wild elephants in a proper way in captivity, since they need utmost care of humans and cannot survive without any help.  Actually, these wild creatures haven’t had any previous experience with humans and it’s provided a proper management system to conserve these largest creatures safely with minimal risk for keeper staff and visitors those who come to visit this place too. Using bull hook is one of the way to control them in the captivity and it is used to guide and cue the elephant with the purpose of ensuring the safety of both humans and elephants. Especially in a free contact situation, where elephants and humans share the same space, a hook should be carried at all times for safety. The tool was developed through thousands of years to allow a mahout to get an elephant’s attention in an emergency (e.g. sudden loud noises or when elephant rampant) or potentially dangerous (potential ingestion of chemical poisons, litter, fallen electricity wires etc.) situation in any situation where elephant may panic. This tool can be used to ensure the safety of the elephant and without causing damage or injury to the elephant. Without carrying a hook is dangerous for both the elephants and people around. The advantage of the hook is that it extends the reach of the arm to allow a safer way for the mahout to signal a command to an elephant. Chaining is another way of managing elephants in the facility. We absolutely do chains only for male elephant here since they are aggressive and boisterous in behavior and it is necessary to keep them under control to ensure the security within the premises. Female elephants in the facility are not chained and they roam around for morning to late evening. In addition to them, we concern their mental and physical conditions to keep them happy and healthy. As a social animal, we have facilitated them to interact with others in compatible social groups, which called herd. They eat with each other, play during bath time, care for their caves, and vocalize array of greetings. We hope you will noticed the efforts, which we have taken to protect and conserve them in the facility. Thank you. From, PEO Team.

Dear Schmumues. A fantastic day from Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage! We thank you for your feedback and your comments are taken in to consideration constructively as we strive to improve with your each and every visit. Actually, as a responsible elephant conservation center, we do follow the international standards of elephant care in the facility and we are struggling to meet your expectations. At present, there are 84 elephants in our custody and we highly concern their international standards such as population control, veterinary care, food and water supplementation, and habitat enhancement to keep up them happy as possible. In a captive environment where multiple elephants and people including tourists and visitors share the same space. It is simply too dangerous not to have an elephant controlling method in case of emergency. Chains and bull hooks are the elephant guiding and controlling tools in the facility and our caretakers are capable enough to use them effectively without any physical pain. Chains are the simplest and safest tool to confine these large and potentially dangerous animals to a specific area because they are more difficult to control especially male elephants are on chains around their ankles to provide a quick and safe means to control them whenever necessary. Chaining are also important for safely restraining an elephant during husbandry. (e.g. foot care) and veterinary procedures. Many forms of restraint, if done properly and with appropriate tools are not harmful to the animal for example halters on horses and leashes and neck collars to lead and manage them in a safe human manner. Actually aggressive individuals can be dangerous to other elephants and need to be control to certain extent. Therefore, we are compelled to use chains to minimize the harmful effects. Activities like fruit feeding, jumbo bathing events are at the orphanage for   visitor’s entertainment and it enhances the interrelationship between humans and animals. Hence, these all the revenue generated are for the welfare and upliftment of the elephants. When conserving these largest and long lived animal, financial stability is a major concern to provide appropriate facilities for them. Indeed, we have to feed 84 stomachs daily, have to keep them up happy and healthy environment, have to maintain daily sanitation activities etc. The maintenance cost is very high in the facility and it is absolutely huge task maintaining the institution. However, we do our best to protect these orphaned and endangered species for the being extinction and ensure the biodiversity in Sri Lanka. Thank you From PEO Team

I visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage just over a week ago and I must say that I was on high alert after a few derogatory articles I had seen written about the facility and its treatment of the elephants. Happily, I found nothing worthy of a complaint. The elephants parade down to the river and anyone who knows animals can see that they are intelligent beings who are used to the routine and are not at all stressed by the watching crowds - in fact, some clearly loved it and were happy to participate and be patted or fed a morsel along the way.  Once in the river they splash, roll around in the water and clearly enjoy themselves. Yes, some did have a loose chain around their necks, but this didn't bother them. When you consider the size of an elephant and the general havoc they could cause to a community when aggressive, it's not difficult to understand that there are times when they must be prudently restrained or separated. As for returning them all to the wild; these elephants no longer have a place in the wild as they have formed new family bonds within their new herd. Many have already been rescued from the wild where they were close to death and others are on medication or special food. So if you want to truly help elephants and not just have a pompous rant about turning them loose, visit Pinnawala, spend a few dollars towards their support and watch them happily splash about in safety.

Reviews of Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage praise and condemn so our only choice was to see it for ourselves. The stamp of the country’s Department of Wildlife Conservation on the park was the deciding factor. Over a twenty year period, Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage hand raised abandoned babies, treated the injured and integrated displaced elephants into a growing herd. Currently, 88 elephants are part of the Pinnawala family on their 30-acre property, making it one of Sri Lanka’s largest tourist attractions. At Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage you will see chains. This is precautionary for large males while bathing, wandering the park – river path, and when a female’s seductive pheromones spike. A full grown male can stand more than 2.5 metres weighing  5.5 tonnes. A force to be reckoned with when they want to get down to business. You will also see mahouts rounding the elephants to keep them in one spot. This is also precautionary to keep them from getting too close to punters. A disappointing observation was people paying some entrepreneurial mahouts to bathe the elephants. The elephant is chained and made to lie on its side during the encounter. This is not approved and is something the orphanage is trying to eliminate. Elephants eat an average of 250kg of food per day, multiply that by 88 of them and you have an expensive grocery bill. Modern veterinary equipment and traditional indigenous medicine come at a price and the gallons of milk required to raise a baby elephant is also exorbitant. Sponsorship programs, donations and your ticket price all contribute to the cost of feeding and caring for these adorable creatures. Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is not perfect, but the care for these elephants is obvious. This is a heavily tourist-trafficked attraction. Vendors take advantage of the captive audience and sell everything from elephant poo paper products (quite an interesting process) to every form of elephant printed clothing you can imagine. Away from this retail madness, however, is picturesque countryside, a meandering river and comfortable accommodation.

We then went to the land site on the opposite side of the road, again elephants are corralled for the entertainment of the viewing public. A very heavily pregnant elephant was trying to get to a water hole at the top of the paddock with some other elephants following, however the mahouts would not let her rest and drove her and her followers to the part of the paddock closest to the tourists. One of the staff stood near me kept saying 'happy elephant'. I'm not David Attenborough but I would say that the elephant was not squealing with delight.  There were also other elephants under shelter which clearly had mental issues and were heavily chained, I do however appreciate that where they have been rescued from may be the cause of their problems and not the place they have come to. Some negative reviews on here and comments concerning the treatment of the elephants. Some are in chains but these are male elephants and are to control their natural aggression to other males. The mahmood’s use sticks to encourage understanding of commands - again for the safety of the elephants and surrounding people. They use the sticks to apply pressure to vital points ( acupuncture points) which do not harm the elephants - if you’ve ever been struck in a pressure point you will know a slight jab doesn’t hurt but does encourage the body to move in a certain way. This is what they do with the Sticks. You couldn’t move an elephant with a shove or a little stick otherwise. If you’re concerned with the treatment suggest research first before judging. Many of the elephants come from farmland where they’ve been trapped in holes dug by farmers to collect water. They often have broken limbs when they come to the sanctuary. Once recovered, most are returned to the forests. Some pictures attached of the time we watched them bathing. One thing to note - from wherever you are you will likely take some time to get there. Hello, I was in Pinnawala last October (2018) and it was a total scam as expected. The tourists arrive in a campus that is completely human-created as opposed to what the pictures seem to show, surrounded by elephant cages and yards where the elephants are being held captive with chains in place and keepers armed with spears. The elephants are paraded every few hours to the ''feeding area'' and the ''bathing river''. Both these areas are places to which the elephants are forced to walk to, clearly displaying signs of stress and resistance to the keepers. The smaller elephants that they call ''babies'' are used for public demonstrations of milk nursing. A local guide explained to us that these babies are in fact adult elephants with over 8 years that are kept in confined places and fed milk so they remain small and cute for the tourists to believe in the whole ''orphanage'' thing. I believe this orphanage started as a place for rescued elephants, but nowadays it's clearly only a zoo for captive mistreated elephants that should be in programs to be returned to the wild. Many guides admit to take tourists here only because of its international popularity, against their own beliefs. IN SUM, if you have the time, for the SAME PRICE of visiting this scam, you can go on a full day safari at the beautiful national parks of Sri Lanka and see wild elephants happy in their proper habitats. Please spread the word and complain to your travel agency as most of the european or any international proposed itineraries in Sri Lanka propose Pinnawala as a must, and this has to absolutely change, together with the overpriced fake spice garden tours.

Spent 2 weeks volunteering here as a family so gained some insight into the orphanage. The orphanage would love to see all elephants in the wild, unfortunately this is impossible with pressures on land use by a growing population.  They cant introduce elephants to an existing wild herd as they would not be accepted.  All elephants in the orphanage have been raised in captivity so would seek out people if released and this would in turn create conflict risking the elephants life. The mahouts do shout and use ashoks with elephants to ensure public safety.  To see behind the public face and watch them tenderly go over the elephants skin for 2 hours looking for problems shows their true feelings towards the animals.  They shout at the cleaners if the elephant houses are not sufficiently cleaned. The prices are fair for tourists and cheaper for locals to encourage locals to visit, learn and take an interest in their own wildlife.  This is a government run organisation so the prices are set in Colombo, not by the orphanage.  The extra fee for feeding or bathing elephants is likewise set by the politicians. The Elephant in the Room - chains.  These are necessary to manage the herd in a small area to keep public, staff and elephants safe.  Injured, sick and pregnant elephants are kept separate, but still taken for free time at the river away from the main herd. There are 19 elephants housed here which have been seized from illegal owners and are awaiting court cases so can't be put with the herd. In all we really enjoyed our 2 weeks here giving us an insight not gained during a short visit.  Volunteering is hard work and not for everybody.  We learnt about the politics behind a lot of decisions and saw the love held for these wonderful creatures by all the staff at the orphanage.

There are a lot of misleading reviews about Pinnawala. I've been twice - earlier this month and 21 years ago - and I've enjoyed the experience both times. The price of 2500 rupees (about £11 per person) is quite high but much lower than I've seen online where it's often stated at $20 per person. There's not too much to do. Our driver went in with us which we thought a bit odd until we realised he knew exactly where to go and when to make sure we got the best experience. We went first to the elephant 'paddocks' where the ladies were hanging around eating and waiting for bath time. In a separate area, the boys were getting ready to go the river. Nothing can really prepare you for seeing a massive herd of elephants on the move. The boys went first, strolling through the orphanage, out to the road and down to the river. Some are chained - for their safety and everybody else's. I don't think it's a bad thing. Once the boys were on their way, the lady elephants followed. We watched the bath time for nearly 2 hours. Our driver urged us to a brilliant watching space in a cafe which we really appreciated. In two hours you have plenty of time to watch and observe the different personalities amongst the elephants. There are the cheeky younger boys, the stubborn old ladies, the frisky and the laid-back all hanging out together. People have commented on the use of 'spikes' or 'guides'. We was the metal guides being used by the mahoots but always very gently and never with any violence. The love of the handlers for their pachyderm pals was clear to all. One old lady - quite possibly the grande dame of the herd - spent an hour standing knee deep trying to avoid a wash. Her mahoot gently urged her into deeper water, taking his time and using his 'guide' to help scrape old mud off her head and back. Eventually she gave in and rolled over in the water to let him clean her properly. Some are chained in the water but didn't seem distressed about it. A couple of young females made a jovial bid for freedom on the far banks and were laughingly chased down and returned to the herd. If you're looking for lots of action, this may disappoint. If you have the patience to watch and wait, you'll probably love it as much as I did. One comment. I think the management should consider rebranding this as an Elephant Home rather than an Elephant Orphanage since it seems to create elevated expectations of lots of babies and at present there really aren't many at all. The purpose of the home is to give safe haven to elephants, not to go looking for unwanted babies. Back in the days of the Civil War, a lot of babies were orphaned by their parents being killed (accidentally or intentionally) so there were more little ones to see. These days they do have a few babies but I suspect that's more an outcome of boy and girl elephants getting friendly rather than any kind of captive breeding programme.

First things first, I saw no evidence of any physical abuse of the elephants during my visit to Pinnewala Orphanage. The elephants look well fed, clean and have no scars from chains or sticks as far as I could see. The keepers used goads to guide the elephants and to prevent the bulls trying to mix with the main herd of females/younger elephants, but I did not see a single one being hit. The chains used on some of the bulls look unpleasant, but they seem to be loosely fitted and not particularly irritating to the animals. Keeping such large and potentially aggressive animals under control is essential when they are in such close proximity to one another (bulls generally wouldn’t mix with the herd in the wild) and to humans. The animals are corralled to be fed and kept in a certain (quite large) area of the river to be washed, but otherwise roam around a large natural reserve. Some of the ‘extras’ put on for tourists (photos with the elephants, feeding/washing them etc) aren’t acceptable. The elephants are wild animals, not playthings or props, and they should be treated as such. A couple of keepers rode some of the bulls back from the river, which again I don’t agree with. Additionally, perhaps more effort could be made to return some of the animals back to the wild, however I don’t know anything about the practicalities  and of course this runs the risk of them being killed by farmers (the main threat to wild elephants in Sri Lanka). All in all, as far as I could tell the Pinnewala Orphanage is not abusive to the animals in its care and is no worse than Western zoos. Keeping animals in captivity is never ideal, but the fraught relationship between farmers and wildlife in Sri Lanka make it impossible for all elephants to live in the wild. Perhaps in the future with better education, people all over the world will be better able to co-exist with animals and places like Pinnewala will be unnecessary. However, for now this place is the best of a bad situation.

Maybe the intentions of this 'orphanage' were once good, they are definitely not now. This is a commercialized elephant breeding factory. Most of the elephants are bred in the park, for the sole purpose of entertainment for tourists. Caretakers are encouraging everyone to take photos and touch the elephants in exchange for tips. You can pay extra to feed a baby elephant, who is chained by itself in a cage surrounded by tourists. When we were there, the baby was freaking out, trying to get out of the chains and hurting herself. They get fed whenever a tourist pays, not only during feeding times. Many elephants are chained up all day in the same spot. They get to go to the river 2 times a day (you have seen the famous photos). Even there many are chained up under water and caretakers push them underwater with a stick so they look like they are splashing around. Many of them are showing signs of distress, rocking back and forth for hours at the time while being chained up. This does not happen in the wild. These compulsive movements cause life-threatening damage to the feet and joints of the elephant. They are in severe distress and don't let them tell you otherwise. People saying that there is no other way to treat them and the elephants would not survive in the wild are wrong. There are way more humane ways to treat elephants in an orphanage and this is not one of them. Please don't participate.

This is a place that has many controversial reviews and so we pondered to whether we wanted to go or not. It was a tossup and I am glad we did go but it did leave some questions unanswered. We missed the elephants walking from the park over the road and down to the river. So we purchased our tickets from the ticket office and then headed over. You have to give your ticket to the ticket man at the start of the road so unpaid people cannot get down there to watch the elephants. We got down there and it was quite a sight. All these elephants standing in the water. The group of elephants was split and I did notice the ones that were chained in place. I also noted a small group that kept trying to get out of the water. The mahout would let them go for a while and then he would yell and wave his hook and the elephants obviously fearful of him would get back in the water. I got talking to another visitor who said she had been a number of times and that the river was really low and when it is low they seem to be lethargic. It was the first time she had seen them so disinterested. The mahout to me seemed to be a bully. Later on when they were prepping them to leave, this particular guy caught my eye and smiled. I gestured to him that I was not happy with his behavior and proceeded to photograph him. I believe there is a difference to being in control fairly and being a bully. Out of all of them he definitely was a bully. The elephants were swapped  around a bit and it was fascinating to be so close and to watch them for a reasonably long period. It was extremely hot that day so we sat up in the restaurants balcony and had a beer etc. to get some respite. They then moved the elephant’s to the water cannon by the exit to the river which they seemed to enjoy and then the main girl elephant, she led them back up the road. They knocked over a hat stand in a store which was funny and they seemed keen to get back. We followed them closely and when we got back they had taken them over the back of the park and they were being fed. We stood for perhaps half an hour and no one told us what was happening- we just stood and hoped there was something more. Eventually they told us we could go over which we did. Yes they were all chained by a foot and they all had piles of food. We stood for a period watching how they ate soft wood, palm leaves and observed what they seemed to prefer to eat, and how they manipulated the food to eat. We then went back to another area where they had younger elephants still on milk. We got talking to the assistant curator and it wasn’t until he answered my questions about containment, feeding, punishment, medical care, that it made any sense. He said there was a lot of misunderstanding and therefore there are negative reviews. I asked why they seemed to be not enjoying themselves in the water and he said, they are just so keen to get back to eat. The main reason for containment is to stop fighting. In the wild the elephants form packs where there is a boss and they will fight if they encroach on other elephant’s territory. They are working on a big open area for them but at the moment containment is the best for them. So this parks environment is not normal, but it is the best they can do and they do their best to stop the animals hurting each other. He said that the elephants do not have to work for their food there and life is quite easy and the care is excellent with medical care etc. and it is a good alternative for the orphans. I suggested they educate the visitors more. There was very little education of the visitors and when you don’t know why things are being done, you come up with your own theory. The experience is not interactive enough. I also complained about the bully mahout and he knew who I was talking about and he has been pulled up before about this. I appreciate what this place is doing but think it is a shame that there are even orphans that need care. If they were just left to their own devices, and humans didn’t interfere, there would be few orphaned anyway. I think they actually do really care for them and give them great care, but they need to connect with the visitors more and explain what and why and how they do what they do.

It's amazing to watch 40+ elephants happy, frolic and even scrubbed by some of the orphanage workers. You can enjoy the view from a cafe or just from the pavement. Proceed back up past the shops selling elephant dung toilet paper ;) to the orphanage where you can enjoy feeding them or just watch them roam about in wide open spaces. Some elephants are with chains which can be a little upsetting to initially see but it appears its only for those that are a bit unruly and could charge off. None are actually shackled to the ground although we did feel a bit taken advantage of by the river as a young elephant with a chain was used to pose for photos with tourists as workers pressed for money for each photo. Try to avoid this if possible as you will have many opportunities to take photos of them in the river, on the road and in the orphanage without lining the pockets of opportunists using them for a photo opportunity. Who wants a photo with chains in it anyway?

One of the oldest places in Sri Lanka where elephants wounded, hurt are cared for. They even breed elephants and leave them out in the open once they are ready. This is my second visit to the place, and was excited all the way through. You can see elephants up close and personal, chewing the greens, with their young ones and in their families. If its a non rainy day, you can even see the herd bathing and enjoying in the nearby river. There is a ticket for foreigners, saarc country foreigners, and locals...totally takes about 1-2 hours, and is on the way to Kandy...

We visited as a part of a day trip from Negombo to Kandy. We arrived early morning, at 0930 and were able to watch the baby elephants being bottle fed. You could also give it a go yourself if you asked. The elephants looked well treated and after  walking around the orphanage, we were pleasantly surprised to be guided across the road by our tour guide to a local restaurant overlooking the rivers. The street was full of shops and people asking us to come in, which seemed decent if your into that kind of thing. We arrived at the restaurant and ordered some food (Western prices) and after a few minutes, saw a huge herd (50+) elephants coming down the streets into the large river to bathe. It was particular great to see they were completely free to play and wash (no chains of ropes) with a few of the handlers simply sat by on the rocks. Absolutely fantastic to see and definitely recommended.

Great experience. Washing & feeding the elephants. We need to pay appx 50 USD for a pack of 4 ( 2 adults 2 kids ). A way of donation. The souvenir shop has reasonable prices compared to the ones that we saw in Bentota & Galle. Try to be there early like 10 am. to see all the ceremony.

I have visited a few elephant sanctuaries in Thailand, but this is the first time visiting an elephant orphanage in Sri Lanka. We were not expecting to see a few elephants chained at their hind feet and neck, but were informed that these were untamed animals. Overall the caretakers did not seem to have a bond with their charges like what we saw in Thailand. It would have been better if there was more narration on how these animals are cared for and managed.

It is an okay place to visit even though I personally against places using animals to make money. It seems to be much better than it was a few years ago. I still feel that animals like elephants need to be in the wild, not in enclosed areas like Pinnawala

We visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage on our way to Kandy from Colombo. Initially I did not have high hopes of seeing anything extraordinary. After entering we had to walk for some distance in the hot sun seeing only one or two elephants chained inside their enclosure. But at the end of our walk, we were treated to a fascinating sight of more than 50 elephants roaming about in an open area enclosed by rocks and railings to prevent them from coming out. Then we watched some elephants being fed and some people were allowed to feed milk to baby elephants in bottles. After coming out, we were told that the elephants would come out, cross the road, walk into the street and take a bath in the river. We waited outside for some time and then the gates opened and more than 30 elephants came out, crossed the road and walked into the street within 5 feet of where we were standing. It is both awesome and scary to have 25 elephants walking right next to you, trumpeting and swaying and one elephant swerved dangerously close to where I was standing. After they crossed us, we followed them to the river by paying the charges and were again treated to a rare sight of so many elephants bathing together in the river. All in all, it was a wonderful and unforgettable experience and I am very happy that I paid a visit to this place. I have no hesitation in recommending this attraction to all of you who are visiting Sri Lanka.

We visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage in May 2018. I would not agree with some of the reviews here because we as locals know where these elephants come from. Most of the elephants are taken in when they are so small and stuck in mud or wells. They have been rescued from near-deaths and taken in to the authorities for recovery. Their unfortunate situation is when they recover they are not in a psych to go back to the forest and survive on their own. They start loving humans because humans saved their life when they were small and when they are released to the jungle they go searching humans houses just to be pet. But when the house people are unaware of this they can harm the elephants in fear. Some elephants are taken in when there is a risk to their lives due to their tusks. Some elephants are calves born at Pinnawala from the orphaned parents. Elephants are intelligent creatures and they are very grateful for the human who saved their life. As I know Pinnawala started in 1970s to protect the vanishing elephant species when it was the era where elephants were to be classified as endangered (still classified as endangered). I must say Pinnawala is protecting them well. I agree that it’s a prison for them. However they are well taken care of. Story may have two sides. Mahot (the iron rod) and chains have two stories too. Some say it hurts the elephants some say they do it in a way it doesn’t. True they are in limited liberty but the last white rhino too was protected like this. Pinnawala has 88 elephants and Sri Lanka have only around 3000. So I believe what Pinnawala doing is right. Once the population grows to a safer level things may change. Our journey was incredibly relaxing. Contrast to the last time I visited here 20 years ago, now they have made lot of free areas for elephants to roam. Feeds them regularly and elephants seems to be well nourished and happy. I’ve been in zoos where animals looked so malnourished and unhappy but this was not a place like this. We contributed to the park to help them with feeding costs. I agree foreign tickets maybe expensive but all the money goes to a good place to keep this tuskers happy. Thank you staff for all the great work, please keep up the great work and dedication. P:S: I attached a photo of the milk feeding ticket since it had the showtimes. And don’t forget to check the info photos and the funny elephant trying to scratch his back ;)

Honestly. I thought I would write something that will help guide your decision about whether to go or not, however it isn’t straight up and simple. I’ve tried to bullet point my thoughts to try and help. 1. Yes there are chains on some elephants. I believe some have shown aggressive behaviours. There are some very not well looked after elephants in extremely worse situations I have seen across the island. 2. The milk feed I am in two minds about. It is done to obviously provide money for the elephants. The two we saw were not in shackles, were boisterously playing around the site and seemed more than happy to keep drinking away, and were more teenager-ish stature. 3. The River. They seemed more than happy to splash about in the river. Some elephants were having their keepers wash them, one elephant didn’t want him to stop, encouraging him when he stopped until he carried on again. Two elephants were chained on a long chain, they had enough room to play and their keepers could leave them safely there. It didn’t seem any different to when you nip into the corner shop with your dog tied by its lead to the lamppost outside. 4. I did see one keeper prodding an elephant with a sharp pointed spear type implement at one point when it appeared to be going off track. This concerned me a little, however no elephant I had a good look at had any wounds, there were happy calves with their mums. They kept the bulls separate to the rest of the herd as they generally get territorial and violent. If you do not like Zoos, do not go. Minneriya National Park is nearby and has wild herds.

ANIMAL CRUELTY This place is barbaric, a poor excuse for an orphanage. We visited this place on our first day in Sri Lanka. Being an animal lover I was very excited. I’ve seen African elephants on Safari but this was going to be the first time I’d ever encountered Asian elephants. We were told that the elephants were down in the river having a bath. We paid our entry fee (Circa 2,500 ruppees each) and headed on down. On our walk to the river a ‘guide’ started telling us about all the other elephant related things available (rides, paper made from dung) - this blatant ‘up-sell’ put me on high alert. If this was a REAL orphanage I would have expected a bit of chatter about the elephants we were about to see. When we arrived at the river we were faced with the reality of this place. All the elephants were in a river huddled together being watched over by 5 menwith large metal pointed rods and large crowds of unsuspecting visitors. Now, I’m no an idiot, I understand these animals used to be wild and appreciate the humans have to have some sort of protection should something go wrong. However, these animals were so obviously scared of these rods. On several occasions I watched a man raise a rod to the elephants (who were not misbehaving) and the elephants coward away. Disgusting. We watched on as a man prodded one of the elephants with the large metal rod so that it would go to the crowds of tourists and place its trunk in their hands. (The crowd had to later tip the man for the pleasure). One of the elephants was in a chain. There is a sign explaining that they have to chain some of the male bulls elephants, for safety. Funny, the only elephant I saw chained was an old female (probably a matriarch). There is ZERO information on the elephants themselves. Nothing about their names, ages, or stories - they have have no identity. As we walked away from the Elephant prison I felt a great sadness that these Elephants were subjected to a life of misery just so us tourists could get a photo for Instagram. What made me even sadder was to see how many people have reviewed this as a positive experience. If you want to see an elephant head to one of the many amazing national parks that Sri Lanka has to offer do not go here.

After some initial concerns, we decided to visit Pinnawala Orphanage and we enjoyed it yet it did raise some concerns. The ticket for locals is a bargain. Foreigners pay much more, but I guess you need to maintain such a place and it's be unfair to overcharge locals. The place is indeed huge, beautiful and well-kept. It's all surrounded by the jungle. The orphanage enclosure is all done with wood and trunks and there is varied and typical vegetation (there are signs for the trees). The fruit feeding of adult elephants and milk feeding of the young ones has a little of a show feeling, but if you try (paying a somehow reasonable price), you'll get the chance to have a unique experience, get close to the elephants and touch them. The unruly young ones were cute and insatiable. The adults seemed to enjoy the fruit and none seemed to be forced to eat. Across the place there are lots of signs with information about elephants and their care and feeding. In a world where human beings are taking space from the wildness to build towns and roads, Pinnawale has a caring aim. Seeing a few unruly young ones chained was cause of concern, yet I want to believe that's the only option to keep the most unruly ones and that at some point, they are unchained and allowed to be in other open areas. It's a different experience from a zoo and a from a circus. I have heard otherwise yet I don't have those strong opinions. These elephants were separated by their own herds so at least they appear to be looked after and they may not have had many chances out there alone.

When I was looking for a place to visit animals close to Kandy, the Elephant Orphanage was indicated and my first question was if they have animals for tourists or because they take care of them, and I was told that they were taking good care of the elephants! Unfortunately, I didn’t like what I saw... the animals are clearly scared from the staff, who handle stick with sharp metal in the end. I have to be honest after reading negative reviews of the orphanage on trip adviser I did not want to visit here and was talked into it by our tour organiser..but I am so glad I did. We arrived early and our organiser bought us tickets to give the babies their milk and to feed an older one fruit.  I was wary of this as it seemed very intrusive but watching the babies playing with the keepers reassured me they were happy and the older one certainly new which treats she wanted first from the fruit basket. Everywhere was spotless and I saw nothing but care from the keepers to the elephants.   Soon enough the elephants were down at the river.   I got a little upset as one elephant had been chained and seemed distressed. On asking our guide why he explained she would run away if not and could not take care of herself in the wild on her own and did not have the social skills to join a herd.   My unrest was soon settled though as some other elephants joined her and she soon settled she just wanted company. Whilst it is not ideal for elephants to be kept in captivity it is however a fact that these elephants need cared for.   Sri Lanka now also has a transit orphanage so hopefully moving forward more orphans will be returned to the wild. Given that the elephants at Pinawalla will always need cared for I recommend you visit if only to help pay for their upkeep.   I see no need though for a breeding programme to be in place.   Tourists would rather see older elephants knowing this is ethically sound than to visit somewhere which is breeding babies to show although we did not see any really young ones.   Something for the management to think about. More and more travellers are now wildlife tourists who care about all of the animals they see.   To end on a positive I do recommend still visiting as it was such positive experience whish put a lot of my fears to rest.

They collect them from the wild for a human spectacle. They are chained and trained. It's quite sickening the way elephants are scared of their trainers.

My favourite animals - elephants.  We spent hours just watching and experiencing them - interacting with each other and obviously very happy.   Watch them come down the street to go for a splash about in the river - they are amazing animals and it is good to see them cared for in a very special way.   Thank you for taking care of them Pinnawala - you are all wonderful people.  I will be back .....

While we love the idea of this elephant orphanage, it was surprising to turn up to see an elephant chained in a small paddock. However, things picked up when we saw the full herd, clearly contented and well-cared for in a large grassed space. The kids LOVED the opportunity to feed one of them some fruit. It was amazing to see the full herd in the river. However, seven elephants were chained in the river and one was trained to reach up to a hotel platform where tourists could touch it - for a price! One tourist couple were hit up by the elephant handlers because they didn’t give a big enough tip. We came to see an elephant orphanage, not a circus, and it felt morally wrong to see the elephants being forced to perform for tips.

Pinnawala for us was really a big zoo keeping elephants only.  Didn’t see any abuse of animals, but a few were chained and being ridden on for whatever purpose.  The best thing was to see many elephants at their bath time (2pm?)  when they take elephants to the river.

Came to Sri Lanka without the intention of visiting elephants in captivity. After speaking to some local tour operators, we were assured that our reservations about how the elephants were treated would be found to be untrue. The government has recently stepped in and at pinnawala, you can no longer ride the elephants which is a good thing! When it came to them being chained up - the ones we saw in "chains" simply had them around their neck to their ankle which would prevent them from running or charging. Only the elephants recently brought to the orphanage had this. We watched the babies feeding and walked with them down to the river where you can sit in a hotel and enjoy a cold drink whilst watching them, and walk down to the rocks to stand near them while they play in the water. Overall a good experience and one I would recommend!

Nice to see elephants bathing in river, some seen feeding from bottles, bit like very informal zoo. Nearby are shops including elephant "poo" items - we saw a demonstration of how the dung is recycled into paper. Interesting place for a couple of hours

Spent a really nice hour here enjoying the beautiful Elephants. Was difficult seeing a couple of the Elephants chained by the ankle but they did seem very healthy and as many of them are rescued the alternative to a chain is far worse. Well worth a visit to see and support these gorgeous beasts.

Went to Sri Lanka in Nov 2017. Landed at Colombo & stopped at this place on our way to Kandy. Did not go inside the orphange but there is a hotel just on the opposite side of the orphange where one can see the elephants bathing in the river below. It was breakfast time and we thoroughly enjoyed our breakfast while witnessing the elephants playing in the river water below. Worth a visit

I had read a lot of mixed reviews so I really wasn’t sure what to think but I’m so glad I visited,one of the best experiences of my life and one I won’t be forgetting anytime soon. We visited yesterday and arrived early to ensure we could get tickets and view the elephants before feeding and bathing started. When we arrived we spent time taking photos and watching them in their natural environment, they had a lot of space to move around, tree branches and water. None had chains on in this enclosure (which we were worried about after reading so many bad reviews) You can feed one of them if you purchase a fruit bowl for 250rupees which is super cheap, you get six big sizes of fruit and you get so close it’s a great experience and good photo opportunities. They then started the milk feeding for two babies, again these didn’t have any chains on in the milking area. We chose not to do this but it was very popular to feed a bottle to one of the babies. After this we headed down to the river where they come down and bath, this is when we saw four of them had chains on around their foot and the remaining chain thrown in their neck (not wrapped around), I asked our tour guide why this is and he said it’s to control them as they were kept away from the herd dude to fighting. Don’t know if it’s true or not but a fair explanation. We went into the restaurant and brought a drink and definitely worth while to get an excellent view of them walking down and bathing. Overall an unforgettable experience and my friend and I are so glad we went.

We arrived early to see the baby elephants being fed, it was ok but not the highlight. You can see quite a number of elephants the highlight however is when they go and swim in the river. Try and get over the road early and grab a seat at the hotel on your left near the river. You will get a great view and you can grab a drink while you watch them. Definitely worth visiting.

I did a lot of research into this orphanage, especially because of the mixed reviews. My friends and I organised a tour with Scenic Tours & Travels, and from Negombo  it was about a 2 hour scenic drive (but extremely bumpy). It’s 2500 rupees for the entrance into the Orphanage. We arrived at about 10:30 and went straight to the river where they bathe. It was a stunning image and we got extremely close to a few of the elephants, an absolute once in a life time experience. At 12, they bring all the elephants back to the orphanage, so to get a great image of them crossing the road, try to get back to the reception area just before 12 to watch them. Then you can go watch the elephants eat as well as pay to feed one. At 1:15, the feed the baby elephants. It’s extremely hot in the sun but bearable in the shade so take lots of protection. Some elephants did have chains but this mainly when they were walking within centimetres of people. I believe the elephants and well looked after and happy, and is an experience I’ll never forget!

Ruchi is very dedicated in his job! The people he works with are really nice and reliable! This is a travel-agency with heart and very special people. Putting together the long time of being of Ruchi Tours as a travel agency, the great experience of the travel guides and the wide and grown network of Ruchi you will experience a unice trip with a lot of special insights of the Sri Lankan culture. We travelled with our 7 year old daughter and booked 3 trips. 2 were with Ruchi, 1 was with our travel angency. The Tours with Ruchi were much better organized and guided. With our travel agency we had the feeling, the guide had a low interest of explaining and guiding trough the Safari Park. Book with Ruchi, you will not be disappointed. It is worth a try!

I went to this place some two weeks ago , i found the place OK , since we were staying in a river facing hotel , where the elephants came for bathing , it really didnt make sense for us to visit the orpahange , the elephants came for bathing once during the brkfast and then once for lunch also at 3 pm . so anybody staying at the hotel with a river few can easily see it and it really doesnt not make any sense to see elephants inside the orphanage . just to note here we had to buy ticket even to reach our hotel bcos the elepehants were visible to us from our room .and frankly after seeing them twice you dont wanna see them again and again

We booked our stay in Pinnawala overlooking the elephant bathing area after reading tons of great views add seeing amazing photos on various travel blogs. After we booked we heard from a local friend that it was not such a great place after all since the elephants were not treated that well. We decided to go and see for ourselves. One of the first things we saw in our hotel was a poster offering people to ride elephants - pretty bad sign. The following day we got up to see the elephants walk down to the river and bathe. Many of them wore big chains and had a guy on their backs with a bull stick in his hand. When they came down to the river some of them were chained so they could not walk 3 meters and others were just standing looking out in the air. Some were forced to bathe and were clearly scared of the sticks. Most of the chained elephants were done bathing and left while others stayed in the bathing area. Since the remaining ones were not chained and walked a bit more free it might look like a nice place for tourists only seeing  this part. After the elephants had bathed in front of one hotel they were pushed towards the next hotel so more tourists could see them. It was very clear that they could not walk freely but has a plan of where to stand and what to do. I understand  that the elephants might be dangerous and I am not a vet who understands elephant behavior but to me it just didn’t look right. I would NOT recommend this place to anyone and I am so upset that I supported this place by staying at one of the hotels overlooking the elephant orphanage. I will however use this knowledge to inform others.

If you are passing through the area it is nice to stop and pay a visit to this orphanage. It feels very touristy though and more like an elephant zoo than a sanctuary. You can feed the elephants but need to buy a fruit basket and elbow your way through the crowds to get close enough to one trunk. If you just want to see the elephants and aren’t fussed about interacting with them, it may be better to just go for lunch at one of the restaurants overlooking the bathing site.

We were in Pinnawala last week, and loved watching the elephants bathe in the water. We only took the general entrance ticket as we had already done the bathing of elephant in a smaller camp nearby. The sight is gorgeous when you see hundreds of elephants enjoying in the cool waters in the scorching heat, while you're lunching with that view. My concern is with the claim that the orphanage and the smaller camps make regarding the safety and wellness of the elephants. These elephants are chained up and their actions to sitting, standing, bathing, eating, riding humans, etc. all seem orchestrated by the mahouts, I hope not out of fear. Having said this, the overall experience of being so close to them and petting them is so delightful.

I was on a tour from Colombo in a group of 15.  This tour was presented by Silver Whisper (cruise ship) and began with a train trip on a classic train, the Viceroy.   We had an excellent guide, Asiri, who told us the history of Sri Lanka and the history of elephants in Sri Lanka and the role of the Pinnawala Orphanage.  Once we got to the roadway used by the elephants to go back and forth to the river, we then had a lovely buffet lunch at the Pinnawala Elephant Hotel followed by an opportunity to feed the elephants on their way back from the river.  We then proceeded to the other side of the road where we watched the bottled milk feeding of some of the elephants as well as larger portions of fruit.  We went back to the hotel and watched the elephants come back down the road and into the river.  I think, for all of us, watching the elephants in the river was the highlight, but feeding them fruit was exciting!  The role of our guide was key to our appreciation for and delight with the elephants, and I highly recommend going with a guide.  We had a reverse trai trip back to Colombo, and arrived happy and tired after a wonderful day!
