After travelling to see this place it is not worth the effort. The elephants are chained up and are at times in small pens during feeding time so that visitors can try to touch the baby ones. If you love animals this isn't the place for you.

Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage takes in and cares for wild Asian elephants and is located at Pinnawala village. When we arrived we saw lots of elephants grazing and then walked down the street to the river for a swim.  We stood to the side as they left the grazing area and then when they passed we walked a bit behind them to the river through the street of markets.  Wow! Down at the river the elephants were treated to a one hour frolicking session.  This was amazing and beautiful to watch.  A whole group of school kids were there too watching from one of the grand stands while we were up close behind the barrier. After the swim the elephants are then taken back up the street to their grazing area.  Unbelievable experience.

Wonderful to see a herd of elephants frolicking in water and trying to beat the heat. The surroundings are scenic and you will also find plenty of small shops that sell all kinds of souvenirs. It was also interesting to see the process of making paper products from elephant dung. If you plan it well, you can also try your hand at bathing the elephants.

This a very good place. They have 87 elephants now. One tusker. We can feed the elephants , see them taking bath...play... There good Rest Rooms in this place.  Very well maintained. Lakshala is also here but small. We need to buy elephant dung paper...they show us how it's prepared.  It's pretty costly but can buy.

At the first place , I didn’t actually get as to why it is called an Orphanage. All the elephants in here are not tamed but rather controlled as being part of the place. I felt it is more of a Tourist Trap kind of a place. There are currently 86 elephants.Indians are charged 700 lkr/person. Foreign Tourists are charged higher 2500 lkr/person. Best time for visiting is the feeding time from 9:30-10:00 am and 13:30-14:00 and the bathing time from 10:00-10:30 and 14:00-14:30 where all the elephants are taken to a river nearby. You can feed the elephants for fruits(250 lkr/basket) and the milk(500 lkr). A tusker elephant is kept away from the normal crowd but can be seen from far. You can expect poops in the middle. If you are visiting during the day, carry a hat as the ground is open and it gets really hot. Not many shades nearby to stand and watch the elephants.

visited the place with the family and overall it was a great experience. You have to be before 0930 hrs , should you need to cover the full package including  of the feeding milk to the baby elephants and bathing. Elephants can be closely watch and enjoy their movements in leisure. The place has improved from my last visit when was  4-5 years back.

Visited the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage with my family on our way from Colombo to Kandy. My experience can be summarized below: What's impressive: - You get to see elephant up close! What to expect: - Most area of the park is uncovered so it gets really hot in the afternoon. - Elephants poop along the way while they walk towards the river. So watch out for those poo! - The elephants will have their usual baths in the afternoon at the nearby river, and if you wish to see them taking their baths while enjoying lunch, there are a couple of restaurants by the river which allow you to take your meal while you watch. Slightly pricey though. What can be improved: - Not sure if it's a Sri Lanka thingy but seems like all entrance tickets for foreigners are rather expensive comparing to other Asian countries. Final verdict: - Attractions: Basically, viewing of elephants - Structures: Not much of structures except for the shelter for the elephants. - Cleanliness: Decent but expect elephant poo along the path! - Food: No restaurant selling food inside the compound, but there are some along the river. - Staff: Couldn't really judge as hardly come into contact with many - Value: Slightly overpriced - Time: Recommended to spend between 1 - 2 hours, unless you with to enjoy lunch while watching the elephants taking their regular baths in the afternoon - Likelihood to revisit: Probably if I happen to pass by

I was a little skeptical about visiting here. I went with a tour that I had organised. Seeing elephant close up whilst they are down having their baths was truly amazing. Walking to the orphanage I was a little worried as I am not a fan of animals in captivity. Surprisingly the orphanage was spotlessly clean and the elephants have great facilities.

It was an amazing experience seeing these beautiful elephants up close and it’s clear that the staff care for them very well. However the whole experience was very unorganised. Once you pay the entrance free the parts you can participate in (milk feeding, fruit feeding and bathing) all need to paid for as add ons, however this isn’t explained. So although I’d recommend going, make sure you find all of the information at the ticket office when you arrive!

This is an absolute must whilst staying in Sri Lanka. The price to get in is 2500 rupees (£12.50) and there is an additional option to pay 350 rupees (£1.75) which allows you to give a baby elephant a bottle of milk. After seeing the herds and feeding the babies the experience gets better as all the elephants are released out of the front gate and driven down the high street hill to the river where they all bathe in the water, again an experience to be had. Note, there is no option to ride or bathe the elephants yourself at this attraction (although this can be done very local to this attraction at a place called the elephant farm -see separate review)

It is very nice to see these beautiful animals here. I myself am very much against the exploitation of animals for commercial purposes. You must respect animals. Before I went here, I read in and read varying messages. Especially because a few elephants are chained and the caretakers walk with prods. That some are on the chain (normal chains without hooks on it), I think that’s because they can be mocking or aggressive. I did not see the prods used by the caretakers, but because the elephants walk through a kind of shopping street and because there are many people around, it is necessary to correct one if necessary. That said, it is a lot of fun to see these elephants when they go to the river to bathe with a beautiful view of the landscape behind it. Unfortunately there is a lot of commerce in the sense of shops and restaurants around it, which is often the case at these kind of places.

We have been reading most of the below comments and we had a hard time to make a decision. Since I am writing it’s quite obvious what choice we made. The orphanage itself is relatively small which allows you to make the most of it in a short period of time. The bathing session happened at 1:45pm and is on the opposite side of the street. It’s worth it to spend a little extra money to enjoy a fresh juice (or a beer) from the terrasse of the 2 hotels nearby. Be there before the bathing since seeing them coming down is definitely worth all the Sri Lankan heat.

It was a great experience to see elephants up close and some activities including feeding to baby elephants, elephants bathing are worthwhile to see. This was on our must-see list in Sri Lankan tour and we heard that this place is a home for more than 100 orphaned elephants.

An all round great experience. Check timings before you go as feeding times and water trips are at particular points of the day. The elephants a free to roam large expanses of land and the work they do to rescue elephants from neglect and injury is admirable. The site itself is clearly well funded and legitimate programmes of care are evident. No riding or exploitation means the elephants are happy. You can however pay 750 rupees to go in and bath with the elephants which I would highly recommend.

I've seen similar attractions in other countries and I'm always concerned about the treatment of the animals. I looked hard to find signs of mistreatment and found nothing. These Elephants are very well cared for. Highly recommend supporting this attraction.

First of all you can see these elephants outside in a lovely environment, then at feeding time for just 350 rupees (about £1.60) you can feed an elephant with a bottle of milk. Then over the road and passed an array of shops and restaurants down to the river to wait for the elephants to come down the same road. Have a drink at the restaurant overlooking the river. Its a lovely sight as 30+ elephants walk passed and into the river for a wash and bath. If you want to go in the river and help scrub an elephant there is a charge of 750 rupees (about £3.50) to do so. Go prepared with an extra pair of shorts etc. as the water goes up to the top of your legs. A lovely experience.

Visited in march, with 3 adults and one 3yr old. Coming from the southern part of india, seeing an elephant had no special feelings for me. But since it was on every tourist list, i obliged. First things first, the place is a tourist trap. With lots of shops/guides waiting to cheat. Be smart and avoid getting cheated. The official ticket prices are separate for foreigners,SAARC nations and locals. For indians its 700LKR. Kids are free below 6. Before getting in, take a picture on ur phone of the various activities and timings, for your reference. Once you enter, theres no guides or help. Only directions to various parts/enclosures. Follow the directions and attend various shows as per timings. Its hot, so carry caps, water,umbrellas as required. Feeding fruits to adult elephants...or feeding milk to teenage ones, are paid activities. My 3 yr old enjoyed feeding fruits. (250LKr) For the elephant bathing shows, you need to exit the park, cross the road, walk past many tourist trap shops and finally reach a river bank exclusively set up for the bath. With metal loops to chain the few naughty elephants. Most of the elephants are free to walk around in the rivet. Once they all get in, a man starts a water gun to spray water jets at the elephants. Not very entertaining, but its what you paid for, i guess. Best to enjoy this by sitting in 1 of the restaurants on the river bank, with a bottle of lion beer 😊 Overall its recommended only if you have NOT seen elephants before or are visiting kandy(the nearest city). Else it can be avoided. Ps- very neat toilets inside the park. Free for foreigners, while locals have to pay to use.

When we arrived the elephants had been taken down to the river , we witnessed one chained elephant being told/held under the water  for the tourists to take photos of him "bathing" , all the men had long poles with hooks on that were used on the elephants , we were offered photos and rides (by young lads working the crowds) this obviously cost more , I found the whole experience  very upsetting , these poor elephants should be released into one of the wildlife parks to live freely , they attract enough tourists to support the elephants , so sad to see these magnificient creatures being treated so badly

Its a a very nice place. Especial the river area is wondeful. You can see the little elephants take their bath and play. There are manyu stores on the way to the river so if you like to buy some suvenirs its easy to find them here ( not the cheapest in Shri Lanka). Its also intersting to see how they produce paper out of elephant s***t. For all the activities there (feeting,bath ect) you have to check their time table

Although the Elephants were fed via a bottle they had loads of them and I am sure this is for the benefit of the tourists but all the money raised is to maintain  the well  being of all of these orphaned animals. Walking with them  from the sanctuary  to the river to see them being bathed and having fun was excellent. A very well run place with  plenty to see and do.

We went on march 2018 to Pinnawala for an elephant riding. The guide brought us to Maha Raja Elephant Safari. They charged us 10'000 Rupees each Person for 30 minutes (about 64 USD)!!! The whole place wheew the elephants were was looking barren and dreary and the creek that runns thru was dirty ant the water milky.

Our tour of SL included a visit to the elephant orphanage.  Most interesting.  Hundreds of school kids were there as well having a splendid time.  Grounds are large so we could easily circulate.  We watched as the first troupe of elephants returned to "nature" after their bath in the river.  We then walked though the little village which is part of the orphanage to the river. We ate a simple lunch in the resto that overlooked the event.  A perfect setting to enjoy the action

The Elephant orphanage is very good place to see the Elephant group. This Elephants is not a wild. Most of they are very friendly with people. There are have more baby elephants. Here we can look Elephant Bathing on the River, Feeding and Milk feeding for the Babies. And We can have a look how the process of Elephant pooh papers.

Arrived towards end of animal feeding and didn't like seeing the elephants fed out of a very small bottle seemingly for benefit of tourists. Next bit much better. Elephants came down to the river and were allowed to play there for quite a long time. Much nicer seeing them rolling round in the water.

Went to see the elephants at pinnawala you can buy fruit to feed one of them watch and feed the baby's with milk for a extra 3.50 rupees then watch them in the river but they are chained at the river side !!!!!! Until one of the keepers takes of the chains so they can walk up the hill to get feed again one of the elephants had a band leg and was still expected to keep up with the rest of the herd sad but true they had the spike sticks too not that we see hem use it but I'm sure they do otherwise why would they have them . I thought this was a sanctuary it seems to be a money making role as didn't see much care only what the tourists do !!!!

Went here for the first sitting (got in as it opened at around 8.30) and saw the elephants being fed, milked and bathed. It’s obviously lovely to see them, some of the younger ones were even rather playful. The bit that isn’t so easy to see is that some of them, especially in the bathing area, and when the elephants are being bought too and from the bathing area, are chained. Don’t get me wrong, there are probably more that aren’t that are and the orphanage explain that there are legitimate reasons for this. At the end of the day you have to accept that some of these are big animals and based on their temperament on the day have to be controlled, especially when they are not in their main enclosures and in public areas. I would definitely advise the visit even if its just to donate the money to help house, feed and look after them.  You can see, just from looking at the elephants, that they are clearly well looked after.

I visited pinnawala elephant orphanage after reading so many positive reviews. Upon arriving first thing in the morning the immediate experience appeared positive, the main heard of elephants were standing in an open space seemingly happy. We then wandered back to the elephant feeding area. What I witnessed made me want to cry, two young elephants chained up with clear symptoms of PSD. Swaying back and fourth on short chains. Very obviously distressed!!! There was no life or souls in their eyes just sadness. The handlers held bull hooks which behind the scenes they would definitely have used frequently as the elephants were very afraid. Next it was time for the tourists to feed the baby elephant milk - this was no longer a baby but more of a teen. The elephant got forced feed huge bottles of milk. While the trainer threatened it if it turned its head away. I don’t understand the positive reviews from other tourists as  it’s very obvious that these elephants are abused! I couldn’t get out of the place soon enough!! DO NOT SUPPORT THIS BUSINESS. See these majestic animals in the wild on safari.  - I filmed videos but unfortunately can’t upload them to show the truth about this place.

Different experience. You will love to see so many elephants together taking bath and moving around as it's a rare view. Kids will enjoy the most. There is comfortable arrangements to enjoy the view. Spend around one hour drinking and eating while watching elephants.

It is nice to see that the elephants are well looked after and the work that the people do for these animals are admirable. The people that look after them deserve all the kudos. A visit to this place should be timed so as to follow the elephants when they go down to the river for their daily bath.

We visited here 15 years ago and was surprised how much it had changed, firstly we stopped to have our breakfast on the viewing area and watch the first of the elephants come down for bathing, the viewing area and bathing area were just as we remembered. The first lot of elephants were what they called the ones with control issues and even though they came down in chains and some were chained to points in the water they seemed ok and well looked after. They really enjoy the water and love been blasted by the water cannon. After this we went into the orphanage which they have really changed and are making into more of a conservation place. We saw many elephants and the place has around 50 plus of the magnificent creatures. Some of the elephants are working elephants but all seem to be happy and knowing the background that they come from we were pleased to see that they are all well cared for. We got to feed the baby elephant with a milk bottle which was fun but they certainly guzzle it within seconds so you need to be quick with the camera. The mahouts are dedicated to their animals. We then went back down to the river to watch the rest of the elephants come down to bath, you can buy packs of biscuits to feed them with and you are allowed to go down to have pictures taken and help wash them if you wish for a small donation to the mahout. The setting is lovely and very tranquil but does get packed with tourists and you always get silly people who try to do silly things with the animals, at the end of the day please respect it is a wild animal. Some of the elephants do have chains round their necks and feet but this is because some have control issues and it is easier for the mahout to handle the animal, even though it is heart breaking and not normal to see they do not seem to be in any pain or discomfort. The orphanage does a great job and it is a shame that they should be needed at all. Brilliant photos from the day out and many special memories to cherish from the experience.

This program was mostly expected in our holiday in Srí Lanka. I was so successful because I was able to touch a baby elephant at first time. We watched how elephants were fed and how they were walking across the street to have a bath. It was realy entertainig watchig such a great amount of elephants with different measure and personality. It would be good to know more about them or to discover the park where they live but we were with a tourist group and have only a few hours to spend there. So next time i will return and visit the orphanage again. :)

We reached there around 12 which was the perfect time to view the elephants bathing in the river and watch them walk back to their homes. The elephants are massive and beautiful. Don't miss visiting the center there which has products from elephant poo. They also explain the process of making paper from elephant poo. We did not do any activities though, but are available at an extra price like feeding the elephants.

A visit to Pinawala is definitely recommended for those who love nature and anmials. The elephants are one of the most interesting animals to observe and you can do so at the Sanctuary here. The dedication and care taken by the workers here is commendable

I believe this place is pretty good for these elephants, although reviews go for and against this place. Inside the park, the free roaming area is so hot to watch the elephants so I believe both them and I enjoyed the bathing time by the nearby river. The elephants did walk there with chained feet - I believe it is for the security of people - as we going back to the actual park, it was time for the elephants to return as well. They blowed a horn when all merchants guided all tourists inside and took their merchandise inside as well. Then dozens of elephants marched through the 200m market street and some bags and t-shirts feel down to the ground as they had passed by so close to the shops. Best place to watch the elephants bathe at the river is in the nearby hotel's covered terrace. Some people payed to go to the river and help clean and bathe the elephants. They however pooped often to the water so these people needed to shower well afterwards ;) Beware of those pretending to be park guide, or palm reader scammers: When we bought our tickets at the entrance, there was a man who guided us over the road the 200 meters to the river. After we started to return to the park, he was there to escort us back. Then we realized he wasn't an employee at all - he proposed us a private elephant bathing and riding opportunity a little off the main tourist street "at the local prize, not the foreign prize". I think that probably was scam, or at least the elephant ride would have been less safe as with proper licence. We turned down the offer although he tried to negotiate price as low as we wanted. Palm reader wanted to "read our future" for a price of 3000rs per person! Beware of them, don't let them scam. At the park, we bought the tickets for milk feeding to the "baby elephants" (under 5 year old elephants that is..). The milk feeding is very poorly organized event, you needed to find your way to the correct place and make sure you got your place at the feeding. Not too many elephants to feed (2). Lots of local school children at the park as well.

My husband and I visited here today. We had been reading reviews and they were extremely mixed, and this nearly put us off. But we’re on a tour and it’s one of the stops. So we figured we would go in and if it was bad, we could at least spread the word about any mistreatment. First stop once in the park - our driver took us to a reasonably sized open area where there were many elephants roaming freely, with what appeared to be an abundance of leaves and branches to eat. Off to the left in a separate area we’re 4 elephants apparently chained to concrete with some of the animal handlers with them. I’m not sure what the area was, it said staff only, but the whole area was in full view of all the park visitors. 2nd stop was lunch down by the elephant bathing area. There were a handful of animals chilling in the water with 1 chained to the rock. The only one chained up seemed to be the most energetic of all, going for the other elephants that came near it, albeit in what seemed to be playful to an untrained eye. 3 keepers came down to move the elephants to a different area. 1 keeper looked after the chained elephant, the other 2 looked after all the others. They soaked them with water and encouraged them to lie in the water so they could get completely covered in water. We presume this was to cool them off for the walk back up and across the road. The chained elephant did look like he was a struggle to handle, for whatever reason. The keepers did carry sharp sticks, but they were not used on these animals. There was a police officer who watched the whole process. Then a batch of elephants (probably at least 40) were brought down to the water. The first small batch had chains round 1 foot but not attached to anything. I think they were chained just along the river from where we were for bathing by the keepers from what we could see. The last large batch (33 elephants) wore no chains. Police also followed these elephants. We saw keepers helping the elephants to wash. At most, the animals were held just at the water’s edge for longer than necessary to allow tourists to take pictures. We witnessed no apparent mistreatment of these wonderful beings. And we were also not approached to be asked for money for anything extra that would have mistreated the animals. This was our experience and what we saw relieved us as we were expecting to see mistreatment from what we had read.

Just your average tourist attraction, the animals seem happy with there enviroment, with a lot of space and a river to wash in, some are chained for safety reasons. You can (for a fee) bottle feed the young and hand fruit to the older ones, its also possible to wash them in the river...

We took the Viceroy train from Colombo to a close location to the elephant sanctuary. The first stop was to go to the river and watched them getting washed. Beautiful natural habitat for Elephants, they are friendly and un suspecting of humans. Donot miss the bathing experience in the nearby river. (even happens twice a day) Be careful of local touts who will take you on a ride and show you some other orphanage nearby.

As much as there are negativities surrounding such facilities (zoos inclusive), I always enjoy visiting to such place to learn a thing or two about animals. 1. The feeding session, I personally found this a bit peculiar - Both elephants inside seemed more like teens than infants. Do teens actually drink milk? A bit boring considering my guide rushed, meandering through traffic to reach before 9.15am. I ended up being more interested in the kicking ‘competition’ between an Asian lady and a Caucasian lady. 2. I enjoyed the washing by the river session. However I noted one elephant that was isolated who was trashing away as if to voice his displeasure of being alone. Overall, worth a trip to kind of watch NGC come alive... but... Yet another instance of Sri Lankans milking tourists... - 2,500 LKR  to enter seems really excessive.. really frustrating.

I enjoyed my visit to the elephant orphanage, and was lucky enough to participate in bathing an elephant in the river, during their daily trips to the river. It was a thrill of a lifetime for me. I would return to the orphanage,and do it all over again.

Visited this foundation on our way thro Pinnawala,  The elephants are all mostly old and have been either mistreated or over worked in their earlier lives. You see and feel they are now well looked after by people who care for them. Our guide explained the complete history and background to the organisation and about each elephant in their care. Also explained their needs and how they are looked after. Recommended if you are interested in these grand animals. Totally fee but they appreciated a donation from your visit to keep them funded.

Despite hearing not great things I was hopeful that the sanctuary really did have the elephants best interest at heart but after seeing elephants forced to lay down, take food and suck up water to spray I was left very disappointed. It's a shame but you feel very much that they're out to make money, picking up on tourists selfish need for a photo with an elephant, turning a special experience for one into a repetitive job, done hundreds of times in a day, for each elephant. It's tough because these elephants do need care, so inevitably need money from us, but hopefully if tourists start choosing to go to safaris instead, or the orphanage listen to these reviews, they will begin to work with organisations such as born free to develop more ethical practices. I would be much happier watching the elephants natural behaviours than being lined up and pressured to feed them..

Like many tourists, I was attracted to this place because I wanted to see elephants up close. However, what I was not prepared for was to be based in an artificial town like Pinawalla that only exists to service the tourists visiting the orphanage. It's grim. A run down street of tourist tat shops and tired hotels that form the main 200m route from the park gate to the river. Around 40 - 50 elephants are brought out of the park gate at 10am and 2pm every day and walked down to the river, carrying their own tethering chains, where they are then tethered to eyebolts on rocks in the river where hundreds of tourists then photograph them for an hour. Whether or not the elephants, enjoy or benefit from, this twice daily parade, it was hard to escape the conclusion that this event was more about raising cash than it was about improving the elephants quality of life. It is clearly successful in that respect but if you want to see elephants then go to the National Parks and see them living free, even if you cannot get up close.

I had heard very mixed reviews about this orphanage but it was part of a day trip and we wanted to see all the other things so we resigned ourselves to having to do this too.  The orphanage itself looks very organised and most of the elephants we saw looked to be well looked after.  There was one teenager in an enclosure near the baby feeding area which seemed to be chained and stressed but I think he may have been upset as he wanted the milk which he knew was coming shortly so was showing his displeasure at waiting for it. I did have one of the few tickets to bottle feed a baby which was in fact the teenager and although I think he may have been a bit old to be fed milk he did enjoy it. I'd heard that sometimes babies are taken from the wild to fulfill this activity for the tourists so was relieved that the only two being fed weren't in fact babies at all but a little older. We then proceeded to cross the road to watch the bathing.  We were seated to the left side and told that the bull elephants would be brought to bathe directly in front of us.  I was distressed to see them brought in chained then shackled to rings in the rocks while the keepers constantly calllled up to us for tips - appalling way to treat these animals and although we enjoyed the rest of the day this tainted it for us.

I was thoroughly disappointed in this place, first we were taken down to the bathing river where one elephant was repeatedly forced to lie down for each tourist to ‘wash it’ which was just rubbing its back. Then we were brought along to to feed them which was not too terrible but the keepers were rushing you to get on the elephant which we all refused. Seeing them chained and led in a circle for rides was heartbreaking really, not to mention the vary sharp spears the keepers carried. The following day I saw elephants in a National Park in Habarana and the experiences were incomparable. Please do not come here if you care about animals and not only their physical health but also their mental wellbeing.

Very nice to see baby elephants being fed. They allow the visitors also to feed. The adult elephants are very nice to watch but they are resting in hot sun which made us feel sad. The elephants are looking healthy. We did not have time to see them going to the river to bath. Unless one has no exposure to elephants there is no need to go to visit this place exclusively. But if it is on the way while going to other places it is worth visiting. If one is not planning to go the river to see them bath it will take maximum 1 to 1.5 hours to see the place.

We heard mixed reviews about this "orphanage" We decided to make our own decision. We arrived a few minutes late. We were not able to see them walk down to the water. When we did arrive, they were in the water. The chains are just low enough in the water that you don't realize they are there. One baby elephant was laying down with the chain pulling at his leg. Another elephant was trying to get close to anther area and the handler poked him. I didn't want to see another minute of this. There has to be a more humane way of showing these animals. I know they are dangerous and need to be treated in a certain way, but this is not good. We left. I believe it was 30 dollars too! Our biggest mistake while in Sri Lanka. Would not recommend anyone who has a heart.  I have been to Thailand and they treat their elephants much better.

Not sure if there are perhaps incentives for hotels / taxi drivers etc to promote this business but I can honestly say, it was the last stop on a 10 day tour of Sri Lanka and this spoilt the trip!  We were encourage to go by our hotel. Elephants in chains were not what I expected. I was with my family. Rs10,000 for four people. We were there for ten minutes, walked out and I demanded my money back. Both from the desk and the incredibly rude “tourist police” desk next door. This is a governmental organisation and I would urge anyone considering a visit here to avoid. If this is considered the best business for the treatment of elephants, I would hate to know what the worst does. Photos attached of some of the staff who should be ashamed of themselves. It will amount to nothing, but the Sri Lanka Tourist board will be written to as well.

Honestly. I thought I would write something that will help guide your decision about whether to go or not, however it isn’t straight up and simple. I’ve tried to bullet point my thoughts to try and help. 1. Yes there are chains on some elephants. I believe some have shown aggressive behaviours. There are some very not well looked after elephants in extremely worse situations I have seen across the island. 2. The milk feed I am in two minds about. It is done to obviously provide money for the elephants. The two we saw were not in shackles, were boisterously playing around the site and seemed more than happy to keep drinking away, and were more teenager-ish stature. 3. The River. They seemed more than happy to splash about in the river. Some elephants were having their keepers wash them, one elephant didn’t want him to stop, encouraging him when he stopped until he carried on again. Two elephants were chained on a long chain, they had enough room to play and their keepers could leave them safely there. It didn’t seem any different to when you nip into the corner shop with your dog tied by its lead to the lamppost outside. 4. I did see one keeper prodding an elephant with a sharp pointed spear type implement at one point when it appeared to be going off track. This concerned me a little, however no elephant I had a good look at had any wounds, there were happy calves with their mums. They kept the bulls separate to the rest of the herd as they generally get territorial and violent. If you do not like Zoos, do not go. Minneriya National Park is nearby and has wild herds.

Oh my where to start, I knew when I was visiting Sri Lanka that elephants had to be part of the experience and I came across this sanctuary.  Looking at the website I thought this is a definite must, milk feeding, fruit feeding and elephant bathing in the river.  We walked here from our hotel which was nearby and this place was just stunning and definitely the highlight of our trip to this wonderful country.  According to our guide there are nearly 100 orphaned elephants here and we got to see them be playful with each other, walk through the sanctuary, saw them being fed milk (members of the public can do this but there is only a limited number of tickets available, if I recall rightly its only 30), but we got to feed them fruit for 250 SL rupees which was just amazing.  What an unbelievable sight it is to see them walking down the street towards the river for their bathing (10-12 and 2-4) although some were down there at 9am which we saw from our hotel but the majority go down at these times.

After reading the reviews we were unsure whether to visit this place or not but decided to give it a go. Wish we never did! We wanted to leave as soon as we stepped in! As we first went in we went down to the ‘bathing river’ which had 3 elephants chained under the water and had 2 men with mental spikes which was being used when they wanted the elephants to lie down in the water so that the tourists could wash them and then they would ask for money! One elephant was being washed so much it was to upsetting to see so we moved on to the next step. Which was riding elephants which for us was a complete no! This was awful to see! This reasons we wanted to go to see the elephants as we wanted to feed them and feed milk to the baby elephants! So we decided to feed them and go. Even the feeding was awful! Was like a circus, they were rushing us to feed them and the same elephant was getting feed by each tourist! Was horrible! There was no baby elephants at all! So all that they put on there website is untrue! The hole place is awful and the men just want money! This place should be closed down! We did a safari where you see the elephants in the wild so much better!

we were disappointed when visiting this place. All elephants were locked by chains, it looks more as ZOO than Elephant Orphanage. Still in constructions, you can see there a lot of building cars etc. ticket cost 2500 rupies per person. Next time better to choose some national park in Sri Lanka to visit than this place

Was very apprehensive about visiting the orphanage however was swayed by all the good reviews. This is a very unpleasant park. All the elephants are clearly unhappy, many of them are in chains. If they get too close to anyone they are quickly threatened and prodded with a spike. Milk feeding time was especially unpleasant when the two elephants caged up were just trying to get out of the inclosure and were clearly stressed. I understand that there are much worse places nearby but that does not make this place acceptable. If you want to see elephants then go see them in a national Park like Minneriya.

This place makes me feel totally confused. The first impression was terrible... Chained elephants which were forced to eat and eat just to entertain the guests (I am aware of how much an elephant can eat but it just seemed way too much). The baby elephants had their legs chained to the floor and they were disoriented, trying to move. On the other hand, seeing how happy the elephants were during the bathing time made me believe they were not as sad as I had thought. The care takers were playing with them and obviously showed some affection. All in all, I truly hope the care takers are good people and the elephants are treated with love and respect.

The place gives you a very close moment to the Elephants which are living in a group of more than 80 animals. The highligth is the bath at the river side. That happens 2 times a day and in this Moment the Elephants are playing without stress with their relatives. a view horney male Elephants have to be places by the side in order to reduce their emotions but that is okay. It is a lovely place and you should not miss it.

Me and my husband visted here on 22nd Jan 2018. We were originally taken to the wrong place. Elephant Village. Trust Me, those complaining about this place need to go there!!!! This place is heaven compared to how others I saw were living....well....more like existing. We loved seeing only 2 elephants in chains.....the rest were free. The 1 was being treated by a vet. The other I'm not sure..... but again, this place was a breath of fresh air compared to what I had just witnessed. Watching them all walk passed us down to the river was amazing. And they stayed for several hours. It was lovely to see. We also saw the elephants showing affection to the keepers....again....lovely. Keep up the good work. If only you could rescue the 7 elephants from elephant village :-(

Was going back and forth on the decision of visiting this place as i dont want to encourage any type of animal exploitation, but after reading many and many reviews and articles we eventually decided to go, and it was surprisingly fine, the elephants in this place cannot survive in the wild because of either sikness or injuriries and thats why they live there, they are a big herd so not lonley, treated well, bathed twice a day which they seem to love , and well fed! Beware though of of all the other places along the way which do seem to be exploiting elephants as they keep one or two lonley elephants in order to make money, seeing them along the way to the orphanage was pretty sad! After chatting with some other tourists who have been on elephant safaries in the south of the island sanctuaries described that jeep cars swarm the poor elephants who are getting terrified, upon hearing that ,i was glad we didnt go to those places, and in light of that this orphange seemed like the best choice to experience elephants without harrassing them.

This was nice to see and enjoy Elephants and bathing and the dance . If you like to feed the baby elephants milk that can be done as well here. Take photos with this lovely animal and spent a lovely time. Arooha tourism arranged us the best guide for us to go to this place and he took us to each with knowledgeably

Was really looking forward to visiting but left feeling it was little more than a zoo. The elephants were undoubtedly well cared for but we saw two babies chained in the feeding station... you could pay to give them bottles of milk. It seems too commercialised. Also saw the keepers using sharp sticks to control the younger elephants. Not saying mistreated just herded down to river twice a day ... I hoped to see more rehabilitation. Go to minereya national park and see elephants roaming 20000 acres of land

So having read reviews and research on this place, I decided to go with an open mind, so here is my thoughts and experience. On arrival, we were shown by our guide (who we had hired for many tours over 2 weeks) to where the elephants were in what looked like a huge paddock, they were quite close as the food is put on ground near to tourists so they get a good view, yes it is slightly touristy but read on for my thoughts on this. It is explained by our guide that some of the elephants are born here in captivity, to help boost the numbers, and around half of them will be transported later in life (usually around 4-5 yrs old sometimes a little older} to the government run National parks. some will stay for breeding purposes, I can see the need to keep it that way. We then went down to the feeding station and watched 2 babies, 1 was 5yrs old and 1 6yrs old being bottle fed, and yes tourist were encouraged to feed them for money, but bearing in mind poor wages I can see the need for some people to try and boost their income. Of these 2 babies, one had a chain quite loose did not hamper his movement at all around his neck and down his leg and around his foot, when he tried mounting the other baby, our guide explained the need for the chain, it seems the boys can get rather amorous and as there is a lot of public about they do need to have some control. Our guide then hurried us across the main road and down the pedestrian strret where we saw lots of elephants in the river being hosed and washed, now I had heard that some are chained to the river bed, in the 2 hrs I was there I saw no sign of this, all elephants were able to move freely, yes some had chains bit like a manacle round neck and down to foot, but I saw no sign of distress or of this hampering their movements, I asked about the chains again as they all strolled past us up the street back to the orphanage and paddock, and was told they were mainly teenage boys or elephants that had shown signs of over friendliness. Yes the trainers were getting public to stand and have fotos and asking for back handers, again it is a poor country with very low education, and poor wages ! We then walked back up the street halfway all of a sudden a siren sounded and our guide dragged us into a shop doorway as the next lot of elephants were walking down the street to the river. ...... So my thoughts IS it commercialised and cruel ????? well I guess the answer is yes and no, 1 It provides much needed income and jobs to the area, 2 some of these elephants are actually brought into the orphanage from the mountains etc and would either be killed for raiding villages or die as their mothers have died for one reason or another. And the government can only provide so much money for help and conservation, so if they were not here they would die.  some of them , and usually as many as poss do get released into the National Parks. Yes they are making money by charging entry fees ! But elephants do take a lot of feeding, not once did I see an elephantr cruelly treated, so I guess its upto each person to make their own minds up. I did not see any person riding an elephant at this place, though it is possible at other very small orphanages close by, we were offered but declined.

Lovely to see and interact with the Elephants although it does feel more like a Zoo than and orphanage, the elephants are now bred in captivity and very domesticated. Don’t get hooked in by the ‘tour guides’ that approach you when you arrive! They will tell you they work for the orphanage and instead they will show you the elephants at the water, wait around for you and then get you into a herbal spice garden for a ‘tour’ and a ‘free’ welcome drink. You’ll either be parting with cash for the drink or buying expensive herbal medicines and when you come out of the garden the tour guide is gone!  The garden was interesting so if it’s your sort of thing, go for it but I got a bit stuck!

I see there are quite mixed  reviews and I completely understand.  We did question why some of the elephants had chains on and we were told that the bulls were kept in chains to help control them less they should charge and that the chains would not cut into them like ropes would.  It is a unique experience to see them up close and as far as hitting them with sticks, we didn’t see that.  When you see them in the river being scrubbed by some of the attendants I wouldn’t say they were being mistreated. It does seem a bit of a ritual for the tourists however and like everything else in Sri Lanka it doesn’t come cheap. The young girl next to me was holding out a small bunch of bananas. The large bull came right up to her to take them and for me personally to touch the trunk of such an amazing animal wa unforgettable

Firstly, this place is entirely overpriced. After paying exorbitant amounts of money for entry, every activity therein is also costly. Secondly, the word 'orphanage' is a misnomer. The elephants are chained up, prodded with sharp sticks, and trained to be controlled and ridden. The elephant baths were perhaps the worst; some of the elephants were chained up to big rocks alone in the water. The most heartbreaking thing was watching one elephant, chained to a rock with a very short length, desperately trying to join the other elephants. When he couldn't move more than one foot onto dry land, he kept swaying his front leg back and forth, as if perhaps he could finally take that next step forward if he just kept trying. Please, don't fund this organisation by spending money there.

This was  sold to us as an orphanage/sanctuary which implied to me that they had somehow been orphaned and were being raised for release back into the wild or stay in the sanctuary.  This is clearly not the case it is a Zoo and a major tourist attraction. Some of the elephants have chains around their neck and foot and are prodded with metal hook tipped sticks and look thoroughly unhappy. If you want to see elephants (ok you may not see so many) see them in the wild visit Udawalawe National Park - I wish I had!

Everyone has seen images and film of the Elephant Orphanage at Pinnawala so often that the worry is that the actual visit will not stand up to expectations. But it does. Watching the elephants being bathed and fed at such close quarters is terrific.

I enjoyed being in this place, the elephants seem happy and the staff looked after them. Of course the care takers trying to get some extra money taking pictures of you with an elephant but why not. It's 1USD. Best thing was when they were feeding the little elephants with milk...ha ha never seen this before. Quite cute. Good shopping around the place available too. And seeing all the elephants in the river for washing was an amazing experience.

I was a little uncertain about how I would feel about this should I think the elephants were not being cared for properly...... The elephants are clearly very happy and content. I got to feed a baby elephant its milk. I thought our dog could make food disappear quickly but she is nowhere near as fast as the baby elephant! Then we followed the elephants down to the river where they are taken to bathe and play twice a day. The elephants clearly know the routine and were delighted to see the river. A huge water cannon is set up and sprays them which they also enjoy. We paid an extra £10 for me to bathe one of the babies in the river. AMAZING experience. My baby was so chilled out and thoroughly enjoying lying there while I scrubbed her with a coconut husk. I felt like the guy in Jurassic Park when he saw his first stegosaurus. Definitely worth  a visit and pay the extra to feed and bathe the elephants. It was breath taking to see them at the river and that they had formed a herd despite coming from different 'families' and that they were very well looked after.

I am a veterinary surgeon and visited Sri Lanka with some other friends , we had seen the reviews for the orphanage and they were very 50/50 with most saying how wonderful the place is . We felt it was best to visit this place and make our own decision on the orphanage and what it had to offer . It is fair to say that it was the most distressing and upsetting visit we made in Sri Lanka , on arrival we were directed to the stream to watch the elephants bathe . This is not what happens all of the elephants are stood broken and bored , if they are not being forced to bathe then they are being touched by people or paraded about , we particularly became distressed seeing the male elephant in several chains , the staff there began to poke him with sticks until the male elephant finally laid down in the water. The sanctuary is very much catered towards tourism and I strongly feel the elephants needs are not met ! Thoroughly upset by this place and hope it makes changes to improve its animal welfare

I should’ve listened to my gut instinct and not gone. This is no sanctuary for those poor elephants. Some were shackled and crying out in pain as they were forced to lie in the river whilst their so called carers scrubbed them clean. Elephants don’t need scrubbing down they are perfectly capable of bathing themselves. This is just a tourist attraction. All the elephants looked miserable as you would be too if you were constantly prodded with a metal pointed stick. It has upset me for days. I wouldn’t recommend at all!

We visited in January and left after 10 minutes. As an animal lover it was horrendous seeing elephants in chains, beaten with sticks and shouted at. It worries me to think if that's how they are treated when visitors are present what goes on earth behind closed doors!

We were looking forward to visiting the Pinnawala Orphanage,  but we witnessed a large male Elephant tied on 3 legs with chains, the poor Elephant was very distressed and could only sway, we could not find anyone to complain to, We were all very shocked at this very depressing and heartbreaking treatment of this poor Elephant. The keepers also had long sticks with sharp metal hooks on the end to control the Elephants, we cannot describe the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage as a sanctuary Elephants should be free to roam not chained, we were all very upset by this incident and very sad we had contributed to their suffering by paying to go in.  Please do not visit this very sad place for Elephants.

Whilst its truly an amazing experience to be so close to the biggest land mammals on the planet, I don't think that they are treated too well and its not so nice to see them in shackles and prodded with a sharp metal edged stick. I came with my four year old son, who loved it.

We loved watching the elephants as we were too scared to go on a wild safari tour.  Make sure you walk down to the river to watch them bath as this is the highlight. Yes they are chained but if you have seen an elephant loose it you will know why.  They were fed and they all looked quite healthy. Costly trip for tourists in comparison to local fees which is sad as a couple of my young children had to pay adult fees.  It is bearable though as it is an orphanage. I had read reviews about only been a very few elephants and about the chains but this wasn't true. there were loads, yes some were chained but they are dangerous animals and hopefully this is monitored but many were not and they were walking free and one juvenile even got out of the very low barricade and terrified all the tourists. So be aware.

This was on our way from Colombo to Kandy. When we reached, it was time for elephant bath. After buying tickets, ( saarc countries get a benefit of discount) we went quickly towards the river where the elephants were to be bathed. Must be 50 odd elephants that parade through from the orphanage to the river through a street that must be 100 odd metres It is quite a sight to see so many walking through the streets. The elephants then go to the river and enjoy themselves to a good bath. Quite an experience

It’s better to book an elephant ride where you can find one to get this experience . You pay foreign rate to get in and there is actually not a lot happening in not a very large space . There is a timetable that runs throughout the day with the highlight being the herd leaving for the river at 2 pm and returning at 4pm . There are maybe 20-30 elephants that go into the river to cool off . This is good for taking pictures . But going for a ride for the same entrance ticket is a magical experience - we found one outside Sigiriya for a reasonable price

Coming from Maldives we do not see a lot of animals and seeing these beautiful animals was a wonderful experience. Have to purchase a ticket for entrance and we are directed towards a lane down to the river the elephants were bathing in. We have to purchase another ticket if we wanna bath them ourselves. Visited with a 10 month old and it was very very hot. So if you are travelling with a baby bring enough sunscreen, appropriate clothes and water. Many souvenir shops were available. You can experience a herbals and spice garden in the area for the entry ticket. Students studying herbal and Ayurveda medicine guides you through this area and gives you demonstrations too. We were 13 people travelling together of all ages. Whole family and they were more than happy to give us each a massage. Foot back and head. We had a guide who himself guided us towards these places and didn't ask for anything in return. That's new in Sri Lanka. We got to see the elephants returning to the orphanage from the river and the next batch going to the river as well. Although we skipped the feeding as my father wanted to leave. He was not happy with how the elephants were chained and ridden on. I also felt that maybe this place was more of a money making idea than actually caring for the well being of these elephants. It's still worth a visit though.

This well maintained park, was well worth the expensive entrance fee because it goes to a very good cause. Although there were a couple of “show pieces “ ie bottle feeding the babies” where the elephants were in a small area, but I think just for the demonstration. The elephants seem to have plenty of space. Witnessing their bathing time was wonderful. Except for a small group of perhaps wayward elephants that had long chains around their legs the majority of the elephants freely frolic happily in the water. AMAZING. It was clear that this was the very best time for all the elephants to cool down. Close by is a very interesting Dung factory. It was fascinating to see the recycling process. I loved the whole experience.

I came to the orphanage in 1998 and it was very different.  You could get up close to the elephants and even the baby ones were out and about to touch.  It is now an expensive tourist trap.  AN extra 350 rupees to feed an elephant and another 350 rupees to give milk to a baby one.  Even ore of a rip of is the Elephant Museum just up the road.  You can pay 5000 rupees EACH to have an elephant ride and wash one.  I would rather see them in the wild in the national parks.  IT would be better if these two facilities were closed down and return the elephants to the national parks as they seem a lot happier there.

Many elephants and would recommend if not for the unfriendly staff and because they beat the elephants with sticks and poked them on there feet with a spearhead. Costed 2500rupies per adult on entrance. The staff wanted "donations" after they said we could pet the elephants, without naming that it would cost. They wanted 1000 rupies, we gave them 500 and they accepted it unwillingly because they wanted more.

Although the visit is informative and fun for children but the expectation were way too much. Sri Lanka tourism need to develop the facilities better and make it more attractive and fun loving place. Overall good experience but could be more better.

Interesting to see but not worth going out of the way to get there.  The park was nothing special. The fun part was watching the elephants take a bath in the nearby water.  Gift shop on the property was filled with typical tourist trap items at inflated prices.

Very far from Colombo, more than 2 Hours by bus to get there. You can see Elephanths bathing in the river ( and it is nice) and other elephants going around in the orphanage. It is with utter disappointment that I have written this. Having spent some time at Patara elephant Farm (Chang Mai) in Thailand, we expected something similar, but left after 5 minutes and we have made a pact never to return to establishments which exploit the animals. We have seen elephants in the wild, in sanctuaries and then at this orphanage, this doesn’t make us experts, but we have seen them at various times and I can say that these animals look the saddest of all. We were assured by our guide that these elephants were looked after and were being taken care of, but it really didn’t come across in the interactions that they had with the animals and all the positive work that is supposedly being done was in no way communicated through any of their collateral. We paid our money and we’re duly pointed down the road to watch them bath. This road consisted of every tourist shop imaginable, all with elephant images on, selling t-shirts, crockery, dung paper etc etc. I suppose we expected more!

The elephants are trained that if they come into the area they will be looked after, they are not kept there, this place is doing everything possible to make sure the elephant population stays up. There are a few viewing points to see the elephants; in the river, walking down the road, a rock area and finally over to the baby elephant feeding. Its well worth a visit and I would recommend that you support this place

Costing about 2000 LKR for just a ride/bath/feed a elephant. well you can get it much better if you have planned Kerala. the place is enroute between International Airport to Kandy. so if you plan to go to Kandy, you might prefer to visit here. Its just a herd of elephants walking/sleeping.eating/bathing which you can witness do activity with if you have children.

I came here for the first time in 1999 and my experience then was positive. I don’t remember the setup exactly but it seemed there were more opportunities to encounter the elephants close up. Now, perhaps because of greater numbers, the experience is more controlled. If you have time to visit one of Sri Lanka’s nature reserves you’ll see elephants in the wild. They look relaxed. They mess about with water. They stroll around. Unfortunately at Pinnawala they just look bored. Yes a couple lie down in the river so you can splash water on them, because that’s what they’re trained to do, and the keeper keeps his billhook over the animal’s back in case it gets any other ideas. The babies are chained by the leg while being fed for public viewing. Overall it’s not a dreadful place, but humans and elephants can’t mix easily without the elephants being strictly disciplined, and they show it in their behaviour, standing listlessly around waiting for the next command. It was disappointing.

I visited this place on the way from Bandaranaike International Airport to Sigiriya. I got a chance to get really close to the elephant. Elephants getting bath in the river was the most beautiful thing to watch while being at this place. It was really a beautiful experience.

Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage  houses orphan elephants including those who have been maimed or injured It is awe inspiring to see 44 plus elephants calmly marching to the river front with their caretakers and enjoying a dip in the river and marching back to the orphanage after their daily ritual.The elephants are given a good scrubbing by their caretakers and the walk from the Riverfront back to the orphanage is no less than a Ramp walk.You can also see them during their feeding time.All in all a different experience

We visited this place but unfortunately were disappointed. The elephants mostly had chains on their legs and the babies were chained front and back legs prior to being bottle fed. Upset me so we left and walked down to the river for lunch. We were lucky enough to see elephants in the river with their mahoot. He kindly took some bananas from me for them. Wouldn't recommend this. Better to see them in the game reserves. I'm sure they are saving the orphans but there was something I didn't care for here.

Been a few days ago, up to 10:00 am elephants are in Orphanage where you can feed them if you have a feeding ticket. After, they lead elephants  to river and bath them. Very positive emotions. Entry about 500 LKR(3$) for person for non feeding ticket.

if you want to touch elephants, but you disagree with riding them, than this is the place for you. you can feed them, you can touch them, watch baby elephants being fed. they will also take you to a river where the elephants will cool in the water. the place is big and the animals are well cared for.

This place should be visited only if you have kids who would be excited on seeing elephants in the open. Otherwise you can surely miss this place. Also, it can be visited only if you are in Pinnawala and the place is near by. It is not something that you should plan for as a special visit. Also, be aware of the main entrance guards as one of them tore our ticket to enter the bathing area of elephants. We came to know about this from the guard manning the bathing area and he let us enter as a special consideration.

Read a lot of negative reviews, so we were very apprehensive about this place. It’s a shame some people can find the negative in something so special. $20 aud is a bargain for the experience and everyone in our group of 9 felt so great full for the chance to interact with these beautiful animals. It is definitely not your typical tourist ripoff and the locals pay much less because they are locals and extremely POOR! Make sure : you get there early for walk to river (check times)as traffic is very slow everywhere. Have cash! and passports to pay at counter. Definitely pay the 700rup $6.00 aud to bathe and interact with elephants. My family loved it. Take plenty of water it’s really hot We rate this as a must do for anyone who hasn’t had a bath with an elephant 🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘🐘.

Great place to bring kids. Don't miss the bathing of the elephants in the river. Also worth visiting the place and watching the elephants eat. May want to skit the demonstration of how they are fed with milk as they don't really have small cubs there

We had just arrived in Sri Lanka and on our way from Colombo to Dambulla we stopped by this Pinnawala Elephant Orphange. We had visited a few in Asia in our travels, Thailand and Nepal and of course each is differently run. We arrived after a downpour and saw some young calves chained up feeding in the orphanage. So we headed across the street to the river front where the mahoots and more mature elephants were bathing. We got very close to the elephants when they were headed back to the orphanage after the bath. Nothing unusual about the place and like most orphanages the entrance fees though some times high are used for the upbringing of the elephants to get them food and supplies whereby in the long term they can breed and increase the elephant population.

Good experience watching these elephants, especially the baby ones.Place is very pricey though - 2500 LKR for non SAARC nationals and 700 LKR for SAARC nationals. Milk feeding session is extra - 350LKR and this I would say is completely worth the money paid. Was real fun. The entire session ended is 20min flat! :-)

I was concerned about the ethics of this establishment before visiting but was pleased to see nearly all of the elephants are free roaming. Given the fact they have been successfuy running the conservation for a number of decades and look after so many is quite a testament. I would much rather see elephants in this environment than at the other establishments nearby such as the many riding centres or at the Elephant project which is home to only two elephants. Which seems very lonely for them. The paddy field is a huge area for then to roam and the fruit and milk feeding it done on a rotation to not over feed particular elephants. The larger animals are chained when they make the walk over the road, down past a row of shops in into the river for the safety of the staff, the public and the herd. They are then unchained to enjoy the water. Or kept chained so the keeps can bathe then and carry out vital health checks. While the keepers did carry bull hooks we never saw them used while we were visiting as the elephants followed when called. It seems they were carried as a precaution. Meeting one up close for a small tip to the staff of 500Rs was worth it for the memories. I just love elephants and wanted to see them up close.

We took three hours to drive up to the elephant orphanage and were v disappointed at the lack of information. No flyers or map. No guides and no information about events that they have through the day. They only allow a certain no of people per day to feed the elephants. So it s difficult for everyone to get a chance. Would not recommend this place. Sorry.

Wow a place filled with elephants. We went in the morning on our way to Kandy from Colombo. First it was time for Milk feeding to the babies and then Fruit feeding to the big ones and you and your kids can feed for a small amount. Then they go in groups to the river for a morning bath thru the narrow street and wow it gives a great feel when you see so many of them in that street. They enjoy bathing in the water. Kids would love this place. Also couple of shops reusing the elephant poop and making paper you can see the process and buy some nice sovuneir if interested.

Not worth a visit especially if you're from India. The entry fee for Indians and other South Asians is LKR 700, & 2500 for other foreigners. Pretty steep. Plus charges for milk feeding, etc. You could view feeding, river bathing, etc plus of course a large herd of pachyderms - many of which a babies. The keepers will demand money and are very rude to visitors. Worth a visit only you've never seen elephants before. The handicraft shop is small and v expensive.

We were driven to Pinnawala and the driver was anxious  to get us there early (think 09:30) as only a certain number of visitors can bottle-feed the baby elephants a day - well worth the rush to get the tickets for this (pay an additional sum to the entrance tickets and we had to pay more as tourists) We then walked up to where a large herd of elephants were being fed leaves and watched them for a while before going on to a raised platform and buying some fruit - 250 rupees per bowl. Then we got to hand feed an elephant called Mina - fantastic! A horn sounded and the visitors were kept back off the roads while the elephants walked down through the town to the river. We all followed and watched these incredible animals having a wonderful time for at least an hour.  They were allowed to wander over quite a big area and some really submerged themselves, while younger ones played together and a member of staff gave another a good scrub. The Orphanage itself was a well-kept and clean site - with good loos and shade if needed!!

Place is pretty commercial and surely not advisable! Prices are hilarious and everybody inside from security to tour guides asks you for a tip so bluntly. End of our elephant tour, the Mahout pulled me by the leg from the other side of the fence and asked me to give him money which was so surprising considering they charge 2000 Rps per tourist. Our overall experience of the place is pretty bad! Surely not recommended as the flow of tourists made places like that think they can rip off people and get away with it.

Valuable conservation work undertaken here and great to see the elephants so well-treated .  You can see the elephants being fed (and pay a little extra - Rs200 or Rs300, £1/£1.50 to feed them yourself) and also being taken down to the river to bathe.  Brilliant photo opportunities.  However, it is a real shame that they don't capitalise on their success and hard work by giving out more information on the elephants and their habits.

It was an impressive experience to see the elephants up close and watch them walk between the sanctuary and river. A steep admission price at 2500 rupees per foreign adult, though. Everyone passed up the souvenir shops. It’s a great experience but difficult to spend more than an hour in the heat.

We were really surprised with the prices: for locals - 100 rupees, for foreigners - 2500 rupees :))) There is a timetable of the elephants - you should follow it to see interesting things : milk feeding, fruits feeding, bathing in the river, just walking around. It seems like elephants are happy there, no chains. We like it very much. You can't ride the elephant, they are free here:)) It's much better than private "orphanages" with chained and sad animals.

I visited the orphanage last week, while I was on holiday and I was really surprised at what I found. All the elephants were really sad, none of them seemed happy and it was very upsetting. We got there to see elephants in the river and our first thought was how down they all looked.  They weren't playing or washing, just standing there in a heard looking sorry for themselves. When they got out and made it back to the orphanage visitors were kept back and told to wait before being allowed to walk up to the enclosure.  When we finally did I was appalled to see all of the elephants in chains!!  From the old to the young, every single elephant was chained up and the younger elephants found it very distressing.  The older elephants were obviously used to it, so they didn't care as much but I care!! This is unacceptable and these large beautiful animals should NOT be chained up on short leashes or look so sad and down.  The orphanage should be a place where the elephants are cared for and hopefully released into the natural parks so they can be even more free. I would NOT recommend a visit to Pinnawala but spend the time to see these lovely animals in a national park like Yala. It was a really disappointing visit and I would tell anyone not to give money to a place like this where I felt the elephants are not being looked after to the best possible standard.

I was left absolutely devastated after I witnessed elephants chained up and men walking around with spears stabbing elephants behind their ears if they didn't move quick enough. I wouldn't call that an elephant orphanage!!! An absolutely abhorrent experience. If you want to see elephants, go and see them happy and free in the wild WHERE THEY BELONG!

We visited this orphanage on our way to Kandy on the 08/10/2017.  Our Guide Luba and our driver collected us at 5:30 am from our hotel, so that we could be at the orphanage as soon as it opened.  It costs about LKR 3000 for adult tourist and LRK 1500 for children.  There is a separate price for citizens   There is also a board at the ticket office indicating the programme for the day, which also indicates the times the baby elephants will be fed and when the elephants will be taken down to the river.  . There is also a restaurant where you can enjoy a meal or a cup of tea, while watching the elephants bathing in the water.

Visited the 'elephant orphanage' with a group of friends, why it is called an orphanage is unclear as a torture camp would have been a more fitting name. The actual herd seemed to have the best quality of life, however, did not really have that much space and no vegetation whatsoever, it's basically just a big dry mud field. The most distressing thing to see is the probably 50 or so bulls chained up with no room to move at all. None of the male elephants had water and only 4 or 5 actually had food. They were all bobbing their heads, which I later read was a sign of distress. There are very few signs throughout the complex so we ended up in an 'off limits' area. Clearly they did not want us to see these elephants due to the horrendous conditions, there was an enormous shed with around 30 young bulls chained up with no food or water, again lots of head bobbing and one particular elephant making this wailing sound which was very distressing. A man then spotted us and quickly ushered us back to the beaten track. We attempted to speak to several keepers about what we had witnessed but they kept deferring us to the head of communication. We eventually spoke to this man, who when questioned, became instantly defensive and stated several times that these elephants were too dangerous to socialise freely and it was purely a safety precaution to keep them chained up all the time. He then started telling us that they did all individually get 1 trip to the river each day. I'm sorry but he was obviously lying. We asked how this was possible given his previous statement about it being too dangerous to move the elephants. He then started stuttering and stumping over his words etc. Logistically taking each bull to the river individually is unfeasible, it would take them all night! We asked what time this started as we would like to see, he originally said 8PM, then when we said he would stay until then, he said it didn't happen on Saturday?! He then got extremely defensive saying that if these elephants weren't here, they would be dead and at least they are still alive! I appreciate his point but I feel that they should make much more effort to care for the elephants properly, at present it seems that the male elephants at the orphanage have absolutely no quality of life. Serious improvements are needed urgently! I would not recommend going whatsoever, I feel guilty for helping to fund such treatment.

Not worth visiting. The elephant looks forced  to take people in rides. They don't put a basket on top of the elephant. Just a cloth underneath you and you can feel the animal moving. You don't have anything to hang on to except for a small rope. When the elephant tries to go down into the river, if you are not holding correctly, you could fall and there is no safety gear. Expensive for a 10 min ride. You can also bathe and feed the elephant for a charge.

Enjoyable 3 hour drive from our hotel in Bentota mix of motorway and through towns and villages gives great insight into how the locals live. The 80 or so elephants of all ages look in great condition. Some are rescued logging elephants and as they can be aggressive when unchained they are lightly restrained. Feeding session was a big hit for the grandchildren. (1.15 pm). We gravitated to the riverside restaurant for 2 pm to watch bathing session and we had excellent lunch. I was lifted up steps in my wheelchair. Commanding view of proceedings as elephants played in the deep pools and the mahouts scrubbed some behind the ears. Elephants loved that. Although this is not a safari and all is orchestrated it’s in natural surroundings and children and wheelchair can get really close. I strongly recommend. Back in our hotel for 6pm. You can do an earlier session leaving your hotel at 5am if you prefer and want to see more sights around Kandy etc.

The Orphanage is doing good work, but the place is over hyped and not worth the time.  The place is clean and very well maintained, maybe a good attraction for visitors from Europe and Americas or Australia where there are no Elephants.

My wife and I visited this place in the second week of October and found the place highly over rated and highly glamorized. Its just a place where perhaps you have very high expectations and end with a whimper. We saw around 30 elephants in all ; ; some bathing ; some walking towards the river for a bath and some young ones being fed milk. There appears to be no communication between the keepers and the visitors ; no elephant show as in Thailand. The entry fees is also high especially for a western tourist and you end up with a lump in your throat after seeing the place.
