Kids really like the elephant form and their bath etc. but ticket are very expensive I do nothing so that it has worth to pay that much. if you have to feed element you have to buy separate food, there are many other smal form where are few elephant and you can have ride on them too. here is no ride option and only elephants. .

A must visit place for Elephant Lovers. 2-2.5 hours are enough for the complete activity. Keep in mind the timings for different activities (feeding and bathing majorly). Ticket cost 2500/- LKR. 50% off for SAARC countries, needs to show your passport. You can get the bundle tickets for Orphanage and Zoo, else you have to take separate tickets.| No need to take any guides with you, everything is self explanatory. Bathing in the River was the nice part. Milk Feeding is paid activity, won't recommend it as it last for only for 10-20 secs.

We visited here on our way back to Colombo airport from Sigiriya and spent a couple of hours here. When we arrived we went straight to see the baby's being bottle fed milk, makes a great picture if you want to pay to do this but the bottle is gone within seconds. We then had a little wander and went to feed a basket of fruit to a massive elephant. I loved this, got some good pictures and so amazing to be so close touching and feeding the elephant, actually having my hand on her tongue to give her the bananas! We then headed over the road to the river where the elephants are taken to bathe. On our way there, the elephants followed us, so we had to duck into the nearest shop so as not to become a target on their way to the river. Some elephants taken there first are chained to the floor while in the water. Then the heard arrives who are allowed to be free in the water and play. We spent a good half hour here watching them all and found this to be the best bit. Glad we went there and a good break to our 5 hour journey to the airport!

If you like elephants, then this is the place to be. I prefer to see them in the wild but they are not always there when you are! It was nice to see them taken down to the river by the handlers, where they bathed and drank copious amount of water.

As we drove from Negombo to Kandy we stopped off here. This broke the journey up a little. We arrived for 11am (feeding and washing time) all elephants are paraded twice a day from their orphanage down to the natural Water pools just a five minute walk. We met the elephants there and observed them all washing and playing. We noted about 30 elephants in that group which was great to see. All of which looked healthy and happy. Price of entry was 2500 rps per adult (western price). After watching them bath for one hour we took a look around the orphanage which also looked nice and spacious. Worth a visit considering admission fees are used to continue the care of these animals. It didn't take long to visit. I would allow 90 minutes.

We visited the orphanage - watched the feeding of the youngsters then went down to the river to watch them in the water.  To be honest if I did this again I would miss out the park and the feeding and go straight down to the river as it was a nice experience to watch them - although clearly not as free as we would hope for. The river part was nice to watch - it's as close as you get to them being natural although behaviour clearly not. A nice day out for an elephant lover with an elephant poo calendar to remember the trip!!!

We were  here a couple of years ago and thought it worth a second visit.  The car journey from and to Bentota  was 'interesting'  as are all car journeys on the Island. Enjoy the elephants and have a meal at a local restaurant. All in all, a good day out

We arrived at Colombo airport early morning on Friday 22nd 2017 and were met by an elderly gentleman who offered us a trip in his car to Pinnawala with his wonderful driver Sudath. You can choose the activity you want when buying the ticket - normally about 40 minutes to an hour. There are 8 elephants of different ages. Different activities include bathing, ride on the back, following the elephant along a track, feeding and the museum.

What useful information and experience can I add to these reviews?    I suppose it depends on how you view things.  It's a zoo.  A nice zoo, but a zoo nonetheless. These elephants have been in trouble during their short lives and have been located to the orphanage and are being made to work for their keep.  This entails being herded to the top of a hill so that tourists can take selfies.  Our trip coincided with a period of rain showers and it was quite funny to see that when the keepers took shelter from the rain, the elephants about turn rapidly and head back down the hill, or even tried to amble out.  Then, there is an argument between the keepers about whose turn it is to get wet and regroup the elephants. Milk feeding time is 13:15hrs and there is a limited number of tickets available.  Basically, a keeper fills a bottle of milk and you feed it to the elephant while a friend or colleague takes a photo.  Be aware, the whole process takes about 20 seconds so do practice your smiles and camera angles.  Maybe add a couple of pre-minutes to work on that. Right, feeding done with, find your entry ticket, hoping you haven't fed it to an elephant, because you'll need it to pass security and get to the river down the road opposite the entrance.  Get to the river and choose one of the restaurants, either left or right; we went left, sit at a table grab a beer and wait for the afternoon elephant washing. Again, during the next rain shower, the pantomime continues.... the keepers take cover and the 30 or so elephants meander up and down stream looking for escape at best or just something more interesting to do.  The real entertainment is watching which keepeer draws the short straw and gets soaked running up and down stream to regroup the herd. Elephant washing done, stroll back to your car passing many spending opportunities.  There's a place that tells you all about turning elephant poo into paper but I missed that looking for a lost phone which magically turned up in the car. Well, they say Sri Lanka is a magical place.

The entire tour is worth taking as also tiresome due to climbing up hill down hill and to be in the cheer drums as well as happy shreaks of fear with fun together. after this tour it was so tiresome that it had injected a full level of fun and satisfaction inside for a very calm evening snacks followed by a very refreshing sleep at hotel to be fresh for next day. the charm, fun, and the joy is unaccountable in words. its all about how as friends or family yu do this tou sitting on a single elephant.The best was we were three on 1 elephant and the joy and adventure of it was worth it that its still fresh in memory lanes tokeep remembering and smiling.Happy journey, my advice never to miss this if in group and its worth it as its very economical .Highly advisable to have only 1 banana to keep up to the energy levels before this adventure as its very uphill and down hill task and to handle ones weight against the height of elephant with all the fun, fear and cherishment alive for the 1 or 1.5 hours.

The elephants can be seen in cautivity in the Pinnawala area. It's very important to know the schedules and visit during bath time, when they cross the road to the river and enjoy a bath so close to the people you can take excellent pictures

See elephants in the wild and don't go here! There is very little orphanage about this place! The elephants are chained up on concrete platforms. Many of them weaving with their heads back and forth. There is no safe zone for the elephants to retreat to if they find all the tourists too much. We saw this inscription in the guest book that summed it all up quite nicely!

The visit left me feeling very uneasy. First we went down to the river to see the elephants wash. Some were chained to the rocks because apparently they were 'aggressive'- they just looked sad to me. The other elephants that weren't chained also looked sad. They did not play in the river or move much (even the younger ones). We then went to see the younger elephants at the 'orphanage'. I was upset to see them in such small cages with no stimulation and a lot of them were isolated. The cages were so cramped and again, the elephants looked sad. A few days later we went on a safari and saw many elephants in their own habitat, which was much better. We even saw some as we drove along the road- this was a much better experience than the orphanage. If you like elephants, then stay away from the orphanage and go on a safari instead. It's a much more enjoyable experience to see happy elephants in their own environment with family.

This is our second visit to the Pinnawala Elephants Orphanage with children. Tickets: there are separate counters for Sri Lankans and non- Sri Lankan's. Arrived in time to see baby elephants being bottle fed. There is a recording explaining how much milk is given to each baby elephant in local language and English. If you buy a feeding ticket (premium) you can bottle feed a baby elephant. Mind you they suck a bottle of milk in a second or so but great photo opportunity. Elephants are taken to the river around  midday. It's where all the action happens. Great sight - large herd of elephants playing in the water. From the last visit most memorable thing for children (around 4years then) was that elephants doing poos in the water! Lots of shops to buy souvenirs. Elephant poo papers are made by the locals and sold in shops as cards, writing paper etc. Toilet facilities are available at the entrance and inside. Some facilities have a normal fee like £0.05 We took picnic lunch with us there are places nearby to get food. Not sure I saw a restaurant inside. Great place to see lots of wild elephants. Would highly recommend. Don't forget sun cream and hats.

I didn’t like the orphanage itself as it looked too touristic, especially the so called “baby feeding with milk”. You pay an entrance ticket of 17$, but if you want to feed the babies (who do not look very much like babies) you have to pay more. They put two smaller elephants in a huge cage around which the tourists are watching the feeding with milk and those tourists who paid extra are allowed to feed the animals, still outside the cage. It looked like a circus. But it is still worth visiting as there is the herd nearby - quite a lot of elephants, some babies.

We didn't and wished we had. Our family are not animal experts, but the sight of these supposedly revered and 'orphaned' grand creatures in chains took me back to the cruel travelling circuses of previous years, mercifully now banned. I've no idea of the true agenda at this place, but the prices are high (£50 for 4) and animal welfare evidently low. Do your research before you visit to avoid the upsetting scenes we witnessed. A couple of hours up the road is the Minneriya National Park, where herds of elephants roam free without the shackles or spikes.

If you have young children like I do They will enjoy it very much and will see it as a Paradise. They only saw the elephants passing by and being fed and bathed. However our driver ,Madane, took us to a very nearby place where my whole family fed, rode and bathed Raja a beautiful big male 5 ton bull. It was a beautiful exhilarating experience.

We set out to visit the elephant orphanage at Pinnawala, about 90 km (56 miles) from Colombo. Those accustomed to traveling by highways and freeways would think it's only one hour or less drive, piece of cake. Not so if you're traveling in Sri Lanka. In fact it took us around 3 hours to reach there because throughout the journey we never broke through what appeared to be a town-like single lane road on whose both sides were shops & houses and people walked lethargically by. While we were frustrated at the snail-pace speed of the car our driver seemed at complete peace with himself and oblivion to the movement, rather lack of it, of the car. That's Buddah's country, that's Sri Lanka, and that's patient, friendly, and accommodating Sri Lankans we have been experiencing ever since we got here. Haven't seen anyone losing his/her tempter in even knotty situations. No shouting matches, no exchanges of expletives, no red noses, just matter-of-factly statements and moving on and beyond. At time I wondered what they do for fun. 😁😁🍁🌺🌻🌼🌷💐🌸 Upon arriving at the element sanctuary we were not sure if it was worth visiting as the entry fee of SL Rupee 2500 per person seemed a bit too exorbitant. After convincing ourselves for not missing out on a life time chance we dragged our feet to ticket window. The gentleman at ticket window asked where I was from? Surprised at the question, and almost shouting back at him "none of your business", the word Pakistan escaped my mouth. He further tested my patience by demanding to see my ID or passport. Luckily I had my Pak ID so I showed it to him reluctantly. I almost fainted what followed next. He charged me SL rupee 700 pp saying SAARC country residents have special rates for entry. My Pak ID never looked so dear to me, and I made myself promise to Google what SAARC is abbreviated for. 😛😛❤️❤️ Finally we entered the elephant orphanage and OMG I have never seen so many live elephants of various sizes in one place and that too so up close and personal. Luckily we were there when baby elephants were fed milk at 09:30 and other big babies were fed fruits and vegetables. Between 10:00 am and 12:00 noon elephants are herded to a river nearby across the street from elephant sanctuary for bathing. It's a very unique sight to watch elephants frolicking in the river water. The mischiefs of baby elephants, trumpets of elder ones, interaction between men and mammoths are such unique events that you wouldn't want to miss out on.🌺🌺🌹🌹☘️☘️🌹🌹 The elephant orphanage by its name shows the intention of a great cause which needs to be supported. Elephants are nourished well and taken good care of as was apparent from their health. However, there is a counter argument which says that this elephant sanctuary is a man-made unnatural habitat where elephants are kept against their free will. The supporters of this argument point toward some of chained elephants, and usage of pointed steel implements by elephant trainers. Make up your own mind.👍👎😱👌😎 By and large the sanctuary is well maintained keeping in consideration of elephants privacy and safety of visitors. The area is huge, absolutely plush green, aptly fenced/barricaded and there are sanctuaries within for elephants to rest & relax, and where visitors aren't permitted. To me it was a life time experience, and we were happy that we had ignored the high entry fee and decided to visit, and of course happier still that we carried our national ID cards.😀😀👍🇵🇰🇵🇰

Great place to visit with Children. Really enjoyed the visit to the place. You could see the way the baby elephant been fed. You could do so too. but of course they charge a little amount for that. There are lots of restaurants around the river. you could see the elephant bathing while having a snack at the restaurant. It's worth the price.

This one is what I understand as a tourist trap. Well, you can see elephants and relatively nice surroundings, that's the good news. Everything is really expensive. Note this: The staff will ask kindly if they can take a photo of you and an elephant with your phone, afterwards demanding great deal of money from the photos. Some of the elephants were chained so that they couldn't move, and they were treated cruelly in other ways too. I was disappointed as I expected more natural experience.

On the way to the International Airpor from Kandy, I arrived here at 12.00 p.m. and stayed almost for two hours. I feeded fruits to elephants and they posed with me. One of my favorite photos was that I put my hand on his nose. I could see milk feeding to child elephants. I took many  photos while they are in the field. At 2.00 p.m. all elephants went to the river to take a bath and I could take photos of them.

Calling this an orphanage implies that the elephants are there for their own well-being and best interests. However, we wish we'd read the Born Free Foundation reports before visiting, as this would have saved us the heartbreak of seeing these beautiful creatures in such an unnatural 'zoo-like' environment - being herded to and from the river by men with metal spiked sticks! Although release into the wild may not be an option for some of the elephants, attempts should be made to give them a more natural environment. The elephants were seemingly in good physically healthy but their mental welfare was certainly called into question during our visit. There was an elephant chained by the river alone, rocking and clearly in distress. This is inexcusable for a so-called orphanage.

The elephant orphanage is a great cause to support for its lovely intention. However, it is best to plan your visit around the times when elephants are taken to the river (around 9:30 am or in the afternoon), where you can see them frolic in the water and interact with one another. Check the schedule on the orphanage's website. Also worthwhile, is the boutiques along the street that leads down to the river. One, in particular, is fun, as it sells all kinds of paper products made from elephant dung. Yes, dung!

I went to see these yesterday but you can tell the elephants look very sad. They were told where to go. The only thing I liked was the baby's when being milked. I would say if you are over here go and see them in the wild at yala or even on the road from kandy to yala they come out. They are free to roam.

Very interesting place to visit.  It's worth remembering that most of the elephants here were rescued as babies and would have died in the wild otherwise.  It's disconcerting to see chain hobbles on the big males, but understandable if you consider they are not rehabbed for release back to the jungle, are living on a "farm" and need to be controlled.  They all really seem to enjoy their visits to the river, splashing around, crowding close to the water spray, and lying down to soak in the deeper pools. Babies play and spray each other, then wrap their trunks together.  Glad we went.

If you come to Sri Lanka , never miss this place. It is located  closer to Colombo -Kandy road.If you are travelling by railway trains you have to get down from the Rambbukkana railway station and travel by bus( Rambukkana - kegalle buses) from there. Their you have to purchase tickets to enter in to orphanage.You can watch lot more activities of elephant sch as bathing, feeding baby elephants, playing etc. If you wish to go elephant safari ,there are private places near to orphanage.

If this is your only option to see elephants in Sri Lanka (which I doubt it would be), go for it. If you rather see them roam a bit more freely in the wild, try and go for that instead. During our time here the elephant heard was bathing in the river quite freely (1 or 2 were chained for safety and it didn't seem to bother the elephant). Overall I felt that the elephants were taken good care of and they weren't mistreated at any time. Only reason for not giving  a higher rating is that the price was quite hefty and I would rather see these animals walk freely in the jungle.

I rode a bus from the port to Colombo where I was served a delicious lunch and then I could walk through the nearby shops for souvenirs. The best part was waiting across the highway where I walked to the elephant orphanage where there are very many elephants that have been saved by the personnel who work there. Baby elephants often get separated from parents and must be saved and cared for. This orphanage is a place where the babies are loved by all who see them. Many find homes in zoos across the world and many remain where they are. A marvelous place to visit!!!

Never seen so many elephants up close and that too of varying sizes. The tour guide usually takes you around showing how they are bathed and fed. The baby elephants are fed by feeding bottles. They are very naughty so you are not allowed to come near them. There's a specific area where you can buy fruits and feed them yourself. You can also get pictures taken with the big tame ones.

Some elephants are also chained up. All have their heads down and you can tell they are sad with broken spirits. A couple times per day they march through town on the way to the river for "bath time," though they aren't allowed to play in the river. A water sprinkler pump goes off and the herders make the elephants stand under the sprinkler. You can tell they don't want to be there. I would recommend doing a lot of research before visiting any animal attraction. Putting the word "orphanage" into the name of this place is misleading. They don't save elephants, they profit off of them.

We thoroughly enjoyed our visit to the Elephant Sanctuary and it made a very pleasant last visit to our tour of Sri Lanka. The highlight was the river bath time where some of the Elephants were taken across the road to the local river for an afternoon swim. The orphanage is split in two by the main road.  One side has the elephants bathe in the river, but some of the elephants are chained up and not allowed to roam free.  Other elephants roam, but if they get too far away are hit with sticks to keep them close to the tourists.  On the other side the elephants are chained up or kept in cages where you can pay a fee to feed them.  While fun to feed them, the fact that they are chained up takes away from the experience.

The 'elephant sanctuary' was recommended to us by a close friend, and we were happy to make the stop along the busy A9 on the way from Colombo to more remote parts of the island. Although not experts on the levels of elephant happiness, we were rather disappointed by the dwellings which the elephants inhabited. A very commercial enterprise, there was more a sense of money-making, rather than wildlife preservation, which could disgruntle and upset some visitors. In relatively small enclosures, the animals are encouraged by the keepers to stay close to the adoring crowds, despite the numerous warning signs encouraging us to stay away from these 'untamed' animals. Keepers with large sticks encouraged the animals closer whilst also keeping an eye on their mobile phones, probably entertaining phone calls from their friends. The baby elephants, in particular, were kept in enclosures that were far too small, standing in their own faeces, and their lack of comfort was tangible. When feeding time came, it was not a particularly comforting affair, with baby elephants all herded under one roof to appease the mass of tourists. Obviously requiring some interaction with their own kind, the elephants would often rub against the bars of the enclosure, whilst still shackled, meaning that their movements were very limited indeed. The small herb garden was the only solace that we found, set back from the rather loud crowds; we would have happily paid the amount requested if the elephants well treated, but we left feeling rather sorry for them.

When you visit here, you have to look at the time table. In the morning the herd of elephants will walk across the street to the river, where they stay a while. Than, around lunch time, they walk back. It is nice to be there when the elephants are walking through this street. There is a nice restaurant on the river side, where you can watch the elephants take a bath, walk through the street, where you have a nice view and can have your lunch. For 250 rupees you can feed an elephant, which my kids really enjoyed. I think the elephants are treated well here and can recommend this place.

We wanted to do a 1 night pit stop in Pinnawala to have a refreshing drink at one of the riverside restaurants while watching elephants from Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage bathe in the river in a relaxed atmosphere. But since recently, the orphanage blocks anyone from entering the whole street leading to the riverside, unless you have a hotel reservation or pay their exhorbitant 2500RP!!! So basically, 3/4 of the city is blocked if you don't pay them. We ended up paying their insane fee to the orphanage guards to enter the city and get to the river bạthing point, since we were there only for this attraction and there's absolutely nothing else to do there. That was a mistake. We ended up seeing elephants from far away packed in an ocean of other tourists behind a fence. We ran away from this horrible town on the first train the following morning. Avoid this city at all costs! If you're in Sri Lanka, spend time in one of the numerous national parks instead of this joke elephant circus called an "orphanage".

Not really an orphanage,more a money making rip off. Whilst it was great seeing these beautiful animals walking down the street and bathing in the river,it was just not right. the 'walk' was so commercialized with tacky souvenir shops and cafes. Wildly overpriced and overhyped, we lasted 20 minutes here then headed off. We arrived just in time for baby elephant feeding, the staff feeding the elephants milk looked as bored as we were. Workers do prod them occasionally with sticks and it is hard to see at times why they are doing this because there doesn't seem to be an objective at times. There is an opportunity to see some of the smaller elephants being bottle fed and the opportunity to feed an elephant for extra cash. The entrance fee for foreigners is 2500 rupees which is a little steep. My biggest criticism is that there was no information boards to explain how the elephants came to reside at the park or  information about the challenges the elephants face. Without this Pinnawala is simply just a elephant safari park and once inside you have no insight into the purpose of the project for which you appear to be paying a premium price. Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage, about a 2 hour drive from Colombo must be on every tourist's bucket list. We have visited a few times over many years in our travels to Sri Lanka and seen it develop to become one of the top tourist attractions today. It's home to about 75 or more orphaned elephants from playful and adorable cute babies to majestic and magnificent giants, well looked after by a team of dedicated staff. Visitors get the opportunity to feed the babies who guzzle copious amounts of milk and follow them to the nearby river for their daily bath when mahouts give them a good scrub. It's a truly wonderful sight to see so many elephants enjoying and frolicking in the river, captured by visitors from all over the world. There are several restaurants dotted alongside the river bank where visitors can enjoy snacks, refreshing drinks not to mention "kurumba" (young green coconuts) or "thambili" (yellow/orange version. The elephant orphanage in Pinnawala should be a 'must' for anyone visiting Sri Lanka. We were lucky enough to arrive early in the morning, at about 7.30, and after waiting for about an hour by the beautiful river and seeing some beautiful and unusual birds the elephants came working down the road for their bath. As it was so early there was only one other couple there so we were able to take some stunning photos and videos. In the orphanage itself you can see elephants feeding from about 6 feet away and our knowledgeable guide was able to provide some really interesting information. The only slightly 'commercial' bit was seeing the baby elephants have their milk but they seemed immune to the people ogling them and were very sweet.

Many Asian countries do make a profit from many of their elephants. Their wellbeing and handling is always brought into question. I have ridden an elephant in Thailand where they were seemingly well treated. However at Pinnawala, an elephant's life seems monotonous and I do not use this word gently, but cruel. Entry fee was 2500 rupees (20 USD) and what was on offer was to go down to the river and see the elephants bathe. The 'carers' steered the elephants clear from tourists by yelling or coming close to them. When the 'carers' approached the elephants, they immediately moved away. Half the elephants were in chains and baking in the heat with little shade or the ability to move to deeper water. We did see the elephants walk back to the orphanage and that was it; we were not keen to see much else. The area near the river is highly touristic, selling products about elephants including the classic elephant dung. It's highly recommended not to visit this area until they alter their style of caring. Trust the comments on Trip Advisor that say it is not worthwhile.

The elephants were beautiful to see and arrived when they were down at the river. But to be honest, the place had a bit of weird vibe and felt very touristy. We have seen elephants in other centres / environments around the world & this was not the best experience in comparison. However, when in Sri Lanka we wanted to see elephants, particularly bathing in the river. The reviews are mixed & I totally understand why now, as it's hugely overcrowded & very staged for tourists. The crowds to watch the milk feeding were huge (& we already saw that in a much more natural environment in Kenya), so we went straight to the river to await the bathing at 10am. We got a great seat (most were empty) & had a cold drink while waiting - definitely recommend getting there early. This experience was mixed as the elephants on the left all had chains (although were being personally bathed by their mahouts, which was great), & the ones on the right were roaming free under a water jet, which was amazing. We are open minded, & were told the reason for the chains is that they are boisterous, but we just couldn't get over seeing the chains. As we had personally fed elephants with fruit in South Africa in a natural environment we didn't return to see that, as I suspect it was again, very staged. In summary, you need to decide if you can watch elephants in chains (whatever the reason) & if you can't then don't visit. If you're OK, then do it as you will probably love it.

What brought me here was my love for animals, in this case elephants. I didn't really know what to expect from this trip, as I hadn't looked it up and wanted to keep it a surprise. When we arrived by the river I was slightly overwhelmed by the amount of people that were there and how commercialised it was. Obviously it needs to be commercialised to fund the care for the elephants, and I understand that, but it wasn't very pleasant, and definitely not how I would have done things. If you are expecting to view the elephants in small groups, this is not for you. The keepers chained some of the elephants up (these must have been the older elephants, who were not born in captivity, and so are chained for their own safety), which was rather upsetting and actually made me cry. They also had almost pike/spear instruments used to usher the elephants if they weren't doing what they were told or were misbehaving, which I thought was a bit unnecessary. There were also a lot of tourists who had been told not to touch the elephants or feed them and were still doing this, which was very frustrating as there could be serious consequences for the elephants if they end up hurting a human, not to mention that they are probably on a special diet. The only up side to this, is that you got to see elephants in a fairly natural environment, which was absolutely beautiful and you could see that they were enjoying themselves, playing in the water fountain, getting a nice scrub from the keepers in the water and playing with each other! It was nothing like seeing elephants in the wild, and I didn't really like to see that this was the best that they were going to get, but they will never be able to go back into the wild and I'm glad that they are not just left as prey for poachers. They do look happy and their keepers obviously care for them, or they wouldn't be in the job. I would definitely recommend this visit, if not for you, for the elephants, everyone that pays to see them contributes to their well being.

Today my fiancée I and two friends visited the pinnawala Elephant orphanage, After reading good things about this place we felt optimistic about our visit. 1st we walked to the far side where lots of elephants seemed to be roaming around freely behind some large boulders and it looked nice as they had plenty of room, then a mahout (elephant trainer) was shouting holding his large wooden stick with metal spikes/ hook on and the elephants either seemed terrified or extremely well trained as they moved away from him with speed. They didn't look so happy. Then we saw an elephant by a fence where people could feed Him fruit (for an extra fee of course) 250 rps on top of the 2,500 rps entry fee. This elephant had chains round his neck and wasn't aloud to walk away as his mahout had the hooked stick ready every time he tried to move, this elephant looked very sad. By this time I realised it was a zoo and not so much something for the greater good may be more for the greater rupees. Although the elephants were well fead and looked healthy they did not appear happy. We then walked down to find some smaller baby elephants, one was in a metal cage about the size of a small bedroom, this baby elephant was rocking forward and backwards with no food or water near by. I knew that this was not good, the elephant was obviously distressed (very sad to see) This elephant was only About 5 - 6 ft High so quite young. Another elephant in a larger enclosure ( size of a tennis court ) was chained to a post with approx 2 feet of chain so he couldn't walk Around, again no food or water near by and he looked very sad. They could of easily let him off his chains as he was already in an enclosure!!! I had seen enough by this time, quite gutted I had contributed to this pain. I'm fully aware that this wasn't/ isn't the worst case for elephants by far as I've travelled around Thailand and seen some nasty stuff. So this isn't elephant hell. But it's far from elephant heaven. We went down to the river in the afternoon where the elephants go into the river, although some were playing and lying down many were just stood there still Looking very sad keeping a mindful eye on any near by mahout who would often shout at them and pointing their sharp stick at them, the elephants looked extremely fear full of the mahouts! Many elephants were chained up with a few meters of chain to move. One small elephant walked out of the water to find some greenery to eat but the mahout commanded him back into the river. Not once during this unfortunate visit did i see any kindness or affection shown to any elephants by any of the mahouts! All the mahouts looked angry or miserable! I saw one mahout sharpening his metal spike with a file. All In all quite a sad experience for me as I have a lot of empathy towards animals, especially ones as beautiful as these greats! Please don't visit this place. On a better note we did also visit Udawalawe national park before this and a jeep safari took us around, this was a great experience as we saw WILD elephants in herds with NO chains NO mahouts NO cages just freedom to roam and graze anywhere they liked for as long as they liked. That was a real pleasure to see them in their natural habitat! I would highly recommend this instead of the elephant orphanage.

We loved this place, it was good to see the elephants with lots of space to roam and bathe in the river. After they have bathed the shop owners board up their shops temporarily so the elephants can walk down the parade back to the feeding grounds. You can feed one of the tamed elephants whilst the rest eat grass and leaves. It's nice to see the elephants relatively happy and most are not tamed.

We visited here as part of a recent trip to Sri Lanka - the only place my mum has ever wanted to visit, with the primary goal of seeing elephants. After a trip to Thailand last month and a visit to an Elephant Sanctuary there where I had the most wonderful experience, we felt hopeful that Pinnawala would be similar. This is not an Elephant Orphanage or Sanctuary, or even somewhere where the elephants are even remotely prioritised. This is a zoo and a tourist attraction. If you care about these beautiful animals and their welfare, do not visit here. Firstly, the majority of the elephants are kept in one area in a large group. They are not free to roam and also do not seem to have access to the large amounts of food they require (elephants eat for approximately 16 hours a day). In addition to this, there are a select number of elephants chained to the ground on concrete slaps. They are within the view of visitors and clearly maltreated - as demonstrated by them rocking back and forth. This is honestly disgusting and how anyone can see this and think the elephants are okay is absurd. Reading the review below, many seem to think that this is because the elephants are dangerous - elephants are very intelligent animals and, treat with respect and kindness, can develop deep bonds with their mahoots. However, even if they are dangerous, is this any reason for them to spend their lives chained to the floor? Finally, there are numerous viewing areas around the park. There is a small area where you can pay to feed an elephant; which in itself is a tourist scam. In addition to this, there is a concrete area which looks like a cattle sale where you can see smaller elephants be fed milk. This is made to be a show and is disgusting to see - and even sadder to see spectators enjoying it and thinking this is a place where the elephants are looked after. Unfortunately, this is a tourist attraction first and foremost and not concerned with the welfare of the animals. Do not visit here or support this site.

About a 100 kms from Colombo , this place is an elephant orphanage . One can see the elephants in their natural surrounding as well as in restricted spaces. The entry ticket is Rs 1200 per person . You can feed them as well @Rs 250. Fun watching this fantastic animal here.

Seeing the elephant herd was amazing, but overall it is just not worth the price. They charged 2500 rupees, but don't even take a credit card. The elephants were at the river when we came so we had to walk through all the tourist traps to see the elephants. That was great, but after watching them for about 20 minutes, you're ready to go. You can't touch or go near the elephants. In my opinion, it's not worth the $16 per person to see these.

This place is on the Kandy Galle Road, approximately , 80 kms from Colombo. There are separate ticket counters for foreigners and we have to produce our passports to buy the ticket. Not sure whether they charge more for foreigners because the guide bought the tickets which were included in our package. The elephants are taken to the river for a Bath twice a day. Not sure about the morning run but for the after noon one we were told to be there by 1400 hrs,  One can see the herd being taken across the road from their camp to the river. All traffic is halted while they cross. There after they splash and frolic in the river while a powerful pump sprays water over the area to give them a bath as well. There are restaurants along the river where you can have lunch , sip beer and watch the scenery around, as well as the elephants. a bit pricey though ! It is a fairly long walk from the road to the river so have good walking shoes and protection against the sun

I really wanted to go and see an elephant orphanage when I was in Sri Lanka, however, I was left feeling guilty for supporting this attraction. Basically, I thought it was just a zoo. We read mixed reviews about this place but we enjoyed the trip.  The tour of the orphanage was interesting.  Baby feeding time divine.  We watched the elephants playing in the river from a hotel balcony whilst eating lunch, which was probably the best way to do it.  Fascinating to watch.  A bit hit with all the children and a treat for adults.

This is a really wonderful place. You can tell that the elephants are well looked after, and that the keepers/mahouts are very close to them. The visit includes watching them drink milk from large bottles, feeding them fruit and then following them across the road and down to the river to watch them bathe. You can get really close to these magnificent animals. The hour watching them bathe went by very fast. A really good tract of wide, shallow river has been chosen for this activity and you can sit and watch them wash themselves, play and tend to their young - a great experience! Some advice - check the website, and make sure you get there for the baby elephant milk feeding and larger elephant fruit feeding (you pay a little extra to get a large bowl of fruit to feed them, but it is not a lot of money.) The bathing takes place just after that. You are best getting to the river as quickly as possible and grabbing a seat at one of the bars overlooking the bathing area. You can then leave the seats to take photographs and to get closer to the elephants later.

It is a park for orphan elephants in Srilanka. One and only in the world. park is not suitable in hot weather. and the big elephants are not to see very close. Elephant bath is an attraction. otherwise it is not recommended. Fee- SAARC countries- SLR-1400, others- SLR 2500

The best time to experience these beasts, is as they walk to and from the park to the river. Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is on the way from Colombo Airport to Kandy/Nuwara Eliya. Elephants which turn Old, Baby Elephants who have lost their parents in the Jungles & others are prevented from people who kill them for Tusks, Hide, etc. There are 2 Restaurants by the River, where you can have Coffee / Breakfast / etc & watch these Giants having funn

We arrived just as some elephants were on their way back from bathing so we got so close to them and it was a great experience. We walked down the road to the restaurant where you get great views of around 30 elephants bathing in the water. They were all roaming freely around but the Mahouts were definitely out to make money and asked to take photos with your camera after getting the elephants in position. We did not witness any cruelty though. We followed all the elephants back to the orphanage where they were led into an enormous open space. There were a few elephants in their own enclosures but it was explained to us that they were rescued from the wild as they were injured and because they have been taken away from their families they were unpredictable and anxious. They needed to get them better before releasing them back into the wild to be with their families again. We only witnessed one that was chained but he was rocking backwards and forwards which is a definite sign of aggression and unpredictability. They can't take a risk with so many visitors. We had a fab day and it was purely looking at the elephants, no rides whatsoever which I was happy about.

We went to see the elephants bathing and also to the orphanage.  The bathing in the river was the first part of what we saw.  Although there were two elephants who were on chains, the others were freely roaming with a keeper making sure that they did not go to far away.  There were opportunities for lots of photos. We then went into the orphanage.  It was clean and appeared to be well looked after.  The only difficulty is that the keepers wanted money to take photos.  They then wanted 50,000 rupee for the photo or $50 NZ.  It was a bit of a shame trying to get money, but that was the only negative.  Other than that, it was a good experience to see the elephants.

The visit to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage was planned well in advance of our trip. I was expecting to see elephants roaming freely within a reserve in their natural environment so I was a little shocked to see the reality of the situation. Make no mistake,  this is a expensive commercial money generator and I just hope all proceeds are ploughed back into the coffers of the orphanage and not some bureaucrats pocket. The highlight is the sight of all the elephants bathing in the River Oya but even here many are chained to the rocks in the river and whilst the elephants obviously enjoy the daily ritual so do the hundreds of stall holders along the road to the river and the hotel who profit from the hordes of tourists who gather there. Everyone seems to be in it for a buck and it's this aspect that detracts from the original intent of setting up an elephant sanctuary/orphanage in the first place. Better to view the elephants roaming free in the national parks around Sri Lanka than in this environment.

I asked our tour guide about this who assured me this was generally the just the large bulls who could be a bit unpredictable but were free when the tourists were not there. Watching them parade through the streets to bathe was amazing and watching the young elephants frolic in the water whilst having lunch was perfect. Whilst I loved it here and would return, visiting elephants later in the week in the national parks completely free made you think about the difference.

The title of 'orphanage' makes the place sound like abandoned elephants are looked after. Quite the opposite. The more I think about our visit here the more uncomfortable I am about it. We expected elephants to be freely walking around the big plain that is located here but every single elephant was chained to the ground in a hut when we went (with a few others dotted around the grounds for tourists to look at also on very short chains attached to the floor) They all had very little space to manoeuvre or access to get to water in the blistering heat. Mahouts were asking for money to pose next to the elephants and we even saw them kicking the elephant to try and get into the right position for a photo. There is so much open space for them to be walking around I cannot understand why the chaining to the floor is necessary. Its a great place for a day out and for kids. Elephant orphanage is little far from Kandy. You can touch the elephants, ride them and watching them bathing. Its not a must do, but if love to see elephants, then one can visit this place.

It was nice experience, my children were excited and thrilled to watch the baby elephant drinking his milk in the bottle....It is a big please but was very hot, you have always to carry your umbrella in Sri Lanka in case of strong sun or rain.

We spent around 45 minutes here.  We saw the elephants going to and from the river, we saw them feeding from plants and also the younger ones drinking milk.  I would have liked to see more informative n regarding education and retiring elephants to the wild.  I also found it upsetting to see some of the larger male elephants chained up so they had difficulty walking.

We had a great spot downstairs at the hotel on the left side othe roadless ingot the river. In the shade we had a drink and watched them from very close quarters. It's was funny watching the street be closed off and all the shopkeepers removing their wares from the sidewalk as they made their way back to the park. My son fed the elephant and for 250r he got a large selection of fruits and loved the experience. The park is clean and looks we'll run.. The elephants don't seem well looked after. Remember - they were not caged. All the animals I saw appeared healthy, contented and well nourished. It was a joy to watch the elephants  and it was clear that the mahouts took the trouble to ensure that the elephants all had a  "turn" to bathe in the deepest part of the river.

While these animals are amazing and it's always an honour to watch their habits, not sure how I feel about the chains and sticks used to move the elephants. When I asked a number of different mahouts, why, was told that these elephants aren't fully reliable yet and need to spend 2 years like this. 2 years!! I get that this orphanage is rescuing them and has does some great work but is it necessary to have these beautiful animals chained in the river for the purposes of attracting tourists? It was distressing. And at 2,500 rupees (17e) its quite a tourist trap. The main attraction really, in my opinion, is watching them bathe in the river there isn't much at the feeding area. Wish I had read some trip advisor reviews before going. Would not return. (Look at left leg in this pic)

Our nine year old loved feeding the elephant from the feeding platform. One of our favourite visits this trip.

After taking a bath, they would walk reeeeeally close to you, without any barrier in between which makes it a bit scary, but from the other side it is really nice being so close to them. If you ask around or try the Sri Lankan tourist board on Galle Road opposite the Cinnamon Grand hotel you might get it from $80 - $100. The cost to enter the orphanage is 2500 rupees if you are non Sri Lankan and if you are a local it is 100 rupees.  It always narks me a bit about the lack of equality but I suppose we have 2 choices - pay or don't go. There are several places to eat and get a drink at Pinnawala and there are quite a few shops selling clothes, bags, souvenirs - it's good to take a look around. Get to the orphanage early.  Bottle feeding of the baby elephants starts at - 9:15hrs sharp.  Don't miss this!! The elephants are then herded at 10:00 hrs out onto the main street and across the road to walk down the pedestrian area and down to the river - it's surreal to see this and a special treat.  Down at the river there is very little water now due to years of insufficient rain so the elephants stand in the little bit of water that there is and a powerful hose strays water over the elephants as it arcs from side to side  They bath for about 45 minutes and are herded back the way they came to the orphanage. It's not sad.  It's the best chance these elephants have got of survival - it's this, or death as many of them lost their mothers for a variety of reasons.  They are fed, watered, bathed and given medical attention as required - there are some humans in Sri Lanka who don't get these necessities so you have to view this for what it is. Enjoy it, it is quite special.

We went to Pinnawala and caught the afternoon feeding and bath. The feeding was fun to watch. Lots of school kids there. They fed the 2 babies in different areas of the arena so all could see. The bath was different as many elephants came down to bathe. There were Kunki's also and Mahouts to keep the elephants in line. It was fun watching the younger ones play and the older ones lying in the water. Also there was a big spray to wet all the elephants. There also was another smaller place where the elephants got wet and one touched my hand there. I like elephants. I appreciated coming here. The old male who everyone gets to feed, I felt a bit sad for, as he only stands in one place but gets fed. He looks to be a bit depressed to me, as he keeps his truck down in a heavy way. But, he is taken care of and fed well. The elephants look healthy.Heavy entry fee for foreigners, but it is used for the upkeep of the Orphanage, and that is fine.

We went to see the elephants bathing as part of our tour. I was surprised to see some of them chained up when walking towards the bathing area. Some of the elephants seem to eat anything off the road and rooted through boxes that had broken glass. This was sad to see. They try to get you to feed the elephants whilst they are at the lake for an extra cost. It was nice to see them being fed but the orphanage felt more like a zoo. They appeared to be well looked after though.

Those poor elephants! I hated this so much! Coming from South Africa and seeing elephants in the wild, this was shocking! Not only were a lot of the elephants chained up and looking miserable, the handlers also often poked the elephants with their hooked sticks and they shouted at them! My heart was so sore during this visit. The bathing was a little better but still some of the bigger elephants were chained up. It was awful, from start to finish. I couldn't wait to leave.

Every day between 10 and noon, the elephants are walked across the main road and down to the river to bathe.  They have keepers with them but are not chained so they have a great time.  At the end of their session a local policeman clears the way and they walk back to their very big compound, where they are free to roam.  It's not expensive to see and it's a great way to support the upkeep of these lovely animals.

Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is an orphanage, nursery and captive breeding ground for wild Asian elephants located at Pinnawala village. Pinnawala is 13 km (8.1 mi) northeast of Kegalle town in the Sabaragamuwa Province . Pinnawala has the largest herd of captive elephants in the world. (88 elephants in the 2011). They were from 3 generations and of one species. Those elephants found here are orphaned unweaned wild elephants found wandering in and near the forests of Sri Lanka are captured and taken care of and protect them here. When elephants go in search of water during droughts, elephants sometimes fall into pits and ravines. Other orphans brought here were either displaced from their wild habitat by development projects or got abandoned before weaning, diseased or wounded. Sri Lanka Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC) established the orphanage in 1975 for feeding and providing care and sanctuary to orphaned baby elephants that were found in the wild. In 1995, DWC created the Elephant Transit Home (ETH) adjoining Udawalawe National Park Previously it was located at the Wilpattu National Park, then from there many shiftings had taken place and they are in the order; the tourist complex at Bentota, the Dehiwala Zoo and finally to Pinnawala village. It is on a 25-acre (10 ha) coconut plantation adjacent to the Maha Oya River at Pinnawala village. The primary residential care area is on the east side of the Rambukkana  Kegalle road having some restaurants and refreshment stands, and management buildings including sleeping sheds and veterinary facilities. The elephant bathing and viewing area along the Maha Oya (river) is some distance from west side of the road. To find finance to run the orphanage, it was planned for the facility to attract local and foreign visitors and it is now has become a real tourist attraction. The Department of National Zoological Gardens Sri Lanka, took over the orphanage in 1978. An elephant breeding program was launched in 1982. The orphanage was established to feed, nurse and house young elephants found abandoned by their mothers. The activities involved in taking care of elephants and the daily routines are bottle feeding of elephant calves, feeding of all other elephants, and bathing in the Maha Oya (river). The elephants are taken to Maha Oya for bathing and they do engage in playing which shows that they enjoy the activity. Tourists prefer to watch them there probably taking a meal/ tea in some restaurants on the banks of Maha Oya found at the place . There are 48 mahouts (handlers) who take care of the elephants.Some reviews I have read says that mahouts have a pointed hook to hurt the elephants.How can the elephants could be controlled if they do not fear the mahout? There was another comment to the effect that they are changed and imposing cruelty.I was a witness when an elephant ran wild and ran ferociously in the Kandy Esala Perahera killing some on lookers, sometime very back; when I was a kid.Don't forget that elephants are dangerous animals and should be handled safely. Can anyone tell exactly when an elephant go wild? Those devices are done for the safety. The female and young elephants move freely as a herd during the day in an acre land. At night, the females are individually chained in stalls. Adult males do some light work such as transporting feed. They are chained and managed individually. Calves born in Pinnawala are fed by their mothers. The ones that are bottle fed are baby elephants from ETH who are kept here and bottle fed as a tourist attraction. The elephants are fed in their stalls. Only little food could be gathered from the area and therefore  large quantities of jackfruit, coconut, kitul (sugar palm), tamarind and grass, brought in brought from outside daily, are fed to the elephants.Each adult animal is given around 250 kg of green matter and about 2 kg from a food bag containing rice bran and maize daily. This elephant orphanage conducts captive breeding of some elephants in its care. The natural environment and healthy care and feeding at Pinnawala made the elephant breeding program a success. The first birth at Pinnawala was in 1984. More than twenty-three elephants were born from 1984 to 1991. In 1998 there were fourteen births at Pinnawala, eight males and six females, with one second generation birth in early 1998. Since then till early 2012, 84 more were born at Pinnawala. 12 elephants were released to temples and private owners since June, 2011. Most of the elephants at Pinnawala are healthy and once attaining adulthood, will be retained within the facility mostly since they have become dependent on supplied food. A few disabled elephants are given residential care. One tusker, Raja is blind, and one female, named Sama, lost her front right leg to a land mine (probably was laid by LTTE). Watching of the cute baby elephants is thrilling. Must see the bottle feeding of baby elephants and feeding and bathing of the big ones. It is an amazing experience. You will not see so many elephants in one place.The kids loved it, watching the elephants take milk from bottles. Mosquito repellent is a must though because of the insects if you visit erly in the morning or around 5 - 7 pm. Try to enjoy the walk around the place and see the elephants bathing and playing at Maa Oya near- by. Watching the elephants bathing and playing in the river is a once in a lifetime experience, Elephants interact with each other while bathing.It is something you will never forget. It is not like watching wild elephant herds in the jungle but definitely this is a great experience specially for kids. You can feed the elephants at specific times, get really close to them. Kids will love it. The site of elephants going to bathing must not be missed. Please do check the timings of elephant bathing before you visit. A very good place for kids to enjoy as they can feed the elephants and also take an elephant ride. The site bathing is a must see.I was there at mha Oya at 11 am and i saw elephants march back in a gigantic pesonality. Its a real magnatic experience. Not big  place, but the elephants look happy , large enclosure for the main herd, best part when 30 + ele's come down the road for a bath in the river, our quide assured us that the mahouts that were I'll treating animals have been dismissed.

I visited the orphanage in late October 2016 (time only now permitting me to record my notes and memories) and was amazed to see up close these huge animals lazily bathing in the nearby river and the new (baby) arrivals being trained by their handlers.  For a few rupees you can purchase a small bag of bananas and feed the elephants as the handlers bring them close to the spectator area.  For one who has never seen a elephant close up, you can imagine this was quite a thrill for me as their trucks came up waiting for me to stuff a banana in their mouth, their big brown eyes watching my every move.  All this was quite a thrill, but I was a bit concerned how the handlers, using what looked like a hook at the end of along pole prompted them to move this way and that... I wondered if the elephants felt pain from this?  They are so gentle.

I am not sure what to think about this place. Sure the helped some of the elephants but the have now as well young once there which are born in the orphanage. My feeling is that it is more a tourist attraction now a days. We have seen elephants with signs of hospitality and some of them where chained. I was really looking forward to this place and was sad when I left.

I had a lovely morning at the Elephant orphanage. I arrived for 9:00am in time to see the baby elephants be milk fed (9:15) and then watched the herd walk down to the lake (400m across the road) to play and bathe in the lake. It was so lovely getting up close to these beautiful creatures. They seemed to be well looked after and cared for. A couple of elephants had chains on but the majority didn't and seemed calm and content. It's quite expensive for tourists (2,500 SLR), it's obviously how they make their money. Make sure you keep hold of your ticket as you need it again when you go down to the lake.

Like a lot of other people I have ridden on an elephant in the past. At the time I didn't realise the terrible cruelty that goes into training elephants to do this. Now I just want to see elephants being kindly treated and not performing in any shows whatsoever. These gentle, intelligent animals should have the opportunity to be well cared for and protected without having to do tricks or stunts that involve cruelty. Please don't go on any elephant rides or see any shows. We visited the elephants being bathed and it was nice to see them enjoying themselves in the hot sand. Some of the bigger ones had chains on them. It was obvious that they were scared of the men with the metal pointed sticks but we didn't see any cruelty. There were a lot of elephant sanctuaries in the area and this seemed the best one. The main area where the elephants live was very busy with people. It did seem very chaotic - different people told us where to go for the toilets, we were quoted different ticket prices and a security man told us that we could not come back in once we had been to see the elephants being washed.

You can appreciate that money is needed to maintain the work of raising the elephants, and of their importance in Sri Lankan society, but the stage managing of the feeding and displays can seem a bit forced. Far better, though, is the river bathing, especially the view from the bars and balconies overlooking it, where you can sit and watch for a longer time, and see the individual personalities of each of the animals. The pots of local tea are also very good!

Thanks to our guide from Blue Lanka Tours Mr. NIhal we had a wonderful tour of the elephant orphanage. We left early from Columbo & took about 2 hours to  get here.  It gets very hot & humid ,crowded & not very pleasant  to arrive later we were told.  We arrived around 10 AM &  saw the elephants as they  arrived  after bathing in the river to the time they were fed. Walked around & took some pictures.  All in all it was nice to see the elephants.

Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is a place where wild elephants are kept. The animals are taken to the river for a bath and at around mid-morning and the larger males are taken down to the river and back around 1PM. The babies are bottle-fed later. That is about it. Do not expect some sort of show or anything like that. It’s fine by me as I just hate animals being taught to do daft things for public entertainment (and for money). You can spend 2 or three hours here if you stop to wander around the shops and have a meal. Overall I am happy that we went there to see the elephants. I got some great pictures. I would recommend this place.

The highlight for me was watching the elephants outside of the orphanage taking a bath in the nearby river.  It was nice to see them in a more natural setting.  Although the orphanage itself was good to see there were a lot of children there on day trips and so a little chaotic.

Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is about an hour's drive from Kandy. Worth a visit if you have half a day to spare. They have an entrance fee of 700 LKR for people from SAARC countries At 10:00am they take the elephant's across the road, down to the river for a bath. These are wild elephants and come a little notorious. You could take up chairs in the café on the banks of the river and watch the elephant's play. At 11:00am they walk back all the male elephants and an hour later at 12 noon they walk back all the female elephants. While walking back to the orphanage the elephant's play around and mess with the small shops on both sides of the lane, if they are in the mood. You can wait till 1:15pm and see the staff feeding the baby elephants. Maybe get to touch the elephant's and get a picture with them. Can be amusing for children. Would be great if they could arrange more interaction with the elephant's but then these are wild elephants. After reading he reviews, we had great expectations from this place.  Not too disappointed, but we were definitely expecting a lot more from here. First of all, if you are a national of SAARC countries, you will get a discount at the entrance, but make sure to keep your passport handy to avail it. The orphanage does fantastic work of rescuing wild elephants and taking care of them.  However, as a tourist attraction, this place is lacking.  There is a milk feeding session, where a care taker feeds milk to the elephants using a feeding bottle.  There is a bathing session scheduled for the elephants which the visitors can see and finally, there is a fruit feeding session.  Of the three, the only one that visitors can interact with is the fruit feeding session. This is one of the drawbacks - personal interaction with the animals are minimal. En route to the orphanage, there are many smaller establishments where you can pet and ride elephants.  For a small price, we managed to have a half hour ride on an elephant and feed the elephants at the same time.  The mahout was managing the elephant whereas another individual took our camera and snapped pictures for us.  In my opinion, this was definitely a better option than the orphanage itself. Not saying that the experience is bad, but if you give the orphanage a miss, you are really not missing out on much.

Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage has had mixed reviews and we had some doubts about this visit. The visit was built in to a schedule with a number of other attractions and so we held judgement till we arrived, deciding we can leave if we didn't like what we saw being animal lovers. I'd like to say we were pleasantly surprised. Start your visit by looking at the elephants in a open enclosure just roaming and feeding. They are watched over by their handlers. Beware of the signs around you, confirming these are wild animals and not to be approached. It's wonderful watching them interact naturally. Move on to watching the babies being bottle fed which is both controlled and dignified. The highlight is then a walk to the river to wait for the elephants to walk down past a row shops, May be 25 or 30 of them. Yes some, maybe 4 or 5 have chains on the rear legs and front legs which as animal lovers seems barbaric and unnatural buts lets put this in to context, it's only the same as we place a lead on our dogs to walk them. Only difference is, a lead on a one ton elephant is going to be much use. Hence chains.  I'd recommend Pinnawala but go with an open mind.

On our way to Kandy we made a stop at Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. It was our second visit in the Elephant Orphanage and I'm quite certain we'll go there every time we visit Kandy, as this is breathtaking and amazing every time we get there. It is so refreshing to see elephants being treated nice and getting to live on their own premises instead of these trained elephants in circus or at hotels that are only there to amuse tourists and who live a horrible existence being chained all day and being tortured into doing horrible tricks just for the amusement of tourists. This is a great venue to visit in Sri Lanka. At particular times, you can watch the elephants at the nearby river. In the late afternoon, many elephants congregate here supervised by the excellent staff at the venue. This is fascinating to watch, not least because the elephants clearly enjoy the water sprays cooling their heated bodies. Only one criticism I have: the ticket prices vary according to your nationality. Local countries are charged considerably less than Europeans. Perhaps they should justify this difference in prices, otherwise, it might seem discriminatory.

The highlight is the milk feeding of the babies. After that the elephants cross to the water, and you can find a shady spot for lunch and watch them bathe and play close below. Nearby is a place you can actually ride an elephant, which might not be for everyone, but they really seem to care for their elephants there as well, and treat them humanely, even lovingly.

What a wonderful experience!   The perfect time to arrive is late morning.  Upon arriving and paying the entrance fee, we went into the sanctuary and to the left, where we saw several smaller elephants who had been socialized to people prior to being rescued.  There were a few employees selling very inexpensive plates of freshly cut fruit that we could purchase to feed the elephants -- about $1 USD.  It makes for a good photo op, to be popping a banana into the mouth of an elephant, and have a friend snap a photo.   It was an unforgettable moment.  (There were other elephants who had not been socialized to people, and we were kept far away from them.) Next, the handlers started to lead all the elephants out of the sanctuary and down the street to a river where the elephants could splash around or play in the stream of the water cannon.  The street that the elephants walk down is lined with touristy shops selling mainly (you guessed it!) elephant-related souvenirs.  It is completely shut down to all traffic except the elephants while they make their treks down to the river and back, but otherwise, you are free to shop and enjoy the local offerings. While the elephants are in the river, you may choose to eat at a restaurant overlooking the elephants, wait for the elephants to be walked back to the sanctuary, or depart for the shops.  We watched the elephants for about 30 minutes, then decided to leave because it was very hot. On the way back up the street to our car, we stopped to purchase fresh coconut water from a merchant who cut off the top of the coconut and stuck in a straw for us.  The potassium-packed coconut water helped to hydrate us for our leisurely visit to the Poo Paper Shop, where they make and sell paper products made of elephant dung.   The store offers a free and brief tour during which the process is explained in sufficient detail. I visited in December 2016, and the weather was very hot for me -- a Chicagoan.  I was grateful that I had brought an umbrella and bottle of water.  A few of the shops have air conditioning (including the Poo Paper store), and many have fans, but the temperature was almost unbearable for me after 1:30 p.m.  I was happy to be whisked away in an air conditioned car, but am grateful to have met these majestic creatures.

However, some are chained as they are "naughty" plus the keepers shout and prod them with large wooden sticks just like a zoo. This was a tough pill to swallow. I would like to see more love , fun and interaction with the animals rather than what I seen.

First of all I would like to say that this is one of the most inspirational and most eye opening places I have ever been to, all so it can be a sad place. The reason for this is that these Elephants have been either injured by Mines, which have been left over from the past troubles or neglected by their mothers. But on a positive note they're looked after to the highest standards, you can feed the little Elephants with a very large bottle full of milk, or you can go down to the river and enjoy the spectacular view of them all being washed by their keepers, whilst enjoying a cold beer or Tea at the cafe which over looks the River. Firstly can I correct a previous review, you can not go and watch the elephants in the river without buying a full ticket, all roads down to the river have park attendants at the top demanding to see your ticket, you are also unable to access the shops or restaurants along these roads without a ticket. There is no information about what the park is trying to achieve, depending on what time you go very few elephants will be visible and those that we saw in the park were mostly chained. We watched the elephants in the river and they did not all look happy, some were chained in the river and trying to get out but we're unable to. This was worse than visiting a zoo.

We had heard a lot of good things about this orphanage so decided to stop off. The entrance fee is pretty expensive (around £40 for the 2 of us). We arrived just in time to see the elephants walking back from bathing. Lots of tourists all crammed into the sides whilst the elephants and instructors walk through the middle of the street. Amazing to see the elephants in such a close proximity (some come right up to you) but a couple of them were chained with their back legs tied. Also on occasion the instructor would use the elephant hook which you can see break the skin of the elephant to make it obey and walk. We found that part rather painful to watch (even if maybe necessary). Our driver explained that these elephants are wild and some of them misbehave (hence the chains) but because there is no information provided by the instructors or orphanage it is very unclear for tourists. Should definitely be information given about the elephants and how they are looked after. Also the instructors encourage tourists for bribes. We watched tourists "secretly" going down to the water to feed the elephant and for a picture. Worst part of this is the elephant didn't want food so was beaten to take it and then when it wouldn't another had to be brought over. Makes you wonder if the instructors have the elephants best interests at heart... Best part was watching another herd of elephants playing in the river for their bathing. You can see them in their natural environment looking happy! Great to see elephants so close up but definitely need to have information provided to you for a well-rounded experience. Entrance fee is expensive which is ok if money goes to looking after the elephants but the whole experience occasionally makes you wonder...

However, tacked on, in usual fashion, to this experience are all the usual grotty cons of sideshow ally. A great visit for the whole family, be sure on your timing to see the Elephants when they're in the river. It's a nail biter of a ride from Colombo, don't do it with a hangover.

I had visited this place with my family. They had different schedules of elephant's daily activity. We saw elephant feeding themselves playing in mud and also saw baby elephant being fed by the care takers. We saw elephants taking bath playing in water and also the panic after a bull elephant made his way to his shelter. Altogether a nice experience for elephant lovers.

Too few elephants and the bathing at the river was equally disappointing, Basically, the elephants were walked and guided to the river for them to get soaked in the waters and mahoots sprayed water on their backs to keep them comfortable. Tourists were made to sit at tables at the restaurants overlooking the river, and there was literally nothing else to do. I thought it was not as fascinating as the tour brochure made it out to be Would give this a miss.

Sight of a heard of elephants just walking few feet away from away and into the river is something you will remember forever. Its just amazing! Like everywhere else in Sri Lanka, this place also checks for passports before issuing tickets, so without a SAARC passport don't argue that you should be issued the discounted tickets that is only for SAARC countries. You will make a fool out of yourself in front of everybody, we watched quite a few people do that and every single one failed miserably. Tip: Before planning your trip, check out their website for the schedule of activities! Elephant bathing happens in the river which is OUTSIDE the orphanage gate, which means you need to see everything inside before leaving the gate to go see the elephants getting in the water. You can't re-enter once you leave the camp. We had to show tickets to get to the river but not sure if it is required if you are not planning to enter the orphanage and just want to see elephants in the water. There are a bunch of restaurants by the river to have lunch and watch elephants bath so at the check port you could tell you are going to restaurant and not need a ticket?? you have to find out yourself. Elephant bathing starts at 2pm, we were at the river by 1.15 and there were few elephants already in the water. If you pay few hundered or a thousand sri lankan rupees to the guys, they will let you touch the elephant, bathe them and take pictures with them.  Not sure about safety and legality, you will have to figure out for yourself. When the elephants are walking down to the river they ask for food from the visitors who are standing at the edge of the road, and we saw few tourist giving bananas.

We arrived mid afternoon & wondered whether the $25 entrance fee was worth it. We were directed to walk down past many shops to the river because it was bathing time. About 40+ elephants were having a great time in the river & we were glad to have arrived when we did. Feeding is OK but all the elephants are chained up so not as interesting.

We went there in June 2016. It was a really good experience. I believe there is a good cause behind this orphanage. Also it is a rare elephants gathering to have all this number of elephants, and you get to see them eating, swimming and just wandering off. And you got to be really close to this magical creatures and touch them and feel them. However it is so commercial, you can do anything provided that you pay the keepers.  I think some of the keepers are so kind of cruel. Overall i would recommend to go, they have a good system. And i hope the system gets better.
