Not a natural habitat for elephants but incredible to get close to these stunning animals.  Beware - we were offered photo taking by the official guides and then "asked" for a ridiculously exorbitant "donation".  Gave them a tenth of the request and then was surrounded by several guides complaining.  Luckily I'm rarely intimidated by such behavior but others might well be bullied into such extortion.  Very out of step with the manner and spirit of almost everybody else on this wonderful island.  More positively the view of the elephants bathing and feeding in the river was amazing with a beautiful backdrop of the mountains - a highlight of our holiday.

I was shocked and saddened when we arrived to see the elephants in the river ( they have 2 hour bathing slots twice a day) that they were being herded around by handlers with elephant hooks, and even worse than that, that several elephants (babies and adults) were shackled in the river (some by one leg, some by two). It was so distressing to see a baby rocking left and right as she couldn't move and be with the rest of the herd. When I asked other tourists they said she was ''wild'' and the handlers were ''training'' her so as not to be a danger to tourists. Honestly- it's wonderful to save and/or rehome elephants back into the wild and several places do this in Sri Lanka. But this orphanage doesn't rehome elephants. Many elephants seemed to have chains round their necks and/or legs.The handlers rode on many. I felt completely uncomfortable witnessing this. If the 'orphanage' could change its practices and allow the elephants to roam freely all the time (like in a safari park), it might make less money from tourists getting 'up close' but I'm 100% sure the elephants would have a better quality of life. Guides told me that 60% of tourists say that to them.  There are other projects eg Elephant Freedom Project that guides take many tourists to locally instead. Animal welfare has moved on since the government started this operation many years ago and hopefully feedback from tourists will encourage them to change their animal welfare practices and allow the elephants to always roam free.  Until then- not recommended.

After Reading all the reviews here I was not expecting must, but it turned out to be a really great experience. The Elephant seemed to be happy here, and they had freedom to bath and Walk alone on a Big natual area. The Elephant bathing is def. Worth to see, especially if you bring children. There was no information given, no explanation of what goes on there, but the primary objective is to watch these magnificent creatures, and that is what this opportunity provides. Very entertaining.

My first time ever in Sri Lanka and an overnight flight from Dubai which arrived in  Colombo at 8.30 a.m. I have organised a car with a driver and Lal was awaiting my arrival. We set off immediately for the famed Elephant Orphanage which was recommended by my wife and several friends who went there in earlier years. A most enjoyable visit and well worth the Lankan Rupees 2500/- one pays as a foreigner. We watched elephants being fed, others being rounded up for their trip to the river for a bath, others returning all wet from the river back to the Park, etc. Plenty of tourists around. We spent close to an hour here before adjourning to a nearby Hotel for drinks and lunch.

The place is quite crowded with tourists and very expensive. Inside the people will charge you a high price for a tiny basket of fruits and they will ask for a tip for all the extras (fotos with the elefants or extra time etc) -even though we didnt pay. i felt like the elephants were treated fine in general, they range inside the park and the water freely only some few are chained -i am not sure why. if you wanna go there from kandy be aware that is very far (1 1/2 hours by cab) and you need to get there in time if you dont want to miss the feedings. bring some of your own bananas if you can. i think its not worth the time and the money. if you really want to spend some time with the elephants the elephant freedom project seems to be the place to go.

Pinnawala is an elephant orphanage located about 2 hours east of Colombo. Bottom line is they have a good number of elephants involved in different activities. If it is watching elephants walk around, baby elephants drinking milk, or feeding bananas to elephants then go to the main site entrance for non Sri lankis is 2500 rouppi. The other more interesting option which I opted for is to ride those elephants. Price depends on trip time, I paid 5000 rouppi for 30 minutes. Until elephants arrive, a herbatologist guy takes on a free tour to his garden where he grows all sort of medicinal plants, he did end up convincing me to buy several products. Elephant ride involves him going into water, spraying you with water upon request, and going out to mainland and then back to base. Experience quite authentic as no chair is placed on elephants' back but rather a person just mounts him directly and holds on to a rope around his neck. You will have an option to feed the animal bananas at the end of the ride for a fee. Finally, don't miss on going to the elephant dung museum where they produce paper from elephant's poo. Very interesting, as they explain to you the whole process, and you then proceed to a gift shop to buy some elephant dung paper or related products if you wish. An absolute must if you have the interest and courage. Don't do if afraid of heights, too old, or pregnant!

I was a little unsure about visiting Pinnawala elephant orphanage but enjoyed the trip. I love elephants and have seen plenty in various countries. I felt the animals were being well cared for and any that were chained was because they were dangerous. We are not talking about miniature dogs here so care needs to be taken that no one is injured.

Fantastic trip to the elephant orphanage. Helped by a friendly 'guide' who convinced us to have a 'private' elephant riding experience. This was clearly not part of the orphanage, and I was absolutely sceptical. But it was probably one of the best experiences of our trip for our teenage children. It helped that my partner speaks singhalese so we were able to negotiate a good price.

Very nice place to visit with kids. However it is not very great. The elephant feeding ( milk and fruit) is something unique and the herd of elephants make a rare sight to watch , any photographer's delight! It was annoying having to again cross the road and walk up a busy street to watch the elephants bathe. The area was crowded and there wasnt much place to sit or even stand. Overall I didnt find that it was worth to travel all the way to visit this place, We happened to be staying near its vicinity and thus enjoyed the experience. I wouldnt recommend travelling great distances to see this.

There are 2 main attractions here- elephants taking bath and elephant feeding. There are specific timings for each of these. there is an entry ticket - SAARC country visitors, ensure you take your passports along since the rates are substantially lesser (around LKR 700, as against LKR 2500 or so). Elephants take bath in a river and one can see them from close view. and in a nearby enclosure, elephants are fed from feeding bottles. When we went, an elephant was desperately trying to bring down the branch of a tree. It was trying again and again, standing against the tree, against the barrier. and there was another one which was doing a small dance. On the whole, a very good experience. There is a hotel near the entrance and we could get some Indian veg. food (though expensive).

There seems to be lots of politically motivated negative comments about this place.  I have been twice the first time in 2011 and the second in 2017.  I enjoyed it on both occasions.  The elephants are relaxed around their keepers and their keepers are relaxed around them.  I do not believe this would be the case if the elephants were being treated cruelly or were unhappy with their lives. Elephants are domesticated throughout a large part of Asia and even the wild live in close proximity with people.  This has been the case ever since there were elephants and people in Asia.  Sri Lankan people and Sri Lankan elephants have been dealing with each other for a very long time - is it possible that they are better informed than a few tourists?

This place is good for family visits carrying children along, so one can enjoy both orphanage camp and zoo. Mostly they brings elephants for bathing purpose. Its a good scenic view. Elephant dung related and other products were sold as part of promotion activities. Near by herbal farms are there but its bit expensive. if one want originality then can go for it. I will suggest to make it half day if travelling from Colombo. one can check all the things in 1-2 hours.

This is not a riding experience. You get to see elephants in numbers and the best bit is watching them in the river area. You can sit in a bar overlooking the river and enjoy. You can touch and play with them but will have to pay the handlers. I enjoyed it more than I expected to.

We were expecting to see happy elephants in happy environment, but after seeing how one elephant was chained in a spot so people could touch him and take pictures for money, we left the place with disgust. Other elephants were beaten with sticks by the staff so tourists could take pictures close to elephants for once again some extra tip. We did stay for bottle feeding, but it was more of a show than genuine care for the babies. Overall, it's a sad place to be.

Visited the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage with my colleague on our day off from a conference in Colombo. We had to leave Colombo at about 6.30 am as the traffic in and out of Colombo is crowded and slow moving. Tickets are inexpensive and quick to buy as there were no queues or line when we arrived and it was just starting to heat up. There are a number of areas to see and interact with these beautiful creatures. There's a covered pavilion to which the attendants bring the babies to feed, a raised platform from which to feed the older elephants who are experts at tugging at the heart strings and rapidly disposing of a small basket of fruit which can be purchased cheaply, and another open area which the older animals roam freely but you have to keep your distance. I has mixed feelings about visiting this place but on the face of it from what we saw, this appears to be a well managed place where the elephants are looked after properly and the configuration of the different areas allows relatively large numbers of people to move freely and observe and take photographs if they want without being boxed in or feeling crowded. Which is probably a good thing as it was a stonking hot and humid day and the sun certainly has some extreme UV in it so preparations for this visit should include a good breakfast-lunch, litres of water, sun hat (not the ridiculous baseball caps which don't cover your ears or neck) and small snacks like bananas or other fruit to keep you comfortable. After this we travelled to a hotel nearby and had a pot of tea - mad as Englishmen in the noon-day sun I know - and sat on a huge outdoor verandah and marvelled at scores of the larger elephants in the river. It was a day in my life I will always remember and treasure.

This elephant orphanage is dedicated to the majestic creatures. It is a sight to watch them cross the road to go for a bath in the river. Though they are not tamed, the staff advise tourists not to go anywhere closer to them unless they are around. Children absolutely love being here.

Overpriced and crowded. It is as far from the meaning of the word "sanctuary" as you can possibly imagine. Tired, exhausted animals. A circus for tourists. I am told the place was  completely different 15 years ago. It has changed beyond recognition.

Park is open for visitors at 8 30am and closes at 6 30 daily. Don't miss below events : Herd leaving to the river is from 10 am to 12 pm and again from 2 pm to 4 pm. Timings for Bottle feeding for baby elephants are 9 15 am and 1 15pm and some selected lucky visitors will get the chance to bottle feed baby elephants too! Gather around that area in advance as the place can get so crowded. A baby elephant usually in the wild drinks milk from his mother up to 5 years so at the orphanage those babies are fed for the same period. Here are some tips * you don't find a decent place to buy any refreshments inside and the stuff you get in a small place are extremely costly. * parking is a real hassle and sometimes you have to manage with roadside parking , still some guys will come and charge you 100 rupees with a ticket * members of SAARC countries get a discount of 50% ,just check with the ticket counter * you will notice that there are some other conservation projects similar to this one before reaching the actual place , might be bogus projects

Fantastic day out seeing the baby elephant's been given their milk and then down to the river to watch them swim. Tip of the day set off to the river and get a table at the elephant hotel on the balcony with a coffee and sandwiches as this was the best view of the swim as they walk straight past you in to the river that's then u see you.

You can see the small elephants being fed milk but again it is very staged, and similar to feeding time at the zoo! I would like to see more of a natural environment here which is not present now. Also we were pestered a lot for money by employees if we wanted to get closer to the Elephants or give them fruit. We had already paid a decent amount to get onto the Park as you have to pay for a 'tourist pass'! It was OK but not brilliant, and if you have a couple of hours to burn give it a look - you may be disappointed if you build your expectations up too much.

We arrived just on time to watch the elephants marching from the larc towars the river. Be there before 10am. Walk through the village to the river when the elephants are taken for some R&R it's fascinating to see them in a natural environment but be cautious of people wanting to give you food for the elephants as they make their way through the village as once you have fed them they explain that the food was for sale and then insist on money. Having visited this place today I feel disappointed with what I saw.Firstly it is expensive at R2500 and no one to explain anything to us about the elephants or the orphange.It is just one big tourist trap.Watching the elephants been fed their bottles was nice and also the bathing in the river was lovely and made some good photo opportunities.However the staff are just out to rip you off,offering to take photos with your camera  then wanting R2000. Quite over-priced at R2500 per adult, considering you watch the elephants have a bath...and that's it. Feeding and touching the elephants is banned, but watch out for staff who will tout for money by offering these services, take your money and then you will get caught and removed by the security guards! Perhaps to ensure the safety of the tourists who get too close... We stopped here for 45mins, but it could have easily been 10mins, is it worth the money?

Our last visit was some years ago and much has changed since then. We visited at midday on a weekday so there wasn't a crowd and no queuing at the ticket counter. As with most attractions there are separate rates for locals and tourists . Elephants are taken in groups to bathe and have a drink of water(several litres) down to the river. You can spend as much time watching these gentle giants interact with each other and enjoy their water play and if you wish feed bananas which they pick from your hand. Feeding time is organised and seating areas set up so everyone gets a good opportunity to the bottle feeding which of course lasts only a couple of minutes by elephant standard (appetite)! Recommend picking your time and day to avoid crowds so you can enjoy the experience. We have been here several times over the years and never get enough of it!

If you have been to Asia before this trip you KNOW this is NOT a good place. When I was in Habarana I saw a lot of chained elephants. I asked our guest house host about it and he said they are auctioned off from the orphanage and that it most certainly is not a good place. They do not rehabilitate the elephants back into h wilds they sell them! Awful

This was fun to see all the elephants in one place however its a big tourist trap, walking through a street of shops to see the elephants at the water. Some of the elephants were in chains. I would say skip this stop and  go to the national park. if you can't make it to the park this is nice.

This is a great place to get up close with the elephants. They do a good job taking care of them but it also is a bit of a show. Many of the elephants in this herd have been bred in captivity but orphaned elephants are still taken in. The whole place has become a bit commercial but it was still wonderful to be able to get so close to these majestic animals and see them bathing in the river. The elephants have almost learnt how to pose for the camera! Well worth a visit.

Just marvelous to see how the orphaned elephants are being tended for. The surroundings are well maintained,  clean and relatively tidy. So glad we made the effort to revisit. Pinnawala. Nothing changes except, like us, the elephants get older.some have sadly died but another generation bring joy to watch. We visited this place on our way from Colombo Airport to Kandy. We were there luckily at 12 pm and got to the the wonderful parade of around 60 elephants walking to riverside for a bath from their stables. We saw the elephants bathing and it was super fun to watch them bath. Some of the elephants were dancing and enjoying their time in water. It was a pleasure. We didnt get to see the place of stay or feed them as we were in a hurry to leave.

When I went to see elephants in Sri Lanka, I was expecting to see a more natural environment as it was a so called "Orphanage", which would teach us about elephants and provide an insight into where they were from.  Instead, we arrived and we saw some in chains and rangers with spiked sticks, along with some that were more able to roam around. Along with the fact you are hassled by the rangers for "Tips", the bottle feeding reminded me of the scene in Taken, where the girl was being auctioned off - a ring of oblivious tourists taking in the "spectacle".  It enraged me. This one certainly wasn't the worst out there, however, it was pretty upsetting to see some of these beautiful and intelligent creatures sad. If you go to Sri Lanka, I WOULDN'T recommend the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage.  See them in the National Parks instead.  🙏🏽🐘

Its a fun place to visit. Baby elephants are cute and the feeding session is quite fun. You can get up close and feed them straight into their mouths or leave it on their trunks. Funny when they exhale and it hits you. The bathing sessions are also quite something to watch. We saw elephants roll in the water. There was also a time when the elephant was tapping on my wife's shoulder when we were taking a pic. All fun and friendly. Do plan to reach in time as all this lasts for a limited period of time only. But it's just amazing to see 50 elephants in one place, in the open, going about being themselves.

My son was super excited about seeing the elephants in their natural setting. He enjoyed feeding them he actually did it three times. The people who worked there gave us background on the orphanage and made it possible for us to take everlasting pictures. All of the pictures that I have posted on facebook has made my friends all over the world interested in visiting this country.

We visited this place on our way from Colombo to Kandy. We reached there pretty early in the morning and i think that worked really well. We were able to see pretty much everything very easily. We saw some young elephants, we saw them drinking milk. We also saw them taking bath which was fun. I would recommend going early morning so you can see everything in a short time. Also on the way dont forget to have the King Coconut on the way, MUST HAVE.

The place is magnificent. You can get close enough to touch and take photos with elephants. The fellow who took us around was very helpful. The elephants here seemed genuinely happy, especially when they are led down to a nearby river to bathe. The entrance fee includes one time entrance into the park as well as the bathing trip. We were quite excited to go for an elephant ride.... an what an experience it was. It will remain in our memories.

This place is magnificent. You can get close enough to touch and take photos with elephants on a plane where they roam as far as the eye can see. Handlers will vie for your attention, quoting high fees to take photos with an elephant. There is no set price. You are welcome to tip a handler if you would like, but it is not mandatory. Some handlers might keep trying to extract a tip, but it is far from necessary. Just remain assertive. The elephants here seem genuinely happy, especially when they are led down to a nearby river to bathe. The entrance fee includes one time entrance into the park as well as the bathing trip.

they basically torture the elephants that they can make money with tourism. the elephants were all chained or in very small cages. There were only without chains that Tourist can touch them or make Pictures. the guards hit them reguarly with their sticks/hooks. The elephants are very afraid of the guards. I left this place crying. the first time I cried during any holidays.

We really enjoyed coming here to watch the elephants being fed. The first one had a prosthetic leg, but he didn't let that stop him from munching on all of the trees. I've been working for 3 weeks as a volunteer at the elephant orphanage and can report that the animals are treated good there. First, I felt like in a zoo but after going with the veterinaries and speaking with the director, who is new and really dedicated, I can give the all-clear about it. Especially, as I've been traveling other Asian countries and saw how elephants are treated there, I can say that the elephants in Pinnawala are doing well. Further, they are working on making more land accessible for the elephants and improving the current enclosures. === About the chains === In general, the elephants are untamed. This means that, though they are friendly animals most of the time, they are potentially dangerous and have to be chained when not under supervision of a mahout. At the beginning, this seems cruel but when you have been standing next to these giants when they started to fight out of nothing while moving WITHOUT chains on the open street, you suddenly understand very well. A rampaging elephant is not only dangerous, it is potentially lethal. But while all of them are chained in the evening in order to prevent them from causing damage, fighting and vanishing, they get enough food to be busy with that until the next morning. Beside this general case, there are a lot of other reasons for chains. Adult male elephants have a so called musth period once a year where they have a significantly increased testosterone level and become quite aggressive. This is not related to mating and they also attack females during this time. This phase can last for weeks to months and the usual treatment for these elephants is to enchain them. However, the orphanage is currently building a special area for musth bulls where they can stay without chains. There can also be medical reasons. Some of the elephants got injuries on their legs from falling into a pit or having an accident in the river while bathing. One special case for keeping a baby elephant and his mother in a cage for a long time was that the mother accidentally stuck a branch into her babies eye, causing it to be nearly blind now. Because the wounded eye could catch some infection when going outside, they had to be kept in the cage. Another important thing was that the mother seemed to be really stressed everythime we saw her while cleaning the stables in the morning. She was just waving her head around really strong and apart from that not moving at all. Of course, one thinks this is because she is caged. But as we learned later from the doctors, the true reason was a social one – the herd was outside. When we were there as the herd returned in the afternoon, she suddenly did not show any signs of stress anymore, though she was still in the same cage.

This is a government endorsed and funded elephant orphanage and I was horrified to visit and see that it is more focussed on meeting the egotistical needs of humans/tourists than the elephant welfare needs. On arrival we went to the river to observe the elephants being washed and having some time in the water with their herd. There are 3 large hotels built on this area and restaurants overlooking the river - music was blaring from the restaurants. We watched tourists feeding the elephants and saw elephants picking up plastic water bottles and trying to eat them. There were many touts there selling bananas  to encourage the tourists to feed the elephants. All of this in spite of the rules on the signs and on our tickets requesting that tourists keep away from the elephants, do not feed them, and do not play loud music around them! Then to make it worse, when we returned to the orphanage across the road, staff were encouraging tourists to touch the elephants and have photos taken with them for a monetary tip. I understand that incomes are low for staff, but these practices are totally without respect for the elephants' welfare and autonomy. If you care about the elephants then this is not the place for you. However, perhaps the more we raise awareness of these contradictions and transgressions of elephant welfare, then perhaps some of these bad practices will cease and elephants may come first. I will not return and in future I will seek more ethical wildlife experiences.

We have mixed feelings about this place. Our Sri Lankan family members recommended this place to see elephants before we left Sri Lanka (having missed them in the wild at Yala). They accompanied us on the day, and enjoyed the experience a lot more than we did. Some of the elephants are chained and look distressed, the mahouts were somewhat aggressive and appeared more focused on making a quick buck from the tourists rather than the welfare of the elephants. I appreciate they are paid little and need to earn where they can. But this place is sold as an orphanage, to me that should be a place of conservation, not an elephant amusement ride? When asking our family about this, they reminded us that the concentration of elephants in Sri Lanka is problematic and these elephants have been relocated to avoid them disrupting farms and villages and being potentially killed. They also reminded us that elephants have often been used as working animals in Sri Lanka throughout history, and this is far better treatment than  working elephants receive. Again, this I can appreciate. Not all elephants are chained, once tame enough, some are allowed to roam free (to an extent, before an angry mahout herds them up). But many of the tame elephants are young - have these been bred in captivity? Does that not defeat the point of an orphanage? Many questions, many mixed feelings, but overall we felt uncomfortable here and didn't stay long. I just hope the expensive cost of 2500rp per person goes back into caring for these beautiful creatures.

What a wonderful place! The Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is such a joy to experience with over 80 wild elephants who have been saved by this organization. These elephants were either abused by man, or abandoned by their herd, but are now able to live out their lives in a safe and lovely environment. Yes, they get pampered a bit by their minders and the tourists, but they remain wild and happy. Bottle feeding for the youngsters begins at 9:15am and later in the afternoon, and you don't want to miss this! Seeing a young elephant down a liter bottle of milk in 5 seconds is pretty cool! After that, some of the big boys and girls gather to be fed fruits by the tourists. Mind you, a small basket of fruit will set you back a few dollars, but when they open their mouth for you to put in the pineapple slice and look you in the eye with gratitude, you feel blessed and good inside. Heck, you just made a new friend! Yes, their tongues are a bit slimey, but it's a good slimey. They will even welcome your touch and love smiles. Around 10 o'clock the herd of larger elephants are taken out the gate, down the street to the waterfall where you can follow and watch the bathe or get scrubbed by their minders. It's quite a sight seeing about 80 elephants hanging out in the river cooling themselves or mooching food from the tourists. Watch out, these are after all wild elephants, but pretty friendly ones, so have a fair bit of snacks on hand for them, and you will have made lots of "friends" on your trip! The orphanage is about halfway between Colombo and Kandy in Sri Lanka, and costs about $17 to get in for adults, but know that your money is supporting a great cause. The 80+ elephants will thank you.

On our tour of Sri Lanka, one of the destinations to visit whilst in Kandy was the Pinnewala Elephant Orphanage. Having read many of the reviews, some very negative, some positive, our group decided to go and see for ourselves. I have been lucky enough to see wild elephants both in Sri Lanka and Africa and of course that is the best way to observe these magnificent animals (or any animals), so I went to the reserve keeping in mind these were captive and therefore likely to exhibit different behaviours. I wanted to see what their conditions were like, whether they displayed any ill health/ injuries and what the overall "mission" of the centre was. All in all, I left feeling relatively positive about the place, although a few displayed signs of stress the vast majority seemed, to me, happy. Their habitat was generally good and they had a good space to wonder around when in the river and back at their enclosure. There were a few younger elephants that were in very small pens but we were assured they were there to be fed and then would be released, these were displaying some signs of stress though. They did not seem overly fearful of the trainers which suggested they were not ill treated by them.  I did not see any elephants with "open wounds" as described in some reports, however some did have scarring from the chains, which were used for both training and controlling purposes. The biggest disappointment for me really was that no one explained what the orphanages' mission was and when we asked questions we received inconsistent answers. Were they being rehabilitated? Maybe. Was our entrance fee going to conservation? Maybe. Was it non profit or commercial. I don't know. For this to be a far more positive experience I would say they need to improve this aspect of the centre. Overall I am glad I went. I would not either recommend or dissuade people to go to the orphanage, however a part of me feels it is important to go and see these things for yourselves rather than just taking other people's views.

We went to the orphanage feeling reserved. We went with a national guide who having read the recent reviews of the orphanage obviously gave us a lot more information than is made obvious at the orphanage, but also stopped us from being pestered as we weren't once asked for any money after entry from the keepers. On entering the baby elephant feeding was sweet, the babies had a good appetite and were beautiful. The elephants roam in herds of around 30, there are also a few elephants that are disabled who are also kept separate but can be seen from the main park so could look to unknowing guests as kept elephants. Having seen the wild elephants none of these were underweight in comparison. Some males especially in mating season can be made separate as their behaviour becomes volatile however the males left in the herd are chained around the ankles just in case so when they are taken to the river the can be chained to the ground. The chains are long and don't restrict their movement- they carry their own chains over their neck when they are on the move. Over all as reserved elephant lovers we were worried - it's not an orphanage as they breed the elephants there and when they are released this isn't into the wild but to "elephant back riding schemes" (only 6 in its history I think) where other people can profit from the elephants and the expense of their feeding is passed on. The funds raised does mean that any elephant who is orphaned has a place to go... The elephants seemed relaxed and happy. In comparison to the zoos we are used to seeing the elephants had access to a lovely bathing area and seemed happy and mischievous was enough for us. The sticks the the keepers had had bulbs on the end when you looked closely rather than spikes, the keepers held them but only used them as a training tool. They seemed to to love the animals and elephant cleaning time was magical. Over all a lovely experience if you're not too worried about the term "orphanage". Not sure if we saw the same elephants as the others who have written reviews but we were pleasantly suprised and our experience was a fun one.

Also number of shops, a museum, etc for visitors to look for products made of elephant dung, etc, Next event inside the orphanage is feeding of fruits to elephants and feeding of baby elephants with milk bottles which can be viewed in close quarters with ample protection for the visitors. Most of the elephants are quite calm and pose no problem to the visitors. The restless ones are kept separately in an enclosure chained to anchors to prevent them creating any disturbances at the premises. The events are covered by tickets which can be bought at the entrance and are quite reasonable. All the evnts can be covered in a fes hours so if you catch the early cycle they will be over by early afternoon. We went on our second day in Sri Lanka. In hindsight I wish we hadn't as there are many opportunities to see elephants up close in the wild in Sri Lanka. I'd recommend Minneriya National Park for getting really close. Yes you can get close to the elephants in Pinnewala but it is much more of a zoo than a sanctuary. Elephants are made to hold poses for photos for tips as well.

Best part is the elephants bathing in the river, must have been at least 50 elephants!! We went between 10 and 12, was fairly busy. Not sure about the feeding and milking within the orphanage but would recommend seeing them by the river!

The Elephant orphanage has been given some bad reviews in travel guides for cruelty, however as an animal lover I found no evidence of this. The elephants seemed happy and enjoying their trips to the river and feeding times. Yes they may not have been reintroduced into the wild, however with dwindling habitat this may not be an altogether bad thing. Some of the elephants do wear light chains on their ankles, but it seemed to be only the adolescents who were quite rambunctious and obviously still in training. The mahouts carried training sticks, but we saw no evidence of misuse and I'd certainly carry one if I was training a couple of tons of wild beast!! Most of the elephants walked freely around the park and down to river for the their baths and they seemed very content.

We visited here while on our honeymoon. A great experience. Seeing the elephants baths was fascinating. What they do for the elephants here is good and we understand why they need to have chains on some of them. Just put into perspective how small a chain is in relation to a large elephant, it isn't causing any injury. The smaller elephants are very playful and it's so cute to watch. We weren't pestered for tips which was a bonus.

First, a disclaimer: if you strongly believe animals have same right as humans - don't go to the orphanage. It's more a prison than an orphanage. If you choose to go there - make sure you are there in the bathing time, as this is the nice part of the visit, where the elephants are kind of loose (they are still surrounded by guards, but at least they are not chained).

Time just passed so quickly, dont bother with the elephant ride, waste of time, washing the elephants was well worth doing and an experience I shall never forget, amazing facts and figures, but they require funding, so a good tip is reccommended

Was worried after reading reviews about cruelty to the elephants and constant harassment from the mahoots, we knew before we arrived if we wanted to do get really close to the elephants we would have to tip, however if you said no you were left alone, the experience of seeing 60 to 70 elephants, most NOT in chains, running down the high street was something we will never forget., we saw no cruelty and those in chains were new elephants to the sanctuary

We have really enjoyed our visit to the orphenage. First, you have to know that there is specific timing for milk feeding baby elephants. However, the adult elephants, you can feed them fruits at any time under the supervision of their professional trainers. You can also ride the elephants. However, what I really enjoyed is the magnificent view from their open elephant "arena" (don't know what else to call it): It was raining today, there were fog on distant mountains (2 of them) and the green was beautiful.

While it is nice to see the elephants cross the road in the town and head to the river to bathe, it is heartbreaking to see them inside the so-called orphanage chained in small stables waiting for the tree leaves to be delivered so they can eat. The more disappointing part is that everything around the river and the elephants is about money, the staff there are focused on earning extra money and they mistreat the elephants and aim at them with sharp spears. I would not recommend donating to such places, the elephants must be returned into the wild.

This is basically an elephant zoo. But man, what a zoo. Watching the babies being bottle fed is the big draw(9am). Also the chance to hand feed a basket of fruit (250 Rs, about $2) to an elephant. Don't go with romantic 'born free' notions. This is a highly specialised zoo, where the animals are not tamed but do interact a little. Sort of how steve irwin would've done it, but with less razzledazzle!

We arrived at late morning. It was our first day in Sri Lanka at we had a great time. The elephants were very sweet and we enjoyed bathing and feeding them with the local workers of the orphanage. One of the most exciting stuff on our Trip was visiting Elephant Orphanage. To see a large sanctuary to keep Elephants is very inspiring. It is said to be 25 acre coconut property. Operational since 1975; are taking care orphaned or injured Elephants. Areas are properly marked. There is a place where you can sit and elephants are just at the back. Then there are areas marked where wild elephants are kept. The highlight of this place is when two young baby elephants are bottle fed by volunteers.

We were given the choice by our guide to go to a Government run (this one) or a private elephant sanctuary, we chose the Government one as we presumed the elephants would be treated with kindness and compassion. How wrong of us to assume this! We gave around £5 and they were demanding more as they were saying one held the elephant whilst the other took the picture and so we needed to pay twice as much! We were obviously feeling quite upset at this point but decided to not allow two bad members of staff to spoil our experience, we were mistaken again as we were then shepherded across the road to watch the elephants being taken down to the river. Once at the river the staff then target certain tourists, we obviously fit the type they were looking for as they managed to cajole our children into "bathing" the elephants. We have read that this orphanage is a popular turist stop and we were not sure if visit it or not. At the end we decide to go but we were disappointed. The elephant are not freet, hey did not look healthy or happy, at the river most were  chained to rocks. They just focus on making money not to help the animals.

We got tuk tuk to take us here from Kandy hotel we were staying at. 1 hour and 20 min ride which is long enough as you start to hurt in the tuk tuk after that. We visited the elephant "sanctuary" last week after being saddened by elephants in chains paraded on the beach for tourists to pay to ride. We wanted to see animals with more freedom. It is definitely better than the bathe and ride attractions but is just a zoo. It costs 5000 ruppees (about £13) to enter. It is much more ethical than the elephant ride places, which clearly beat the spirit out of the animals and abuse them. There were around 50 elephants at the orphanage. Most of the male bulls are in chains or enclosures and can only take about one step in either direction. However, there is a herd of around 30 that are a little more free. Tourists aren't allowed to ride the elephants which is good for the animals, but the keepers are corrupt. They grab white tourists and let you touch the elephants, whilst keeping them in place for your photo with bullhooks. The elephants are clearly scared of the keepers and try to pull away. Keepers also compete for the most tips from tourists for the photo, requesting up to £20 and laughing at tourists foolish enough to pay. You don't HAVE to pay them anything, but 100 ruppees was accepted and we walked away (70p). This being said, it was good seeing the elephants acting semi-natutally, together in a herd and seeing them bathe in the lake was a real highlight. Again, the bulls were chained down at the lake, whilst the females and babies were free to roam, swim and relax. They looked like they enjoyed it once the keepers left them alone. Lovely to see such majestic animals, but much preferred Yala safari and seeing them in a natural environment without corrupt zookeepers, who were just in it for the money.

I've visited many elephant orphanages in Africa and south east Asia. Many of them were built to give the elephant a pleasant life and to even prepare them to go back to nature. That's not what this orphanage is about. They just focus on making money. The entrance fee is steep for what you get. Over 20 euro's. When you enter the park you need to walk a bit to see a large herd of elephants. When you are nearby you will directly be invited by the elephant keepers to take a photo and they will ask for money immediately. All elephants have chains around there legs and are trained to work with tourists. It's just one big circus with elephants...

I had my reservations about this place typical of a westerner looking at the animal welfare of the developing world. You by your tickets and go down to a riverside restaurant to watch them bathe but the whole experience seemed contrived and over the top and not a genuine conservation project.

At first we were excited, especially when we saw the herd of elephants passing by, but then when we were watching them in the river, we started feeling sorry for them. Some of the elephants could across the river, some of them were enjoying the water, but several elephants had to stay at the bank, and they had to stand there with tourists so that the tourists could take a photo with them. Every photographing was carefully charged by the staff of orphanage and when someone gave them small amount of money they pulled a face and demanded more money. The elephants which were used for posing with tourists were in chains and we noticed that they wanted several times to join in other elephants in the river, but they couldn't because of the chains. I mean that initial plan of the founders was undoubtedly good, but nowadays it is just an atraction how to get the most money from the tourists and the happiness of elephants is not so important.

We arrived at the orphanage just in time to see the elephants troupe down for their morning bath at the river. Note: you must get a ticket at the orphanage before you head to the river or you won't get through and it's a bit of a scrum so be careful if you have small children. You can get a great view from the path of all the elephants in the river playing and being washed by their keepers. Some were sadly chained by the side but still enjoyed the water. On the way back a good tip is to leave the river around 1145 so you get a prime position on the road to see them go back up for their lunch. We also fed the elephants back at the orphanage. Yes it's touristy but done well and it seemed as if the animals are well treated. Recommended if you like elephants!!

We arrived at the airport and headed straight for Kandy, stopping at the river to see the elephants being washed.  We didn't go to the orphanage itself after reading mixed reviews.  The river washing was worth it.  Cost nothing (apart from our beer and chips at the restaurant overlooking the river) and we had a nice break from the car. There were about 40 elephants being washed on our day, some chained up (the "naughty" ones) and some free to roam about.  It was interesting to see them climb up to the far banks and then be called back by the mahouts.  Some came back and then left again straight away.  They covered themselves in dust from the river bank and then when they came back to the chained elephants, seemed to "share" it with them - letting the chained elephants wipe it off their backs and spray it onto their own. This was our first taste of Sri Lanka and after being scared by our Australian doctor, didn't feel the need to pat or touch the elephants ourselves.  We had our fill of looking though and got lots of lovely photos. Bought a hat from the stalls going down to the river.  Do your best haggling as they expect it.

We visited this place because we presumed the elephants would be taken care of and be happy there. This made us feel like we had just paid to contribute to the mistreatment of the beautiful creatures. When the baby elephants were being fed it was nice to see them so excited, however the minute they see the spear like stick they run for their lives looking terrified. I would not recommend this place because it is over priced and only harms the animals. I genuinely believe that the orphaned elephants would be happier on their own in the wild...

We arrived in Sri Lanka very excited to see elephants so thought we would stop by on the way past. Mixed feelings by doing so. I know there's a lot of controversy around this place, but we had a really lovely visit. We arrived at 1200, on my birthday! and headed straight to the river, where we watched eight elephants bathing whilst we ate our lunch. Then we spent some time in the more zoo-like area before watching 30-40 elephants at the lake again at 1400. Only some of the elephants were in chains and we were reassured that these are the elephants who had not-so-good times before being adopted into Pinnawala and therefore could attack (as elephants never forget!) so they had to be more controlled. Majority were not tied up and they seemed relatively free to roam and were well fed. Once they are back in orphanage you have the chance to feed them and take photos with them with the guidance of a staff. Fruit baskets are sold for feeding the elephant.

I enjoyed seeing the elephants and the scenery around here is lovely too but I just don't know if it's right. There is no information given and it really felt like 'here they are, the elephants. This is and has been one of the most controversial places to go in all of my travels. After some hours of hectic journey you visited few elephants how do you feel ?Really very disappointed this time ,previously i had been visited 2 times but this time terrible very few elephants and some area restricted to visitors poor maintenance any where.

They then took us to a hidden corner and pushed me towards the elephants in the river, grabbed my phone off me to take a picture, then as I tried to leave 5 men blocked the stairs to get out and demanded a 'salary' for taking pictures which were not asked for. it was incredibly uncomfortable experience throughout ruined further by the men that worked there. I would definitely not recommend this place as it is not an orphanage.

The orphanage is a popular tourist spot full of elephants, elephants bathing in river, feeding & bottle feeding are popular activities but the elephants are not kept properly, you won’t find a single adult elephant having Ivory, the elephants looks weak, they are earning from elephants but not maintaining them well.

The entrance fee is quite high. I went with my family and missed the bottle feeding so there wasn't really anything to do but watch the elephants bathe in the river. The restaurant by the river is horrible. We ordered hamburgers that tasted like cardboard so go there before lunch time or after.

After reading the reviews about the mixed feelings we thought we needed to visit it by ourself to judge. It didn't felt to me like a commercial activity. I also saw some keepers asking tips for photo's, that's not good, but mostly they were busy helping out the elephants eating, washing etc. What I was really missing was the storytelling; what's the story behind each elephant? Why are they using their methods? What's the goal for each elephant? Rehabilitation? Offering? And what's the historical proof of their work? This storytelling and educational function would make this orphanage a outstanding organization and will bring a better understanding to all visitors.

As an experienced traveller and animal lover having visited many animal orphanages across the world, I must be honest and say that visiting the Pinnawala Elephant orphanage was not what I expected it to be and leaving me feeling saddened, disappointed and guilty for visiting. The Elephants did not look healthy or happy, most were always chained to rocks in the river leaving some of the elephants swaying left to right (mentally unwell with their back legs also chained so not able to move freely) and leaving sores around their legs. Just so cruel. The caretakers had sharp weapons they used to control the Elephants, whilst also aggressively shouting at them and forcing them to lay down in the river so that visitors can take photos with them. The whole experience and environment was not natural and did not seem to be for the Elephants best interest but for the caretakers to earn some money. I would advise not to visit here.

This is a big place with lot of elephants. Many friendly baby elephants, where we can feed by hand. Just need to be little careful though. Elephants going to the river to have a bath is a sight not to miss. Try to visit the feeding times. There's parking, few souvenir shops and a cafe around too.

A nice place to start our Cross Country trip on Sri Lanka, after some hours drive out of Colombo we arrived this place. A beautiful place, were the elephants whom has had a tough start in life are taken care of. Those who are ready for going back in the woods are going be released. Enden up with a nice lunch by the riverside, watching these beautiful animals having there bath. Entrance fee is approx. 15-18 USD per person,

It was nice to see the elephants in the water, we thought it would be more natural, the elephants stood there and the caretakers threw water on them. The caretakers always asking you to take a picture and then asking for money. (There were some complaints by guests so there are also some game and wildlife officers on hand) The elephants walk from the river to the orphanage to get their daily exercise. We went up to the main area, the babies are separate and feed according to the scheduled times - the elephants were so cute but the feeding ritual was disappointing. You can buy a basket of fruit and feed an elephant - this was nice. We had our own guide for explainations however it would be good if the orphanage would organize this for visitors. Overall a little disappointing for the price

Fairly expensive 5000 for two adults. The animals are well fed and look in good condition. However some are chained and terrified of the men which made me question their treatment behind closed doors. The cafe with the view over the river is very very expensive.

We loved the baby elephant feeding. Big shame on the Indian government that a small country like SriLanka can manage such a great activity but Indians are busy in looting the country. Pinnawala offers a baby feeding and elephants bath in river show. Both are great thing to watch. If you have little kids than do plan this activity. They will cherish most precious memories for the life.

We had an awesome visit, however somewhat spoiled by the aggressive elephant handlers who were demanding a lot of money after encouraging us to have our photos taken with the elephants.  Make sure you're clear up front what is expected and don't be bullied into handing over excessive cash!

Pinnawala is a must visit when in Sri Lanka. It's an enjoyable place for the entire family. If you go early in the morning, you can see the elephants walking to the river. You can also buy elephant dung products from the shops lining the street...

After visiting an elephant sanctuary in South Africa, set in glorious countryside, just allowing small groups, riding for ages and helping at feeding time - all with red tea and snacks in a lovely villa  I was really keen to see the Indian elephant. They are lovely and it was great to see them in the river and being washed, but that seemed to be all there was on offer. No rides through the countryside. Nothing but pay extra to buy fruit, then pay again to feed it to one chosen elephant. While jostling with dozens and dozens of visitors. Nowhere even to sit and watch them after bathing - we were herded in and outjust like the animals. Sri Lanka seems to have a policy of charging foreign tourists many multiples of the price for locals. While it's great that locals can get to see their attractions, and many, many do so. I object strongly to being charged 25 times the basic price because I'm neither from SL nor their area of economic cooperation ( which is 4 to 5 times the SL local price).

The visit to the orphanage was a nice start to the trip. The best time to visit is between 10 - 12 Am, when the elephants are taken to the river for a bath.  Post this you can feed the elephants in the orphanage. This is a government run orphanage and does not let you bath the elephants.  Your driver may take you to some private places where you can ride an elephant and bath it.  However, these are sad places with 2-3 elephants and should not be encouraged. At the pinnawala orphanage, you can see dozens of elephants bathing and frolicking in the river and the banks. The near by cafes offer chilled beer or a hot coffee a you may prefer...with a view of the Elephants.....What more do you want!!

Orphanage?  Crowded place - the animals were well fed though. Their mahouts asked for money to have pictures taken with the elephants. I the river most of the males were shackled and some of them had adopted "repeated motion". It was clear that the beautiful animals were scared of the mahouts just showing the stick made them back of. Please don't visit - there are other places to go to in Sri Lanka. Photo shows shackled female :-(

no one else has mentioned that most of the elephants are chained and our driver said they have to chain the crazy ones! To me it is a money making site, photos and feeding all cost extra. I am no expert but some of the ones that could be fed look very overweight. Also there is no information on what they do. When we went down to the river bank they were chained on the front and back legs and their carer prodded them to sit down and roll over. If they provided information so that their rescues are clear I would have felt much happier. We went away feeling distressed and I would not go back.

Best ! Life time experience. Worth visiting. [25/06/2016] Visited Pinnawala village, in Sabaragamuwa Province of Sri Lanka. According to 2011 census there were 88 elephants, from 3 generations, living in Pinnawala. Now the number has gone up considerably.  This Conservation step was taken up in 1975 by the Sri Lanka Department of Wildlife Conservation.

Mixed feelings. A beautiful place where you may see lots of elephants of all sizes and even pet them. Baby elephant feeding isn't what you think. You just see a kind of boring show off of baby elephants making small stops for bottle feeding by their trainers (and not you) on a round circle. Seemed more than a circus really rather than an act of kindness to the species. Elephants seemed to be in good condition, not harmed and you should definitely go up the small hill to see them in a more natural environment. In Sri Lanka whatever you do a local is there to help you and ask for a tip (even when no help is needed). Elephant touching and a photo means about 400-500 rupees per local..

It was a decent experience.  It's definitively not worth the $30USD equivalent but your already there so you feel obligated to pay and go in just for the experience.  Being a foreigner they really overcharge you.  Its good for some photos and touching an elephant or two.  Its best to follow guides on the street outside and ride one of the elephants in the river, this didn't seems to be part of the actual orphanage though.  Its cool to get up close and personal with the Sri Lankan elephants

What a wonderful experience if not a little bit of a tear jerker. These wonderful animals are so gentle yet very much taken for granted. It is quite a busy place with an initial visit inside the orphanage and then a short walk to the Riverside to watch the elephant's bathe and get scrubbed down. They were all impeccably behaved except for a baby that tried to do a runner. I would highly recommend a visit here if you are in the country because you would probably regret it if you didn't visit.

It was a 4 hour drive for us but was worth the drive. Got to see so many elephants in the natural environment. Best part was it rained for a while whilst we were at the orphanage. It was a sight to see all the elephants enjoying the rain & playin by themselves splashing mud all over them. Kids would love it too as they can touch the elephants & even feed the elephants under supervision. Once we finished the orphanage we got to see the elephants bathing whilst we enjoyed a good lunch.

The site is split in two parts, the actual orphanage and the riverbank area where the elephants taken bathe / cool themselves during the day This is ok for some photos, but definitely not worth taking a detour. Plus I can see elephants in multiple other places across Sri Lanka

After 3 hours of driving through the beautiful jungle from Negombo to Pinnawala. Words alone are not enough to express how wonderful and breathtaking this place is. The air was so fresh and clean, the elephants so cute and friendly, the trees so green and skies so blue. (If possible, ask for Anurood to show you around. Very informative and helpful with bargaining) If you're able to go to the elephants when there are less people there, the men will allow you to feed the elephants and they'll let them play with you & pose with you for the camera. They will ask for high tips but you can bargain your way out and pay way less. If that's not enough, I only paid around $14 to ride and elephant into the river and have him spray me with water while on its back! Somewhere between the markets on the way to the river, there's a secret garden hidden where you can also find herbal medicines from the trees! There, in June/July, only men can get a free massage/treatment since the female masseuse are only available during high seasons. Everything used/sold in this garden is natural. So beautiful and worth it!

Yes it costs to get it, and yes nothing is for free. This place gets too much bad press considering its supported and licensed by the Sri Lankan government. Call it a zoo if you like, i enjoyed seeing these elephants being fed, washed, mothered and looked after because if this institution didn't, nobody would. Suck it up haters. 5 stars.

As other reviewers have stated it is a small zoo with just elephants. Watching the elephants swim in the river across the road from the orphanage was pretty good except that you are continually harassed by touts trying to sell you food to feed the elephants and then the keepers will get you in for a photo with the elephants, then sting you for some money for taking the photo! All the while there are signs telling you not to feed the elephants and not to get close to them! The best time is when they bring the elephants back up the road to return them to the orphanage from the river. Its a pretty spectacular sight. Would I return? probably not.

It is on the way to kandy from colombo.entry fee is 700 lkr for a saarc country citizen.bt small area for tourists.most of the arra is forest.a bunch of elephant can be seen bt all are small elephant.only one elephant was feeding milk by tourists.in front of shed no 5 there was 15-20 elephants open bt with a lot of mahut(guard) surrounded.otherwise all other elphants were in shed.no area map inside,only one at the entrance.a restaurant is situated at the entry ticket counter.overall a over rated tourist destination.generally european tourist who dont see elephant in their country are the main visitor.

I was a bit disappointed with the way some of the Elephants were treated by the caretakers... but then you need to remember that the animals are not domestic & tamed ... they are wild and dangerous... so the care takers need to show who is the boss.... the feeding time is just awesome with the baby elephants... be careful looks can be deceiving... they are bloody hell too strong....highly recommended

If you are an animal lover you will enjoy this place. It was a nice experience seeing the baby elephants play with each other. Also, there is a small river where the animals go for a bath. Apart from that there is nothing else to see in this place. Entry charges 700 Srilankan Rupees per person. I rate this place as "good" solely because I love animals.

We had read mixed reviews of pinnawala orphanage so were not sure if we wanted to visit here. However, my love for baby elephants won and on our last day in srilanka we went there. Am I glad that we did!!! This place should be visited only if you love animals and  enjoy watching them doing their thing from up close. This is all that you get to see here! We reached at around 1315 hrs and first up saw baby elephants being fed milk from Guliverian milk-bottles. Baby elephants look very cute, gulping down liters of milk in seconds. The milk feeding is at specific times during the day. These may vary with season so it's best if you find out in advance and reach accordingly. Moving around the orphanage, we were fascinated by the way baby elephants play among themselves. We also saw how adults feed themselves with dexterity - removing all the tough outer skin and eating the soft insides. Our last leg of this visit was to a river bank just outside the orphanage. Here the elephants go for an afternoon bath. They are playful animals and it was fun to watch them splashing water over themselves and their friends. There were a few that kept lying in the river while some tried to play truant and moved upstream. We also saw three adults protectively surrounding a few months old baby all through this bathing time. There are a couple of restaurants overlooking the river. One can take a place there and spend hours looking at elephants whilst you  enjoy a meal or a cooling beer. There is an entry ticket for pinnawala orphanage. The cost of it is different for locals, SAARC regions nationals and others. So do keep this in mind when buying the ticket. Kudos  to the people who take care of these elephants and follow such a disciplined schedule. Im very sure that it is not an easy task!

Not an orphanage but an overpriced zoo with poorly treated animals. Disgusting. I went to the orphanage in Nairobi a few years back which was an amazing experience that I highly recommend. This was a complete waste of time and money. If I could rate it a zero, I would. They charge 2500 LKR to get in then the staff harass you to take a picture or touch the animals and then demand another 1000 LKR from you (which I did not do, but heard this from others who visited). Do not go under any circumstances!!!

Located in Pinnawala this location is a haven for orphaned elephants from around Sri Lanka. Sponsored by the government but dependent on public donations this sanctuary provides a worthwhile service. There are activities set at different times of the day so check before you go if there is anything in particular you want to see or do. We visited when the elephants were bathing at the river & it was fun to watch them enjoying themselves in the water. For a small fee you can feed the elephants treats, supervised by the guides/caretakers. Watch out for hawkers. There are many.  Entrance fee for foreigners is 2500 LKR.  Recommended.

We wanted to go to somewhere which was known to really care for the elephants, we arranged it via viator/trip advisor and it included pick up from our hotel & the entrance for the sanctuary & lunch overlooking the elephant watering place. The staff looking after the elephants, try to encourage you to go across the chain fence and stand next to the elephant and they take a picture of you and the elephant, of course they then say after we need to pay for this experience 1,000rupees each !! And if you dont pay they become pretty rude with you, obviously this is not a huge amount of money in the whole scheme of things but i dont think its correct, there are also signs around saying dont approach the elephants or feed them, and the staff just allow you to do so. They also prod the elephants with spikes to get them to perform for the photo, which i really didnt like. However to be so close to an elephant and to pet them was a special experience. Lunch was a simple buffet on a terrace closeby, food was included in our trip price but drinks were not. All in all glad we did the trip, but I would have prefered if our guide had told us about the photo tourist trap in advance.

One had heard a lot about this place, but I didn't quite like it. It is an over rated, over commercialised place. The staff virtually forced us to take photographs touching an elephant and then demanded money for the 'service' pleading that their salaries are too low. I also did not like the exhibitionism around feeding bottle milk to baby elephants. I tried to save some time since we were travelling to Colombo from there and decided to have food at one of the cafes just outside the place. The only way to describe the cafe is that the people running it are thief. They charged me a rate which will rival in nice four star restaurant for pathetically poor food. I got a feeling they have two price cards for pretty much the same food. Already feeling cheated, as we were coming out, the guys tried to extract more money from us in a rather threatening manner. I would urge the Sri Lankan tourism authorities  to look into it so that another visitor doesn't go back with such a poor experience.

We visited as part of a two day trip booked though our rep and really enjoyed seeing the elephants. There were elephants of all different ages from very small ones to fully grown adults. They are very tame and so lots of photo opportunities. We got to see the baby elephant being fed and boy can they drink milk lol. It was nice to see all the elephants given such a large space to roam around virtually free and so well looked after.

My tour guide cum driver brought my family to the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage on 19/6/2016 during our 5 days tour in Sri Lanka We do not know how much was the fee as it was a package tour but we certainly enjoyed ourselves. It was an amazing experience to watch and observe so many elephants  and to interact with them closely. We loved watching the many beautiful elephants bathing and playing in the river. This is the most memorable experience in our Sri Lanka's tour as we have never seen so many huge elephants in such wide open spaces . Coming from an urbanised city, the sight of so many elephants is certainly a great experience to us. The down side of this place is that the elephant's handlers were rather pushy in getting our cameras to take photo so as to collect tips.

On a small road from Colombo to kandy, Pinnawala elephant orphanage was a totally unexpected experience to me The vast area on which it is located, the green bambo trees and the innocent eyed elephants were a beautiful sight to be remembered for long The elephants were fed milk with big bottles and the sight was truly amazing

Seeing a herd of elephants walking amongst market stalls, and then bathing is an amazing, unforgettable sight. Buy your tickets before 9am, and you can see the babies being bottled fed. You may even be able to grab some fresh leaves off the feeding trucks to hand feed them. Be prepared to give a tip to the handlers when they ask you over for a photo with the elephants- nothing is free. I understand that the elephants aren't orphans, and have been born in captivity. Some of them are chained up when they are swimming. You don't get any commentary from the handlers, and there is little information available on these elephants. When the elephants are swimming you are constantly being asked by hawkers to buy fruit for the elephants, and you can pay the handler for a photo with swimming elephants. We did enjoy the visit, and we were looking forward to seeing wild elephants later.

We have visited pinnawala on our way to Kandy. The experience was awesome. You should reach to the place well before 9.00AM as the elephant feeding start at 9.00 AM. You can collect your tickets at the counter and the same ticket needs to be submitted to enter in to the elephant bathing place. Hence please make sure you carry the tickets safely. The elephant bathing is happening at a separate location. Once you see the elephant feeding and the elephant cottage, slowly start to the elephant bathing place and make your comfortable view there. The elephants are lining up for the bath is a great visual for the eyes. Also they spend an hour in the water with their naughty moves. Trust me, you will get a best rate on money exchange there. You will find people walking there with local currency in hand and they offer the best rate than any banks, exchange centers in sri lanka. Our tour guide helped us to exchange the money there. There are few shops around the elephant bathing area, however you should be very careful as you can be ripped off in these shops.
