I had an amazing experience visiting the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage, but there are concerns about the intentions of the place that cant be ignored. Some of these elephants are genuine orphans but there is now a breeding programme in place that questions overall motives. Male adult elephants are chained to 15ftsq concrete platforms and are never unchained. Elephants are openly managed with bull hooks and trained to pose with tourists for photos, for cash payments obviously. The positive highlight of a visit is the view of the elephants bathing in the river, and you dont have to pay the 'orphanage' entrance fee to see that. Just wander down the street opposite the car park and there they are. Though most are chained to hooks sunk into the riverbed rocks while they bathe. And again, cash payments get you up-close photo opportunities.  Check out the Born Free Foundation for more info on care standards at the orphanage, apparently they have withdrawn their patronage.

There were a lot more elephants than i expected. And surprisingly enough, even though they peed and pooped where they stood, they didn't actually smell bad. especially with how many there were. Horses smell way worse and thats only if here are a handful. Anyway, i was surprised with how close we were able to get to them, and they weren't in any cages or fenced in areas or anything, but there were maybe half a dozen handlers there to make sure we were safe, so no worries. some would try to get close to you, and i was able to touch a couple of them, its a bit scary because of how big they are, but they were so mellow so it was fine. I saw spotted a few babies too! a bit later on they brought the to the river so they can cool down and bathe, and that was on awesome experience, i don't know the route they took, but i went down through an alleyway where they were selling wares and food, i grabbed a coconut to drink. And when i got to the river, it was a pretty amazing site, some just jumped in and laid out in the water, others just stood around spraying themselves, and few played around with each other. It was really cool to see. I recommend.

Extremely sad. Many of the elephants are chained up, shouted at and hit with sticks. It wasn't what we had expected from an 'elephant orphanage'. You are much better off going to a national park where you can see the elephants in their natural habitats.

I have no knowledge how to tame an elephant, but for some reason I think it takes more than just good words. The orphanage should put more effort into explaining people how it works and why, because otherwise it really might seem for a lot of people an exploitation of animals for money.

Make sure you are there for the feeding time. We reached in the evening and saw the elephants bathing in the river. even though it is not permitted there were a lot of hawkers selling fruit packets for feeding the elephants. The full heard moving back was an amazing site. It was fun to watch the baby elephants drink milk from giant feeding bottles!

The orphanage didn't worth the foreigner price, 3500 rupees. Honestly, those elephants hardly moved and were not treated nicely by the guardian. But by the river near the orphanage, we found impressive view of dozens of elephants playing in the water. It was just fantastic and amusing!

The orphanage is home to hundreds of adult and baby elephants that roam around a beautiful piece of land and bathe in a big river. We were late to feeding time, but managed to catch the bathing time of the elephants in the river. We had some drinks at a restaurant directly facing the river where you get a nice view of elephant families interacting with each other and enjoying the water. Some workers gave the elephants a good scrub. What bothered me though, was the chains that some of the older elephants had over their necks and feet :( This place was established to protect and take care of injured and abandoned elephants in a safe environment, so I don't see how chaining these animals fits the picture, it is rather cruel. p.s The washroom needs major upkeeping, it is not in good condition

Love it! There are hundreds of elephants who wander down to the nearby river after feeding time, twice a day to take a long cooling bath. You can follow them down to the river, feed them bananas and take as many selfies as you like. Costs are interesting tough, foreigners pay 10x more than locals... even though rates are low, it seems a little bit distasteful.

Amazing way to view the elephants as they are mostly roaming free (with minders around) although the minders are very pushy to take your camera and snap a pic so you'll tip them. Make sure to plan so that you can catch the elephant feeding and bathing. 2500LKR entrance fee (well worth it)

The Pinnawala Elephant orphanage is an amazing way to view elephants in the wild. As you walk in, you see them roaming freely (with watchful minders all around) the minders seem a little pushy trying to take your camera and "help" you take a pic so you'll pay them. Otherwise a nice experience petting the elephants and just watching them. There's an area with the wild elephants that are a lil more temperamental (clearly marked so tourists dont go too near) Go in time to watch the baby elephant feeding time, so adorable to watch. We had lunch by the river afterwards. Food was expensive and crappy. But they time the elephant bathing so it overlaps lunch time leaving you with no choice but to eat there. Entrance Fee is 2500LKR (well worth it!)

Loved being at the riverfront watching the elephants batching and playing in the water. We ate at a restaurant which had a birds eye view of the river and the kids wouldn't budge from there. They wanted closer views and went right next to the river. Everyone enjoyed seeing the elephants march up the road at the end of the ritual. A treat to the eyes.

We were staying in Kalutara and travelled for a half day trip to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage first thing in the morning. Before going I had some reservations as I had heard the elephants were in chains. However, the majority of the elephants are running around free over a large spot of land. The only animals I saw with chains on were not actually chained up but just had chains on them while there were people about apparently because they are aggressive. Firstly you see the feeding of the young elephants, and then you go down to the river and watch as the herd of elephants all run down to the water to play and wash and explore. You are able to get pictures with the elephants and the handlers will ask for a tip which is fine, but I'd recommend only taking out small denomination notes and do not get all of your money out in front of anyone as they will demand a bigger tip. Overall a lovely experience, seeing the elephants in a nice and very big environment which to be honest is much nicer than seeing them in a zoo in England.

I had reservations as I thought this may be a cruel circus, overall I was impressed with what I saw, our guide explained to us that some of the elephants were saved and others were evidence in an elephant theft crime, whether or not this was true I don't know but made me feel more at ease. I thought the walk down to the river was wonderful, though amazed at the stupidity of some tourists who stood between the elephants and the river. Overall I found it an interesting way to spend a morning and the animals were stunning and didn't seem to show any signs of mistreatment. Yes the staff want money for everything but this is just the culture. Worth a visit.

I went to visit the orphanage thinking the elephants would be free to walk around instead the elephants were chained sometimes chained with both front and back legs to a pillar. The workers were shouting at the elephants demanding they follow instructions and I also witnessed a worker prodding an elephant with a metal spike. Two baby elephants were stuck in a dark concrete pen with no water or food and they looked in distress. Not only was the orphanage bad but when I thought it couldn't get any worse I was taken down to the elephant hotel were I saw elephants chained to the rocks in the water and people just stood there taking photos. The elephants looked miserable and how they can call this place an orphanage or sanctuary is beyond me. It was like a prison. Overall it was a horrible experience.

The elephant orphanage was interesting to visit but the handlers were very pushy for money after taking photos of our party with one of the elephants in the main paddock, best part was watching the elephants bathing in the river & just loving the cool water.

The thoughts with the elephant orphanage are very good, but not enough. Most of the elephants seemed to be in a very good condition, though some of them were leashed. One of the leashed elephants was unable to get any water at all. Also be aware of whatever the staff is offering you, they want money. Even if they tell you its free!! With all this said, I think the place is better than many other similar places.

Maybe it's some cultural difference, but i was shocked when i saw kids AND parents throw stuff at the elephants from behind the fence. When the animals came closer they even started kicking them while yelling and laughing! Also one of the mahouts said that the elephants had a good future.....because some of them will be sold to zoo's around the world. Not an orphanage, just another breeding program!

My parents visited here a few years ago and told us we must go. It is beyond words.... The orphanage is amazing. Took us about 20 minutes from Kandy to get there but when we arrived we went into the park which was a small charge to look round, watched a couple of baby body elephants get fed bottles of milk which was amazing. The staff were good, they encouraged you to go and stand near the elephants. If an elephant is on a chain it's best to keep your distance as they have a temper! We then watched them walk out the park down to the river where they were washed and chilled for a long time. You don't need to pay to go into the park. I think it was about 2pm when they were taken down to the river, it's free to watch this. I would say it's worth paying to go into the park though.

We undertook a visit to Pinnawela from Colombo, where our cruise ship was berthed, and this involved a 2 1/2 - 3 hour coach trip from the port. Once at Pinnawela there was a walk of maybe 500 yards downhill past a number of souvenir and clothing shops to reach the river in which a number (20 - 30) elephants were bathing. We spent a short while watching this, in fairly uncomfortable heat, before moving to the Hotel Pinnalanda, on the bank of the river, for buffet lunch which was quite pleasant with offerings of spicy and non-spicy dishes accompanied by a beer or a soft drink. Following this, we returned up the hill and over the main road to the Elephant Orphanage itself to see some very young elephants being hand-fed and to see others grazing. This was followed by a 2 1/2 hour return trip to Colombo. The overall trip was spoilt by the fact that the seating on the coach was very uncomfortable with seats much too close together and also the pitch set at an angle seemingly designed to produce backache. The guide appeared quite knowledgeable but was not always easy to understand and was not over-friendly either. It has always been a dream of mine to see the elephants, We travelled to Sri Lanka and decided to visit the elephant orphanage, we have read some bad reviews before going, and yes some of them I can understand. The staff there do just expect you to give them money, but we found this in most places we visited in Sri Lanka, After having long conversations we some people working there you can see how amazing these elephants are, watching as they are walked to the river to bath was amazing, we had the opportunity to help wash one in the river which was incredible! I certainly loved this place, and highly recommend visiting! I'd just advise that tips are expected, and staff can appear rude.

The orphanage is a popular tourist spot and our guide helped make the visit more special as he was a regular and able to tell us a lot about the place and how it was run. There were many elephants and there was an opportunity to watch the baby elephants being fed and the whole here at the river bathing.  That was a wonderful sight and they appeared happy and calm (except when the presidential helicopters spooked them!) a good alternative to visiting the national parks where you can see more closely how they interact with each other and to see how curious and playful they are.

This was by far one of the most memorable experiences I've had.  It was so nice to see elephants roaming free, playing, and enjoying life.  Prior to this experience, I've only ever seen elephants confined in a zoo with very little room to roam.  It was good to see these gentle giants in wide open spaces.  They look like they are treated very well by the caretakers.

One of the most amazing sites I've seen in long time. The management team must be appreciated for all the amazing work they have being doing. The sight of numerous elephants (mostly untamed) are very well taken care off. The experience was indeed amazing. Kids would surely enjoy the park as we as adults surely did. Only one word to sum it up... 'Amazing'

Elephants belong in the wild. This Orphanage has turned it into a circus, under the pretext of conservation. Shame on them. On top of this, they charge tourist 25x the gate fees for locals. The staff are very rude. Avoid this place. If you really want to see these Elephants, go there during the bathing time, which is between 2.00pm and 4.00pm, when they are paraded across the road to a nearby stream for their bath each day. You can see all the elephants you want, free of charge.

We visited this elephant orphanage on route to Kandy as suggested by our driver and my friend was excited to see the elephants. The whole experience is quite overrated and you get to see the elephants close by and elephant bathing. There are specific timings for elephant bathing and feeding- so do check else you will waste time waiting. The ticket for 2 costed us Sri Lankan Rupees 1400 (its for SAARC countries citizens). Once you are inside you can roam by yourself and no need to waste money on the local guides. Max. stay at this place for an hour. Things to keep in mind if at all visiting this place: 1) Carry hat / sunglasses as it tends to become very hot in June 2) Wear comfortable shoes as there will be some walking involved 3) Watching the elephant bathing is avoidable 4) Dont buy the magnets from the shop where tickets are sold- rather walk towards the elephant bathing area- there are plenty of small shops selling it for half the price (I paid 200 Sri Lankan Rs for a magnet from the small shop, where as the shop inside the orphanage sells for 450 Sri Lankan Rs.) 5) Carry your own water / soft drinks. One Coconut water costed us Sri Lankan Rs. 100 which is on expensive side 6) Can have tea / coffee at this small cafe called Cafe Chana- we spent Sri Lankan Rs. 360 for 2 tea (again expensive!)

Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is one of the best places to get a close look at the behavior of elephants. There are few activities to do around. Enjoy elephants bathing in the river, hand feed giants and take a journey around on top of an elephant. There are few shops around to buy souvenirs or other traditional Sri Lankan handcrafts. Be careful though, you can be ripped off in these shops.

I didn't know what to expect when the tour I was on arrived here. At first it appeared ok and we saw baby elephants been fed and there was photo opportunities. We were them taken to the main field where some of the other elephants were kept. Here, I saw 4 elephants chained up. They were distressed and constantly straining against them, trying to break free. I walked towards where one female was chained and there were repetitious patches of blood on the floor indicating that an injury was possibly on a leg. She kept trying to pull her chains to return to the herd and when one baby elephant tried to reach her the trainers threatened with shout and hit the baby with a stick with a spike on the end. All very upsetting.

There weren't much activities other elephant bathing and elephant riding both of which were very good . Most staff around there were expecting a tip even though only one or two actually conducted the activity. Elephant bathing was indeed a fun experience.

We boarded a private restored historic train to reach the orphanage and were not only able to see them in the river at bath time, but the parade of elephants back through the village to the sanctuary.  Be prepared to tip park staff for each experience with the elephants.  If they offer to take your photo they will expect it.  Gift shop is very expensive but good.  We enjoyed this experience and the herd has been increased due to the efforts of this sanctuary.

We visited Pinnawala around 10:00AM just in time to see the elephants walk down the road to the river. It is a tremendous sight to see the big, little & large elephants trundling along just feet away. The road then gets closed off for a few minutes ostensibly to allow the elephants to enter the water without the crowds, but some elephants were definitely chained up on the rocks in the river and they did not seem too happy about it. The crowds are allowed to follow down right to the edge of the river & there were around 40 elephants in total. It is a magnificent spectacle to see all the elephants in the water, walking up the small rapids. Some were certainly playing, others were just standing there with a sad look and others more interested in looking for food so there were some people selling bags of food for a price. You could also get up close and touch the elephants or take a picture with them, again and 'informally' for a price. There was no riding elephants at the site which at least was a positive aspect. Back up the road the elephants do seem to have a very generous open green enclosure, albeit they had left that area by the time we got there so it was hard to judge the adequacy of the open space. Again there were a few elephants chained up in the enclosures who did not participate in the earlier parade. I have to say we enjoyed the experience and it is certainly one for families as all the kids were getting a great kick out of seeing the elephants up close. We did leave with some reservations about why a number of the elephants were chained up. I am sure there is a health & safety aspect as some of them could react negatively to the crowds, but you were left wondering how staged the whole attraction is and with the money changing hands for photos etc - has it lost sight of its original purpose and moved more towards a commercial event?

Pinnawala is all about elephants. Orphaned elephants in captivity - both adults and infants, Following their day time activities, feeding elephants, souvnires made from elephant dung and many more.. The orphanage houses more than 70 elephants and cares for them. It is located on the route between Colombo and Kandy at about 45 minutes from Colombo. Tourists eed to pay an entrance fee and special discounts can be availed by SAARC country tourists. After visiting the enclosures, head off to the river area where elephants bathe in the afternoon. This is a treat to watch. You can enjoy the elephants afternoon activities at a close proximity. The place has many souvenier shops as well. Overall, a great place to visit for an experience of a different kind with nature,

This orphanage is on the road between Colombo and Kandy, some 2 hours from Colombo. I won't say this is a must visit but its definitely one of its kind and a treat for nature lovers. You can give the elephants a quick shower and take a ride on its back. There are different charges for each activity. We bought the shower and a short ride which cost us some 3000 Sri Lankan Rs per person. You can also feed the elephants (you have to buy the fruits) and take pictures. There is also a mini museum which you can visit free of cost and a souvenirs' shop. If you haven't been so close to Elephants before, you are going to enjoy this place!

Time your visit to view the feeding of the baby elephants, a charming experience where the babies are hand fed from bottles. then walk to view the 60 plus elephants being gathered in by their mahouts from the large area in which they roam. Then it's a short walk across the road and down to the river to view some of the elephants being given a bath and the others playing and drinking in the water. At no time are tourists allowed to touch or ride an elephant, which is a good sign. Finish the visit by seeing how elephant poo (there's a lot of it) gets turned into paper!

Ohhhhhhhh What else is there to say when you see these babies frolicking in the waters of the river  below the hotel where lunch is served. Twice a day a group of elephants of all ages are walked from the orphanage down the "street" to the river for their baths. Each elephant has been brought to the orphanage by locals because they have been abandoned, attacked, lost numerous reasons. We were delighted to hear that the orphanage now has breeding elephants and so not all were maimed or disfigured. The orphanage includes a 24 hour veterinarian and practice and amazing keepers who bond with each pachyderm and delight in their elephant "humour". We were curious as to why a couple were just laying in there water. It seems they were having lazy days and just didn't want to stand up! It was amazing to see how they manoeuvred their trunks to almost wave to the onlookers from their prone positions. Each animal appeared healthy and happy and we saw no evidence of any maltreatment. A local show makes elephant poo paper which is another way of recycling the continuous supply of fertiziler! When the swim time is up the keepers sound a siren and the group lines up far better than any class of human student and amble back up the street, across a main road and back to their pens. Heart warming to see animal breeding and conservation in action.

I am not sure how great the ones in the rest of India are. But even a visit to the ones we have in Karnataka are good enough. Its a good experience, no doubt. And they do a good job caring for the elephants - but my sense is that it is more of an attraction for those who haven't seen sights like these before. Must visit? I think not!

Pinnawala was our first stop from Colombo airport. If you want to see elephants up close then this is the place to be. You can even touch and feed them. And that's possible only because these giants have been tamed. It's really saddening to see the elephants pose and put up a show. However, the good thing is that they very well taken care of. Having said that would still recommend visiting one of the national parks and watching the elephants in their natural habitat. Contrary to few reviews below, we didn't experience nor see tourist being harassed for money to pose with the elephants.

We visited here fairly early in the morning to catch the bottle feeding of the baby elephants at 09:15 and the walk to the river at 10:00.  This means we got to sit at a riverside restaurant drinking tea and watching the elephants bathe and play in the river, and we could have happily stayed there all day. The elephants themselves are beautiful and seem entirely happy in their environment, some of the male elephants had their freedom to roam at the river restricted with chains but that is obviously a necessary part of stewarding such large and potentially aggressive animals.  If animals are to be in any sort of captivity then this is the lightest touch that is sensibly possible. Some of the smaller elephants walked right past us in the orphanage itself, and we had a chance to interact with some of them.

Coming from India , Elephants don't hold a great deal of attraction . Its nice to see them bathing in the river but thats nothing spectacular . The toilets stink!! However if there are kids with you its nice for them to see them finish bottles of milk......a lesson for a finicky eater , perhaps :)) . So don't miss feed times.

It is a good visit for the travelers who are coming to Kandy. There are several other Elephant places privately run,  before you reach this government run orphanage and our tuk tuk driver tricked us twice to stop ate the private business places so that he can get a commission from the establishments. Any how we reached the real place at last. It is well run but questions came in our minds whether the animals were treated well or not by the keepers.

This is nice to see the elephants to take a bath in the river but to be honest I feel a bit sorry for them having to be chained up, they look quite sad 😞 especially compared to the wild elephants I've seen. There is a restaurant that you can eat at and watch the elephants bath, the food is average. A large amount of shops to buy souvenirs and practice you negotiating skills.

Price for the ticket is astronomical compare to what locals pay , even if you not visiting for the sanctuary and just watching elephants bathing in river it will cost £8 per person plus tips tips and more tips Also if this on the way to Hill country your time will water here so plan 2 hrs for watching them nothing more Elephants ride are not my cup of tea why you want to trouble them if you really love the animal There are enough places to watch them in jungles so we choose them Ornaments are not really authentic around here so we bought it thru state timber coop outlets with bit of haggling

We arrived in time for the bottle feeding which was recommended to us but the best part was definitely when the elephants went to the river to bath. Incredible watching the number of elephants bathing. Yes some of them do have chains on them but I didn't see any mistreatment of the elephants. There could have been more information available for reading about the purpose of the Orphanage.

The Sanctuary is hard to reach (3+ hours by cramped buses from the nearest town), overpriced (plus the staff demand huge tips on top of it), and provides visitors precious little info on the elephants (unless you're willing to pay out more). While most of the elephants have space to roam and do not appear to be mistreated, others are inexplicably chained in small pens. They all seemed dejected. This upset me and I left after 30 minutes. I should have done more research and my lesson is definitely learned...

First I must say that all the elephants were in good condition and happy. We saw the babies being given their morning milk then we got taken to the paddock with the mums and babies. One of the keepers pointed at our camera and he took photos of us with one of the elephants (He wanted a tip to do this) I also hosed of a juvenile which was amazing (Again the keeper wanted a tip) We then went to a platform where we could feed some of them fruit (This has to be paid for too) Finally we were taken down to the river to await the elephants, first was the bull, he was huge, so much bigger than expected, then followed the rest of the herd.  What a sight it was seeing them enjoying being washed by their keepers. It was an amazing experience and I would highly recommend it.

Visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage as part of a tour. It was an experience to see so many elephants and there were some very young calves who were a delight to watch as they played in a waterhole and with a hosepipe. Across the road, past the shops that inevitably sprinkle up around an attraction, you can watch the herd play in the river and this is truly amazing and what I travelled to see. Be careful here as there are locals who will grab your hand, read your fortune and demand money. I personally was to polite to refuse and my Britishness cost me. On the flip side there are elephants restricted to the site who are restrained with chains to their legs. I am no fundamentalist and I understand the power of these creatures and the damage they can do if so inclined but seeing such magnificent beasts so restrained was crushing. Overall I feel the Orphanage is a necessary evil, keeping young elephants safe even if their practices with the older ones is shameful.

Children had a wonderful time watching the baby elephants being fed.  They were able to feed fruits to the grown elephants too. It was a nice sight to watch the elephants being led to their bath. Be there by 9am as the baby elephant feeding starts at that time until 930-945am. We could get plenty of close-up pictures.

I went with a local here who knew about their good work.  Yes you see a lot of elephants and see them bathing.  You can also find nearby opportunities to ride one...however.....they really didn't have any information about elephants so educationally left a big gap.  The posh shop really needs to be converted to educate people about Elephants.

We witnessed elephants in chains, being prodded with pointy spears and having there ears yanked in whatever direction the trainers wanted them to go. The elephants moved away from trainers when approached by them. These elephants aren't orphans, they are bred purely to be pranced around in front of tourists. Unfortunately, the weather was bad when we visited and therefore we were unable to witness the elephants bathing in the nearby river. The park is very small, considering the size of the elephants. The majority of the park as closed, though this did not effect the 2500rp entrance fee. Trainers expect 1000rp tips and upwards for photos.

See hotel review details that I put up This place is ideal to visit the orphanage and watch the elephants go down to the river, the elephants go down at 8 am which is a small group, the large group maybe 25 or more elephants go down at 10am and back up at 12, then a group of 7 go down at 1pm. You can follow them down to watch them go in the river a few elephants have chains on their foot but they loop the free end over their neck, it only one of these elephant were chained on the dock I was told that this one would run off if not chained he was rolling around in the water and considering all the others waded out even to the far side of the river doing their own thing It seemed a reasonable explanation.  At about 12 the lead guy blows a horn and all the elephants start walking to the gathering place on the river edge, a guy is in the water and throws buckets of water over their backs to ensure they are all soaked. Then at some sort of signal the lead elephant "matriarch" makes her way slowly up the rock where you can stand to the edge and she checks with her trunk if anyone are offering food bananas and coconuts she did take a coconut from one person dropped it crushed it then ate the pieces, I wished I had something to offer her she put her trunk in my hand to check if I had anything. People are instructed to get off the road when they are walking back and the shop owners just pull their racks of clothing back in their store for the few minutes the elephants walk on the road, once the matriarch has passed the onlookers the rest who are lined up waiting to go all start following her, you need to be quick on your feet to follow them back up the road as the elephants are surprisingly fast.  The elephant handlers expect a tip and they are looking at least 1,000 rupees I only had 500 in change so gave them that they muttered but I had already feed the baby elephant so they couldn't do much. They get a lots of tips for doing this so don't feel guilty if you haven't got much change they just move on to the next tourist. Locals also try to sell you a few eg 4 bananas to feed the elephants with for 200 rupees which is about £1 but it's worth buying a kilo on the way there for 80 rupees about 40p as its very enjoyable to feed the babies and like all children are disappointed when you run out!

The way people rave about this place was the reason for me visiting it. In short.... WHAT AN ABSOLUTE DISGRACE. Orphanage to my mind is where you take care of creatures who do not have any other place to live. This place might be "looking" after the elephants... but the poor creatures are nothing but slaves. They struggle to move around due to being chained. To top this, the chains are so tight around the ankles and also too short for normal movement, it breaks my heart to see this. Nearly all the elephants have chafed in the chained area with open wounds. I have seen one with such a short chain that the walking motion is restricted to the point where it is limping around. Another has a stiff front leg making walking very uncomfortable. Upon enquiring why the chains, we were told that they are dangerous animals and kill humans. Question. How many humans have been killed by elephants opposed to the number of elephant killed by humans. To my mind, being an animal lover, such an orphanage project should not be a tourist attraction where the animals are getting forced to perform. Money making racket where the wellbeing of the elephants are not the top priority. Sorry if I sound bitter, but this is a project that is failing dismally. If I knew what the state of affairs are before hand, I would not have visited this "orphanage"....

It is nice to see the elephants from close up but it is sad the way they get treated chained some have the to back legs chained together so they can not run and they are constantly puked with a sharp pointy metal spear if they miss behave

The Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is nice place to visit with children. You get to watch as the baby elephants drink milk and see adult elephants in nature as they graze. You can even interact and feed them different fruits. I would suggest bringing a bag of bananas along for the ride, instead of purchasing it at the orphange itself. The setting is great for photos as they aren't particularly fenced in by ugly cages, so in photos it would look as though they are out in the wild. Afterwards, you will need to walk for approximately 10 minutes towards the river, where the elephants have their bath. That too, is a picturesque scene. Moreover, if you are looking to ride an elephant, don't expect to do so here- you can do that a location nearby, but you will have to ask around. Overall, the orphange makes for great photos but it would help to have more signs up to direct tourists on where they should be heading. I will just say about my experience as others have already written in depth. I went with my guide. There are now 80+ elephants here of all ages but mainly over 4y.o. I paid £3.50 for a basket of mixed fruit to feed the selected elephant at this time. The handler was good with him, allowed me to stroke him and have photos taken. No hassle. I did see a tourist lose their camera because they got too close. The young elephant had a new toy. I think the tourist needed a new camera by the time it could be retrieved. Everyone must remember they are wild animals who choose when to listen. At 1.15 pm they fed 2 young elephants milk. Quite amusing. The handlers try and move around the arena so all get that photo opportunity. The elephants ran down from their pen, they knew what was in store. After this you may be fortunate enough to see them cross the street back from the river. All the events occur several times a day so make sure you ask & get an answer from your guide otherwise you can be hanging around for too long. Nice for the children who do not ask as many questions as adults. 1-2 hours is quite sufficient unless you want that 'perfect award winning' photo.

The Pinnawala elephant orphanage was interesting and looks like a "happy place" for elephants considering the alternatives. Having said that, it's a pity to see they have to be kept there instead of roaming their own habitat. Humans interfere too much with Nature n have to do damage control later. The orphanage was it! Saw a wild elephant across a fence along our drive, feel it was better off sans vet, bottle feeding etc. "Give me freedom or give me death!" Saw some disturbing behavior of elephant in chains. It was doing the side2side, trunk/head waving 'dance' characteristic of one 'disturbed' Sad!

To take things in order..... Travel to and from the elephant orphanage was very good. Only my wife and I went from our hotel and we had a car take us there and back. The orphanage visit....bathing in the river and walk back to the park was incredible..these are really majestic animals. The feeding time for the babies was nice to see and the babies were quite funny in their attempts to get more milk ! At this point the guide was nowhere in sight....almost like he knew what was going to happen. All in all though a nice part of the day. The next bits were where extra costs that unexpectedly came up.....the saree shop.....if buying expect costs in region of 45000 rupees, you don't have to buy one, but this is the approx cost if you wanted to....the tea factory...very interesting and the tea tasting a nice touch...again you don't have to buy but you do feel like you should. Finally on way back to hotel you visit a herbal medicine place.....very informative and again no obvious cost....but you do feel obliged to buy something....expect cost in region of 8000 rupees if you decide to. These additional visits don't ask for payments but you do, as I say, feel obliged to spend something and in that case expect about 10000 rupees outlay. Overall.....good day out...nice experience....slightly spoiled by the aggressive manner of the picture opportunity staff and the feeling that the guide was possibly doing people a favour taking you to the other places To summarise....overall a good visit to the orphanage and bathing site. Do your homework on who you book with to hopefully avoid the slightly negative aspects of the experience

I really wanted to go here and was aware of some of the reviews in Tripadvisor and elsewhere, but decided to go and see for myself. There are around 80 elephants here now and none are released back to the jungle, unlike the country's Elephant Transit Home in conjunction with the Born Free Foundation where they are "real orphans" that are released back into the jungle. The original number of elephants here at Pinnawala was very small and over the years have developed a healthy number, probably too many for its size. There are two types of elephants here, what they call "working" elephants and the the herd elephants. Exactly what work they do is difficult to establish and is certainly something that could easily be done in another way on the "orphanage". These have chains at all times and a handler, the way that thy are trained is clearly seen at the river when they are bathing. At first you think that it is great that they are lying down in the water and "enjoying" the flowing river....until you see that when they stand up they are told to lie down agin by their handler.....this is just for the tourists watching. This is very clear when they bring the herd to the river, as they are released and NONE lay down in the river!! The handlers do allow humans to touch and have pictures taken with them for the expected tip! The feeding of the calves with the milk bottle is also a spectacle for the tourists. While there is a balance between the need for looking after the "institutionalised" elephants and the real orphans there seems to be no need for the "trained working" elephants and a need for stricter control of the way in which handlers use he elephants to simply obtain tips with photos and feeding. This was a mixed feeling about the experience, if you want to be amazed by the relationship that humans can have elephants, then go. But realise that the relationship is based upon the use of the dependency upon food and the potential to be prodded in sensitive areas that cause pain. There is a balance that does not seemed to have been obtained or even strived for.   This is a big money spinner for the government it seems.

For most, there are likely more elephants here in one setting than seen elsewhere before. The most rewarding was to watch the elephants led down from the park and to the river where some cooled off from the sun and heat of the day (and it can get pretty hot in Sri Lanka too).  Not sure if it is numerically accurate but one of the mahoots shared that there were 93 elephants at this "orphanage".   And while we did see a few "baby" elephants, they generally were larger elephants (vs. a plethora of babies one might expect from the name of the facility).  And, yes, a few of the elephants are chained at the leg.  Our guide says it is because they are "naughty".  Hmmm ..  Even in the river, a few are chained at the leg in the water. We assumed this is for the safety of the visitors who wanted to approach closer. Some other notes: (1) Do your advance reading on this place before you come. Best you always know the background of a place before you visit. (2) The entrance price is 2500 rupees per person. Though relatively high, we considered it a contribution to the elephants. Hope they get most of the benefits. (3) Try to be there at 2 pm when they have many of the elephants trek one after the other from their main area, across the city street, down to the river. (4) The area does have restaurants (and hotels), We followed our local guide's advice to eat elsewhere. (5) Last, there are elephant poop products for sale at the stores which flank the path down to the river,

It was an enthralling and most rivetting experience that one had at the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. From the young elephants who were gamboling about, gleefully accepting milk and fruits from adoring visitors to the bathing glory of the water spouting beauties... the experience will remain etched in my memory forever. God Bless Sri Lanka for taking care of their loving and docile mammoth friends

We took our 9 year old daughter who loved the whole experience of getting up close to the elephants and being able to feed a baby elephant.  its great to see them roam around and look so happy.  When we visited they were due to go down to the river to have there wash. This was amazing and my daughter got the chance to wash one in the river.  Please visit this place its well worth it.

I went to the elephant orphanage under the impression (as it is advertised) that this was a place they rehomed and cared for injured or orphaned elephants. This is not true. The elephants are chained up and treated horribly by the mahouts. One young elephant was alone in a tiny cage pacing back and forth and when I asked why he was in that condition the mahout replied it was being tamed. This is all a big show and totally misrepresented. There are also touts outside offering rides on elephants. When I saw the condition of one of these elephants chained up I was in tears. They have scars on their skin from the chains and are clearly in distress. An awful place. A total rip off for naive and unsuspecting tourists.

This is a great place to view so many gentle animals. You can get very close to the elephants. We missed the feeding part of the baby elephants but were able to catch the animals in river in their full glory. Baby elephants are too cute.

I visited the elephant orphanage as a part of a you're and it was incredible! The elephants are in an enclosure but seem happy. Some are chained for reasons unknown but I assume this could be because of visitor safety. There are babies there who get fed in front of on lookers which is great to watch. They are full of life and even mischievous which is so fun to watch! Although they are enclosed they are free to roam at the lake which is a short walk away. This was where my experience really was amazing. The chains came off and these beautiful animals were free to interact with each other. The elephants should not be touched or ridden here and there are fines if you do. Some members of staff will all for money for you to touch or wash the elephant I didn't witness anyone riding them but they are still wild animals so approach any invites to touch them with caution. The overall feel we had from the elephant orphanage was that they were cared for and loved. I went for my birthday and it will definitely be hard to top! A great experience for everyone!

Stunning up-close views of elephants bathing in the river.  Seeing elephants in their natural habitat, against a backdrop of distant mountains.  Bottle-feeding baby elephants. It all adds up to a more respectful interaction with the gentle giants.

Not a huge place but great to see these graceful animals being looked after, all of these animals end up here after coming into contact with local farmers or generally being in the wrong place and become threatened. Watch the babies being bottle fed and then watch them cross the road on the way down to bathe in the river. fantastic to see them just wandering down the street. Get yourself a bowl of fruit and hand feed them .

We didn't know what to expect and if I had known we would have never visited this awful place that sustains animal slavery. Thanks to strict regulations in Sri Lanka there are hardly any elephant orphans anymore on the island. If this place was just taking care of baby elephants, there would be 2 animals or so. Instead they keep around 80 animals locked in cages or chains. The mahouts (elephant caretakers) are very cruel tot he animals, constanly poking them with their bull sticks in their feet. They don't care about the animals : There are signs all over the park not to feed the animals but the mahouts themselves will sell you bananas to feed the animals,and for an extra  tip of 100 rupees, and up they let you inside the cage, so you can pose in front of a gentle giant for a picture. As a consequence of their cruel treatment, the animals suffer from tics and stress,show repetitive behaviour  chew the bars of their cages, repeat the same gestures over and over again. This place has nothing to do with animal wellfare but everything with the exploitation of these poor mammals. By visiting this awful place, you sustain this. Go visit the elephants instead in their natural habitat in one of the many national parks in Sri lanka. it's so much more fun and at least the animals there are free and not bullied by their caretakers

This is the second of two animal 'orphanages' in Asia that were in my bucket list (the other was the Tiger Temple in Sai Yok, Kanchanaburi, Thailand). Glad I've done both! Have deliberately singled out 'orphanage'- the starting cause of rescuing, treating and raising injured and orphaned elephants was noble no doubt, but after decades of operation they are more inclined in running most of its activities towards profitability. Specially artificial breeding programs to increase the number of this majestic creatures in captivity should not be endorsed. It was learnt that they also sell few elephants to outsiders for commercial use- deplorable if true! The elephants are kept in fenced enclosures and visitors can go very close and even interact with them, which  should not be allowed to give the animals some chance to retain some of their natural instincts. Basically these are not being given any chance of surviving in the wild once cured or grown. Apparently they don't want that happen either! Even in their enclosures some of the young adults are kept heavily chained. My daughter and me felt very sad to see the incessant attempt of one rebellious young elephant to break free from its chain, it was not taking its food even! Getting a chance to see so many elephants bathing in the river is a sight to behold. The playful juveniles in the other side of the river is also quite a display. At the same time seeing so many heavily chained elephants even during the bath and frequent use of pronged stick on them is a shame. And I wonder why most of these elephants have lost the tip of their tails including the tail hairs! Its such a pity! Could not find an answer from anyone nor from the net- anybody? Well, I'm glad that I've done this but it did not even remotely meet my expectations. I expected a more natural raising of the elephants from where at least some could get a chance to return to the wild. IMHO its not worth just to visit this 'elephant farm', go there only if you are passing through nearby. In our case we visited en-route our Colombo-Kandy journey.

There many places around the world where you can see wild elephants. This is one particular place where you can see them in there true sense. Cover across 70 acres you can actually go and see elephants in to the wild. Baby elephant feeding is an interesting option one can pot for.

It was lovely to see the elephants, especially when they go to the river for a wash. However the Orphanage is a total tourist trap and the elephants are paraded around by the 'keepers' all who are looking for money each time you approach or try to take a picture. They are keen to help you out but then keener to ask for extra money (typically $20). Feeding the baby elephants is just a circus show. Nice to see elephants but not the best place to do that. I think you can just see the elephants at the river without paying to go to the Orphanage - It was quite expensive to get into the orphanage and is really only worth an hours visit.

A great place to visit. For me, the highlight of a trip to Sri Lanka. forget what others have said about the elephants being chained up, they are extremely well-treated by the mahouts, and watching them in relaxing in the river is something I will never forget. The drive there is a bit tortuous, but if that keeps the place form becoming too commercialised, then I am happy for it to stay that way.

I am not one for seeing animals in captivity - I much prefer to see them in the wild. However this is not like a Zoo. when we arrived the herd of elephants probably numbering around 50 Elephants were roaming free and bathing in the river. It was a relief to see that were no chained in place. Great for kids , a chance to get very close to almost wild animals.

I was apprehensive to go to this as it seems to have had a lot of negative comments about elephants being chained up etc. We arrived at approx 09am and watched the baby elephants get fed their milk bottles, not chained up and they seemed to respond with the various noises the keepers made, they was also tapped with a thin stick to push them in the right direction, we made it down to the river where the tamer elephants were getting bathed by the keepers, they did chain approx 10 of the elephants close to the shore (possibly they were not as tame as the others or were prone to running off), I was concerned at first but then I thought - I put a chain on my dogs neck when I think it's going to run off! These elephants were play fighting and bathing in the water with each other but the others approx 20-25 were wandering around on the other side of the river, exploring the jungle and play fighting with each other . Beautiful scenery and the elephants looked well cared for. Only negative was that some of the keepers were trying to get you to give them cash for a close up shot with a chained up elephant

For those who genuinely care about animals please avoid Pinnawalla orphanage. As others have mentioned it is not an orphanage and more a tourist attraction with the elephants acting solely as entertainers for hordes of tourists. Despite a number of signs noting the issues between human - elephant interaction we realised the handlers are willing for a tip to allow tourists to pose for photos etc. One upsetting example we came across was a very young elephant chained to a rock in the water which was showing real signs of distress. After asking why it was chained up we were told it was a trouble maker and therefore needed to be restrained constantly despite it being very unhappy.... Since visiting we realised that the poor treatment and welfare of the elephants at Pinnawalla has been widely publicised by the born free foundation and others.

Horrible place. None of the animals or caretakers seemed relaxed or happy. Lots of small and male elephants in chains and showing signs of anxiety and stress with the head bobbing (some people think they are dancing...it's a sign of severe mental stress in elephants). It opened as an orphanage and evolved into a money making scheme. Elephants from here sold to overseas zoos. Great photos down by the river... If you can avoid the bull hooks which they are not afraid to use. The Elephant Transit Center was opened to do the right Tung as Pinnawala became more corrupt. Not a place to support.

Please do not be fooled by the name, these elephants are mainly poached from the wild, the only most of the larger elephants are chained to the side of the hill in the water, that are also hit if they react in a non robot like fashion. We have both pictures and footage of an elephant that was smacked on the forehead which resulted in a cut. We also witnessed the distress of a younger elephant tied up by both one front and back leg in the water several times it called and struggled to get free. It was a distressing sight for any animal lover knowing you paid money are now somewhat responsible for this animals suffering. Having seen elephants looked after with no chains around there neck or legs it simply shows me how the excuse that the trainers give that they are dangerous animals is rubbish. Please be aware that by tourists continuing to visit the animals with suffer.

While I enjoyed seeing the elephants here, it was quite distressing how they were being treated.  This place is not a refuge for elephants, it is a side show about making money.   Elephants were chained up to posts away from the heard and were clearly upset.  The staff we not friendly to the animals or the visitors.  I came away upset and greatly saddened by the treatment and conditions of the animals.

We visited Pinnawala and the elephants were great, roaming free in the waters. Took 2 hours drive to reach from port and another 1 hour drive to Kandy. Also had an elephant ride next door which was on my "to do list" when I left for this trip. Loved the serene experience.

We made the very long trip from our holiday base to see the elephants and the children weren't disappointed. Thoroughly enchanted by the sheer number of elephants and the proximity to which you can get. They loved feeding them and watching the babies be bottle fed.  We were being rushed through by a laconic tour guide so I may have missed it, but it would have been nice to have more information about the elephants around to read whilst there. Also, it wasn't really possible just to stand back and watch them without being harangued into posing for photos that you didn't want, were badly taken and resulted in demands for payment. They looked like they had lots of space and were content. Like all zoos, I have a slightly uncomfortable feeling about captive animals but there is conservation work occurring. The kids loved it and would never have seen so many elephants so close otherwise.

I have really mixed feelings about this place.. the elephants in the park where they are wandering around seems very beautiful and serene but then you see the chains and cages and it was just not what I had expected ...naively. .. I understand the reasoning as they are wild animals and there are safety implications for the visitors and staff but it just left me feeling rather sad...

Love elephants, they're beautiful. Took us 4 hours to get there from Negombo but it was worth it. Got to feed the elephants although it  was a bit scary at first cos I never met an elephant face to face but the Mahouts are on hand. I fed them Mango which I bought there but whatever you do don't carry bananas in you bag. I had some in mine and the Nelly's had their trunks in there trying to rob em, little tealeaves.I suppose with a nose like that you can tell a banana a mile off. After visiting the park you can browse the shops on the way to the river and then watch the elephants as they are led down for their daily bath. You can even help to wash them. I sat at the bar and watched a renegade group make a bid for freedom over the river only to be turned around and led back. I believe they are very well looked after and you can watch feeding time for baby elephants with giant bottles of milk. Word of warning - dont handle your cash in front of the Mahouts, they will swarm you.

We wondered about visiting as we had read some less than flattering reviews, however we were so glad we went in the end.  All the elephants we saw were well fed, healthy and happy bathing and splashing about in the river, or just wandering around. It was so nice to see them in their natural, and very beautiful environment.  Not sure it's an orphanage as such anymore, but it still needs the funding.  Well worth a visit.  Such lovely animals.

If this is your only chance to see elephants then visit it.  We watched them at the watering hole...it was ok but I am pretty sure that the 'orphanage' name could be dropped from the title. I would recommend trying to see the elephants in the wild, plenty of opportunities in this country.

There are mixed reviews about this place. We were aware that some found the orphanage a depressing place for the elephants to live. We didn't see this at all. I'm no elephant expert but they all looked happy enough to us. They are able to wander about in a large area, & the opportunity to get right up to these wonderful creatures is not to be missed. The walk of the elephants down to the river is just fantastic. Get to one of the hotels overlooking the river, grab a table &  just watch the elephants have a fantastic time swimming, playing & just enjoying themselves! Highly recommended.

We visited this orphanage early. It was a pleasantly nice seeing the whole herd of elephants bathing in the local river and the babies being bottle fed. It does get very busy here, they seem to be treated nicely here. You can plot up near the restaurant and have a beer while watching, and taking in your surroundings. I'm glad I went to see this and would return.

If you can visit place early in the morning, somewhere around 6 am, to late afternoon, you can have a good idea about this giant marvelous animal. In this place most attractive one are, feeding little elephants, watching their bathing, take a few snaps with them. Mean time you can buy lot of survivors related to elephants.

This is a fun place!  You can watch the baby elephants being bottle fed!  Try to get in the front row if you want to take photos.  Walk up the hill and watch the mature elephants feed, then walk down to the river, find a table in the restaurant, eat cheap and watch lots of elephants bathe in the river, tended by their mahouts!

Got there for before the gates opened. Walked around a bit and watched the baby elephants being bottle fed. Then walked out again as was not convinced that it was really worth spending any more time there. Was approached by a gent at the gate who suggested we go for an elephant ride (outside providers) and decided to do this. That was a good experience priced at Rs 5,000 for myself, wife and daughter (all three on one elephant) and a ride lasting about 15 minutes in total during which the elephant sprayed water on us (the mahot asked if this is ok prior to getting the elephant to do this - we were told this is for good luck).

It is amazing to hear that there is an orphanage for the baby elephants which ones literally abondened in the forest. It is really amazing to see them while they are having a bath but it is also sad that it is kind of a zoo. We human beings are there to watch and disturb them. The only thing I am so happy about that they have got a huge environment that they can actually not being caged. For kids it is so lovely to feed a baby elephant with a giant bottle.

we reached in after noon. It was very hot and humid. Tickets are very costly. Luckily it was elephant time to bath. which across the orphanage. so we directly went to see bath of elephant. Worth to see bath. But we exhausted because  of humid and hot weather so we not gone back  again to orphanage.

Real touris atraction,an rather expensif,to see feeding small elephants.Not value for monney Much more nicer to see the elephants at the bathing place in the river.At 8 o'clock are comming a few elephants to the river,,but at 10 o'clock so manny,nice to see how much they enjoy the bath

It seems they are taking a good care of orphaned elephants there. You can see the feeding "frenzy" whey the keepers drive in with the fresh food. You can buy a bag of bananas and handfeed an elephant. Nice. Then you can observe a baby elephants get bottlefed. You go across the road and down to the riverbank to watch the elephants taking bath in the river. They take the whole herd. Try to get a good spot on the restaurant balcony above the river, order youself a cold beer and watch the show, priceless almost!

An experience I will never forget, to get up close and personal, to touch and have ones photo taken with them, to see the babies being fed,  we then went to the watering hole and had the chance of feeding them there, a dream come true and a memory never to forget. The down side was lunch at the Elephant Bay Hotel. Not a good experience the food was really bad.

it was an amzing sight to see the elephants bathing and playing up close! in the rest of the site they don't have too much space which is sad. and we heard that it is no longer custom to move the elephants back into the wild which was the original motivation for the orphanage...

Our family of four enjoyed this because the kids liked the elephants. However, when walking down to the river where they bathe, we were stopped by a hand reader, who didn't tell us he was going to charge us R5000! Also, another hawker sold us bananas despite the signs saying not to feed the elephants.

We went to see the elephants at the orphanage.... I am a bit of an elephant freak! We did have a guide with us & he was brilliant. Get there early to see the babies bottle fed, about 9.30 am. We loved it... 7 litres of milk in a matter of no time! They are so funny to watch as they run into the area they know they are being fed in. After you can go & feed the bigger elephants, a bowl of fruit is about 200 Sri Lankan rupees.... £1!. Great experience. Then you walk through to see so many more all wondering around. Fabulous! At 10 am they blow a horn & the elephants walk down the street to the river. Make sure you get yourself on the right hand side facing down the street they will walk, that way you can just turn round as they come towards you. It is fantastic to see them amble down the road! There is a restaurant over looking the river. If you go in at street level, buy a beer & they are happy for you to sit there & watch the whole of the herd bathe. It is truly an amazing experience. Don't miss it!

Went to Pinnawala elephant orphanage & what a treat to see them in their own environment, watched babies being bottle fed & then the best part of the visit as 30 odd elephants are walked down to the river for a wash & brush up which they really enjoy. Something i will always remember & on a par with my visit a couple of years ago to the Taj Mahal both majical experiences.

Excellent visit - wonderful to see so many elephants in the river and being treated with kindness and courtesy by their handlers.  Lovely spot - great views; lots of stalls and food outlets.  Seeing them bottle fed was interesting.  Obviously this is a must do site if you go to Sri Lanka. I was impressed....

We went to Pinnawala reluctantly as we had previously been to elephant sanctuary in Kuala Lumpur - we saw some the elephants wondering round took pics with some and watched the feeding of milk to the little grown babies - time to go - then our driver cum guide walked us towards the river on the opposite side of the road through a narrow passage with shops and a balcony facing restaurant - four elephants walked passed us to the river - as we were watching them bathe suddenly a herd of 30 small medium and big elephants thundered passed this narrow passage and into the river. It was the most amazing sighting of so many at one time Best time 2.00 pm worth the fee

It was incredible to see the elephants, some of them were chained up and this can be upsetting to see but we were told that these elephants were unsafe. We saw these magnificent animals walking from their bathing area to the sanctuary so managed to get up close to them. Beware of the man reading palms - he approaches you as though to shake hands and before you know it he's holding his hands out for money.

It probably started out with good intentions but they are now keeping their elephants chained and training them for tourists.  Not what it promised to be.   Funniest part was when my partner stood too close to the fence of one enclosure with his straw hat tied to his backpack.  Baby elephant came and a tug of war erupted with the straw hat being ripped in two: one half down his throat an the other assigned to the bin.  Read the signs and don't get too close to the fences.

It was on my bucket list to visit this place and it was wonderful to see the elephants up close. The kids loved it - they got to give an elephant a banana and see them bathing in the river which was truly special. My two ten year olds also got to wade in and help bathe a baby elephant. Only for a few minutes and it cost £20 but I guess we thought it was worth it. What was also really, really good about that was I miscalculated the amount on paying and handed over the equivalent of £125!! But the guy was soooo honest. He argued with me (at first I thought he was after more and I was getting really annoyed) but then I realised my mistake and he said " yes, I told you you have given me far too much" and he handed it back!! Brilliant. The mixed feelings are because some of the elephants are in chains. I think it's for health and safety which I can accept, and they weren't chained up all day or anything like that. Overall I think the elephants are well treated and they have quite a bit of freedom to wander around. However, there's always the odd guy who torments and uses his power wrongly. I saw one man slowly poke his elephant in the eye to make him lie back down in the water, and another hit his elephant with a stick and shout at him. I just don't accept that this was necessary. Such a shame as I would have loved to give this place five stars.

A nice place to visit though a bit hyped. Definitely a must go for elephant lover. Check out the times for milk feeding and bathing of elephants for best experience. Elephants walk through a narrow lane towards the river which is exciting to see. Entrance fees is LKR 1400 per person. You will have to bribe the caretaker if you want to bath the elephants.

There are around 2 Elephant orphanages close to each other. One is run by the government and another is privet. We went to the privet orpahange as it was said to be the 'cheaper' one.This facility is just to make money. They charge you for the entry, elephant bath and a tiny museum. These is an elephant ride as well but offcourse with an extra charge. We paid around 500 LKR per person for the entry and elephant bath. The only good experience was bathing the elephant for 10 mins. Rest was all just ok.

Visiting the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage was one of the highlights of our trip to Sri Lanka. The baby elephants playing in their pens were so cute and fun to watch. The baby bottle feeding was interesting to see. I was able to feed fruit to one of the older elephants - getting up that close was wonderful. Our favorite was going down to the river to watch the elephants bath. It appeared to be a hundred elephants that were brought down to the river to bath and play in the water. It was wonderful to watch!

Pinnawala is a home for almost 100 of elephants of different age. Of course especially young animals are very cute. The best is observing them when bathing in the river. You needn't buy bananas from local businessmen because it's prohibited to feed the animals. Interesting is when the animal go from the areal to the river when they must cross the street and go along shops with souveniers.

This place was on ur way to Kandy. It has a Rs. 2000 or 3000 entrance fee which they say is used for the elephants. The place has a small museum with lots of elephant bones and skulls. We rode the elephants which was a nice experience. We had ridden elephants In India before but this was better since there were no seats. The place said that we could bathe the elephants in the river but were told that this would take place after a couple of hours. This was a good experience but the place should spend some of the money to maintain the facilities.

This place is well worth the visit.  You can see the babies being feed large amounts of milk, feed other elephants, and have your picture taken with adults.  Don't miss the trek from the orphanage to the river by all of the elephants.  They then bath in the river for several hours and you can watch from the riverbanks or restaurants on the river.  Also you can buy elephant dung notebooks, and other articles on the walkway to the river.

The Pinnawala orphanage was on our list of what to see in Sri Lanka from the beginning. It is not exactly wildlife experience, but you will get to see big group of elephants together. Be careful for any offers to touch them or feed them, you'll be asked to pay for that. Highlight of the visit is baby elephants feeding and bathing of elephants in the river. The river is actually out of the Orphanage area, so you have to walk a bit there, also the feeding and bathing run only in speific hours, so be sue to check and arrive o time.

Lots of differing views about this place but it was nice to see the elephants walking down to the river and roaming freely around once they arrived. For a few hundred rupees  (no fixed fee just give what you want) you can get in and help bathe an elephant  for me that was magical.

We were actually excited to see the elephants especially I am with my nephew who is 4 years old. We wanted to see the bottle feeding. When we reach there, we felt sad by looking at them. According to our guide, the elephants who are on the orphanage can't get back to the wild because they do not know how to find foods for them because all through out their life they were given food. But still I suggest you to come and visit the place. One way also for children to learn protecting our environment for these elephants. The bottle feeding time is 9:15. Then they go for bath 2x in a day. Morning and afternoon down in the river.

I was so excited to see the elephants but i was very disappointed. The entrance fee is high, the grounds are extremely busy and the elephants look miserable! This was our first tour on day 1 of our honeymoon. Initially we were very excited to be visiting an elephant orphanage but the experience left us cold to be honest. The elephants looked sad and institutionalised. While it was nice to be able to get photos and touch the elephants it just didn't feel right.

Thoroughly enjoyed our visit here. Our guide showed us round the orphanage and we got to see so many elephants. It was great to see the elephants up close and be able to touch them. These large animals were under constant supervision by their handlers and seemed well cared for. Watching the animals bathe in the local river was inspiring and witnessing the interaction with the staff. Very enjoyable.

We were excited to be seeing so many elephants, the day we went it was absolutely crazy with visiting school parties. Great to see so many elephants, but on closer inspection there were quite a few elephants in chains around the park which we did not expect. Elephant bottle feeding happens every morning, but these elephants are 3 and 4 years old so hardly babies. The high light of the visit is the elephants in the river, and they are taken from the park across a main road and down a side street to the river. Expect to see aroun 50 elephants which is great and some make a bee line for the mud on the far side. Sadly a few are chained to rocks in the river during bathing and this is the keepers chance to make a few bucks out of tourists by inviting them down to participate. Keepers more interested in making a fast buck than caring for their animals. For the best views grab a beer in the restaurant overlooking the river. Amazing to see so many beautiful elephants but there is a dark side that is not so nice.

There are many elephants here of various ages, some have been bred here some have been rescued from the wild. Could get really close to these amazing creatures but you are not allowed to touch them.some of the larger elephants are in chains, but I didn't see any mistreatment, watching them in the river was the highlight of the visit.

You can walk right up to the elephants. It's a little scary because, in some areas, there is NOTHING between you and the elephants but it's also amazing for the same reason. Rather minimal as far as things to do but if you go across the street to watch the elephants bathe in the river it is a truly unforgettable experience. They are so affectionate with one another and the little ones love to play with and tease one another. Absolutely worth the heat. My suggestion is to get there early if you're planning a day trip so you can get a seat at one of the restaurants until the crowd dies down a little. DON'T let that stop you from going down to the edge of the water though. Don't let anyone read your palm either(there are men walking around who will strike up a conversation and then take your hand to read your palm. After that, they tell you that you owe them money).

Pinnavala is located a little off the main road. Beware of local tuk tuk folks as they might try to take you to a privately run elephant center. The orphanage has over 85 elephants while the local ones have hardly 3 or 6 elephants each). Try to reach there before 10am if you want to see the first round of elephants going for bath. It is quite a ceremony to follow them. The next round of bath happens at 1:30pm. Don’t forget to take the SAARC discount. While the normal entry charges are 2500 SR for foriegners, for SAARC people it is 700 SR. You can feed the elephants while they bathe without even paying the exorbitant amount inside the orphanage. Overall it is a very nice place with lots of elephants around. dont forget to see them going for a bath and while bathing...the entire thing looks like a procession

We went to the orphanage en route to Sigriya and reached there by 12:30pm... just before the elephant feeding time as explained by our driver. There were a lot of elephants roaming freely and the mahouts were around to ensure they don't go out of hand and kept their distance. Great show of the elephants showering themselves with water and then spraying themselves with dust.... We even got to feed an elephant.. Good overall time there for around an hour or two. Best to stop by than to spend an entire day just traveling to a fro from the place.

We went to Pinnawala elephant orphanage not really knowing what to expect. We initially watched them bathing down by the river, whilst it was nice to watch, clearly the male elephants were chained to the side of the river at particular points to stop them causing trouble. I found this quite hard to watch & struggled ethically whether this was morally correct. The elephants did seem to be in good health & enjoyed their bath. As we visited at the end of March, lots of school trips were there also so it was very busy. After we went up to the orphanage I found the entry to be quite expensive overall about £13, in the orphanage again lots of elephants were chained and some were struggling again this. I found that rather uncomfortable to watch. It appears we missed other activities such as washing an elephant/feeding a baby elephant both of which I would have liked to do. People were also volunteering there. Note some tourist operators from the UK will decline to take you as they do not agree with the operation as they think this is unethical. Overall if you like elephants probably worth a visit & you can decide for yourself.

Wasn't sure whether to visit the sanctuary after reading some negative reviews but I can honestly say it was a good experience. Most of the elephants are roaming free and to see them walking to the river is great. I know there are some elephants that are chained I know it doesn't look ideal but I'm not sure how else you control animals this size, let's face it people keep dogs and still have to put them on a lead regularly! Some reviews say this place should be closed down I don't agree and where would you then put the elephants .... I say go and have a look we enjoyed it

I visited the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage as part of a daytrip from Kandy. I gather that this was once an orphanage but nowadays all new elephants are born on site and the whole thing has become mainly an expensive tourist attraction (Rs 2500 the entrance fee for foreigners). The bottle feeding of the baby elephants is equivalent to what you see in zoos, feeding fruits to the adults cost you extra money. The walk to the river and the opportunity to watch the elephants bathing in the river were more interesting, though. And on the way back to the car park you can stop in one of the shops and learn how elephant dung can be turned into paper (of course they will then try and sell you souvenirs made of "elephant paper"...).
