Hardly worth a visit as there is little to see here. Some elephants in compounds, some chained and a few roaming free. A half hour visit will suffice. There is a distinct lack of signage and information, we just wandered around. Most workers/keepers were asking for money if we photographed any elephants. This money was going into their pockets, not towards the 'orphanage'.

We went to Pinnawala as part of a drive around Sri Lanka and, as a wildlife writer and zoologist, I felt I should judge the place for myself. Trust me: this is not a good way to care for elephants and only if tourists stop going will the authorities take their responsibilities towards elephants seriously. We watched the elephants bathe - all ok - but we sneaked around the back to see the captive elephants, chained with limited potential for movement or expression of natural behaviour. They had sores around their ankles and were showing repeated, stressed behaviour. The elephants here are bred and kept purely for tourism, this is not a sanctuary and the Born Free Foundation, and others, have highlighted welfare issues. Elephants are extremely intelligent animals that live in close-knit families; they deserve better than this.

The orphanage is nicely laid out but there is really very little to see, which cannot be seen in any decent zoo. The trip though the small steet packed with turist, elephants, shops (and turists) down to the river is of course something else. It is nice to see the elephants in the river, but the entire experience of the caretakers trying to get people to pay to get to wash a chained elephant, nailed the overall experience as a complete turist trap. We went 5 minutes down the road to the Club Concept Elephant Riding and museum and had a much nicer and calmer experience washing and riding an elephant.

Really do avoid going here. It may once have cared for orphaned elephants, however now it's really a zoo. There is no information on the conservation or care of the elephants. It appears that they are being bred and kept. The handlers encourage you to take pictures and then demand money At the riverside some elephants are chained for pictures and to be fed (for a price) some looked quite distressed. As the tourist industry expands this place, if left unchecked, will get worse. Avoid and go to a national park instead

While we travel from Colombo to Kandy DJ travels took us nice place in Pinnawala 86.5 km away from Colombo its took 2h 35 minutes to drive there. We could acknowledge regarding milk feeding time as first feeding is 9.15 a.m. and the 2nd feeding was 1.15 p.m. 12 O' clock elephants coming to there living place by the river and they going back again 2 O'clock . We could see around 100 elephants there and small elephants are very interesting thing in this orphanage , specially among the children. We can stay this place more than 3 hours , its so interesting.

Arrived for the afternoon feeding session. Initially, you come to a large area where there are elephants and 'keepers'. The keepers invite you to come up to them for a photo opportunity. They have trained the elephants to react to their commands so they are able to manoeuvre these large animals into a position for photographs. After about a minute of photographs comes the 'demand' for money. If they are not happy with what you give them they have no hesitation in asking for more. If you decline, they effectively ask you to leave that particular area. Then comes the feeding times for the 'baby' elephants. Limited shady viewing area here, so need to get there in good time. The trainers give milk through feeding bottles and are happy to pose for photos, no money requested this time! The best bit of all is when animals are all herded down to the near bye river. We had an opportunity to watch from one of the near bye restaurants, and as they are in an elevated position the view is good. The elephants clearly enjoy this session and 50 of them can be seen rolling / playing in the river for nearly 2 hrs. For us, this was the best part of the whole experience

While I agree it is for tourists still it provides the opportunity to see and photograph dozens of elephants close up and of course the children are beside themselves with happiness feeding and caressing the smaller ones. Much better than seeing them do tricks in a circus and being hauled around in trucks from city to city!

Here we found lots of orphaned elephants protecting by wildlife department of Sri Lanka.Bathing view is nice at Maha Oya twice a day.Among the group there are few baby elephants as well.I noticed some out side business parallel running around the orphanage.They will offer you to bath,feed..options for elephants where you might not have chance in official park.But remember then your contribution will not goes to orphanage

As a visitor we paid 2500 rupees each (£12.50) locals pay 100 rupees (.50p) feeding time is ok if you're there first or are 7 ft tall as viewing places are limited. Viewing at the river is the place to be so reserving a table at one of the riverside resurants would be prudent.

Pinnawala Orphanage is such an amazing experience! We have never been so close to the elephants!  The best time to go there is the early morning, as the first bottle feeding time is 9.15 and at 10.00 starts the elephant transfer to Maha Oya (just across the road), this is where the bath time is. It is unique to see so many elephants walking so close to you. You can touch them, you can wash them in the water. The entrance for overseas visitors is LKR 2500.00 (Adult) and LKR 1250.00 (children), Sri Lankans pay LKR 100.00/LKR 30.00, SAARC visitors LKR700.00/LKR 350.00. Staff inside the orphanage will aks you for extra money if you want to wash them or when they take you closer to touch them. Do not pay, as all this is included in your ticket, plus compare the rates, I can't see any reason why shall we do so, because the money goes to the pocket not to the orphanage itself. Guy by the river asked me for another LKR 2500.00 which I refused to pay. It can be very annoying, however you need to ignore this, otherwise you can run out of money very soon by tipping everyone. Overall very unique place, which worths to visit!

I have mixed feelings about this place...it was enjoyable seeing the elephants...but using them to make money was not so okay with me...it was a very hot day...they were in search of water...I felt really bad...milk were fed as a show...I don't get the point out of it...I felt funny being there just to see something like that since it's nature ...there don't need to be exhibition on it

Feeding was very interesting, two babies were there, they are very headstrong. Always calling for milk! You can see them from close. Than half of the group went to the river. Keepers are bathing their, some of them just chilling in the water. There were 2 or 3 "teenager" elephants, who was on chain, I think because on that they you can feed them from close, it was a little bit sad, one of them really wanted to go play, but can't. I hope they are changing everyday. Cool to see them just chilling in the water.

We left the Elephant Orphanage with mixed feelings. On the one hand it was nice to be so close to Elephants but on the other hand I felt sorry for them. They are being used as an attraction to make more people come visit this place and I can only imagine how stressed they have to be while being fed in front of hundreds of tourists. I visited here hearing it was an elephant orphanage that the elephants had been rescued, only to arrive and see some of them including very young in chains being forced to be washed by tourists, when I asked why they were in chains I was told they are in training!!! I have mixed emotions as I wrongly assumed they would be in as natural environment as possible, not being trained to be touched by humans... very sad to see this

Was there in Oct last and it was an eye opener. We arrived there with our guide who made sure we there In plenty of time. It is important to be there for the feeding and for a small charge you can feed the young elephants and all the money goes to help the elephants. Be there At the right time of the morning also all the elephants are brought down to the river to get washed and there also one can help wash them for a charge and buy food to feed the elephants and get your photo taken with them. There is a restaurant where one can sit and eat while watching the elephants.

From the look of it, it was extremely crowded – the street, the ticket counter. It was bound to be. It was after all 25th Dec, a holiday. One last time I tried to dissuade the duo, but they refused to re-consider. Elephants we have come to see and elephants we shall see, they retorted and went off for the tickets. I, on my part, recovered from a feeble OK and went up to the ticketing area to see if they had anything for disinterested souls like me. Yes, there was —  Sri Lanka’s famous memorabilia store, Laksala. I hovered around the store while Jayant and Niharika, squealed and ogled at elephants eating their lunch and eating veggies off their hands. The orphanage is popular with kids and grownup alike (as you can tell from the interest shown by my family) since it offers a whole lot of attractions, such as, bottle feeding thrice a day, bathing in the river twice a day, once in the morning and once, late afternoon. Tickets are fare for Rs 2500 for adults and Rs 1250 for kids. If you belong to one of the SAARC nations, tickets will cost you Rs 700 and Rs 350. Poo Paper-Making Center: This center is right opposite the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. The staff there take you through a tour of the paper-making techniques through the elephant’s poo, and then take you to the adjacent shop where you can buy products made of the paper you just saw being made. Quite an educational tour for kids. It is free and not binding upon you to buy the products. We’d recommend you to go, take a look.

I visited Pinnawala orphanage two days ago and have some mixed emotions. I don't understand why are some reviewers complaining about elephants who are never going to be set free after their time here because the orphanage internet site clearly states that this isn't the case since the animals become dependent of feeding and the rituals and I understand that. I really love elephants and it was a once in a lifetime experience to see them being bathed and bottle fed. I liked the fact that we, the tourists were able to buy the food and feed them on site and I truly hope that the money we'd spent there didn't dissappear in some pockets because that's the real problem here! I find it extremely unacceptable to be using them as circus toys! And that's basically the case. They'll let you pet them, bathe them, take photographs with them - anything for a tip and this was disgusting! But there are some real idiot tourists out there who would do anything for a picture with an elephant. What?! As long as this is the case, the problem will remain existent. I love the elephants and I loved the visit, but the behaviour of SOME trainers/workers is to be banned and punished.

We had taken this off our itinerary as we didn't think we had enough time. Our driver said we would have time after kandy and on our way back to Colombo. We'll talk about timing , as we arrived it was 2pm and the elephants were just leaving the sanctuary and heading down to the water to bathe, we enjoyed a blissful hour watching them bathe in the water. Unfortunately we didn't have time to see anymore of the sanctuary but would visit again with more time. Costs about £10 each to go in. Worth to put on your itinery, just get your timing right so you can see the bathing.

You'll see elephants and they seem to be well treated - however, it's important to be realistic and realise that this place is not really an orphanage any more. We really enjoyed seeing elephants in the wild by the side of the road or on safari and recommend that above Pinnawala.

Visited in late February 2016. Although it was a treat to see these magnificent creatures at close quarters, there are plenty of locals who will tell you that they are not released into the wild. Apparently these animals are bred on site and kept in captivity for the rest of their lives, never experiencing freedom. There have been a number of protests by animal lovers. It's quite expensive to visit if you are a foreigner... Much cheaper for the Asian community. It seems to be a money making venture at the expense of these lovely animals. Go on a safari in one of the nature reserves instead and see them in the wild.... Where they should be.

I support helping elephants and would like to believe the publicity of the orphanage but after a visit I can't decide if it''s being run for the benefit of the elephants of for the commercial exploitation of tourists ... and the elephants. It is a very organised tourist attraction which obviously brings in large amounts of cash which the orphanage can then spend on the elephants but I got the distinct feeling that the elephants were being used as performers. The other worrying sight was the 5 or 6 adult elephants that were chained because their behaviour was unpredictable - 2 of them were repeatedly swaying from side to side and looked distressed.

This was our third visit and we were disappointed to see how commercial it has become.  The handlers want money for any photographs taken with the elephants - several elephants had chains on their feet - the water was very low this year and they seemed very unhappy to how I remember several years ago before all this very commercial expensive enclosure was built. One would only hope that money is put back into releasing elephants back into their natural habitat  - all in all would not go back and came away not feeling very happy about the whole experience - not to be recommended I am sad to say as someone who loves elephants and would never use them commercially such as rides etc.  A lot of improvement is needed before I would visit again.

I visited the Elephant orphanage on a Sunday in March for a few hours. The elephants were majestic and I enjoyed every minute when they walked around and played with each other. One of the best moments of my entire Sri Lanka tour was when the elephants crossed the street on their way back from the river and looked around at all the people waiting for them. But some moments were quite different: I saw an elephant by himself in a small area behind a fence, desperately trying to reach water next to him who was held by a chain around his leg. The employees also offer you to touch the elephants for a tip when no manager is looking. While the elephants have plenty of space and are not abused for rides, it felt wrong to have them pose for pictures. I nevertheless strongly recommend going there!

Maybe our guide didn't give us the full experience but we came away feeing a bit cheated!! The sight of 30 or 40 elephants of all ages having a bath was wonderful but we thought we were coming to see the orphanage in action and maybe see a bit more? Any way what we saw was great but nothing we hadn't already seen in the wild in Kenya for example. The place is very busy and hideously commercialised!!

its fun to watch is elephant's bathing time on the river. Baby elephants do some funny and cute things while they are bathing. This is not a must visit place when you travel to srilanka but if you can easily reach to pinnawala then you can visit the orphanage.

If you have seen the elephants in the safari trip and rode an elephant and took pics with it in Kandy, I dont see a reason why to visit Pinnawala. We couldnt feed baby elephants which was our reason for going, if you go closer to the elephants you will find yourself surrounded by soo many Keepers asking for a tip. I think it was a waste of money.

This was the first stop in our tour of Sri Lanka and did not know what to expect. Turned out good with a great chance to see many elephants and when we arrived they were being bathed in the river. Not an expert but they did appear to be looked after well. I'm sure others might disagree. I did get the chance to hose down one so got close and it deal feel good. However, there is no question it is geared towards tourists, but the money made appears to be going to help orphaned elephants.

I admire this place for its "social" cause, namely protecting the elephant orphans. It was also lovely sipping my cider while overlooking the elephants playing in the water. However, I was left wanting to see more elephants in a more natural habitat. Visitors are only allowed entry to a very limited number of areas.

The idea behind the orphanage is sound and to be commended though the facilities for the elephants need to be enhanced and given the amount of money I'm certain is being generated I can only hope that some of it is reinvested (as I'm not sure where the money is going), particularly in building enclosures for the male elephants who are restrained in a life of mental torture swaying from side to side, as far as their chains allow when they're not being allowed down to the river (or any other supervised activity I'm unaware of that they participate in). I would have been nice to find out if they were doing anything to support the elephants in the wild, if they had managed to release any animals into the wild (particularly if there are wild elephants re-homed there after finding themselves in the wrong place). This was our fist experience of the power/expectation of 'tipping' in Sri Lanka as you're expected to tip to have photos taken near elephants etc. - I do appreciate that wages are low but would have preferred to pay my tips into a fund to improve staff conditions overall as well as contributing to the improvement of the facility.

My wife and I went here en route back to Colombo before flying home the following day. Admittedly we were hot and tired but found the elephant orphanage to be over priced and a generally an unpleasant experience all round. We arrived at lunchtime when the elephants were in the river bathing. The entrance fee was £12 each, not a huge sum of money but a lot more than other attractions in Sri Lanka. As others have commented it does go to a good cause. Beware of people selling fruit to feed to the elephants on the riverside - they seem to have a scheme going with the people in charge of the elephants. An elephant will be brought up for you to feed whilst they take photos of you - then you'll be expected to pay 1000 rupees each to several people. When we refused to pay that amount they became unpleasant towards us. Although this does break to journey up nicely from Colombo to Kandy I would have preferred to do something else instead  - e.g. roadside restaurant or spice garden.

A fantastic place to get up close and personal with these wonderful creatures, whilst contributing to a very worthy cause. My wife and I both approaches this with slight trepidation as we were concerned about ever present animal cruelty issues. These proved to be unfounded in the Elephant Orphanage. Part of the experience is seeing elephants in a relatively natural habitat, and getting very close to them through the keepers good management. Also, follow down to the river around 10:30 where you can help wash them! All staff expect tips for photos/activities, don't feel pressured but do give something.

A novel experience. The baby and young elephants are all orphans, or rejected by their parent elephants. They are not all there because of man kind's cruelty. We watched baby elephants being bottle fed and then a large group were led to the river where we watched them bathe. It was clear that these animals are well cared for and were happy in their situation. There is a programme for releasing them in groups when they are mature enough, that enables them to adapt back into their natural environment and to be accepted back by others in the wild.

I would not agree with some reviews that I have read here. This orphanage took elephants that were abused, and takes care of them. Yes, they charge visitors for an entrance, feeding them and taking pictures, but most of that money goes through proper channel to fund this orphanage, as long as I could fathom. Elephants are chained from neck to foot because fast running elephant could harm people, it is the same thing that is done to cows and oxen before taking them to graze. Also, those animals are saved from killed parents, abusive tourists that rode them, so I think that paying to feed them and take pictures is not an abuse and it doesn't harm the animals. Try to come from 10 to 12am, or 2 to 4pm, when they bathe the elephants, because whole herd looks impressive. After that visit them in orphanage, observe them, because I found it more interesting to look at their behavior instead of endless and pointless picture taking. Each one or pair does a different thing, they are quite individual. They are very friendly animals, and babies like to be cuddled at head and forehead. Also there was one elephant couple that had a "fight" who gets to bathe in small pool, and they looked like lazy people pushing each other from a couch. Great 10 minute show that I have enjoyed. 1:15pm is baby bottle feeding time, but I missed this because my group left at 1pm.

The Pinnawala Elephant orphanage providing care and protection to many of the orphaned unweaned wild elephants found wandering in the forests of Sri Lanka. The best place to see and feed Elepahnts. If you are lucky you will get the chance to bottle feed the baby Elephants as well. Elephants will walk to the river two times a day for bath and it will be a wonderful opportunity to watch them having a bath.

Reading a lot of reviews before going but actually. After sitting with a local gentlemen who explained the chains and sticks. It was for our safety. Do remember that these are wild animals. The animals we happy with the tourist and the bathing was amazing. Had lunch whilst watching the elephants.

This visit was part of a guided tour of Sri Lanka and we spent a couple of hours there.  My overall impression was good. You will not get a better opportunity to see so many elephants in a controlled but semi-wild environment.   Three are three main facets to the visit.  First you can go to the river and see them bathing followed by a processional walk on the road back to the orphanage.   This area is very commercial including a restaurant and several shops and vendors.  Intriguingly you can also see the process of converting elephant poo into paper! Next there is the large area where the elephants roam free and this is probably the best.  Here you can see them feeding and generally enjoying themselves.  We did see a couple of animals with chains and were informed this was for their own safety as they had not yet got used to captivity. Finally there is the entertaining but rather less satisfactory area where the public is very close to young elephants being fed with bottled milk etc.   This is very commercially organised. This is not a zoo but an orphanage where elephants are cared for in circumstances where they might well die in the wild.  I understand that the fact that some are chained would upset animal lovers, but I think it is a case of the greater good bringing more safety to a large number. I'm glad I went but will not revisit.

Anybody who loves animals - don't go there. They make a lot of money with the tourists, pretending to "help" elephants. First they charge a high entrance fee, then you are ushered all the time to pay again: to feed the elephants, to wash them, to take a photo with them etc. It's all about money. Which would be ok if it was for the elephants. But this is not an orphanage, this is animal hoarding. They don't have a lot of space, the babies are isolated in a small concrete arena with no place to hide and no grass and nothing. Some of the big elephants had bad diarrhea. When they are led through the city down to the river (thank god they can bath in water at least), some elefants are tied to a short chain so that tourists can "wash" and touch them. For money of course. There are many zoos with much better conditions. Pinnawala is just a circus. We felt very ashamed having gone there...

Why go to see elephants chained and corralled with hundreds if not more tourists when it is relatively easy to see them in the wild at Minerya Nat'l Park, Yala NP and Udawalawe NP? Seeing them en mass in the river was a thrill but it felt more like a circus than a sanctuary. There is no information about the elephant rescue program on site and apparently no efforts to return elephants to the wild. This seems to be a breeding ground for temple elephants. They look reasonably well fed and certainly better off than left as orphans in the wild, but (again, lacking better information) how many are truly rescued vs being bred on site?

While it is an exhilarating experience to watch elephants being splashed with water in the river, having an opportunity to feed them and seeing them all file back to their 'orphanage', the whole experience is negated by the feeling of animals being exploited for tourists and being not much better than a circus act. Native Sri Lankans are totally disillusioned as the orphanage did start with very worthy aims and intentions. Animals are chained so that it is possible to get very close to them at feeding time without them being a danger. The alternative would be for the animals to roam free in an enclosure and be seen from a distance. The overwhelming feeling is of animals being exploited. The touts angling for money for supplying food and taking photographs of visitors (with visitors own phones or cameras) feeding and stroking the elephants are aggressive and very unpleasant. If the money goes to the orphanage this would be tolerable but there is a strong suspicion that it does not. I have very mixed feelings about my visit. Elephants are magnificent creatures and it is a great experience to see so many at very close quarters. This is offset by the behaviour of the touts and a feeling that this is now a money making zoo with elephant welfare a distant second. I don't think they are ill treated but rescue and return to the wild doesn't seem to happen much if at all.

This place markets itself as an orphanage but is really just a place that horribly exploits and trafficks elephants. It is no better than the elephant trekking places who have beaten those elephants to make them submissive and safe for human contact. If you care about animals, do not visit these places. Do your homework for the animal's sake.

This is one of the must go places in Sri Lanka. To see the elephants drain bottle after bottle of milk, use their feet to break out the middle of trees to eat and appear to just inhale large chunks of fruit is fascinating. The high light though is to see them just wander across the road, down to the river and then enjoy themselves, ambling about in the water, rolling around and spraying each other, smashing. Their are not many signs in the attraction and a general lack of information so you need to be on your toes if you don't want to miss out. The staff are not allowed to take tips so beware of them offering to take your photograph and then demanding money, don't pay,

Its a great effort to maintain this sanctuary for these elephants.With human elephant conflict on the rise in SL maybe they have some protction here. Ever seen Elephants Bathing,Having food & Playing with thier Lil oNes??? head to Pinnawala elephant orphange if u would love to watch all this. it was a amazinnggg & altogether diffrent Experience.however they have a spcific timings. you can always confirm it & visit

Visiting Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage seems to be obligatory for all foreign tourists. We left Kandy very early to be in time for the baby elephant feeding – the baby elephants looked to be at least 4 years old so not tiny. They were fed milk out of empty alcohol bottles in a small rotunda that visitors stand around. After the feeding you can walk up to a large corral and for an extra cost can hand feed large elephants with watermelon and bananas. After this they are walked to the river for a bathe – all very civilised but we don’t know what goes on behind the scenes. At the river the mahouts almost drag people down to pat the elephants and have their photo taken with them – again at a price. Apart from that there isn’t really much else to see or do at the orphanage so if you aren’t there at feeding or bathing times it wouldn’t really be worthwhile.

This visit was sold to us as the ultimate in elephant orphanage - best place for them to be looked after / see them feeding and bathing in their natural habitat etc etc. The truth is a little more disappointing. Our guide/driver described this as a highlight so we went here on our first full day in Sri Lanka. I was a little bit hesitant because of the past reviews here that described the orphanage as quite cruel. It's of course hard to say whether or not those elephants were actually orphaned or otherwise, but the ones that were there looked very well cared for. The admissions was LKR 2,500 per foreign adult, paid in cash. 9:30 am was the bottle feeding session (though the bottle fed elephants were already 3-4 years old and not tiny - they could easily have done some damage) and we walked around a bit where the mahout were allowing people to get very close to the elephants, touch them and take photos with them. We opted out of that because as our guide said, the mahout (elephant keeper) probably shouldn't be allowing that close contact with untrained strangers and elephants as they are, after all, still wild and can be violent animals. The real highlight was at 10 am when they walk the elephants to the river across the street. Grab a seat at one of the cafes (ideally the one on the right hand side when you're facing the river) and watch the elephants splash around with glee! The mahouts also scrubbed them down and the elephants looked so happy spraying water on themselves and playing with the mud. Some of the elephants were in chains and according to our guide, they are the more aggressive ones. But the majority were not chained and generally looked well cared for. I'm not sure if I would go back but definitely enjoyed the experience this one time.

Observed. Eventually the tracker falls off, as the elephant growsWe were lucky to have a knowledgeable guide taking us around. The elephants are not released into the wild ,because they are with the orphanage from birth ,or as a calf ,and being reared in captivity where they need to be for 4 years means they will not survive on their own in the wild. Other places, where baby elephants are reared, do not accept tourists, so the elephants are reared close to nature and are rereleased with a tracker, so they can be observed at how they cope in the wild. Also the elephants, who are shackled ,is for safety ,whilst the public visit. I have it on good authority that they are unshackled ,once the public have gone. We also saw 2  baby orphans whose mothers were killed on a railway track. There was also an adult elephant who had fallen on its side and was propped up in irons, because an elephant's lungs are on the side of its body and when it falls over the lungs can be damaged. To let the lungs heal is the reason it is tied in the metal contraption, not to be cruel to it. We had some photos taken with the elephants as a memory of this event and paid a small fee of 250 rupees, for this experience. Unfortunately, we never saw the elephants in the water or being bottled fed. Worth the experience to see.

We went to this attraction in February, 2016.  We only went for the bathing time.  Admission was $16 USD.  Buy your ticket first and then you can enter. At 10AM they walked the elephants to the river and bathed some of them (I guess they have to take turns).  You can sit in the restaurant that overlooks the river to have a drink or a bite to eat (or not).  Great view for pictures.  At 12 noon, they walk the elephants back to the enclosure. The elephants looked well taken care of.

Pinnawala is touristy; and very busy. Elephants certainly looked well cared for and the site is well managed. If captive animals are not your thing then don't go!

This was a great experience and especially wonderful to watch around 90 elephants bathing in the river Maa Oya, their procession at noon back to their compound and then see them there. Some moaning on tripadvisor about mahmouts asking for tips for photo opportunities with the elephants. Yes they may well do, but these are very poor people indeed in comparison to the tourists, they do a very good job, and the amounts involved are very small indeed and help supplement their income and their families.

We went to this place on commendation of our driver as we wanted to do a day trip from Colombo.  This place is about 3 hour's drive towards Kandy.  They look after abandoned elephants from temples etc there.  We booked a short ride for about an hour.  The tickets cost about £10.00 each which included a tour of the establishment, a short elephant ride, which was sufficient to give a good idea of a relaxing ride.  If one wants, they can wash the elephants in a nearby river as well but you need not have shorts and sandals if you don't like wet clothes.  They have a small restaurant for snacks and drinks.

Yes the elephants are rescued. Yes the elephants are having the daily bath and scrub. I am not sure the Orphanage is doing it gest to bring the elephants back in to the jungle. It is good to see lots of Elephants in the river. To enter this site you have to pay some thousands rupees to Gowerment again. As part of our visit this place was included and most of us liked the way the orphanage keeps and look after the elephants, feeding them and bathing them. You can see a lot of elephants of different age and breeds. Place to spend an hour and see the wildlife in urban style.

The elephant orphanage is a great place to understand how the Sri Lankans have and continue to treat elephants. You get to see the good and the bad. The elephants are being rescued but still in chains. There behavior is corrected in a very physical manor which may strike some people as cruel. If you know what to expect. I would say this is a great cultural experience but not 100% warm and fuzzy. It is much better than what would have happened to these elephants if not for the orphanage.

There are always questions about whether we should be charged Rs2500 (£12) when locals are charged only Rs 50. The ticket states part of the cost of the orphanage is met by its earnings. This is my third visit to the orphanage. The highlight is always watching the herd including baby elephants walking gracefully  to the river for their fun time. It is mesmerising. One needs to spend two or three hours going to different sections to watch them feed, being fed or just resting. If it is just to watch them bathing, or being bathed (buckets of water thrown over their body which they seem to love , some tourists talked about buying drinks/ lunch at the restaurants overlooking the river without purchasing the entrance tickets.  These had clear views of the elephants but difficult to take close up photographs. This is my third visit to this orphanage. In addition to the increase in number of young elephants there are certainly a huge increase in the number of tourists who go there. There was one elephant chained at the riverbank looked distressed and restless moving its head side to side. It was upsetting to see this. I first came here in 2000 and loved it. We now have two young children so wanted to show them the elephants. We booked in to a hotel which was a clean and comfortable b&b but nothing special but we were right by the water so could see the elephants. The place has become much more for tourists with coach loads of people arriving regular. The main walk down to the walk has all the same stalls with little gifts to buy. It is very hot in the little walk way and the kids found it a bit much. But they loved seeing the elephants. We didn't get hassled much although our two blond girls do draw a bit of attention! We had an elephant ride in a very quite place that was recommended to us and it was amazing although be prepared to get wet!!!!! My parents are residents here so get into somethings cheaper. But I think the orphanage is a bit expensive for what it is.

This is the second time we visited the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. Both times we had the forenoon session. We were quite fascinated by the baby jumbos playing, the milk bottle feeding and the river bathing. One should know the timings before visit. 9 am  to 10 am watching the elephants play, feeding milk to baby elephants and public fruit feeding. between 10 & 12 noon is the batching of elephants in the river. What I still could not understand is why some of them were chained and a few of them poked with sharp tools that was a bit rude. Absolute joke! Your better off going to the Zoo. As most of SL attractions it is completely overrated and overpriced. The Elephants are not really orphans and treated really badly. Most of the big ones are chained at two legs to keep them in place so the tourist crowd can take pictures. CLOSE THIS PLACE DOWN!

A fascinating place but without a guide or access to information about the orphanage and its activities/aims etc was limited. The baby feeding was moving but the highlight was the movement of the elephants to the river. One of the elephant attendants offered to take a photo of us with an elephant. We came to understand that foreighners are seen as a source of tips on any possible occasion. It was interesting that you could use Mastercard to buy at the  merchandise centre but not 200 yards away to pay the entry fee, which left us in the position of borrowing funds from our driver. I had very mixed feelings visiting this place. I wanted to visit a place where the elephants are truly well taken care of. I believe this place used to be like that but now I found it too tourist oriented. The elephant caretaker came over and pulled me to take a picture with an elephant. I was surprised but very happy to be so close to it and tried not to interfere with it's activities to much, but being so close to it for the first time in my life, could not resist posing for pictures and hanging around it for a short while - just love these beautiful creatures :) After that the caretaker expected a tip. It just didn't feel like the people taking care of these animals were really devoted to them. They also let you feed the elephants and have a few selected little ones to be bottle-fed in front of the onlookers (supposedly most babies are raised on mother's milk). Unfortunately, being on tight schedule with our tour, we missed the elephants going to the river to take a bath which many people review as the best part. I'm against animal exploitation and avoid all the acrobatic shows and the zoo but if you're looking for a true animal sanctuary there are for sure better out there.

I visited the orphanage back in 2000 and 2001. Then, there were just a handful of elephants and their attendants looking after them, but you really go to see and hear how the elephants were being cared for.  I recently returned and was shocked at the changes. There were so many tourists, and not enough staff to control where people went. The tourist ignored the sign, slipped past the fence, and ran up and snapped photos wildly. This agitated the male tusker significantly. There was no real information given on the care of the elephants. People lined up to see the babies being fed. The place is more like a zoo, now.

We were really in two minds as whether we wanted to visit the orphanage after reading the reviews, we love elephants however! We arrived in time to see the elephants walking to the river, an impressive sight to see a small herd. We were on the corner, behind a little shop rail and they were so close we could have touched them, they are certainly huge magnificent animals and I must admit a few times I stepped back against the shop window, when they stopped right in front of me. Took some great photos we then spent time looking at the shops and waited to view the elephants returning to the river at 2.00pm. For us this was enough and we didn't feel the need to purchase the tickets to see more.

Good experience. Good or bad I won't know. Elephants are chained yes. But, the question is... As against what. Roaming free ?? The mobility in the venture needs to be appreciated. Orphaned giants are cared for. Some form of care is better than neglect. The little ones were the cutest and kept running around. Worth  a visit if not for anything at least the fee you pay which I hope reached the elephants or their needs. I'll try to spend more time here. Don't miss it...its worth a visit..

I visited the orphanage in January of 2016 and instantly became upset with the fact that most of the elephants are chained. We did enjoy the lunch they had down by the river and enjoyed seeing the elephants bathing my advice to anyone would be just to do this part of the trip.

I brought 3 US friends who wanted to see the orphanage. Immediately upon entering we were called over to a chained elephant to get our picture taken. One worker came up to one of the women and I suggested she give him 100 rupees. He wanted 1000 but I told him he was only getting 100.He walked away swearing something rude. We did view the elephants being bathed in the river while eating lunch across the street from the facility, that was a really great experience that helped us forget the terrible experience inside the orphanage. My advise-stay away or refuse any picture taking etc.

A 1h30min drive with the tuk tuk from Kandy you will be seeing elephants galore. The trip from Kandy to Pinnawala is most agreable: the hill scenery is quite impressive. If you are travelling alone or as a family, be sure to ask for the orphanage as 3km before the orphanage there is an elephant observatory which is not the same. The troups of elephants leaving the orphanage to take their daily bath is impressive. You can view the bathing on front row seats at the hotel, but be ware of sweaty old men wanting to read the palm of your hand: you'll unwantingly hear that you'll be 92 years old for 3000 rupees - I only had 250 rupees and almost did not make it till 43... A visit to the poo paper factory is nice and they do not push you to buy. Do not visit the obscure spice garden: there are nicer gardens (and better sales men) along the road between Matale en Kandy. I didn't stay for the feeding (at around 12h30) because I wanted to combine with a visit to the botanical gardens on my way back to Kandy.

Unfortunately this experience didn't live up to any of my expectations. I don't know what I was expecting but to see the poor elephants being yelled at and poked at with spears was definitely NOT it. There is nothing joyful or free about these beautiful elephants and supporting this place made me sick to my stomach. The elephants were being hurt and they were clearly very scared of the mahouts which is absolutely NOT how their relationship should be. The only purpose of this place is to entertain the huge crowd of tourists with absolute no regard towards these majestic animals and it was therefore absolutely acceptable for the mahouts to use hooks on the elephant's ears to force it to lay down in the water and look cute. I highly recommend the Pinnawala Elephant Orhanage!! The elephants here seem to have an amazing life. They have about 25 acres of beautiful land to roam freely in. They have plenty of food and shade. Twice a day they get walked to the river to bathe, explore, and play at their leisure for a few hours. The facility costs 2500 rupees for an adult admission and it is well worth it! You can watch the baby elephants get fed by bottle; and for an additional 250 rupees, you can purchase a basket of fruit to feed some of the larger elephants. Then you can follow the herd down to the river and watch them have fun in the water and river banks. So many photo ops! Please do not confuse this government ran orphanage with a couple of the local businesses who own elephants for tourist joy rides. Who knows how well those elephants are treated or how they came to own them. I assume any negative reviews on how elephants are being mistreated are actually about these other businesses. Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is in Sabaragamuwa Province of Sri Lanka on the way to Kandy. The orphanage was founded in order to take care and protect orphaned wild elephants found wandering in nearby forests. The Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage was established by the Sri Lankan Department of Wildlife Conservation for feeding and providing care and sanctuary to orphaned baby elephants that were found in the wild. This is situated in a 25 Acre coconut plantation area near banks of river Maa Oya. Elephants are taken in groups for bathing to Maa Oya River .We were told by the guide that there are around 60/70 elephants consisting of baby elephants and grownup ones... The orphanage feed, nurse and house young elephants found abandoned by their mothers. Young elephants sometimes fall into pits and ravines in their quest for water during drought period. These elephants are brought to orphanage and cared for. Veterinary care is provided for wounded elephants which are adopted by this orphanage. An entry fee is charged which is Rs.700 /-(SLR) per head. The orphanage is open for visitors from 8.30 AM to 5.30 PM. One can watch the elephants being taken to river for bath in herds at 10 AM and 2 PM and return from river after bath at 12 noon and 4 PM.  We went from Pinnawala orphanage to River Maa Oya which is just across the orphanage to watch elephants bathing. There are a lot of Hotels offering good food. This is must visit place if one is visiting Kandy in Srilanka.

We got there at about 12:30am - it was about 2 hours from a very busy Kandy - when you arrive it may be very busy when you go to get your tickets - look for the foreign ticket office as this is where non Sri Lankan / Indians buy tickets and 'we pay more' 2500 rupees and half price for under 12's - keep your tickets safe because you'll need to show them again when you follow the elephants to their bathing place. In the orphanage itself it was great to be so close to them and my kids even our eldest 18 enjoyed feeding the little ones and we got some great pictures of the kids with some of the herd literally side by side. When the herd went to bathe this is across the road and you follow them through an alley of shops - what a experience that was seeing them in the water cooling off literally 40 meters away - and please wait until they leave the water - watch them come out and walk toward you as the herd heads off back to the orphanage. We loved watching these beasts coming up out of the water and heading towards us! Do not use the loo's outside the orphanage unless you are used to wet washing toilets and carry your own paper with you. The best thing was these elephants looked really well cared for and 'happy' I loved it and get real it is not expensive - great value for money in my view.

I was not planning to take my family here as the reviews made it out to be an overly commercial place, aimed at taking as much money from thrust as possible. However, an opportunity arose and some local friends took us. I must say, it was not a bad experience. The journey from Colombo takes about 2 hrs, leaving at 6 am. The drive back took around 3 hrs. The only negative aspect was the entrance and trying to get into the place. Absolute chaos! Once through, the orphanage is good with plenty of opportunity to get up close and personal with one of nature's most magnificent creatures! My 1 year old boy could not get enough. Next, a walk down to the river to check them out bathing. Another nice experience, although the elephant handlers are always trying to get tourist to wash or touch the elephants and then ask for money.  A reasonable rate to pay is RS300. In summary, a good place to visit but go early in order to mitigate the awful traffic.

The orphanage has three parts where we enjoyed our company with the elephants. Part I: Shower in the river During the day, the elephants will be led to a river opposite to the orphanage for a shower. To my surprise, the elephants do not shower themselves but they are waiting for the caretakers to splash them with buckets of water! You get really close to the elephants and there are lots of them. There are also seats by the river so you can get a sip while watching. Part II: Feeding At 1:30pm, they also have a feeding session. Several elephants juveniles are fed with milk. The feeding part itself is a bit "plain" - basically pouring bottles of milk without much actions. Not as spectacular as the shower. Part III: Walking around the orphanage At any single point of time, there are dozens of elephants in the orphanage where you can see them in a really close distance. For those who love elephants, it is a must go!

To say that we were right above the elephants bathing is not an exaggeration so close providing an almost intimate experience. Approximately 50 elephants of all sizes from babies to full grown adults having the most fantastic time in the water staying there for well over an hour. The view is magnificient. Could have stayed for a lot longer just soaking in the atmosphere but I guess even Elephants know when they have had enough.

After an early start we travelled from Bentota to Pinnawala village and settled into a cafe overlooking the river for a cup of local tea. Shortly after we had arrived there was a ringing of bells as dozens of female and young elephants walked down to the river past shops and cafes for their morning splash about. The sight of them all playing in the river was incredible. Later on we went up to the orphanage where we were able to bottle feed baby elephants, and boy were they thirsty! I am not an animal-rights activist. However, I was dismayed at the lives of the poor elephants at the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage, and outraged at what is clearly a for-profit tourist scam at a place that bills itself as a do-gooder orphanage. Elephants are in chains, and are scarred, terrified, stressed, and unhealthy looking. Elephant handlers demand large tips from tourists after pressuring them to touch and take photographs with elephants, and then intimidate those tourists who refuse. The orphanage's existence has given rise to a number of copycat orphanages in the region where elephants are kept in far more despicable circumstances---i.e. chained to heaps of junk all day. From a tourist's point of view, this is a bad deal. - The entry fee is very expensive: $25 per person. (How is this money spent? The orphanage makes no effort to assure its guests that their money is being spent improving the welfare of the elephants. The orphanage has an obligation to do so.) - It's far from Kandy and Colombo. Several hours from each city by car. No train or bus access. Save your cash and go on a wildlife safari instead in one of Sri Lanka's national parks.

Our guide from Walkers Tours (arranged via Virgin Holidays) was incredibly helpful and took us to the orphanage in time to see smaller orphaned elephants being fed, then led us down to the river to see them bathe. We saw two orphaned elephants being bottle fed which was amazing as they were so close to everyone and seemed very happy trotting around, coming close to everyone so you could stroke them until some tourists lured it over then shouted loudly at it (which made the people around them as well as the elephants back off). Then down to the river which was even more amazing - the elephants looked in their element, rolling around in the water, squirting water on them selves and each other through their trunks. An absolutely incredible experience that I will never forget, and I'd definitely do it again if I'm ever back in Sri Lanka. The staff at the orphanage do try to coax you close to take a picture then demand money, but that type of behaviour isn't limited to Sri Lanka so you can't hold that against them. Just say no or even ignore them and they soon stop. Yes SOME elephants are chained up at the orphanage and at the river, but if people would stop to understand WHY they are chained, their experiences of the orphanage would have been much more enjoyable. It was explained to us that the ones chained in the orphanage were the 'naughty ones' and males (preventing overpopulation I'm sure). Think about it this way - you wouldn't keep a badly behaved dog off a lead then wonder why it got out and hurt someone, so why can you expect a wild orphaned animal (of their size/weight too) to be any different? And no it's not a 'cosy cute' kind of place where they make every animal better then release them back into the wild - simply because they cannot. Wild elephants would smell human on them and reject them. So, if you're not ok with seeing SOME elephants with chains on them then save yourselves the energy and money and just don't go. I'd read all the bad reviews and almost didn't go myself, but I tried to focus on the good things people had said so I could form my own opinion. I ended up having an INCREDIBLE time :)

But we enjoyed anyway sitting in restaurant drinking tea with milk, listening rain drops on the roof and watching so beatyfull animals enjoying their bathing.

Having heard a lot about this place we stopped here first during our visit to Sri Lanka, from the airport enroute to Dambulla. The entry fee for foreigners is 700 LKR (if you are from one of the SAARC countries) and the gates open around 8.30am. We watched the elephants in their enclosures, during their feeding time and then being led down to the river for their bath. The mahouts seemed to know the animals well and we hope that the care offered is of a similar nature. Apart from the fact that the place is quite large and house the world's largest number of captive elephants who are offered care and protection, there was nothing major about this attraction. We hoped that the proceeds from the tickets would contribute to the upkeep and maintenance of the place. Overall, loved the baby elephants waddling around, full of their antics and feel that this place is a one time visit and can be dropped if you prefer to see elephants in the wilderness without being chained or enclosed.

It's one thing being an elephant orphanage for elephants that have been worked and abused, which is what this place sells itself as, however, that is not the case. The elephants are inbred meaning that the disabled traits have been passed down to another generation and now the 'orphanage' has too many elephants for it to cope with. The elephants are apparently only chained during the mating seasons when they become more aggressive. It is understandable that they cannot be out in the open where there is no protection for guests however there are other methods of keeping them without the use of chains which harm them. To make things worse we went on a blisteringly hot day. The elephants in the main area were clearly distressed and too hot. They in theory have a relatively large area to roam  compared to some of the other elephants there. And in theory have access to watering holes but the reality is that they're not allowed to go there. The elephants herded by the workers shouting with elephant hooks forcing them to congregate in from of the guests for photos etc so that they get more money and tips.. This meant that the elephants were unable to get water to cool themsleves down. This is exactly the kind of activity that the orphanage is supposed to have rescued the elephants from. I believe that the principle of this place is right however somewhere along the line the meaning of this place has been lost and it has now turned into a money making scheme. PLEASE, go to a national park. Minneriya is fantastic- its a chance to see the elephants in their natural habitat and believe it or not they look happy!!

If you want to help keep Elephants on this planet then visit here.  Yes, you will see some elephants chained (not to my liking) but you will also be able to touch/feed others that are not chained. It was wonderful to see a couple of baby elephants playing together, it makes you wonder why people want to hurt/kill these majestic creatures.

My wife and I visited the orphanage as part of our tour around Sri Lanka. We had read previous reviews which were rated low and complaints about the elephants being secured by chains and looking generally unhappy. Personally we could not see the problem. Yes some of the elephants were chained up and some even excluded from being with others. We asked lots of questions which were answered by the keepers. The animals were chained during some feed times as this is protection for the staff as well as for the elephants. What you have to remember is the elephants are orphans and did not have the luxury of a role model hence some of the animals fight with others and this is dangerous to humans when feeding hence the chains. I can say I was observing two of the younger elephants fighting and as they came towards where I was standing with the fence between us one of the elephants reached out and hit me in the stomach with its trunk. So you can see why the elephants are chained. On the whole the experience was amazing especially when the heard when for a bath in the nearby river as we sat and watched them from a diner overlooking the river. If you speak to the staff they are very knowledgeable and are happy to explain what they are doing. I would highly recomend a visit as part of your tour. Oh I forgot you do get to feed the elephants if you like.

If you have an iota of love for these gentle giants, you must head for this place. You will be able to feed them and pat them. You can watch them march towards the river and have a good fun there. A must go place for children. Although you might read some negative reviews also but that is not going to stop you or your children from having an experience of a life time. Do plan your travel as the elephants are taken to bath at 10AM and 2PM daily. You need to see them march towards the river. Absolutely must go place in sri lanka.

Very expensive entrance.  I hope most of it goes into conservation - but I did not like to see so many elephants chained.  We were told that these were newly rescued and possibly a danger to the public and I hope this is the case. Those who were wandering were a delight.  The keepers however were very cheeky, demanding quite large tips for  ensuring you get good photos - they must make a fortune. Be aware!

We were taken to this location as part of our tour.  I was looking forward to visiting here but perhaps we arrived at the wrong time for the feeding of the babies.  We were given the opportunity to having our photo taken with an elephant but it came out very badly and the "photographer" demanded another very large tip to retake it." (This was not a big deal but it was irritating and somewhat spoiled the fun.)  We then watched the elephants being bathed in the river - something was part of the admission price but most of the other viewers just came in from off the street.

I understand that the opinions about this attraction are mixed. I think it’s a beautiful place to see elephants although I think it’s touristic and animals aren’t treating always right. The sanctuary is a good way to help the elephant, since a lot of them are being killed by local people because they destroy a lot (harvest, buildings,…). You can watch how people milk feed the very exiting baby elephants or feed an older elephant some fruits. If you want to do this yourself, you need to pay extra. In an adjacent area you can watch the big group of elephants. It’s amazing to watch the animals. At certain moment the supervisors brings the elephant to the river. This is nice to see. Elephants are moving in group to the river through a small shopping street. We were lucky there was a very small baby elephant in the group. He was very cute and funny when he was playing in the water. Unfortunatly the male elephants are all chained. The explanation:  Male elephants spread along the river and climbing into the forest next to it, so they will be lost. Be aware: there are some supervisors that keep some elephants out of the water so you can come closer to take some pictures with them. Those people ask for a lot of money. It’s just meant as elephants can enjoy the water. Those moments (twice a day) are short and valuable for the animals. The supervisors inhibit them to enjoy their stay at the river. You can see that the animals really want to go into the water but they are being kept at the sight. This also happened inside the sanctuary. Guides who want to take pictures for money.

I personally found our visit here quite distressing, I'd like to think they are doing some good but the whole place felt more like a zoo with Elephants chained up and being controlled with bull hooks for the entertainment of visitors! I broke down at the sight of the Elephants being pulled by their ears so guides could earn money taking tourists photos with them! We left almost immediately! The previous day we had visited the Elephant transition centre which I would recommend to anyone, I liked that the Elephants were being nurtured and rehabilitated ready to be released back into the wild where they belong!

It has been a nice experience to see the elephants so close and without barriers. The Orphanage is doing a great job and it is worth supporting it by paying the ticket to the premises, even if you can see the elephants without paying when they go down to the river. It is so funny to see these pachyderms roll and splash in the river.

Getting up close and personal with the elephants was a truly wonderful experience.  The orphanage was well maintained, the elephants seemed to be cared for gently and the experience was remarkable.  Don't miss this stop if you are in Sri Lanka

I visited this place with wife. To start with was having different impression. But was surprised to see the place. It is big area with lot of elephants of different age. Unhealthy or alone small or big elephants  are brought to this place from forest. They are treated  with due care fed  properly and once they become healthy send to forest. They are taken to near by river for bathing three times a day. Sufficient no of care takers are with them. elephants are in the river for about 45 minutes each time. Arrangements for Baby elephant feeding by tourist against additional fee. lankan Rs 500 is entry fee. Any way place,river view,and elephants of different age was a pleasure to meet with. Also see Elephant "Dung PAPER" Paper factory. Were happy to see and know.

Two sessions a day. The heard is walked down the street by their handlers and then they play in the river, splash and wash each other. Opportunity to feed them bananas which can be purchased at the site. At the end of the session they are called by their handlers and then walk back to their enclosure where they can be viewed and you can be photographed with one. A must visit

I'm sure that this place does some good things for elephants but a major part of it is still like a zoo and making elephants perform. They take elephants for baths twice daily and when we for there, there were elephants whose ankles were chained to the rocks so they couldn't move. One particular baby elephant was really struggling against its chain and it was sad to see.

We enjoyed this visit very much but it is very tourist- orientated. There are elephant handlers who will invite you to stand close to an elephant for a photo but then they expect to be given money. You can pay to feed the young elephants but again, this is very much set up for tourists. It takes about 5 seconds for the elephant to drink the bottle of milk so if you want a photo you have to be very quick or, as many people do, pay again. If you wander away from the crowds and the handlers you can often get pretty close to, and even stroke, an elephant or two without being pestered.

You will find many elephants roaming freely in designated area and you can take pictures holding their trunks. Also watch baby elephants being bottle fed with Lactogen baby milk in bottles. A time pass place but good if with children. However the entry tickets are priced steep. Though visitors from Saarc countries get these at half rates.

The first thing to say is this is not an orphanage! The elephants do not look happy and they are chained, fed and washed for the amusement of tourists.  I personally saw six elephants chained by the back legs to trees, allowing them only to move side to side with the front legs. I was told they were chained because they had not been trained yet! The entry price was also expensive compared to the rest of the attractions in Sri  Lanka. Please do not attend this attraction if you have any love for wildlife!

This is ok; there can't be many places in the world where you can see so many elephants up close. There are lots of dilemmas with this sort of place and whether it is the right thing to be doing with wild creatures and if visiting it is encouraging the keeping of elephants in an un-natural environment. However it does help preserve the elephants and does this in as a dignified way as possible - all things considered. The main attraction is watering time where the elephants leave the compound, walk down the main shopping street and bathe in the river. This is the one that attracts the crowds. In some ways it is worth going after they have returned as the crowds leave and their remain a few elephants in the river allowing you to watch and get close without the crowds around. There is a lovely little hotel/cafe at the end of the road that overlooks the river and you can watch from here in peace.The main orphanage is open and you can walk around to see the elephants and feed them also. There is the usual tourist shop and facilities are good. The only down side is that in a very typically sri lankan way, the staff appear to be being helpful by taking photos of you with elephants only to fleece you for money afterwards - so be ware of that. Otherwise a nice experience. There is a smaller orphanage down the road, which we didn't go to, but if you set-off early enough you could easily see both attractions in a day

Its worth visiting, if you do not visit you never come to know that they people really tack so much care for elephant, specially baby elephant. They even train them, tack care of them, special health care for un-healthy babies and much more.

I'm not sure what I was expecting when I got here, but it certainly didn't live up to the billing. The place was completely mobbed and the river where they bathe the elephants is not even inside the orphanage, not that I'm adverse to the walk but it just made everything feel bitty. Some of the guys who walk the elephants are rude and just in the job to see how much money they can squeeze out of the tourist. I bought some bananas off one guy to feed the elephants, when I took a photo of an elephant being fed one of the bananas  the keep hounded me to give him a tip, almost to the point of being aggressive. If it hadn't of been my first day in the country he would have been picking himself up off the riverbank. Don't get me wrong, not all the keepers are like that, but there are a few, and they need to be told by the tourist board. It was nice to see these majestic animals close up, but sad that they have to be kept like this.

A friend told me this was one of the best things he saw when in Sri Lanka a few years ago, so decided to make the effort to drive out of Kandy to see it. It's a great story behind the establishment of the orphanage, but having seen elephants in the wild in Sri Lanka, it was sad seeing them in captivity. We watched them bathing in the river, and playing in the mud, which was fun, but some were chained and there were the ever present minders with their sticks. I don't think I'd bother.

They don't look happy because they are chained and shackled amongst their own faeces. Tourists are constantly feeding individual elephants - one of them walked away because it was so full, however the mahout grabbed it by its ear and dragged him/her back to let the tourists continue feeding the elephant who then went on to spit the food out. Seriously needs a review - maybe it started with good intentions, but doesn't seem to be now! Only profits in mind, not the welfare of elephants.

Must visit for all Srilanka bound tourists to feel humanity. Great care and abundance of love may be felt the way caretakers nurse the baby elephants and grown ups too.Discipline and army columnwise marching for their baths,are sights one shall never forget. Affection showered to the really needy,must say.

Pinnawala is on the river Oya, west of Kandy on the road to Colombo. It's an orphanage, nursery and captive breeding ground for wild Asian elephants and has the largest herd of captive elephants in the world. There were 86 there when we visited. Try to be there at bottle-feeding time and don't forget, when you leave, to go through the village to the river as the elephants are regularly led through Pinnawala to bathe in the river.

Disappointing visit, received no history of how this orphanage came about, was not made aware that the entry fee would support the elephants.  Elephants chained to trees and made to perform for tourists.  Baby elephants did enjoy their rollick in the rain and it was delightful to watch them do this.

This is a breath taking experience to see these wonderful animals at such close quarters to photograph touch and even feed from milk bottles at feeding time. Superb setting on this location the hill by the river. (see our review also the Ideal Island for that Special Occasion John & Jady 2013 )

Extremely disappointed with Pinnawala 'orphanage'. You can tell from the start once you've paid and entered that this is far from an orphanage, no introduction is given explaining any history of the 'orphanage', their work, what your money goes towards. Elephants are chained to trees on a chain no longer than your arm, you'll find them swaying with frustration and crying. Not cared for as you thought. I asked a member of staff there why the elephants were doing this, he laughed and told me they're 'dancing' then I asked why their dancing, he laughed again and said they're the 'aggressive ones'. Elephants were poked with metal spears if they didn't do what was expected of them. Really and truly disgusted that I paid to enter such a place. Please please do not support the torture and unethical keeping of elephants purely for human greed. This place should've been closed down already.

I work as a travel agent and my husband and I just completed our 3 week honeymoon in Sri Lanka. Having never travelled to Sri Lanka before I did lots of research and found that Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is a standard inclusion on just about every set tour/itinerary, so we decided to include it on our itinerary. I regret this decision immensely. The elephants are treated terribly, chained by by both front and back legs in one place in the river. The babies are not as I guess they are easily controlled by the cruel pokers the staff carry and toerment them with. Children were throwing rocks and yelling at nearby elephants (and seeing as they are chained there was no escape) and the staff did nothing. Why would you go here when there are literally hundreds of free elephants in National Parks nearby that you can go to see. They are free, happy and protected. DO NOT SUPPORT THIS CRUEL TREATMENT. I will ensure that I tell all my clients about this inhumane "orphanage" and tell them to avoid it. If you want to see happy elephants, unchained and free then Udawalawe National Park is a great choice.

We were sad to see the way some  baby elephants were in  enclosures and children shouting and pocking them. The elephants on their return from the river were given free range in the plains although some were chained due to being aggressive,There were a lot of elephants but very few handlers who really wanted to have their pictures taken to get money. There is a large wide open space where the elephants roamed which is more what we wanted to see. We went down through the village to the river and watched a small group bathing which seemed much more natural .There was a shop in the village which made paper from elephant poo, which was very interesting as they explained the process. We did feel by purchasing an item we were helping the elephants a litle

I could not figure out how this place was different from a zoo. Yes there were elephants who were roaming free in a well watched area by their handlers. But most of the elephants that were meant for visitors were either chained or in an enclosure. Also nobody had an answer to how these animals are being rehabilitated to go back to wild. Felt more like a zoo. My kids did have good time feeding the elephant.

We visited this elephant orphanage (there are many other choices to see elephants) because we felt it was the ethical choice but we were very wrong. Elephants are captive here, some chained to fences and to rocks in the river for the amusement of tourists. We were strongly encouraged to take photos by staff handlers and then after doing so pressured to pay the staff handlers for this. We of course did not pay - but combined with the chains we came away feeling this place is not about the care of elephants. There is no educational material & it was all about tourists. Sadly it is just another profitable way to exploit elephants for personal gain. Avoid.

Pinnawala was not what we expected at all and we cut our visit short because we couldn't bear to see the elephants being treated this way. The male elephants were particularly distressed having been kept in isolation, chained to trees with no water or food in the blazing sun. Little effort appears to have been made to reintroduce the animals to the wild and I would describe it as more of a zoo than an orphanage. The baby elephants were forced to feed so tourists could get a picture and they appeared to be scared of the mahouts. We visited Yala National Park and saw wild elephants which was a fantastic experience and I would recommend visiting this instead.

Pinnawala is an elephant orphanage where the baby elephants whose mother are dead and the lost elephants are take care of and rehabilitate,until they can live in their own in the wild.Go early in the morning so you can catch they are bathing.Also  you can feed them.Baby elephants are so adorable and playful.Great place for kids.Don't forget to buy recycled elephant duck paper note book.

We had a bad experience at the MEF so this seemed much better in comparison however there are still elephants chained to trees and infants kept in isolation. The Elephant Freedom Project seems to get good reviews so I would try that over the two attractions we went to.

A good experience. You can interact with elephants and feed them  (with a bottle or fruits- this is a paid activity). One you are done with this, you can hop over to the other side, where there is a lake. There you can witness these elephants being bathed while you enjoy lunch at one of the many hotels that are over looking these lakes. Overall, it was fun and recommendable.

This is one of the best success stories in the World on helping wild elephants. I really enjoyed the Elephant gathering there, specially their bathing time and feeding time. Baby elephants are really loving and children love them. We had seen many generations of Elephants living there and there are considerable number born at the Orphanage. Most Elephants are orphaned as a result of continuous Human-elephant conflict, recent civil war at the country, lost from herds, loosing their parents or other. It was wonderful to see how these herds move within the park under a matriarchy system. We really enjoyed every movement of these gentle giants and irrespective of their sheer body size, these orphaned elephants bring a tear to visitors. I recommend this place for everybody who are interested in wild as well as a good place for little children. They just love Elephants!

I have never seen so many elephant at one place and since I love elephants I enjoyed this place. Could have stayed there all day. :-) Such cute elephants. We saw them having a bath. There was even a teeny-tiny baby elephant, which just lay down in the water in between the legs of the huge elephants without any worry of getting trampled.

I was actually really looking forward to go here, but when we arrived it just didn't felt right.  Some elephants were chained on both (front and back) leg, so they could't move. You could see that they were not comfortable. It just basically felt ike elephant ZOO.

This is a great place to see elephants and you can even get close to them. The best time to observe them is when they go to the river for their bath. They really seem to enjoy themselves in the water and the scene is so natural. Fully worth the ticket price.

No idea about anyone else but since watching Dumbo and the Jungle book I have loved elephants. I know there are loads of people saying "its irresponsible tourism" and the elephants are sad but thats all nonsense, this isnt Black Fish people.  This is a land species that takes a lot of space and man management.  You dont moan at elephants in a western zoo and they are thousand of miles away from their actual climate zones. The Mahut's seem to love their animals, you might get a shock when you see chains but an bull elephant in heat is a dangerous concept.  Elephants kill local villagers and damage lots. The sanctuary is fine but basic, you get to feed the elephants for a price, along with seeing excited baby elephants. Sri Lankan's love elephants.  Anyone that says they are mistreated can take a run and jump.  There are always nutters that do bad things. Don't listen to these negative nancies.  Sri Lanka is a tiny islands with millions of people on it.  The only way elephants and people can coexist is with places like this.  There are lots of huge reserves just for the wild elephants and the government tries to get the sanctuary elephants back into the wild.

The elephants aren't treated in a dignified way. Many of them are chained and the mahouts will bring them up to the fence where tourists can pay to over feed them and bottle feed them. The elephants are supposed to be released back into the wild at some point, but I don't see how they can successfully be reintroduced to nature after being taught to be so dependent on humans and to not fear humans. This orphanage is irresponsibly managed. Stay away!

Perhaps my perception is skewed because I understand the freedom of the African elephant in the wild. Pinnewala looks after orphan elephants - but our group of 19 cut our excursion short because we so distressed by what we saw at Pinnewala. The elephants appear to be afraid of the mahouts. The adult elephants have chains from their necks attached to their front legs which restricts their ability to walk. We spent 11 days in Sri Lanka - for all 19 of us, Pinnawala was our worst experience.
