It was a great experience to visit this place I would say. We planned to just spend less than an hour initially, but ended up spending close to 4 hours just watching the elephants bathe :) The river side restaurants were pretty decent. It was a scenic beauty of course, can enjoy the nature :) We got to see the elephant feeding,  it was cute!

Elephants are treated in the worst possible way here. They hardly look interested in entertaining the visitors - they are forced to go down the river or even walk as per the instructions. If the elephants seem to not listen they are struck with a needle ended stick/weapon - that most definitely hurt them greatly. The most heart breaking sight to us, was seeing tears in the eyes of the elephants because of all the pain and mistreatment. Visitors should avoid this place and authorities should take immediate steps in improving the treatment and management of the elephants.

For young and old, a great experience.....an opportunity to feed the baby elephants in a controlled environment too. An adjacent area gives the chance to be up close with the adult animals, great pictures against a wild backdrop. WARNING: a well meaning Mahout offered to take our picture as we stood next to an elephant ,but instead, successfully deleted all my shots taken in India prior to our arrival in Sri Lanka....they don't all do that of course, just be aware!.....If you can, cross the main road outside the orphanage and walk down to the river, the adult elephants are there in numbers for a bath etc., at 10.00 and 14.00 hrs.....Some criticize this place, but, without it the elephants would probably be dead!

By far our worst experience of our Lankan trip. A detour on the way to Kandy from Negomobo airport. This is a hugely overrated place which has a small stream, a few overworked elephants and a small museum. The package consists of a 100 mtr elephant ride which is the only takeaway of the tour. The Mahouts literally demand tips from you. At LKR 2k per head its sheer wastage. Specially for Indians, for whom citing elephants is no big deal.

The smile on my childrens' faces as they got to pat, then feed elephants of all sizes brought tears of happiness to me, one of my parenting highlights.  To then see 50 elephants bathing in a river, surrounded by natural beauty, unrestrained by mankind surpassed anything I've ever seen in Africa.

Yes, elephants can be dangerous, but to see them constrained and managed in this way is so sad. I could not help but compare to an elephant conservation park I visited in Thailand where the mahouts and elephants seemed to have a genuine loving relationship and the mahouts played games with the baby elephants. Many of the Pinnawala elephants were shackled and had a handler with a hook close by. They are marched down a dusty shop-lined street to the river. They did not even seem to enjoy the water very much. None of the male bull elephants were brought down to the river. If you have not seen elephants before, here is an opportunity to do so at close hand, but there are better places.

We visited the elephant orphanage with a tour guide. He was a great help as new where be at certain times to watch them feed and bathe. Watch out for the people selling bags of bananas sa we were told not to buy them as the bananas were small and the elephants snatch. Was amazing watching them all walk down to the river to bathe. It was a fantastic experience

I went to Pinnawala with a sense of trepidation as I had heard reports of poor treatment of the elephants. But I thought my kids would enjoy seeing elephants up close so off we went. These reports were unfortunately confirmed as the handlers seem to use their positions mostly to get 'tips' for photos. I get it, its a developing nation and everyone has to make a living however they can. But there did not seem to be any love from the handlers we saw. And the elephants seem very scared of that pointed stick with what appeared to be a blade attached they brandish at them. We also saw one elephant chained very awkwardly so that one leg was too far forward and one too far back. Who knows how long it had to remain like that? It seemed very uncomfortable and its trunk kept feeling at the chain on its front leg - heartbreaking! Another was chained to a fence in the blazing sun for the morning so that tourists could stand with it - again for photos. In a land of rapid development I hope that the government steps up its treatment of these elephants. Its obviously making a lot of money from them. The least it can do is see that they are treated with dignity.

Excellent Tour. Get there early, for the ritual feeding of the baby elephants (tickets on entry have to be sought). A most enjoyhable visit, the cleaning of the elephants in the river late morning was a site to be seen. heard that some people were asked to pay 2500rps (£12) for getting wet and cleaning them, but be careful of this. Really will never forget our trip here.

Getting to Pinnawala is a breeze as the roads are excellent. Parking is along the road and easy to find a spot :D SAARC residents get tickets at a cheaper price but should be carrying an ID. Please note that the milk feeding and bathing tickets for the baby elephants sell out really fast so it's better to come early [around 11-12pm] if you want to do those activities. Fruit feeding happens all the time and tickets are those available on the spot. You get to feed Mohini. The fatso female elephante :P You can observe a lot of elephants here eating, bathing, playing and some simply roaming around. Water and food is available at a particular spot. Very few spots to rest / relax. Many people have commented on the poor conditions of the elephants here. Sadly, most of it is true. Wild elephants take some time to be tamed and during this time they are kept chained. The chains rub against the elephants' skin causing lacerations and sometimes infection. Handlers also hit the elephants with more force than required and it's very disheartening to see that. Avoid if you cannot see the above.

Im unsure whether to love this place or feel sad for the elepahnts. Don't get me wrong it seems as if the care takers look after the place but it's also cruel to make money off feeding these beautiful creature. Most of the elephants are chained in order to allow people to feed them hence I didnt particularly enjoy the sight. However, watching the elephants bathe in the nearby river was a magnificent sight as the animal seemed free and relaxed in its natural environment.

First off, be aware it costs foreigners 2500 rupees to "see" the elephants. This includes the option of walking down a public street to the river to watch them bathe. You cant get down to the river without a ticket as the police stop everyone going down the road. At first I thought this was a lovely idea. So I sat by the river in the restaurant enjoy a drink in the sun. Then proceeded to watch the elephants, who wanted to enjoy themselves in the water no doubt, have stones thrown at them and be beaten with sticks by the handlers. These same handlers carry what can only be described as spears, to which the elephants seem petrified. and it doesn't take a genius to know how animals became afraid of things like that..... Back at the actually orphanage, the remaining elephants are chained up eating. Which for 350 rupees a go, you can feed them. This is no more than a cruel zoo, designed to attract money and tourists.

It's fair to say that we absolutely love elephants and the " idea" of this place sounded just up our street but to be honest I could not in good conscience recommend this place to anyone. Too expensive for a zoo, not for those looking to see rehabilitation of orphaned or injured  animals nor is it really for those wanting interaction - the crowds put paid to that idea. Everything seems rushed and stressed, hard to see how any part of this could be enjoyable for anyone, especially the poor elephants.

We were so excited to go and watch the elephants, unfortunately the entrance fee was too expensive and not worth it at all. More over the day we went it started to rain. We opted to go to  Kandy Dalada Maligawa – the Temple Palace of the Tooth Relic. Thank God we went there as during that time, they had more than 100 elephants around for the full moon festival. We were not lucky to even go to the river to watch the elephants bathe which was across the orphanage area as they are men who watch people, and ask for you tickets. Police will also be around there. Its a public area, but when the elephant go to the river, only people with tickets are allowed to be there.

My whole family went to see the elephants on the way to Kandy and we wished we didn't. The price was extortionate for Sri Lanka, a tourist trap. It was just a money making exercise, extra costs to feed the elephants, extra costs to take photos next to them. Not nice. They elephants we chained up to eat at feeding time so tightly they could only move about 50cm in any direction. We thought it was cruel and therefore would not recommend. Go and see them on a safari in a national park where they wonder around without chains.

A must place to visit. We skipped getting into the orphanage and went straight to the river to see the elephants having a bath. Never would you have seen so many elephants in one place together. My kids enjoyed watching the elephants and got loads of photographs. On the way back from the river, do stop at one of the shops which makes paper from elephant dung. They also show you the entire process how the paper is made and you can buy the paper as well in the form of earrings, bracelets and notebooks. Do not miss the elephants marching back to the orphanage after their bath.

We love elephants and were not disappointed here.  We got to feed two of the cutest baby elephants who were just like little puppies. Also enjoyed seeing the elephants in the river.  They all seemed pretty happy with their lot. Worth a visit for sure

We decided to be here enroute to Kandy to show elephants to my little one and also to make him feed the baby elephant/s. He was so thrilled at the eight of these lovely animals. We saw the entire herd being taken for the bath. We got to feed milk and fruits to the elephants. And we even got to see them bathe and scrub them. There is a cost attached to every activity which is not high and am sure its put to good use. Its an experience you wont forget. Try to be there before 930 am to experience both, the feeding and bath sessions.

We decided to go to this orphanage as it was midway between our drive from Colombo to Kandy and moreover because we love elephants. Its quite expensive and the entire routine hardly lasts 3 hours.We reached around 2 pm which was time for elephant bath on the nearby river. Parts of it were absolute fun. Around 25-30 elephants were taken for the bath by the mahoots. Young kids around were so excited to see the baby elephants jump around the shallow waters.Elephants were then taken back to the orphanage where we fed the smaller ones. You can even feed milk to them for a hefty cost.The sad part was to see them tied and forced around by rods by the mahoots. Felt more like a zoo but still better than the typical ones .Also for those who don't know much about elephants, the male ones are difficult to control and those few of them there , were tied with heavy chains.Overall would recommend the place only if you have young children or if you are doing Colombo-Candy route.

The moment we arrived I knew this place was going to be dreadful, with throngs of locals, tourists and school groups, there were cars and buses and tuk tuks parked up double and triple on both sides of the street. This place is so ridiculously touristy and I really don't see how it can be of benefit to the poor elephants. We sat in a bar overlooking the water as a group of about 20 young elephants bathed, watched over by 3-4 mahoots with big metal rods. There was one particular elephant who really looked unhappy, chained up and rocking back and forth. I hope he was in that state before he came to this place... The elephants are then marched up through the streets where particularly the local tourists are the worst thronging around and being very loud. It must be terrifying for the poor animals. You are also encouraged to buy bananas and sugar cane treats for the eles which the locals pushed in to the hands of their young children and thrust them in front of the oncoming herd, smart phone in the other hand at the ready. We also took part in, much to my disgust now, in the hand feeding of the baby elephants. This is essentially when a huge group of loud excitable people gather round a concrete circular enclosure and two or three small eles are brought out. There are feeding stations where those with a special pass and have paid extra can stand for about 5 seconds with a glass bottle of milk and pose with it in baby elephant's mouth before a mahoot screeches for the next person and the crowd jostles you out of the way. Money making scheme posing as conservation effort, I wasn't buying it and neither should you.

A great opportunity to (pay extra to) get up close and personal with elephants. However, this is essentially a zoo, where animals are kept in small enclosures/areas, some are chained and all are trained to respond to being jabbed with a sharp stick. We enjoyed our visit although entry for tourists is expensive and there is not enough there to warrant a full day trip. We stopped for the morning on our way from Kandy to Colombo airport.

Be aware that tuk tuk friver will insist to take you here instead of real Elephant Orphanage cos thy are getting commision for every tourist they bring there. I was convinced by my tuk tuk driver to go there. I was planning to go to Elephant Orphanage but tuk tuk driver was persistant and suggesting that this is better and cheaper  option to go and see. You can get ride and bath elephants in chains, after that people working  there will asking you for more money and tips.

This is about a 2 hour drive from Colombo but worth the effort. Walk around with the Elephants on the 9 acre Orphanage. There are about 90 Elephants there of all ages, you can feed fruit to the adults and you can feed milk to the babies. The kids will love it. Once you're done make sure you go down to the river and watch them have their daily bath!

The elephant orphanage in Pinnawala is a must go place if you are coming to Sri Lanka. Place is located around 100KM from Colombo, however the travel totally worth the experience. You are able to view large amount of elephants in a single place, which are living in the place. Most of them were orphaned or captured from the wild. You need to travel along the Colombo Kandy road and turn after you pass Kegalle to reach the place. You can view elephants bath in the nearby river and also you are able to feed baby elephants during their feeding time. Note that they request you a fee when you feed and elephants. Note that all the personals visiting the place are required to obtain a ticket to enter the place.

This place is a lousy tourist trap. The guys who take care of these amazing creatures doesen't seem to care much for the elephants but rather for the money. When they were in the river, the keepers would yell and use their bullhooks to make the elephants pose for photos with ignorant tourist who doesen't seem to notice the sadness or how these people act behind the scenes when there is no audience. They were really afraid of the bullhook. Everything for a good selfie. Do not support this kind of activity. Instead go to one of the countries national parks where they roam free. It is much more satisfying and beautiful to see.

PLEASE NOTE!!! I write this review for our elephant ride in a small town between Badulla and Polonnaruwa, I am not sure if it is Habarana or another place. We called the day before to book it, since our driver-"guide" mislead us earlier, so we missed the elephant ride in Sigiriya. A 40 minute ride around the lake (or river) and in the village, was arranged by our local friend for 20 $ per person. When we arrived there, they asked for 40 $, we reminded them the call the day before, so they said OK, 20 $. Of course, the ride was 150 meters on a field near the village and back, lasting merely 25 minutes. As I say every time I write about my experience in Sri Lanka. I REPEAT!!! Very beautiful country, very sweet people, BUT most tourist industry workers are ignorants, appauling and they don't miss an opportunity to show their dislike to foreigners.

There are now seemingly a number of smaller elephant rescue places just along the road but this is the biggest and with the largest number of animals. These are clearly not wild creatures (more is the pity) but are largely rescued from the wild as orphans or because they can no longer support themselves. Since our last trip the whoel place has become much more commercialised (as to be expected) but the keepers clearly adore their charges and do their level best to keep them happy. It is sad to see some of the animals chained - but these are said to be the ones with "issues" and who will not mix with the rest of the herd. The highlight of any visit is feeding time for the babies (for a few Rs you can even get a bottle to feed them yourself) and the trip to the river for their bathe. Its wonderful to see them all running down to the river together and then just doing their thing while you watch on. The rout to the river is now largely taken with shops and the cafes overlooking the river provide a great place to watch the antics going on in the river below you

The first place I liked most in Srilanka is Kandy to Ella Train Journey.  The second place I liked most is Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage in Srilanka. For Asians the entrance fee is 700 Srilankan Rupees for other foreigners it is 2500 LKR. Asians should have passport with them. Two times in a day elephants are taken into the river for bathing one before noon 10 am to 12 pm & one after noon 2 pm to 4 pm from the Orphanange which is 200 meters apprx from the river on the other side of main road. At the ticket counter one can find complete day's time table chart of elephants activities. I have attached it in my review. You get to see elephants from very near in fact you get a chance to touch them or feed them bananas. There are Srilankans at the river selling bananas at a very affordable rate to be fed to elephants. The thing I liked most is the scenic beauty around the river with elephants bathing in the river. In the orphanage you can feed milk to the elephants at extra cost, you can bathe elephants that too again at extra cost. Please see the photos to get the real feel of the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage.

So if you have not seen Elephants roam free, and if you are in SriLanka , you must go here, but start early and catch the 9am feeding, as the day tends to get too hot . It's nice to see the elephants and their young roaming around and hanging in their habitat, the elephants are well looked after and are kept well , so that is very heartening ..

i had my reservations about this place from the reviews, but was pleasantly surprised, when we saw the elephants walk down the high street to the river to bathe. They looked happy as they frolicked in the water and were given free time. Went back up to orphanage and hot opportunity to hand feed what I thought was a baby, but was actually 7 years old.

Hello, My name is Bogdan Muncus and together with my girlfriend we visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage on Septmeber 2015. We have to say that is a very beautiful place to see baby elephants, how they care and feed them and of course the main event is the river bath. It is a very wonderful experience to see this creatures playing in the water. We'll definitely recomand this place when you come and visit Sri Lanka! Best regards, Deborah & Bogdan Romania - 15.09.2015.

Be prepared for it to be busy. At one side a village style shop /souvenir Street. The elephants are taken through to bathe in the river. You have to get well back out of the way.  You can observe them bathing easily. The scenery is great for photos!  Cafes, toilets available.  At the other side where the elephants are kept. Enclosures are spotless as are the surroundings. Large groups are also in a large open area. All looked after well.  Some people comments about them being chained. It's not all the time and do these people realise they are very large and can be dangerous animals.  They all looked healthy and happy. Really worth a visit.

This isn't a 100% free range elephant sanctuary. There are still chains and cages but the majority or the animals are out in the opening. I didn't see any elephant rides at the time of visiting and not quite sure whether they do exist there. Generally speaking the elephants looked in better shape here than other elephant set ups I've been at. It was a nice sight to see them taken down to the river for a wash and a play. At the end of the day the "orphanage" has a commercial element to attract the tourist so it will never be fully humane toward the animals

I was awed to see more than 80 elephants in one place - all shapes and sizes :) Definitely a must visit for somebody who loves animals. When I heard that they actually pick injured elephants from the wild and then that the entry fees is half for SAARC countries - it just enhances the overall experience.

Very much a place to rake in money although it is nice to see all the Elephants in the river. Sad to see these magnificent animals in chains and prodded with pointed hooks. Best to see them in the wild in one of the numerous National Parks of Sri Lanka.

If you care about animal welfare please DO NOT visit this tourist attraction as it is just that and not a sanctuary in any sense of the word. I  went as my mum visited a few years ago and described the elephants playing in the water and feeding the babies and there are plenty of reviews that say the same thing however I believe this is contrived set up activity for the tourists that happens at particular times. We arrived as the orphanage opened at 8:30am so there was no set activity happening, instead the majority of the elephants were just standing in a paddock.These were not chained but a few were rocking/swaying and they were certainly scared of the staff who had bull hooks and ran away when threatened with one if they came too close the few tourists that were there. This was upsetting enough to see but there were also several elephants who were not in the paddock but were chained up. One in particular was rocking quite violently and our driver said 'look he's dancing'. This is not dancing. This is absolute distress. I asked why he was chained and we were told because he's naughty!!!!! Another elephant was being hosed down but his front left leg and his back right leg were chained to the ground with no room for movement. They were making him lie down to wash him but it was very difficult because he was so inhibited by the chains. I was only in there for 5 minutes as it was too upsetting to watch. I have no idea what we would have done for 2 hours until the 10:30 river walk and bathe as there was nothing else actually in the park but I am pretty sure if we had waited we would have seen the tourist show. I will be contacting relevant animal welfare organisations to report what I saw as I strongly believe that what most tourists see is not the true picture of this place. However I should say on that point that there was about another 20 tourists there at the same time as me, seeing exactly the same thing and they were smiling and posing for pictures like it was all lovely but sadly ignorance to animal welfare only adds to the problem. The entrance fee is about £12 each and I would happily pay double, even triple this to support a genuine animal sanctuary but Pinnawala is not that, it's just a tourist attraction. Beautiful animals like elephants that need rescuing and safety deserve respect not an audience.

Took a 3 hour train ride to reach Rambukkana from Colombo and then to Pinnawala. Its a little tricky to get here since there are not a lot of trains/buses which come here directly. However, it was wonderful spending time with the majestic creatures. They are kept and fed well, although one might feel they are kept in captivity. Make sure you go in the morning or evening during bathing time to visit orphanage and see elephant bathing. Beware of elephant keepers, they will try to make money off you.

It is a money making outfit, run by the government on the tourist trail.  The 'keepers' are only interested in taking your money - for a photo with an elephant, to give them a bottle of milk or whatever. They 'encourage' the elephants along by prodding them with a spike on the end of a long pole. These are not happy animals and I regret paying my entrance fee to see them.  Your money is better spent at the place in Udawalawe or wait to see the elephants on a safari.

It was a great experience to see the elephants up close but with all attractions they want money to take pictures and they seem more interested in that then the elephants, they were roaming free mostly however did seem to be chained up to eat. We only caught the end of the bathing in the river, this looked really cool and loved how they just walked them through the street  back to the park however it was very busy there. We only spent an hour here and much preferred our trip to Yala to see them completely chain free.

Located about 30kms off Kandy, this is probably the first thing on your to-do list if you're on a package tour in Sri Lanka... And definitely it lives up to the expectations! Housing multiple elephants of various size, it's certainly a treat to watch the ever-smiling gentle giants! Going close to 10AM, you get to see a herd of elephants walking across the road to the river for a bath.. Although a Government run site, I believe the entrance tickets to this site is much beyond worth it considering the brilliant maintenance of both the surroundings and the wonderful elephants.. It's certainly a delight to click several photos with different sizes but watch out not to get too close to the younger / smaller naughty ones.. they love to snatch anything from you.. In short, don't miss it! :)

This orphanage was established in 1975. With a 4 baby elephants who lost there mother and the group. Since then there was born more than 45 babies and having more than 85 elephants. Elephants are taking to bath from 10:00 to 12:00 or 14:00 to 16:00.  More than 30-40 elephants are taking to bath. It is interesting to see how baby elephants are playing in the water.

If you are travelling to Kandy from Colombo, do not miss this 20 km round trip off the highway because chances are, you would never have seen so many elephants together after Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (or were they Oliphaunts?) Kids love this place, some of them positively exploding with energy at the sight of so many lumbering giants. It feels great to see so many elephants living a normal, non-tormented life, trumpeting from time to time. Many of the elephants are in chains but that is just a safety mechanism and animals are not treated harshly here. You may or may not want to entertain touts who would take your money in exchange for an elephant ride but it is certainly not allowed(officially) in the orphanage. Food and water sells at 1.5-2X outside the orphanage so come prepared.

We visited the elephant orphanage which seemed to be a nice place for the elephants to live and they appeared well treated. That said, this is obviously a state run tourist attraction and the emphasis is on making money. When the elephants came down to the river at 10am, you could see the delight and pleasure that they had in getting into the river and having a wash, that was lovely to see. It was quite dear to enter and the staff were less than polite.

This was apart of the tour I was on, and had I known that the poor Elephant's were beingtreated so bad I would not have gone. It is very expensive and also a huge tourist trap attraction which exploits the poor animals. They do not appear to be treated very well, considering it is a orphanage,  most of the elephants are in chains and shackles when the are in the river playing and back at the orphanage.  They give you the excuse that they are wild and mis behave. They don't seem to be looked after very well and I could not help but leave after about 30mins in total from down by the river and the orphanage.  Stay away if you care about animals and have morals.

Very very interesting and so exciting and a bit scarey to see those huge creatures so close up - no fences between you and the elephants. A wonderful experience. Watchiing the babies bathe in the river while we ate our lunch at a nearby cafe was a once in a lifetime experience.

We went there with our cousins in September 1st week. It was an unforgettable experience to me becaz I was never been there before. Some elephants were dancing in the river. Some were fighting. They were like babies.. We really enjoyed well.. It is pleasure there is such a good place for orphan elephants to stay calm and quite.

Drove through and stopped here on the way to Dambulla from Colombo.  There are different events going on depending on the time you go.  Entrance fee is 2500 SRL, if you park across the street in the market they ask for 100 SRL.  You can pay to watch the baby elephant milk feeding (not really that great) and once you enter the orphanage you have the option of paying to feed the elephant fruit. The area is really small despite what the map looks like.  I really only paid to enter with my friends because they wanted to.  Once inside, it feels more like a circus than an orphanage.  See photos, the handlers were poking elephants with a sharp pole to keep them in certain positions for picture taking.  Following that, they would ask for money.  I never gave them money and eventually they wouldn't let the elephants pose with me.  Some of the elephants are chained from their neck to their foot. I'm not much of an animal rights activist but it just seemed like a really sad place for the elephants to be.  You won't need to spend more than an hour here.

A beautiful sight to see elephants bathing in a river. Such graceful creatures yet there was an undertone in our opinion. We had to pay 5000 Rupees as "foreign" people with locals paying 1400 Rupees (per couple). Insensitive marketing. We saw a heavily pregnant female. Not unusual I guess except this is an Orphanage!  Breeding to generate more babies for tourist cameras? Seems that way. The keepers had poles with vicious looking spikes on one end. When weiled, the elephant concerned backed - off quickly. That said they had first hand experience of it.... Cannot fault the overall purpose though. Homing orphan elephants is very commendable.

Quite expensive by Sri Lankan standards but that didn't stop the tourists! Probably the busiest place we visited for a very up close view of many elephants although the most unique aspect is watching them walk down to the river for their bath. Kids loved it!

Expensive to enter but you get very up close and personal with the elephants. A baby elephant even groped me! The 'rangers' constantly encourage you to get even closer to the elephants for pictures and then they want paying. It wasn't pleasant to see the elephants chained up and some were obviously very bored where they were being kept but at least they weren't being forced to carry tourists around on their backs. Unless you are an elephant fanatic you will probably be done with this place in under an hour. Not really their natural habitat but better than being on the street.

Absolutely amazing place, arrived early to catch the bottle feeding of the baby elephants. Had our photo taken with the elephants by the handlers, our guide told us to give them 100rps even though hey asked for 1000! When the elephants go down to the river try and get there early and you can get a free seat at the riverside restaurant on the left hand side at the bottom and grab a cold drink under cover with a great view of all the elephants in the river. One of our best memories of Sri Lanka

if you love elephants, especially baby elephants, and if you love spending time looking at them, this is the exact place you should be. Ideally you must spend at least three hours to cover their daily routines; from feeding to bathing in the river. Make sure to take lots of photos since they will definitely make you smile later on. Call them and check the feeding times and bathing times if you are visiting for a short period of time.

This was a fantastic place. We loved our visit and went with three children 17 15 and 12 . Yes it isn't cheap but it wouldn't be in the usa or uk!!!! You can pay to fruit or milk feed inside the park we didn't. There are loads of elephants the only ones chained are aggressive males. You can see babies who have been bred there . the place to see orphaned elephants, they are taken care of some good keepers and few money minded people as well, many places they offer for photos in return of money. the day we visited they had general elections so we had to wait 2 hours for the milk feeding due to staff shortage and change of schedule, overall our visit was a wonderful one,

A fantastic visit We arrived when they had gone to the river to wash and play and it was wonderful to see them in a natural environment There was bulls females and new born who they all surrounded They then walked through the town to the orphanage to feed They seemed very happy and well cared for and it was wonderful to get so close and be able to touch them A  very enjoyable experience

entrance fees is quite expensive for non srilankans.. since i was with my senior citizen parents we directly went to the place where the elephants are taken for a bath.. watching them bath was ok and not worth the money spend on the entrance fees.. if you want to touch them and take pictures or feed them then better do at temple of tooth relic,kandy...

This is a place not to miss if you happen to be in Sri Lanka. The trip to get there is rather long because of the roads, but it is worth it. apart from different things you can do; i.e feeding the elephants, washing elephants, you can also enjoy either breakfast or lunch or just drinks, watching all elephants being washed in a river. Our children liked that a lot, especially from one of the restaurants which gives a lovely view, looking down at the elephants in the river, (about 15 metres or so from the restaurant). You can also go down and nearer to the elephants, if you wish. Along the way to the river, you can buy a lot of soverneour, which include books or stationary made of elephant pooh! Some of the prices of different things on sale are very high, so be careful!

Visited Friday 28th August! Me and my partner left bentota at 5.30am in order to get to pinnawala elephant orphanage... It was definitely worth it! I was very worried about the reviews saying lots of elephants were chained up but this was not the case! We arrived at 9am and had chance to take pictures of over 30 elephants roaming free (without chains) on the grass area! Men were around with whips but didn't use them! Our tour guide said this was only for emergencies. One guy asked me if I wanted to touch one of the elephants... He stood by me whilst my partner took my photo! Then another guide got my partner in too and took the photo! Both men then asked for money! You do not have to give them money it's your choice! We then moved on to the feeding which was at 9.15! The place was rammed! So make sure you get to the front to take lots of pictures! You have to pay extra to bottle feed the elephants and the milk literally lasts less than 8 seconds! The workers have to assist you too which doesn't allow you much chance to join in with the feeding. I bought a bag of bananas from outside the orphanage for 200 rupees which I went on to feed the elephants when we moved onto the river!! Feeding them bananas was a much better experience! We then went down the market street towards to river. Sat and ate breakfast at a restaurant whilst over looking one little elephant bathing in the river! Then 8 more elephants came along! I walked down closer to the river and was asked if I wanted to wash an elephant! Again someone was taking photos whilst me and my partner were washing the elephant down in the river!! Again you will be asked for money! Up to you if you wish to give donations! As we were about to leave we went towards the market shops and were told we had to move out the way... Over 60 elephants were being freely walked down to the river! (NO CHAINS)! Two elephants were chained and escorted at the end I can't physically explain how big these were (so probably chained for people's safety). Such a wonderful day and amazing experience. Unfortunately the pinnewala orphanage does not allow people to ride on these elephants as they have all came from different backgrounds. There is a place close to the orphanage where you can ride the elephants for 20 minutes for 2000 rupees. Think it's called 'upalis elephant safari' also worth a visit!!!

We went here on part of a guided tour and enjoyed the experience of first seeing so many elephants roaming free in the orphanage, a few of the older and stronger elephants are chained, i was relieved to be honest. They were moving logs around the site with their handlers. The youngsters are adorable, bottle feeding the babies is something i will cherish forever. The walk down to the river with the elephants should be seen from a distance, follow slowly or go before them, watch from the waters edge and enjoy the fun of all the elephants doing normal stuff. I know it's all for the tourist but some if not all of the elephants would have died without intervention of this orphanage. Go and enjoy

Every time that I go to Sri Lanka, I make it a point to visit Pinnawala. Watching a herd of elephants at such close quarters is an absolute delight and if you love animals, this is the place you must definitely head to. Try and get there early in the morning when it's time to feed the baby elephants. You can also enjoy watching the elephants while they are bathing in the river. The restaurants by the river are quite expensive and the service is not very good. You'll find some people trying to sell you bracelets saying that it's made of hair from the tail of the elephant and that it brings good luck. Please take that with a pinch of salt.

A must visit! When you first go, make sure to watch the elephants move from the river to the general area. You may be alarmed when you see chains around some of the elephants but these are only around the elephants with a violent history. If you want to feed the elephants do the fruit feeding and not the bottle feeding. For the fruit feeding you get given a basket of fruit and you place the fruit into the elephant's trunk. There is plenty of space for photos and videos to be taken as well. The bottle feeding was rather chaotic - people pushing and shoving with no room for photos. You only get about 4 seconds to feed the baby elephants which seem to just wait for the tourists to feed them. If you walk to the top there's a place with the adult elephants and a few babies. The keepers will encourage the younger family members to have a photo with the elephants first, then the older females and finally the older males. Expect to be hounded for about a 500 rupee tip from the keepers (some say this is too expensive but it comes out at about 2.25 british pounds). If you have a guide he will probably take you into the 'elephant poo paper' factory where they make toilet roll from elephant poo. Try to avoid this if possible because it seems like a waste of time. About 10 minutes before the elephants are due to go to the river, walk up to one of the small restaurants for a drink. They all overlook the river so you can see the elephants in the water. My key points are: Bring a camera Bring small notes for drinks and tips Fruit feed not bottle feed I hope this helped and you have a great time:) - char (16)

There are a lot of mixed reviews on this place, but we really enjoyed it and hopefully can debunk a few things. Our guide/ driver came in with us. We went up to see the group of mother/ child elephants, and they were all there freely. There was a gorgeous, tiny baby too. They tended to stick together in a group, protecting the baby but also they were really curious and wanted to investigate everyone! Sometimes they got a bit close, so the keepers would ward them back with a loud noise and clapping. I only saw a stick used once as a gentle prod when a huge elephant got very close, otherwise they were nudged away. They bring two young elephants out for feeding time; it gets crazy busy and crowded here so it's best to wait until it's quiet. Our guide was mates with the security guard, so we went back and my husband got to bottle feed one! I also got nibbled which was a funny sensation. Our guide explained to us that some elephants do have chains on, especially during feeding, but this is because they are newly rescued from the wild and so aren't used to close human contact yet. Even so, after feeding time they could wander round freely. One they are used to being around people, they relax this and then remove them completely. The best part is if you go across the road to the river. There are a lot of souvenir shops here (which are much cheaper than the actual gift shop) and also a cafe where you can watch the elephants bath and be washed over lunch. You could see that the elephants were genuinely content and were free to amuse themselves; the keepers just sat nearby when they weren't washing an elephant. It is a truly beautiful sight watching them playing in the water. A couple of cheeky ones tried to get close to people. We really enjoyed it. I was nervous because of some reviews I had read, but take the time to listen to the reasons behind the way they do things there and make up your own mind. Also, once you get in the grounds, lovely toilets.

The journey is definitely worth the effort. The best part of the orphange is watching the elephants go down to the waters to bathe. Fourteen years ago this had the appearance of a genuine orphanage, there was a three legged elephant who had trodden on a land mine, another who was blind... All were being cared for and roamed freely, the only shackled ones were the disturbed or dangerous ones. Now things have become more commercialised. Most of the elephants are chained or being herded around and their keepers constantly badger you for money. We were literally grabbed to have photos with an elephant and the keeper immediately held out his hand demanding money. We gave him a token amount but he demanded "thousand" which we refused to hand over. Feeding the baby elephants costs 350 rupees but the bottles are much smaller and last about 5 seconds, a manic affair! It's an experience that is unfortunately spoiled by the greediness of those who work there and the ambiguous nature of the place, the beautiful mammals are not as carefree as you'd like.

After the hour journey from Kandy in Sri Lanka we visited the Elephant Orphanage. Our first impression was it was costly at the equivalent  of $25 entry - but that  was to help the elephant orphans - right? We felt the main goal here was to remove cash from gullible tourists - as there was an extra charge of you wanted to place your hand on a milk bottle when feeding the 'babies', another charg if you wanted to take turns feeding one elephant a small basket of fruit, and another charge when you have your picture taken - oh sir that will cost you. not even sure if this is an elephant rescus area or just exploitation. Our driver was keen to get us there to feed the baby elephants as they do this at 3 certain times a day - but it seems everyone got this advice too as it was very crowded. The main herd of elephants you get to see are separated back with rocks that they could step over but it prevent them getting close to you. There are also lots of 'keepers' with sticks and hooks to tap them back. I can't say I saw any of them use it overly agressively but it wasn't nice to see. The other main attraction is small herds of 8 or so are walked down to the river for bathing. They are changed up and cross a busy road before heading down a tourist street. At this point they are chained up to hooks on the river. The standard thing to do is stand on the river bank and watch but if you were to go to pinnewala, I'd recommend getting lunch in one of the restaurants over the river and watching. It avoids the crowds and gives a good view of the whole river. At the point the handlers beckon tourists forward to have photos with the elephants or bathe them, they do expect tips for this. I had a photo and paid a couple of hundred rupees but I did hear them getting pretty forceful with one lady who washed an elephant in the river and demanded 2000 rupees for it. Entrance for tourists is 2500 rupees and claims to be run solely for the protection of elephants. If you want to see elephants up close then go - but be aware it's by no means a nice environment for them or you.

Our visit to the elephant orphanage was totally different from the description given in many of the negative reviews. Arriving at 1 pm, we were able to be hands-on with some young elephants in enclosures, admire the large herd wandering freely in the scrub and watch up close as a couple of elephants had a hosedown. We then followed the elephants down to the river (you need an orphanage ticket for this) to watch the elephants bathe whilst we had lunch, which was a fabulous experience. At no point did I see any of the keepers mistreat any elephant in any way. Yes, they carry pointed sticks, but at any time when it looked like any elephants were going to get too close to the visitors, all it took was a shout to get them to move away. The chains that the elephants wear are used to tether them from time to time, but since these are animals that weigh upwards of half a ton and can carry four people, I suspect the weight of the chain is no more of a burden than a rope would be to a cow. Personally I much prefer the freedom to roam that the elephants have here compared to the average European zoo, and I suspect the elephants would agree. There was one chancer trying to charge people 1000 rupees to touch an elephant: don't bother, just wander down to the enclosures by the milk-feeding area to have a free stroke. But definitely visit the elephant orphanage - it's a unique experience.

This is a MUST for anyone travelling in Sri Lanka. Make sure you time your visit to coincide with the feeding and washing of the elephants. Early morning  ( we were there before 9) or early evening. The "orphanage" is a huge parkland with fenced off areas for feeding the babies or training the older elephants but it is spacious and as close as you'll get to seeing herds in the wild. You are free to wander about and there are signs telling you where you can't go. We went with a private guide so I can't comment on any tours provided by the centre. We were able to feed the babies and got our photos taken for 350 rupees each although it was all done by "tipping" the military looking guard in the enclosure so not typical, I guess. Don't use the toilets outside the orphanage but wait till you are inside where there are "western" toilets that are really clean and well looked after. After visiting the orphanage , you come out the main gate and cross the main road, walk along to your left to go down to the river to see the elephants bathing.  The highlight of the visit was watching the herd of elephants walk down a narrow street lined with little souvenir shops on the way to the river to bathe. There is a viewing gallery at the bottom of the street but we tucked ourselves in a side road at the bottom on the left hand side and got an amazing view of them towering over us as they ambled by. It was incredible. There is lots of space around the river to watch and you can choose where to stand. Watching them freely wander about in the river is a beautiful sight and some cross over to the sand to throw sand and have a sand bath. Mahouts wash a small one for the tourists to see but the rest roam freely in a naturally beautiful setting. You could stand and watch them for hours but we moved on, so again I can't say how long they stay down there. Go! It's unforgettable and really worth it.

However the viewing point is bit of a circus, with souvenir shops, restaurants and bars, and crowded with tourists. Some elephants are in chains, and the people tending the elephants ask money for allowing you to take a picture next to the elephants. Across the road there is a zoo park where the animals stay and feed between baths, which is somewhat less crowded. The entrance fee is 2500 rupees - quite steep. It has ticket SLR 1000.  The location has number of shopping outlets for clothing, accessories, handicrafts and restaraunts.

Book a cheap guesthouse in the street where the elephants walk to to river and you will get to see and bathe and cuddle them for free. 2500 rupees for a very tourist-ish spot was too much for me. You can see it in a few hours so no need to sleep over. Although I did so I could see them bathe twice!

Big elephants, chained tuskers, baby elephants, seemingly drunk elephants, hungry elephants, freshly bathed in the lake elephants......it was an Elephant's day out indeed... Grass-eating herd of elephants, quietly enjoying their day not bothered with the flock of tourists around them, posing for pics and i actually stretched my hand out to an elephant and he extended his trunk to reach my palm. Not sure if he was expecting goodies or giving me a handshake - felt privileged and exhilarated with that experience. Loved the time out that day with the Elephants in Pinnawala.

We took a taxi from Kandy to visit the Pinawalla Elephant Orphanige. After a discussion with our landlord in Kandy we chose this over the Millennium Foundation, because this is government run and supposed to be more 'natural'. We found it disappointing. There were many elephants but a lot of them in chains. After being invited to pose with an elephant we were immediately asked for money. It was great to see these giants up close but all in all we were disappointed.

Visited the orphanage, can't remember the price we paid to enter. There are a lot of adorable elephant babies in different enclosures. The elephants get washed in the river across the road from the orphanage. Nice to see them play around in water. You can also feed the elephants here, you can buy fruit and bananas. There's a restaurant overlooking the river which has decent food and juices. Great place to relax and watch the elephants.

Great facility set up by the government to look after orphaned elephants. Feeding time was great to watch and the elephants looked in great condition and were well looked after by the staff. Only surprise was the price which at 2,500 Sri Lankan rupees per person was very high.

there are various places in Kandy, where you can see Elephants. but there is a catch. many of them are operated by private organizations and the tickets are really expensive. specially for foreigners. however, for SAARC countries the ticket prices are less. the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is operated by government. for SAARC Countries adult the ticket price is around 750! and for foreigners it is 1500 rupee or may be high. in comparison to other places which charge more for tickets, this one is better. you can feed the Elephants but than you have to pay again. you get to see a great view of Kandy from the site.  the place is huge but you can only roam around to certain points.Lakshala have a souvenir shop here, which is really nice. and price of some of the items are relattively cheap than other places. there are numerous souvenir shops outside the orphanage. overall, it was fun.

This was my third visit over the past 14 years, the last being 11 years ago and what a dramatic change has occurred! To begin with it cost 5000 SriLankan rupees for my husband and I to enter (approx £25). To our disgust, this did not include anything and once inside the gates we were asked for money from the majoots (touts) to touch the elephants (one asked for 2500 SKR to just stand next to one near the river!) Obviously we didn't succum to this daylight robbery. The total disorganisation of this Singalese Government run place is clearly evident from the lack of clear directions to the rudeness and small mindedness of the 'security' men. I am very fond of elephants and having been here before wanted my husband to be able to enjoy the wonderful experience I had 11 years ago here before it had become a tourist money making trap. There are very few elephants inside, no where near the numbers they once had. (From the sheer number of places along the same road offering elephant rides it's likely that they rent the poor creatures out, not for the elephants' benefit but to line the government's back pocket.) Every elephant now is chained in some way unlike 11 years ago when the mahoots were able to control them in the traditional way without metal enforcement. I am so sorry to say that Pinnawela elephant orphanage has sadly lost the charm and beauty it once had. The greedy Singalese government has gone too far and appear to be utterly blinded by money. In my opinion don't bother going. You'll see more elephants in the myriad of tourist tat shops nearby, made from wood.

We arrived at Pinnawala at 9am just before the morning feeding. The entrance fee is expensive for what you get at 2500SLR each. We also paid 350SLR each to feed the baby elephants. The orphanage is set on a very large piece of land. We started by going to a penned area where we fed the babies a bottle of milk...the whole process is done in less that a minute! Then we walked up to a large field where a herd of about 20 elephants were grazing. We were able to watch them close up and took photos. Beware of staff wanting to take your photo for an additional fee. We then crossed the road and watched as the herd followed and went down to the river to bathe. It was amazing to watch so many elephants roaming free and playing. The pictures that people have posted are an accurate reflection of what you will see. There were very few souvenir shops that we came across in our travels in Sri Lanka so you may want to take the time to do a little shopping here while you have a chance.

Visited this place in the month of December 2014 along with my wife..we reached here in the afternoon, wherein all the elephants were taken for bathing in the river..it was a fantastic experience to watch those elephants play with their calves in the water as we enjoyed our late lunch...

The best part of the visit is to see the elephants bathing. This was truly amazing with over 40 elephants in the water.  We also saw the baby elephants being fed which was disturbing because the elephants were basically being fed as customers paid to hold the bottle. This was chaotic.

My wife had visited here years ago and was able to wash the elephants in the river. My daughter was really looking forward to this only to find they've stopped doing it. However, you do get to be really close to the elephants, and at times there are no barriers between you and them. It's worth a visit, and try and time that visit with when the elephants go down to the river as it's nice to watch them bathing.

The place was a bit smelly.... But it was great experience to look at the elephants pretty close, even we touch the elephants :) Watch them fed, our guide was a great guide, he took us there right in time when they fed the elephants, and the best part was to see them took a bath in the river. Again, we came right in tike because of our tour guide. There was an elephant with no ear, sadly a leopard bit him/her ear. And also there was a 3 legged elephants caused by mine trap.

It was amazing to see so many elephants so close. The problem was that several elephants was chaned and couldn't move freely - that was an upset :( The location itself is great, we stayed at night there but there's nothing to do at all at night - only sleep. The view on the river from a hotel we stayed was just perfect. Elephants shown up in the morning.

I went there in nov 2013 the weather was perfect. everyone must go and see the elephants taking a shower in the river and how the trainers speak with the elephants. you must see the old and the young elephants . don't skip the paper factory :)

The van ride from Negombo to Pinnawala took us about 2.5 hours - a rather bumpy ride as the roads are not the best. But once you reach there you are just so amazed by these wonderful creatures!!! The orphanage is on the right side of the road but everyday they take the elephants for a bath across the road to the streams. Such a splendid sight!!! And at the orphanage they have an area for the blind elephants, an area for the wild ones, for the pregnant ones and my fav - the babies!!!! There are many small shops around the area and you can buy souvenirs there. There is also a restaurant that serves buffet meals. Not the cleanest though. But they have a shop in there that sells paper made out of elephant poop!!! Just 5 minutes away from there is a tea-factory - make sure you visit it & get a cuppa!

Really enjoyed seeing the elephants here, two main locations: The river where they bathe in the mornings and a large area of plains where you'll find them in the afternoon. The place itself I very well maintained - with great toilers surprisingly. You can leave the complex to go see the elephants by the river and come back inside as long as you still have your ticket. The elephants themselves are in good shape and were mostly well treated except for two younger ones that we saw in chains and another two that were stuck in a very small pen with no obvious shade. Other than that they are free to roam the park and guides will constantly offer the chance for an elephant ride or a photo for a fee. I had a very good day out here and would recommend, but the sight of a small minority being less well treated did taint the experience somewhat.

The elephant ride, elephant shower / bath is a nice experience. All the folks there ask for a tip! You will anyway end up giving it to the "guide" so do not give it to anyone else unless you want to. Elephants are in an OK shape. Being with the elephants make you feel good. Dont expect as per any pamphlets that you get to see. Nowhere near that for sure. No baby elephants when I went. But definitely a must visit.

Take some time to visit the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage...you will not be disappointed.  Make sure you go in time to feed the elephants and then stand back in the shade and observe as they quietly walk past on their way to the river for their daily bathing ritual.  Absolutely magnificent! Once they have crossed the road you can stroll down behind them through some lovely little souvenir shops on your way to the river.  Take up a position on the balcony of one of the little restaurants overlooking the river and sit back with a cup of tea or a cool drink and observe the antics of these gentle giants.  You can stay as long as you like and if you're lucky you'll get to see them walking past again on their way back.  This is an amazing experience and something that really must be seen to be believed.

The Pinnawala elephant orphanage was my second trip in Sri Lanka. I was not given much pre-information about the site and I also had not read about it either. I was expecting to see an education/information center giving some background about the institution, how the elephants had come to be there , about elephants in general but this, as far as I could see was not available, which was a great shame. The day I arrived (a Friday), there were roughly 8 coaches there as well, and when we were inside, realised that these were full of children. Looking at the other reviews it seems the site is regularly overrun by school children so keep that in mind when visiting. The elephants themselves seemed to be in good health - I did not see any elephants showing signs of distress as per some of the other reviews but it looked like they slept in concrete  zoo like facilities which I was not expecting and it was not clear to me how often they were allowed to roam free. When I arrived, the elephants were all out in grasslands, with the Sri Lanka country side as a beautiful back drop. It should be noted that the elephants do have chains around their legs although it does not seem to disturb them walking. It does mean however than if one elephant wanted to wander off a little further than the others then it could not but that's not to say that they are tied together and don't have any freedom. You'll see by the pictures that when not walking towards the rivers, they have alot of space. There are many guards  with long bayonnet type poles who walk alongside the elephants and keep them within the pre designated areas. While the elephants were grazing we were able to get quite close to them. I noticed in some parts of the site the elephants were getting friendly with the school children as well. Most of these elephants were previously kept as pets until they were rescued and so in the majority of cases they are domesticated. The highlight of the visit is when the elephants are taken to the local river and bathe.  I am unclear how long they are there for but we spent around 20 minutes watching them in the river and it felt as though they were going to be there for a lot longer. The river where they bathe is extremely picturesque and worth seeing. The walk down to it is filled with tourist shops etc. Each elephant gets literally hand scrubbed by a couple of the elephant guards. The elephants seem to yield quite easily to this activity, many of them submerging themselves completely in the water as they get cleaned Overall it was an interesting experience but I found the schedule and activities quite confusing - there are no signs, or timings, or information as to what happens when, what can be seen where etc. It was so confusing that we nearly missed the whole elephants bathing in the river spectacle simply as we had quickly nipped to the toilet. The site needs better organisation and communication. I also felt that the guards were aggressive towards the guests. I would have had a better feeling about visiting this site if the mission of the organisation was a little clearer and if there was more of an educational/conservationist aspect to it. It was however a good chance to get up close to these magnificient creatures, and I wish we had been allowed/welcome to spend more time getting to know them

Lovely to see the elephants - once you arrive you'll get the chance to book various tickets - worth paying a little bit extra to feed them.  You'll get to stroke and feed them. All the elephants are taken down to the river once a day so be sure to ask when - it's an amazing site. On the main road back there are many other places you can visit which provide an opportunity for you to ride an elephant, feed and bathe them for around 1000 rupees - worth stopping.

If you are interested in getting an excitement fix during your holiday probably Pinnawala is one of the few places where this excitement laced with a bit of fear, astonishment, surprise, and the feeling that "what am I suppose to do now" definitely exist. I went to sri lanka for my honeymoon in november 2014 - mainly to go and see the elephants. I had read reviews of the orphanage before hand and admittedly had seen both excellent and terrible reviews. I was really debating about going to the orphanage when one of my colleagues told me that she had visited 10 years before and that it was absolutely fantastic and the elephants were treated well. So with that in mind I was so excited when our rep told us there was a trip to go and see the elephants at pinnawala and was literally counting down the days until we were due to visit there. When we arrived, i couldnt get out of the car fast enough to get into the orphanage. As we walked in, i was shocked to see men everywhere with bull hooks. I understand they need them for protection, however, these men were stabbing the elephants with these bull hooks for no reason. My husband and I then went over to see the baby elephants, just in time to see them fed. There were men there, hitting the baby elephants with branches, which upset me even more. There were elephants chained up, which we swaying and looked in distress. And the workers tried to get money off you for everything. My husband was hounded for money for taking a photo himself of an elephant. Then one of the men was very persistent about getting me close to an elephant and then charged us for that too! I think we were in the orphanage for roughly 40 minutes when i had seen enough and left very upset. One of the reasons we chose sri lanka is because my husband knew how much i loved elephants and wanted to visit some, however, although an experience, it is one i never wish to repeat again and really regret going. The experience really affected the rest of our honeymoon.

Boy do I wish I had read the reviews before coming to this place. As a huge animal lover I found it extremely distressing. Many elephants were chained up and looked clearly distressed, swaying repeatedly from side to side. The mahouts were money-grabbing and quite threatening to the elephants and it really felt like a zoo. If it were a true orphanage why were there so many older elephants which could have been released after a certain age? It is a complete tourist trap, I left in tears and feel haunted by what I saw. These animals should only be seen in the wild.

The way they treat the elephants at this place is awful! Chained up, hit for bad behaviour and expected to perform all day for long hours. There are others nearby, for example elephant freedom project, which protect the animals and treat them well! Do not go here! Don't harm animals by riding them and giving money to this awful place

As the picture suggests, there are many organised school trips to the elephant orphange. When we arrived it was very difficult to see anything due to the number of children. Also photographs were difficult until the school party had moved on. However the essence of the orphanage needs to be praised and encouraged as it provides a home for disabled elephants.

It is difficult for me to judge how the elephants here were treated, but for the most part they seemed healthy. A few things struck me as off-putting and dangerous, but it was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity and a memorable portion of our trip to Sri Lanka The good: Elephants seemed healthy, not scarred or hungry looking. Mostly chain-free. The bad: Few barriers between guests and elephants, employees ask for tips to bring you too close to elephants. Male elephants were tied up to one side, seemed agitated. Especially a giant tusked elephant that was chained and swaying side to side. Attendants seemed rough with the elephants at times. They yelled orders, swatted with sticks (arguably not hard enough to hurt an elephant), and threw rocks at one elephant that was messing with another one. They also used pokers and a knife at one point. The ugly: I saw an elephant try to grab a toddler at the fruit feeding area. Please do not let your small children sit with their backs to adult elephants while holding fruit. This is a recipe for disaster and it put me on edge for the rest of the visit.

Visited orphanage with our family (5kids and 2 adults). We were unsure what to expect given varying Trip Advisor reviews but we're pleasantly surprised. The elephants were in the river when we got there and had freedom to roam as they pleased, only a small few had chains and it was explained that his was for the ill tempered ones only. The mahouts seemed genuinely caring towards the elephants although they were all keen to get a 'small tip' for setting up a photo op. Again this was no big deal and we were happy to oblige. In the orphanage it self we saw more baby elephants that appeared to be well treated. We understand how some might see this place as cruel but we could not agree, and would simply ask 'What would be the viable alternative for the baby orphaned elephants that are brought here?'. Overall, we loved it and would highly recommend it for a visit!

I parked my car in the orphanage's car park in front of the main gate. There was no indication, no sign board or a person which/who mention about a parking fee. When I returned to the car, a man appeared from nowhere, with a ticket book in his hand, and asked for Rs 350 as the fee. I was surprised, but paid it,and when I asked for the receipt, he said no need a receipt since I'm leaving, and rushed back into a restaurant nearby. One of the highlights of the holiday was visiting the elephant orphanage. The place is a must for any visiting Sri Lanka and love to see elephants up close. The tickets are cheap and well worth it. Excellent toilets inside the orphanage.

After reading a lot of reviews I was concerned how I would feel about the elephant orphanage. Much to my surprise I could not disagree more that the animals are treated "cruelly". This is just categorically not true. They looked healthy, happily tooting away and had plenty of space for the number of elephants there were. We were there for the bathing time in the lake which was so cute to watch the animals splashing each other! The fee to get in is around £14 for two people which I felt was reasonable in comparison to some of the other tourist prices in Sri Lanka. The only irritating thing were the workers who love to ask for a tip! You give them 200 rupees and they state they are unhappy with 200 and want 2000...bit rude really!

Boy, what an awful sight!  I was so excited about visiting Sri Lanka's Elephant Orphanage for my 50th birthday, and although some reps said it was better to go to the Elephant Transit Park, my husband and I thought it was just sales talk.  Boy what a shock, it was just awful!  This has turned into a money making place rather than animal welfare.  Everything is about bleeding money from tourists!  The elephants are in chains and the men guiding them have long wooden poles with metal hooks on to stab the elephants in their poor little trunks.....I just started crying!  My husband took me away from the main area to a fence at the back.....and what we saw will haunt us forever!  There were individual elephants heavily chained to trees flapping their ears and thrashing their trunks on the chains and swaying hard to get away from men that kept stabbing at them with these hooked poles.  One elephant had blood on its trunk....my husband shouted out to them to stop, I was hysterical.  When the men saw us, they stopped and one approached us to talk to my husband.  He said they were wild elephants that needed to be trained, they didn't have pain!  Just their behaviour of flapping ears and trunks and swaying back and forth told anyone that they were stressed, please please don't go here.

Felt uneasy as it seems more a tourist attraction rather than a refuge for the elephants.  Quite a few of the elephants are in chains and the feeding of the baby elephants no more than a show for the tourists.  We saw the mahouts taking bribes to feed the elephants at the river and have photos taken.

This place was one of my favourite visits. Elephant watching was so calming and Breathtaking. The feeding times were awesome. For 500 bucks we can buy a fruit platter and feed some pregnant elephants. That was so cool. There were baby elephants which you can feed milk from bottles. That was a cool experience too. It was really nice. And near the elephant bathing place there are some nice restaurants u could have lunch while watching them bathe. Overall a nice day out. And was glad i went there!! Kids really enjoyed it too.

I've visited Pinnawala Elephant *Orphanage* (with a wink) several times, often to take visiting family who of course want to check it out, there's not many elephants in Birmingham, UK. Firstly, this is by no means an orphanage. Secondly, the treatment of the elephants can be a little off-putting, and the persistence of some of the handlers towards tourists for pictures with the elephants posing, or to feed the elephants is not regulated or controlled in any way. This of course in exchange for hefty (by Sri Lankan standards) tips. Your opinions/morals/ethics/standards towards animals in captivity will influence whether you enjoy your visit to Pinnawala, it is an absolute tourist trap and the elephants could clearly be looked after better. However, it is also a once in a lifetime opportunity to see so many elephants in one place at one time, and the elephants themselves are very entertaining and make for some good tourist snaps. THERE IS NO POINT IN GOING TO THE ORPHANAGE OUTSIDE OF BATHING TIME, although a quick tour round after you've seen the elephants bathe is okay, but you're not missing anything if you leave without seeing it. Don't waste your money on any of the shops, the Poo Paper shop is the best of the bunch and there is a free tour on how the paper is made, and in fairness not too much pressure to buy from their shop at the end of the tour. Although everything is extortionately over priced. Finally, don't fall in to the trap of staying in or near Pinnawala, get up early if you're in Colombo or Kandy and it's doable in a day, it's quite easy to detour to Pinnawala on the way to Kandy from Colombo, even if you're using public transport - although I wouldn't recommend this if you have young children.

I love elephants. The only one I'd previously seen in Sri Lanka was chained up at a Hindu Temple in Colombo and it reminded me of one I saw in a zoo once many years ago. Not a happy memory. However, this was something else altogether. We travelled from Colombo by car and arrived in time for 49 elephants of all sizes and ages to be washed and enjoy the beautiful bathing area. It was a sight I will never forget. Their size belies the grace of these magnificent creatures.They stand, sway, lie down and play in the water, seeming to enjoy the attention from the 100's of onlookers. Later, in the park I was almost overcome by the scene. Few elephants but some of the most beautiful scenery Sri Lanka has to offer. Later still, having enjoyed  the milk of a young coconut, I watched in awe as the now bathed elephants were walked up the path between the numerous shops and stalls, inches from me. It was a sight I will never forget. I have read in other reviews that you can be ripped off at Pinnawala, and yes, westerners are charged more than locals, but that is clearly shown. And yes, you are encouraged to feed and help to bathe the elephants ( and pay for the privilege ), but a polite "no" is accepted if that's what you want. And yes, some of the elephants are chained, but I asked about that and for some it's because they could wander off and get lost or hurt and some are a little cantankerous in their old age, and most aren't chained at all. I found the staff pleasant and helpful and the state run gift shop well stocked, reasonable and a good place to dip some shopping. ( there are other shops and I used them as well )

Ok, first of all this is an orphanage but also a business, so keeping that in mind I can say I liked it. They keep the elephants there and it seems they take good care of them. We saw them bottle feeding them, we took pictures with the elephants and we saw them going for one of their many daily baths.

Having read previous reviews, some good some not so good, I formed the belief that this place is very well run and the animals are well looked after, those that have chains around they're feet are the problem or rogue elephants, and they are not mistreated. I especially thought it was funny that all the store keepers shut up shop when they are walking the elephants to the river, but after seeing can fully understand, it would be like the proverbial bull in a China shop scenario other wise. The train trip from Colombo Fort station to the Rambukkana Railway Station was very picturesque and well worth it.

The elephant orphanage itself was kinda sad as the elephants were paraded around like a zoo (ie baby milk feeding etc) at 2500LKR, it is also pretty expensive. Some of the elephants were chained too. The keepers like to pretend to help you take photos or let you go closer to the elephants, but all they really want are tips. Try not to do that as it encourages the keepers to b "corrupt" The best part was at 2pm when the elephants are led to the river for a bath. It's really crazy to see so many elephants in one place! That was worth the admission for sure. The river backdrop plus the elephants make for great photos! So do come at around 1pm to visit the orphanage as well as get to witness the river bathing too!
