Wow I never thought I'd be allowed to get so close to wild animals.  You can view the elephants playing in their river and have a chance to feed the baby ones or bath them.  Make sure you have small currency with you as keepers and helpers all ask for tips.  The elephants then get lead up through the village which is amazing.  You can get so close.  In the main park you see them being fed and trained, you can for a small price give a baby elephant a bottle of milk. There's lots of shops selling tourist gifts.  As we were a group we had a guide who was very good.

we had heard about this place from some friends and decided to visit sri lanka after seeing their photographs....however some reviews spoke of the way the men were mistreating the animals. when we reached there it was definately a beautiful place...but you could see the chains on the elephants legs. however they were allowed to move around everywhere and we got the impression that only when they are in some areas (where people can feed them after paying a fee) they are chained. we followed the elephants to the river to watch them having a bath...since it was a hot day it was lovely to see the elephants lying down in the river to cool off.  the ticket costs 700SLR for foreign people belonging to the SAARC countries. it is definately worth a visit! the gift shop there has many things that are really pretty and i was tempted to buy them...but i thought id wait and see if i could get it in Kandy since it was just the beginning of the trip,...i did not manage to buy the same things that we found in pinnawalla...so i would suggest that if you find something you like you pick it up there itself.

visited on 5th of june with my husband .. place was very nice. we were lucky. we reached at 9 am and that was the feeding time for elephant .. we enjoyed it . after 1 hr (10am) we convert to other side to see elephant bathing .. everything was good .. the place was fully crowded with students.. i liked this place & i will be back with my children on my next visit to srilanka

This is probably the biggest shelter house for the elephants . I've seen many elephants earlier in sanctuaries and other places but had never heard of an orphanage, so decided to check it out. This is a very well established commercial orphanage with a huge tourist attraction. There's an entrance fee to visit the orphanage where the elephants are taken care of. They have proper time-table for bathing the elephants and feeding the baby elephants with a bottle of milk. If you want to feed a baby elephant yourself with a bottle, you have to buy an extra ticket. The timings  are set in such a way that you can do both the activity one after the other . It's a commercial tourist attraction with the limelight on the elephants. Please feel free to like and follow my FB page Suejatas Lifestyle and also check my book out on travel , enjoy !!!

It is real delight to see Elephants in their natural environment and without chains. Atleast 70-80 elephants ... Kid elephants, old elephants... Bathing in river (Mahavelly Ganga). Definitely good for a 3 hour stopover. Ticket money for us (non local visitors) is high.

It was first established in 1975 with 7 orphan elephants and gradually became a scientific captive breeding program for Elephants. The timings are as follows 0830: Opens 0915: Bottle feeding of elephants 1000: Herd leaving to the river 1200: Return from the river 1315:Bottle feeding of elephants 1400: Herd leaving to the river 1600: Return from the river 1700:Bottle feeding of elephants 1800: Close Make sure that you arrive in time so that you get to see all the activities. Cost for bottle feeding/ milk feeding of elephants is SL Rupees 350. Cost of entry for adults from SAARC countries is SL Rupees 700. (You will need to carry your passport for proof)

I thought riding an elephant would be up there as one of the most memorable things to do when travelling. However, the experience has just left bad memories of seeing elephants being treated in such an inhumane manner. Shouted at, beaten with sticks with sharp hooks on the end... Left lying in water chained and looking almost dead or like prisoners which people are most probably irritating them by throwing water over them. The only enjoyable part was feeding the elephants which u need to also pay to buy the food. Only then did the elephants looks happy. Please do not support this cruelty. Naturally we all love to be close to such amazing animals but the more people who go there just encourage it to continue. These animals should be free and happy in the wild and I would rather see them in such conditions even if it means not being so close or riding them.

This Elephant Orphanage is situated close to Rambukkana,  Pinnawala. There are several routes that can be used to get here but we came through Kegalle. There are two time slots that the elephants are fed and then taken for a bath during the day. feeding starts at 9.15AM and then they are taken across the road to the river for a bath. The evening time slot is 1.15PM. They take a good 1-1.30hours at the river for the bathing time. Fee for a foreigner is Rs.2500 & for a local Rs.100. There is quite a disparity here in terms of the fee charged. What is most interesting to watch is an elephant so up close & how they interact with other elephants, how they eat & how they bathe. By observing there is a lot you could learn. It is sad to see though that people feed elephants almost anything although it said not to. Be wary of the individuals who stand outside and try to get you to take elephant rides etc... as it is not very clear if they are part of the staff or some outside outfit which is legally allowed to do this. Lot's of souvenir shops around and even has shops selling recycled paper made out of elephant dung. Only downside is that it can get very hot and sunny so use that sunscreen.

My partner and I visited here while in Kandy for a couple of nights. After reading the mixed reviews here I was a little apprehensive of what we would see but I needn't have worried. We arrived early and we didn't see the bathing at the river so our experience was limited to the main compound. This was large and well kept. The herd had obviously had some training over the years as they all stayed behind the rocks away from the public area, and there were clearly animals which were or seem stressed or disturbed. That said there was no sign of mistreatment during our visit. There were a lot of animals and the feeding progressed well. Again, one large elephant was trained to bring the food supplies but again, no mistreatment seen. I would recommend a visit if you're in the area.

Elephants in chains, their keepers constantly yelling on them to come closer so tourists would be able to take pictures, pushing them to stay in a space without any grass to eat, taking money for everything - touching or feeding the elephant...horrible...The best moment of that afternoon was watching elephants in the river (I mean the ones who weren't in chains or pushed to lay down in the water)

We travelled to Kandy and then on to Pinnawala to see the Elephants for my dad's birthday. It was an experience like no other, we washed and fed the Elephants we sat on a balcony of the nearby hotel where the Elephants approached us for food. It was unbelievable, my 5 year old daughter had the best day. I've read quite a few bad reviews on trip advisor saying the orphanage is cruel however all that we saw was the love and care they have for these incredible animals. In the orphanage itself they do not allow for any elephant rides so if that's what your going for, you will see places on your way to the orphanage where you can get an elephant ride and an elephant shower. It may be there that people find the treatment of the Elephants cruel but the orphanage itself is there to protect and care for the Elephants. Beware it can become an extremely expensive day out as everyone wants a tip!

It was a nice visit with all the elephants at the orphanage. We really enjoyed watching them all walk through the small town down to the river to bathe. During the bathing we had lunch at one of the close restaurants. If you want to watch the elephants while enjoying your meal make sure to reserve spots at the restaurants.

This place is on your way while going to Kandy from Colombo airport. Takes around two hours to visit and roam around. You can view the elephants eating , bathing and relaxing in the river. The beasts ate treated very well and no nonsensical "rides" are allowed on these elephants. Respect and loved the way they keep these orphan elephants.

It's a nice place to see baby/adult elephants in a well kept condition. There is an option of feeding a baby elephant which I tried and was a wonderful feeling. Would definitely recommend it if visiting Sri Lanka. Make sure you check the correct timings so that you may be able to do/see everything. The elephant bathing spectacle is very unique and relaxing.

We went to this place on our way to Kandy. Reached there at 9 am. After few initial feeding shows we were taken to the river where elephants come for bathing. It's a real fun with few scary moments to see nearly 30-35 elephants running towards the river barely at a distance of 3-4 feet from you with nothing in between. Please stand at some height of possible.

Try to walk around the grounds to see the elephant feeding, elephant hospital and baby elephants bathing. Really enjoyed the experience...Worth a visit.

This is a great place to see the elephants. There are loads of them here! It's nice to wander about & see them but it's not so nice to see them all in chains. Also the baby elephant feeding is a rip off. You pay 350lkr for about 5 seconds of holding a bottle! You cannot fail to fall in love with the elephants. To see or be involved in feeding the baby elephants is a real must. When you think things cannot get any better, make your way to the river where you may get the chance to bath the elephants. This really is impossible to better. A fantastic experience we are never likely to forget.

Our eldest son, Luc, got married on the 11.04.2015 to his fabulously beautiful and pretty Princess Hiranya at the fantastic venue of the Chaaya Tranz Hotel in Hikkaduwa. A day tattooed on our skin by the hot sun in the bright blue sky of Sri Lanka. Our memories still filled with the perfect angelic and romantic wedding and warmth from our new families. How could anyone keeps a gang of visitors and tourists like our group, still dreaming of exotic memories with our eyes fully opened? Thanks to Luc and his father in law, Lalit, for their already great understanding of keeping us on our magic carpet, well cocooned amazing cloud. Luc's brother, Max, was to see, touch and feed elephants for his memorable 29th birthday. It was 06.00am and 16 of us prepared for a long trip from Hikkaduwa to the Orphanage. The old coach looked the part, ancient enough to have seen the creation of Ceylon and modern enough to have became the new Sri Lanka. Equipped with air conditioning perfectly working, new curtains for shading those white skins from the sun's big smile and a driver who was up to top World Racing a Driving League. His elderly co-pilot had the added function of jumping out of the vehicle when we stopped for a break and slide a big piece of square wood under one of the back wheels. Brakes were excellent but handbrake had a mind of its own. The Chaaya Tranz Hotel had provided us a take away European breakfast type with drinks, fruits, croissants, bread, butter, jam, yogurts. Damn, damn, damn! No dhal and rice noodles this morning. We were lucky. It was the 14th of April and New Year day in Sri Lanka so a Bank Holiday on a Wednesday. Not many people worked but not many were on the roads either and we made it in 4 hours instead of the usual 6 it would have taken a different day. We stopped once for cash money in a town and like everywhere in the country, the ATM worked wonders.  Another stop in a small village in the only restaurant there and closed for the day. The owner was sitting under the shade of the enormous covered terrace and our driver persuaded him to allow ladies to use his toilets. Men did too and he personally took me to his own brand new bathroom, adjacent to his bedroom. I felt very honoured and borrowed a cigarette from my younger son and change from my wife to thank him. The coach driver took us right at the gates of the Orphanage. Personal belongings were left in the vehicle and off we went. The entry tickets were expensive but not as extravagantly as in Europe. Elephants do eat a lot and need many staff to keep visitors safe. Although smaller in size than their African cousins, they are still big and remain wild animals. As such, the first one we all met, had a heavy chain necklace and chained legs to restrict their head and members' movements in case of a crises. The keeper was equipped with a long spear like tool with a hook at its top. The elephant obeyed to its keeper's voice and not once during our 5 hours there, I saw one keeper use the tool in order to hurt an animal. We went straight to the metal built parasol like open shelters. Several elephants of all sizes, ages and genders were wearing the usual heavy chains and only allowed to move a few centimetres. Under the supervision of several keepers, visitors could approach one mastodon at a time and queue to stroke the animal's trunk or its discoloured ears. Brig branches covered with fresh, green, shiny, juicy leaves were fed to the stoic pachyderms showing how agile they could use their trunk. Also how powerful their jaws were while shredding to purée the flexible wood. Children and adults alike were surprised by how soft their skin was, expecting their grey brown protective shell to be like concrete. A young 3 year old female was being taught how to carry a stack of heavy wood with her trunk. She demonstrated how intelligent she was. Cleverly, she would push the stack against one of her enormous feet and then roll her trunk around the beams. She then would go down a few steps with her load. She did it several time, only restricted in her steps by the heavy chains. In safe enclosures, baby orphans were on show and parents lifted their youngsters to stroke what in their mind must have looked like a Walt Disney's cartoon figure. All those beautiful Dumbo were as magic as the flying legend, only responding to caresses by softly and gently shaking their handsome heads. We, unfortunately due to our long trip to reach this heaven for orphan elephants, missed the bottle feeding of the youngest ones. Apparently, a spectacle by itself, the babies can drink 30 litres in a few seconds. We saw the herd coming back from the river and it was impressive. One, two, three, four, twenty, they keep coming and parking themselves in a gigantic shelter to have their feeds. What a special sight, a magic instant, an alien experience! It was time to go to a purposely built high level platform where a basket containing fresh fruits could be bought. Then one at a time, one person was able to sit near the far side of the terrace and with directions from a keeper, slides the fruits one by one in the docile elephant. This one had a great job. Visitors paid their dues and the animal got fed. People resplendent with pride, smiled happily, this memory engraved in their minds until they die. The ice cream stall did extremely well on this New Year day in Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. At the entrance of the Park we found a modern low building which accommodated the 16 of us and we had lunch, traditional food, pizzas, chips, anything one had fancied. Well cooked portions, serviced with diligence and at the right price. The afternoon was even more extraordinary. We met the herd crossing the main road and not one pedestrian, vehicle or even a tuk tuk dared pushing through. We waited until all went down the street leading to the river then were allowed to follow them once our morning's tickets were checked. The street had touristic shops selling rainbow coloured clothing items and artisans products which were displayed in and outside their shops. Not one elephant had disturbed the spray of the items for sale. The herd had descending a sharp steep rocky formation and was spread in the wide river, bathing, drinking under the tall stature of the bull elephant's protective aura. They appeared to be free to do whatever they felt like doing, an old mother using her trunk to wash a lone baby and two trunks embracing, making an almost perfect heart shape. Was I dreaming? No, we were all out of breath by the simple amazing beauty of nature at its best. The chains were still present around the necks and legs of the majestic beasts but no keepers, no spears, no ordering, they appeared almost free and in their natural environment. A pregnant female was kept apart, far away from the herd. She had been carrying for 2 years and was due to give birth in 2 weeks time. She was lying on her left side in the water, showering herself with heavy and strong jets of water coming out of her trunk. I went as close as I felt safe and took pictures. One keeper asked me if I wanted to go in the brown river and wash her. I thought he was joking but he wasn't. I took a few steps and remembered to ask how much it would cost. Too much for me but what unique experience it would have been! The way back to our coach was filled with today's many stories and experiences. Not one person complained about the long hours on the roads, the heat, the price of hiring the vehicle, the entry fee, the tips, the long day. We had another long, hot drive to Hikkaduwa but it was worth a small effort and a previous short night sleep. Thank you for this charitable human gesture towards these marvellous animals. Their park is well designed and safe for people of all ages but parents will want to keep their children close by. There is a fantastic view of higher mountains and deep thick green jungle in the background perfect for pictures of the Wild. On our way back, we stopped in Colombo and celebrated Max's birthday with the New Year meal at the Mount Alvinia Hotel and an enormous cake brought by our eldest son's mother in law, Jeevani and her husband, Lalit. A magic day like so many in Sri Lanka.

The tour operator arranged this trip which was worth visiting.  My wife also accompanied me on this trip and it was fun watching elephants who were returning back to their normal life after being taken in care by the Sri Lankan authorities.  It is a great job.  Took couple of photographs and mixed around with the elephants as if were their care takers.   It was great to feed them with the permission of the orphanage house.  A memorable visit I must say (date of actual visit is Nov.2014)

Nothing is like an elephant as another elephant. Well, there are some differences between the African and the Asian elephants but if you already made some elephants (or Big 5) safaris in Botswana or Zimbabwe you really don't need to visit the Pinnawela Elephant Orphanage.

If you are in Lanka.  Then you must visit here.  It's a really nice experience Shops for souvenirs are available You can encounter the elephants in different situations -feeding -bathing -and at the park The schedule for each place can be seen in the photo I have attached. Chairs are available for elderly (haven't seen wheel chairs there though) It's situated in the way between Colombo and Kandy.   So can visit while going back to Colombo before leaving the country (that's what I did) Bad thing about the place is the sellers in the shops. They will be annoying you if you cross by them trying to make you enter their shop obviously Overall.  It's an excellent experience

We visited in Sept 2002 and had a magical day. We were with our guide Dia and he got us right down into the water with the elephants.we washed them and spent a wonderful half hour in the water whilst crowds of people watched from above.a truly magical time.unfortunately I don't have photos uploaded on my computer,they are in 2 albums that are guarded with my life.

If you are going to Sri Lanka this is a must-see! The elephants are in their natural environment and you can go right up close to them. The staff try to sell you fruit to feed the animals with but it's a bit of a rip off. There's no need to feed them really, just seeing them was enough!

Pinnawala orphanage : 1.5 hrs drive away from colomobo, can be reached by taxi. One of the places to visit and spend ur day with elephants instead of humans Nicely maintained orphanage where there are timings for elephant bathing, fruit feeding and milk feeding with charges for each activity. Its good to see a handful of elephants marching towards the lake for bath for 2 hrs and enjoying the water with their trunks.. Better be prepared for the heat under sun as its all in open and difficult to find shade.. Way back to the orphanage from lake there are shops selling gifts made from elephant dung in a nice n recyclable manner. All in all nice experience,however tickets are costly for foreigner, so do check out before going.

It was great to take a stroll among the elephants and even better the elephant bath. The horrible think was not only the price of the ticket but the incredible amount of money the guards had requested for taking a picture with you / your kids with an elephant (8 USD at the park and 16 USD at the river). This behaviour spoiled the whole visit.

I went here for my birthday and was sadly disappointed. To me it was no different to a zoo? Some of the big elephants had huge chains around their necks which seemed to be some kind of "control" thing, plus quite a few had chains from one front foot to a back foot, quite sad to see? The nicest part was seeing them being taken to the river to bathe, but again, is there really a need for huge chains on their necks? All in all I felt it wasn't worth the 4+hours journey from Bentota and would not go again. The baby elephants seemed bored standing under a shelter and displayed symptoms of repetitive movements, again very sad.

Watching the elephants walking down to, bathing and walking back from the river is what this place is all about.The oprphanage itself is nothing special and some of the elephants are chained so it can be a little upsetting. You are told to get a ticket for the orphanage before going to the river but it is not legally required, Just go into the riverside hotel and have a drink.

if you are interested in observing little elephants in flies quarters ,this is the place for you. Don't expect acrobatics ,but they do put on a decent show with the elephant feeding routine. Visitors from Kerala might find the place a little boring especially if they have been to Guruvayur temple and its elephant enclosure

I visited this place on my way to kandy. We reached there by noon so that we could see the elephants coming back from their morning bathing session. This place gets crowded fast and hence need to be aware on the timing ( refer to attached ). If you are in a hurry but want to see elephants you can catch them up if you go near the main gate by 12.30-1 pm ( no need to by tickets for this.

There is plenty of space here for elephants but something struck me as wrong about this place. Elephants are chained, presumably so they don't run away, but what I know about elephants is that they need room to roam. The keepers don't seem to care too much about the wellbeing of the animals but that is just my perception. I had high hopes for this place but it seems to be just a cash cow - charging visitors to feed elephants in addition to the entry fee. I have mixed feelings about 'working animals' but this is a supposed orphanage where I guess the elephants are safe, but don't seem to be that happy. I felt guilty about spending my money here.

I found it fine. The elephants seemed calm and peaceful.. Some did look a tad skinny but overall they seemed alright. it was nice to watch them bathing and taking their own time to do it! We went for the 2pm session. Yes there are particular times they are brought out to bath.

A short walk from the highway takes you to the river where the elephants bathe twice a day.  You can pose with a baby for photos and have a nice lunch at one of the hotels or restaurants along the river.  After bathing, the elephants march down the street connecting the highway to the river, cross the highway, and re-enter the sanctuary which is extremely well maintained.  Lots of gift shops with interesting items.  Unforgettable.

I could argue the case for how much money is made off these creatures, but I'm never going to get this close up to so many lovely creatures. There are some animals who have been beaten, abused, saved, ill, trapped and now have a life. They are sometimes scarred, missing limbs, but they all seem very happy indeed. I enjoyed this place. It is a tourist trap, but so what. Scrubbing a full size Jumbo in the river with my 6 year old will stay with me for all my life. Good day out for the whole day. Expect to get wet.

We were not sure what to expect from this trip and ended up somewhat disappointed, especially after a 5am start to go there! There are something like 90+ elephants apparently. Most seem to be adults. The main objective seemed to be for the staff to get as much money from visitors for photo's. It was nice to see the elephants going into the river to bathe but overall we wouldn't have gone if we had known what to expect.

This place was terrible! It's not an orphanage its zoo. They do not care for their elephants and they treat them with no respect. They train the baby elephants early to fear a stick that they smack them with. I was here a total of 15 minutes and couldn't handle seeing how they were treating the animals anymore. When we were walking over to where the larger herd was feeding I saw two elephants chained to trees and both had less than a foot of chain. You could just see how confused they were on their faces--animals do not deserve to be treated that way and that type of treatment is what develops psychological problems, especially in creatures as intelligent as elephants. The larger herd all stuck closely together while they were feeding, which in elephants is a sign that they feel threatened, and other elephants were forced to walk around with chains on their necks. People get a clue! If this place was actually an orphanage/hospital then why would the elephants have chains around their necks and why wouldn't this "orphanage/hospital" place the elephants back into the wild after they had been treated? Please I beg you do not go here. Do not support this business. It's disgusting and extremely disappointing to be in the presence of people who feel they can treat these beautiful creatures with such disrespect. Also do not ride on elephants' backs in those baskets. Elephants have backs as sensitive as our own, and those baskets are actually terrible for their backs. If you want to have a true experience with elephants than I would encourage you to do the safari tours in Sri Lanka. I, personally, did not do a safari, but seeing elephants in the wild would be a much better experience than seeing them at this pathetic zoo. I would also encourage true lovers of elephants to check out the Elephant Nature Park in Chiang Mai--those people truly know how to treat the elephants!

Booked the trip through our holiday rep, virgin, at our hotel. I had seen reviews saying about elephants in chains etc but i choose to go and see for myself. Yes some elephants have no chains and are roaming around free but only in certain areas and if they cross the 'line' as such, then the guards get very aggressive and point spheres at them and shout to get them back. Which doesn't seem very fair when they aren't looking suspicious and are seeming to look for food. Some elephants are chained and apparently this is because there not tame yet. But some looked very distressed moving from side to side waving there trunks around. We had a guide stay with us from our hotel the whole time so had no trouble from the staff! When it came to feeding the babies it was nothing like i imagined! Such a disappointment! It was like a circus act the guards picking who would be next to feed the elephants, and after a while the elephants seem to be full and started to wonder around but the guards would push and poke them and shout at them to feed again! Such a waste of money!! Then it was bath time so we walked out of the orphanage across the road to the river. We went and sat in a hotel balcony watching. Some elephants were free and roamed around the river which was nice to see, however the other ones in chains were then forced to lay down in the river while the guards got people to wash them and the elephants had no choice if they got up they were made to lay back down again! I know everyone was saying its for there safety to be in chains until there tame etc however after going to walk with lions in Africa  where we had nothing but a plain 30cm stick which the lions were controlled by i dont see why the elephants needed such  big chains and sharp hooked sticks! I will never advise anyone to visit! Defiantly not a orphanage more a money making circus

I visited the orphanage as part of a short organised tour in Sri Lanka so hadn't particularly researched the place beyond looking at a few promotional photos. While you certainly get to see elephants cooling off in the river, what the photos don't show is the small village worth of gift shops and restaurants at the riverbank, making this place more like a zoo. To add to this impression, a number of the elephants were chained and swaying back and forth clearly uncomfortable. My guide advised me this was because these particular animals were likely to run at guests or their keepers. I'd read mixed reviews on the elephant orphanage but wanted to go in with an open mind as a friend had recommended this to me. The only positives I can take from this was that it was lovely to see all the elephants together bathing but in hindsight I shouldn't have gone as all in all there were more cons than pros.

This is a great place to see elephants and have a bath with them too. Get here early 9am to feed the baby elephants. But please be mindful that the minders ask for money to feed touch and photograph the elephants. Pay no more than 150 rupee to feed the babys nothing to photo the big ones at the back and 1000 rupee at the river to bath with them. The men will try and say the get little money but be firm or they will take you for a ride if they hustle you just walk away. But this place is a great place to visit and a good trip to see the sights on the drive there. Enjoy Sri Lanka and have fun.

even if your tour operator or guide suggests this place please avoid it. please do not pay money to these pimps who are prostituting our orphaned baby elephants. they are torturing them and when grow a little older gift them for prostitution to Buddhist temples and to overseas zoos.

Disgusted with the way these animals are forced into submission. Pinnawala has a great opportunity to be a force of goo; instead they are going from bad to worse. First of all the staff just wants your money and pushes you next to an elephant in chains, grabs your camera from you and takes 2-3 pictures and then shouts "money" to you. Infront of us the hitted the elephants whith sticks and and the elephants were running away from the staff when they came towards them. Will not recommend this.

This is nothing more than a zoo with clearly distressed elephants chained up to poles or in chain shackles. We visited because our children wanted to but having since done an elephant safari in Sri Lanka and seen huge numbers of wild elephants, I really regret having gone to Pinnawala and given them our money. It is essentially a zoo not an orphanage and there is certainly no element of conservation here - it's just a tourist trap. And a very expensive one at that. Yes, there are some elephants roaming free in an open area but there are staff with huge sticks standing by them in quite a aggressive manner. Some of the elephants are in chains and two in particular were clearly distressed, swinging their heads from side to side which was very upsetting to see. Some tourists were feeding the baby elephants crackers and other junk food and none of the staff stopped them. People were also climbing over the barriers to get closer to the babies and get a better photo, it was sickening. The bathing in the river is the 'best' part of the generally distressing experience although again, some of the elephants are in chains. AVOID AND GO ON A SAFARI TO A NATIONAL PARK INSTEAD, thus supporting real conservation.

Tons of elephants in the most amazing natural backdrop. The highlight for me was seeing the herds of elephants, big and small parading through the  orphanage, crossed the main road and all the way to the river to bathe. Important to check the times when they bath before you go so as not to miss it. When water level in the river is too low, the bathing time might be adjusted. So do call ahead to check before you go! Best place to get cashew nuts is on the way to Pinnawela. There are many stalls selling them along the road. Be sure to bargain!

Learning about the elephants and interacting with them will help those children learn to respect the wild ones in their country. The elephants all looked healthy, well fed and happy, particularly the time they spent bathing in the river. The glee was obvious as they rolled and played in the water. Such a personal way to learn about elephants and the unique place they hold in Sri Lankan culture and life!

The orphanage itself is great, many elephants to see and feed, the baby elephant feeding is especially good. By far the best experience is going down to the water side to watch the elephants bathe. Surreal experience as they are all led down the tiny street to then sit in a restaurant, have a drink and watch tens of elephants enjoying the water just meters in front of you. You can purchase some bananas to feed them if that's your thing or even get down in the water with a handler to help the bathing. A must do in Sri Lanka.

It was lovely to see the elephants in the river, they were left to wander, swim and mess about in the mud.  You could probably watch this for free as they are led down a street from the orphanage, but it you want to see the orphanage you will need to pay - still worth it.

We only visited the bathing of the elephants in the river, which was great. We were there around 14.00. You have to pay the full price (2500 rupee pp) even if you only want to see them bathe. Easy to get there by public transport. Great to see the elephants go down to the river.  You'd be better off taking the bus and staying at one of the places by the river for the day. Entrance fee to the so called 'orphanage' is a rip off.

I am not usually one for these types of animal attractions but I think it was very worthwhile. Particularly at 10am and 2pm you will see many of the animals along with the mahouts (elephant handlers) leave the sanctuary and head down to the river for bathing. Watching the elephants stop traffic to cross the road is quite a spectacle. The animals will spend a couple of hours in the river and then return home again. The elephants living here have been displaced for a range of reasons and many would not be able to return to the wild. While I am no expert I don't necessarily agree with critics of the way the elephants are handled. Some of the bigger bulls are shackled and the handlers all carry hooked sticks to herd them with. While this does seem unkind I have heard that it is necessary for the mahouts to let the animals know who is boss or run the risk of being trampled. This all begs the question why they are in captivity in the first place. Some are orphaned, are dependant on supplied food and cannot return and others are pests that cause damage to farmers crops and in doing so face the risk of retribution. In any case worth a visit to come up close (but not too close) to these amazing creatures.  Remember to get there for bath time, you will need to purchase a ticket for around $25USD that will give you access to the sanctuary where the animals roam free and the river for bath time.

I understand why this place gets mixed reviews as it is hard to see the elephants in chains but I would not have missed seeing them having fun down by the river the seemed to be happy and enjoying themselves there, it's a tourist attraction but locals as we'll lots of animal lovers attend so hopefully that will improve these amazing animals lives.

We travelled a few hours from our hotel to visit here and it was well worth it! Amazing place to see the elephants up close, the babies being fed, the herd being taken to the river for a drink and bath. A couple baby elephants in a pen that they won't even allow you to feed on your own, the guy has a iron grip on the bottle while you are holding it as well feeding baby. But what is most disturbing is the treatment of these marvellous creatures. Baby got stuck with a horseshoe shaped piece of metal with spikes in the end to move him along. At some point you can follow the herd down to the river to bath. But I suppose if you are early you can get the river yourself. All in all not worth the money.

If you want to have a photo taken with the elephants you can expect to pay circa 1000 rupees, give them a basket of fruit again more money & I'm not convinced that it would actually go to the care of the elephants but more likely to the staff members pocket. I appreciate there are not many opportunities to get up close & personal with elephants for us Westerners & that the staff are probably earning a pittance but in reality I think it is a circus with the elephants performing at the whim of our requirements & in a true environment with a wild state encouraged I do believe that there would be acceptance to just view & not touch to encourage a true rehabilitation as should be the target of any organisation possessing the state of orphanage.

The 'orphanage' was included in our tour of Sri Lanka and having read the TA reviews I did have my concerns about going. The two main issues seemed to be that of animal welfare and keepers ripping you off for money / tips. We asked our tour guide who was quite honest in saying there had been an issue on welfare with a couple of keepers in previous years but they had been sacked and it had all been cleaned up. From what we saw, we would agree. On animal welfare I think there are improvements that could be made but on the whole I didn't see anything to overly concern me. Yes, some elephants were held by a chain to keep them somewhere, but if I want my horse or dog to stay where I've put them I tie them up! Obviously this wouldn't be acceptable on a continuous basis, but I believe it's just for some of the individuals who aren't safe roaming freely while the public are there. Yes they could be penned, and this is one of the improvements I'd like to see, but they had water and shade where they were and didn't seem too concerned. The other area I would improve is the baby feeding. These babies aren't 'orphans' as it's clearly now a captive breeding programme and I felt this did cause some unnecessary stress, while getting money from the tourists to feed them. I can see you may want an interactive focus with the public but there are better ways - maybe Q&A sessions? So we didn't stay for the feeding and instead headed down to the river to get a good table at the cafe to watch the bathing, which we enjoyed. The second main concern from visitors seemed to be the fleecing of the poor unsuspecting public by the keepers for tips / money. My husband and I went ready for the 'onslaught' but really never had a problem. Yes if you fall for the 'have a photo', 'take this bag of bananas' 'come and wash the elephant' then the keeper is going to ask for a tip, but from what we saw they really weren't hassling. If you said no, politely, they just left you alone. I can only assume those people complaining haven't travelled very widely as we've experienced far more pressure in places like India and Egypt. I actually did decide I would like to help wash one in the river. The keeper was only too pleased to help me out to 'my' elephant, and I tipped 500 SR (about £2.50). I was allowed as long as I wanted to bath him, and when a different keeper helped me out the river and asked for another tip I told him that I'd already paid his mate and that was it, he didn't try anything else to get his cash. What's the problem? On the whole, yes it's a tourist attraction but that in itself is not a problem and the elephants are living in a large herd in a natural setting, so far better than most zoos. Yes the keepers will ask for a tip if you interact with the elephants - just be prepared to pay what you want to pay, but don't worry about being unduly hassled. No, it's not an 'orphanage' but surely a breeding programme of these wonderful animals in a natural setting can't be a bad thing. We would recommend going and enjoying it for what it is.

When we first got to Pinawala, it appears to be a well organised Zoo! I don't like Zoos and never go after a childhood of being taken to Glasgow Zoo which had a poor polar bear with repetitive stress behaviour. Pinawala is odd, at first seeing elephants chained up doesn't sit well. The herd of 60 elephants seemed happy enough, it's a huge area for them to roam, not sure though they aren't chained up at night? Feeding was a bit touristy, but when can kids get that close to elephants in our world of health and safety. I thought the elephants bathing was the good bit, at least they seemed free enough and the staff washed them. I never saw anyone hit, annoy or be horrible to any elephants. Yes, the handlers ask for money, the average monthly wage is £5. In short, if your at all Squeamish about Zoo's don't go, but it's not all doom and gloom. Sri Lanka has been domesticating elephants for thousands of years as we did with horses, cats and dogs, it makes for a good day out and kids will love it. There are other elephant "orphanages" nearby which looked really exploitative, elephant rides etc- those you need to avoid!

Firstly, I am an animal lover and i can hand on heart say this place does not mistreat these animals. They have a large area to roam, are bathed twice a day and looked after. They also do fantastic work saving these elephants and releasing them into the wild once they have enough of them to form their own herd. The problem is we tend to be very sensitive and want elephants to be roaming free in the wild. The truth is: - Elephants are Sri Lankas working animal and have been for centuries, just like horses and dogs are for us - Because of this they are trained to obey the keepers - The keepers have sticks with a sharp point in case the elephant disobeys (you try pushing a 2tonne elephant in the direction you want it to go) - They don't draw blood or cause any harm to the elephant - The keepers will shout at the elephants if they arent behaving, just like we would with a horse As for elephants being chained, there were 3 chained up when we were there. Our guide (not employed by the orphanage) said that some had to be chained if their behaviour was poor as they pose a threat to the keepers, visitors and other elephants. The only thing to watch is the keepers down by the river, they will charge you a fortune to touch or feed the elephants. You can do this for very little inside the orphanage. Please visit this place, it was absolutely fantastic. People are too sensitive and don't realise how much good this place does.

If you want to support genuine orphan elephants go elsewhere. AVOID Pinnawala.

Other than at the entrance, there weren’t information boards/plaques anywhere. I wanted to know what they did as an orphanage- like where the elephants are from, do they rehab them, do they tame them, do they breed them etc- but nothing!! I’d like to know what my money is going to/support. Second, there are elephants in chains and in distress. My guide wanted to take a picture of me next to a little, chained elephant with its handler. The closer I got to it, the more uncomfortable it seemed and wanted to walk away but its handler kept poking him with a metal-pointed stick to force him to stay. Maybe this didn’t hurt for the elephant, but it was being forced to do something it clearly did not want to do. My guide then took me to the side where there were large, tusked elephants. Beautiful animals but chained to a tree and standing on concrete. How unnatural is that for them? All they kept doing were swaying back and forth, and making a lot of noise. Animals in distress in captivity usually show abnormal repetitive behaviour like swaying (ref: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereotypy_(non-human), http://www.aps.uoguelph.ca/~gmason/StereotypicAnimalBehaviour/library.shtml). That was disturbing to see. My guide said these were old, untamed elephants thats why they were isolated and chained. Well, why can’t this 44-acre (according to my guide) place give a few acres for old elephants to roam?? Maybe there’s a good reason (can’t imagine what) but you wouldn’t know because there’s nothing around to inform you!  You, reader, are smart. Do a bit of research. There must be another place in the country that does a better job at taking care of elephants or at least not exploit them. I wish I did. There were a few smaller places with elephants around as we drove away the ‘orphanage’.

Spent some time there and witnessed babies through to adults. I am not qualified to comment on whether they are being well kept. They "seemed" to be well kept. I think they should do away with bottle feeding the baby elephants they "seemed" to get distressed as the time went on. Look there are some spectacular events going on, like the walking to the river and bathing. I think maybe they should do away with  touristy things and let them just be natural as much as possible. It's hard to know what to say I would like them to be totally free but is that realistic. Why are they there in the first place?

It was not a tourist friendly place to be at. The entrance fee was RS2,500 per pax (SGD25.00) for tourists, while the locals can get it at RS100 per pax (SGD1.00). It's definitely a ripped off! Once you entered this orphanage, though a huge place, it's not sheltered or covered, thus you gonna expect a hot and warm visit.(Prepare an extra clothing & wet tissues.. You gonna thank me for that advice 😉). There are many person in charge of the elephants, they will be very friendly to ask you to go close to the elephants to take photos, but you gonna tipped them afterwards, some will still request for more tips as they are not contented with what you have given. Next, it's the milk feeding. You get to feed the elephants but at the price of RS350 per feed (SGD3.50). It's just a very short while, one or two mouthfuls and time is up! Only the elephants shower is the highlight for me. I get to see many of them being released out in the river and they get to roam around freely enjoying their own baths. There again, you get to see some locals giving you bags of bananas for you to feed the elephants. Once finished feeding, you know what? Yes! It's time to reach for your wallet again! It's tipping time!! Well, be positive, I gained my exposure to see so many elephants at one go, and hopefully with the money we contributed, the elephants can lead a better life!

I first visited this Orphanage in February 2005, 6 weeks after the Boxing Day Tsunami.  I was delighted to see how well the Elephants were looked after and watched them bathing in the river and interacting with each other.    In February of this year I paid a return visit to the Orphanage.  We set off very early in the morning so we would not miss the Elephants bathing......as soon as we arrived my friend and I realised that things had changed quite drastically.   As we were parking our car we were bombarded with various people trying to sell us Bananas/Milk to feed the Elephants, these we ignored and went to pay our entrance fee.  The next unpleasant thing we encounter was a big sign informing us that Locals would pay Rupees 500, but Foreigners would pay Rupees 2,500 - quite a difference.   We proceeded into the park and then it became apparent that we had made a terrible mistake.   Elephants were chained and stood in the blazing heat and we were being encouraged to take photos of these magnificent beasts (for a fee) you could see and feel the misery they were enduring (especially the unfortunate Bull Elephants giving a display of moving huge logs from one place to another in blistering heat).   My friend had promised her grandson that she would take some photos for him so we moved to the covered enclosure, where the horror was complete when we sighted one baby being tied by his tail to a stake, to make him stay still for the photoshoots....an incredibly ugly sight!    They had a beautiful thing taking in orphaned Elephants and nurturing them with love and compassion, now 10 years later it has turned into a cross between a rogue Circus and a Zoo!   We had only been there 15 minutes, but had seen more than enough!   We went to the shop to see if I could purchase some hand carved Sandalwood Elephants  (as I had 10 years ago) and found the shop was full of mass produced gaudy tat!  the disappointment was complete and we literally ran out of there fighting the desire to cry....as my dear friend said, that is the last time I go there and I will never recommend it to friends and relatives who come to visit.....so in conclusion,  Greed wins and Elephants lose...shame on you Sri Lanka the RSPCA (or a similar organisation) should intervene on the Elephant's behalf!

Visited the elephant orphanage post several recommendations. It seemed that this was going to be a positive experience where the elephants were looked after. It seemed that activities such as milk feeding and fruit feeding where for the benefit of tourists and visitors not for the elephants. The elephants looked visably upset during these activities. We saw several elephants in shackles and chains. Whilst waiting to decide what to look at next we observed to orphanage employees striking two elephants with a stick for no apparent reason, leaving the elephants visably distressed as well as yelping. Disappointing to see people wanting to make money out of something that could have been a positive educational conservation. I wouldn't recommend unless you support animal cruelty.

We travelled here for a day and had a good time but found this over commercialised. There is a 2 tier pricing system for europeans and Asians ( european pay double). The orphanage was very clean and the animals appeared well cared for, but we were a little confused about the purpose of it, as we believed that the animals were being prepared for release, but they were also training some to be working elephants. There are some locals  a the entrance who catch you and give you bananas, then demand 200 rupees per bag, but don't give change. If you go to the river to watch the elephants bathe,  beware of doing anything extra, such as feeding,  or helping to wash them, ( which the staff encourage), as they will let you do this, then demand money from you. I offered 500 rupees and they were looking in my purse, and telling me that it was too small and i had to give double - just to give the elephant a few bananas. Overall, this is well worth seeing and i would go again, but i would be more alert next time.

I have been here on each of my five trips to Sri Lanka, and always look forward to seeing the elephants, particularly at the river. On previous visits, access to the water for tourists had been relatively unrestricted, but they are now kept back behind a chain. Whilst this could be to protect the elephants, or for the safety of the tourists, I suspect that it is simply to allow the mahouts to control who gets to stroke and bathe the elephants so that they can maximise their own income. Not that I begrudge them making something from this, but it has taken away a little of the spontaneity of it all. There are good views to be had from the restaurants overlooking the river, and the food is passable if not exciting. As well as restrictions at the river, the public are also prohibited from walking in the main field, but there is still plenty to see. Feeding time is a joy, although it seems as though separate payment has to be made if you want to bottle feed the babies. We weren't offered this on entry, as our guide purchased our tickets. The place is still a must see though for anyone travelling between Colombo and Kandy or Habarana.

The best bit without a doubt was seeing a large herd of elephants tramping down a street of shops heading to the river to bathe. It was a truly awesome sight. Could have sat for hours watching them washing in the river. A must see for any family in particular.

This place is a sanctuary for elephants found wild and is open to visitors, predominantly foreign tourists on a high charge, to finance its operation and proabably for a good profit. There are mixed reactions to the elephants being chained (some feel cruelly and roughly) and driven to demonstrate milk feeding and bathing in the river, although from we observed during our visit, nothing untoward appeared to have been done to the animals and visitors, ourselves included, enjoyed the sight of their marshalling through the park and the bathing as well. The best place to watch the elephant bathing would be from the restaurant of the Riverside Hotel overlooking the river.  Food is a little pricy but for the comfort and vantage position over the scene of action, it's worth paying for..

Not sure why there are mixed reviews about this place? Its a must see place while in Sri Lanka. If u get your timings right ( I think around 10am) - you will be able to feed baby elephant! That was a wonderful experience. Elephants are really looked after & cared for there. River bath is an icing on the cake! Try to get there before lunch time, so can see them crossing the road & making they way there. Make sure you get your camera ready for the elephant "fountain"! We stayed by the river and had amazing photos. Please go and visit- entrance fee isn't much. Of course you will get asked to pay extra for feeding, but I got so much joy out of it, that it was worth every penny.

chained animals clearly trained to entertain the masses! these animals are so far out of there natural habitats I don't know what to say without throwing up on myself! I'm going to make it my life's mission to close this place and every place like it on the planet down!

Pinewala Elephant Orphanage is a beatiful place, where you can see all age of elephants. We have been here in Mar 2015 and my doughter enjoyed it realy very much. The entrance for foreign visitors is 2500 LKR per person and you can view more than 80 elephants at one place. The nature around is so lovely such you can see at pictures. But I really was frustrated with ride of elephants. It is not provided by Orphanage, but other providers so this is realyy cruelty to animals. Walking in a cirle with a man which stings elephant into legs and trying to move him forward. So enjoy Orphanage, but you can miss ride.

Don't visit these places or ride elephants anywhere in the world. As to control elephants in any way these enormous animals have to be broken and hurt to entertain us humans! Elephants deserve to be free and are too intelligent to be used for human entertainment. Although used for many years as transport etc for local Asian communities it is wrong that these incredible animals are used for tourist entertainment any where in the world! I made a choice to avoid this during my tour of Sri Lanka, as I will anywhere in the world, as I totally disagree with humiliating these gorgeous and amazing creatures. I am not an animal activist or anything like that but please be aware of other reviews. It also broke my heart to see a chained elephant outside an elephant ride centre near Sigiriya. Ironically she was there to attract tourists into the ride centre but she wasn't even the elephant taking people out on her back as clearly she hadn't been 'broken' yet. She was out in the blazing sun with no food or water, inches away from the speeding traffic. She had every foot chained tightly to the ground where she stood so she couldn't move more than 6 inches in any direction. In the UK these people would be jailed for animal cruelty. When I looked into her eyes and looked at her face she showed her desperation in her physical movements and I wished there was something I can do. Fair enough I didn't visit the sanctuary here, but surely if our entertainment is eliminated then no cruelty will be required to keep these animals in any controlled environment. If you don't believe me google it! Elephants HAVE to be harshly controlled to perform in any way.

The Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is a sanctuary for Elephants. It's a wonderful hands on experience where you can observe, feed and touch these beautiful animals. The Orphanage grounds are well kept and very attractive, giving way to gardens and typical tropical wildness. Safety rails are in place in various places for when a large group of elephants pass from one section of the sanctuary to another. Some creatures are rather large and daunting if they were Rides are available at a reasonable cost if desired, either bare back or with the option of a seating device. If a device is used the elephants skin is protected by various fabrics. Elephants are clever, graceful and intelligent. They can be trained to paint, or indulge in sport or creative dance routines without looking ridiculous. They seem to love the attention and the food that follows after either performing or obeying instructions. They learn quickly and most Sri Lankan elephants respond to the same words irrespective of who is using them.  The best part was watching them bathe in the river which is a short journey across the road and down a walk way leading to the river. On route there are several shops selling typical tourist products such as scarves, hats, sarongs, paintings, batik, jewellery and paper products made from elephant pooh. There is a demonstration of the production of elephant pooh paper. It's interesting and the products are appealing souvenirs. So take your camera and thoroughly enjoy your elephant experience. The entrance fee is not expensive and it is possible to make donations to this wonderful cause.

Our Sri Lanka tour itinerary included a visit to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage as we travelled from Sigiriya to Kandy.  As part of our planning for this holiday, we had checked the internet reviews for Pinnawala and noted there were mixed comments from visitors.  Whilst we had reservations, we decided to visit the orphanage but asked our guide to ensure we arrived just before lunch.  This would enable us to see the elephants returning from the river, tour the orphanage, watch the feeding of the young elephants and then have lunch at one of the restaurants overlooking the river when the elephants returned for their early afternoon bathing. This visit left us mixed emotions.  We came away with more positivity than anticipated even though Pinnawala has developed from its initial orphanage concept as some elephants have been born here and we saw one female which was clearly pregnant.  It was wonderful to see a herd of elephants lumbering down a narrow street and then bathe in the river.  On the negative side was the ever visible presence of the mahouts attempting to persuade tourists with cameras and parents with children to part with a disproportional amount of money for a photo opportunity.  Arranging for a table at one of the local restaurants which overlooked the river meant we had fantastic views of the early afternoon bathing session. In conclusion we think it would be relatively simple to implement changes which would enhance visitor appeal.  Information on the various elephants would help tourists understand more about the facility and its objectives.  For parents with young children a safari may not be a practical experience but a visit to Pinnawala would be a worthwhile experience.  However, if you have convinced yourself it is going to be a horrible experience, then it will be.  If you go with an open mind, you should enjoy the experience for what it is.

Thou I felt their ticket prices are too high for the experience, I can't deny I have a lovely time with the elephants. Just a few pointers - - Do not fall for paying extra money to feed the elephants, once you inside you will get enough opportunities - Do not pay the Mahouts any tips for letting you touch and pet the elephants. Its illegal, not appreciated by the orphanage and you will get to do it anyways. - The bathing time is 10 -12.30 noon, it is a brilliant site, please try to reach around this time. Also, the bathing river is outside the orphanage across the road. Nobody bothered telling us this and we wasted a lot of time looking for it

This was the feature stop between Colombo and Kandalama, and did not disappoint. The herd was bathing when we arrived and look most content in a beautiful natural setting.  All done, they walked back up the road to the parkland and onto a large field to graze. Very picturesque There were a small number chained or in pens and once again, most looked happy - pretty much like a zoo setting - but one was fastened front and back legs and was swinging his head continuously back and forth, reminiscent of the "polar bears gone mad" in London Zoo in the 60's when their cage was too small, so this wasn't so great Maybe this last animal wouldn't survive in the wild and will calm done over time, but he wasn't happy on the day we were there Net-net, however, a worthy enterprise giving education and perspective on these stately beasts

Lovely to see the elephants enjoying a relaxing time in the river. The chains around some of the elephants legs were a bit of a concern at first but the animals do seem to be well cared for. Feeding milk to the baby elephants was fun and worth a few Dollars donation. Overall, definitely worth a visit if you would like to see these animals close up and not behind bars as they are in most zoos.

This place is a must on the journey from Colombo to Sigiriya or Kandy.  Be there at bathing and feeding time and it is truly wonderful to see the elephants up really close and even get to bottle feed a baby one.  It is easy to spend an hour or two just watching the elephants in the river and at the feeding site and getting up real close to touch one and see them squirting water or  dust from their trunks. You will come away with plenty of great photos!  A really worthwhile stop on a long journey.

Undoubtedly one of the best places to see wild elephants in sri lanka. You can take photographs with elephants. You can see them drinking milk. You can get really close to them. Staff take them to bath. Kids love this place. Very nice orphanage. Wonderful isn't it? Yes. But most people dont see the worst part of this commercialized circus. So called caretakers hurt these big fellows by poking them from sharp sticks until you click a good snap. They are chained and tortured. Orphanage(yeah thats how they call it) just need your money. They dont care about poor animals. Go there. You will realise.

If you value elephant welfare don't go there. Being one of the first ones there I took time to wander around and came across an elephant chained up by one front foot and by the opposite back foot and doing the usual step/sway step/sway step/sway that all animal lovers recognise as a distressed elephant. When I couldn't stand watching any more I went to complain to the director who tried to fob me off with a story about the elephant having problems with it's shoulders and they had her tied up to stop her jarring her shoulders, when I tried showing her the video of the elephant doing just that because of the way she was chained up she wouldn't look at it saying 'I know which elephant you're talking about'. The second gripe I have is that when you first walk in and go up to the top to where the elephants are 'hanging out' you are met by the local 'handlers' encouraging you to 'come and stroke the elephants' which they will then try and charge you for but after paying 2500 LKR I'm not going to spend even more money on something that should be free. Which leads me to my finally gripe, the fact that tourists have to pay three and a half times more than locals is scandalous, I don't mind paying a bit more as is the norm in some other countries but they are just being out right greedy which in an apparently buddhist nation is laughable.

Even though the orphanage name suggests a very innocent interpretation as one expects poor animals are given shelter by people with good intention the truth is not really so. What you will see when you go there is more like the commercial version of the truth: - The area is quite small as compared to where they naturally roam aroand - chained animals - the fact that the caretakers are more interested in the money in your wallet than the elephant. Even when you get close to the elephants, they will start saying "tip" multiple times. (I gave 200 RPS and they told me that they want 1000 each of them 6 mahouts around, and they call this tip) If you really think that taking a photograph cost extra money, just increase the ticket cost. What these mahouts are doing is not just decreasing the reputation of the facility but the whole country, as this place is a stop for many tourists visiting there.

I read opinions about this place here and wanted to see it what is the reality. Its very expensive but you pay for good thing (thats what u think at the beginning) and then everything extra: if u want to touch or feed elephant (or feed baby elephant  - comedy with hundred of tourist and you can hold bottle of milk for 5 sec in baby's mounth for 350 rp). Upper part is nice and group of elephant is free but they still use some for photography with tourists  (extra paid) and forcing them with hooks. In back side you can see "not tamed" elephants on chains - very sad and stressed. Ok, maybe they are really dangerous but why they have them also in the lower part where are tourist? And also older babies? They have TWO chains and cant move at all, they are stressed. When I asked why they are like this, worker answer: they are dangerous. Ok so left them somewhere in back side behind the fence and not like this! Or you think that this is happy animal?: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x7lrFVn1Zfw&feature=youtu.be Also bathing in the river is like march prisoners and workers are not nice to them and they are scared. Why dont they let them free in national parks? I visited Eco national park and elephants are free and happy - dont spend your money in "orphanage" becouse its more like a prison. Spend your money in park and you will see wild animals. They should live like this - such a beautiful animal deserve it!

This attraction charges foreigners R2500 but Sri Lankans lay only R700.  As this is government owned, the Sri Lankan Government needs to stop treating tourism as a milch cow.  By and large foreigners rarely or never pay more than locals in Australia, New Zealand, Philippines or Singapore. Watching the elephants bathing in the river was great except that there and on land, some were still chained, including as they were paraded down a street full of tourist gift shops. This is obviously now a commercial venture.  One wonders how many have really been released into the wild.

We were offered this visit as an additional part to our tour of Sri Lanka.  IT was lovely to be 'up close' with the elephants and when they were taken down to the river it was a magical sight.  Wouldn't have missed this visit for anything.  quite a highlight of the tour.

I am so sorry for the elephants. Why one has to humiliate this big fellows so much? What is the fun to pick all day them with a long stick. If the most very youthly staff goes on this way, one day the tourist and the income stays away.

People need to really need to think about the facts they know before moaning about this place.  Think about what material they would use to hold a grown elephant during a medical check, clean, or to keep it away from the elephant it keeps attacking whilst on heat.  Think about how they would fund an orphanage and feed the 250kg of food to each elephant.  It is a genuine orphanage taking in young elephants that would have died in the wild due to development projects.  They claim (and i mostly believe) that 100% of the money earned goes back into the orphanage. It is not to say I agree completely with everything they are doing.  Captive breeding without the intention to release back into the wild is certainly questionable but again maybe necessary to bring in tourists to pay for the care of the orphans.  Not to mention the priceless spreading of the word and interest in other people to protect and care for these magnificent animals world wide. I enjoyed my visit and would encourage the support of Pinnawala as an orphanage.

I cannot believe that in this day and age people are still of the view that chained elephants, wild animals herded with barbed sticks to get a 'great photo  opportunity' and circus style rings with a chained baby elephant feeding from a bottle - to look cute for an audience, is what you consider 'a great experience' or 'a great day out'. This so called orphanage is nothing more than a money making scandal. There is NO reason at all that can justify chaining elephants just so that people can get a good snap for their holiday album. Hopefully in a few years time we will have moved on as a society and in the same way that 'most' people see having wild animals as a performing circus act as unacceptable, people will see that this 'petting zoo!' is in many ways no better!

Pinnawala orphanage really has a large number of elephants and calves. they don't teach or have any material on elephants and their care though. the bottle feeding of the calves was exciting for my kid, though i felt bad looking at the calves desperate fr the milk.  the restaurants at the river side have an excellent view.

The good: you can get up close to an elephant. The bad: this is not an orphanage where any attempt to move the elephants onto a 'real life' is made.  They are tourist attractions and are herded constantly into the bottle feeding/bathing cycle. Having previously seen wild elephants joyously bathing and playing it was truly awful to see them taken to the river to bathe.  A few were made to lie in the river, stretching their chains - yes chains - to the limit.  Most distressing was to witness the bottle feeding where young elephants were running after the keepers from one side of the enclosed ring to the other, chasing the bottles for a drink. I really didn't like this experience at all.

Clearly this is not just an orphanage - some elephants were born here, already in captivity.  This is now a very commercial venture.  Really liked seeing the elephants in the river, especially the youngsters who were having a great time. Did not like seeing some of them in chains, dragging their chains up or down the road as they travelled to and from the river. Handlers seemed overly aggressive with the elephants and focused on the money. Once inside the orphanage, there were some animals showing signs of distress/neuroses (swinging trunks and feet backwards and forwards repeatedly). Although this is one of the main attractions on the tourist trail, I would not recommend it and would not go again.

We were given a free trip to the orphanage as part of our honeymoon package, after reading some of the negative reviews we nearly cancelled but we decided we would see how it was and if we didn't like it we would leave.  Can honestly say it was nothing like some of the scare stories I have read on here, in the park the elephants are roaming the plains (bar the sick ones which are in pens as part of their treatment). The walk to the river was truly amazing, seeing the elephants wander down and frolic in the water is a sight to behold, we saw two elephants their who were chained, we were told that is because they were disruptive animals who if they did not chain would attack the other elephants, whether this is the case of not is open to discussion but it wasn't as bad as people on here make out. We also read that we would be constantly be hassled for people wanting to take photos or sell us stuff, during our time there we were only asked once which we politely declined and we weren't bothered again. I found the main site almost distressing because the animals were chained and paraded around but when the elephants went to the river it felt almost naturally wild. We stood watching them and stroking their trunks, yiu can buy bananas at the river edge for a few hundred rupees or if like us yiu have lunch at the restaurant which over looks the restaurant yiu can take a couple from the buffet table. You can't watch the river washing without buying a ticket.

This place gives mixed emotions. On the positive side it was truly amazing to see a huge heard of elephants go lumbering down the street, cross a busy road then bathe in the river. It was truly amazing to be able to buy a bag of bananas (200 rupee) from some hawker looking to make a buck and have an elephant come over and gracefully be fed. The difficulty for me was the ever visible presence of the handlers with huge pointed sticks who shouted aggressively at the elephants. None of the elephants had any obvious physical signs of mistreatment apart from one or two of the bigger ones who had chains on their legs. For non south Asian visitors 2500 rupee entry to the facility but the main act of bathing in the river happens outside of the facility and is not ticketed so you don't have to pay to see the elephants in the river. We paid to get in, see them walking down the main strip then out of the orphanage. They are brought to the river twice daily at 10am for 2 hours and again later in the day. We went back inside the orphanage 2 hours later to see them come back and go back to the reasonably sized paddock. The orphanage apparently takes in elephants who were injured in the war, who have lost their parents through poaching etc and provides food and vet support. This is not a place where you can go for an elephant ride. There are places very close to the orphanage which have chained up elephants for tourist rides.

Having been around elephants before there was not exceptional about this time. Nevertheless, we certainly appreciate the work of the orphanage. We did not get to see a feeding or elephant bathing. Seeing those activities might have made the experience better. There was a light on and off rain during our visit, which resulted in open umbrellas.

We watched the elephants walk down the road to the river , then you are allowed to feed them,it's a great chance to get close to them. It's not cheap but in relation to hotel prices all  attractions in Sri Lanka are expensive. We had a drink at the hotel overlooking the rive and observed the elephants enjoying the water and lying down for a bath.

Stopped here on the way back to Negombo on the last day of our Sri Lankan tour. Whilst our guide got our tickets (lot more expensive if you are a tourist!) saw we could have got an extra ticket to bottle feed a baby elephant but were a bit late arriving to take part in this. As it turned out it was a bit of a free for all as a lot of people had bought these tickets. We were happy to watch and take photos and were amazed how quickly an elephant can demolish a bottle of milk! We walked around the orphanage taking photos, noting that some elephants were chained to trees with a none too convincing explanation as to why. Also took the opportunity to feed one of the elephants a bowl of fruit (for an extra charge of course). We went to one of the restaurants by the river for lunch and waiting for the elephants to be brought down to bathe which looked lovely. The mahouts then beckoned people down to help wash some of them (again for a "tip") and while I did take part in this did feel a little uneasy but enjoyed being up close to such lovely creatures.

I disagree with the earlier review in that what is described in the guide books is exactly what is available to be seen in reality. We did not stay for the feeding but did witness the herd of elephants paddling in a Leiden but shallow river and seemingly enjoying themselves. We.had morning tea on the terrace of the hotel on the left hand side where the view was excellent. A treat for the whole family.

If you love animals and you do not want to experience a horrible visit to view the full sorrow and suffering of animals - do not come to this place. Shackled in chains elephants, elephant standing in front of the entrance forced to hold on his neck a large billboard WELCOME. Crowds of tourists who are more interested in taking picture with an elephant than to really get to know these wonderful animals. Sadly, disrespectful to animals place. Also a terribly expensive tickets and the lack of any information about elephants. We came here specifically to Colombo - that was our greatest failure - we advise you not to repeat it. We were so disgusted with this place that we went to the office of Director of this sad zoo - to express our displeasure and ask for a refund of tickets. Very unpleasant woman avoided talking with us. First she agreed to refund tickets - leaving us with a bodyguard. When the poor guy didn’t not know what to do with us - he sent us back to her. This time, she said that cannot have our back - and that she never promised to return it to us. It’s not worth talking about it.  Anyway ... certainly you can find many other great places in Sri Lanka - we advise you to avoid the mistake that we have made.
