I recently visited this so called 'elephant orphanage' and whilst I was there I witnessed a group of elephants feeding on grass and appearing to be quite happy and as free as they can be until I noticed a baby elephant was chained with a chain around its leg. They give lots of lame excuses for chaining adult elephants but what reason is there for chaining a baby??? None what so ever! The feeding time for babies is nothing more than a circus act with workers who show little feelings for the babies and their enclosures are bare and made form concrete, why are babies kept in such horrid condition away from the herd? The only happy time that I could see for some of the elephants was the time spent in the river but sadly I saw some adults chained down in the river, not allowed to stand up just so tourists could 'wash' them, another circus act. How can this be classed as an orphanage when the workers here show little feeling for the elephants?

This elephant  orphanage was a heartwarming sight,,housing elephants from huge to little new borns. Its amazing to see the different personalities they all have, some love being sprayed with water, and actually jump and splash in their enclosures, while we saw one little fellow run for shelter at the first hint of spray! And they all have different jobs,,,one big fellow carries banana tree trunks to another elephant who strips the trunks to get at the juicy cores, which are then given to  visitors like us, so we can feed the other waiting elephants.,The centre opens at 8.30 and closes at 6pm daily. Bottle feeding is at 9.15am, 1.15pm & 5pm and bathing time at the river is at 10am and 2pm. We had a wonderful guide in jayantha Gunashekhara (Jaan), who was with us for the entire 10 day trip.

After reading some of the 'terrible' reviews, we thought twice about going. We are a family with a 3 yr old son who is obsessed with elephants and since we landed in Sri Lanka, started to ask where they were and when we would see them ( and kept asking!). We didn't want to support an organisation where some of the reviews here on trip advisor made us think the elephants were being mistreated and many were saddened by the place in general. We thought about a safari to a national park instead but with a 3 yr old and a 4 hour road journey before reaching the safari for another 5 hr jeep ride ( where you can't get out) this was just not a viable option right now. Having read some of the 'excellent' and 'average' reviews, we decided to go. After a 4 hr car journey from Wadduwa, we reached the orphanage at 9am which was perfect to find a good spot to watch small baby elephants have their milk. First impressions were quite positive compared to the negative reviews. The babies were fixated on milk, some visitors had paid extra to hold the bottle. We chose not to. We then went up to the main field to see the older elephants grazing on an abundance of green leaves and branches with their young. Here people had the opportunity to touch some of the female and older elephants. Our son wanted to touch and we had some photos. We offered a 300 rupee tip. He was not allowed to touch a baby as he wanted as the mahouts informed, the females would not like it and neither the babies. We did see 4/5 elephants tethered. They seemed ok. 2 elephants were swaying from sidet to side, these were a little further away, away from the public, but we could see them. Our guide said that some are chained for safety of public and elephants. Of course this was upsetting for us but without the full information,history, previous life before the orphanage I didn't jump to any conclusions, but they were obviously displaying distressed behaviour which I felt sad about. The trek down to the river through the village area was nice to see. Elephants eager for a dip! We got a great spot to observe them and watched them playing and enjoying the water for an hour ( they were there for 2 but that was enough for our 3 yr old which meant we left beforetp the crowds.) I thought this part of the experience was ok. Yes, 5 elephants are chained near the river bank restaurant for tourists to pay to wash them and have a photo. I personally think this is unnecessary and 1 female didnt want to comply - grunted when having to lie down. This was not a positive thing to witness. We, however enjoyed seeing 45 elephants playing and enjoying the river. The scenery is breathtaking. As you leave the village, you are called to buy souvenirs etc. we expected this. To conclude, pinnewala is what it is - right now. This is Sri lanka; the elephant orphanage is a no. 1 tourist destination;  the animals are elephants; there are lots of people, I think safety for tourists and elephants is the orphanages priority. We didn't see any mistreatment, we didn't see any elephants with sores around their legs. The mahouts have to guide and manage a large number of elephants for people to see. I do think improvements can be made. Information on the individual elephants is key to understand more about the facility, how that are cared for, displays of behaviour and certain practices removed. If you have small children and cannot do a safari, they will enjoy Pinnawala. However, if you have convinced yourself it is going to be terrible, then it will be and don't go. If you go with open eyes and an open mind, you should enjoy the experience for what it is. It is NOT a safari park or zoo in the UK. It's a government run elephant orphanage in Sri Lanka.

really looked forward to seeing the elephants and made sure that this trip was included in our tight itinery. We did not arrive until until 3.30 so elephants were down at the river bathing which was an amazng sight and would not have missed for the world, i also took the opportunity of going down to stroke them at the water edge that was fabulous. great sight to see them all walking back up the road to the orphanage,  we then went into the orphange and like other posts was really upset to the elephants in pens and chained so they could only take up to one step ( other than the babies) when i asked why ? i was told they could jump over the fence i said i would rather higher fences and no chains! no evidence that an orphanage now just a tourist attraction. would not go again

We reached around 3 pm when the elephants were in the river nearby for a bath. It is a scenic beauty to watch them play and bath in the river. Some of the naughty little ones are travelers delight. we enjoyed watching for almost an hour and half . Worth a visit and it is a place one must visit.

I have just visited the Government run Elephant orphanage and was very impressed with the whole operation. We wondered if some previous reviewers had been to the privately run elephant operations, rather than the legitimate one. And a minor point, having travelled Sri Lanka for 2 weeks, the 'foreigner' toilets at the orphanage were excellent, which is a good indication of the whole place.

Tricky one this... as you can see there are many conflicting comments about this place We visited after going to the truly awful Millennium orphanage down the road (avoid!!!), and I must say it was an improvement on how the elephants are treated... but not perfect The positives: - The habitat the elephants stay in is big and looks like a healthy natural environment - The elephants appear to be pretty well looked after, fed and healthy - Ive certainly not been anywhere else where you can get so close and (for a small additional fee to the staff) actually touch and feed them Negatives: - the staff often seem to be more interested in generating a bit of money on the side by asking you repeatedly if you want to touch, stroke, feed the elephant etc. for a tip... although they probably arent paid that well by the park so one can hardly blame them if they can get away with it! - when the elephants were bathing in the river, one of the staff ushered one of the older elephants up to where the tourists were gathered and had it perform a 'trick' of standing on a concrete post and rubbing its side on a wall... Ive no idea why they make them do this but it was pretty pathetic to be honest... AND the staff member carried with him a sharp spear like weapon. I know this is commonly used to keep these untamed animals under control and also protect tourists and staff but the whole charade was unecessary and made us feel uneasy that the poor creature was in danger of being stabbed if he made a wrong move - there has been some bad press about cruelty in this place in the past... Im not suggesting it still goes on but some people might be put off entirely because of that - the elephants were chained up whilst being fed.. necessary in some ways but its a bit uncomfortable watching them pull against the chains to try and grab food that is out of reach Still, it was overall a positive experience and we left with good memories and photos but there were a few things that will make some people uncomfortable.. so its something of a moral dilemma until the park decides to make a few changes...

We had read the mixed reviews about the orphanage on Tripadvisor, but decided to visit it anyway. Big mistake. I was last in Sri Lanka in 2010 and I visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. I had to revisit it again on this trip and I still marveled at these wonderful creatures. I  agree with other contributors - one needs to be prepared to be hassled to pay for extras like having your photo taken with an elephant; feeding them etc. Plus the prices at the market/shops over the road are a bit hiked up. However, it is lovely to see these creatures bath in the river and a great photo opportunity. Just be prepared in determining if you want to pay for anything extra - it is a money spinner attracting tourists which at times in Sri Lanka - the locals think that it is okay to target in a 'rip off' manner.

Two in our group were very keen on elephants, so reading some reviews of Pinnawala Orphanage would have probably had them stay away. However, the opposite was the case - they thoroughly enjoyed the spectacle. The 'orphanage' itself is predominantly just a large open field where scores of elephants can wander about unrestrained, with relatively small section open for tourists to interact with them. Other areas are devoted to a visitor centre, an elephant 'car' wash and, most popular, an elephant feeding arena. While the milk feeding show was fun to watch (never seen milk disappear so fast!), the highlight of the day has to be the parade across the road, down a lane between the shops and stalls to the river. The river had flooded 2 weeks before, but on the day was perfect - low and clear. Those who wanted to wade in and wash an elephant could do so for a small fee, although apparently the authorities frown on this since some elephants are not far removed from the wild. A good vantage point is from the elevated areas either side of the roadway as it ends at the river. We took advantage of Hotel Elephant Park's riverside seating, ordering a snack lunch and drinks, and watching the elephants enjoying lying about, splashing themselves in the cool water for an hour or more. Many were being washed by their mahouts, some by tourists and others just wandered - even to the far side and up the bank. Once the bathing was over, the parade up the street and back to the orphanage began. With so many elephants at a slow pace, it's easy to interact and get some great photos. We all thoroughly enjoyed the spectacle. Probably the most annoying thing was the mahouts, and often others accompanying them, playing 'interference' by getting in the way when they saw a visitor posing in front of a wandering elephant. They'd encourage an elephant to stop in front of someone just watching the parade, a friend would take an impromptu snap, then money would be demanded. Once you figured it out, you could get much the same photo by just waiting for a bunch of well-behaved elephants to go by with no one leading them. While some chains were apparent, our personal guides explained that these particular animals were fairly new to the park, and especially the street and river bathing. While most elephants would be free to wander on their own and bath without any attendants, if an elephant had proven unruly in the orphanage, its river trips were limited to one a week, or when it had been 'good', in the hope it would make the connection. Those criticising the chains and bullhooks should understand that in elephant husbandry (Google it) these are approved devices when used in the correct manner. They are huge, strong, thick skinned animals - a chain would be like a lease on a dog (what's a dog choker collar, if not a chain?). If not for some form of control, these animals would be a risk to everyone in the countryside and people would take matters into their own hands. An alternative to chains is expensive concrete and steel bars - and lots of it. Much like some zoos - not a pleasant sight and not a happy animal. And releasing 'domesticated' elephants out into the 'wild' of a national park isn't a simple task, putting the animal at considerable risk unless done with care and great expense - something a small developing nation cannot afford. So if you're easily upset by dozens of elephants wandering freely down a street, enjoying a bath in a very pleasant river setting and wandering back again to a large open field with lots of food and shade, then you'll not enjoy your day here. But we did.

Yes, it's touristy but where can you get so close to elephants in a natural ( like) setting? We enjoyed our visit to Pinnawala despite reading negative reviews. A few of the elephants were chained by their feet but im sure this was for the protection of the public. They had plenty of vegetation to eat and were busy stripping bark off branches. Lots of photo opportunities with the elephants

Its a nice place to visit If you want to get up close to elephants. Specially if your with small kids they might enjoy it. But nothing like seeing the Elephants in the wildlife in their natural habitat like at Minneriya National Park.

I am sure that this orphanage started off with good intentions, but it appears to have turned into a money-making tourist attraction, to the detriment of the animals.  While I enjoyed being able to feed the baby elephants, I was extremely disturbed by seeing some of the elephants tightly chained up and looking very distressed.  I was also disappointed by the lack of information available about the elephants and the orphanage itself. I much preferred seeing many wild elephants later on in our trip!

Visited the elelephant orphanage at Pinniwala. Nice to see the elephants with a lot of grounds to roam around on and not in small compounds. The keepers seem to be remarkably annoying By constantly managing to get in the way of photo opportunities until a small donation is offered. The best part for us was when the elephants were taken down to the river to bathe. I would definitely recommend getting there a bit early and having a drink on the outside bar of the Elephant hotel. And watching them come down the road and into the river. Definitely the highlight of the visit.

Never seen so many elephants together,,,specially the cute little ones.Elephant orphanage is well maintained and the majestic march of the elephant herd to the river for bathing is just too good to watch...lots of shopping in the viscinity as well. A Must See for all visiting Srilanka.

Lovely setting, but very much a tourist attraction. The Hotel we had lunch in leaves a lot to be desired. Food not covered and service a bit ad hoc. Not sure about the chained elephant situation - kept an open mind with regard to the explanations as to why they were chained but overall a little disappointing. Was so disappointed by what I saw. I've been to Africa and have seen elephants in the wild. They did not act like these elephants. Opt to see them on the National reserves instead.

An elephant ride costs 2500 rupees, and as soon as you've payed they urge you to hop on the elephant as quickly as possible, they litteraly push you on to the elephant, no introductions, nothing. The reason for that is they want to work as fast as possible to make as much money per day as possible. When you're on the elephants back one guy walks ahead of you and is really friendly and takes a lot of photos with your iphone. He expects a lot of tip. When we got off the elephant after 30 min my girlfriend accidentely dropped a 50 rupiees bill on the ground, he quickly bent down and snatched it for himself, and only reluctantly gave it back when we asked him for it. Then we gave him a very poor tip because this was actually one of the worst experiences we've ever had as tourists and we regret bitterly paying for this. As you can understand all the smiles and friendly conversation disappeared when he realised he wouldnt be able to squeeze money out of us.

I booked the hotel here but wish I had read the reviews on here first. I have never witnessed such brutality from the keepers that bring these beautiful elephants to the water. While having breakfast we were disturbed to see a mahout deliver brutal training with a hook to a baby elephant that was chained both one front leg and one back leg. The elephant had no clue what to do for the best. Most of the larger elephants in chains already have broken souls! They just stand in that river scared to move. What the hell is this place? It's a circus not an orphanage. I am disgusted that this is happening and that the Sri Lankan government are in business with them!! Please please do not go to this place! Don't make the same mistake as I did! I will never forget this place! A prison !

We've been to several elephant orphanages and this is unlike any of them. This is more like a tourist attraction abusing the use of elephants. If you've never touched or been around them then this is an opportunity. Many however, were chained. Some were young/teenage boys that needed to be for safety's sake. There was a young one though that was severely chained and weaving incessantly. Very sad. No animal should be treated like this. I was ready to leave but we had scheduled lunch at the Elephant restaurant. Glad we did. We were able to see the march down the street and see them play in the river. Most were left free, and a few were able to cross the stream to eat and play over there. This went on for over 2 hours. Of course some of the boys were chained, but they were still able to play in the water and a few girls would come over and visit them so they weren't alone. So I'm glad I had the opportunity to visit, but once is enough. Go with reservations.

Horrendously expensive, no information or interesting guide. Some (not terribly happy looking) elephants going up and down the path with you bareback on them (terrifying). Having to pay again for the guy taking pics from it-with our camera. Nope not impressed.

first of, yes, a visit to the orphanage is still worthwhile and entertaining. Especially the bathing ceremony is fun to watch. But you wanna come early in the morning and not wait for the later sessions. Apart from that the entrance fee is horrendous, the mahouts obnoxiusly demanding tips and some of the elephants do not look well treated (some were chained up and swayed back and forth like no normal animal would). In general it feels like the initial idea of an elephant orphanage has shifted over the years to a circus show.

The Orphanage concept seems really sweet and with good intention, but this place seems more a tourist attraction than anything else. We have been told that a part from the orphans there are also elephants that have been injured during the Tamil war and have lost a leg or ear etc. so this is good and the entrance fee at the end of the day is just a small up keeping for the work. We decided to go just as a charitable gesture as I found very sad to see these elephants to bathe in the river for the pleasure of the cameras.

I have to say after reading some comments below I was a bit scared. I love  elephants and I was worried  I would  be upset. But this place is really amazing. .Some of them run free.of course If you want to see them close they are  controlled sometimes chained, but what do you expect? ?They can run away and the place is full of tourist,some of them are children. They took some pictures for us and they didn't want money but it's true if you give the cam to a mahout they always expect a tip but it's sensible. If you want to go,mandatory is the bath time at the river..It makes a huge difference. It was sooo beautiful! We loved it

Opinions are divided. Lots of adult elephants and a few babies. Difficult to see how they can be orphans. Double-daily parade down the hill from the centre, across the main road and down to the river for swim/wash is impressive. Good views from the Elephant Hotel verandah. Some were chained, which is a concern. They seemed frightened of their keepers who brandished nasty looking spiked poles to keep them in order. At 0930, for a small sum, one can feed the babies. Is it a real orphanage or just a revenue generating business? Go there and you decide. Worth a visit, but there are concerns.

Not to my taste really, the animals appeared unhappy with chains on their necks and swaying and pulling at the chains on their feet. I am assured they do good work but seeing them in this environment isn't the best. The only positive was to actually see the elephants with some degree of freedom wading across and through the river.

Steer clear of this place. It's depressing. Tickets are purchased from an office at the roadside and you then walk down a road full of tacky tourist shops to the river. The elephants are taken to the river twice a day from their "orphanage" for tourists to see them. There is no information about any conservation programme or how the elephants are kept when not on view. Some are shackled at the water's edge and visitors are invited down by the mahouts to feed them. Beware of this as, although enticing, the mahouts are really aggressive. Before you know it you've paid £5 for a bag of bananas to feed the elephants. Once you've finished feeding the elephants the mahouts insist on a tip. My tip was considered inadequate and I was told again very aggressively that I should be giving them the equivalent of £10. At this point I'd had enough and told them to get lost. There are great opportunities to see the elephants in national parks in Sri Lanka which is a much better bet.

This place is definitely not an orphanage, more like a jail , is being advertised very nicely as a beautiful orphanage where animas wonder around free and theya re happy, they have pictures of happy elephants  being washed in the river,also some baby elephants but when u arrive there besides the 2500 rupee entry fee and the fact that they want money for everything , like feeding them or taking a picture or watching them being washed or touch them etc... all you see is chained elephants they are all in chains with blood around their legs, not 1 was free and not 1 was happy, very strange how they wore chained from front right leg and left back leg ..... u could see some of them barley reaching for food, it made me very sad, as many tourists were taking selfies and failing to see the reality of facts

My expectation was that this Orphanage was going to be like the Elephant camp in Chiang Mai, Thailand, but I was wrong....  The elephants are in an open area when you arrive, but their "guards" are always present and are very pushy for tips when you are done taking photos.  The animals themselves seem very sweet and at one point I saw an elephant that wasn't going in quite the right direction and the guard was quick to smack it with his stick.  The bottle feeding sounded like fun, but was over in like 2 seconds as the babies are very hungry.  The bathing was a forced march down to the water, where the guards and caretakers urge you to come down into the dirty water with the elephants to splash water on them and subsequently take your photo and demand more tips.  As soon as I got a couple pictures of the bathing I got out of there....

We had a lovely time at the orphanage today observing the elephants at close hand, but this is all wrong.  It moves me to joyful tears to see these beautiful creatures, and I love elephants, BUT BUT they are not free, they are in fear pf the mahouts and their pointed sticks, and I hate to see that.  They are a massive money spinner - 40 elephants led down to the river every day - what's not to like?  But they are clearly leading them down there and letting the young babies come close to us and take bananas for OUR entertainment, because we have paid a lot to see them.  Once the banana has been taken, the mahout then beats it back again.  It was a hot day and they all clearly wanted to go home - it's a shallow river and not deep enough to stay cool.This is a Government organisation and I invite the Sri Lankan govt and the managers of this place to think more deeply about elephant welfare and conservation, and ask themselves if it's right to have the pachyderms tied up, trained and subject to human routines and bred for profit and entertainment.

Thinking this would be a tourist trap, I was  skeptical and was pleasantly surprised. I was astounded that the elephants had so much freedom given the close proximity to the people and thought the mahouts handled them well and with genuine concern. Yes, they wanted tips, but so what? Who knows what they get paid. The absolute best part was seeing the elephants walk down the road and into the river. This happens at 1000 and 1400. Missing that is missing the best part of the whole thing and you absolutely should time your visit around it. You can have lunch at a restaurant with a breath taking view of the river and watch them cool off and enjoy the water....even ask the mahout if you can wade in and throw some water on them yourself. The river experience changed this from a 2 star to a 4+ for me......don't miss it!!,

If you have never been close to elephants then consider visiting the Pinnawala Elephant but in any other case I would recommend you better see them in their natural environment or at a National Park. In Pinnawala they look very sad and are all chained. Even though the entrance is already expensive enough (for Sri Lankan standards) at LKR 2500, once you are in you will be charged for everything else like feeding, bottling, bathing, in a very very greedy way. The guides have long pokes with a blade at the end and they deliberately use them to push the elephants to pose for photos. They even use the sharp pokes to try to put the elephants in funny poses to convince you to take photos (they will charge tips for taking photos even when you haven't asked for the photos or they just took the camera from your hands). The whole thing feels like a circus and even though I loved seeing the elephants, I felt bad about being part of this.

This place is terrible. It is meant to be an orphanage, but most of the elephants are chained up. One young elephant was being kept separate from all the others and was pacing. After asking why it was separate, we were told it was being trained for work. They provide the illusion of freedom by allowing these poor elephants the chance to go down to the river twice a day, with chains still intact, and with their behaviour kept in check at all times with a stick. I tried to imagine if this was a children's orphanage, they would not get away with using the word orphanage. Last but not least, you have the horrific workers there, who try to get money out of you at any chance, if you interact with any of the elephants. I heard one guy corner a lady and tell her that she should give him the equivalent of 10 pounds, after having her photo taken with an elephant, stating "10 pounds is not much for you." Really terrible, if you love and respect animals, I can't believe this would ever receive positive feedback, it is disgusting and left me thoroughly depressed.

So brill to see these most amazing animals up close where you maybe lucky enough to feed baby elephants its a good experience its always busy with locals to plus its a point to go between yala national park which is amazing.....i love sri  lanka its amazing

While called an Elephant Orphanage, I'm highly skeptical that any elephant has ever left once entered.  The cost is high for entry and then everything you do from touching an elephant to taking a picture incurs an additional 'tip' to the elephant 'handlers' who carry sharp spikes to control the elephants for I assume when their chains prove insufficient.

This is a terrible place - looks more like a zoo than an orphanage. First, it cost 2500 rupees to get in - and if you at all look or say hi to the staff they will ask for tips. But the worst is that this does not look like a goodt place for the animals. And when elephants become adults, they are sold/shipped around the country and to other Asian countries. Spend yout time and money on something else.

Thoroughly enjoyed my visit, great experience to be up close & touching so many elephants. My wife enjoyed feeding a fully grown elephant with fruit & a baby with a litre of milk (which disappeared in 3 seconds!!) A herd of elephants go down to the river at 10.00am every morning (& again at 2.00pm I think) to bathe, we went down 10 minutes early & there were already 4 elephants in the water, one of the Mahouts called me into the river, I needed no second invitation, & was able to splash water on the great beast, scratch his back, trunk & ear. It was a great feeling to be able to interact with such a beautiful creature in its own habitat in that way. Having read quite a few reviews of Pinnawala before my visit I had some concerns but for me the elephants looked in good condition & appeared well cared for, yes some had chains but they did not look in discomfort & were happy to be petted (if that is the right word for patting such a thick hide?) If they were badly treated I dont think they would be prepared to be so docile. Lastly I could not believe some of the reviewers complaints of cost!! £12.50 to get in, £2 for a huge bowl of fruit, £1.75 for the milk & yes the Mahouts all want a tip, 50p here & 50p there and £2 for the Mahout in the river. I have mixed feelings about my recent visit to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. I am an animal lover and therefore cannot deny that I loved going to see the elephants. Perhaps most disappointing was the way in which everything was catered around money, you want to get up close to the elephants and take memorable photos but can't do so without being hassled for money. I would recommend visiting the Orphanage to see these amazing animals as they trump any negativity you may have towards the establishment.

We visited the orphanage on our honeymoon trip across Sri Lanka as a stop off between Negombo and Kandy. We were very fortunate to have an excellent guide with us throughout our honeymoon. I am no tree-hugger, no animal activist, but what I saw today in Pinnawala elephant orphanage disturbed me and filled my eyes with tears: all animals are treated horribly there! Regret having financially contributed by buying an overpriced entrance ticket. The elephants are merely a tool to make as much money as possible. I absolutely love elephants, they're one of my favourite animals! I first visited pinnawala on a family trip to Sri Lanka when I was 13 and thought it was amazing! When re-visiting Sri Lanka at 21 with my partner we were thoroughly disappointed, when seeing the elephants playing in the river, many elephants were in chains and swaying on their own as if they were mentally ill. Some of the elephants didn't have chains on however you could see the chain marks on their ankles! All the guards had sticks with spears at the end, which we felt was not necessary! Many of the tourists bought bananas to try and feed some of the elephants, however every time the elephants came close the guards would poke them with a spear, and every time the elephants wouldn't come close to the tourists the guards would again, poke them with their spears and often charge at them! One baby elephant got so fraught we thought he was screaming and we thought it going to attack the guard! Some of the elephants were left to reign free and play on the other side of the river in the mud, which was beautiful to watch. Me and my partner tried to tell ourselves that the ones in chains must be because they misbehave, however it seems to me that these elephants are all healthy and smart enough to live in the wild. I love the idea of an orphanage or rescue centre where elephants get taken to get treated and looked after until they are well enough to get released into the wild. If you don't care or aren't that bothered about animal welfare then go ahead, I love zoo's and I'm not an animal rights activist or anything, but it what pinnawala was doing was so wrong. The price was extremely expensive, the attraction is extremely touristy and in the end we just felt so much empathy for those elephants! I know that there are elephants out there who are treated 10x worst, but it seems as if Sri Lanka just keep these elephants in captivity to rake in the money from the tourists! It's a great way to see elephants but saddening.

Just returned home after nine days in Sri Lanka. One of the attractions on our list was the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. Our main interest was to be able to make it in time to feed the baby elephants. On arriving we paid the entrance fee and were told that we would have to pay extra  in order to feed the calves at the pen itself. When we got there the pen had a few policemen within the feeding area along with the orphanage workers who were handing over the feeding bottles. When we asked if we could have a go, we were told that we needed to pay at the entrance. We explained to them that we were told to pay at the pen itself. Then we noticed the strangest thing, the policemen were assessing the crowd with the orphanage workers and we were then told that it would be 200 per head to feed the calves. We handed over the money to the workers who then gave the money to the policemen. It seemed like there was a side deal going on there and when we were given the bottle it was literally for a few seconds. We then moved on to the open area where all the big elephants were lined up with chains around them. Most of the Mahoots carried long sticks with barbs at the end of them and every time a tourist wanted a photo they would poke the elephant in its mouth for it to pose. This did not seem very humane. Once the photo was taken by the Mahoot, he promptly came up to ask for a tip. The whole experience lasted about 10 mins. Everything seemed very rushed and also not very nice. The animals did not look happy and it felt like being in a circus. I would not recommend going to see this as you do not come back with a feeling of seeing a majestic animal in its natural environment and HAPPY. Sadly the whole place felt like a money making racket. On a last note, if you are from a SAARC remember to carry ID with you when you go or you could be charged a full fee of 2500 Rupees for  nationals of non - SAARC  countries instead of 700 Rupees for SAARC- none of the money seems to be being put towards the elephants anyway! Kerala elephant experience - Much more natural. Happy animals and well looked after by genuine elephant loving Mahoots, who carried a small cane which they used for pointing and directing rather than prodding. In Thekkady, the Mahoots simply spoke to the elephants which was wonderful to see.

I visited this place (after planning for years!!!) yesterday, and it was a great experience. My 7-year old was absolutely THRILLED to see elephants up close and in a near-natural setting. She is no stranger to elephants, having been to the Kandy Esala Perahera only last August which featured close to a 100 beasts (and we were in the front row:literally just an arms length from them),  but Pinnawala is a whole different kettle of fish! True, some of the animals are chained as they are either new to the place or maybe because they are a bit excitable, but they are in no way treated cruelly. As is the case anywhere in the developing world, the local animal keepers would try to coax a couple of dollars from the foreigners. The admission fee of about 20 USD for a foreign tourist could hardly considered exorbitant, though it looks high compared to what the locals pay. Again, only a handful of Sri Lankans would be able to afford if the fee is any higher. I just had to write this review as I was almost discouraged to go after reading some of the negative reviews here, but I am very happy that I decided to see for myself. The experience can be made more pleasant by training the animal handlers on etiquette of interacting with the visitors (these are very poor people coming from neighbouring villages, and sometimes do not have any school education, let alone experience in receiving good "customer service" so they don't think what they do as unusual).  Perhaps it's high time the authorities look into this aspect.

The Good:  It is my understanding this place was started to take in orphans from the civil war.  It is fun to go to the river and see the elephants bathing, and the large herd crossing the river.  There is a great dung paper factory at the end of the lane - stop in and take the short tour - very interesting. The Bad:  They don't have enough room or electric fences to let the bulls roam free.  So they are chained to posts - looks like 24/7.  Standing in their own urine and feces.  What was upsetting was the chain was clearly tight and only a couple feet long - so they could barely move.  What I don't understand is why they aren't making any effort to try to reintroduce animals to the wild.  This has been successfully done for decades by the David Sheldrick Foundation in Kenya.  There is no signage about the elephants - how old they are, where they came from.  Our driver told us that they are breeding elephants there so they always have small ones - which is what tourists want to see.  Also, didn't know this until after I fed them bananas - apparently bananas give little elephants constipation.  And like others have said - avoid getting pulled to the other side of the ropes by the river - because every trainer will have his hand out for a tip. The Very Ugly Mahoot:  I was very put off by one trainer that yelled at and hit a young elephant.  The little elephant was scared and screaming.  Anyone who is an educated animal trainer knows you do not have to raise your voice or hit an animal - positive reinforcement is a much better training approach.  I have posted pictures of the rude and abusive trainer. If you go - just do the river portion.  They go to the river from 10-12 and 1-3 (check the timings).  Skip the orphanage part.  It just made me sad to see the elephants chained up - so I asked our driver if we could just leave.

We almost didn't go to this place due to the negative reviews here. If you haven't been you might think the elephants were all very poorly treated, beaten with sticks and chained up for no reason. If you don't think elephants should be kept in captivity and that any form of restraint is an abomination then don't go and don't read this review. The tickets are priced differently for locals. It is either that or most locals couldn't go. Happens in lots of countries. The price as compared to what we would pay in Australia was very reasonable. The mahouts keep the large (free roaming) herd of elephants away from the tourists who want to approach them. Seemed sensible to me as they are very large animals some of which are clearly not tame. If you think the people and mainly wild elephants should just mix freely then maybe you should go to Pamplona.  You were still able to get pretty close to them and they are amazing animals. The baby elephant feeding was great. Yes the bottles of milk (which are pretty big) disappear quickly. The babies are thirsty. You have to take a quick pic and hope your kid isn't frightened. One of mine was one wasn't and he loved it. You could pat the other babies that were in an enclosure close by waiting for their turn. Some elephants have chains. When some visitors were (quite rudely) questioning one of the keepers he said "training". I took this to mean that the elephant might be new to the orphanage and not ready to mingle with the herd. When we went down to the river one of my children and I got down into the water and splashed some water on an elephant that was bathing and rubbed it for a couple of minutes. The elephant didn't seem to mind and when the mahout asked afterwards, I gave him a small tip worth a couple of dollars. Yes he wanted more but that is how they survive. Some posters seem to resent being asked for tips. It is expected here. They are are not extortionists. The main herd of elephants came down shortly afterwards and they clearly enjoyed getting into the river. They were given a lot of freedom though one was chained. Presumably this was because he would either run away or do something else they wanted to prevent. All in all a great experience and one I would recommend particularly if you have children.

After reading mixed reviews my partner and I wanted to see for ourselves what the Elephant Orphanage was all about. We travelled in from Colombo to make it in time for the 10am elephant bathe. We paid 2500 each to get in which is about £13. You can take as many pictures as you like but be quick as there are so many others trying to do the same of course! The most exciting part about this excursion was when it came to bathing time. At exactly 10am the elephants from babies to adults all together head for the river- this was beautiful and I captured this on video. Once at the river they bathe for roughly an hour. At this point you can come close to the river and take pics. Try and take pics yourselves (selfie if you must!) as any of the locals will charge you for their services. We had lunch at a restaurant close by which had a stunning view. You pay for the view more than the food if you get what I mean! The orphanage is definitely worth a look BUT the place I actually recommend is a small animal hospital which is about 4 minutes down the road... the place is called Club Concept. You can check the out at www.milleniumelephantfoundation.com At this place my partner and I were able to bathe, ride and learn more about the elephants with the help of our one to one guide. All this for 2000 each which is £10. We got to ride the elephants for 10 minutes together which felt much longer at the time. We tipped the Matout (elephant keeper 200/ £1 for the ride and we tipped our guide 500/ £2.50 for being so good and also taking fab shots of us throughout our stay!) This place is a MUST if you want to experience a more intimate experience with the elephants. Of course the orphanage is completely separate and does cost more. Hope this review helps when visiting Pinniwala :)

You only need to read these reviews to realize this (and other) elephant orphanages in Sri Lanka are quite controversial - my friends and family went and enjoyed it thoroughly and some took part and some sat and watched.  Here is everything we did/learned. Firstly, the orphanage looks after orphaned young elephants that wander into/near villages in a bad state. They are well-fed, and looked after into adulthood and remain in captivity. Some babies are born in captivity from the older orphans and remain with their parents in captivity. Secondly, they are taken twice a day to bathe in the river where tourists get the chance to be close to the younger animals and the females who are more docile. The larger Bulls (males) of which we saw 4-5 were indeed in chains and spent much less time at the river as we were told they are aggressive. We were told the chains are for "control". And I do understand how that would be necessary  to have human handlers control such massive animals. Thirdly. We did buy the bananas to feed them and paid 200 rupees for them. We also tipped the handlers the 500 rupees to do so. However their "boss" came and shouted at the handlers for taking tips from us. I must say, being so close to these animals was exhilarating. And I completely see how some people saw this as cruel. But out of 40-50 elephants (maybe more) only the large males were tied up and the remainder were left to roam free in and out of the river. Finally, all ticket proceeds go to funding the orphanage, and there is a paper factory of which all sales proceeds go to supporting the orphanage as well. Without which, the alternative to this is a lot of young elephants who won't survive. I would recommend it, and encourage everyone to go enjoy being so close to these majestic animals.

The Pinnewala Sanctuary is just off the main road from Colombo to Kandy, and is one Sri Lanka’s most popular animal attractions. Although the conditions of the elephants are in general better than at some other establishments in the region, the welfare of the animals is a cause for concern for many experts. Elephant at Pinnewala (c) BFF Photo showing ankle wounds from chains - taken in 2006 The site at Pinnewala covers 25 acres, and was founded in 1975 with five young elephants. There are now around 60 animals, ranging from those born at the facility to some estimated at 40 years old or more. The main site itself has a couple of restaurants / refreshment stands, and some management buildings (eg sleeping sheds), but little other infrastructure. The animals spend the night in the main site, and in the mid-morning they are led down to the Maha Oya river, around 500 metres away, for a two hour bathing session. This walk takes them down the main street of town which is lined with gift shops, stalls, restaurants and other tourist facilities. During the bathing sessions tourists can watch the animals playing in the river and being washed by the keepers. More adventurous visitors are encouraged to touch the animals under the supervision of a mahout (elephant trainer), who expects a tip for this service. I fed the baby elephants with bananas and of course, I was in the water at the bathing session with them!!!!!

As part of our tour of Sri Lanka we detoured off here on our way from the airport to our accommodation in the cultural triangle. Sadly it was not what I was expecting.  At first sight the elephants appear well looked after and content, however our driver then started to explain about the history of the place.  It was started as an orphanage for injured or orphaned elephants years ago, however since then, commercialisation has overtaken the welfare of the elephants in the management's priorities.  We learnt that once elephants have recovered they are not re released back to the wild, and new baby elephants are kept in captivity for the amusement of paying guests.  This is exemplified by the feeding sessions where punters are invited to force a bottle of milk down the babies throats.  There are now over 70 elephants held in a 23 acre site so it is actually quite cramped for them too. I'm afraid we left with an overwhelming feeling of sadness for the elephants.  I wouldn't recommend this for anyone that loves animals and dislikes zoos, as this is essentially what this place is.

We landed early morning and asked our driver to drive us here before heading to our accommodation in habarana. I wish we hadn't bothered. Plenty of other opportunities in Sri Lanka to see happy and healthy elephants. The elephants at the orphanige seemed stir crazy with not enough space. Apparently once rescued from the wild they are looked after and not released back to the wild. Instead they are kept at the orphanige to attract tourists. The feeding time of two seemingly healthy baby elephants was actually a little upsetting to watch as the crowd pushed forward to have a go and the elephants were paraded up and down.

I've visited this so called orphanage many times now and the more I do so the more I feel like the whole operation has lost the plot! It has turned into a breeding program rather than a place of care for a lot of these elephants. I remember seeing not too many months ago two elephants - one very large older one that was blind and another that had lost its foot to a land mine. Upon visiting the orphanage recently these two elephants we're no where to be seen! - yet there were a number of young elephants. Like everything in Sri Lanka you pay the manhouts for their supposed time or rather your time with the elephants and upon giving them a 100 Sri Lankan Rupees I was told it wasnt enough. I told them not to be cheeky and moved away. After paying to take pictures with the elephants the experience just isn't as special. I've done the same at a true elephant orphanage in Thailand and experienced what felt way more natural and a true experience with the elephants there. The Millennium foundation for elephants is a much better program for the elephants I found as it seems this operation is far more touristic and seems to have lost its vision.

After an extremely long drive from Colombo we arrived at Pinnawala excited to see the elephants. I was so overwhelmed at the amazing sights at the time I didn't notice any specific cruelty, but now looking back and reading other TA reviews I realise that the elephants welfare isn't necessarily top of the list. I did obviously see the chains and a few solitary chained elephants around the park. Glad to say I never witnessed any beatings or chained babies, just the constant money grabbing.No warmth or friendliness from the mahouts, no talk of welfare or protection for these animals. I do feel guilty as I thoroughly loved seeing the elephants in the river splashing about seemingly having fun. I just hope that the SL authorities do something to promote health and welfare for these magical creatures, but with a somewhat heavy heart,I fear this will not happen. It sadly is all about the money! Our guide did take us to the botanical garden, where we were given a massage and learnt about herbal remedies, and had some herbal tea. All very relaxing and good fun! Did part with £100 (apparently locals prices!!) on some products that I hope will aid me in my quest to stay young looking! Our lunch at the hotel was disgusting- would recommend taking a packed lunch. The museum was simply the entrance to a gift shop, where a lady told us how they make elephant poo into paper, then showed us products to buy. Hope conditions improve....soon

Basically all you can do is look from distance. The elephants are treated as an object to make money of. The feeding was literally a nightmare. My family was disgusted. We paid for it, it meant touching a bottle - while somebody else holds it - and force feeding little elephants which are held on a chain which is less than a meter long. It was very disturbing. This is clearly one of Sri Lanka’s major tourist attractions, it isn’t an orphanage in the sense that most people define orphanage, however it does look after its primary guests, the elephant. It would be foolish of them not to do that of course, because these elephants need to be willing participants and healthy. Some visitors here have made some negative comments, which make you wonder what they expected when visiting the attraction. Families will enjoy the day here and there is the opportunity to feed the elephants, wash them and ride them. For most of their life these elephants have been in captivity, for this reason they have chains on their legs, preventing them from running around too vigorously and harming the baby elephants, while at the same time restricting the option for these elephants to run out of the designated park area, outside they could easily become injured or a target for those who might wish to harm them. There is a fee charged to visit the elephant orphanage attraction, part of the fee helps maintain the environment for the elephants and provides food and medications and health treatments. No doubt, part of the fee goes someway to paying the staff on hand at the attraction. You can expect to pay additional sums as a tip to just about anyone you meet who lives and works in Sri Lanka, this seems to be the norm and on occasions, or at least until you are familiar on how the system works there it can be pretty overwhelming. If you are unsure on what to tip, it is 200 Rupee for just about every tip. Visit and enjoy the day, it is an incredible experience and one to be enjoyed.

We visited the elephant care home ( not an orphanage to us in its strict sense ) on our way back to Colombo from Kandy. It's 40 km down the Kandy - Colombo road near Kegalle town on the side of Rambukkana road. All types of elephants , male,  female, old , young and even calves , abandoned or lost in jungle are living free and breeding there in 25 acres. A project launched by the Wildlife Department about four decades back is now managed by the National Zoological Gardens.Every day the elephants are taken for their bath twice to Maha Oya river about half a kilometre away on the other side of the road . On reaching the place we were spellbound to see a long parade of elephants marching one behind the other for bath. There are about 50 mahouts  who care them like children . From 1984 onwards there is breeding and there are several families according to the mahouts . You  can  closely watch the daily routine of these pachyderms , all left free. Bottle feeding to mass fruit / vegetable feeding . You can also watch their  bathing in the river. The mahouts even permit you to feed them. We enjoyed a whole day with elephants . True , elephants are big wild animals but they are lovable ones !

First of all, can I repeat that this is NOT an orphanage and has not been for at least three decades. Elephants are bred here and remain in the 'orphanage' permanently as they have been exposed to so much human contact that they would not survive in the wild. This place is an elephant zoo and a tourist attraction.  This does not mean that the elephants are not well cared for, but the name 'orphanage' is misleading to say the least. There were originally four orphaned elephants, who are all still resident. It is now a breeding zoo. We did not experience any hassle from the mahouts, but did not particularly like feeding time for the babies. Visit if you wish - the animals do seem to be genuinely cared for - but please, please see this place for what it is, or rather isn't. Definitely NOT an orphanage.

We visited this Elephant Orphanage in July.  I felt very uncomfortable actually with the "Milk Feeding" of the baby elephants as it was just too "touristy" and not in the best interests of the animals.    We did witness some elephants with nasty red welts on their legs where the chains had cut into them and that soured things a bit.  That said, the trainers who took the elephants to the river for a swim genuinely seemed to care about their welfare and the animals appeared happy enough in the water.  I think the intentions of the Orphanage are good, but I also think a Reserve for the elephants where they can wander freely and be observed by tourists from a safe distance would be a better environment for these animals.  The other thing that bugged us a bit was that some of the workers managing the elephants in the large enclosure were trying to scam tips in return for photos.  That money doesn't go to the elephants by the way.  We have no problem with paying tips to the many wonderful people we met in Sri Lanka, but we do object to being exploited just because we are tourists.  A better option would be a donation box that tourists could leave tips in which could then in turn be distributed to the workers.

This is absolutely a great experience to see elephants. We arrived around 1:00 pm, which is the feeding time and fed a bottle of milk to a baby elephant. They enjoyed being in the water and I enjoyed seeing them because it was my first time. This journey was enjoyable!.

We visited Pinnawala as part of our family tour of Sri Lanka in August.  Having read some very negative reviews on trip advisor , we weren't quite sure what to expect. We arrived to see the elephants enjoying the river, which is quite a spectacle. My daughter fed the elephants bananas. I'm not sure why you have to tip the mahout for doing this?? They are quite aggressive in their manner and when the Elephant came out of the water the Mahout was poking it in the eye. We had lunch at the riverside restaurant which was nice. However, when my son went down to feed the Elephants bananas by the river on his own, the Mahout was very aggressive to him demanding more of a tip. When I intervened and said it was enough, he backed off.  We didn't see any signs of neglect in the orphanage and a lot of the elephants roam quite freely. However it was extremely distressing to see the poor Elephant who had stepped on a landmine propped up against the bars where it remains 24 hours a day. In my opinion this is certainly not a tourist attraction with everyone staring at him  and i m certain it would not happen in the UK. He looked very sad and Im afraid it really upset me. The children enjoyed giving the babies milk. Our guide did say that the orphanage do rely on the tourists to supplement the feeding as milk is expensive. All in all we enjoyed our visit but the Mahouts definitely spoil it with their aggressive surly attitude wanting tips at every turn.

Was very apprehensive about visiting after reading all the awful reviews but went with an open mind and I believe that a lot of the comments are based on ignorance.  There is absolutely no evidence of the animals being ill-treated or unhappy. As for the chains, they are to prevent the elephants from running and charging at people – the weight of the chains is the equivalent of us wearing a necklace so doesn’t cause them any suffering.  It was a joy to watch them happily trotting down to the river at 10am for their morning bathe and there is a cafe with a viewing terrace with superb views.  Didn’t particularly like the babies’ feeding time – felt a bit too much like a circus show, but other than that a very memorable trip.

Unlike some reviewers I could find no evidence that the elephants were being badly treated. Some of them are wearing chains, although these are either bull males or lively youngsters, who cannot roam as freely as the other elephants due to visitor safety considerations. We got very close to the herd. Feeding the baby elephants from a bottle is a quick experience, but still worth it. The elephants walk to the river for their bath and we would recommend sitting at the Elephant Park restaurant  for a great view.

Having read some of the mixed reviews on here I came from Kandy with an open mind thinking this was some kind of an elephant "Orphanage", how wrong was I ?  The first thing I noticed was the sign informing me that all "Foreigners"   pay around 2,500 rupees each while locals get in for next to nothing, now in my country if we displayed signs like that the "Ethnic Minorities" would be out in force rioting in the streets. Perhaps a sign like "Tourist" or "Over Seas Visitor"  would be a nice touch.?  It would also seem that us "Foreigners"  are seen as cash cows and are routinely fleeced across Govt, controlled attractions in Sri Lanka and this place is no different either, as I saw in their overpriced souvenir shop, I also purchased the same articles in the shops in Unawatuna for a fraction of the price. Upon entering we went over to an elephant and were met with a surly mahout who insisted on cash for some pictures to which I refused however I just quietly used my tele lens to get what I wanted. Later on I witnessed the daily circus routine of the elephants going to the river some with chains some without, on the way down just be aware of people selling food for the elephants as we bought some only to be told by a grumpy, moronic mahout "No Feeding" , so we went down to the river and I must admit I did enjoy seeing the elephants bathing while enjoying their short freedom.   As we watched I began to notice a pattern developing with the mahouts, they appeared devoid of any real interest in what they were doing and were just going through the motions it would seem. The elephants were also well aware of the ankus being wielded by their mahouts, and would run with fear from them when brandished, this did not bode well at all as we saw later with a baby elephant. By this time we had retired to the restaurant above the river for a snack & some drinks, when I noticed a curious baby elephant approaching some tourists below who were behind a fence , the mahout started shouting at it and then raised his ankus and brought it down so hard on the elephants foot the poor animal screamed in pain upsetting many tourists in the process, totally unnecessary and made me want to go down and punch this moron so hard. Yes I do know that elephants have many pressure points in which the mahouts control them but this was way over the top, and before anyone thinks I'm some eco limp wristed rookie traveller,  well I've been all over Africa, India and Thailand watching and seeing elephants in the wild and captivity and have never seen elephants treated like this. After an hour or so, the elephants are lined up to go back to the "Orphanage" and a guy with a siren sounds the warning for the shopkeepers to bring the steel shutters down as the last time an elephant took a wrong turning and it ended up in a shop full of tourists. As for the "Orphanage" when we returned one could see the elephants feeding etc, and for a hefty price my wife got to feed a baby with some pineapple but, it just seemed so money orientated. Moving along I did notice more babies some were chained both front & rear and one was even doing the characteristic swaying side to side a sure sign of distress, not a pretty sight.  I left here feeling guilty for patronising this elephant "Gulag" I didn't even see any signs of conservation or anything educational to be honest, just a money making tourist trap. I can only assume the people on here who are leaving rave reviews are the ones who've probably only watched the movie "Dumbo" and never seen a wild elephant in their lives, I would suggest going to one of the national parks like Yala, or Walawe  like we did, and seeing wild elephants or even going on a safari to Africa.?  This was a low point during our stay in Sri Lanka,  and I honestly found the Millennium Elephant Sanctuary along the road more educational as they work with the local farmers in protecting their crops against the wild elephants in a friendly conservation way which benefits both parties..!

Oh what a treat, I was a bit dubious thinking it might be a bit touristy and circusy but it's wonderful so lovely to see them in the water enjoying it, then walking up the street back home, and what a wonderful,treat to,see them being fed. Thoroughly recommend it.

I have read a mixture of reviews for this place, I decided to go with an open mind, yes every two minutes they are looking for ways of getting tips, but to be fair its like that everywhere, I didn't see any evidence of the elephants being in distress I actually loved the place and thought it was one of the highlights of the trip to Sri Lanka

Go to the one which is maintained by government, having Elephant Orphanage board. At 1:45 PM elephants go for bathing, thats a pretty good sight. With few hundreds SL rupee, you can go close and touch and bathe elephants. Children will like it very much

I really love elephants and for me it was very hard to see what is happening at this place. The mahouts don't treat this beautiful creatures right. They hit them with sticks and hooks and throw stones at them when they don't listen quick enough. Some mahouts like to hurt them for fun, just to show them who is boss. One word: disgusting! A few elephants were chained and were very, very stressed. It hurts me so hard I had to cry. And then the price.. You pay a lot of money just to see the elephants being abused. You can feed baby elephants milk out of a flagon, but hey, they have a mother right?? If you want to see elephants, you should go to one of the national parks, where you can see happy elephants in the wild, just where they belong.

When we were initially walking around the orphanage we were a bit disappointed - very little character and seemed just an opportunity to exploit the elephants. We were hassled for tips, make sure you don't let anyone take a photo with your camera for you - they will expect a tip! However the experience was saved when we walked down to the river. Seeing such a large number of elephants in the water was really amazing and I could have watched them for hours. The rest of the orphanage was nothing to write home about and I worry about how happy the elephants are when they are in the small pens but they seemed very happy and free to have a wander in the water!

We visited this place last week. We reached there around 12 30 and we were just in time to view the elephant procession for their bathing.It was quite an amazing experience to watch the herds of elephants walking around. we watched the elephants take bath from the elephant park restaurant.also, the feeding time was fun to watch as well. Overall its worth it and also there is a market place near the orphanage to buy souvenirs and gifts.

This was a highlight for me, I had read reviews prior to our visit and I wasn't disappointed. Yes the handler's did have sticks, but they were only used to coax the elephants; remember elephaphants, even the babies are heavy and need to be kept uncontrolled for the safety of all. Feeding time with the baby elephants was busy but enjoyable to watch, they love their milk and drink very fast! Bath time is a sight to see, the elephants are walked down to the river, they leave the orphanage, cross the road and amble through a narrow shop lined street. A siren is sounded to warn of the elephants arrival. The huge bull elephants have chains on them, again this is for the safety of all and I did not feel this was cruel, I am an animal lover and at no time did I feel the elephants were being mistreated. Once in the river the elephants can bathe, play and relax. The handler's scrub the elephants and this is appreciated, the elephants relax down in the water. The elephants are clever and I witness a couple which used sticks to scratch their skin and clean their own ears. This is a great day out for all.

I visited Pinnawala with some trepidation, having read some fairly damning reviews here on TripAdvisor. My fears were allayed when I visited a different orphanage: the Elephant Transfer Station next to Udawalawe National Park, in the south of Sri Lanka. At the ETF they rehabilitate young abandoned elephants – mostly it is those elephants that might have got themselves trapped somewhere so that the herd had to abandon them. The purpose of the transfer station is to feed them to adulthood and then release them back into Udawalawe National Park. They have released many into the park already. However, not all elephants can be released back into the wild – they are either too docile and accustomed to humans, too violent or incompetent in fending for themselves. When these elephants get to about 4 years of age they are sent to Pinnawela This basically makes Pinnawela a repository for elephants that won’t fit in elsewhere. The alternative to keeping the elephants would be to put them down. At Pinnawela, there are quite a few elephants chained up and not free to move. The majority seemed to me to be bull elephants. These elephants would have been attacked by the matriarchs of the herd – so the chaining was to prevent violence between elephants. Having said that, Pinnawela is still a money making venture and a tourist spot. It just isn't quite as evil as some people might think.

Before I went to Sti Lanka, I did a lot of research about things to do etc... And when I found that I could see elephant, I almost cried! We got to watch the baby elephants being fed, which was incredibly sweet (they are chained, but this is so they don't hurt themselves-I asked my "impartial" guide and he assured me that the chains didn't hurt the elephants). Then we went up to a large area of grazing elephants - there were so many, and seeing them was amazing! Then we went down to the river and sat in the restaurant waiting for the large herd to come down for a bathe... There were already 5 or 6 larger elephants in the water... And out of nowhere some of the guys who worked at the park grabbed us and said "follow us now" so we did... They brought us down to the water and let us wash the elephants!!! An experience I will NEVER ever forget! I was stood in a river in Sri Lanka, washing an elephant! The only thing that ruined this was a gentleman who had sat on the side the entire time and didn't really do anything as far as I was aware, stood in my way back up to the restaurant and demanded a 3000 rupee tip... I understand that tipping is expected and I would have happily tipped the person who brought me down to the water... So that has slightly soured an incredible memory of mine... Even just watching all the elephants in the water afterwards was worth it, when else in your life will you see a herd of 80+ elephants?! I would say this is definitely worth a visit! Get down to the river early and

We arrived whilst the elephants were bathing in the river and it was such a beautiful sight that I was quite moved! We were lucky enough to go with our personal guide, who was extremely knowledgable about the whole set up. Yes the large bull elephants did have chains around them when they were taken to and from the river, but this is only like putting a lead on a dog. How else would the keepers control them when they are amongst people and crossing a road? There were also some kept in a distant enclosure and those are the ones that are in 'musk' and can become aggressive, so they can't mix with the herd. We didn't experience the feeding time so I can't comment on that, but what I saw of the whole set up was very positive. What is the alternative? For them to be hunted and shot by the farmers who's land they destroy, or for the babies to die in the wells or the jungle. Maybe it's not the ideal situation for these lovely creatures to be in, but it's far better than the alternative..

We paid Rs 2.500 (but on the ticket was printed Rs. 2000) You can see all the Elephants chained and eating and go to the river to see how they take a bath. Unfortunately this is no longer an orphanage, it is just another touristy spot.

We had researched elephant encounters before we arrived in Sri Lanka and were excited by an opportunity to feed a baby elephant at the Pinnawala elephant orphanage. It was a huge disappointment. Admission for foreign visitors is 2500 rupees, plus 350 rupees to bottle feed a baby. Some mature elephants were feeding freely in the forest, and we could see a large herd past them in a covered area beyond these free range elephants. Signs warned us of the dangers of coming close to the elephants, so we didn't venture any closer. Back in the enclosures, about 12 chained elephants were feeding. They seemed fairly oblivious to visitors. 2 baby elephants were in a separate enclosure, and these are the ones we fed. This took about 2 seconds so was a very fleeting experience. The worst part for us was the behaviour of the handlers, who offered to let us pat a baby elephant, then stood over us and demanded 4,000 rupees each. This left a sour taste in our mouth about the whole experience. That said, the elephants look to be well cared for. It is from the orphanage that elephants are taken across the road for bathing. Some are taken across chained, but the vast majority are not, it is a sight to see the large number of elephants enjoying a cool drink and bathe in the river, and the youngsters having a play.

This is absolutely a great experience to see elephants but it is not the personal one-on-one you might have hoped for. The feeding stations are very busy and the opportunity to give a bottle of milk to a baby elephant has to be for shorts to shoulder with all the other people will also bought a ticket. This said there are a lot of elephants here and wandering around the rest of the sanctuary did you get the opportunity to get up close and personal with a number of elephants. This was magical and a lot more real as interacting with the elephants was not time-limited. Some of the elephants are chained up for feeding time this is not cruel given the size and potential risk involved with these animals but just be aware of in case this distresses you. If you want the opportunity to see elephants up close are interested in the animals then this is exactly what you're looking for. For an added experience make sure that you go to watch them wash in the river approximately 2PM this is a rare opportunity to see them interacting with each other without the keepers supervising too heavily.

I was a bit sceptical about visiting here and having read some of the other reviews, perhaps on the day I went things were different, but the elephants were roaming free around the huge expanse of land including a new born baby elephant who was roaming around freely with its mother.  We then witnessed the stampede down to the river and clearly the elephants loved this part of the day and were afforded ample time to bathe and play with each other.  I visited some other elephant orphanages around the world (the worst of which was near Kuala Lumpur - avoid at all costs!) and Pinnawala offered the most freedom of all of them and was more about tourists having to respect the animals rather than them being on show and performing.

I am travelling out next Wednesday to sri lanka and this is definitely on my todo list. Could someone tell me how much it is to visit the orphanage. and if you have any other feedback on what to do there that will be much appreciated :)

We were a bit sceptical before going, but hoped for a good experience. Started by looking at elephants being bathed by the river, but saw lots of staffing not treating the animals well. They all have spiky sticks to move them from the river to the park and sticks to move them around. In the park all the elephants are chained, both a front and back leg, including the young ones. They all stay in this spot, besides the daily trip to the river, which just feels wrong when they have all the land that they could've roamed around in. You wonder also why there are so many baby elephants there and I guess more for breeding and keeping the parks revenue up rather than being rescued. The staff also are mainly trying to get you to pose with the animals for a hefty tip. There's also hardly any information about their 'orphanage' work in the park, which you would've thought any decent organisation working for animal welfare would do. So all in all, I really recommend everyone giving this place a miss and trying a elephant safari instead.

Pinnawala is synonymous with elephants and its overwhelming to see sooooooo many elephants. I haven't seen such a herd other than on TV. We arrived around 1:00 pm which is the feeding time and fed a bottle of milk to a baby elephant. It was a 1-litre bottle and the baby finished it in 3 seconds !!! My lunch was at the Elephant view restaurant located next to the river where all elephants are brought at 2:00 pm for a bath. They enjoyed being in the water and I enjoyed seeing them because it was my first time. I read the comments from other reviewers about chaining the elephants and being cruel. We cannot deny the fact that elephant is a wild animal and much much bigger than a human. With so many tourists around, the only safety method is to chain them.

First of all the people visiting here should understand that the workers are handling elephants not horses or sheep. Also certain accusations are incorrect. Having visited the place on the 6th of September same as the Wizhmazter below I must say that the herd was present on the day in the river. Also LCM808 says that the elephant was repeatedly poked in the eye. Which is ridiculous. I did not see any of the keepers beating up animals. They do carry ankus but that is to guide the elephants which goes in a herd crossing a main road to the river. i think it is a necessity

The elephant orphanage was one of the things we came to Sri Lanka to experience... and I can't really say if it was an elephant orphanage or just an elephant exploitation.  The amount of hooks, pokers and chains were alarming to say the least (made my wife very upset).  And the handlers demanding money for allowing you to take your picture with an elephant didn't help.  On a good note it was awesome to pet and feed an elephant.  But all in all if you want to have a pleasant time here just skip the feeding and head down to the water to watch the elephants bathe.

Don't go to this expensive tourist trap where the elephants are beaten, shouted at, and pushed around. This is a cruel zoo, not a safe haven for orphaned elephants. Some elephants are chained up, some are able to move but get abused if they stand somewhere the keepers don't want them too (like in the shade or on the dry land rather than in the water). One keeper was particularly bad - poking the elephant in the eye and beating them as hard as he could - he seemed he lost his temper with them regularly as some were terrified of him and others just stood strangly motionless whenever he was near.  Please don't go here - go to one of the safari parks where you can see elephants in their natural habitat and not distressed or damaged.

We travelled as a group, my partner, dad and myself in March 2014.  It was very hot and not a great deal of shade around.  We felt saddened by seeing elephants in chains, but they have to control them somehow,when there are so many tourists walking in amongst them.  Towards the rear of the tourist area, you could get closer for photos - of course, like everywhere - you have to then pay "photo money" to the guide!  not sure if this money goes to the individual, or the attraction itself? The facilities were good, excellent bathrooms, plus eating facilities and water, so you could get out of the sun etc. the main attraction of course is the elephants and they are absolutely beautiful.
