This was the attraction the whole family had looked forward to most before our trip to Sri Lanka. To see the elephants march to the river for their bath was going to be the highlight of our two weeks. We got there, paid the expensive entrance. But that was going to be worth every penny we thought. Oh my good was we disappointed when we got inside... At first we took some pictures of a young elephant getting a bottle of milk, beautiful. Then we started to prepare going to the river... then we overheard someone saying they will NOT go to the river. We asked around, and got the bad news. No river bath today, because of too much water in the river due to heavy rains in the hill country. Maybe nothing to do about that, but the big disappointment is that noone told us at the entrance, and no signs or info whatsoever!! We were so disappointed, and our children even more... we skipped the rest of the days plans and got back to our hotel in Kandy immediately. The worst money ever spent...

Very upset with myself for going as knew what to expect but had to go for research purposes for my company. Cost is $20 but the whole thing is a scam, a lot of the elephants are chained and swinging which is negative signs of captivity, certainly not dancing as many like to believe. There are sticks and ankus'' (an iron spike) everywhere and the elephants are clearly scared of the mahouts. They had very little room to move and during feeding are chained with no interaction. There are also many political issues with elephants in Sri Lanka - so my advise is got to Minneriya Park and see them in their natural environment as they should be. After all the elephant interactions i have encountered through India and Sri Lanka, this was beautiful to see...save your money on the 'scam' tourist attractions and go on a safari to see them truly free.

This place is such a delight. I was really surprised at how much room the elephants had. They are fed well, and visitors can feed them for a small fee, which was fun. There are all ages of elephants, but the babies are so funny. The caregivers really seem to care as well. The animals are treated well...better than zoos.  Bathrooms are really nice and clean. There is shade everywhere, but bring water to stay hydrated. There is a vendor there with some water and snacks as well. You can stay as long as you want, but a few hours are sufficient.

Just had a wonderful day out! Travelled from Negombo to Pinnawala by car; even this journey was enjoyable! The Elephant Sanctuary and Orphanage was superb. Arrived to see the elephants assembled in a large group in the main compound. There were elephants of all ages and sizes, all seemingly contented and well cared for. Why wouldn't they be...it is a Sanctuary! The entrance fee is used to feed and care for these wonderful animals! Visit here is far cheaper than a day out at a theme park in the UK! Next was baby elephant milk feeding time. Then down to the river to witness the entire herd walking into the river where some were enjoying being scrubbed was laying in the water, others walking slowly through the shallow but fast flowing water. I'm guessing there were 50, 60 maybe 70 elephants in the group. How many people are able to say they have seen so many together at the same time? Truly a sight to behold! Wonderful day....to be highly recommended!

Okay, let me address the obvious criticism that many reviewers have of the place - the handling of the elephants. I did see some of the elephants in chains, and a couple of times the handlers poked them to move them in a direction. This is my first visit to such an elephant sanctuary and so, I have nothing to compare it to, but the fact that only some of the elephants were chained seemed to indicate that the handlers know which of them are safe around people and which might act a bit aggressively. I would prefer not to see the animals being poked, of course, but I am not sure how elephants are managed in other similar places. What we did enjoy was feeding the elephants fruits and milk, and being able to touch and pat them from so close. The baby elephants were full of energy and clowning around, which certainly makes us laugh. When the whole group of 20-30 elephants are led for their bath, that is also a good thing to watch from the viewing area, as the young ones charge ahead and the older ones lumber in and plop down on their sides to be scrubbed. It is a good place to visit on the way to Kandy, although it does get a bit crowded during the feeding time.

this place is amazing we watched the elephants bath in the river then there walked up the street to the park a lovely place for orphan elephants to live ,you can also feed the baby elephants a bottle of warm milk amazing experience I will never forget

Costs Rs2500 and more to feed baby elephants milk or big elephants fruit. Then watch the elephants rush by into the river where you watch a few working being washed while the rest play in the water and you watch from nearby restaurants if you purchase a drink. The act of watching the antics of the young elephants playing was totally delightful. No participation possible and if you came around 10.30am you could walk down and see the elephants in the water without paying such a large amount of money.Some elephants are chained and others free. Overall it is very overpriced for foreigners.Ok if you are desperate to experience seeing a large amount of elephants in one place

We visited the Pinnawala Elephant orphanage during our stay in Kandy - although it is accessible from most places in Sri Lanka. It was an amazing experience seeing the great work they do for the orphaned elephants. Ensure you get there to experience them in the river and for baby feeding.

I appreciate that visiting somewhere as special as this site is going to cause controversy, but the memories of the day will stay with me for ever.  I felt very privileged to be among these majestic mammals and their off-spring.  It is expensive to go in and you are constantly having to pay for everything, including a permanent expectancy from the mahouts for tips.  They, unfortunately, do complain about how little they receive in wages making tourists feel obliged to put their hands in their pockets. However, apart from this, I thoroughly enjoyed my three hours there and would willingly do it again.  I was spell bound.  At no time did I feel that the elephants were under any kind of duress.  The 'baby' elephants though were much larger than I thought they would be!  I did bottle feed one but it downed the contents in 1.8 seconds!  I was very close to a sedate elephant who carefully extended her truck for a photographic opportunity - another tip required. There was one isolated elephant being given special treatment as it had huge injuries and deformities - rather distressing I thought. The only time during my visit when I was perturbed. Down at the river was extraordinary while these creatures awaited their baths.  It was an hilarious sight to see one elephant totally submerged, with the exception of one ear, the tip of the trunk and part of her belly awaiting her massage.   There were five very mischievous baby elephants (about 2-3 years of age) all frolicking together in the water having such fun. You had to laugh.  (But not at the people trying to sell you bananas while you watched!) This is a tourist trap - but I loved every moment.

Elephants, elephants and more elephants. If you have a passion for pachyderms you can get your fix in Pinnawala, Sri Lanka, home of the Elephant Orphanage. The orphanage,about two hours from the capital of Colombo, takes in (usually) young elephants that are orphaned or injured or abused. Right now there are 95 elephants housed there, ranging in size from under one meter to giants well over three meters from the tips of their toes to the tops of their heads. Every day from 10am-noon and from 2-4pm they are herded down to the river by the Mahouts (handlers) for their twice a day bath or frolic in the cooling water.

The mixed reviews are unwarranted... This place is great. The cost is high for foreigners and yes it is a little like a roadshow but the animals are well cared for. I am happy to pay extra to ensure that the orphaned elephants get a chance. There are chains on the animals but not in a painful way just to keep them generally in the same area.

Our misguided guide brought us here. It was hugely expensive and all we saw were elephants chained up and keepers looking for tips every time you turn around. Even the kids did not enjoy this experience. If you love elephants go to the Perahera in kandy and see them for free in a far more positive atmosphere

I had read several review about the orphanage and with concern advised my fellow travellers what we might be seeing. A vote was taken and the decision was made that we would not visit or fund this orphanage as there are several other was of saving orphaned elephants. For some strange reason our driver did take us to the attraction, as our lunch stop was planned around this. I paid my due money under duress and went in. If you knew any thing at all about elephants and their behaviour you would soon find out that these poor babies are not well cared for. Yes the do look well fed and they do get to go for a swim ..... But being hobbled (more than one leg tied up), really !! In these modern days it is absolutely not necessary to hobble animals to display them to tourists. There are many other ways to exhibit orphaned elephants. Mahouts are supposed to be kind to their giant friend, but instead the were poking and prodding the poor beasts to stand up for people to have their photo's taken with them. I had a mind flip as a photographer and decided to take a lot of photo's to make travellers aware before they enter the at action to make a informed decision about what they are going to see with their own eyes.

There is a separate ticket purchasing counter for foreigners. If you are a foreigner please ask your guide to use that counter and respect the locals by NOT abusing their power to purchase your tickets thought the counter for locals.

This is not an orphanage. It is a disgusting, moneymaking zoo. Firstly, Sri Lankans go for free. 'Foreigners' (as written at the entrance) must pay approx £13. We were disgusted to see all elephants with chains around their legs, unable to walk around. There were no barriers in places, just single elephants standing alone, chained up. By the river, elephants are ordered (by the staff with large sticks with a spike on the end) to stand in an area where 'foreigners' could have a photo with there favourite captive. The staff then demand that you pay them after having a photobtajen. We did not take any photos but we saw many people. The elephants were clearly scared of the staff who had obviously used the spike sticks in the past. Do not go here!!!!! It is horrible and cruel. THIS PLACE MUST BE SHUT DOWN.

The only attraction in Pinnawala.There are several decent hotels to stay if you wish but there no attraction or things do there. One can visit from Kandy. Best time to go is the morning and watch elephants are taken for a bath at the near by river . Nothing much to see and the orphanage except feeding of elephants etc. Surrounding  reminds me of mines view park at Baguio with similar type souvenir  shops.

Visited March 2013. Only good part was watching the elephants bathe in the river, otherwise very upsetting watching them being chained (esp when the tourists can 'buy' a bottle of milk and feed the orphans) some getting more than others. Just didn't like the experience.

We went there expecting an orphanage for baby elephants and sort of a conservation project and rescue centre for disabled elephants. What we found was elephants chained and lined up as a tourist attraction. They are trying to get more money out by people feeding the baby elephants with milk and adults with fruits and also taking pictures close up. Apart from the entry you have to fork out extra for every picture taken. The nice part was seeing the elephants bathing in the river where they can enjoy a bit of freedom and seem to be more relaxed and less of a tourist attraction. It is a shame that this is apparently a government funded place.

I am an animal lover and was excited to see a place where animal welfare would be put first - but when we got to the 'orphanage' I was a bit upset and disappointed to see that it didn't seem to be a wonderful place for elephants. Some were in isolation and seemed to be exhibiting boredom behaviours and many had chains on their legs. There were so many people there and it all just seemed to be a money-first rather than elephant-first place :( I hope that I am wrong. PS The bathrooms were very smelly.

We'd saved this till last on our trip as we expected it to be the highlight of our holiday - but what an unpleasant experience! It's run by the Sri Lankan government and we expected a conservation project raising money for elephants by offering visitors opportunities to see elephants up close and learn about them. What we saw was upsetting and degrading to both visitors and elephants. Mostly it involved mahouts shouting, pushing people out of the way and demanding money for photographs. What could have been such a special experience - bottle feeding a baby elephant - involved my daughter putting her hands on a feeding bottle for a few seconds before being yelled at to move away so the next paying customer could squeeze through the crowd to where the creature was chained. We were concerned about the welfare of the animals although accept there may be good reason for some of the apparently cruel practices (chaining, keeping animals in isolation) however as no attempts were made to educate the visitors we remain sceptical. Overall the experience left us feeling shocked and upset. The management need to get a grip of their staff and save what could be one of the best attractions in Sri Lanka. Sent from my iPad

I recently visited Sri Lanka and the orphanage was a major low point of my trip. The workers are interested in their own financial gain at the expense of the helpless mammals. There were many distressing sights including elephant's chained to trees and kept in isolation for indefinite periods - I would urge anyone thinking of visiting the orphanage to stay away, a truly disgusting establishment.

The Orphanage provides a great opportunity to see elephants up close.  However it doesn't provide much else and the helpers spend too long trying to persuade you to get your photo taken touching an elephant and then asking for money afterwards.  If you are just passing through then a visit will be an experience but I'd recommend instead staying a night at a local hotel like the Elephant Bay hotel and you can see the elephants close at hand when they come down to the water twice a day to wash.  Here you can pat and stroke them and avoid the expense of paying to get into the Orphanage (approx. £10 pp).

SAARC countries have a different entry price, so keep your passports ready. We paid srilankan 2450 for 2 adults, 3 kids and 1 driver (local). It is a delight to watch the river bath and their walk up the street to get back into their shelter. Kids enjoyed every moment of our stay here. Beware of guides wanting to take you for a elephant ride away from the orphanage. We left Kandy at 9AM and reached the Pinnawala at 11AM. The road is a single lane and it is very difficult to overtake slow moving vehicles as there is oncoming traffic at all times. So plan for 2 hrs and 30 mts from Negombo to Pinnawala.

We were taken here on a Hayes and Jarvis tour. It is called an elephant orphanage but it felt more lime a zoo. All the young males are chained up separated from each other. One of the baby females walked over to a young male and they embraced with their trunks. Then a young man with a hooked stick went over and shouted then put the hook on her head to lead her away.  Another young male was rocking from side to side, swaying its head. I left after 20 minutes as I found it too distressing. I understand my view is subjective but The Born Free group have written a much more objective account that I suggest people read. It was interesting from a cultural perspective as our guide didn't see anything wrong and was happy to explain that the males need chaining up as they are difficult to control. It didn't seem to occur to him that they shouldn't be in captivity.

we heard of so many kinds of orphanage but not of elephants. it was so touching that department of national zoological gardens of srilanka taking so much care for sick and disabled elephants. it starts from 8.30 am to 6 pm. for foreigners fee is 700 srilankan rupees with a valid id.

I think this place started for the right reasons but tourism is taking over from its main purpose and they're getting carried away with the feeding and photos.I found my trip to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage very uncomfortable It's worth the visit, but just be prepared that it's a tourist attraction, not an animal rescue organization. I had something else in mind . Was very disappointed .Those elephants have shackles on their legs and chains around their neck.

I've never been on a safari or seen animals in the wild so visiting the Pinnawala elephant orphanage was big deal for me and was well worth it! Our group was staying in Hikkaduwa for 4 days but made sure we dedicate a whole day, takes 3 hours to get there from our hotel, just for the orphanage. We loved it and it was an amazing experience to see so many beautiful and grand animals just chilling in the wild. It's a breathtaking scene that you can not completely comprehend until you see it with your own eyes. Two great features of our trip to Pinnawala was riding the elephants, I must say they were a bit cranky and the carers tried to ask for extra money once we were out of sight from their managers. BEWARE OF (baby) LEECHES if you wish to ride. The other thing you should check out are the little shops that sell elephant dung souvenirs, they can also take you on a tour to see how it's done. Makes for a great gift!

After seeing elephants in work, it was amazing to see elephants at play. Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage provides a safe home and sanctuary for Sri Lankan elephants. Once an elephant joins this herd, he or she is retired.  They practically run to the river for their morning swim. A highlight of my day was to observe one of the herd try to stay at the river longer that the time allowed. He or she was just so clever in the way s/he slipped the handler. Good naturedly, she rejoined the herd.

I was taken here as part of a group tour. It is difficult to make judgments on the basis of one visit, but I did not like this place and would suggest others think carefully before going there. The elephants in the river certainly provide an attractive opportunity for tourist photos, but I wondered in retrospect whether they enjoy having to stand in the river for a couple of hours at a time. We arrived towards the end of the morning session and by that time the elephants were just standing, not being bathed or doing anything else much.Some had chains attached to their legs and at least a couple were chained in one place. In the main part of the facility, which we visited next, most of the elephants (presumably those which had just been brought back from the river) had been taken to a large bare area, without shade or food, so visitors could get photographs with them. I do not know how long they were required to stay there. A few elephants were chained in the roofed enclosures. Particularly disturbing was the sight of a baby elephant, chained up alone on a short chain and rocking compulsively back and forth in what appeared to be distress. We were told that some of the elephants are orphans but there is also an active breeding program, which raises the question of whether the baby elephants which visitors can pay to feed are orphans or babies taken from their mothers. I would be glad to be convinced otherwise, but I had the strong impression that, whatever good intentions there may have been when this place was founded, the welfare of the elephants now comes a distant second to their commercial exploitation.

The Elephant Orphanage in Pinnawala, Sri Lanka is one of its kind in the world. It is an orphanage, nursery and captive breeding ground all " under one roof ". Elephants that are driven away from their herd, those that have fallen into open wells, tanks, or slipped and fallen down a hill side are all brought here, treated by veterinary doctors specialized in elephant care and domesticated. It looked as though it was the largest herd of three generation of elephants, in the world - I may be wrong. There are over 50 mahouts to look after these elephants. There are quite a few young girls looking after the very young elephants. There are quite a number of them there, many of them are so young that they are bottle fed. Very playful young elephants. There is one big elephant there which was badly injured when it stepped on a land mine. He cannot stand on its own and is propped up by supports, one leg is bent. I was told that it has been standing like this for the last 22 years. No one is allowed to go near it, but my niece managed to up to him, talk to him, and as though he understood what she was saying, put out his trunk to caress her. I don't understand why the orphanage is making suffer like this, he should haven put to sleep when they found that he couldn't have a normal life. Any way, it was nice to watch the large herd of elephants following a young elephant, who I was told was the " leader " to the river for their daily bath.

The elephants seem to be looked after very well.  They go down to the river twice a day for several hours - so have plenty of fun and recreation.  They are well fed - 75kgs per day each.  And even the elephant with only 3 legs - land mine - seem happy. There was no evidence of pacing back and forward or other signs of distress.  We enjoyed our visit. There are plenty of reports and stories about these elephants being sold to temples and others who may mistreat them; NOT seeing them at the orphanage probably doesn't change that and hopefully the entry fees are put to good use. We were offered a closer encounter with the elephants - hand feeding the bananas - and then asked for cash but once it was clear we didn't agree to any payment, we were left in peace. A firm no was all it took.  Otherwise, an very interesting and enjoyable couple of hours.  I'd recommend it to friends and family.

I wanted to make my own mind up after reading all the reviews. I left still not knowing how I felt and slightly concerned at the 2,500 entry price. I think this place started for the right reasons but tourism is taking over from its main purpose and they're getting carried away with the feeding and photos and touching them etc (none of which I did) It's a sight to be seen but obviously the best thing would be to go and see elephants on safari.

Widely divergent reviews a feature of this attraction. My view is somewhere in the middle. On the basis that we believed that orphan elephants were being rescued we were happy to visit. On the day we went there no tourists being obnoxious! Some elephants (younger ones) were roaming freely away from the visitors, some were walking freely but with legs dragging a chain, presumably to prevent them from running off and a few, mostly adult bulls were chained up. The babies being bottle fed were chained to their feeding station but not so tightly that they could not move. Frankly it is fairly naive to believe that elephants are going to be allowed to roam freely amongst human beings. Even the National Parks containing elephants have strategically placed electric fencing. We were not approached to be photographed with an elephant and we saw no evidence of cruel treatment by the mahouts. The land mine damaged elephant is not right next to the main visiting area but it is plainly in view some 50 metres away. This is an ill-considered decision by the management. It is an upsetting sight and this poor creature should be humanely put out of its misery ( my opinion of course). The cost is approx UK£7.50 per adult and if this is supporting orphan elephants then all well and good. However there is not a great deal to keep adults occupied for any length of time. The highlight is the river bathing, described by other reviewers.This is not in the orphanage but down a public highway opposite the entrance and is free. Again we saw no evidence whatsoever of ill treatment and the male elephants who went down first at around 10 am were happily lying in the water and were not chained down to the rocks although they were wearing leg chains. The site of the females coming down at around 12 o'clock with their young and entering the water and being washed down by the mahouts and then playing in the water is something that I shall remember with pleasure for a very long time. Again we saw no evidence of ill treatment. We were not hassled in any way by traders along the street apart from friendly banter. My suggestion to anybody who has misgivings about the orphanage is to request that your driver  take you to the river only. arrive at about 11.45, the males will already be there and the females will come a little bit later. Go up one floor of the restaurant on the left hand side and you will have a perfect view and can have refreshments or even lunch as we did and you will be away from the hustle and bustle and dust of street level.

Our guide took us for an early morning visit to the elephant orphanage. He knew we needed to be there by 9:15 in order to feed the elephants. So worth the early start. This is the biggest orphanage in Sri Lanka, with over 40 elephants in situ. After you have helped feed the babies with bottles of milk and given bananas and palm leaves to the older elephants. You then walk down to the river - ahead of the elephants, to watch them then walk down at 10am for their daily bath. Fascinating and delightful in equal measures. Make sure you have Rs.400, if you want to tip the elephant workers to be able to feed the elephants. Very very worth it.

first of all, this place is full of tourists! we went to the milkfeeding in the morning and when you see those little cute elephants in chains, who cannot move at all, you just want to cry! after that we went to the river & yes it's nice to be on the terasse having tea and watching the elephants, but honestly it feels wrong and the elephants dont look happy at all! overall it feels more like a huge business, the focus is on the tourists and not on the elephants!

We went to Pinnawala with our guide and we were very pleasantly surprised. We travelled a lot in Asia and we found that in Sri Lanka the people care for the animals very well. Pinnawala is one of the examples of that. The elephants literally walk freely and are treated very well. Ofcourse there are a lot of tourists, I mean we were there as well. But it is worth the trip, seeing the elephants like this is really a great feeling.

It's a bit of a tourist trap, but still interesting! We passed the elephants that were tied up and fed by children Go to a open area and ask if you can feed some. We did, and it was great! Then we went to the river. We had a table in the restaurant by the river, downstairs. It was a great view to the river and a sight when the elephants came to have a bath. The shops in the area were nice, but very overpriced. Don't shop here. You'll find everything you want somewhere else.

It is definitely a high volume tourist attraction but they manage groups very well.  We travelled in a minibus with an English speaking driver which meant we didn't have to find the car park and had a great guide. I was disappointed to see so many obnoxious tourists imposing on the elephants space and getting far too close with cameras.  When we arrived we walked up to he main area and bought entry tickets.  We didn't stay too long and walked across the road to the hotel Pinnalanda to have some lunch.  It is situated right on the water and to our pleasant surprise there were elephants being washed.  Right throughout our meal we got to watch these wonderful animals bask in the sun and enjoy the water. After lunch at 2pm as we were leaving a larger herd were being escorted down the road towards the river for their turn in the water.  Truly magical to see them so close. I definitely would recommend this attraction to children and people of all ages.  But please don't feel the right to pat them and force cameras in their eyes.

This was a distressing visit for the family.  Not sure what I was expecting, but it was certainly not to see elephants in chains - most weaving. We arrived in time to witness 'bottle feeding the elephants' where three baby elephants were chained - we did not stay there, but decided to walk around where we saw other elephants in chains.  I told our guide that we did not want to stay, but he suggested that we watch the elephants visit the river.  The first elephants that came down were chained on rocks and made to lie in the water.  When they tried to rise the mahouts prodded them with  their spears - awful.  Other elephants were brought down unchained. I wish that I had not given money to this so-called 'orphanage'.  Don't go.

This place don't look like orphanage. The elephants are chained all the time and led to the river twice a day for bathing. The bathing time seems to be the time when all the workers try to take you're money. They tell you to take a photo with the elephants and than ask for tip. Sorry but I don't think it's something I should tip them. They're just standing there and doing nothing. Of course the entrance fee was too high.

It was amazing to see the elephants, I was in awe.   The sight of the elephants going to the river was incredible.     Watch out for the workers - they will offer to take your picture with the elephants and demand money - fortunately we had been warned about this but I saw a number of surprised and irritated guests.

We were on a tour of Sri Lanka with expats going back for a visit after 10 years.  What use to be a rescue center has turned into an abusive tourist trap.  The treatment of the elephants is terrible, the only thing worse is possibly the treatment of the non locals.  Go to the gathering in the northern parks to see these remarkable animals in the wild and how they should live, not chained up and abused.

but somehow still worth it. Try to get there, when the elephants are brought to the river to enjoy a refreshing bath there: it´s really a nice sight and fascinating to watch, when somewhere around 30-40 elephants come strolling down the street to get to the river. Don´t miss to go to "Elephant Poo Paper" a little store on the right side of the street that leads down to the river, where they make and sell products made from elephant dung. No entrance fee and you even get a guided tour, where they show you the whole process.

We thought we would take our 3 children here to see the elephants up close. As soon as we set foot in the place, we wanted to leave! The elephants were 'guarded' by the mahouts who encouraged the children to step closer to the elephants to have their photos taken and then demanded 1000 rupees. The baby elephants are chained up and you have to pay extra if you want to feed them. We observed several elephants swaying side to side (not natural behaviour). One attraction was an elephant who had stepped on a landmine and couldn't walk. He was horribly disfigured and was sadly propped up against a fence away from all the other elephants. The sight of the elephants being led to the river was quite something but they all carried chains around their legs. You follow behind them, conveniently down a street where you are hounded by people trying to sell you things. The elephants are then forced to perform once they are in the river. Men sell bags of fruit for you to feed the elephants but as soon as you try the mahouts chase the elephants back into the water. A sad and depressing place. If you want to show you children elephants take them to one of the national parks and see them in the wild.

We were both looking forward to seeing the rescued elephants at the orphanage but were ver ysad to see them all chained up. People can walk freely around the site but the elephants can barely move. We were expectign it to be the other way around, with the elephants walking around and the people safely behind railings etc. We did get to stroke and feed the baby elephants and see these majestic animals but it left us with a sad feeling that they had, essentially, gone from captivity to captivity. it's a very profit-driven place with everythign costing a little extra. If you want to see happy elephants in their natural habitat, go on a safari in one of the national parks.

We visited this orphanage and were very disturbed by the treatment of the elephants. We arrived and were welcomed by the mahouts to come and see the herd who then took pictures on our phones and aggressively demanded money, one of our party was surrounded by 3 of them demanding money. We would have given a tip anyway but this aggressive behaviour was not a good welcome. The main herd of elephants looked healthy and happy, but when you looked to the side you could see the bulls who were chained up looking very unhappy, one was swaying from side to side which is common knowledge that it indicates the elephant is not happy. we then went to the babies being fed. Once again another disturbing experience, one was being beaten so much it collapsed onto the floor, yet many tourists were oblivious to the cruelty as they were too excited to feed the babies. The feeding is just a money spinner for the orphanage, i watched people holding bottles for 30 seconds and being charged for the privilege. We have seen elephant sanctuaries in Thailand and there they are so well looked after, the managers of this orphanage would do well to travel there and see how to really look after their animals.

We visited even though we had heard some less than brilliant reviews on the basis that we should make up our own minds.  Altogether, I wish that I hadn't visited as I feel it legitimated the behaviour of some of the mahouts. I realise that a good job is done here in some cases but I very much felt that, particularly with the older elephants, they were being manoevered around for photo opportunities and the ensuing payments to the mahouts as the primary concern.  I left feeling very uncomfortable and wouldn't recommend visiting.

On our first day we went to the Orphanage. We arrived in time to see the elephants bathing and playing in the river. We certainly got up close, our friends managed to touch and get photos with the elephants as they came out of the water. My husband and I also had photos when we were in the Orphanage. Be warned, the handlers will grab your camera and demand money, and what you give them, they will demand more. We didn't mind paying, they are just very rude about it.  We went to the Orphanage to see the feeding, this wasn't as pleasant seeing the babies chained up and several in distress. They also have an older Elephant who is injured and chained up, very distressing to see.  After visiting we would have said you must go, however, the next day we did an Elephant Safari at Minneriya National Park, now that is a must!

The Pinnawela orphanage for elephants is a must see. We found it one of the highlights of our holiday to meet with such a large herd of elephants walking freely (under a lot of supervision) and witness the bottle-feeding of the babies. Never mind the outrageous price difference between admission for locals and westerners. True, very true, it’s not all love and care, but one must realise that the majority of these animals would not have survived at all in their natural habitat as they were abandoned shortly after birth. At least now they get meals, medical care and a bath twice a day. I was quite astonished to see how the matriarch keeps an eye on her herd and how youngsters were being corrected by their (foster) aunts. You must realise and understand that chains have be used to control members of the herd who do not listen and, perhaps because of their natural urges, would upset order, not to mention cause havoc amongst the watching crowd. (There was a huge bull in heat when we were there.) We can learn a great deal here. Just look at these babies being fed, the ones that already had a few bottles, of milk to be precise, will still fight any other baby to get their trunk around a full bottle so; they must be chained. The chains for babies are also needed for equal treatment; remember that elephants have an extremely good memory and will remember very well who was treated different. Follow the elephants when they walk through the main street when they go for their bath in the river or, if you are clever, leave a bit earlier. (Please ignore the man with the unfortunate snake who wants cash for a photo.) Not only do you not have to slalom to avoid the mounds of droppings, (if ever the reminder: “Mind your step…” was appropriate!) but you can also find a seat at the terrace overlooking the river and have cold drink. It appeared to be quite safe to go down to the river with the elephants but be prepared to grease the palm of the nearest herdsman. I did not go down myself if only because, for instance, if the nearest animal does not like the colour of your shirt, you might get very wet! Plan the trip either early in the morning or enter the park shortly before 2 pm. and stay until closing time to see everything. One thing is clear; once you have seen the elephants you do not wish to ride these magnificent ever again. They are willing to work hard and can push and pull tirelessly but were definitely not suited to carry people.

The first thing you notice when entering this "orphanage" is the sound of chains and the constant noises coming from distressed elephants. This park claims to be helping and caring for elephants when their actual goal is to suck as much money as possible out of tourists (€12,5 of 2500 Rupees entrance fee, and in 15 minutes you have seen the whole park) without any care for these animals.   Every "care-taker" walking around in the park holds a speer-like stick, poking and hurting the animals in the neck when they walk in the wrong direction or don't do what they want them to do. Some elephants have wounds on their ankles from the chains. They have one deformed elephant displayed for the visitors. This animal is clearly in pain, as he or she is constantly leaning on a large branch. Instead of taking proper care of him or her or maybe even releasing him or her from the pain, the elephant is left there to take care of him/herself.  DO NOT GO THERE.   If you are keen on seeing happy and healthy elephants, go to nature parks, like the Yala Park. There you see many families of elephants living free and happy. If however, you are staying near Pinnewala, you do not have to pay the fee to see the elephants. At 14h the elephants walk to the river to bathe. To do this they exit the park, cross the road and follow a public path. So if you go to the park at 14h you will see the animals without having to go inside and thus without having sponsored this horrible circus. They stay in the river for 2 hours and then return to the park via the same road.   It is an absolute shame that this park is advised by many people. I was ill after having paid for this horror show.

When we visited the Pinnawela Elephant Orphanage I had mixed feelings. We watched the elephants take a bath (I think it's from 11:00 - 13:00). You can take a picture with them for a tip (we didn't do it because elephants are forced into position). When you sit and watch the elephants bathe it is a really nice experience. However it is made for tourists and people really want to sell you different things (statues, pictures, bananas). We just sat in the back and enjoyed the view! We walked back to the orphanages and saw the old elephant that stepped on a landmine. He can barely walk and doesn't look happy. I think they should end his misery and not let him live to enjoy the tourists. Some of the elephants are free to walk within their space and some are chained, not very tight and they can walk a couple of meters. The watchers are taking good care for the elephants!

I was in Sri Lanka for a month with 15 kids trying to help wild elephants. We went here to see what it was like and though we were warned about the terrible treatment of the elephants we were appalled at the active abuse that is leveled at these elephants! The mahouts scream at them and poke them with sharp Steele pokers. The chain them on short chains for hours at a time. This is unnecessary. Elephants are lovely and can be treated with kindness in order to co operate. There are no real elephant behaviors left in these poor creatures.  They have been trained to beg only. Please don't go here! Riding elephants is a terrible abuse of these lovely creatures! If you want to see elephants go on a safari and see them in the wild.  If you go here you are actively participating in animal abuse.

In April, my family and i had the chance to visit the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage while on holiday in Sri Lanka. It took us three hours from Colombo 3 to reach the site by Kangaroo taxi. We were guided by our chauffeur Mr.Sanjiva who was a very courteous person. We visited the elephants when they were bathing in the river and my husband and daughter had the pleasure of riding Sita, a very friendly elephant. We also experienced the process of recycling elephant dung into paper. It is really interesting and it is a must see for visitors. We had a memorable experience and we will surely visit this place next time we are in Sri Lanka.

Visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage ,on early July 2014, the tour was organized by BlueLanka tour ,our guide/driver was Mr.Janeke.Took about 2 hours + from Colombo 03 Colpetty to reach Pinnawala.Entrance fee was Rs 2500 per person.Near the ticketing booth ,there's a souvenir shop. The elephants , including the juvenile , old and crippled are kept on a huge shelter .We saw several elephants are disabled , and old .These elephants are rescued from the jungle, because of human activities destroyed their habitat. Later we proceed to the bathing site.The view was stunning. We manage to hand feed the elephants , with bananas , for Rs 100 , then we give gratitudes for the keepers ,Rs 100.Overall it was a nice experience .Worth to be visited !

I would definitely recommend a visit to this place even if you are used to seeing Elephants. They have done quite well to make it interesting and seeing over 40 elephants being herded through the park to the river is a sight to behold. Try and make it to see the feeding of the baby elephants. The little rascals are adorable.

We went to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage with some trepidation after reading some of the negative reviews.  However, after having visited, I have to say that I really enjoyed it.  Yes, some of the elephants did have chains, but they seemed to be free to move around when we saw them.  The young ones were chained when visitors were feeding them, but I think that was necessary to keep them still.  Staff appeared to really care for the elephants. When we first arrived the elephants were all in the river bathing, which was incredible to see.  We had lunch at a restaurant overlooking the river where the elephants bathed.  Back at the orphanage we were able to give some young elephants milk.  It was amazing to be so close to them and be able to touch them!  We also got the chance to feed fruit to a very large pregnant female.  She had no chains and was clearly enjoying the fruit! We also saw elephants wild in Minnerya national park which was amazing.  However, I still wouldn't have missed the elephant orphanage which was a completely different experience. Tip:  The toilets near the ticket office are very basic.  Inside the park there are much nicer, cleaner toilets which are free for ticket holders to use.

We visited the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage with the entire family as a day trip(Colombo to Pinnawala and back). The visit was a unique  experience for the kids and adults alike,being able to get in  close proximity to these giants(and giant babies!). Since we were local we did not get hassled too much by touts and the like,however we observed foreigners being chased by local traders trying to sell items ranging from DVDs' to miraculous herbs! The Elephant mahouts too seemed to be making some easy cash on the side by allowing visitors to pet the animals at a price! The visitor center and park was reasonably well maintained and it was good that we timed our visit with the bathing and feeding times for the elephants(between 9 am to 1 pm). I would also recommend visiting on a weekday and avoiding weekends which could get crowded. Whilst stating that this is a unique place to visit in Sri Lanka I must also stress that the experience may not necessarily be a satisfactory one for conservationists who would prefer that these animals have little or zero physical contact with humans.We were made to understand that the National Zoo would be relocated to this area in the future,which would then mean that the overall facilities would surely improve in time to come.

Who could visit Sri Lanka without seeing some elephants therefore I headed to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage in the hopes of possibly adopting an elephant to preserve the species.  I was in awe of the animals but was slightly upset by the commercial selling of the animals as a means to get money.  I went with a hotel guide on a trip to the orphanage and was quickly goaded into buying bananas by a local street seller.  I then paid a high entrance price, which I was fine with as I felt it was going for a good cause.  I was greeted with a large pachyderm walking down the path.  We were quickly brought to the baby elephants that were in a pin and many chained to large post.  This to me was a bit upsetting.  The babies were apparently enjoying getting bottles of milk and bananas from the visitors.  I was able to feed on baby, which was a neat experience. We were then ushered to a pavillion and shown the injured and very sick looking elephant propped on a fence.  This was very disturbing, but understanding the poverty of the country it seemed the elephant was being fed and cared for as best as could be.  I would have liked to have skipped this show of pity. It did not encourage me to give any money for the center and would be better not used if they are trying to get donations. Next we were led to a field where elephants were eating.  Some had chains, one could chalk this up to a control method.  Shortly afterwards were were walked through the town following the elephants down to a river.  Here is where the magic happened for me and made me give this place a four star rating.  It was amazing to see the elephants enjoying the river and dirt embankment.  I was a little upset by the few elephants that were chained, one in particular was chained by the front and a back leg and could do little but lay in the water.  I don't know if this was because of miscreant behavior, but again not what I would like to see. We eventually went down to the river bank and had picture taken and fed some more bananas to the elephants, a visceral experience. At the river you will be approached by many street people, beware.  The "palm reader" grabbed my husband's hand and started reading his palm despite our protest.  He then demanded 1000 rupees.  He would not relent. I volunteered at the orphanage for a month in 2013. At that time the orphanage had two babies that were kept in a separate enclosure and bottle fed. Three times a day they were taken to a feeding place were houndreds of tourists could watch them bottle feed. The tourists could also pay extra to feed the babies one bottle and have pictures taken. I witnessed on EVERY occasion that the babies were in distress and it was heartbreaking to see. If they walked the wrong direction towards the feeding place their handlers would hit them with wooden sticks. At the feeding place they were then chained in one front and one hind leg. They always pooped on themselves which I have later learned is a sign of distress, you could see the panic in their eyes and they were always screaming. The zoo staff told me that the babies were rescued orphans found in the jungle, abandoned by their mothers, that they had fallen and got trapped in water pits whereas the mother was force to abandon the baby. I have later read from organisations such as PETA that the babies are not rescued in the jungle but born at the orphanage by the adult elephants and that they are taken from their mothers at birth - in the purpose of making money such as the bootle feeding occasions. I also witnessed the adult elephants being bullied and tormented by their care takers, and at one point I saw the "chief care taker" beat an elephant repeatedly with an umbrella. During opening hours the elephants ran free over the orphanage but as soon as the orphanage closed the elephants were chained in stables THE ENTIRE CLOSED TIME, not being able to move for a good 12-14 hours a day!!! Adult males in musths were chained in all four legs and kept in separate enclosures which tourists were not allowed to see or even aware of. I recommend readers to google about musth in elephants if you want to know more, but I have learned that keeping them chained extends the musth period and causes the elephant a great deal of physical and mental suffering. They suffered wounds around their feet from being constantly chained and were not allowed to be shown for visitors until the wounds were healed. Although the orphanage is better than nothing for the elephants, I cannot recommend tourists to visit the orphanage from an ethical point of view, since I believe tht visitors are decieved and that the main concern of the staff is to exploit the animals to make as much money possible.

This place has recently been in the news for maltreating of elephants in Sri Lanka and I think with good reason. I did not like to see how the lazy mahouts allow the elephants to walk to the river with their way too tight chains on. Some elephants got the chain caught on rocks in the river and had issues breaking free. One baby elephant with a huge chain on his hind leg came up to us, raising his foot as if asking (I am sure he was) to please take off the chain. It made me almost cry. The mahouts have to prove their manlihood by being rough with some ellies. Really a stupid thing to do with tourists around. I hope they will seriously address these issues as I believe the place is need for the "war elephants". Also, there is one elephant that just stands there. He lost half his front leg in a mine accident and refused a prosthesis a German Dr. applied. So, now, the poor  creature is sitting in the same place day in, day out, eating, being sprayed down with water when needed and cared for. I think there is a time and a place when animals need to be put out of their misery. This one is literally begging for it. Anyhow, please go and see the place though. It's still worth it.

Apparently this place was set up to look after orphaned elephants - the sole aim now seems to maximise the revenue from tourists. All the investment seems to be going into guest facilities (a brand new toilet block that wouldn't look out of place in a 5 star hotel) and not much for the elephants. As for the mahouts - their sole aim is to get money from tourists. The guy who took a couple of photos of me demanded (substantial) payment for himself and his 4 colleagues - leaving a bitter taste in the mouth from what should have been the archetypal Sri Lanka experience. Sorry to say but avoid at all costs.

This orphanage keeps the babies separate from their mothers so tourists can spend money on food and feed the babies. The babies are very distressed at being away from their mothers and cry a lot. God knows how the mothers feel. The babies are chained front leg and back leg so they can hardly move. They are cruelly beaten and constantly prodded by their mahouts who are supposed to care for them. Anyone going there should know they are supporting a very cruel trade. Just don't go!

Prior to my visit to Sri Lanka I read the reviews about the elephants and they were split for and against. Some implored me not to go. As part of our day trip the tour representative provided details of how the orphanage was established and how it works. It took several hours of driving the interesting narrow roads of Sri Lanka. Appears if you honk your horn before you overtake its ok if a bus is coming the other way. I digress. The elephants are in a reserve and are taken the river along a path. Over time commercial businesses have established and offer sometimes forcefully their wares. Its fine just to decline. The sight of the elephants in the water was amazing. It's free to take photos but be warned. Be very warned. If anyone offers to take your photo with an elephant be prepared to pay. They have your camera and then ask for a "donation" this is never mentioned before the offer. We spent an hour looking at these graceful animals. They love the water. They then are lead back up the path to their land area. The young calves are fed with milk and they can drink this down without much effort. There hide is tough and their hairs like steel wool. we thoroughly enjoyed this visit.  Amazing to see all the elephants, especially the babies.  Great location, they seem to be well looked after but take lots of small notes as you will be constantly asked for tips - for everything and equally told if it's not enough!!

In 2011, there were 88 elephants, including 37 males and 51 females from 3 generations, living in Pinnawala. Like most Srilankan tourist attraction, if you are from SAARC country you will have to pay less for your tickets. Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage consist of the main complex which houses the Elephants and also there is a river called Maha Oya nearby where you can see the elephant bathe..You can find many shops in the lane which leads to the river and you can buy good souvenir here at a relatively cheaper rate. There are elephants of all ages here and you can spend an hour going around. If you are from India, you can spend an hour or two here.

This being one of the most sought after attraction, we did halt by to see the elephants. The entrance fees are LKR 700 for Neighbouring Asian Countries (List displayed on the Board), an addition of LKR 250 for feeding fruits and LKR 300 for feeding milk. It was a good experience watching the elephants and even feeding them. However, work needs to be done on making this place truly a home for these elephants. Do patronise by visiting the Orphanage.

It is about an hour (ish) out of Kandy. There are so many elephants here being fed and then bathed down at the lake. However alot of them are chained, something we did not expect to see. You have to pay extra to feed the baby elephants! Be wary when you go down to watch the elephants in the water the guides will let you touch and take pictures of the elephants but then they ask you for money..something they should have made clear at the start!

I have to agree with other travellers that this place is rather a tourist attraction where elephants do not get a proper treatment. After visiting i am now clear to say that the best place to witness the mighty animals is only safari.

Never seen so mant of these magnificent mammals together. An awesome experience. Pity it is necessary but one gets the feeling that they do it well. The toilets by the way better than a lot of good hotels which is a bonus. Worth the journey from Kandy

When I first read on our itinerary that we were going to an elephant orphanage, I wasn't too excited because I didn't think there was anything new about seeing elephants (have already seen a lot in Thailand). When we went, I was  surprised and it turned out the whole scenery took my breath away! It was a completely different elephant "scene" to what I've seen before and I definitely recommend travelers to stop by here! We started out with lunch by the river and from there we could see a couple of elephants drinking. After lunch, we went into the orphanage and witnessed feeding time. There were several roofed areas where they fed the elephants. A few minutes after, we heard a commotion and we saw that all the elephants were being lined up and started hustling towards the river. We followed their path. The path to the river was like a road that was filled with lots of touristy shops selling SriLankan merchandise and elephant poop paper. (yes they use their dung to make paper!) You also have to be careful where you step because the droppings are everywhere. Once we got to the river, the scene before us was magnificent and just breathtaking. Imagine all the elephants in one place drinking and playing in the water. I couldn't get enough of it!!! You have to be there in person to drink in the whole experince. Lots of great photo opportunities! So yes, this site is definitely a must see while in Sri Lanka!

Elephants chained up for three months to 'break' into submission. Enjoyed seeing the elephants roam with acres of land in sight, until I realised that the elephants were huddled together and had chosen to keep in sight of the humans. All of the elephants had puncture wounds from being prodded. The elephants were hurded across a main road, past shops and down to the river. The highlight was seeing them bathe which clearly made them happy, for a short while.

If it hadn't been for watching 50 or so elephants bathing and playing in the river, this would have been a bit of a tourist trap. Entrance fees are steep and it feels a bit like a zoo. Feeding the elephant babies with milk bottles (at an extra fee) certainly was not worth the long drive from Kandy. But the river bath made it all worthwhile, we watched for hours.

Well that was the first place I visited in sri lanka so it was fun to see all this elephants and be so much close to them ... but the disadvantages were the that there was specific time to see the elephant in the river and the high entrance fees . but in general was fun and deserve the visit

I too will echo many of the other reviews about this "orphanage". Pinnewala is built on tourism and getting as much money out of the toursits as possible...an understandable goal given the ease that tourists part with their money, compared to working hard for a living. I was fortunate enough to be accompanied by a Sri Lankan friend and his two young sons. Understandably it is much cheaper for nationals to visit than tourists, which is just as well given their wages in Sri Lanka. I brought two milk feeding experiences to give to the boys. These were 350 rupees each and not something their father would normally afford for them. We wandered in at opening time (around 8.30 am). Found the elephants in the field eating fresh food trucked in by the workers. My fried took photos of me with the elephants behind, but one of the handlers encourage me to come nearer and pose with the elephant to take a photos. It seemed I escaped him before I could give hime a tip (which I didn't realise was the reason for their insistance to take a photo of me). At the second photo when he menacingly demanded 1000 rupees for pressing the shutter once, I laughed and told him he must be joking. I gave him 100 rupees and learnt my lesson fast that as a white tourist, I am considered rich. We watched the babies being 'fed' which was more a 3 second guzzle of a small bottle and is effectively a very brief photo op. At 9am the aimals headed down to the water. They were only letting visitors who held a ticket through to the lane which led to the river. Lots of things to buy, but maybe a bit early for agressive sellers, or the fact that I was with a Sri Lankan, meant that I did not get hasseled. A little expensive, and not sure that the intentions are completely honourable for this 'orphanage' as there were only a few babies...it did seem to be more a tourist trap zoo, but as I was only able to have a quick visit to Kandy, I wasn't going to see elephants up close in the wild, so it was my only opportunity to have an encounter. I don't regret going, but there are some practices which the western world would not agree with.

It costs 12.50gbp for a foreigner to enter and 100 rp for a local.  We arrived at 1pm, the Elephants were already walking across the park to go and have a bath.  We followed and the next thing we are out on the street following them to the water.  The clever tourists did not buy tickets but stayed in the street.  Many had already great positions in the restaurants and cafes by the water.  If you want to spend the whole day at the orphanage and watch then being fed the price is still extortionately high.  Best thing to do is get there about 12.30, find a good seat in one of the Cafes / Bars; sit have lunch and watch at your leisure.  The Elephants bathe twice a day, once in the morning and once from 2pm to 3.30 and you can get right up close to them as they go down the street.

This is definitely one way to get close to an elephant. If you too the guys, they will give you priority to go up to elephants and feed them. The best bit is when they are walked down to the river. It was unfortunate that they changed the baby elephants up for tourists to feed them milk (didn't participate) I hope they read their feedback and stop doing this, but they probably won't as people will keep tipping them to do it. Yes it's expensive to get in compared to everything else in Sri Lanka, but it's still dirt cheap, and well worth it.

When we first came here in 2010, the entrance fee was 500 rupees. In 2014, we were shocked to find out that it was increased to 2500 rupees. 500% increase in 4 years!!!!! Locals only pay 50 rupees. What were they thinking? Obviously they think people with white skin are made of money. I emphasized white skin because they don't charge nonwhite tourists this much. Although I'm a British citizen, I'm originally from Sri Lanka and I feel ashamed. I wouldn't mind paying 2500 if I was absolutely certain that all the money is spent on looking after the elephants but knowing Sri Lanka, I know that half the money ends up in politicians' and their henchmen's pockets.There is no transparency. I feel sorry for those who look after the elephants because they get paid a very low wage. Restaurant is a pure ripoff. Milkshake is 550 rupees. In the UK I can get 2 milkshakes for that money.Restaurant was dirty. Don't ask me about toilets. On the way back to our vehicle, so many people tried to take money using various techniques. That was totally unacceptable. Watching elephants was enjoyable though.

Whilst you get to see a lot of elephants up close, this place is not nice. Watching elephants tug at their chains to break free during feeding time is not pleasant. Watching them be forced to lie in the river to be bathed by tourists, again, isn't nice. It tries to pass off as an orphanage, it is little more than a money making zoo (2,500 RPS - £12.50). It is much more rewarding to see them in the wild and I suggest if you want to see elephants, go to one of the national parks in Sri Lanka instead. After going to Pinnawala I went on a safari in Yala National Park. We saw so many elephants, a massive herd roaming free. It was amazing, and whilst you cannot go and touch them, you don't want to, you are just happy that they are free and it is such a surreal experience rather than going to a zoo. Save your 2,500RPS and spend it elsewhere!

I know that this is the number 1 attraction in Sri Lanka but I would really advise all tourists to stay away. It is not an orphanage and I really do question the motives of this government run tourist trap. Yes you can see elephants up close and can pet them, but the conditions were upsetting. Baby elephants were chained to railings so that tourists could pet them - they were clearly distressed. These are wild animals who were clearly unhappy. The cost of admission for Sri Lankans is 100rs but for tourists its 2500rs - it is a complete rip off and I doubt any of this money goes towards elephant conservation. It's a money making scam for the government. Please spend your money elsewhere! Go to one of the national parks and see elephants in the wild - it will make you far happier to see the elephants happy too!

Not sure why this is consistently top of the rankings. Yes. it does what it says on the packet and has lots of elephants  but if you've been fortunate to see elephants in a setting like Yala National Park, Paying what is a (relatively for SL) large amount to get in to see these majestic animals chained to the ground or being herded around a dusty compound for your entertainment is just a bit disheartening. Our opinion - its total tourist trap and our holiday would not have suffered at all if we had missed it altogether. I would suggest they are very adept at "looking after" the guides and drivers. Our driver certainly seemed unusually keen that we go there and had lists of reasons why other elephant related attractions in the area were definitely not to be visited. Cynicism aside, if you have not had the chance to see elephants anywhere else then they are definitely here to see - but I do wonder what this place does for the money that other elephant zoos (sorry, "sanctuaries" or "orphanages") wouldn't?

This was a short stop during our Sri Lankan travel. We came during elephant bathing time, so we saw lots of them. As there were no children in our group, feeding and petting of the animals were not so important, so some time for elephant observation and making a few nice pics did well. As some of the reviewers have noted, the place is quite commercialized, but if at least some money goes for maintenance of elephants, it is OK. Actually, the idea of making paper out of elephant poo is cute and a small souvenir made of poo paper was fun to buy and to give while coming back home.

The Good: There are LOADS of elephants. The Average: Very rushed tour and very crowded. We only had about 30 mins in the Orphanage before the elephants were herded down to the river to bathe. This meant all the tourists (and there were a LOT) had to do what they'd paid for in a real hurry. You can buy extra tickets to feed milk to the baby elephants and to feed the adults fruit. HOWEVER...... The Awful: The babies are chained up to the iron fence in the feeding area to stop them wandering off and with so many tourists having bought tickets to feed them, the atmosphere was more like a force-feeding station. It's amazing to see such a huge herd of elephants on the move together and that was great, but if you want an experience that is more about the welfare of the elephants, more relaxed, unrushed and with real access to well trained and happy elephants I would recommend you save your money and go to the Elephant Freedom Project down the road. Yes, they only have 2 elephants instead of a whole herd but you get to walk with them, wash them, feed them and play enrichment games with them. They're also well trained so they respond to vocal commands rather than being dragged about on chains or prodded with pointed sticks. My 8yr old son was very vocal about the differences he saw. The experience at Pinawalla was made more disappointing by the fact that one of the mahouts encouraged us to touch the elephant he was looking after and then aggressively hassled us for money. That, and my son cutting his finger very badly indeed on a thoroughly pointless piece of barbed wire. If it's quantity of elephants you want, then this is the pace for you. If you want quality time and a personal experience go to the Elephant Freedom Project.

Were able to see so many elephants and it was worth every penny going there.Elephants are well taken care.We were able to see feeding and bathing of elephants.Also were also were able to see them roaming on a open ground. Was a incredible experience!!! A Must Visit place Caution be aware of people who will try to  cheat you.

Good chance to see many elephants up close, but in a very touristy environment.  If you want to feed elephants, to be photographed with elephants and buy any manner of souvenir this is the place to come. It is a good place to practice saying no toall manner of peolpe who want tosell you stuff. This was the first attraction that we visited in Sri Lanka and most of the attractions we visited after this were better.

We visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage mainly because of my 4yr old twins and their joy and excitement made the trip completely  worth it. The experience is amazing and very very memorable -  you can feed the elephants and watch them bathe. The elephants were also quite well looked after and most of the caretakers are really nice and friendly. A few tips to note a. Watch out for the fake elephant sanctuaries that have cropped up all over the road to Pinnawala. Don't get taken in by your car driver into these and insist on going only to Pinnawala. b. Go well before feeding time. While there is plenty of scope to feed fruits to the large elephants, we couldn't get to feed milk to the little baby elephants. That part is really crowded and they issue only about 5 tickets per elephant. So make sure you go well in advance and book your ticket. We didn't and my kids cried their hearts out - so they let our boys pet the baby elephant c. Keep your passport along when you visit - if you are from an ASEAN country, the tickets cost much lesser if you can show your passport. d.The mahouts who accompany the elephants to the bathing are sometimes pretty commercial and ask for extra money to let you touch the elephants.  I watched horrified as one asked 2 Caucasian women standing next to me for money in lieu of taking them close to the elephants and were pretty rude to them when they said No However this was a very tiny blip on our overall experience which was fabulous. On the whole, a must visit!

It's a great visit for toddlers & children as they are totally mesmerized by the mere existence & behaviour of these gentle giants. We loved watching our son being 'wowed' by the baby elephants. This is a must for any traveller visiting the island. It can be arranged as a day trip from Colombo or stopover between Colombo & Kandy.

This Elephant Orphanage is doing an extremely good job. Not only is it a fantastic tourist attraction it is also caring for injured and orphaned Elephants. The tea rooms and restaurants provide an excellent service and photo opportunities are plentiful. Well worth a visit.

This is a bad place.  The elephants are sad, distressed and wounded!  The keepers are rude, uncaring and money grabbing.  It made my hackles stand on end to be there and makes me heavy with sadness to think of it now.  A big black mark for Sri Lanka!

I went to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage with my wife when we were on a trip to Sri Lanka. We had booked the trip through Ravi Tours near our hotel. We arrived in time for the feeding of the young Elephants and our guide had pre ordered a ticket for my wife to hand feed the baby elephant.  Not many of these tickets are available, so if you do go try and get the ticket in advance, your guide will help you on this. My wife thought it was a great experience and really enjoyed it. You really do get up close and personal with the beautiful creatures. Make sure you take your camera with plenty of film and batteries. You can buy fruit to feed the elephants in the grounds and have you photo taken feeding the larger elephants. After the feeding the elephants they will go down to the river for a relax and cool down in the water. It is really great to see the elephants running around playing in the water, especially the younger ones. There is a restaurant by the river where you can get some food and a drink.  There is also some toilets. You can get a seat and just watch the elephants at play. You will also have local people come up to you trying to read you palm, they will want money from you, they asked me for 1000 rupees to read my palm. You can just tell them that you are not interested. One of the people we were with paid 100 rupee, so there is some bartering to be done. The down side to this trip is most of the elephants have a chain around their leg and the Mahouts have a stick which has a point on it and they do use them if the elephants are not doing what they should be doing. It could be to make sure we are safe. They do have a culture in Sri Lanka, of they do not put the animals down, even if they are in pain. They have an elephant which had stepped on a land mine and has only three legs and a stump for the fourth leg. This may upset some people as in the UK we would have put the elephant to sleep. It is quite clear this elephant cannot move very far, however it is feed and watered. I think they should be raising money for this elephant to have a new artificial leg so at least it could try and walk down to the river for a cool off and give it some sort of life.

This was along our trip to and from Kandy area, so wanted to have a see.  It was perfect timing that the animals were bathing in the stream when we arrived (10-12pm? and 3-5pm?); worth getting the time right.  The rest of the orphanage was quite empty awaiting the elephants' return up from the river, but can always find a few things to see.  We watch two adorable 2 yr. old elephants play in a pool/bath!  Also have some good photos of some children feeding a big elephant - trunk up, put food in, … and one little boy in background was looking way into elephant's mouth!  adorable.  Was HOT, but shaded areas, refreshments/at cost,  and nice toilets INSIDE.. those pay ones near the gate were pretty rough. I agree with other people's statements about 'the trainers' on the make for money… sad, but sorry, typical for Asia.  ASK first… hope the organisation reads these reviews and tries to get a grip on this… as they ask for ridiculous amounts!  Are we stupid!?!  I hope the elephants are well looked after by these guys!

It was great to see how Sri Lanka is looking after it's minimal elephant population and trying to increase the population. But to do anything interactive with the elephants such as bathe, feed calves or ride (which I find cruel might I say) you have to pay more. I know they need money to continue the good work but it just didn't feel right. Probably wouldn't return myself, although I would recommend going to others

I wasnt visited real Elephant orphange, but be carefull abou fake one, so this is only warning. We did managed to get to Pinanawala crossroad by bus. There we took tuk tuk to orphange. We were at the orphanage april 11th. Seeing the elephants is a very nice experience, but be prepared for the rangers who will try to make you tip them for the slightest of services such as taking a photo of you. After paying 2500LKR per person this is most embarrassing. Their attitude is a shame to the park. We witnessed rangers who after being given 500LKR pulled a face and even asked for more! One Japanese tourist apparently was so intimitaded that she gave and incredible amount of 2000LKR and still we couldn't see the slightest signs of gratitude in the face of the ranger. Shameful. Another socalled highlight is the feeding of the baby elephants.with cash you can buy your way into the line of feeders. My advice: go and see the orphanage. But stand firm against any ranger who tries to force you into tipping. And if they show you an attitude turn around and walk away. I understand people want to earn money, but the behaviour of these greedy rangers was a great disappointment.

We took our 2 girls 11 and 7yrs, both of whom are animal lovers. We were a bit wary as a few reviews on trip advisor made us think twice about going. In hindsight we had nothing to worry about. Yes the workers occasionaly have to use pointy sticks to control the animals but they have 2 inch skin and weigh more than my car so that's understandable, i think some people are a bit unrealistic and over sensitive. It was idyllic watching these huge beautiful animals bathe for a couple of hours. Then onto the orphanage itself which is laid out brilliantly and the animals are not mistreated at all. Please ignore the negativities in some of these reviews, its a great place doing great things.

It was not what I expected. The elephants are great but there were still quite a few elephants tied up. We opted to pay extra to feed baby elephants but it was so busy and not well organised so I wouldn't recommend. Take local currency they do not accept dollars.
