It's a good place to visit - the worlds largest elephant herd resides there. I traveled there with my wife and friends.  The train ride from Colombo is good and the orphanage is half way to Kandy. We arrived early and went for a cuppa and breakfast at the Elephant hotel waiting for the attraction to open. We were over the moon when the keepers brought 5 females and 2 babies down the hill to bathe while it was quiet. We were invited to help bathe the elephants and enjoyed a good hour feeding and washing them,  We enjoyed so much so that the actual attraction was a bit of a let down. Take my advice and do what we did.  Even if the elephants don't turn up the tea and toast was excellent.

its a wonderful place to see elephants.  you are bombarded for tips. .....but I find that describes asia in general. ......I was happy to pay extra to touch and feed the elephant.   I don't think any zoo looks after animals  any better. ....and it was very special to be able to get so close to them.

We were attracted by the fact that it is supposed to be an orphanage for mistreated elephants, but once there we were very disappointed. Now it seems like a circus business where the caretakers are dragging you the elephants to take a picture with them, 'bathing' an elephant countless times, and almost forcefeeding milk to elephants, only to win some tips that they are even unsatisfied of. If you want to see happy elephants, go to any natural park in Sri Lanka

Loved seeing so many noble beasts at such close quarters but weren't so sure about the chains or the quality of life for the disabled elephant. Watching the river swim showed how much the elephants enjoyed this part of the day, though.

My partner & I first visited here 9 years ago & really enjoyed it. This time, we travelled with friends on their first visit to Sri Lanka. I have to say that I was a little disappointed at how commercialised it has become & how often you are now expected to dip into your pockets for tips. It was still good to see the elephants bathing in the river but I felt that feeding the baby elephants was now too impersonal & a bit of a mad circus. It has definitely morphed from being memorable special experience to a hectic tourist attraction. As you make your way down the street from the "orphanage" to the river, you are bombarded by people trying to sell you tourist tat.

We went there around 11:30am , the elephants were already bathing. There will be this guy come and sell you banana for 200rupees saying you can feed them, do not trust him and do not buy. There is a sign saying no feeding. We understand that the place needs to make money to sustain this project, but it feels quite commercial as there are too many extras you can pay for. You can even bribe the guards while the elephants are bathing to feed them. The elephants seem hungry as they kept trying to get close to the tourist hoping to be fed. I have seen similar place in other part of the world, they are taking care of these elephants orphanges but at the same time they want more income so it really comes down to whether you want to see a big group of elephants bathing in the river up close or not.

The orphanage itself is well worth a visit, particularly at feeding time but also walking down to see the elephants bathing in the river was a real spectacle.  Get a seat at one of the bars/restaurants overlooking the river and you can enjoy the elephants as well as having food and drinks at a reasonable price considering the location.  We sat here for an hour and just watched, amazing!  The elephants in the orphanage were tethered to prevent them running away which was slightly of putting but once you understand the history and that after starting with just 4 rescued elephants they now have many many more, quite a few who were born there but more importantly that they regularly release them back into the wild in the rain forests with ongoing checks on their welfare.  Makes it worthwhile.

I enjoyed this place but is not perfect. It is government run and associated with the zoo. The animals on the whole are free to roam in the fields and brought for bathing in a large river twice a day. You can bottle feed the babies and feed the animals for between 250-350 rupees (1.50e-2e) You aren't given a lot of information regarding their work. Also there are many optional "extras" like getting your photo taken or feeding them at the river which the workers will try extort you for tips (they say 1000-2000 rupees, don't give more than 100 rupees for anything) I also had an issue with an elephant they had which had been injured by a landmine. The poor animal was leaning against a fence and looked very ill and had no quality of life. I don't know why this animal was not euthanised as it would seem less cruel.

Myself and my friends visited here as it was a government run elephant orphanage so we assumed the welfare of the elephants would be paramount.  The reason we decided on this park rather than a cheaper one down the road was due to the fact we were told the purpose of the park was merely to observe the animals and not to ride them etc.  this is what we wanted,somewhere to observe good work being done on behalf of orphaned elephants. First off all there is absolutely no information that I could see based on how the orphanage was established,the work they do, the situations in which they have rescued the elephants etc....surely the centre could not only be a place to observe these magnificent creatures but also one of learning?!! This seemed very strange to me and something that is really lacking here and made the place seem more like a tourist attraction! Secondly I must mention that yes they do not allow you to 'touch' the elephants, yet our friend was encouraged by one of the mahouts to have her photo taken with a baby and was told she could touch him....however we soon realised this was only made available to her in exchange for a backhand of rupees to the mahout.  They need to create a policy and stick to it or else people's belief in the work they do (or claim to do) will diminish! We paid extra at the gate to partake in the bottle feeding, which in hindsight was a bad decision.  We expected a one on one experience with the baby elephant, instead there are about 5 babies led to a circus ring and chained and 100''s of people just gather round and crowd them, there is no order to it and no queuing system for those who paid to bottle feed....as a result the whole thing is very rushed and people are crowding and pushing to get to the rails to feed the baby which can't be a good experience for the elephants either!! All in all this was not the most pleasant of experiences and certainly not what we expected....it is referred to as a orphanage but there is little evidence of that actually being the case so there is little in the way of differentiating it from a zoo! The elephant bathing is fun to watch and it is a good place to go for an up close experience but there is a serious amount of work needed here to live up to its ethos! Try yala national park for a much more natural experience of elephants living in the wild but within safe parameters of the park!

I found the baby elephant feeding very depressing. They were kept chained by the ankle and several where distressed. I find it hard to understand why they should have to have been shacked while waiting for food and while being fed. They was a three legged elephant that had had its leg blown in a land mine that was kept alive, I believe for tourist to ogle at. Its other food and trunk were deformed trying to cope with holding up its wait. I understand that they do good and have to control the older ones as they could be dangerous and they are giving them a better life and the time they took the larger elephants to a water whole was good. I tried while there to get an answer to the treatment of the baby elephants but to no avail. I am researching a way to convey my feeling to the appropriate people.

If you don't have another event planned to see elephants, this would be worth it. We did this, then went on an elephant safari in one of the parks and saw the elephants in the wild-much better. Here you can see tame elephants eat and walk to the river. If you have time, go to one of the national parks and see the elephants in the wild instead.

I wasn't sure about going here but it was part of the trip. It was lovely to see so many elephants and I thought that perhaps they were really being helped. It seems to be just a tourist attraction. The mahouts poke the elephants with a stick with a sharp hook on it and you could see they were very frightened. There were disabled elephants there struggling. A lot of the elephants had chains round their feet, especially the babies which was very upsetting and you could see the scars caused by them. I asked why they did this and they said to protect them from running around and to protect the visitors...One large elephant in particular was chained up severely and could barely move. He was on his own, it brought tears to my eyes. Apparently he had been naughty??? It was lovely seeing them walking to the river. I thought they would be very keen as it was so hot but most of them seemed to be scared, especially the babies and did not want to go in, they just stood on the rocks but were poked by the mahouts to go in. The mahouts just lazed around and did not interact with them at all. Foreign visitors have to pay a lot more to get in than nationals.

Just to get your attention do not go this place it is government funded and a tourist trap. We arrived excited after seeing heaps if wild animals in Minneriya national park the day before we were keen to get up close and personal with some orphaned elephants and babies. However, when we arrived got to the top of the park there were heaps (maybe 30) of elephants but only in a dust bowl no food to be found. The next was an middle aged elephant chained so close to a pole that he could not move, and a mahout who asked for money and for us to feed him the money was going in his pocket not the orphanage. We walked over to the males with tusks who again all five chained so tightly to poles and trees and making a move with their head. Obviously a sign of mentally ill animals doing repetitive actions due to their constraints We were finally told by our guide the baby feeding was to occur; in come four beautiful babies into a pen and again chained up so tight that they were all trying to run so hard to break the chain but in fact all they were doing was hurting their legs. A mahout comes in shoves a bottle down their mouth so heard that they spat half of it out, and onto the next one. By this time my wife and I had enough and wanted to leave. I had read in lonely planet that its a vicious cycle because tourists want to come and will continue to come and the government will continue to get money hungry and do more. I'm told they are now breeding here when their initial goal was to look after orphaned elephants and injured ones. One relief is seeing them go to the river at about 1:30pm and you can eat lunch at a restaurant watching them in the water play, but by this point we wanted them to run off the other side of the river and free themselves because this was as worse as being in a circus or caged up! The Sad thing is there are too many people from around the world who see this as acceptable and laugh and take photos as if this is an amazing experience and while this is still happening I hold no hope of this ever changing. I promised myself to report this on trip advisor and the more who do realise this is a disgrace maybe Sri Lankan officials will think about what the purpose of this place was actually all about. Apparently about 10minutes down the road there is a new sanctuary set up and reviews so far are good. So maybe try that first and see if its what we are really meant to see. Please if you do go and don't like post so others don't support animal cruelty. The worst highlight on an amazing 14 day honeymoon!

Being animal owners and lovers we were always keen but wary of what we might see at this orphanage. We didn't need to be wary. The elephants were in magnificent condition and had plenty of space to roam in. Some of the larger males were kept away from the herd but the majority of them were wandering freely around the place. The opportunity to wander amongst them while they roamed freely was greater than we had expected. Feeding time for the babies was amazing and Linda had the fantastic opportunity to bottle feed one. A few complaints from people around the elephants being restrained but we understood that even a baby elephant can do some major damage just by leaning on the handler. Also kept the babies calm enough to feed properly. Great to see so many locals visiting this place and learning about these amazing animals. Would be great in an ideal world to have them all out in the wild but unfortunately we don't live in an ideal world and this is a very good second best to ensure these magnificent creatures safety. Also fortunate enough to see them walk freely through the village down to the river and have "bath time" which you could see they thoroughly enjoyed. They were left to their own devices and great to see the babies playing together while some of the older elephants laid in the water and appeared to fall asleep. Unlike some other reviewers we were pleased with the level of professionalism and respect that the handlers displayed with these animals. The discussion we had with the head handler left us in no doubt he understood and loved these beautiful creatures.

It was to be the highlight for me of our Sri Lankan tour in February 2014 but sadly from the moment we arrived I thought the whole thing was horrible.  A tourist circus,  I washed a young elephant in the river - its mahout had no empathy with it  at all.  It had three circles of gensian violet on its head around wounds obviously inflicted by the metal hook that the mahouts use to control the animals.  The babies were fed at a certain time - all were chained and in distress. I would not recommend anyone goes there.  We went to the park up in Yala where we saw wild elephants which I would recommend most highly.

We visited in February 2014 and saw: The big male who is kept away from the herd during certain times The herd grazing freely on a very large open space The orphan elephants being bottle fed Two disabled elephant who would have died in the wild - one had his ear chewed off by a leopard and one lost his front feet on a landmine. We were able to get so close to all the elephants, except the alpha male which was a bit dangerous. It was a terrific feeling to be up close, seeing every aspect of their behaviour in such detail. I felt very privileged and very humbled by the size of these magnificent gentle animals. Our guide was fantastic and told us so much about the situation of elephants in Sri Lanka and what the orphanage does. He was very knowledgable and educative. Later we saw the elephant herd "running" through the street down to the river. Very powerful. It was great to watch them in the water, some going deeper, others including a baby were very timid of the water. Go with an open mind and a good guide and you will learn a lot.

It was nice to see the elephants and they did appear to have a nice big open space to live in, not to mention the river in which they bathe each day.  However, it was hard to see the elephant with its leg blown up standing alone and with difficulty. The staff were pushy and did not seem overly caring towards the elephants or keen to ensure visitors have a good time.  If they offer to take your photo expect to be asked for a hefty fee afterwards. Also, if a man tries to sell you bananas outside the facility to feed the elephants, it's a con as you can't feed the elephants outside food. It's also expensive for foreigners and completely over-run with tourists.

This place confused me. I was expecting a nice happy place with beautiful happy elephants who had been rescued due to being orphans. (we were told that elephants have babies there so that's not the case) Anyway, we went down to the river and my first glimpse of the elephants in the river!! Wow. I watched mesmerised for five minutes. Then i noticed that they weren't actually doing anything, just standing.they looked bored.i noticed that one nearby had scarring on its legs.then i noticed one had chains and it was chucking its leg about and i saw the the chains were so tight that they had dug into the elephants leg.that's what the scarring was on the leg of the first one.many had tight chains and were clearly upset and hurt by them, many many more had bad scarring. keeper uses a metal ended (boat) hook on the elephants' ears to move them on.corruption is seen here too.a keeper let my partner under the chain and took a photo for him, then tried to get 20 dollars out of him.he settled for 200 LKR in the end.a bit saddened, we made our way up to the centre where first we saw two babies.they were clearly put there to satisfy the needs of us visitors to get up close and personal with the elephants.. We then saw two poorly disabled elephants both had bad legs and were tightly chained in a shed.nearly having had enough we were ushered to see the babies being bottle fed.we stood for 20 minutes waiting for this during which time we saw the five babies, on 2 meter chains, all clearly distressed calling loudly, trying in vain to reach each other.there were branches in the middle which they were trying to reach for distraction but the keepers just told them off and pushed them back.there was no comfort offered to them by the keepers.after 20 minutes of this and no feeding in sight we left, dismayed and sad at what we had seen.not sure what is going on here but i feel its just a government sponsored money maker taking advantage of the fact that people like elephants.If you want to see healthier happier elephants go on a jeep safari at Minneriya national park instead.

My main problem was the dying elephant kept on it's own. It's leg has been blown up by a land mine and it's quality of life was horrific. It spends it's life leaning up against a wooden log and has a sore on it's leg from where it was previously leant against metal.  It was hitting it's sore with leaves and was obviously uncomfortable.  It rarely moved at all and when fed a banana, simply chewed it up and spat it over its back in a failed attempt to cool itself down....I am guessing it was not being made comfortable by it's keepers. Meanwhile, 99% of other visitors were distracted from this scene and by baby feeding time.....crowding around a small enclosed space where the baby elephants were being chained and fed bottles....it was like a circus....hundreds of people. It is only right that the ill elephant is put down, as it is clearly in distress and is distressing to see. It was not all bad at all...the elephants were not hurt at any point and have a lot of space to roam.  Other than the injured elephant, they all seemed very well looked after, and have a lot more space than any elephant in a zoo!! As a big animal lover I would have rated this place much higher had I not witnessed the suffering of the ill elephant.

The Laksala shop in the entrance sums up this whole experience - a shopping/money making project for unthinking tourists. In my opinion, the welfare of the elephants was well down the priority list. I wish I had paid attention to my gut feeling and turned back at the gate. The higher entrance fee for foreigners is understandable - but is it really benefitting the elephants - I have my doubts. This was my least pleasant visit in a four month trip to Sri Lanka.

if you arrive in the morning at 9.15am you can see (or do) the feeding of baby elephants (drinking milk from the bottle), at 10.00am all elephants are walking across the road to the river, you can watch how about 60 elephants walk by 2 meters from you, I can say it's quite impressive, and then how they play and relax in the river... afterwards we took an elephant ride in one of the places offering it down the road

We found this place that good we went back 2 days later for more. This place is a must as we have never been lucky enough to witness as many elephants in one place before. From  6 month to 40 years old and have a total of 86 elephants. To see them trooping down the road and in to the river is a sight i will never forget.

You can see many large and little elephants here, orphans and wild - they are so nice really. Our children was happy, it was best place for them, best trip in Sri lanka. We rided elephants here in nature. They have bath in river. Beautiful country and river, and all. Only problem we must give money to people that are working with elephants. It is busines but it is ok.

On the positive side of things the Elephants appear to be taken care of with large areas to roam and twice daily walks to the river to swim. On the negative side and the reason for the 2 star was that it all seems for show and to attract tourists. The handlers were not nice and only want money off you but a stern "no thanks" and they don't persist, preferring to move on to the next tourist who wants a photo. To me this indicates they do not really care for the welfare of the elephants but use them as a money maker. The feeding time with the baby elephants was one big circus with tourists being charged extra to feed the chained up babies for a photo opportunity. Didn't like the atmosphere at all. Also we were told that the park BREEDS elephants, so how can it be an orphanage? The government is raking in millions of rupees through this park with absolutely no information about how its going to the benefit of the elephants. Overall, I got the impression its a money maker that's all.

The orphanage houses wild elephants by the dozens. Handicapped or blind elephants are also sheltered. Visitors can get up close with the elephants with or without the care-takers around. Photographs are possible with the elephant with a nominal tip to the mahout. The best time to visit is when the elephant herds are taken for their daily baths across the river by crossing the main highway. Particularly attractive are the younger ones who struggle to keep pace with the bigger ones. The place also sells paper and other stuff made out of elephant dung. the whole place is a bit expensive though.

Well managed and run, with the orphans of various ages obviously well cared for by the mahouts, in a large scenic park.. Babies can be fed milk (small charge) and empty 2 litres in a blink of an eye. Another docile female can be hand fed fruit via a bespoke stand.The main herd are led out of the park and across a main road to a river where they bathe for an hour or so, before returning, somewhat bizarrely through a narrow pedestrian only shopping street. The only criticism, was the sight of a adult nelly whose front leg had been shortened to the knee by a land mine on one side and the other front leg obviously broken, its existence only possible by keeping it propped up in a barn.With such poor quality of life, euthanasia would seem the kindest result. Despite this well worth the visit.

Before visiting I read a lot of mixed reviews on Pinnawala. The resort provides fantastic opportunities to get up close with the elephants. I'm unsure how ethical it is although following the elephants down to the river sees them enjoying wide open spaces to roam. I would advise going but maybe enter with an open mind.

Excellent experience, it costs approx £12.50 which basically get you entrance to the viewing area to watch the elephants bathing, feeding etc, some nice shops, stalls, restaurants etc all down the small rad that leads to this area. When visiting it is well worth stopping at a herbal/spice garden, very interesting and enjoyable

This was day 1 (22.2.14) of a 5 day tour of Sri Lanka. I am not an animal lover but elephants have always been my exception......we arrived early and the elephants from the orphanage were down in the river cooling off. It was a sight for sore eyes!!! So, get there early!! At 1pm, they walk up the road back into the orpahage,quie an incredible!!! I didn't like the baby feeding session.....but I can well imagine it earns alot of  welcome cash for the orphange!! I have to say, it's an incredible experience!! Is it right though?? Hmmm!!!

A once in a lifetime experience. You can feed, touch and ride elephants, and the orphanage is the best place to do it as other sellers do not treat the elephants as nicely. Don't get me wrong be prepared for chains and a few whips, but on the whole the elephants seem well looked after. You get to watch them march to the water to bath for an hour which was lovely, and the riding of the elephant was such a great experience although hard to hold on! It was 2000 ruppes for the ride and 2500 ruppes to enter the main orphanage.

A really awesome experience to see so many orphan elephants coming back from the river, the bigger females keeping the smaller ones safe against the public. It was interesting to see the way the Poo Paper was made too. Such ingenuity! We then went on to wash an elephant and ride on one. Totally wonderful.

I love elephants and especially baby elephants, but this experience left me a bit cold.  I did not like to see the babies in short chains.  I understand the explanation that this is for their safety as well as the tourist.  The chains just seemed way too short for small animals.  The orphanage seemed more like a business rather than an orphanage because of lack of compassion by those taking care of them. The best part of the day was watching the elephants in the river at lunch.  The views were lovely and watching the elephants play and roll around in the river was delightful--except when the mahouts walked over and whacked them with a pole when they went some place he didn't want them to go.  Food at the restaurant overlooking the river was good.  Service very slow.

As we were with a guide fro 5 days (the best way to tour around Sri Lanka), ven if the attraction was full of tourists, we could avoid the crowd and watch the elephants in the river (closely and at lunch-time) and baby feedind (extra fee) relatively at ease. We could also be close (too much close...) to the marching herd when they went back to the herd's farm from the river, because we were buying clothes from one of several stores in the compound. The elephants of the orphanage (now a breeding facility), are domestic and, as we didn't went to a natural park (perhaps next time...), so we only saw one wild one at the board of a road.

A tourist attraction which raises money to look after these elephants, that may have started as orphans. There is not a great deal to see, & mahouts ask for money for any extra.  The best bit is seeing the elephants in the river. Try to visit at lunchtime as this seemed to be the time when all the coaches left, but if you live near a zoo that may be a better option!

I had read other reviews and so entered with an open mind...our tour guide had previously worked with this facility and it is more a breeding facility now than orphanage .... he felt that they were doing a very good job of looking after the herd. The elephants in chains is necessary for everyones safety as these huge beasts can get out of control easily....watching the moms and babys cooling themselves with dust is fascinating...but the best part was when the elephants were brought down to the lake....we were sitting in the cafe and could watch as they went into the water and were spraying themselves and some were rolling in the water to cool off....they seemed very content. Worth a visit!

A very commercial attraction. You will be asked to pay for everything as an extra once you enter ( getting close to elephants, feeding baby elephants ). It is very busy, particularly at feeding time, and unless you can get an early front line view, then children will not be able to see.Just about worth a visit if you are local as it is nice to see the baby elephants, but I wouldn't drive 2 hours in a car from the coast to visit

Good time to spend. Unfortunately, tickets are Rupees 2500 for tourists and 250 for local. Feedinf elephant 250, bathing, giving milk etc... in every step you move you have to pay. I feel something wrong. Also, it's too far, we drive two hours almost to reach there. In general, it's a good experience especially for kids. They enjoyed more than us.

This orphanage is very well run and although people have commented about the chains on some of the elephants, this is for the trainers safety and yours. Baby elephants are being fed with chains on but obviously they have to be kept in one area or they would just run riot. The whole experience of being beside these magnificent creatures should be marvelled and watching them whilst you have a snack and a cool drink at the river restaurant is a great idea.

We had high expectations of witnessing "something special" at Pinnawala, but were rather let down by the experience. Whilst it is true that one could be at very close quarters with the elephants, both young and old, but one left with the impression that this was very much a commercial venture (not inexpensive) rather than an orphanage. The whole process of visitors  feeding the young a bottle of milk through a tube was very undignified as visitors were crammed shoulder to shoulder and then managed just 20 seconds of holding a tube whilst the keeper filled it with a funnel.

This well known tourist spot left me with mixed feelings. First, it is not an orphanage. 15 minutes there and it is obvious it is a business, and all the babies I saw had their mothers with them. Next, the conditions were far from ideal. There seemed to be a lot of "disturbed" elephants. That may account for the abudnance of chains they have to wear. However, the highlight was undoubtedly being stood next to the exit gate as the whole herd of 30 or 40 headed to the river. I have never been that close to elephants before. Awesome. TOP TIP: Do not bother going into the orphanage, but head down to the riverside hotels, order tea & brunch and wait for the herd to come down & bathe.

Great afternoon feeding the young ones and then sitting by the river watching them all play in the river whilst having a long cool drink and a snack This is the 5th time and I'm  still  mesmerised by it all could watch them all day

We were there with our kids. Looking at elephants with chains on legs is destressful. People who should take care of these animals want only one thing from you - MONEY for everything. So you pay a lot for a ticket, then you have to pay to tips for a photo, for giving a corn, for touching an elephant. A real project for orphan elephants is in Kenia - I highly recommend visiting this place near Nairobi. Pinnavala is not a necessary point in your Sri Lankan schedule. The only interesting thing is paper producing from elephants' poo.

If you care about animals you will find visiting this attraction very distressing. There is a large paddock where the elephants can roam freely but many of the poor animals are restricted by chains. However it the feeding program that concerned me the most, prior to the event the baby elephants are brought into the enclosure and chained to posts. This causes great distress to them, they try to pull away and interact with each other but the chains are too short to allow this, also they are surrounded by humans which is not natural for them and appears to add to their distress. I had not checked any reviews of this place prior to my visit as it formed part of an organised tour, however if I ever visit sri lanka again I would boycott the place and would encourage fellow travellers to do the same.

Very busy when we were there, and in many ways quite disturbing to see the chains restricting movement and the use of the metal tipped poles. I suppose in many ways these methods have to be used to keep potentially very dangerous animals under control but in many ways wish we hadn't gone. There are so many other opportunities in Sri Lanka to see these great animals in the wild.

If you actually love animals, don't go here.  This is a tourist trap with elephant victims.  Chained baby elephants and prices that are 100 more for foreign tourists.  I recommend going to one of the other rescues or orphanages in the area, or if you just want to see the elephants go at the end of their bath time and watch them cross the road, because that's free and you're not paying money for cruelty.

It's good to have the chance to see so many elephants in one place, especially when they are going to bath. It's a good idea to produce paper from elephant dung. The reason I don't want to give a higher rating is that the place seems to be too commercial.

The elephant orphanage left me feeling a huge range of emotions, happy, sad, upset, confused all in one. As you enter there are elephants located at different spots to interest tourists. The baby elephants are in the centre, chained, which to me looked quite painful all so that the tourists can enjoy the feeding time. While the baby elephants are being fed, the tourists are literally falling over each other to get as close as possible and take pictures which did scare the baby elephants a few times. The worst part for me was the poor elephant who had an injured foot apparently a landmine injury. The elephant is chained in an enclosure alone and simply moves from side to side, with no stimulation or company, how can this be acceptable? There is another elephant who is a fruit feeding attraction and this one was quite nice, there were no chains at all and you simply feed fruit. There were some free elephants but a few still had chains which had been loosened for the little free time. The elephants also went down to the river and it was nice to see them playing about and enjoying the water. However, as a place that calls itself an orphanage, there is no information given at all about what rescue services they provide, how they take care of the elephants, what happens to the elephants or how they ensure all the elephants are healthy.

Poor elephants - crying small (2-3 months old) elephants which are chained to the concrete pole and cannot move (morning feeding), scared to death due to crowd of people / screaming pupil. Bathing looked less violent but still it's a prison for those lovely animals. And, of course, poor Sri Lankans asking form money in any occasion...

In my opinion this is a bad zoo, many of the elephants have leg chains, they are clearly breeding them since some are pregnant and they have babies which you can pay to feed. This is good for local employment and is a money spinner for the government but not good for the animals. They feed them and take them through the shopping area to the river to bathe which looks pretty but the chains and leg scars are painfully visible. I think we should boycott the place, the animals are suffering. Bull elephants are chained to trees and pull at the chains and stomp from side to side like crazy zoo animals. Many many tourists come here generating lots of money for the government. It needs to be stopped.

We had the best shore excursion of our cruise, from Colombo to Pinnawala. Our guide from Tour East, Pradeep Ratnayake, explained that elephants travel in families. When an elephant is poached and leaves a baby, or when one falls in a hole and cannot get out, they are rescued and brought to Pinnawala. Until newcomers are "welcomed into the group" they must be chained to prevent them from hurting others. We were able to pet elephants, watch them being fed, follow them to the river for playtime and then follow them back up to the park. If the orphanage gets overcrowded, the older elephants are given to Hindu temples for care since they cannot be let back into the wild where they will not be accepted into a strange group. The area outside and across from the orphanage is VERY commercial but there was no pressure for us to purchase anything unless we wanted to. I would highly recommend Tour East, who were very professional and knowledgeable.

My wife and I love elephants and have seen loads in the wild in Kenya. This is different and we went thinking it was for rescued baby or young elephants. I am none the wiser as very little info available. Was upsetting seeing the babies chained up but assumed that stopped them hurting themselves although one or two were doing that repetitive thing. Feeding them was a bit of a money making ritual as they only give them a bottle and if you want to do it they charge you for thirty seconds of doing the same, just enough to get a photo.There are some injured elephants there so I suppose they are being helped although they just seemed to be chained up in one place. Lots of the elephants do seem able to roam about and feed and I guess they are ones that have been previously trained. When the elephants charge over the main road and down to the river is fun and they definitely seem to enjoy that bit with many of them being given a personal scrub. So, if you havn`t seen elephants in the wild this is a good way of getting close up. Obviously there is money involved and the question is " what would happen to these elephants if this place didnt exist ". So I guess I would err on the side of better to have it than not but it is sad as well.

I was so sad when I visited this place. First of all the staff just wants your money and pushes you next to an elephant in chains, grabs your camera from you and takes 2/3 pictures and then shouts "money" to you. Infront of us the hitted the elephants whith sticks and  and the elephants where running from some of them when they came towards them. Handicaped elephants that barley couldnt walk was keept alive, when asked why and if they were given any painkillers they laughed and said "landmine". Later when you are supposed to see the baby elephants... the staff have chained the babys to a wall  3 meters away from each other, they cant barely move at all and the stupid fat tourist are standing there lauging at them and taking pictures. When the elephants went to the river one of the staff members layed a stick over the elephant (that he had used to beat him with)  so he layed there for over 30minutes to afraid to move. DO NOT VISIT .. I cried on the way home.   At the picture I added, look at the elephants legs... one of the legs is dislocated.. the other leg is too short too stand on.

It's just a tourist trap. You're locked up and they only want your money instead of giving you the opportunity to get in touch with the elephants. The staff are not sincere at all. The place is more like a place to train elephants to earn instead of an elephant orphanage.

Very disappointed in this 'orphanage', there was absolutely no information anywhere about the history or conservation efforts of this place. Extremely expensive tourist trap, we have no problem paying that kind of money for a worthy project but this quite clearly seems to be some kind of breeding centre (we saw at least one very obviously pregnant female), potentially providing elephants to the nearby elephant riding centres.

Although it was incredible to see these magnificent creatures up close it was hard to see them in chains although seeing previous Elephant "Sanctuaries" this was by far the best. Just a shame that tourism has made it feel like a bit of a money maker.... I guess we are all guilty of this. The best part for me was when they all got to go for a swim, chain free, it was a sight to behold and one you wouldn't forget! At around £25 its a bargain for what you get to experience, I wouldn't suggest feeding the baby elephants... They look distraught and everyone crowding them makes them agitated.

There's always a slight edge to seeing large animals in captivity and some in chains but the overall experience was great. The babies are chained to keep them from being panicked by the tourists and the bulls are chained to keep them from panicking us. But the sight of the mothers and their calves walking to the river was majestic and I loved the sensation of feeding an elephant as its soft pink mouth took the melon.

This is one of the best place in the entire Sri Lanka to observe natural habitats of elephants. There are so many places in Sri lanka to observe elephants; but to observe natural habitats in a close range pinnawala is the best place in the entire country. If you are visiting Pinnawala do not forget to go in the early morning and to bring children. children loves this place.

My husband and I love elephants and we were so happy to go to the orphanage . When we first got there ( few minutes before the feeding) all tickets for the feeding were already sold and we were really disappointed . We still paid to get in even though we were staying at the elephant park hotel and could see the elephants from our hotel.  After walking in without feeding tickets we first felt like it was not worth it but we soon saw that most tourists leave the orphanage once the feeding is done and the baby elephants are by themselves in their corral. We spent 2 hours but the baby elephants corrals touching them and observing them . It was absolutely fabulous !! We were so happy and felt it was worth every penny !!! What a great experience

On the one hand it is an orphanage and nursery for elephants and the other hand it is a overpriced trap of souvenir trade aimed for tourists. But it seems that Ellys have enough food, care and space to be play, going to bath everyday at 2 p.m so as long as the Ellys are OK - that's fine.

Obviously a sucker trap aimed at tourists with a massive gift and souvenier trade but on the other hand where could you send an orphaned elephant to be looked after. Not a lot of technical info on research or vetinary care. On my trip an elly was killed by a train between Galoya and Trinco, it could have been a mother leaving a youngster. Sadly the leg chains give a bad impression, especially on the very young ones but then stupid tourists cross the security fence to prance in front of the adults ellys in an effort to get their photo taken. One injury to a daft American woman that I witnessed and the elly would suffer. Remember they are highly intelligent creatures and deserve our respect (the ellys not the American). The grazing ground looks far too small for the numbers but they seemed content and well cared for. I would not go again but on balance I'm glad I've been.

This review is the subjective opinion of a Tripadvisor member and not of Tripadvisor LLC. Tripadvisor performs checks on reviews as part of our industry-leading trust & safety standards. Read our transparency report to learn more.

I loved to see the elephants but the place did not feel sincere. It feels that its organized around tourists with a standard routine to keep us amused. The worth for me was to see the feeding of baby elephants which starts by handlers chaining babies who are clearly distressed I just could not stay to watch. I have not seen any evidence of ongoing research or how they re-introduced them back in to the wild. One enclosure had an elephant with a broken leg that heal badly and I did not see that he got any support. This is more of a circus than anything else.

If you have never seen an elephant before then maybe this will be an opportunity that you might just take if you have nothing else to do that day. There was no evidence of rehabilitation, research or anything other than commercial gain from hordes of tourists paying to selectively bottle feed chained up baby elephants.

Having read the reviews we were a little anxious. We did not see ANY ill treatment in the 4 hours we were there. The only animals that were not allowed to roam freely were the 6 or so that were obviously not fit enough to join the herd. One that had lost a leg standing on a land mine, another with a broken leg & one with only one ear. We were told that most of the animals there had been injured either in the war or by angry villagers. There is often confrontation between villagers and elephants as the population increases & therefore the need for more land for crops. Yes, the babies got imapatient when feeding time came around - don't all babies start hollering when they want feeding? We watched them playing & bathing in the river & they appeared to be having a wonderful time. Yes, you do pay extra for bottle feeding etc but imagine how much it must cost to keep a herd of 67 elephants healthy & fed. We can only speak as we found & we had a wonderful day.

Analyzed all the Trip Adviser reviews before we went to Sri Lanka and was unsure as to make the visit to Pinnewela elephant orphanage or not. We did and also visited the site before the orphanage to bathe & ride the elephants. I can only speak as we found. We did not see ANY sign of poor treatment of the elephants during our visit. Yes it is a tourist attraction and you do pay for the privilege but the elephants do look well treated. I met one of the British volunteers who was with us bathing our allocated elephant in the river (resident on site) and she confirmed that the elephants loved to be washed in the river every day. The chains around their legs and feet do look unsightly a bit like taking a dog for a walk .These elephants are no longer wild animals and are kept in captivity with limited freedom. A tourist attraction that may not be for the purist but it was something i will always remember. Elephants are wonderfully animals. Its your choice.

Like many that visit I have mixed feelings about this place.  Like others we witnessed baby elephants straining on chains to get fed and others being prodded and poked by the mahouts.  We saw one in particular that appeared to be getting some pretty rough treatment, it was only after watching for quite some time that we realised they were trying to sedate the elephant (presumably to take it for some form of veterinary treatment) to stop it from standing and possibly falling over as the drug took effect.  I am not trying to defend the place but I guess my point is that we are not always sure what we are witnessing. That said, the reality is that this is no longer functioning as an orphanage but a money making machine now designed to exploit the tourists as well as the elephants.   Given the structure of herd that now lives there it would be much more preferable to see them in a national park and allowed to move freely in their natural habitat.    I give the orphanage itself only one star.  Seeing the elephants go to the river to bathe is not to be missed.   By the way, check your change VERY carefully before stepping away from the ticket booth!

Pinnawala is a great place to see elephants. All the elephants living in this place are abandoned and disabled once. Many elephants are trained and given really good care. Foreigners and other visitors are allowed to touch them, feed them etc.

This place is a business exploiting the elephants. Two generations have been bred here in captivity and it only exists because of tourists. Chains and horrible gaff hooks are used by the keepers to control them. The elephants aren't allowed to roam and have to follow the same routine every day just like a zoo. It is an absolute disgrace and totally hypocritical. Please don't go and support it - I am ashamed to have done so. We went on Safari and saw elephants in their natural habitat which was fantastic.

I am going to strongly put my point across about this place as I am an elephant lover and to see somewhere that is supposed I look after them, put any mystery at all to the elephants makes me mad.they only use the elephants to make money, they do not care about them, chains and the pointy sticks are used, well in my opinion if you have a sanctuary to protect them, those harmfully items should be burned. The only care I see are the visitors. The only good side is when you see them in the river, that's as free as they get, even then they are restricted to where they can go.also do NOT do the elephant ride as that is the Sam thing, I ly they ate treated even worse!

This place has to be seen for the sheer number of elephants found together.  From baby elephants which are less than a month old, one can see giant mature elephants and tuskers. Most are injured elephants which are in the process of recovery or have recovered. Apparently, they are not put to any work.  As is usual in Sri Lanka, the place has been maintained immaculately with lot of greenery around. Visit at 9.30 am is best as one can pay some money, and feed milk to baby elephants at that time. How the babies crave for milk is something worth watching!  At 10.30 am all the elephants are taken to the river bank, which is across the road from elephant compand about half a kilometer away.  At this time, the traffic on the roads is stopped and about sixty elephant lumber along the street and reach the river and leap into the water for bathing. The institution takes sufficient precautions, including use of hand held sirens to provide sufficient warning to the public.  One who visits at other times cannot see these wonderful sights.

Good photo opportunities when the elephants are being washed which happens twice a day, so you need to time the visit right.  The morning session is between 10 and 11.30, but most people come with tour guides so they will know.  There is a bog group of elephants of all ages including some noisy young ones.  You can't ride or touch these elephants so be prepared to be taken to other (quite expensive) places for an elephant ride (uncomfortable) elephant washing, and elephant shower if you don't mind wet clothes afterwards. Good souvenir is elephant poo paper! V environmentally friendly

We have seen animal sanctuaries in various parts of the world where animals have been treated with care and kindness..........but not at this place in Pinnawala! Our first stop was at the baby elephant feeding ring.  The babies were chained and desperate for their milk.  The only ones that got any were those whose milk was paid for by the tourists who wanted to hold the bottle and feed them.  One little elephant (8 months old) was nowhere near the people who paid and had to watch the others have their milk. He was straining on his chain and trumpeting in desperation. Finally he got one bottle compared to nine bottles given to his neighbour. We begged the keepers to give him some milk ( we were nowhere near the kiosk to buy tickets) but they just ignored us and carried on taking the money. Over feeding some babies while others had nothing. Next we went to the restaurant and watched the elephants in the lake.  The keepers hit them with sticks to keep them huddled in a group.  There was no splashing or cooling each other down as elephants do, they just stood subdued, wary of the stick and the keepers. We were in a group of 25 and all were horrified and found the whole experience very distressing.

It's not an Orphanage - they are breeding elephants for making profits. The conditions in which they keep the animals are unacceptable - the misstreatments are obvious - bleeding wounds from the hooks and beatings ... DON'T SUPPORT ANIMAL CRUELTY

We visited the elephant orphanage and I was lucky enough to get to feed a baby elephant. It was nice, but again, very touristy. In hindsight I felt it was something we probably could have dropped from our itinerary. After the feeding time the masses made their way down to restaurants to watch the elephants bathing in the river. It was what it was, it was the equivalent of paying Sheraton prices at the dog on the tuckerbox in Gundagai, but we were happy to cross it off our list and continue down to adams peak.

My experience at Pinnawala actually went some way to changing my views on the elephant tourism industry in Sri Lanka in general. The whole park is not for the elephants' benefit at all, but to attract paying tourists. The elephants are not well treated - some looked malnourished, others were chained in individual cages and most were abused by the mahouts, who welded and were not afraid to use long sticks with hooks at one end and points at the other. A number of elephants had visible wounds from the chains and/or the treatment from mahouts. The baby feeding time, which should have been a great way to get close to the elephants, turned into a shambolic crowd of tourists pushing towards babies chained up behind bars and fed bottle after bottle. They weren't allowed to roam freely and were clearly distressed, crying out and straining against the chains. The only pleasant experience was watching the elephants bathe in the river - skip the orphanage and go for lunch at one of the riverside restaurants. You will get a great view of the whole herd (about 50) of elephants coming down to the river to splash around, bathe and play. Do not visit Pinnawala, you will be supporting mistreatment and are far better off spending your money on visiting one of the national parks, where you can see elephants how they are supposed to be.

Baby Elephants with long nosy trunks following their moms & the herd of large hairy beasts are a cute set of creatures to watch.  The Slow & gentle stroll to the bathing pool & their play in the river is a joy to the eyes & a memory that will stay in my mind for a long time. Fellow travelers to Kandy shouldn't miss this marvel of nature.

It’s a joy to see so many mammals up so close, the place brings one closer to nature, and it leaves one amassed as these giants a so friendly. Must add in your to do list, in Lanka. The Laksala store outside the orphanage is also the best place to stop for souvenirs. They have a wide range of products. Just mentally be prepared as the staff is extremely greedy for constant tips. This unfortunately may put u in bad taste.  But simply prioritizes as pinnawala is all about the elephants.

Our trip started in Negombo, and our next stop was a pineapple farm. On our way to Pinnawala we stopped for a quick round on a elephant, where the animals were treated very badly. Next stop was the Orphanage and we walked around, observed feeding, but enjoyed the bathing ritual at 10:00 the most. The animals are lead from their habitat thru the village off to the river and obviously enjoyed that part the most. So did we! Could have spend more time watching them, but we had to leave for our next stop in the botanical garden in Peradeniya and the tooth temple in Kandy.

I would love to know the qualifications the people who give this place a bad review. Yes the Elephants are quite heavily handled (I wouldn't say cruel like some people on here). . . . but come on.... ITS AN ELEPHANT! It was amazing to see them bathing, was a very nice experience as we sat in a Cafe and watched them after taking some photos. This bit is a MUST SEE and if you only see the orphanage and not this bit, well you are missing out. I mean the ZOO analogy that some people say I can understand. There are something like 70 elephants there. There is quite a large area for them to roam and the ones with tusks are kept separate from the others. The ones that are chained and kept in other areas are ill or being kept there for a reason. We saw one that had been bough in with a broken leg, the work they were doing to help was incredible. The baby feeding was the only time I felt a little uneasy. The idea is great, but these are babies. What happens to your baby when they are hungry and want food? They kick and scream until they are fed. . . . . Yup, you guessed it, elephants do the same.... They were bought into a controlled area, but in the time the workers were organizing all the people these animals were starving and trying to kick off the chains etc. Once they were fed, they were happy!!! I would say go and make your own mind up about this place. Its a must do if you are in the area. If these elephants weren't here, they would be dead... So that put things into perspective for me!

If you are a citizen of SAARC country, please carry your passport to avail the discount applicable. If you have never seen a lot of elephants at one single place, you will be happy to see many elephants here. BUT - Please note that this is an ORPHANAGE. Just like a human orphanage, no one comes here willingly or by choice. These elephants have been rescued from compromised or difficult situations; they couldn't have survived by themselves in the wild. Every elephant has a tragic or unhappy story behind him/ her. So please don't expect very healthy elephants with huge tusks and all, playing happily, eating and bathing at will. Just like a human orphanage, elephants have to follow a daily routine of eating and bathing at specific time. Normally they wouldn't have done so had they been fortunate enough to live in the wild. It's nice to see so many elephants having a bath and meals. But it's very sad to see baby elephants chained to pillars at the time of bottle feeding. Poor little innocent ones get scared with so many people around them. I really appreciate the effort put in by all the people managing the orphanage, but I think those babies should be set free instead of tying chain to their leg. I humbly request all those who visit to not bother the elephants, or crowd and stare at them or make noise. Just put yourself in their position and ask yourself how you would feel if someone did the same to you? If nothing, at least pray for the well being of the elephants.

The orphanage is more like a zoo and the baby elephant feeding is terrible. We went into the orphanage and were able to pet the elephants which was kind of interesting but the whole experience was not very good. We did cross the road to where the elephants are taken to bath twice a day. This was an awesome experience, we had lunch and watched the elephants roam around the river. You want to get there before the baby elephant feeding is done so you can secure a seat on the balcony.

There are far too many elephants crammed into a tiny space. They are not rescued elephants but they are breeding, which they are not supposed to do. The staff are unhelpful and misleading and treat the elephants with careless aggression. The elephants seem unhappy and unhealthy. It felt like a business, and cruel. The place next door, same side of the road but further on, is much nicer. Only a few elephants but some serious education and conservation going on. We arrived wanting to bottle feed the baby elephants ( a bit misguided) and we knew the times for feeding. Due to very heavy traffic (Saturday) we arrived 5 minutes after the start time. We asked the ticket seller if we could definitely feed the babies even though we had missed the start and we were told yes. We explained that was the main purpose of our visit. We paid a lot of rupees to get in 20,000. We hastened to the feeding area to be told  'no, you cant feed them, you are too late.'  We explained that we had come especially and the traffic from Kandy had been terrible but there was no room for negotiation. We returned to the man who had sold the ticket to ask for a refund - no go there, and then remonstrated with the manager, who said we would have to go to the head office in Colombo (not really an option). We had heard from local Sri Lankans and tourists, and read in the guide book, that this outfit is not meeting standards, and having experienced it first hand I definitely would avoid it.  My 24 year old daughter was so upset by seeing the elephants treated this way that she cried for an hour afterwards.

I love elephants. Visit the orphanage where they are being trained and fed with huge baby bottles, again some chains are off putting but required for training. sad to see the disabled elephant who lost legs in a bomb now deformed as weight all transferred to back legs.after feeding the elephants all cross the main road , traffic stops and they travel doe to the river for leisure time. we sat on the verandah of the elephant park hotel for a drink amazing views.

Elephants are my Favourite animal and while it is not ideal for the elephants to be seen in this enviroment, It should be remembered that is an Orphanage and Rescue Centre. Most of these magnificent animals have been rescued due to serious injury many from land-mines during the many years of war or "gone rogue" killing/injuring Villagers. Some are also there for rehab after years of hard work and possible mistreatment. whilst some people may consider Pinawala to be a tourist trap they should also realise that it is expensive to care for these animals and that all Donations/entry fees go to thier care and the businesses/tourist stalls at Pinawala are paying rent which also go to the running of tis magnificent place. Is it better to just let them suffer and die??

If you want to see elephants - do a safari - we did 2 and saw lots of herds of wild elephants. This place claims to be looking after injured elephants - there is an old one there with half a leg and an other broken leg - its chained up and leaning on a post and cannot move - Its very distressing to see an animal suffer like this . We went to the shop over the road and bought a photo album made from the dung - we were assured we could bring it back in to Australia - when we declared it it was confiscated - $80 for an album that we no longer have ! All in all - a big tourist trap

I would give this zero rating if Tripadvisor allowed me. Do not support this horrible institution and go and see the elephants in the wild instead. We saw people feeding the elephants when there were signs saying don't.  Then the elephant is punished. There was NO information on any good activities here re saving elephants. From what I could see, these elephants are in the equivalent of a circuis. The place is a disorganised zoo. There were lots of other issues here that I won't go into. I will simply say avoid it

This place is an absolute must ! You can not leave Sri Laka with out visiting this park. It is actually an elephant sanctuary or orphanage, so the animals aren't help captive like in zoos. They're cared for and looked after, and you can experience an incredible life experience : elephant riding (extra payment). You can also feed baby elephants (extra payment).

It would be hard to go to SL and not see elephants, and I suspect this is the 'least worse' place (except for guided trips in national parks). Having said that, I still feel very uncomfortable with the treatment of the elephants. Many had clearly been chained up all day on a small patch of concrete with a few leaves around, whilst the others were paraded around in chains. We were there for feeding time, at which point the baby elephants looked like there were going to seriously hurt themselves trying to get out of the chains around their legs, and a number looked fairly distressed (though I'm hardly an elephant expert). There must of been about 50 elephants there, and it was a bit hard to believe they were all orphans. Considering the cost of entrance, the time to get there from Kandy, and the treatment of the elephants I would find it hard to recommend.

Visited during bathing in river. Elephants 50+ seemed quite relaxed in the river bathing session and playing. Coffee on the patio with a very serene and picturesque background. Mahouts were keeping them in check with mostly verbal commands. No rides or tricks which seems like the most humane treatment of elephants we have seen anywhere. $25US admission seems steep but if most of it goes to the care of the animals seems worth it.  Travelled from Columbo 2 + hrs enroute to Habarana.

I had the impression that the elephants in the orphanage would be able to live as close to a natural life as possible. But I was so wrong, these poor elephants a forced around by the care takers. They cant walk around freely and have to stay within a very small perimeter. The elephants have to role their trunks for tourists who wants to take photos or standing in a chain inside a circus lookalike arena while tourist can pay to feed them. I feel so disappointed!!  Its nothing better than circus tricks in a elephant zoo.

I visited here 20 years ago & it will always be one of the best days of my life, the elephants were happy & well cared for & we had no hassle from the staff at all. I can't believe the reviews I have just read & how much it appears to have changed. I have always said I would take my children there - maybe not now - based on what i have read. How sad! I have rated this as excellent which it was back then & had to put the date as Jan 2014 - although it was Nov 1994 when I was there!!

This was the highlight of my cruise on Voyager having sailed to Dubai, then five ports in India ending up in Sri Lanka. The weather was hot and humid but the views of these mostly unshackled great big animals being led down a street to bathe in the river was awesome.  The sight of the 3 legged elephant in the hospital wing coping with his disability, and the orphaned babies making one hell of a noise at feeding time - truly a day not to be missed if you are in this vicinity.

2nd visit here and could not believe what I was seeing and how different it was from the 1st time. the elephants were treated poorly at times. The elephants were trying to climb the banks of the river to get away from the sticks which the keepers were pokeing them with - I would never advise anyone to go. This time we went to watch the elephants by the river and did not go into the orphanage as other guests were saying how awful it was. These elephants need help to let them live a happy life.

Echo all previous comments on cruelty ... purely a money making mafia including all of the nearby elephant riding places..the elephant handlers are only interested in aggressively extracting tips even though you have paid the entrance fee... how the government has not closed this down o have no idea... they mush be taking some big backhander s to allow it

My fiancée and I went go the orphanage because we support the cause for providing refuge for abandoned and injured elephants. However, we were quite shocked to see how poorly the elephants were treated at times. When we arrived, we saw a beautiful herd of elephants grazing on copious amounts of food in a large open space together. They seemed content and stress free. We can see that a good amount off the tourist tariff goes to feeding the large mammals their greens and providing milk for the babies. If you do not support animal cutely then DON'T bottle feed the baby elephants. At the time, they had 5 baby elephants chained in a circular concrete terrace waiting to be bottle fed. They were screaming and pulling very hard on their chained foot to the point that they were extremely frustrated and could possibly hurt themselves. It was difficult to watch tourist buy a bottles while the elephants were in such disarray. We also witnessed a few trainers beating an elephant with their pointy sticks. We were told that this particular elephant had lost a part of it's leg from an exploded land mine and was rehabilitating. However, constant screaming and beating this poor elephant for over 15 minutes to the point that it was angry, could no longer walk and used a wooden fence and it's trunk to support itself is CRUEL!!!! I was in tears....and in disbelief. I am aware that they are trying to help the animals rehabilitate but there must be more humane ways of doing so. It was truly heart breaking... The only good part of the orphanage was the elephant bathing. At 10am, the trainers herded a large number of elephants to the river where they got to bathe and enjoy the river for 2 hours. The trainers would wash a few elephants with coconut husks and you could tell that the elephants enjoyed it. We strongly feel that this elephant orphanage should be inspected by animal rights. The orphanage is a great cause but the methods need to change immediately. It's hard to say not to visit this orphanage because without the tourist monetary contributions ... The conditions would worsen and the health of the elephants would beat high risk.... Animal rights specialists need to step in.

We were SHOCKED by the treatment the animals received here. Our driver warned us that this was "touristy" but we needed a break during the long drive and love elephants.  We  witnessed the cruelty described in previous posts, where animals were whacked with pronged posts. I hope that animal rights groups discover this scandal and get in there to save the animals. I was in tears when we left.

An hour and a half by taxi from Kandy, it was not worth risking your life on the crazy roads with the suicidal drivers. I didn't appreciate the keepers who urge you to have your photos taken with the elephants and then demand a tip even though you had just paid a special tourist tariff to get in.  I also didn't like how the baby elephants were tied up on short chains, in obviously distress watched by a curious mob. However, there is a road opposite the orphanage where at end of it is a river where you can chill at a restaurant and watch the elephants bathe.  You do need a ticket to access this road. This was by far the best part of the trip.

I went here 15 years or so ago and it was then a place where orphaned elephants are helped and fed and looked after. Larger elephants were fed greenery and we were able to watch them being fed, if they wanted to wander off they could. The babies were fed by tourists in a coral of metal barriers, from bottles which the tourists paid a small sum to be able to give them. The babies were not restricted in any way and were treated kindly. The milk was mixed beforehand and was put in the bottles ready, these bottles were then brought out all at the same time and the tourists (yep! - I was one of them) were safely behind the barriers awaiting the rush of babies, who were let in en-mass. Each baby made a beeline for the nearest tourist and they all got fed. It doesn't happen like that now? The babies are chained up, each one by a back leg, to a large metal ring, which is stuck into the middle of the floor in the middle of the circle of steel barriers. The poor baby elephants are then frantically tugging at the chains whilst the dopey keepers decant the milk into the bottles in front of them, driving them crazy. Then the tourists are wheeled in and positioned in front of a desperately stretching baby elephant. The tourists are then schooled in how to give the milk and ONLY THEN  are the babies fed. Surely this needs better organisation? OK you need to make money to run the place and this is a good hands-on way to do it, but surely there is a better way than the way they feed them now? We saw the larger elephants being herded into a bunch, so that the tourists can see them eating the greenery. They animals were not permitted to wander around and I witnessed three elephants (two quite young and one about 6-7) being beaten back into the group with a pike. The keeper (I use the word loosely to describe the young idiot doing the beating and who was entrusted with the animals welfare) ran after them and chased them back into position swinging the long pole with a steel hooked spike on, which he also jabbed sharply into the flanks of the animals. There were also several smaller baby elephants with long chains around a back leg, which were obviously causing them distress. THEY SEND HOARDS OF SRI LANKAN SCHOOL KIDS HERE ON EDUCATIONAL TRIPS - WHY? TO WITNESS CRUELTY? I also understand that the 'orphanage' is allowing a captive breeding programme, in order to have enough babies to keep the money flowing - surely this is totally against what the 'orphanage' is there for in the first place? In my opinion the following is true: Is it run for the benefit of the elephants - NO Is it run as a money making venture for profit - YES Would I go there again - NO Should it be inspected by under-cover animal welfare bodies - YES YES YES Should it be forced to change its cruel practices - YES Would I recommend you go there as it is now - NO NO NO NO NO - DON'T GO

I'm not an elephant expert, but hitting an elephant with a metal-pointed stick so that it screams and pees itself is not what you should see in an elephant orphanage!... and that was just one of many (bad) impressions we've had going there. I WOULD HIGHLY NOT RECOMMEND GOING THERE!!

Difficult, on the one hand it was great to see so many elephants and so many different age groups and to see them being looked after. In a way, this is a must see, in another, be prepared to have your heart tugged at. Would recommended the river bathing, quite impressive and certainly a little more palatable.

We visited this place on 15th Nov, 2013 and if any one wants to see a huge number of elephants at one place ( available in a all sizes, shapes and age), this is the only place. If you visit any elephant safari places, ( in Thekkady or Kabini in South India or Amboseli in Kenya), you can see only few or a small group of 7 to 10. This place is amazing! We watched these elephants very up and close for about an hour and finally, the mahouts assembled the entire group and lead them to their sanctuary at 1 pm. This elephant march across the lane and crossing a busy street was the highlight of this place!

I beleive the elephants here a very well looked after my only dissappointment was that when I last visited 18 years ago it was far less commercial and you could feel the babys for free, the admission is now £10 plus extra to feed, I do not begrudge this admission but feel the commercialism is spoiling it. If you want to see elephants up and close, this is the place to be. We stopped at the place on our way from Colombo to Kandy. Though there are a lot of elephants in the park, the best part are the baby elephants. For a nominal amount they even let you feed them which is pretty cool. The place opens around 9 and two hours is more than enough for the place. Would definitely recommend this place to everyone.

absolutely wonderful experience.  I love elephants and it was great to see them and understand what the orphanage does for the elephants.  I saw a number of babies that had been born there as well as one elephant that had his leg injured due to a landmine from the war.  It was heartbreaking to see him but at least he is being taken care of versus just dying in the wild. we went down to the river to see about 30 elephants in the water.  Unbelievable sight - like nothing i've ever seen which is why i came to Sri Lanka.  A must see experience in my opinion! You will see the elephants chained on one leg when they are up at the orphanage eating  - so they do not run wild but you have to also remember that these are orphaned wild animals.  If they were not being cared for by the orphanage here (and that is what the fee is for), they would have been killed in the wild. It is sad that they do not have the place to roam free as they did many years ago - as humans encroach on their habitat but you have to put yourself in the place of a local and not think about it from your own country's perspective (unless you happen to have elephants in your back yard already).  It is not the best scenario for these animals, just like so many others but at least they are being taken care of and can live hopefully a happy long life.

I love elephants and being from Ireland seeing them was amazing...in Yala Park they are free and it is fantastic. In Pinnawala the elephants looked sad, probably because the place is less focused on conservation and more focused on profit. The baby elephants were hurting their legs because they were desperately trying to get free from the chains around their legs. some of the elephants roared out when they were chained up and surrounded by tourists (I don't blame them!) When they roared the tourists LAUGHED. I know the Orphanage MUST be doing some conservation work, one elephant was getting it's leg treated but it all seems overshadowed by chained up elephants being used to get money off tourists. I asked our guide 'how come the elephants have no tusks?'. He wouldn't answer but showed me one elephant (male) chained up at the back of the orphanage with huge tusks and said that he was very dangerous. The poor elephant looked miserable. As they were 'bathing' an elephant we walked up to the little pool. They wanted to charge 1,000 rupees to 'wash' the elephant. The elephant was chained down with the elephant hook left on top of the poor creatures head. The elephant kept on throwing the hook away with its trunk and looked distressed. On the way to the 'orphanage' there were several elephants chained up along the road with signs reading 'elephant rides' beside them. They looked MISERABLE. I love Sri Lanka and the wildlife but as an animal lover I cannot help but feel like this is cruel and these majestic and beautiful animals are being used and exploited for profit. The baby elephant feeding (which I imagined would be magical and an amazing experience) was shocking with the baby elephants screaming and pulling at their chains while tourists had to show their purchased tickets to feed the elephant a bottle while grinning idiotically at a camera.....animal rights? set these creatures free :(

The entrance fee is 2500 rupees per person which is a total rip off to begin with... After you pay you get to see chained up elephants that get beaten and shouted at by the so called "trainers". I loved seeing the elephants! They are so gentle, and having the opportunity to feed two, you can see their eyes are so gentle and knowing. It's apparent that they are very comfortable with people although you recognise they're still wild animals. Also, it was really wonderful to watch them enjoy their time in the river! Watching the baby elephants play and dive, swimming around the adults and pulling on their tails, it was like watching children at the park. The only negative was seeing the chains they use on the animals - but it looks as though overall they're well cared for. While I didn't buy any, I was actually impressed with the ingenuity of using the elephant dung to make paper :)...

It was lovely to see the elephants being cared for, fed, watered and generally enjoying themselves. We then followed them to the river. Whilst we waited, my brother in law was hassled by a "palm reader" who failed to introduce himself as such, then demanded money. A little later, I was asked to come and stroke one of the elephants while it bathed, then charged 4000 rupees (about £20\30 USD) for the privilege of having my picture taken using my camera.
