I visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage with my Sri Lankan friends in April,2013.I was astonished to see how well these majestic animals who had been orphaned or abandoned were being looked after in this elephant orphange.It is beautiful to see how these elephants were taken in the procession to the near by river for bathing and how they are fed and looked after with love and care.It is a must visit for the young,old and the children to Man ,Elephant and Nature in perfect harmony.

Great seeing the elephants up close, and i would definitely recommend feeding one of the adult elephants, but be aware of the guys who work there letting you touch the elephants... They will demand money after wards. Just do NOT give them your camera to take a picture of you, some people apparently then have it taken ransom! Lovely seeing the elephants bathing!

Wow - we left our resort at 06.30 in the morning to make sure that we reached the Elephant Orphanage in good time for feeding.  It was extremely busy but we were lucky enough that our guide had already pre-booked tickets so we were able to progress straight through (there is also a separate queue to tourists).  The baby elephants being fed were very cute and it was also good to see how the centre cares for disabled elephants as well.  There was plenty of room for the elephants to roam and they seemed very contented.  We got really close to elephants of all ages and got some amazing photos as memories.  Mid morning the elephants walk through town to refresh and play in the river (quire surreal) - i think this is the part of the day that the elephants love the most! There are some great viewing spots and the whole experience was well worth the early start.

I have always loved elephants and wanted to volunteer at Pinnawala Elephant orphanage. If you look around, there are many companies that offer accommodation including access to the orphanage which gives you hands on experience with the elephants. I am sad to say i was a bit disheartened with the whole experience. I understand that Sri Lanka needs income from the tourists but feel the advertising for the orphanage was misleading. The elephants we were allowed to get in to contact with, the mahouts expected money for allowing you to stroke them and feed them and myself and another volunteer did see levels of neglect. The worst experience however was the actual "co ordinator". He was a very unprofessional man who offered us drugs on the first day, showed a lot of anger, sexual harrassment to another volunteer and was drunk every evening -i would warn anyone- especially a female to sign up with this guy. I should have gone with a more reputable company like i originally planned. Sadly i opted for his "company" because he was much much cheaper- i guess you get what you pay for. I will say there ARE better companies to go with that have had better feedback, so i would recommend NOT to opt for a cheaper Sri Lankan based company like i did,. I am unable to say the person's name, but it is one man running it and he has a blog spot, not a website, so please be vigilant. The country of Sri Lanka was nice however and  i would recommend people to go there- and the orphanage, but sadly this guy has put me off the whole experience,

I had read very mixed reviews about Pinnawala before visiting Sri Lanka, however, I would definitely recommend a visit. Don't bother paying to bottle feed a baby elephant - certainly the worst (and only negative) aspect of the day! Other than the bottle feeding of the baby elephants who were all chained to the floor, the rest of the visit was very pleasant.  The elephants all look content and well cared for, and have plenty of natural space to roam around in.  Mid-morning they let them all walk down to the local river where you can see them splashing around and enjoying themselves! There were a few elephants with chains but generally large males for safety reasons.

What a wonderful place. Elephants of all ages that have been abandoned or orphaned, there are also some that were injured by the mines left by the Tamal Tigers which is heart renching.  I got to feed milk to one of the babies which was over as quick as it began but worth it & afterwards we walked down to watch them having a bath in the river which was brilliant. Highly recommended.

The elephant orphanage is a wonderful place where the abandoned baby elephants are brought in, nursed and then released back into the wild after a few yrs. Having seen elephants from a young age in every zoo and wild life sanctuary in India, I was curious to see if pinnewala would still excite me. It definitely lived up to my expectations. There were several elephants walking on the road, bathing in the river and we could sit back have our lunch and watch play around with each other. It was fun seeing them push each other around playfully and try and race with other in the wild. It was also nice to see that they were consciously doing their bit for the environment and the elephant dung was being recycled as toilet paper. There were also a number of small shops which had great genuine leather bags for one third the cost when compared to the airport. Definitely a great buy, but you would need to bargain to get a good price or you would end up paying as much as you would for it at the airport. There is also an option to go on an elephant ride and bathe them, but I chose not to do that as it was too hot and I preferred sitting in the shade. But if you are up to it, it might be a great option as well.

A site of about hundred elephants bathing on a rocky river, with lush green pastures and hills around , tends to make you an artist and a poet. We all have drawn such pictures as a kid. It is a dream come true. The naughty babies are a source of delight for all ages.

Visited the Elephant orphanage, on way to Kandy. The road is one way and narrow but luckily not much traffic. The sanctuary itself is a nice place with lots of elephants of all ages which can be seen in quite a proximity. It gives an impression of on-foot safari. Babies were being fed with bottles whereas one gets opportunity to feed a grown elephant. General condition of the animals was quite good. Entry tickets for SAARC countries was half the normal price. There is a nice souvenir shop too. Bought some fridge magnets and t-shirts.

Housing the largest captive herd in the world, Pinnawala is located in Kegalle  about 90 kms from Colombo, an orphanage for the wounded and abandoned elephants. My best friend drove us down winding roads thick with vegetation. The orphanage is a tourist attraction . There is an entry fee, tourists can watch elephant feeding, bottle feeding of the calves and bathing in the Oya river. One can find disabled elephants well looked after. The entry fee is utilised for elephant care.There are various tourist shops en route to the river, selling Elephant Poo paper, leather bags, etc.

be ready to experience elephants at really close quarters and, if you can spare some cash, you can touch, bathe and ride them. Go here only for the elephants and nothing else. If you go by tuk tuk or a paid taxi, you will have a few halts for the spice gardens before it. I returned with mixed feelings. This is an orphanage where the elephants are looked after by having to work their way through. Not so bad, when there is only a very dark alternative.

I went there last summer. I had read that the workers are "animal lovers", that they actually take care of elephant orphans, and that they release them in the wild when they're 5 years old. It was the whole opposite. Those elephants are took away from their parents, and some actually got old but they're still there. They're chained, they're forced to move forward by using dangerous sticks... It's expensive and tourists can't even come close! It was just a horrible show... especially when cute baby orphans try to wander a bit, just to get beaten by some worker in order to come back. It's just a commercial place, nothing related to animal loving. DO NOT GO, do not support these animal abusers.

Visited this orphanage with mixed feelings after reading some reviews but elephants seemed happy and healthy. They were wandering around a large area freely . They also had a paddle in the river which they seemed to enjoy. Baby elephants were fed with bottle but only a few tickets available each day. All on all worth a visit if you want to see elephants.

We took an elephant ride but did not want the water sprayed as it did not look very hygienic . You can sit beside the river and watch the elephants bathing and spraying riders. It was fun to see them drinking water and playing. Apart from this the place had nothing to offer and seemed overpriced.

This place was basically to see elephants closer than you usually would in city zoos and such. I was able to take a ride on an elephant who also went into a river and sprayed us with water as part of the ride which was extra when paid for. Nice to watch the elephants take a bath in a large river area and be right next to them on the rocks as they did. I was also able to feed the elephants fruits which were bought. Entrance fee is 2500 ruppees for foreigners, and no explanations of how the park is run or why its run and so on. I did not like the fact that the elephants where chained/shackled and that the trainers used barbed sticks to keep them in line. I feel the elephants were not handled with enough care.

We were lucky enough to arrive here when the elephants were down having a bath in the local river. There are about 90 elephants in the orphanage from babies upwards. Down at the river we had morning tea as we watched these incredible animals playing in the water (just like human children), and just standing around gossiping (just like human adults). Time's up, and they all very obediently filed up through the market place (most of the windows had temporary metal shutters up while the elephants went past), and back to the orphanage to be fed. We were able (for a small fee) to feed them and be photographed with them. These are elephants that have been found abandoned or orphaned as babies in the wild. They are not returned to the wild but are cared for, fed and trained by the wild life authorities.

We all loved this visit. You see the herd behind the boulders and in the river which was enchanting to see. The cute baby elephants are chained but as well as being cute they are heavy. My daughter fed one of the elephants which she enjoyed because she felt safe. These animals are orphaned and need to be fed though I do realise this is a way to raise money or maybe pay for the bottle of milk that you feed the orphaned elephant. I think its worth remembering that they would die in the wild ortherwise. They also bring in from the wild adult males who have tusks so that the poachers don't kill them, an elderly elephant who is chained was one such elephant. I find it more alarming that there are some other elephant riding places between the orphanage and the Millenium Elephant Sanctuary on relatively small pieces of land.

This is no more an orphanage than a kitten tied to a stick and pelted with stones is an orphanage. Foreigners pay 2500 rupees to get into this exhibit and Sri Lankans 100. Neither gets any explanation of the work of the orphanage, the need for such work or how the orphanage is investing our 2500 rupees into bettering the lives of the elephants in its care. As you walk around, you start to realise why - there is no focus on education or familiarisation at all - and no evidence of any focus on animal welfare whatsoever. This is spectacle, not conservation at work. It's actually mildly revolting. The animals are chained, some exhibiting clear locked-in syndrome behaviour. The 'mahouts' control the animals using barbed pikes. You can feed a (unhealthily fat-looking) elephant a bowl of fruit for a fee and have your photo taken. You can watch others eating leaves as they wander about in puddles of their own faeces in concrete pens. There's no clear signage. There's a shop you have to exit through. Crossing the road, you can watch the elephants bathing. This daily spectacle is best viewed from two restaurants with balconies overlooking the river. The elephants enjoy the water. Two of the elephants are encouraged - in front of the more expensive hotel balcony - to immerse themselves. This is achieved with pokes and scratches from the mahout's pike. It's all heart-warming stuff: the exploitation of animals for tourists gawping from perches in concession-paying outlets reached through an alleyway of tourist trap hucksters pushing 'elephant poo paper' and various other knick knacks. Government-run, you do wonder if this is not some strange microcosm of Sri Lankan governance, but this is the route to acute depression, so it's time to move on and never return.

Do not go here! This orphanage is not an orphanage but a glorified zoo. The elephants are not all rescued but born there. The handlers whip and poke the elephants with metal tipped sticks. Many of the elephants we saw wore heavy chains. This was a very sad and overpriced operation.

We went despite the negative reviews as it is "on the list". We wish we had not. If you want your elephants as chained exhibits then you will not be disappointed. This is more like a petting zoo. Granted baby elephants are cute but if you have to chain them front right foot and back left foot so that paying punters can hold a bottle of milk and have their picture taken feeding them then to me this seems wrong. I am sure this is all for the safety of the public or some such but that misses the point. The public should not be there in the first place. If you want to see these beautiful creatures there are parks in Sri Lanka where they have more freedom to roam. Go there, not here. To be fair there is an open area where the elephants can roam without much interference, when they are not being exhibit of the day, but it does not make up for the other part in my book.

Having read some very mixed reviews on the elephant orphanage we decided that we had to see it first hand and draw our own conclusions, and having done so it is well worth the trip and to support such a venture which looks after animals that cannot fend for themselves. What people need to realise is that this place is probably the only option for orphaned elephants to survive, and the centre is doing an excellent job to ensure they do. Yes, some elephants are chained up, but this is for their own safety and that of the general public who want to get up close and personal, which in most cases would spook the gentlest of the great beasts. Do not miss the bathing of the elephants in the local river as this is a sight to behold where a large herd travels down the narrow tourist lined street to wallow in the running waters. Tourists do pay a lot more for the privilege but hey, we do earn a lot more than the locals, and why should they be priced out of their own natural wonders.

A difficult place to review.....not sure if it is totally for tourists, as others have said chained up baby elephants for feeding etc. On the other hand the elephants seemed to enjoy their time in the river which was enchanting to see. Have to admit to being upset at the baby elephant feeding time.....

Amazing place. A must see if you are visiting Sri Lanka. Lots of elephants. You get to feed them, watch them bathe and you also get to see a couple of babies. Sad to see some of them chained but that's what happens if you really want to be up close and personal with them.

Our visit to Pinnawalla Elephant Orphanage was very distressing. The emphasis is on cruel exploitation to make money from tourists, NOT on elephant conservation. Some of the animals are chained and many appear distressed. The handlers use sharp spikes to herd elephants. Some elephants are forced to lie in the water so handlers can make extra money by inviting tourists to ‘wash’ them. The tusked elephant was constantly engaging in repetitive movements—probably a sign that he was stressed and bored. We strongly suggest you give this cruel and inhumane tourist attraction a big miss and take a jeep safari in a national park instead to see wild elephants.

This is animal exploitation. Be aware that you will encounter young, frightened elephants rooted to the spot by chains in order to give visitors the privilege of 'feeding the orphans' (which is a 3 second experience). The animals are terrified of the stick wielding guards who take every opportunity to trick the guests into handing over more money. The place is run in an unethical manner, it is unworthy of its orphanage name, it is dangerous and exists for one reason only - the exploitation of innocent animals and gullible visitors. My advice - stay away!

I witnessed one mahout punching the lead elephant in the trunk repeatedly to try and get her to turn away from a calf so he could make the calf hurry up across the road. The last elephants in the road crossing were also hit with the ankus to get them to move which was distressing the calf's. The elephants were crossing from the river back into the main "orphanage" but they were not wet so I assume they were not allowed to bathe properly. Also the elephants tail hair is plucked to make bracelets which is not on.

Visited this as part of our 17-day Bunnik Tours. We stopped for lunch at a hotel that overlooked the river and it was here that we were able to watch the elephants enjoying themselves in the water. They were then recalled back to the Elephant Orphanage compound by 3 blasts on a bull horn. After lunch we walked across to the Elephant Orphanage and . . . watched as 3 baby elephants were chained up so that the tourists could feed them! The youngest was so distressed it shate everywhere. The oldest of the 3 was continually trying to break its chain so that it could reach the greenery that had been left on the ground just beyond its reach!?! Because the monks have said that they can't kill any of the elephants, and these live for 70-odd years . . . there is one there that has a leg shorter than the other because of stepping on a land mine, consequently its back is hunched and the adjacent left is severely bowed to compensate! You could pay extra Rupees and feed the pregnant elephant; we didn't. If you walked up to the top of the hill you were then able to view the herd of over 80-odd elephants. Off to the far left was an elephant, and several others, continually swaying, the effect of an environment that does not challenge them to keep active or where there is a lack of stimuli. Off to the right, slightly behind where you would be standing was an elephant chained up, something which should only occur for no more than 4 hours / day. Overall the experience was unsettling, yet on the other hand where else or what else can they do . . .

I worked 5 minute on another an elephant safari, part of the Pinnawala orphanage group for three weeks. I visited the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage a few times during my trip and it was wonderful! To see all the elephants together, then walking with them to the water and watching them in the water! It was amazing! You can also feed a baby elephant for 250 rupees! (£1.25!) If you visit here you should also visit the tea factory just down the road!! Good for the whole family! I imagine the hotel looking over these beautiful creatures is good also, although they are only in the water twice a day.

This review is the subjective opinion of a Tripadvisor member and not of Tripadvisor LLC. Tripadvisor performs checks on reviews as part of our industry-leading trust & safety standards. Read our transparency report to learn more.

My husband and I went to pinnawala elephant orphanage in march 2013 .. We feel its all about having a good guide from your hotel as they seem more respected by staff. We were able to get in the water with a female elephant and we bathed her as she lay there!! It brought tears to my eyes.we then rode her through the grounds and I was lucky enough to feed a baby with its bottle!!! We then followed them down to the river on their daily walk all I can say is WOW!! Tipping is very effective and this can depend how close you get to the animals and the staff there deserve every penny... If you love animals this is a fabulous and wonderful experience which I would repeat every day if I could.

We visited this elephant orphanage as we had our 6 and 8 year old girls travelling with us.  We found the whole experience depressing.  There are a few elephants in chains. We felt comfortable about this when a man explained it was because they were working elephants.  Then another man told us it was because the elephants were 'frisky' males.  With two different explanations we decided neither was probably true and that they are chained because they are perhaps a bit aggressive. The elephants were swaying and didn't look happy.   The cost was 2000 per adult and 1000 per child. I recommend if you come here that you take the option of having a soft drink at one of the two cafes along the river to stop people constantly asking if you need a guide, bananas (which you can't feed the elephants) or generally trying to sell you something.  We left this place feeling a tad sad for the elephants.    We didn't use a guide and used the excuse we were meeting up with friends.

I visited Pinnawela because, me and my family are animal lovers and we thought it might be nice to see the elephant herd. Sadly i was very disappointed, the elephants were chained both front leg and back leg, even the baby elephants. They looked very unhappy and always tried to walk which was unable for them because of the chains. The bottle feeding was terrible, i thought a small group of people would be allowed to pet the babys and feed them. Instead hundreds of people surrounded the chained baby elephants desperately trying to hold the bottle once , to get a picture, this was repeated every 2 seconds. The baby elephants also roared because they were so uncomfortable with all the people looking. I do not recommend Pinnawela, its just a place for commercial and mass tourism, if you really are a elephant lover and want to see them in peace and quiet visit some tempels they have their own elephants, or the national parks.

A wonderful place to go and enjoy as an ecotourism attraction. We enjoyed seeing the elephants. I shared details (pros and cons) and pictures here http://www.createwithmom.com/2013/09/all-about-elephants-at-pinnawala.html I hope the orphanage will keep caring for the animals and keep its motive to care for the elephants rather than a way to make money.

One of the reasons we visited Sri Lanka was for the elephants. I enjoyed the visit but question the way the elephants are treated. I feel they have been commercialised too much. We followed the elephants down to the river and my husband was lucky enough to go into the river with the Mahoots (fully clothed I would add) and wash one of the tucked working elephants. The river scene is so much nicer as they are free to do what they should be doing. Overall enjoyable but a little sad.

On the whole we enoyed Pinnawala, they have a large number of elephants of all ages and it's amazing how close you are able to get to them. A few of the elephants are in chains, as previous reviewers have stated, but we didn't get the impression that the elephants were especially distressed by it.  The mahoots can be quite strict with the elephants, too, but in both these examples it seem largely to ensure the safety of those visiting the orphanage - it's a bit of a no-win situation as if people weren't in it wouldn't be necessary, but without visitors the orphanage wouldn't exist... Only thing to warn about is that some of the staff will allow you to have your photos taken with the elephants, but there is an expectation that you pay them for the privilege.

Visited the elephant orphanage,and found it a terrible sight! Baby elephants chained (both legs) while the mahoots try to make you pay to feed the baby's,seems like they don't get fed unless you pay the extra to feed them!! I had to leave as I thought this place would be doing good things for poorly/injured elephants. But it wasn't!! Absolutely disgusted with this place do not visit unless you don't care for the welfare of animals!! Go look at them in the wild it's a lot better!!

impressive facility for elephants' care. The staff is dedicated and friendly on the whole; however, elephant attendants expect gratification for letting you touch or have a pic with elephants & my advice is not to disappoint them. It is a good educational ground for kids. Please, do not forget to wear a hat or carry an umbrella & water during the visit.

At the nursery they introduce you to their program of protecting the injured elephants,and are given a chance to feed them. You get to see real giant ones and the view of all of them coming to the river for a dip is something worthwhile. The highlight of our visit there was the ride on the giant, never knew they were so tall. That part was the best. Some shopping and restaurants are there. A different experience but nice one!

I've spent a few minutes reading other reviews of this place and can see reviews fall into one of two camps. We are quite firmly in the terrible camp. The place was strange and Disney-like to us. Clearly it was well set up etc but there is a huge number of elephants and no explanation of any conservation work done by the organisation. We were not told the history of the so-called orphaned elephants and this was of the reasons that we concluded that there was probably not many orphans. There was one elephant who had apparently trodden on a land mine but the poor thing was so badly injured that you have to question whether it would be kinder to put him down. We didn't stay for the feeding - to the absolute despair of our drive - and instead we beat the crowds and went to lunch over looking the river. I have to admit it was a joy to watch all the elephants come down and bathe in the river but after a while we did find ourselves rooting for them to make their escape. I would say if you have never seen a wild elephant before - which my partner had not - then maybe this would be worth a visit, however, afterwards you'll feel slightly grubby and ashamed about the whole thing. One final thing, we did go shopping along the Main Street down to the river. Elephant poo paper shop is a delight and all of the shop keepers were well behaved and not at all pushy.

If you like and enjoy animals is the perfect place to go. Besides the opportunity to touch and pet the elephants you will be able to see how Handcrafts are made out of elephants poop.Nice Postal Colorful Cards,Agenda and others Gadgets are available at very reasonable prices

We got to Pinnawala just before lunch in time to see the elephants down in the river. I have never seen so many elephants in the one place! The mothers certainly look after the little ones. After some time a signal must have been given because suddenly they all turned and began to process from the river back to the actual orphanage area.  After a good buffet lunch in the river restaurant from where we viewed the elephants we then went to the actual orphange. For safety the elephants were then on chains. It must cost an enormous sum to maintain this orphanage.

On the way to the river you would pass by a long street with different touristy shops .Just make sure you know the time schedule for the elephants bath in the river otherwise you have to wait quite some time.It was unique experience to see that many elephants in the river.Expect to pay higher entrance fee than the locals.

we decided to go after reading the mixed reviews on our way back to the airport and can unfortunately say it was a big mistake.  there are essentially 3 parts to the 'park' - the first one up the hill is where a large number of elephants (mostly unchained) are "loose" besides the mahoots.  this is good for pictures...while up there, you notice some odd behavior from the elephants (odd rocking, head movements, etc.) as well as chains on some of the younger ones.  the older ones have been 'broken' to understand that if they disobey/act natural, the mahoots will attack them with their hooks.  this was the best part. the second and third part are next to each other...the calf feeding area may be one of the worst things I've seen..these baby elephants are chained (two legs) and are surrounded by a bunch of tourists.  the baby elephants were kept pulling at their chains and trying to rip themselves out of the massively stressful situation but to no avail...besides the visible strain on the chains, it appeared the babies eyes were about to pop out of their head from the stress. the third part contains 4 to 6 grown elephants chained under a canopy.  they were all acting odd, again the rocking, swaying, etc. as they were literally insane. the orphanage argues that they help the elephants, but they actually breed the elephants for profit...I understand you would breed the elephants to keep up the population, but why exploit them by this public feeding...let them live on captive lands in a wild habitat..why domestic them?  oh, right for the money. terrible place that left a sour taste as we were leaving the country. stay away and go to a national park to see wild elephants.

I am a frequent visitor to this elephant orphanage. I am writing these few lines to place some facts correctly specially after seen some of the adverse comments. 1. This orphanage is started to shelter the injured wild elephants or little jumbos separated from their heard. Idea was to have much needed space and water.Over several years the number of elephants has grown up. Now captive breeding is taking place and there are couple of baby jumbos were borne there for our delightness. Kumari is one of the oldest jumbos born here. 2. It is a delightful thing to watch how these baby elephants are being fed. 3. You can not go to any of the National Parks and watch the elephants so closely as they are dangerous and unpredictable. I love to go and sit some where and watch their bathing, some little ones are playing in water, some are fighting, occasionally a large elephant would trumpeting ( Making their mighty noise with the trunk up) 4. You can not compare a care you give for your pet dog and the care given to these elephants. In a wild elephant heard the leader is the oldest female  referred to as Matrya. All the elephants in a heard is under her control. I have witnessed how young elephants are being punished when they do not obey in the deep jungles. Unfortunately since all these elephants are orphaned  here no hierarchy and the Mahouts has to look after these elephants. There is a  language they used and that spike thing is an universal instrument that they use. This so even in India or Thailand. So this is not cruelty!. 5. Of course some grown up elephants have to be tied or place chains to a leg to control them. If any one get boisterous here one can not imagine the damage that can take place. Even the elephants participating in the  Buddhist pageants  are chained. 6. Lots of scientific researches are in progress here today. This is a much large tamed elephant population. I am not aware about a this big tamed heard elsewhere in the world. 7. To maintain this place and to feed the elephants the Department of Wild life is spending a huge amount of money. So it is quite understandable they charge a fee which is quite reasonable. 8. Every body who visits Pinnawala orphanage see the big elephant who lost a limb. If this elephant was left in the wilderness it would have died long ago due to the injuries or else due to starvation as it can not find it's food. This is a flagship for the good work of the staff at the Pinnawala orphanage and I salute to them!!!. I hope I have straightened some facts!!

I love going here and watching the elephants. You can feed the young elephants, have a photo taken with them and follow the herd down to the river and watch them bathe. Look out for the elephant with only 3 legs, he lost one when stepping on a land mine in the war.

I felt the elephants weren't being treated well by the orphanage staff.  Quite a few were chained and the staff hit them with a stick a bit too much. I expected to learn about how the orphanage rescued the elephants and what they do to look after them. However, no information was given. Upon buying the ticket, we just went to see some elephants eating and only 2 baby elephants being fed with a milk bottle. You have to pay extra if you want to try feeding. I felt this was all for a show! Bathing time was also disappointing. Elephants arrived and all of them just stand in the water. Some were still chained. They looked to sad to even play in the water. Only good thing about the orphanage was free clean toilet for foreigners as we paid for our entrance tickets. I would not recommend this place as it is better off watching elephants in the wild in many of national parks in Sri Lanka. I felt sorry for the elephants here.

Liked: The elephants were cute and the greenery in the area was nice. Also we were able to get out of the taxi and stretch our legs enroute to Kandy. Disliked: The handlers were rude and oh-so desperate to earn off these poor animals. Kind of boring.

This location is situated close to Kandy along the kandy -Colombo main road. It is an orphanage for wild elephants where a wide range of elephants are seen of all ages.The elephants are taken to the river for a river bath in the morning.You could watch how baby elephants are fed milk with a giant bottle. You also get some elephant who lost their legs due to land mines. some animals are chained due to their stubborn behavior. A must visit place and lovely scenery of elephant river bathing specially for young kids and animal lovers.

We went there two weeks ago. This is situated little away from Colombo Kandy road passing Kegalle. It is an important place for elephant lovers. for tourists a word of caution you ticket price is much higher than the locals but you have no choice. But taking photos and standing next to elephant you need not pay to any one. Unfortunately the workers (Staff and care takers) always demad money from tourists it is very ugly and demeaning the tourism concept of the government. Considering the situation I may suggest please have some change 50 and 100 rupees notes (1 US$ is about Srilankan Rupee 132) it will be less than a dollar tips. Keep change. Make sure you are there in the morning or afternoon to see the elephant bath, it is really nice.

I am writing this review whilst in the Elephant Bay Hotel Pinnawala. After a very short visit to The Pinnawala Elephant "Orphange". The entire place is purely aimed at generating cash and the welfare of the elephants is definatley lower on their list of priorities. After paying a hefty entrance fee and I broke through the turnstile bursting crowds a strange Disney Land dejavu was felt. I joined the mob of camera happy tourists as we were herded down to a large covered area which reminded me of a cattle market. Circled around two baby elephants were hundreds of people. The "trainers" or guards with there large hooked pointed sticks standing beside them. The elephants had a chain on one back leg and one on a front leg and were desperately trying to break free. The noise an sheer amount of people must be stressful for such a young animal. With there mouths open gesturing for food at all the people it was a very sad moment. I didnt stay long enough to see the actual milk feeding but this was enough to make up my mind. I left the feeding "arena" to check out the large open space where the other elephants roamed. They wasnt chained but they had all been herded up the top of the hill so the guards could exploit them even further by demanding money for photos you take of them. In the distance  I could see a large elephant franticly rocking this one had clearly been chained out of site. I left. After exiting through the gift shop my fifteen minute very sad ordeal was over. I would strongly advise anyone against visiting the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage.

We visited the orphanage from Kandy and drove for just under and hour and a half to arrive in time for the 10 am feeding. We hired a van for about for  £25 and included a stop on the way back at the Peradeniya Botanical Gardens. The driver was a registered tour guide. For our approx £10 per head entrance fee to the orphanage we were able to: •	watch and participating in the feeding of baby elephants with large bottles of milk; (if you wanted to jostle into the line) •	visit three sick elephants, one who had trod on a land mine; •	view the remainder of the herd feeding en masse in an open field; and then •	escort the herd down to the river and sit back with a cup of tea and watch them bath. (it is fair to say that this time the herd did not seem all that interested in the water). The faces of the grown-ups as they took their turn to feed the baby elephants; sneak past the staff to get their partners to snap pics of them touching the babies; or feed bananas to the elephants as they walked down to the river, said it all. They were enchanted. The mahouts and feeding attendants seemed to respond well to rupee notes of large denomination. As always there were touts hanging around outside hoping to convince the gullible that their entrance fee includes accompanying them to see an elephant skeleton, a spice and herb shop or garden or some other ‘attraction’. If you have never seen a large herd of elephants close at hand then this an opportunity not to be missed.

There appears to be ine price for natives and an overinflated price for foreign tourists which isn't disguised by the fact there are 2 booths separating us with their entry price not visible and ours clearly showing a 2,000 rupee entry fee despite our guidebook saying it was only 500 rupees. Feeding time wasn't as described in the guidebook either and many of the elephants chained up which we found distressing. The only good part of the experience was being taken by our taxi driver to a restraunt across the road where we were given seats on the balcony by the side of the river where they brought the elephants to be washed. It was wonderful to watch. But some of the handlers take back handers from foreigners to go up to and toch a bathing elephant thinking they'll pay big money. Not worth 2,000 rupees in the orphanage itself but the river experience is one not to miss!

It was wonderful seeing the baby elephants. It was troubling to see the old, injured elephant that could hardly stand. It was exhilarating to be walking down the street to the river and look back to see a herd of elephants coming after you. We conveniently ducked into the closest restaurant and enjoyed a cold one while we watched the elephants cool down in the river. Where else can you have an experience like this?

There are two part on this visit: The first one is the visit to the place where the elephants live. There are clean and well kept shelters and some elephants (the sick ones) There was an elephant who was injured by a landmine... sad!!! The second part is by the river, where the elephants play and bath... There are shops and plenty of hawkers but if you are not interested on their stuff just say no... with conviction and they will leave you in peace. One of the highlights of our SL tour

This Orphanage is situated about 90 kms from Colombo. a car drive will take about 2 hrs. Enjoyed this visit.  In the morning they allow the elephants to graze where they allow the visitors to get close. I don't know if it is safe. I was not harmed at least.  Then then allow the visitors to bottle feed the baby elephants. Later they take the adults to a nearby river for their bath where they are washed and scrubbed. Good time pass and a photo opportunity.

Great to see the elephants enjoying the river 'relativey' free, then walk their way up to the freeground across the road. Babies funny to watch playing in their enclosure. Unfortunately when it came to feeding the babies, the largest rupee note spoke the loudest-not an opportunity for children to feed the elephants, but whichever western tourist could waft a large bill for workers to pocket. Such a shame. Having to watch a grown woman cooing over the elephants made me want to retch as she pushed her way to the front bloccking the view of children who had been waiting patiently to see the bottle feed.

This is an elephant orphanage.  You can view elephants up close when they are bathing in the river, being lead back to the orphanage and at the orphanage.  At various times you can also view, or for a small sum bottle feed some baby elephants.  It is a great attraction.

After reading the reviews i would disagree with a couple of comments, i didnt finr the place run down. They where in the process of building new shelters for the elephants whilst we was there, and everywher looked clean, tidy and well kept. The mahoots will try it on, but you are under no obligation at all to give them any money, our guide informed us not to let them offer you anything as they cant give you anything that you cant already do. Just get another tourist to take your picture for you, less hassle and everyone wants the same thing at the end of the day! Please go and see the elephant who was injured by a landmine, badly disfigured legs means he is left in one place. He loves human contact and if you could hear an elephant purr it would be then. We was fortunate enough to witnes the parade of the elephants going down to the river and you could happily watch them bathe and play for hours. ther are alot of people wanting your trade there...what do you expect. but for me it is well worth the visit, however give the gift shop a miss...you become a conjoined twin the shop people get so close to you as they follow you around. Oh and for you information their is an ATM 2 minutes walk away from the centre.

Our visit consisted of 3 parts:  viewing the elephants grazing, watching the babies feeding, and observing the elephants in the river.  Upon arrival, we saw groups of elephants freely walking around and congregating in a grassy area.  Soon after, we moved to where the baby elephants were fed by bottle while a couple of older, infirm elephants were bathed.  (Yes, the babies were chained during the feeding but walked into the arena freely and did not seem distressed at all.  With all the tourists observing, it was likely safer for all involved.)  At a designated times, the elephants crossed the road and entered the river where they drank, bathed, socialized, etc.  (I did not see any elephants being treated cruelly.)  I found it much less depressing than seeing elephants confined in small groups in a zoo or animal park.  In fact, it was a unique opportunity to see them in a low stress environment. Yes, there are vendors along the road selling their wares or wanting to charge tourists to give the elephants bananas but this is a poor country and almost everywhere we went, locals were trying to provide services in return for tips.  If you don't want to, just say no and walk on.

I am horrified that this place is put on the itinerary of unsuspecting tourists to Sri Lanka. My husband and I have just come back from there. We had a wonderful holiday until we visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. All the animals, some very young were chained by their back legs and were trying to stretch themselves as far as they could to a) reach food and b) touch each other. The most terrible sight which reduced us both to tears was of an elephant which had, apparently stood on a landmine. It's leg was very swollen and swaying in mid-air as it leaned on railings, incapable of standing up straight. A Japanese man was so upset he shook his head and left. Something must be done to releave the suffering of theses animals. Even when taken to the river, they stood still, not wetting themselves with the water that they love so much. When a mahout came close they kept a very wide distance from him; obviously used to having pain inflicted on them. I have written to Travelbag about it and I hope that people will avoid supporting the continuation of this cruel, moneymaking nightmare.

There's something not quite right about this place. Entrance fee is expensive, and although seeing the elephants bathe was exciting, the rest was just awful. All elephants on short chains, rocking from side to side and kept in sheds. A few large males were isolated from the other elephants and looked extremely stressed. The worst part for me though was the babies. They were also isolated from adults, and clearly hungry for milk, but they wouldn't receive milk unless a tourist paid 1000 rupees to feed them. Disgraceful. One "mahout" asked me if I'd like to touch one of the  elephants, I said "ok". Next thing I know, he asked aggressively for my camera and took some photos of me, then demanded a 1000 rupee tip! This place clearly once had good intentions, but is now just a tourist trap.  You will leave feeling sad.

Elephants are quite good in number but it is in poor condition. There are no signboards which can guide you inside the orphanage . We could get into the elephant orphanage without paying the whole amount for the tickets, seems like the ticket guy was collecting money for himself and letting people in. But the place s really good. Lots of well kept elephants. None of them seem to be tortured. But they didnt allow me to feed the baby elephants :( saying that it is not allowed. There appear to be about 90 elephants presently there.  We saw about half of these bathing in the river, then they walk back up the street, very close to the tables and cafes etc. It's undoubtedly fascinating to see the baby elephants playing in the river with each other and on the way back up the hill, all are so close you can see all the features at very close quarters. However, my reservations arise from my western urban sensitivities seeing wild animals short-chained to steel loops on the floor, tugging repeatedly at the chains. I'm unable to comment on the general husbandry of the sanctuary, or indeed how long the animals are chained thus - maybe it's only briefly. So, it's an interesting visit, but be aware that it might leave a lingering feeling of distaste.

From what I saw this was a safe and health place for elephant orphans. You can feed the elephants, watch them at close quarters roaming and large open area, see very young elephants with their long ginger hair protecting their young skin and watch them bathe in the nearby river whilst you have something to eat. THere were some sad cases of elephants wounded by land mines. Watching the young elephants fed milk was particularly special. If you are in Sri Lanka you need to see the elephants and this is a good place to do it. Butdo visit one of the reserves as well to see these magnificent creatures in the wild.

The Elephant Orphanage is a great place to see various sizes of elephants.  I had the opportunity to see them bathing in the river and also fed a baby elephant.  The overall place is a bit run down and could use a makeover.  I would definitely recommend visiting for the experience and to help support efforts to help orphaned elephants.

I liked this place a lot more than other reviewers. The elephants were obviously well cared for by gentle and loving keepers. Sadly I didn't get to see any elephants in the wild as we were strapped for time, so this was lovely. The elephants were led down to the river for some wallowing and water play. They had ample space to roam within the park. There were sad cases of elephants injured by land mines, which can never be returned to the wild, but were cared for none the less. I personally don't mind spending more than the locals for this. It is part of the education for the children there, wages are very low in SL, and these orphanages are supplemented through taxes, which the locals pay anyway. I think British museums/sights should consider doing likewise.

Tourists  turn up by the busloads and pay  4 times more than locals. There is no structure, bilingual signage  or structure for informing the public about the history or role of  the  "orphanage". If you are merely satisfied in viewing cute baby  (and adults) elephants up close, then you will be happy with the outcome. If you are looking for something more, you will be disappointed.

While Pinnawala is a good opportunity to see and interact with elephants if you've not done that before, and the elephants all seemed to be well looked after, I was pretty disappointed with this place as an 'orphanage'. I guess with a lot less wild and working elephants since it was set up there are a lot less orphan elephants now. There were two when we visited, both quite young, but these seemed a sideshow for the rest of them - a herd of around 40 including a number of young ones. I am assuming this was a breeding herd - assuming because there was no explanation for anything anywhere. Apart from a map at the entrance there were no information billboards, and the staff inside were either not able or not interested in explaining anything about the elephants or the centre. Even during the much hyped feeding there was no explanation or discussion about the elephants. That is not to say the staff were not interactive. You could not go near one of them without them saying 'come, come' to drag you over to take a photo with, or feed an elephant..... and then hold out their hand for a tip. I know elephants are expensive to feed but the entrance fee was about the highest we paid for any attraction in Sri Lanka, so this sort of aggressive tip-seeking was not appreciated, nor were the disdainful looks when we said we just want to sit and watch them for a while. Even during the baby elephant feeding, the only people they were interested in were those paying extra to hold a bottle while the elephants drank it. I have since learned that there are several other 'elephant experiences' near by where there are good explanations, presentations etc which, while I did not go to them (and don't know the prices), are probably better value than this place, which is an average single animal zoo with an small functioning orphanage attached. It's a pity because it seems a great cause and was probably once quite ground-breaking, but without a major revamp is just trading on it's past laurels now.

After reading the reviews on here, and being a real animal lover, I was a little apprehensive about what I would find at the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. However I left the orphanage pleasantly surprised. The majority of the elephants are able to wonder about free... I was expecting all the elephants to have chains on but this was not the case. There are a couple of the male elephants that were chained up but this was only while they were moving the rest of the herd. The baby elephants had a small chain on one leg during their milk time, but this was only to keep them in one place. One of the babies escaped their chain and started wondering around. At no point did the staff attempt to frighten the baby back, they were guided back carefully and the staff thought it was just as funny as we did. When the elephants went down to the river again only the male elephants had a leg chain on and as soon as they got to the water these were all taken off while I was delighted about. You can of course argue the ethics behind the centre... Yes they are breeding and maybe more should be done to attempt to reintroduce these elephants back in to the wild. But on the whole, I felt as though the elephants there were well looked after and were happy. If you want to feed a baby elephant (again not possibly the best thing but it helps towards the cost of milk) then you need to get to the orphanage for about 8.30 as there is a limit to the amount of people who can do it. At about 9.45 make your way down to the river, you can get a very reasonably priced drink and prime viewing spot from the little cafe/restaurant and watch as the herd comes racing down the street. Unmissable!

This place takes in injured elephants and also allows them to breed in the care of professionals. Okay so they have a chain on one leg which is attached to a hook on the ground for when they are in public and getting washed or fed. This may be slightly cruel but it is for everyone's safety and they tend to go for runs and some may attack but they do spend a lot of time roaming free around the orphanage land and in the river. It is amazing to see so many elephants. you can see some are injured with missing legs or missing feet and some a heavily pregnant and there are little babies which you can feed milk with an extra ticket which is about £2.50 or 500 rupees. You can touch them and feed them and it amazing! Twice a day they walk down to the river and get a wash and have a play and I could sit there all day and watch them. They are amazing creatures and I would recommend going their. This orphanage seems the most official one in Pinnawala, there are other ones but they seem to just be robbing tourists and treating elephants badly. In Pinnawala you can find places to ride an elephant too. But this place is definitely the best, you pay around £5-£10 and you can stay there all day and watch them. You can feed them fruit too for about £2.50. Definitely a must!

It's hard to call this place as an Orphanage, as it is a zoo-like attraction that the local area depends on very heavily to bring tourists and their money, and seems more to do with making money than saving elephants. It's probably not fair to make a judgement of the people who work in and around this attraction, as I'm sure some of these elephants would have been killed if they weren't brought here, and the locals are making a better life for themselves. I'm sure some good is being done, however it's still sad and depressing to see animals being exploited and tourists having to pay a hefty price to see it. We were lucky enough to see wild elephants, without chains around their legs and without 'handlers' threatening them with sharp sticks, which was far more exciting. Save your time and money and go on a safari further east and see wild elephants!

Its a must visit place for any animal lovers. The elephants are all very cares for and visiters are able to get right up close but you will be asked to pay something. The actual site also has an entry fee, one rate for locals and one rate for tourists like everythink else in Sri Lanka!

This place was pathetic. It was a tourist trap ... All you get to do is see elephants and take pictures. There is no thrill to that. I mean let's face the facts it was a waste of time and money. 1500 rupees. I was quite sickened that the staff would chase the elephants even the baby ones with sticks for the "protection" of the tourists. And seeing a baby elephant chained to the middle of a building was disgusting. It could only walk around in a small circle while people take pictures of it and it gets bottle fed. I would rather have donated my money than have had to walk into this dump again.

One should get there by 9 am sharp or even a little bit earlier and go straight to the ticket counter as the feeding bottles finish fast. The first feeding is @ 9.15 am...feeding the little fellows is the best experience ! You can also buy fruits @ the feeding pavillion inside and give the guys a treat... Then they're all left to roam around freely (with guides around ofcourse) and you can take as many pictures with/of them as you like...it's lovely to watch the adults caring for the younger fellows... If the weather is good, then they're taken for a river bath

This place is closer to a zoo or Disney land  than any thing else. First it is a rip off and 2nd this place clearly lost it s initial purpose. We saw elephants in such places in few parts of Asia and this was the worth of all. Now we were warned as the guidebooks said it but we wanted to try , after all we also went to Disney land ... ( apparently the millennium park a few km befor is much better). That said too see elephants the natural reserves are much better.

At an hours drive it is a good place to spend first half of the day. Elephant bathing seen is interested. They offer 50% discount to Saarc countries tourists which we availed. You can spend time with elephants of almost all ages. Milk feeding is also an interesting activity. Overall a good attraction around Kandy. It is also approachable from Colombo.

Stayed two nights at the Elephant Bay Hotel. Interesting experience in itself, but great for elephant watching. We didn't have to pay to see the elephants bathe, as we had a hotel reservation, didn't go into the 'zoo'. Saw elephants from 9am - 4pm every day in the river. Must say, they looked happy, well fed and not mid-treated at all. Would recommend this visit.

Visiting Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage was a hilite in our trip to Sri Lanka. We were on our way to Kandy and we made a quick stop at Pinnawala, arriving there at the exact moment when the elephants were taken to the river for their morning bath. It was for sure a lot of fun! I've never seen so many elephants at the same time. All ages, all sizes! Playing among themselves in the water and apparently enjoying it! All injured or orphan baby elephants rescued in the different regions of Sri Lanka are taken to Pinnawala, where they are fed and watched over. The newcomers are in quarentine until they can join the whole group. It is fun and, at the same time, you are helping them taking care of the orphans, injured and elder ones. Pinnawala is famous for having the largest herd of captives Asian elephants in the whole world. Don't miss it, or you may regret forever. Enjoy!

We visited expecting an orphanage but found this more like a zoo. There seemed no attempt at conservation and they are breeding animals. Many elephants were chained up and looked miserable. When questioned the staff told us these were dangerous. Highly recommend giving it a miss and going on a safari to see them in the wild instead.

On our visit to Sri Lanka we made it a point to visit this place. It has all wounded, injured or small baby elephants who are taken care of so well. It felt so nice to see man attached to them so emotionally when rest are all just finishing their chances to survive Salute the selfless people who spend non stop hours to rake care of them.

It is about an hour's drive from Kandy so plan to arrive around 10am which is when the elephants are taken down to the river to bathe. There is a nice hotel right on the water so we got front row seats in return for spending some money on a pot of tea for the four of us.

we make it a point to visit Pinnawala as the first stop from the airport as we head for the hill stations on the colombo- kandy road. The first thing that hit my mind at Pinnewala, is the location.  Elephants are taken for bathing to a heavenly river, which has picturesque view. 30 to 50elephants of all ages were there, enjoying their time. But the saddest parts is, elephants seem to be tortured & hungry. Their legs are tied with chain, that's why there is obvious scar around their legs which seems to be very itchy & painful. That is really pathetic. It's called an 'orphanage', but doesn't work in that way. And I couldn't stop wondering, why there are so many restaurants & shops beside the river? Isn't that a government own place? All these shops & restaurants have just reduced space, both for the elephants & tourists. Instead of settling those shops, space could be open so that tourists would be able to see the bathing elephants from different views. All you can do beside the river, is standing at only one point & get pushed by other tourists who are also trying to have the view of elephants. But watching so many elephants at a time is really a enjoyable thing for the tourists. I think there are still so MANY things to improve in this place.

Every time we returned to Colombo from Kandy, we made it a point to see Pinnawala. Pinnawala can be reached by A1 Colombo Kandy road with a turn off at Kegalle. It’s approximately 85 kms from Colombo and is a 3 hour ride. It is a unique elephant orphanage where orphaned elephants are lovingly taken care of; something unheard of in most parts of the world when elephants are killed for their tusks. Both adult-elephants and baby elephants maimed or orphaned in the crossfire during the war or by villagers protecting their paddy fields are sheltered here. Tickets costing around $20 are a must. The best time to visit Pinnawala is after 1 pm. We were always in time to watch hordes of these majestic creatures lazily strolling towards the river Maha Oya for their bath. Watching the baby elephants playing in the water is really a sight to behold. Photos can be taken up very close. At 5pm, one can participate in the bottle feeding of the elephants at the main center where one can watch the babies greedily quaffing the milk. The fun part is the shops lining the lanes leading up to the river. One can buy interesting souvenirs ranging from leather bags to elephant-poop papers and bags. Bargaining is a must. All in all, a wonderful experience.

We had our day trip organized by Azamara Club Cruises as part of our SE Asia cruise. When asked for the highlight of our trip my wife and I both nominated this day. A interesting bus trip through the Sri Lankan countryside then several hours watching and interacting with the 73 elephants at the Pinnawala Orphanage/sanctuary. Here visitors must take it for what it is. It's a sanctuary - not a free range nor a zoo!! It's a wonderful and unique way to spend time with these wonderful animals. The elephant trek to and from the river, the bathing and then the roaming on the open field all had you fascinated by being up and personal. The only disconcerting aspect was the chains restraining the baby elephants while feeding and that was probably only to protect the handlers and public. Then the return to Colombo in the refurbished Viceroy train through villages, plantations and paddy fields!  A truly wonderful, memorable experience.

Its advertised as a sanctuary for wild elephants that are in danger from poachers. Yet some of them are chained up, u. d to mske money from tourists who pose with them while the elephants strike a specific pose. Most are herded from one place to another by the herders to suit a tourist schedule e.g. 1pm feeding, 2pm bathing etc. At least they dont let tourists ride them. Then it would just be a circus. My expectation was to see wild elephants roam free in a protected area. I was dissappointed. If you still want to go, you take the bus there (follow the instructions in lonely planet). If you take a tuk tuk, make sure they take you to tge right place. A competing park called 'millennium' pays tuk tuks commission for bringing tourists there instead.

The best bit is to see the the herd walking down the road to the river and the bathing. We did pay the 2000 rps and although this is high it was lovely to see the elephants at the river. However if you stand at the top of the road without entering the orphanage you would see the elephants on their way to the river. We were approached and asked if we wanted our photographs taken closer to the elephants but this isn't necessary as we took plenty of photographs ourselves. My advice is to have your hotel call in the morning you intend to go to make sure that the elephants are going to the river.Sometimes due to heavy rain the river bathing is cancelled. I personally would not want to go unless it was to see the bathing.

In one sense, the Elephant orphanage was great. Being able to see such a massive herd of Elephants in the river was really a sight to see! Great for families, without a doubt! I think what really brought it down, in my opinion, was the level of human interaction with the Elephants. I'd much rather watch them from afar, just being Elephants. It was more of a circus than what you would call an "orphanage". I respect the animals, and seeing them like this really dampened my day.

What an amazing experience. Seeing elephants so close, feeding baby elephants milk and adult elephants fruit, watching them feed and learning about the orphanage/breeding program. It is seeing to believing because you stand in front of a large herd feeding and then going down to the river to bathe. Unfortunately due to heavy rain the previous day it wasn't possible to see them in the river, however a DVD I purchased shows what it was like. A fantastic morning and well worth the visit.

Well worth a visit on your way to Kandy. Its lovely to see the elephants bathing and you also get to feed them in the evening at a specific time. Feel that the elephants could have been looked after better at times. Much enjoyed by children and a must see on your way to Kandy.

We visited Pinnawala with our two children and our impression is that this has little to do with an orphanage. The main goal is to shake out tourists as much money as possible. The day we were there, the river was too high to bath the elephants. Although this is the main attraction, the admission price of 2.000 SR per person was the same. For this money you can see a zoo with some elephants standing around. If you want to come closer to them, you have to pay extra. If you want to take picture, you have to pay. If you want to feed bananas, you have to pay. For 250 SR they offer you to give a bottle of milk to a baby elephant. This is also a misunderstanding, as the staff gives this bottle and you may also touch the bottle, which is finished in 3 seconds. The staff is unfriendly and hardly communicates with visitors, other than harsh orders. They just can't care less don't wether you are satisfied with your visit or not. If you want to see elephants, there are plenty opportunities to do so in Sri Lanka. If you want to see them and leave with a very unsatisfied feeling, this is your place to go!

We took visitors from Canada to the elephant orphanage last week-end. The location is about 5kms off the Colombo - Kandy Road at marker 60kms. Admission is $20 for tourists and $2 for locals. Best time to get there is either 09:30 or 13:00 as the 50 or so elephants are paraded from their compound, across the road and 200 m to the river at 10am and 2pm. You can first go to the compound for a walk to see them roaming about and visit the 'baby' area. You can even feed the babies (for a small fee) if you wish. Also a mahood (trainer) will offer to take your picture beside an elephant (small fee). The best place to see them is at the couple of restaurants down by the river. Sit, have a snack or a beverage and just watch the antics of the elephants, especially the younger ones. You can ask a mahood if you can feed an elephant (small fee) but it is quite the experience. A well worth visit if in Sri Lanka.

If you like the combination of a zoo and a circus with mahouts or helpers constantly asking you for money to have your photo taken with an elephant then this is clearly going to be somewhere you will like. But for us seeing elephants constantly being harassed by mahouts with hooks, males out of the main public gaze on chains constantly weaving and the feeling that this is all geared to money making made us feel very uncomfortable. We tried to see through all this and witnessed the bottled milk feeding of two very young orphans, the older elephant with the bottom of a foot missing who was clearly very well looked after by his kindly mahout. At the river one elephant struggled down with massive chains on and only the babies seemed to enjoy the experience. One sensed that this started off as an orphanage with good intentions but has slid in to something which at the end of the day made us feel very sad and hope that there will be changes coming.

It was a magnificent view to see so many elephants walking one behind the other to go for a bath and then back.  There were two baby elephants too who were so cute looking and you will fall in love with them.  When the elephants are arriving for their bath it is followed by music and everyone in the crowd also follow them around.  Its fun watching them have a great bath and enjoying themselves.

The very first place we went to in SriLanka. we had breakfast at a restaurant between the orphanage and the river. After a long trip, the Breakfast was Awesome (now to think of it, it was ok). we saw the elephants going to the River for their bath time, and i had to run to get myself tickets to be able to have the chance to experience bathing them. inside the orphanage we were taken to see the wild elephants that are still chained to be trained. i wanted to stand close to an elephant to take a picture and touch it, but got really bothered from the trainers/workers there, for which they stick to you and keep asking you to help them i.e. tip them. when i went to help bathe the elephants at the river, i was given a bucket of water to pour on the elephant, and again everywhere i went, the workers were trying to get tips, by sticking to me, holding my hand to listen to them, (cries of help, help help everywhere) i found that very disturbing. anyway, i wanted to buy some souvenirs, my husband thought that we should see other places first, in case we found cheaper shops. but i insisted on getting something from there because i didn't know whether or not we will pass from this road or not. (and i was right, we didnt find anything in other cities about the orphanage). i advise you to visit ALL the shops on that Road, and get the best price, and keep bargaining. i was very happy from the things i bought. this was my first time seeing an elephant live, and they were ADORABLE!

I'm not usually a fan of seeing animals in captivity but this was a somewhat different experience. Watching the baby elephants being hand fed is fun - if a bit of a battle to see anything - but seeing the injured animals is very disturbing. I do think that the orphanage is doing good work for them - what would life be like for them if they weren't being cared for here I wonder? The road down to the bathing area is lined by shops and sellers cashing in on the whole elephant thing - be aware that most of the items are available for a lot less in most Sri Lankan towns and shops - so don't get ripped off! Watching the elephants from the viewing areas was interesting - not at all interactive - and I think I was surprised that it was such a sedate activity for the animals - my over active imagination expected to see them spraying water all over the place with their trunks and rolling about in the water - this wasn't the case and probably emphasised the fact these animals had other problems and needed the care they obviously get to some extent in the surroundings. I'm glad I've seen it- and I am happy to pay for the privilege if it indeed goes directly to the care of the elephants - but the jury is still out for me I think...

We visited Pinnawela on our way from Negombo to Sigiriya. We made the stop especially for the children. They liked it, but the adults found the whole site a bit sad. Chained elephants, had the feeling some elephants get to much food, rather expensive for foreigners.

What a sight to see the elephants crossing the road and walking down to the river for bath time. The combination of fully grown and babies made for an interesting couple of hours, we had lunch in a cafe overlooking the river and then went to the Orphanage for the bottle feeding at 2p.m. It was a great opportunity to talk to the staff about the elephants and the reason that they were in the orphanage. Worth the expense to do this.

This is a nice trip, the elephants you see are able to roam free and are not chained up. You can also go down to the river at certain times to see the elephants bathing which is probably the best bit. For more money you can give baby elephants a bottle of milk. There is also an area where disabled elephants are which is quite sad - it is good that they are so well looked after and able to be rehabilitated, but it is upsetting to see them chained up. Would recommend a visit, but the elephant transit home further south is also good.

What a great experience. Make sure you time your visit to arrive just before the elephants make their way across the road to the river. We positioned ourselves right next to the gate and got some great footage. You can then follow the elephants down to the river for more great shots. In the orphanage you will have the opportunity to feed an elephant and talk to the keepers. Enjoyed every minute.

This is the best place to observe elephants very close, in hundreds.. If you choose this place, try to fit the time covering the feeding time which you love to see. Common schedule is as follows, 08.30 AM - Open 09.15 AM - Bottle feeding baby Elephants ( You can participate for feeding….) 10.00 AM – Bath time - ( Maha-Oya situated about 400 meters away for two hours bath.) 12.00 AM – Return from bath 1.15 PM - Bottle feeding baby Elephants 2.00 PM – Afternoon bath - ( Maha-Oya situated about 400 meters away for two hours bath.) 4.00 PM - Returns from bath 5.00 PM - Bottle feeding Baby Elephants 6.00 PM – Close Make-sure to Be prepared with water bottle/ Hats/caps and sunglasses to protect you from sun when you get down from the vehicle... (if in the rainy season the filed can be bit muddy..)There are some nice restaurants near by the river where they go for bath, you can have some food, relax and watch them in the river... You have to buy tickets around 16$ for a foreigner..

This was one of the main 'must sees' for our honeymoon and we were not disappointed. To be able to sit and eat lunch while watching the elephants bath is something we will not forget. After lunch we walked around the grounds of the orphanage - taking in the sights and sounds of the elephants in a habitat/environment they are happy in. The only down side are the 'tauts' who are quick to grab you to have your photo taken with the elephants and want tipps for appearing in the photo and for taking the photo. As we did this on our first day we were not savvy enough to negotiate first!! So having been caught out with larger denomination notes, the day ended up a little expensive, but didn't detract from the experience. There are toilet facilities but these are 'squatting' facilities and a shock to the system if happening them among them for the first time!
