We've been here before about ten years ago, mid afternoon on a really wet day and wanted to see the experience properly. I must say we saw absolutely no signs of cruelty, in fact quite the reverse. The best part of it was that there's actually quite a lot to see and do, watching the babies being fed, feeding the elephants yourself and following them down to the river. Timing, it seems is everything and arrival between 08.30 and 09.00 is best. By the way, the shops on the way down to the river are excellent with a good choice and reasonable prices for local clothes and the hotel verandah is a great spot to watch from while you enjoy a refreshing drink.

This is the best place to see Sri Lankan elephants in close look. The price may be bit high for foreigners, but worth to visit this place since its kind of a unique experience. Now the place has renovate a bit with bigger car park and good toilet facilities. You can feed baby elephants  or give fruits for elder once for extra cost. Be sure to be there at elephant bathing time (10 am and 2 pm). Its always guarantee to have a good photo of you with lots of elephants in your background.

We thought it was done well. Be early for feeding and before the heat gets up. There were no signs of cruelty, one of the babies refused to take milk and it wasn't pressed. It was taken back to its mother. The elephants are allowed to frolic in the river for 2 hours ever day, it all appeared laid back. Yes it is touristy but where else will you  see 100 or so elephants having a swim. They are not easy to see in the wild here so appreciate the experience.

Ensure you are there by 9.15 for the feeding of the elephants, then at 10.00 they walk down through the village to the river which is amazing to watch and be part of as you walk with them..there are some beatuiful restaurants down by the river where you can have a refreshing drink or something to eat, We witnessed three of the smaller elephants behaving just like naughty teenagers, very funny and the scenery was breathtaking.  Just down the road from this attraction you can also ride the Elephants and let them shower you, whilst bathing them in the river.  Very moving experience these animals are so large yet so gentle.

Established in 1975 for orphaned elephant babies the orphanage has over 40 animals. They are daily bathed, fed and herded at specific times of the day, which can be witnessed by people. The very small baby elephants are also bottle-fed. We witnessed the bathing of dozens of elephant babies in the river that is a lifetime experience. The favility has also bred babies and there is facility which makes eco-friendly paper and other artefacts from elephant dung.

Gates open at 830. We paid 2000 rupees each to get in, which I did not feel was real value for money. Bottle feeding of baby elephants was at 915 and was a pretty great sight to see, though only a few got to hold the bottle over a metal railing into a baby elephants mouth.  After that, we walked up a small incline to see a large open field of about 50 or so elephants and watched them for about 20 minutes.  At 10 am they take they rally the elephants and take them to a river about 500 meters away, I will add that this quite a sight to see this mass of 50 or so elephants walk down a small lane and into the river, it also look like they really enjoyed their time cooling off in the river. Going here I thought I'd be able to play around with baby elephants, though there was not much touching of the elephants at all, which I guess may be safer for both parties. There is a lot of places around the area, like within 1km or so, of riding and bathing of the elephants if you're interested. Getting there: One cost effective option is to take the train heading towards Kandy from the Colombo fort station, you can find the times online. Get off at Rambukkana station  and take a rikshaw to the Pinnawala Elephant orphanage for 200-300 rupees. After seeing the elephants you could go back to the station and jump back on a train heading for Kandy. Or if you're gonna stick around for a bit there is a pretty cool tea factory, Glenloch, just down the road from the elephant sanctuary, they will give you a full tour and also allow you to sample some of their teas, I thought it was quite interesting to see.

As many of the 1* reviews of this "orphanage" state, it is a shameful sight to see the way the elephants are treated here.  I saw one chained bull get so frustrated that he picked up a huge log and flung it 20 feet!  I went here on a ship's tour (Cunard Queen Victoria) and relied on the brochure literature - I know - dumb!  But I was on a round- the- world trip, on my own, with the 12 day ship segment thrown in.  I had so-o-o many other places to research that I naively believed the brochure.  It was a long 3+ hour bus drive from the port, with winding roads that gave me car sickness since I couldn't secure a front seat on the way there.  The tour completely left us on our own with only times to meet for lunch.  I was the last person out of the restroom (yes - hole in the floor - I would rather have a tree!).  My entire group had disappeared.  I followed some elephants to the river, snapped a couple photos, and then a very strange feeling came over me.  I hated what I saw, elephants being mistreated.  I became over-whelmed with the heat and the dust and this cruelty.  I went back to the entrance to try and find a breath of A/C.  None to be had - no gift shop, restaurant, or across the street in the tiny village.   I finally went back to the buses and one lovely driver (not even from my group) ran the A/C for 1.5 hours and gave me bottles of ice water.  I was very ill from the heat and don't know what else I could have done.  He literally saved my life and well deserved the $20 tip I offered him (that he refused for the first minute).  When that bus needed to leave, my bus driver appeared and did the same for me.  I spent almost 3 hours sitting on the buses as a captive.  My lunch was a bag of peanuts I found in my camera bag (not the included lunch someplace by the river with no A/C). I felt badly about the bus fumes and the environment, but had no option.  I couldn't find a taxi there and knew if I had that I didn't have enough $ to go 3.5 hours back to the ship.  PLEASE save your money and don't go to this tourist trap.  I complained once I got back on-board and only got a bottle of wine and no other compensation.  I still need to write to Cunard.  Oh, they did say they may reword the brochure to say the "tour" is unguided.

See elephants in a herd walking from the Orphanage to the river for a bath. From the different hotels/restaurants you will have a good spot to see the elephant in the river or when they are walking to or from the river. You can get close to the animals and even touch them when lucky. I didn't buy any food to feed the elephants, but when you do so they will guaranteed get close to you. The curiosity of an elephant made it possible to touch one for me. In the orphanage itself there isn't much to see, but when you are there you should at least give it a visit. After that, try to have a ride on an elephant at one of the many places you can get an elephant safari. You have to do it once!

It was really neat walking around and having the elephants walking near you (I guess since the elephants have hanging chains on them, they think they are chained up and don't run away). The elephants were beautiful, especially the baby ones getting a bath. I loved when we crossed the road to the other side where there were tons of elephants in the water. The scenery in the background was gorgeous! I really wanted to help bathe, feed or even touch an elephant but was not given the opportunity. I did a 15 day tour and let my tour guide arrange everything, so maybe I should have requested something in advance. But I did not see any signs advertising these opportunities. That was a let down, but it was a pretty place to visit.

We visited here and I have to say I was in two minds when we got there. There were two baby orphaned elephants calling for their mother and just pacing I was so moved I felt the tears falling down my checks, their mothers had been killed and they were found down a well and were in quarantine, just tragic that mankind can be so cruel. The little orphans are bottle fed and are well looked after at least they are alive and cared for. The other elephants have loads of food and lot of land to roam. It was an experience to see them all trekking down to the river for their daily swim and frolicking. It was so lovely to go down and watch them all interacting with one and other. The Mahout’s do look after their charges. There are also some old tusker elephants which were superb to see. This orphanage is not a zoo and is not for everyone but it is helping elephants survive in our every changing world.

Dont get me wrong. I loved elephants. Every moment I see them It makes my day. So friendly, so familiar, so lovely animals. But since the last time I was here 7 years ago, the only improvement of this place was the ticket booth and the souvenir shop. It clearly don't put the money in taking care of the animals. Something that is very common in this part of the world. To do business by torturing animals for tourist. You can see all the time how the only way of interaction between a "keeper" and an elephant is with a stick. The hit them all the time to sit and do tricks or just move around the huge amount of tourist. Everything has a price inside so just be careful of been to friendly with the elephant cause they are gonna charge you. If you wanna go just pay the entry fee (2000 rupees) and keep your camera inside of the bag to avoid the "camera fee". Avoid any interaction suggest it by a keeper cause its gonna cost you.

We visited the orphanage with a guide, who took good care of us throughout our visit. He was able to arrange for me to feed the baby elephants and got us a river side seat in ont of the hotels as the elephants were brought down to the river for their daily bathing. To see these great creatures so close up, and to be able to touch and interact with them, is something that neither my wife nor I will ever forget.

I thoroughly enjoyed my visit. There are two tiny babies, still with fluffy hair, absolutely gorgeous,plus lots of other elephants of varying ages. However, the highlight for me was enjoying a front row table in the restaurant which overlooks the river (reserved for us by our tour operator), and eating lunch watching the elephants enjoying themselves splashing around in the wide river below us. One or two elephants decided to go exploring on their own and came back waving palm branches that they had found in the water. Others had fun playing with each other. A truly magical experience, only beaten, but in a different way by seeing wild elephants, including a baby, in Yalla a few days later, but amazingly still as close up.

We were unsure about visiting this orphanage as we are not keen on animals being kept in captivity but given that some have been injured or orphaned at an early age they are at least cared for here. We arrived at lunch time, saw them out in the open then watched them feeding - sad that they have to be chained. Our teenage daughter fell in love with the two baby elephants. The entrance fee then allows you to cross the road and find a convenient restaurant where you can sit and watch them come down to the river to bathe. Don't forget camera and video, it was lovely to see them enjoy the water and try to escape their mahouts! We had lunch whilst we watched them, then bought elephant dung paper products after being shown how they make them!

a truly wonderfull day,elephants so close you can touch them,they rush down to the river and the younger ones really enjoy splashing about and laying in the water,great photo and video action we know they are in captivity,but obviously very happy,and whats the alternative,they are being cared for.....enjoy

..... but I have to say that the National Park at Minneriya was much the best experience with elephants. Nothing beats seeing them wild and in their natural habitat. It was great to see the elephants being cared for so well, especially as many of those that were injured had injuries inflicted by man. Yes, so we should have to pay good money to see that they are looked after properly. The best tip is to get there by 10.30 so you can witness the herd beingtaken to the river for their daily bathe. Get there early and get a good seat in the cafe by the river and watch in comfort

We started off to this orphanage early in the morning but it really important you know the timings of the orphanage which currently are: 0830 Open to visitors 0915 Bottle feeding (We missed this) 1000 Herd leaving to river (Awesome)* 1000 - 1200 You (kids will love it) can see the elephants having a lot of fun bathing and the odd elephant getting into some playful fights. Be prepared with food and drinks as everything around there is pretty expensive. You can also buy some original 'dung paper' which is paper made out of jumbo poop. 1200 Return from the river 1315 Bottle feeding 1400 Herd leaving to the river 1600 Return from the river 1700 Bottle feeding 1730 Counters closes 1800 Orphanage closes Overall it was a superb visit and was quite educational. Elephants are in any case majestic creatures with good social structures so you can learn something. But I would not stay their for longer than a bottle feed and perhaps an hour of bathing! I have a short video of it at http://tinyurl.com/d6lghbr

Ok, The elephants are in captivity, so you will have an internal conflict on whether this is a semi zoo or a natural space. You will not be able to get too close to the elephants, and sometimes you will see them unchained. It is expensive to get in ( 20 dollars) and then they charge you if you want to feed them ( i have never figured out how) or wash them ( same here). Now, if you go to Sri Lanka, this is the only place where you will see so many elephants together, in a nice landscape ( stay until they take them to the river at 10h30), get amazing pictures for you and your kids, see babies and patriarchs at the same time.. You will also pass by a factory where they recycle the elephant dumps and make paper out of it.. sO Yes, I recommend the place, despite the negative aspects.

We visited the Pinnawala elephant orphanage whilst travelling around Sri Lanka amd found the experience a little strange. We got there to see the elephants bathing. There was a lot of them and they all seemed to be gravitating towards the walls which was a bit odd. There were quite a few elephants that had chains around their feet and you could tell they weren’t comfortable as they were regularly squirting water on them or trying to take the chains of by pulling at them or scraping their legs. We got tickets to feed the elephants which we did. It was over very quickly as they drink very quickly but a lovely experience and probably the highlight. It was a very odd day, not quite sure what to make of it. There are a lot of tales of elephants being abandoned by their mothers and I don’t doubt that happens but the majority of elephants are extremely maternal and the numbers attributed to abandonment didn’t really add up so unsure. The elephants looked well fed but I would recommend perhaps sticking to safari if you want to see them in their natural habitat and perhaps not looking so stressed out. On another note, the places to eat were a little restricted around Pinnawala so take snacks and water with you. It’s obviously massively overpriced too due to the location.

Pinnawela elephant orphanage in Sri Lanka was started in 1975 to house the abandoned and the wounded elephants.  The number of elephants has increased to more than 40 now, including baby elephants brought from various parts, as well as babies born as a result of the captive breeding programme.  The best time to visit is the feeding time of the baby elephants from 0930 to 1000 hours and the bathing time from 1000 to 1030 hours where all the elephants are taken across the road to a river close by.

As part of our tour round the 'Triangle' we visited here as our first stop. How delightful & what fun! An endless herd of pachyderms roaming a large paddock. Time for their feed? Marched down to a covered area and feasted on sundry items of vegetation. Time for a bath? Once again marched out of the park, over the road & down the hill into the river. What a spectacle. To have such a photo opportunity whilst eating lunch is unparalleled. A most worthwhile and rewarding visit enhanced by the orderly schoolchildren on trips from nearby towns. It was like stepping back into the 50's, clean, scrubbed, well-behaved children adorned in clean, freshly pressed uniforms walking two by two in 'crocodile' fashion. Sarf' London and the rest of urban Britain look an learn!

Make sure you arrive before the 10.30am "elephant walk" from the orphanage, across the main street, & then down between the tourist shops to their bathing area in the river! It is a wondeful sight, & is a MUST SEE for anyone visiting Sri Lanka. For once I was not bothered about paying for this worthwhile attraction, & knowing that the money is going to a good cause makes it a better experience.(unlike all the Buddhist Temples that charge exhorbitant rates!)

We missed the feeding but joined in for the elephant bathing in the river. It's just a lovely location and nice to see the elephants enjoy themselves. Our daughter loved it as well and we took a lot of good pictures up close. A few of the more big and rambunctious elephants have some chains as they can behave in a more wild manner. Don't be put off by that, it's for their own protection and for everyone around. One of those male elephants put up a great show as he rolled around in the water and played with and sprayed some of the other elephants. A really fun guy! Admission price LKR 2.000 = $16 (March 2013). We sat down and had drinks at the restaurant right next to the river. Waiter was a bit pushy in getting us to buy more and expected more tip as well.

This was one of my favourite days out whilst visiting Sri lanka. It was nice to see young elephants being fed milk and I got the chance to feed an elephant as well (200lkr). The highlight however was watching the elephants go in the river for their bathing session. We sat watching them for over an hour and could have spent all day there as it was great to see. The cost of entrance is 2000 lkr for tourists which I found to be one of the most reasonably priced attractions whilst in SL. My only negative point would be that there is no info given about the elephants. I would have liked to have found out more on their backgrounds, I.e age, how they came to the orphanage etc! Overall though a nice experience.

I visited the Elephant Orphanage in Pinnawala during my trip to Sri Lanka. It was a great stop-by side trip on my way back to Colombo from the east central part of the country.  It was an amazing experience to feed the Asian elephant with fresh fruits. I'm glad that my tour guide/driver knows the feeding time, 9:30 am, otherwise I miss the chance to feed them for a great photo shoot. The foreign entrance fee is 2,000 rupees and feeding elephant is optional for extra 200 rupees. I enjoy feeding the elephant with fruits than with milk, which are two separate events. Do include another hour in your visit to witness the elephants bathing in the river on the other side of the orphanage. At least 30 elephants I saw bathing after feeding.  Be sure to take great photos and they are great unusual picture moments. There are rows of souvenir and handicraft shops, but of course, tend to be pricy. The parking could be challenging, but you will find spot if the local driver/guide knows the area very well.  It was my first time to visit the orphanage but it looks like morning visit and feeding time tend to be very crowded, plus there were many school-age children and high school students on a field trip that day. I visited March 28, 2013 and it is the peak time of tourism of the country and this is a tourist attraction.  A two to two and half hours visit will be suffice if for sightseeings only.  Be prepared for a hot and humid weather in March. I recommend Elephant Orphanage in Pinnawala, Sri Lanka! It was a wonderful experience.

This trip was a dream come true,I have always loved elephants and loathed the thought of them being poached for their ivory.The orphanage is a haven of peace for these animals.It was amazing to witness these noble creatures enjoying the space and safety that has been afforded them.A highlight was to watch a small boy bottle feeding one of the orphaned babies.My husband and myself will never forget this wonderful opportunity.Thankyou to all involved

This place is wonderful and so worth a visit. This was our second visit. They now ask visitors for ID/Passports. We hadn't been told this and had left ours at the hotel. We did however offer some rupees and we were allowed to buy our tickets £10 each. We happen to go on the same day as all the school children which was utter chaos and in the heat was quite stressful with everyone pushing. The elephants are taken to the nearby river to bathe twice daily for 2hrs each time. 10 and 2pm and that is a must to see.

Although very touristic, we really had a nice time in the orphanage. We arrived there a bit before 12.00, right at the time that the elephants left the river and crossed the road to the orphanage. If you want to see the big group in the river you have to come around 11.00 am. After seeing the elephants up close when crossing the street, we had lunch at the restaurant on the left side overlooking the river. It's fine for a simple and price worthy lunch with a nice view. After 15 minutes a small group of elephants came to the river to have their daily bath. This was fantastic. Our 2,5 year old son couldn't believe what he was seeing. After lunch we went inside the orphanage (2000 Rupees p.p). Here you can give the small elephants a milk bottle if you have booked it in advance. Our driver arranged it for us on the spot for 200 Rps. This was nice. You can wonder inside the orphanage but be aware that if you want to have a good picture with the elephants their keepers will ask for a money. Up to you if you find it worth the money. We highly recommend it but be aware it's very touristic.

One of its kind in Asia, Pinnawala is an elephant orphanage where the elephants abandoned or left behind by their groups are sheltered, nurtured and are fed so that they can live their lives. Pinnawala is also one of the largest centre on captive breeding of elephants. Our tour guide and driver, Krishantha informed us that there are about 100 elephants which includes tuskers, male elephant, female elephants and calves. We enjoyed, elephants bathing in the close by river  'Ma Oya' at about 11:00 in the morning. It is fabulous scene, to see the elephants bathing in the river and socializing among their group. The bathing site has few cafes on the river bank, where one can take the seat and enjoy a cold beer or Ceylon tea while watching elephant in action. At about 1:00 PM there is elephant feeding program, where the baby elephant are fed milk, by the glass bottles. The revenue for Pinnawala are collected by sale of tickets and by selling tickets for feeding the elephants. Our guide informs that the elephants are also put to commercial use in religious procession and for other jobs, which helps in generating the revenue for running the orphanage. Then there are several self help group which generates revenue by selling elephant souvenirs which includes elephant mugs, fridge magnets. stationery products made from elephant pooh. Families should not ignore the place and should also buy souvenirs from nearby shops which are are unique in themselves. Bargaining do happen at small shops but not much.

My family and I made a visit to this Elephant Orphanage in Pinnawala recently and we left feeling a little deflated. It was advertised that we could feed milk to the elephants but not once were we offered the opportunity to feed them. As for the bathing of the elephants, I personally wouldn't class one man throwing water over one of the elephants as bathing them. However, these points aside, the orphanage appears to carry out good work in taking in the animals and, barring the odd one or two elephants, do not appear to chain up the animals and mistreat them as some reports suggest. Watching the elephants feed and bathe each other was a wonderful sight to see. The young elephants played happily with each other. I only hope that the entrance fee charged is used for the upkeep of the orphanage; however, my personal thoughts differ.

I enjoyed very much looking at the elephants while they were bathing , but it broke my heart to see that several elephants were chained. Altogether this felt more like a zoo than an orphanage. On top of this it is extremely expensive for foreigners: 2000 rupies! To ne it seemed just another of many tourist traps you find all over Sri Lanka. You are better off if you go to Yala National Park, wheee you can see free elephants.

Have seen some of the very negative reviews on here and cannot help wondering if they visited the same place! We arrived in Sri Lanka with this attraction firmly on our list of must do's.  We also met a couple at one hotel who had already visited and they were most upset by what they saw and the fact that the elephants were chained!?  In addition our guide was also quick to point out that that there are other 'more hands on' elephant places to visit such as Millenium just down the road. In the end we decided that we came with the intention of visiting and would likely regret it if we did not.  So glad we did visit it was wonderful. We arrived at the river about 12.00 and the elephants were already in the water, so we saw them bathe and then return up the shop/restaurant thoroughfare and across the road back into the 'orphanage'.  I should point out that it was clear that we picked a quiet day/time to visit as there were fewer than 100 people there. We did not hang around for the feeding as this was delayed to 14.00 and we had a long journey ahead, but instead took a look around for ourselves.  Starting with the darling baby elephants (rescued from wells) we got up fairly close to a few larger elephants as they ate the foliage provided for them and also saw the one with the shortenned leg due to a land-mine.  These may have had a chain on then (for use when required) but they were certainly not attached to anything. We used the 'foreign visitor' toilets and these were sparkling and signs clearly stated that they were FREE.  Some of the cleaners may have appeared to be looking for tips, but this was easily ignored.  After purchasing water and pringles at very reasonable prices, we walked up to the 'open' area where most of the elephants roam freely under the watchfull eyes of their keepers. Fed one elephant and that was a highlight and photo opportunity - just 200 Rupees (£1) I think and you get an official ticket/receipt.  Entrance was 2000 R each. Bumped into a delightful set of children visiting with their teachers and they were keen to speak with us as was typical of the Sri Lankans generally on on our trip. VERY pleased we didn't get put off visitnig by the minority of objectors.

This was the main attraction that I wanted to see on my trip to SL in Oct 2012 and what a sight it was!! We saw these fellas in their large groups both feeding in the orphanage and also at the riverside having a bathe and a bit of a play around for the younger ones. Was great fun, could've sat there for ages just watching them at the river. Also got a chance to feed one of the baby elephants and have a few pictures taken. It's a decent sized orphanage. Was a privilege to also see the original elephant from when the orphanage started up as well as one who'd had one of his legs blown away in a land mine accident (during the war, i think). The place is unique and looks like the elephants really are treated well! Even saw a group of disabled elephants being treated the same in terms of trips to the river and feeding (albeit in a separate group, to stop any trouble i'm guessing). Tip: be prepared to have a bit of cash on you if you want to feed the elephants or even have some close up photo's taken with them. It's well worth it!

I first visited the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage in 2003, returned in 2010 and revisited in 2012. In consequence, I have had the chance to observe developments and changes over the course of a decade. I am also aware that there are some sharp divisions of opinion regarding the place, and have read a selection of derogatory comments from some visitors. To them, I simply say that I do not recognise picture they paint. There is also about some of the comments an aura of rather priggish 1st world condescension, which is unappealing. Let's, therefore, try to inject a sense of proportion as well as, I would add, fairness. Sri Lanka is an impoverished country. Furthermore, it has only recently emerged from a bitter civil war, which claimed the lives of well over 100,000 of its citizens, not to mention a huge expenditure of scarce resources - financial and otherwise. On top of this, it was ravaged by the appalling tsunami of Boxing Day 2004, from the effects of which it is still far from having emerged. Against these unpromising and unhelpful circumstances, the orphanage has continued its work, almost always on a shoe string. Happily, there are indications that it is now being run on a less restricted budget, and infra-structure is in place which was assuredly not there in either 2003 or 2010. Naturally, the orphanage is a tourist hot spot but is not just a cynical 'tourist trap', and, yes, you do have to pay. It is also true that non-Sri Lankan citizens are charged more, although not that much more. One might reasonably ask what on earth do foreign detractors expect? Looking after two or three score of large animals doesn't come cheap, even in a 3rd world country. Moreover, the reality in 2012 was that native visitors far outnumbered foreigners. The suggestion from some that mahoots and other staff are grasping is a small minded canard. My own experience has been quite the opposite. Friendly engagement and a willingness in a small way to help economically produces a reaction that is forthcoming, cheerful and helpful. To whingers who bellyache about having to part with a few tips, my response is "Change your attitude. After all, you are the visitor in their country, and you have vastly greater resources than those you choose to criticise." All of which being said, overwhelmingly the most important consideration is, and must be, the welfare of the animals. On every occasion that I've visited, with a couple of exceptions which I touch upon below, they've always appeared to be satisfactorily round and healthy. They are plainly well fed, and twice a day they are taken down to the river to bathe, wallow and powder themselves in the dust bowls on the far bank. We are not elephants, and so cannot know with certainty what they are feeling. All we can do is try to deduce their state of mind from observation of their behaviour. On this basis, my own estimation is that life for them is great. Someone has written that they observed repetitive behaviour indicating unhappiness. At Pinnawala, I have seen NO such thing. On the contrary, the elephants appear calm and contented. By way of example, there are few species which will placidly tolerate the approach of a complete stranger to a calf. At Pinnawala they will not only tolerate an approach, they will allow gentle petting of the offspring. If one is lucky enough to experience this, it is life enhancing and, at Pinnawala, such enhancements are commonplace! It has been suggested that the staff maltreat the animals by prodding and striking them. It is true that mahoots do both but, in my experience, never viciously. It is also true that some, though by no means all, the animals are shackled. Perhaps those who complain might care to reflect that an elephant is a bloody big animal with a thick and tough hide. They are not going readily to respond to a brush from a powder puff! They might also care reflect that staff probably know a little more about their charges than they do, and that staff have a responsibility for public safety. So, what of the less happy members of the pachiderm community? So far as one can tell from a fleeting visit, the few examples that there are seem to fall into three categories. Firstly, there are those which are plainly a little skeletal, probably the old and the temporarily sick - well, one hopes. Secondly, there is one splendid and awesome old tusker, formerly a ceremonial elephant from the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, who lives alone in his shelter. His desperately sad fate was to be shot and blinded after some fool (as like as not a cretinous tourist) threw a Chinese fire cracker under his feet, causing him to panic and run amok. That said, for all his imprssive bulk, he too in wondrously placid and gentle. Of course, if some idiotic tourist does something stupid, there may be a danger that he will be trodden upon - though, for my money, not nearly hard enough! The third, and most poignant of all, is a little female  first encountered in 2003, who was the wholly innocent victim of human wickedness. She had had her right forefoot blown off by a land mine, and had been rescued and nursed back to something approaching health. Though obviously kindly meant, it remains hard to know with conviction whether or not, in the long run, this was in her best interests. However, for eight or nine years, she was able to manage with her chums, and with them each day hobbled down to the river. In December 2012, she did not seem to be in great shape, and my own feeling is that a bullet might actually be a kinder option than a suffering extistence. That said, I do not see her regularly, and so am assuredly in no position to be judgemental.............and neither is any other occasional visitor! In summary, Pinnawala is not perfect. It has its flaws, but these are slowly being addressed as funding is made available. It is most certainly not simply a cynical money making venture. It needs, and deserves to get, support. Foreigners should regard it as a privilege to be in a position to provide some. RW

I thoroughly enjoyed a recent visit to the Elephant Orphanage in Pinnawala.  When we initially arrived, we caught the end of the lunch feeding.  Some of the smaller elephants were being bottle fed. In an enclosure nearby, there were two baby elephants who were under 12 months old. After the feeding, we walked up a hill to see a number of elephants roaming free around a field.  It was lovely to see them roaming relatively freely although a number of them had chains around their ankles. After a while, we walked across the road and down to the river where we stopped and had a bit of lunch and a cool drink.  Shortly afterwards, the Mahoots herded the elephants down the street to the river where the elephants were able to cool off in the river.  One large elephant was almost completely submerged in the water, all you could see was the tip of the trunk.  In all, I counted a total of 60 elephants in and around the river area. The entrance fee was 2000 Sri Lankan Rupees which is about €12.00.

This was part of my package to Kandy Temple etc. and I was not disappointed.  It is a huge orphanage for the elephants of all ages, where they are well looked after.  To feed a baby elephant with a bottle is a unique once in a life time experience.  They charge for the orphanage, but to see them bathing and playing in the river is free and is really delightful.  Twice a day they are led from the orphanage down to the river for play time in the water.  The best view is from the restaurant which is right on the river bank.  I enjoyed this sight while having a drink or two there.  It is very interesting to watch how they interact with each other.  I have seen elephants in lots of other countries, but not so many in one place.  One thing I did not like was the chains some of them had on their feet.  Opposite the orphanage, there is an interesting shop called POO where they make and sell so many useful articles like paper etc. from the elephant dung.  They have an on site small workshop where the whole process from cleaning it in the beginning to the end product is shown to the tourists.

it was lovely to see them when we went there it was nice to nice them as i never seen ashian elephant before in the wild they had plenty of space to roam and the keepers were in the know about their parentage and we goot to touch a blind one i have been in love with elephants since

If you want to see elephants, there are plenty of other more worthy places in Sri Lanka to see them. This place is simply a slick business designed to part you from your cash at every opportunity. Want a picture with an elephant? PAY! Want to visit the washroom? PAY! Want to feed an elephant? PAY! Want to ask anyone anything? PAY! The staff will actually argue aggressively with you if they think your "tip" is insufficient. This place is no orphanage (and hasn't been for many years). It exists simply to exploit both elephants and tourists. At least I had the choice to leave: God help the elephants...

It was amazing to be so close to these amazing creatures.  It is a breathtaking experience to be right next to them as they make the walk down to the water for bathing and playing.  This is a great stop for adults and children.  Wear a hat or bring an umbrella- shade is very scarce and it gets pretty hot.

We visited the orphanage in November 2012. I did not expect to see so many elephants and have so much contact with them whilst there. It was great seeing the elephants eating and bathing in the nearby river.  A wonderful experience

specially when you travel with kids, the Orphanage is a MUST! Maybe you will never have the chance again to feed an elephant baby with a bottle of milk and you can have direct contact with this wonderful animals. The staff is so friendly and if you give them some pocket money they will give you foods to serve elephant

Having returned home and read other reviews I feel we were so lucky with how our visit to the orphange went.Having fitted 7 days touring into 4 we were running a tight schedule.When we arrived at the orphange, our driver went to buy our tickets and told us the elephants were already down in the river,so we went straight there.Seeing them bathing and playing was amazing we were also lucky enough to be taken in amongst them stroke them and have our pictures taken with them.Yes the handlers asked for money and we gave them some but no where near what they asked for and they were not at all rude or aggressive. Having read reports about the actual orphange we are glad we then left with happy memories and some great photos.

Especially when you travel with children, the Orphanage is a MUST! Maybe you will never have the chance again to feed an elephant baby with a bottle of milk and you can have direct contact with this wonderful animals. The staff is so friendly and if you give them some pocket money, they will take the time to show you everything and let you to the babies too. Twice a day they walk the group to the river for a bath. Well worth viewing this spectacle.

Visited the orphanage today and was fascinated by what they are doing but somehow gained the impression that they now operate more as a commercial concern than as a sanctuary for elephants. The reality doesn't quite live up to the story on the web-site. It now seems to be organised as a tourist facility where the exhibits are elephants rather than an elephant sanctuary that allows tourists in as a by product. I understand why, it must be an expensive facility to maintain but seeing staff on duty whose only objective seemed to be to keep the elephants under strict control rather than controlling the visitors so that they didn't affect the elephants any more than they had too just seemed wrong. Don't get me wrong I think the original objective was fine and worthwhile, it just seems that the elephants now take second place to the tourists; and maybe I'm as guilty as every other visitor for encouraging that.

Pinnawala is approx. 3.5 hours from Bentota, 2.5 hours from Colombo; and 45 minutes from Kandy. We included this as ‘rest stop’ as we transferred between hotels in Bentota and Kandy.  (Toilets at orphanage are clean and there are a number of cafes/restaurants nearby).  If our schedule had permitted we would have preferred to see elephants in the wild at one of Sri Lanka’s many national reserves (e.g. Yala).  But our tour operator and our local guide assured us that the purpose of the orphanage was to care for rescued elephants which had been abandoned or injured and which could not be returned to the wild for a number of reasons.  We were prepared to keep an open mind and on balance were glad  we went even though it did feel a bit regimented and commercialised. The entrance charge for foreigners is 2000 rupees (about £10) which we were more than happy to pay on the assumption that this the money would go to care for the elephants.  Some reviewers seem to object to the lower admission charge for locals (200 rupees) but this is not unique to the orphanage but in our experience this is common practice not just to many Sri Lankan attractions but most of Asia and some parts of Europe. We arrived in time for the 09.15 morning bottle feeding – four elephants in a large concreted area under cover (the elephants were chained by one leg for the safety of visitors).  We also saw two baby elephants in a separate small fenced enclosure; some raised log platforms where elephants were being fed bananas and greenery; a bull elephant being hosed and obviously enjoying the bath; plus the main herd(s) roaming unfenced under the watchful of their keepers. Despite signs at the entrance that visitors should not give tips, most of the handlers solicited 200-2000 rupees from visitors wanting to feed, have their photo taken with or otherwise interact with the elephants. Whilst we were personally uncomfortable with this, the fact is that the elephants are used to human interaction with their handlers (to ensure that they feed at the rights times and don’t endanger visitors). At around 10.00 am the elephants are led across the road to the river.  We spent a lovely 30 minutes relaxing with a drink and snack at the riverside restaurant whilst we watched over 30 elephants freely bathe and romp in the water (there are plenty of riverside tables but I would still go early for a seat with a good view).  Even the bull elephants were unchained for their bath. Some nice gift shops – just say ‘no thank you’ firmly if you are not interested.

do not spend more than an hour for this.. especially if you are from south-east asia and have seen elephants before. I did notice that european and japanese tourists were very excited. This is a delight for tourists who haven't seen elephants before. There is a herd of elephants at the orphanage. The 'King' elephant is blind and chained at a corner of the orphanage. There is another area where a couple of baby elephants are chained and fed. Nice opportunity for a photo-op. The staff there assist you in posing for and clicking pictures, expecting a tip.. Given the fact that in Africa and Kerala (in India), you can have a ride on elephants (bigger ones), i'd rate this elephant orphanage as average.

I truly don't understand how anyone can enjoy this experience, unless they've never seen elephants before. It is hyped up by locals and even guide books as a 'must do' but in truth it's all rather sad, and one is left asking 'are the extortionate fees for foreigners merely a pretext for fleecing them at the expense of the animals, some of which are chained and tethered and appear 'disturbed'. There is absolutely no information giving background on the orphanage, which comes across as a glorified zoo, and a poor one at that. Two people sharing transport from Kandy will pay about 35 dollars each for the trip inclusive of entry, currently Rs 2000. As other visitors have observed the saving grace of the entire venture is the twice daily elephant walk down to the river (via the colorful but tacky handicraft stalls - there were hundreds of tourists around but no one was buying). I almost imagined the elephants as free and wild once in the river, but alas they were soon rounded up and taken back to their compound. I should add that drinks, snacks and ice cream are all sold there but price inflated (more than double the regular price).

Long drive from Colombo arrived and told to pay 2000 rupees each but refused and got away with 500 by saying we were indians from India luckley got away with it.Anway seeing the elephants and young ones in the river was very enjoyable and then we went to the orphange where they stay which was very vast and open but they are chained...We ate at the hotel restaurant overlooking the river and the main attraction is the elephants and the locals know that and just do not leave you alone for money money as they say makes the world go round.... feeding times are at 9.15am and 1.15pm and 5pm plus down to the river at 10am to 12 and then 2pm to 4.00pm leave early as the road to Pinnawala/Kandy is a busy one. Day tour 13,500  rupees Visted 22nd Feb 2013

Had a really enjoyable day out to the elephant orphanage had a long trip to reach it but well worth the visit particularly enjoyed seeing the baby elephants. Great to see the elephants go to the river for their daily bath. Fantastic scenery too.

When we went we were under the impression that this will be the place with rescude elephants, it was not the case though.....absolutely commercilised place. Good things, - So many elephants, different age groups at single place - Well trained elphants - You can see a full family/herd Bad things, - Nothing much to do - Feeding time is converted to money making activity Good for one time watch.......30 mins enough (Go if you are planning to travel to Kandy this will be on the way)

My wife and I spent about 3 hours here and had a great time. We spent quite a lot of money giving tips to the handlers to get up close with the elephants and at one stage where in the middle of the herd, which was quite scary but the experience was fantastic. Go with the idea that you are going to spend a few thousand rupees on the handlers and you will be treated to a great experience. we fed the babies, washed the teenagers and stroked babies and their mums in the herd. Followed them down to the river to get some great pics... a great time and well worth the effort to get there. Go if you can!

Travel forums, both TA and others, tout the elephant orphanage at Pinawala as a must-see. The orphanage itself is a ticketed site where visitors can view the rehabilitation process. The real attraction however is when the elephants are ‘let out’ to play in the nearby river. Watching these elephants, big and small, romping in the river with the forested hills in the background is a memorable experience.

This was a delightful visit.  The elephants are so close you can touch them.  They are curious and playful and fun to watch.  Yes, they try to get you to buy bottles to feed the elephants but you can politely walk away.  Make sure you get down by the river in time for the elephant bath if you go in the morning.  It is fun to watch them all come down the street and then romp in the river.  One old elephant decided to lay down and take a nap in the river while a young one tried to escape from the crowd.  It was as much fun to watch the tourists as it was to watch the elephants.

We went to see an elephant orphange. To see elephants who had been rescued and being cared for. NOT THE CASE!! To start with one price for Sri Lankan people, (200 rupees) one price for foreigners, (2000 rupees) Then when you go in to see the elephants especially at feeding time, a few are kept on a concrete floor under cover, chained up with the food just out of reach, you are then asked by the handler for 500 rupees to feed the elephants! There are baby elephants who are teased with a bottle again the handler asks for 500 rupees to feed the elephant ( even after you have paid at the gate 250 rupees to feed the elephants. ) There is one area where an elephant is chained up close to a log stage, if you climb the stage you can feed the elephant a piece of fruit again at a cost of more rupees. There is a large area where older elephants feed together on open land! A mass of leaves and what seems an excessive amount of elephant dung covering the area, keepers then come and grab your hand saying come,come see the babies. You are lead into the middle of the elephants, told to hold a wooden pole and your camera is taken from you, they take your photograph and then demand 2000 rupees before they hand your camera back. In one area behind the toilet block there is a large elephant chained up stood on a piece of concrete and surrounded by rubbish, the elephant rocking backwards and forwards obviously distressed. It is nice to see the elephants in the river but most still have chains around their ankles some cutting into their flesh. It was a very distressing day. We have no objection to paying a fair price if the money is going to care for the elephants but its just like a badly run circus, a money making ploy with little regard for the elephants. How anyone could enjoy what they where seeing amazes us as it was just awful. NOT a place for families.

This place is quite simply dedicated to extracting as much money as possible from tourists. It lays claim to being an orphanage and it is probably true that a few of the elephants were orphaned but very few and, frankly, how would you know that the small elephant on display "fell down a well and was rescued by a local farmer because its parents abandoned it"? The elephants are driven down to the river in groups at the point of a very sharp stick so that they can be seen bathing and so that their handlers can hustle tourists for having their photos taken with them. Then they are driven back past the tourist shops to be fed. They display crippled elephants like some freak show and many are in chains. In Sri Lnka there are some 6,000 wild elephants in much, much better condition than those in the orphanage and it is not hard to see them. We saw  several beside the road driving between Dambullah and Kandy and there are a number of safari trips available where you can see herds of them. Avoid

We made it in time for the 9.15 am feeding, and there was a 9 month and 10 month old baby elephants who were being bathed seperatedly in a little pond before feeding. They were loving being in the water. I don't understand why they needed to be chained - or some other elephants who were chained. Maybe it is to ensure that thhey don't run wild? But it is a sanctuary?? The charge for foreigners is Rs.2000 (appox £10) and local rate is Rs.100 - Seems a little unfair - but it is calculated against earning power in Sri Lanka so that makes some kind of sense. But after paying for your ticket, if you wanted to feed the elephants you have to pay extra the caretakers?? Somehow that does seem wrong. See the following link for feeding times and details http://www.lanka.com/sri-lanka/pinnawala-elephant-orphanage-in-sri-lanka-94.html Bathing time, was lovely to see this heard of elephants walking down to the river and getting in - although it was the babies who seemed to emnjoy it the most, and the adults looked like they wanted to be elsewhere. Do leave soon after the feeding and make your way down to the river along the path directly opposite the sanctuary gates. Retain your ticekts -you will need them to go through the barrier furthe ralong. Then pick the hotel on the right hand side (it has a huge elephant as its entrance) and sit along the tiered seats facing the river to wait for the elephants to come down the path. Do visit the elephant dung paper museum opposite the sanctuary. All in all it was nice to see these majestic animals - but I felt that there isn't enough care given to them. P.S. be aware of the extortionate prices at nearby places offering elephant rides. In particular the Millenium Elephant foundation - which charges a min Rs.2500 for a 5-10 minute ride around the small area with a v.sad looking elephant, and charges a min Rs.1000 just to enter the place if you don't want a ride (which we had to pay just to take a photo of our friend having her elephant ride). It has a small area which they term ' a museum' - not worth it at all. Actually not sure where this money goes to? Ofcourse for a one off chance to ride an elehpant I'm sure its fine...but I beleive there are better places like in Sigiriya for an elephant ride.

Such a wonderful place to see so many Elephants. I was there 5 years ago and remember feeeding a young elephant with only one ear, so I was so thrilled to see him again grown up now playing witha very young elephant. I could sit there all day watching them down at the river as they are so enjoyable to watch. This time we saw two very young baby elephants with a sad story, however they are both doing well and adjusting to their new safe life at the orphanage.I aggree with another comment someone made that the handlers take advantage of the tourists wich does spoil it a little. This was definatly the highlite of my trip to SriLanka !!!!!!

Pinnawala is a 2 1/2 hour stop/start, dodge/swerve drive from Colombo and cost 2,000R per person to get in.  We arrived at about 10am just as the elephants were crossing the road to go down to the river - a very impressive site.  After reading many different reviews we had wrestled with our consciences about visiting the orphanage, but we decided to go with an open mind and we were very glad we did!  Watching them in the river is lovely, a beautiful setting and seeing so many elephants in the same space is quite breath taking.  They are so tactile with their trunks, constantly touching each other.  Hassling was quite minimal really.  Yes, we were asked several times over did we want to feed the elephants, did we want to touch the elephants, but a firm "No thank you" was all that was needed, the same in the shops on the way to the river.  There was an elephant that had chains on its back legs, but we figured this was probably for good reason - you don't want chaos breaking out in a herd of this size.  We only went inside the actual park on the other side of the road to see a couple of babies (6 and 9 months old - ahhh) - they were genuine orphans that had become stuck in an irrigation ditch.  They were absolutely enchanting.  Again we were asked if we wanted to bottle feed them, and again a "No thanks" was all that was need.  No hassle at all.  All in all it was a fantastic experience.

Dear fellow tourists ..its with mixed feelings as i write this review on pinnawella elephant orphanage.  be aware there are two entry prices tourists and sri lankan locals i paid 2000 rupee  approx $18 australian dollars  this entitled me access to the herbal garden aswell  just outside main facility.. the health of elephants looked quite well  there was a section of injured ones from previous wars . which saddened me. .however the upclose and personal experience i cannot falter  for a small tip you can touch and get photos taken. ( note the handlers will haggle for 1000 rupee but refrain from this as 200-400 rupees is adequate)   you can also feed some banana s  this will incur a 200-300 rupee cost yes alot of money making goes on. there are three sections all together . baby elephants are also in a specific area... elephant rides are available for approx 15 to 20mins this will cost approx 2500 rupee  if you have a local friend price will be 1500 rupee. (bit of sneaky play is in order)  i enjoyed my elephant ride with my partner  was enjoyable please note a guide will take your photos  and will ask for a tip again 500 rupees is adequate as is 500 rupee for the trainer ,. do not get caught up with the sad story they give.     as in one given day they make over 10,000 rupees which is decent in sri lankan currency.. there is also a short walk to restaurant where you can see 20-30 wild elephants bathing in the river this is a great experience times vary so will need to ask  details. .. there was also a snake charmer near restaurant with two cobras and another snake quite thrilling. other gem shops are near by.... the 2nd entry your ticket gives is to the herbal garden i found this quite interesting.  as guide was informative and passionate about his work. they do  sell products which most customs will allow you to bring back.( hair removal, hair tonic, massage and joint oils, weight loss, etc just to name a few all are herbal based no added toxins)  overall this  was a good day . i tipped too much but in hindsite  it dosent work out much in western dollars pinawella  elephant orphanage good place to see.. travel from colombo is approx 2 hrs east inland so driver will be necessary around 6000 rupees for return trip $60 australian dollars  decent price for the return distance... enjoy your time and be safe and smart regarding giving your rupees out. regards gawain kearse brisbane australia

Its a good lace to watch the elephants bath and feed and nice interaction with them close up. I used to come to this place many times per year and had not visited for 6 years or so, I recently went back and much to my surprise they were now charging addition to this area where as before it was few and donation based. also there are many guys willing to get you a close interaction with the elephants and then want a ridiculous amount of money for their assistance. 1000 or 2000 rupee might not be allot for us but in the big scheme of things when the local population makes less than that per day.. it's just a chance for someone to take clear advantage of a tourist… not impressed. but the elephants and magnificent.

It is less than one day trip from Colombo. It is a bit sad ,but still the elephants are impressive. Nice lunch places by the rive where the animals go to bath. Foreigners will pay many times more ,unless you are a resident.the site is beautiful.

A well organised venue, a it touristy, but fees go towards homing orphaned elephants. Can watch them taking a bath in the nearby river and assist with feeding. Watch out for the keepers asking for money to have your photo taken beside the elephants!

We really enjoyed our visit to the Elephant Orphanage.  When we arrived they were down in the river bathing so we went down there first.  It was pouring down but of course they didn't mind!  The full herd went across to the other side to roll in the mud, so lovely how the adults look after the babies on the way across!  There was one with a chain round his leg, but the others were free.  Apparently the one with the chain was a naughty one!  The road down to the river is full of gift shops and the shop sellers of course want you to look, if you say no thank you, they aren't offended.  We had a toasted sandwich, chips and a couple of beers for lunch in the cafe where you can view the river which was lovely and very cheap.  We then went up to the orphanage.  Seeing the elephants wandering free was lovely to see.  There's a couple of injured ones which is quite upsetting and a couple of babies by themselves, but you can tell they are well cared for.  It's possible to pay to feed the elephants milk bottles but they drink the bottle in about 5 seconds flat so not worth doing that, that is just a licence to print money for the workers!  Some people have complained that the admission price for tourists and locals is different - who cares!?!? These attractions have to make money somehow!!  Admission was 2000 rupees per person, £10 each and certainly worth it.  We would definitely recommend this attraction.

We get to feed the elephants and watch the elephants having their baths at the river side. Like the elephants parading from the feeding grounds to the river side for bath. They were so close to you that you can reach out an touch them. The baby elephants will shy away from tourists with cameras, very cute.

Having been to this attraction over twenty years ago I had made a special request to add it to our itinerary Before we were due to visit there was a lot of adverse publicity regarding the orphanage  so I was apprehensive about going We arrived in time for the 9.15 feeding of the young elephants which gives people the chance to feed them IF YOU PAY /TIP  the handlers ,I felt they were rushing the feeding to make money!!It was a very hot day so they were washing an old elephant  ,this was done with care .You had the chance to  visit the area where the elephants were being feed bananas and greenery ,again you could have your photograph taken up close to the elephants or hold the bananas if you PAIDED / TIPPED  the handlers.????Again the older ,blind elephants were being treated kindly Going over the road to the river where the elephants were brought to bath ,leading down there were shops and a restaurant ,it was an amazing to hear the elephants coming down they were obviously excited to be able to bathe Yes some did have chains on but these are big mammals     . Once again I  enjoyed my visit to the orphanage but I do feel that the handlers should be forbidden to ask for or to accept money !! The travel company I travelled with have since made the decision NOT to organise visits to the orphanage !!!

Its quite a commercial place and a famous tourist spot for Lanka, there are two admission prices for locals and tourists making it accessible to all. There is a small cafe, with adequate food. It was amazing to see so many elephants up close, there are hundreds of free roaming giants there. The animals are well looked after and clearly very happy- watching suckling babies, elephants in love and meeting the three legged elephant with no fences was an experience I will never forget. Unfortunately missed out on the ele washing, but next time... The only bits I didn't like as a big animal softie, was the prods to get the big bull who was chained to raise his trunk for photo opportunities. I went on a elephant ride before which i regretted as it distressed me greatly due to the animals condition and treatment, so it was amazing to see such happy elephants in a lovely environment.

It is amazing watching these beautiful animals playing in the river and sliding on the muddy river banks (hilarious!). For an additional tip you will be allowed to touch the young elephants and make pictures with them. It is worth visitng as there are not many place where you will be able to see so many elephants together in one place.

If I could give it less of a rating I would. Firstly this is not an orphanage at all, that is a scam to get tourists in.  The whole place is exploiting elephants that have been in this place for years, and are being born into this hell.  All day long the elephants are dragged by spears for tourists to take photos and for the rude and aggressive staff who go on and on and on trying to persuade you to take advantage of these huge, beautiful, intelligent creatures as they are. As you can see any positive reviews of this place are from selfish people who are so happy to touch or get close to an elephant but clearly couldn't care less about their welfare.  These are the people that I must have seen posing and smiling in front of an old, blind, elephant who is tied by a chain to a wooden column, unable to move more than a foot.  I know that this particular elephant has been here for at least 20 years tied up, most probably longer. Other elephants are also chained up constantly within the reserve, even in the water when they are taken down to drink.  Various stories come from the workers about why this is occurring, all of them different, none of them matter, as it's quite clear that when the doors are closed these elephants are treated even worse than how we see them treated.  I can't bare to imagine, but the fear in the eyes of the elephants, both grown and infants, when they run away scared from the staff here makes it quite clear that they have been beaten by these spears and sticks before to make them behave in such a manner. Elephants are animals that are constantly munching away at grass also as they walk along and I could see scarce food for these elephants, they are fed once a day, one guy told us, this isn't enough and so all day long the able sighted elephants spend their time trying to steal from the blind elephant, who is given an abundance of food, is surrounded by leaves, that he doesn't want, but is given by tourists who will then be goaded into paying the incessant workers there a fee. As well as all this, this is one of the highest one off payments for an excursion that I paid for in the whole country, one I so regret seeing, £10 to see these elephants or £8 (even less if you can haggle further) to go on a safari, in protected land, where hundreds of elephants roam freely, and happy, amongst the jungle with greenery to munch on until their hearts content.  And iff all of these elephants can do it this so called orphanage is a complete unnecessary disgrace.  Being inside this place made me so angry, it was the worst town I visited, I had found the people all over the country to be friendly, here they were exploitative, pushy and rude. I am so sorry that I saw this place but if my review makes people not visit, then it would have been worth it, I took hundreds of photos of the place and tried to capture how badly the elephants are treated, please see the few selected below. If you want to see elephants in Sri Lanka see them on safari, they look so much happier and content and they are free and left alone to do what they want to do, they are not here for our amusement, to be tied up for years on end, uncomfortable, these elephants are just prisoners that are being exploited completely, it is not an orphanage, it is just a zoo, where for a fee and the cost of an elephant's freedom you can touch an elephant or have your picture taken with them.  I heard visitors reciting how it's better from them here they are protected from poachers, I know that I would rather be dead, not chained up by metal chains that have been there for so long, my leg now has a space for them to fit into, or being constantly dragged about by a man with a spear in my head. But they don't have to be dead either, they could be put back into the wild, where I'm sure they were snatched from in the first place and put into this reserve, they certainly are not orphans.

It was my first experience with elephants, so for one hand I loved it. I really enjoyed seeing their river bath, they were with happy and relaxing behaviours. But on the other hand I was disappointed, first because some of them were in bad conditions, always with chains and expressing many signs of captive stress, it was painful to see. Even the hose bath of the little ones was doubtful, I couldn’t understand if they enjoyed it or if they were obliged by the handler. I also noticed that many elephants had serious diarrhea, I suppose they don't treat them. Please DON’T GIVE TIPS! This must come to an end, they have signs in the entrance not to give tips and never the less that place is all about tips: to make a foto, to feed them, to touch them. Let them be at peace, enjoy looking at them and help stop this parallel business that doesn’t help the elephants.

Just brilliant to see so many elephants of all ages wondering aorund. Our guide who took us there steered us away from the staff looking to make a few pennies and as such we were able to do so much with them. He had even arranged for the "golden ticket" so my wife could feed one of the baby elephants and although I knew this would have been in the price I had no problem with that. One up for Ruuchi Tours!!!

We have been to several elephant attractions in thailand which were very good but this one is just a money machine for the handlers as soon as you are in the park the handlers are prodding the elephants with spikes to get them closer to you so you can have a photo taken next to them as soon as you have taken a photo out comes the hand for money from the handler this happened throughout the visit in the end you are to scared to look at an elephant because you know if you do there will be a handler behind you pestering you for money. All the money the handlers pester you for goes in there pockets and not to the orphanage we were also told we would be able to feed the baby elephants but in fact these were not baby's and were chained up and rocking backwards and forwards like they were going mad and as usual as soon as you had fed them out came the hand of the handlers begging for money all in all i would not recommend this trip you may as well go to a zoo. The toilets on site were disgusting and as usual if you needed any toilet paper there was a lady or man outside willing to give you some for a tip of course. When they took the elephants down to the wash area it was the same situation pestered by beggars and handlers for money nice to see the elephants in the river but be prepared to be hassled for money.

As we walked through the entrance towards the bathing area, I couldn't help feeling as though the place was set up more for tourists than conservation. There were shops lining the street and vendors tried to hawk their wares as we walked past, although the elephant dung shop near the baths (where they don't hassle you) was quite interesting. At the actual bathing area, the elephants were interesting to watch for a little while but they didn't look like they were having much fun. Restaurants also lined the edge of the water.

Our son loves elephants and had great expectations but it just turned out to be a moneymachine! Not a single chance to watch the animals without being ripped off by the staff at the park. Remember to ask "how much"? whenever they suggests anything...

I'm torn.  What I loved about it is also something that concerns me: you get really close to the elephants.  It's hard to tell how the critters feel about it when, through no choice of their own, caretakers take bribes to let you touch them for a photograph.  I could tell the 3-legged elephant (injured by a landmine during the civil war) did not like being touched, and yet hundreds of tourists daily are pestering the poor thing.  It does seem to me that the caretakers are otherwise respectful of the elephants and know them well.  I especially enjoyed talking to the man who cares for the two babies.  Feeding time with the big elephants is another sight to see, as it's not often you see such large beings breaking trees for a meal. When you leave, visit the elephant dung paper factory.  Proceeds go in part to support the orphanage.

Part of a long day trip out this orphanage was worth the visit, in that we had not seen an elephant orphanage before.  Very much for tourists not so sure if all the elephants are having fun !  However if some of the money spent by the tourists is helping to provide a better lot for these beautiful animals then good. There were a lot of us buying elephant dung products, there is a lot of it. An easy site to walk around, with a steepish hill down to the bathing area. All well organised with a lot of people looking to make you spend money

Similar to a review I did for an Elephant park in Thailand, I have mixed emotions for places like this. Clearly it is designed for tourism, and conservationism is about 404th on the list of their priorities. The fees are high, and there are unashamedly two prices - local and foreigner. The elephants don't sing or make any noises, that was probably the most troubling thing for me. There is only one tusker there now too, which is also a shame. Classic catch-22 here - you still have to go, because quite plainly to stand in amongst a herd of these amazing creatures is a true once in a lifetime experience. Just do it with your eyes open?
