I was really excited about visiting pinnewala but was very disappointed.  I felt really sorry for the elephants, 365 days per year they are marched back and forth to the lake for 'bath time' twice a day and when they were there, they did not splash about and enjoy water.  They just stood there huddled together.  The staff will try and force you to have your photo taken with the elephants, then demand massive tips.  When I went to tip the one who had snatched a[our camera and refused to give it back, he told me it was too cheap tip and trued to barter for more!! It really ruined it for me!  In our experience people who were trying to take photo's near the elephants themselves, the the mahouts would come along and move the elephants away.  I also felt really sad that some of the elephants were chained up.  On a positive note the baby elephants were very sweet and it was amazing to see so many elephants in one place together.  But I left the experience feeling quite sad.

We visited the Orphanage with our 2 young children, and it was an amazing sight.  Saw about 50-60 elephants bathing, although it was a bit distressing to see some of them were chained to rocks (not sure why). The staff / caretakers seem to do a good job, as all the elephants seemed to be in good health (except for the chained ones). It's worthwhile to get up close to the elephants, as the photo opportunities are amazing, and the elephants are surprisingly prickly!  You will look back at the photos you took in disbelief. Our kids loved feeding the elephants on the elevated platform, which provided lots of giggles and great photos. We went on a hot day during the week, so it was relatively quiet... but hot!  Take lots of drinks & sunscreen, as it's mostly exposed without much shade.  Wear comfortable, closed shoes. Must go early in the morning to make the most of it. For families - take a carrier (backpack-type is best) for toddlers or babies, as there is no way to manouver around with a pram / stroller, unless you want to carry it all the way around (which we did, d'uh!) Note re Fees - the foreign rates are hugely disproportionate to the local rates, but the tourist dollar / Euro is what keeps the attractions going, so it's worthwhile to preserve these attractions.

Do not bother coming to this place if you live animals, it consists of an expanse of dirt with many elephants and their young hearded around on into extort money out of tourists for photo opportunities. The elephants are hit and shouted at and do not look happy. There is no information about conservation or plans for the future of these elephants. The entrance fee is high and obviously goes straight into the hands of some corrupt management. Don't waste your time and energy.

We got to Pinnawala at around 7:45 in the morning. It is a couple of hours away from the airport. We waited for the ticket counter to open at 8:45. The tickets were priced at LKR 1000 a pop , but being SAARC citizens we availed a 50% discount. From the reception it was a short walk to elephant playland. It is a flat open land with no trees or shade , so be sure to carry a hat or the sun will kill you ! And then the excitement - tons of elephants , EVERYWHERE and of all sizes also . Watching them at such close quarters was amazing , especially like us , if you have not been too close to elephants before. We spent a good half hour , just watching and (trying to) touching =) There are however , elephant caretakers who try to make money on everything - be it a photo op or touching the elephants. A highlight for us was the two baby elephants they had there at the time who were 3 and 6 months and in a separate enclosure. SO CUTE ! Elephant feeding time is totally overrated . Dont waste your money on the bottle feed , for two reasons . Firstly they have very few legit coupons available at the counter (a quota) , the rest are all in black through the caretakers and secondly you literally place one finger on the bottle for 5 seconds and the elephant is done =) Before heading to bath time , we walked around the premises. For a government run place , Pinnawala is remarkably well maintained . Its very clean - be it the elephants areas, the reception or the bathrooms. Bath time at the river was super fun. Be sure you get there fast so you can get a good vantage point. On the way there tons of tiny overpriced tourist stalls , dont buy anything from there - total tourist traps . Actual bath time was lovely. The river with its backdrop of greenery is beautiful and the sight of so many elephants playing and splashing in the water is oh - so - adorable. There is a gift shop that sells elephant related products. There was a lot of cute stuff , but the cost is real high, so we didnt get anything . After checking out the gift shop and drinking a cool and relativly cheap king coconut water , we left with some great memories.

If you really want to enjoy your lunch go to the river embankment around 2:00 pm when the herd is taking its bath. Enjoying some fresh juice and food while watching the calves playing near their mom was great but no need to be blind- it's sad to realize that the aim of the orphanage is gone because  even though I enjoyed the view of the elephants in the river, was really shocking seeing some of them chained in the orphanage. I asked why so and no answer from the keepers. Our guide told us that some of the animals there were sick but as I could see most of them are healthy. If there are so many sane and healthy elephants, why don't they free them? Rescuing and healing them is GREAT, undoubtedly but why keeping them after their recovery?????  Money seems to be more important nowadays than the well-being of those lovely beasts...

The mahouts genuinely seem to care for their charges.  The elephants seem very well cared for and have the appearance of being content.  I was particularly impressed w the Poop-to-Paper campaign...elephants do consume 250 kilos / day & poop 90 kilos per day!  So, the concept of making paper from their poop for sale to support their care is an ingenious one.  Hope it succeeds!

if you love animals this is a place you cannot miss! i spent one afternoon there and had they let me would spend a lifetime =) the elephants are the sweetest creatures ever and there are all sizes. I got to pet them, kiss them (well thats me! ) and just shared of their wonderfull energy and great disposition. we saw them bathing in the river, playing like babies (yes even the grown ups), we fed one female elephant who happened to be pregnant and had an enormous appetite ... my definition of Heaven. We didnt do a few things bcs we wanted to spend as much time as we could at Pinnawala and do not regret one bit

If you are anticipating a place where you can learn about elephants, then you will be disappointed. the orphanage is just a place where you get to see lots of elephants roaming freely around you (no cages, etc). In certain sections of the orphanage, you can feed the elephants. We went there in time to catch the elephants going to the river for their bath (1400 hours local time) - quite a sight to see 20-30 elephants crossing the road, going down the path that leads to the river.. After the visit to the orphanage, look for a place called Channa for lunch (about 2-4 km from orphanage, on the way to Colombo)..

We went to see the elephants having their bath in the river. Before you go, enquire what times the 'show' is on to make the most out of it. Note: this is not very friendly for anyone relying on wheels for transport within the attraction. Also, as foreigners, expect to pay triple as what locals are charged. The place is very crowded and there are all kind of flying sellers and other adventurous types. All part of the experience. There is a hotel on the river bank, where you can sit on the terrace and watch the spectacle while having a refreshment or meal (also clean toilets there) and some relief from the constantoffering of buskers/ sellers. The elephants walk down the road and into the river, really beautiful to see them up so close, perfect for photos too... expect 1 - 2 hours

Was looking forward to my visit to the elephant orphanage. Did not really get to spend much time there but the little time I had, it was a sweet and memorable one. Its amazing to see how these huge but gentle animals actually make their way to their bathing spot by the river by having to first cross the road from the orphanage, then make their way through a tiny lane crowded with roadside tourist shops and tourists themselves (of course) and then head down a little slope into the river. It is really heart warming to see how they enjoy and play in the water. However, I think the orphanage has not been maintained too well. It is in quite a badly maintained state. I see some stalls with one or two elephants (one of which is the oldest one who is also blind). The other one is for tourist to feed the elephant. And the rest of the elephants roam freely in an open plain area. You have to be careful when getting near the elephants to take pictures. The caretakers will be standing close by to collect a small fee for taking the pictures for you. Some may even be daring enough to demand for a higher fee. Unfortunately, there is not much information about the elephants and the cause. But I was privilege to get insights and information on the number of elephants, how did they end up in the orphanage, where did they come from, why are they here, etc from our great driver and tour guide. Despite the place seemingly commercialised (which I think it is), but I have to say that I think they do try despite the country being out of the civil war barely only after 3 years.

So here we are, driving for some hours to this place. Yes, there are a lot of elephants. And yes, they had a bath and it was special when they walked all together up to the orphanage. We had high expectations, told the kids etc. And then after 2000 rupee for adult, 1000 rupee for child we came in and it was just a hill where all the elephants were eating and standing. Just like in the zoo. It was not worth all the travel.

Perhaps the Elephant Orphanage started with honorable intentions... but it turned into a commercial circus. We were mainly interested in the cause of the place, to learn about elephants in Sri Lanka, the problems they face, etc... . But there is NO information at all (except about two new arrivals). This place should, because of its commercial success, be the leader in raising awareness for the Sri Lankan elephant. Sadly a missed opportunity. We also do not get why they have a breeding program when it should all be about helping orphan, wounded or old elephants... instead of breeding more tame elephants. But again, no information. The handlers were sometimes very rough with the elephants, and seemed more interested in collecting tips from as many tourists as possible. The milk feeding was fun, but lasted about 5 seconds... keep your camera ready! We recommend going to the Millennium Foundation (also known as the "Elephant Bath") instead. Besides learning about the cause, you actually get close encounters with the elephants (e.g. by giving them a bath). All earnings at the Millennium Foundation are used to support their programs to cure sick or injured working beasts, free of charge. They do not breed (besides one 'accident') and provide good guides which will tell you everything you want to know about these wonderful creatures.

We arrived just in time for the Elephants to finish their bath in the river and head back to their shelter for food and rest. Feeding the Elephants with Milk and Bananas was a sweet experience indeed! The restaurants next to the shelter are not very impressive in terms of decor but their kitchen makes up for it.

We arrived rather late at Pinnewala and just missed the elephants who had finished their bath at the river but as we were browsing in the shops the elephants returned from the river. QUITE A SIGHT to see 50+ elephants walking down the narrow street with shops on either side with their mahouts. That was quite a special moment as I could have reached out and touched them. After a lazy lunch on the terraces of the restaurants facing the river, the elephants came back for their next bath after 2 hours. Great location to get a good photo from the terraces of the restaurants.

We started by going to the orphanage after paying the entrance ticket. I don't mind paying the ticket since it's supposed to help elephants in bad condition, which you can see they do. They had a couple of youngster that had been found hurt in the forest. BUT I do mind that the staff seemed to be more interested in getting additonal tips/fees for "everything" inside the orphanage. They were friendly and fotographed us in front of the male elephant, but asked for money, you could feed the "babies" if you pay an additional fee etc, etc. Really sad. The big experience was to watch the elephans go swimming in the beatiful river.

Let me begin by saying your holiday is defined by your EXPECTATIONS. It your closest experience with a elephant was seeing Disneys Dumbo as a child or watching the one scene on Blue Peter where Lulu the elephant pees and poos next to Peter Purves as he does his best breakdance impression to recover from the turd slip in the BBC studios, then you will thoroughly not be disappointed with this place. This is where you get the Tripadvisor 5 star ratings from. If like me you actually have a brain and have done a bit of travelling and have at least an ounce of common sense you'll know why I gave this a 1 star rating. First of all, it is a far place to drive to, so once you are there you feel compelled to see some sort of elephant "show" (or orphanage as they refer to it). Make sure you leave plenty of time if like us you are travelling from Kandy. Feeding begins at 930am. You pay your entrance fee of 2000 Rupees (USD$15). Noone explains to you what to do and where to go and maps for visitors are non existent (bargain for $15 entrance!). Pretty much like all Sri Lankan extortionate entrance fees. We follow the crowds of snap happy tourists to the feeding pen where there are 4 elephants. 1 large one leant over the railing in some sad pain left unattended with a wonky leg, one chained down for you to spray a water hose on, the other chained within trunks reach of some shrubbery to tempt it and the last one used as a showcase for drinking milk bottles. It was a tourist frenzy. A lot of people snapping away wanting photos of themselves pouring 250 rupee bottles of watered down milk into the elephants mouth. Bottle after bottle after bottle. I haven't seen so much milk consumed since I accidentally wandered in the breastfeeding clinic as a child when I went to get my tonsils out!  There is no one available to explain anything to tourists. It is a pure freakshow event performed to take tourists money. And guess what? 90% fall for it. You are constantly asked to come and feed or take photos with elephants in exchange for the begging hand that comes out after the photos have been taken. I swear I've never been wished a Happy New year so many times followed by the  words "money" and "tip". Here's my tip for sensible travellers. IGNORE. Don't even make eye contact with the mahout and they won't hassle you. As soon as you make eye contact you engage in conversation then it's your game to price fight your way out of the situation. The elephants are clearly frustrated, over fed and in need of care and loving attention. They are in the enclosure purely exploited for money.  Feeding continues until the tourist rupees decline and the zoo operators (local men who have no clue how to speak English and have no clue about elephants) move onto the other prosperous areas. We follow the crowd onto the main part of the zoo (notice I'm not calling it an orphanage) to see about 30 elephants all eating freely in front of us. Clearly if they decided to go AWOL we'd all be in trouble but our safety comes after the rupee. Again we are surrounded by local zoo keepers who hassle you to take pictures in exchange for money and if you want to take photos yourself they push elephants away with spears or chase them away with their weird elephant noises. Very childish I thought. As I said. If expectations were to see loads of elephants this is your best opportunity to get close and personal and get some great photos. If you have a conscience you'll be disgusted as I was. Next was the chance to feed the elephants. Was it free? He'll no. More money for some tired old fruit I didn't buy. As soon as I asked about the elephant, e.g. How old he was, they looked away and went back to their conversations, probably talking about who had the longest mullet. After this we left the zoo compound and headed out into the road where we waited for the elephants to be walked out of the zoo onto the main road and through a busy street that seemed to sell amongst many things, recycled elephant poo. The elephants processing down the road is an amazing sight and you have to be careful and stand back. Tip of the day. Make sure you go earlier and walk down the street all the way to the end where they bathe otherwise the police hold you back and may check your ticket. In reality you don't need a ticket to walk down a road of shops and hotels so if you get there early and are not bothered about the zoo you can see them bathe for free. If they do ask you, then you can always say your hotel is on that road or make up some other lie. Bathing is also a place where you can grab some great shots. I was lucky or unlucky enough to see a bull mount a cow and try to mate with it. Unfortunately I had just ordered a banana smoothie so not the best time to be sipping that whilst watching two elephants go at it like two distressed teenagers. Needless to say again the mahouts try and hassle you for money to take photos. If you don't pay they push the elephants away. This is the end of the show. We bought a few tourist gifts from the shops. One being a thank you card made from recycled elephant poo but I left the place with a more bitter taste in my mouth than elephant poo could ever make. Not a place I will ever go back to. Some great photos but seriously Sri Lanka, sort your tourism out otherwise you'll have none coming back in the future.

This orphanage is located just off the Colombo-Kandy Highway. Ideal time to reach the orphanage is just before it opens at 8:30 am. This allows you to start interacting with the elephants as they are being let out of their enclosures. There are not many people in the morning as well and this allows you to take your time if you are interested in the bottle feeding or the fruit feeding. There are around 100 elephants of all sizes here with the youngest being as young as 4 months. After the feeding session, the herd is taken for a bathing session to the nearby river, this offers stunning photo opportunities with the Palm trees and mountains as a fabulous postcard backdrop. A must visit location for anyone who wants to come close to experiencing elephants in their natural habitat.

I was keen to view this so called orphanage on my Sri Lankan Trip and thanks to my guide who had no fear of asking my questions I found answers.  This place is not about conservation, integration or for the love of elephants, it is just a money making scam that now breeds majority of it's elephants to attract the money from tourists. One of the first elephants you are introduced to is an old bull elephant, he is blind, been at the orphanage for 12 years, he is chained up and fed and watered by the keepers when the tourists are around with rupees.  For a nice little "tip" you can stand right next to this elephant and have your photo taken.  The Bull Elephant is blind and if you take the time to look at him as an elephant rather than an object then you will notice the muscle wastage in his front legs and that most of his body is propped up against a large pole.  When asked if he goes to the river or has a walk around I was initially told that because he is blind he has to stay in one place, when I pointed out that elephants have bad eye sight and rely on hearing and smells I was told that they once took him to the river when he first arrived but he couldnt find his way back so has never moved in 12 years from where he is.  They now claim he can't walk because of arthritis. In the main "free" area the elephants (especially the babies) are dragged up to tourists to have there photos taken, all for a price of course!  Some of the older elephants tried to make a move from the main group, one of the keepers moved them back with his voice and pole, when the elephants got back on the right side the keeper than ran after them with the spear like hook on the end of the pole in anger at them. Then moved down to see the two alleged orphans who are in a pen of their own opposite a very bored un naturally chained up female elephant and her baby.  The mother was extremely distressed, keepers kept bringing tourists down to stand next to the baby to once again have their photos taken after handing over a couple of hundred rupees.  When I asked why they were chained to posts I was told that they were sick.  So sick elephants are chained up in the middle of the park?  I asked how long and was told "only a day or so", the baby elephant had clear pink and not the grey skin on his legs where the chains had rubbed his little legs and then had been changed to the other legs. Two elephants who have now been trained to this circus walk down twice a day to be bottle feed, this involves them being chained up and then parents paying lots of rupees for the child to hold a bottle of milk for the calf to suckle. This place is an absolute disgrace to the extent of animal cruelty to a sickening degree and every tourist that paces through the gates is lining the pockets of a management who only care about profit and not animal welfare.

Elephants everywhere. we watched the elephants bathing in the river. the small elephants were very cute. it was such a nice sight to see the elephants bath then take mud bath and walk around. and if you have to get close to the elephants you have to tip otherwise you can politely refuse. we loved this place a lot

Whatever this orphanage used to be, it ceased to be that a long time ago. Our driver and hotel staff said this was a great care facility for orphaned elephants and it had good reviews on trip advisor, so we went. Be aware though... your driver will likely take you to another elephant place called millenium. Insist that you do not go in. It is an elephant farm/tourist scam that is in no way fair to the animals. Pinnawala has a steep price of 2000 rupees per foreigner and once inside I immediately regretted it. The grounds are small and crowded with far too many elephants, most of which we found out are bred just foe the park so tourists can see them. I felt horrible looking at the animals chained down to be fed. You read that right. You can feed the animals for an additional steep fee and they are chained to one place so they have to accept what tourists give them. The bull male is chained so he can stand and do little else, so people can get a snapshot next to a full grown male with tusks. The whole park is a disgrace to animal welfare and an overpriced tourist trap. If you want to see elephants in natural settings, visit one of the amazing national parka in Sri Lanka.

If you want to see elephants up close and personal it's a great place to go. We reached when the herd was being brought back from the bathing in the river. That was a great experience for the kids. They loved it! Inside the facility, there does not seem to be a good guide or tour. You are pretty much on your own. We just strolled around and found our way. Milk feeding is a big eye wash, firstly they didn't tell us we needed tickets. Then when we saw what they were doing during the feeding, I'm glad we didn't buy the tickets even if it was a mistake :-) the mahout holds the bottle and let's you touch it and take a picture. Nothing to die for! The food stall at the entrance is a rip-off. They asked my for 200/- sri lankan rupees for a bottle of water that was list price for 70/-. She says that was for locals. I got it at a lot cheaper in the area where they were feeding the elephant. Funny chaps... We did get very close to the elephants once in the park. You can ask the mahout to bring the elephant to wait till you and your family take a picture. They do expect some tips. We paid 100/- and they were happy. If you are local or look local they may not bring the elephants closer to you unless you are willing to walk up to them and say you will give them a tip :-) Overall, worth the visit. Try to go there if you can.

We were quite shocked and disappointed when we visited. Firstly it's very expensive but we wouldn't mind that if we thought the money was used for a good cause. In exchange for your cash you are provided with no information on elephants either in general or here in particular. You just wander around and  there's little point asking any of the staff - they seem to have no knowledge or interest but are just there to extract 'tips' out of the visitors. Walking around with our 6 year old son he kept getting grabbed by the arm by staff to make him touch / stroke / squirt water at an elephant regardless of whether he wanted to or not. Of course each such encounter leads to grasping hands and demands for more cash. The atmosphere is just horrible and the staff are just using the elephants as an extortion racket. My 'tip' of 200 rupees for my son to stroke an elephant was dismissively turned down by the staff member who demanded more. When I put the money back in my pocket and turned away he physically grabbed me. We've been to a similar but much less well known elephant centre in Chiang Mai last year which was infinitely better - informative and with staff who seemed to have a genuine interest in both the animals and the visitors. Catering facilities are pathetic. There is a cafe but they would provide cooked food only for locals (??) - we had to make do with crisps and chocolate for lunch 'Feeding time' just means you pay extra cash to touch the feeding bottle while having a photo taken. 'Washing

80 elephants in the river - from tiny babies playing to massive bulls standing a bit aloof to one side - and you can get to within a few yards of them on the banks of the river. Fabulous! We spent Jane's birthday there earlier this year and it was probably the highlight of our visit to Sri Lanka. The mahouts seemed to know their stuff and treated the animals firmly but affectionately.

At Pinnawala, you can see the elephants which have been orphaned due to many causes. Some of the new generation elephants have been born in captivity. Hence I am not sure whether they qualify as "real" orphans. However, this is a safe haven for elephants as they are protected and fed at this place. You can feed the baby elephants at this place and you can also touch the elephants. Although the workers might ask the foreigners for tips, the foreigners are not bound to give any. The elephants are taken to a river which is situated close by at certain times of the day and the bathing elephants are a pleasing sight. Closer to the Elephant Orphanage, you may find a lot of shops which sell different products that can be kept as souvenirs of your visit to Pinnawala. They might be over priced though. However, there is a place where elephant dung products are sold. They are expensive but they are worth the money that you pay. There is also a small workshop at the back of this shop and if you request them to show you how the elephant dung products are made, they will take you to the workshop and show you how it is done. This is one of the things that I liked the most about this place!

The trip to the orphanage can be done quickly, though try and feed them (very cheap). But get down to hotels next to river before the crowds come to watch them bathe in the nearby river. And be sure to get as close to street edge when they all march down.

this is a good place to see Orphan elephant. tickets price is high for foreignes. You can come this place by bus. You need to get down at " karadupana" junction in kandy - colombo road ( A1 Road) or go to kegalle and take a bus to " rabukkana. ( From karadupana junction to  Orphanage it's only Rs.15-20/= .. Distance 6KM . public bus service available ) In karadupan junction many taxi drivers try to offer ride to foreignes. They may tell to buses to not to stop for you.many people are there to offer many things because near places give very good commission money who bring tourist to their shops. Trick ~ If you are not intersted in watching feed, You can see elephant bath free .. :) becasue river is on other side so they bring elephant to other side. Go there before the bathing time and directly go to the river. They will ask show the tickets, Just tell them we are going for b'fast to the restaruent or  we have reservation on elephant bay hotel or pinnalanda hotel or we first go to check room and evening we are planing to see elephan. they can't refuse because you are go to a private place. so directly go to a hotel and buy a drink and watch elephant free

The milk feeding is not worth to go. The elefants are not quite small ones. Children, but to large vor babes. The zoo is nice and you can get a picture touching the elefants. The drawback are the guards. They constantly want money for doing nothing. The best part is the river bath. For me it is the only time elefants can be elefants. The babes are playing in the water and at the river side. It is at 2pm and goes for 2 hours. It is very nice to see.

If you want to see an elephant, it's cheaper to go to a zoo in England. This place used to be a real elephant orphanage, now it's just a tourist trap. The main object of the keepers is to prod the animals into a position so you can can have your photo taken with them and then they will ask for a tip. It's a great shame, for I remember  the great charm that was here originally and the genuine affection the few locals had for the animals. The times they are a changing. Pedroofpobla

Our guide explained that, of the 90+ elephants currently at this "orphanage" only about 3 were real orphans, while another 4 were in need of special attention (including one who lost a leg in a landmine blast, one which is blind, and 2 very young ones rescued from wells. Being animal lovers, this made us apprehensive as it started to sound more like a zoo than an orphanage. While most of the elephants were free to roam a relatively large enclosure (surely too small for such a large herd?), we were not so happy to see the elephants chained down for "feeding". Or the bull elephant in must, also chained down and in a separate pen as he would be too aggressive during this period. It was great being able to get so close to the elephants, even touching them while the handlers kept a close watch. But I am not convinced that this is something I will do again.

Before writing about the orphange I would like to warn tourists that some of the travel agents or van/tuk tuk drivers insist the tourists to visit other places like the Millenium Elephant park which are on the same road.These places have very few elephants and they have different packages(bathing and ride,feeding and ride,short ride,long ride etc etc) which are expensive.Please dont visit these places as they are run for fully commercial purpose and they are not orphanages.We also got confused at first but took the right decision of not going there and instead visit the main orphanage. We had to pay 500 LKR as we are Indian nationals and other people outside of SAARC countries have to pay 1000 LKR entry fee.This place is very nice as you can see so many elephants roaming freely.Being from India,we knew that there will be mahauds who will be asking for money to pose with or feed the elephants.So we kept these options out and just enjoyed seeing the elephants and striking pose with them on our own.There are two very young(one 3 months n the other 7 months old) elephants which are not to be missed out its rare to see such small elephants. At 2 pm the elephants are taken to the river on the other side of the road for bathing and we enjoyed it clicking some shots. All in all its a nice place to spend 2-3 hours with these lovely creatures.

Supposedly this is a sanctuary for the elephants and orphaned little ones .. It might just actually be that but you also get the feeling its designed to get the all important US$ .. Hopefully that is going towards the pachyderms to give them what they need .. I did see some injured and really old animals that seemed to have a free hand roaming around without the use of a stick or mahout .. Depending on time of day though, you will see the elephants being driven down to the river for bathing and then made to pose for photos, and careful how much you tip .. Dont miss the old elephant with tusks .. Looked like he was in Ice Age At the bathing river there are of course the rows of soveigner shops (overpriced), and a snack bar .. You can have a bite and watch the elephants .. If the intention is right (the future of elephants), you should take a visit there and see them ..

Excellent place. Must visit. Good no. of calf's. Entry fee for SAARC country citizens is SL Rs.500, for milk/fruit feeding Sl Rs 250 for other foreignors SL Rs.1000. Everyday morning and evening the elephants are taken to the nearby river. Tourist are allowed to take pictures with elephants, though you may have to give tips. Nearby restaurants are okay to have light snacks/refreshments

What a unique experience to get up close and personal with elephants at the Pinewala Elephant Orphanage.   The reality is this a commercial venture and costs of managing an operation on this scale must be tremendous.   I am grateful for the opportunity to come into close contact with such gentle giants.    It was heartwarming to approach the young elephants and heartbreaking to see elephants that had lost limbs due to land mines in the region.   In such cases of political consequence, a sanctuary like this is an injured elephant's only chance of survival.   I am grateful to have experienced and contributed to the well being of the Pinewala Elephant Orphanage.

They breed elephants here so they'll have a steady supply of babies.....which they solicit money to have tourists feed them bottles of milk.  The elephants are not free to do what they want here.  They are on a tight display schedule. Some are tied up for photographs.  I witnessed a worker chasing elephants from one area where they were eating to another area with the big stick - for no apparent reason.  Our group witnessed elephants lying in the river which were given "the stick" multiple times to stand up -- just to pose for a photograph with tourists for $$.  Elephants only get a limited time in the river; they are driven back to the main display areas. This is NOT a sanctuary!  These elephants are poked and prodded all day, if not chained.  Very sad!

The Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is a great place to visit and spend a few hours. They do a great job in rescuing abandoned and injured elephants and the entrance fee goes towards the cost of operating and maintaining the orphanage. Some parts of the orphanage looks like it is taken advantage of the tourists (ie. buy a bottle of milk to feed the younger elephants) but they need the revenue to maintain the huge amounts of food that elephants consume each day. All the elephants look like they are well looked after so I say good job to the management and staff members!

This is a must see if you are traveling nearby. Since we have been traveling around Sri Lanka for a few months, we brought our passports and our admission was at local price. So if you are staying in the country for a longer visit be sure to bring your passports since the local fee is 100 LKR compared to the tourist fee of 2000 LKR. The orphanage contains elephants that have either been rescued or born there. It has a minor zoo feel, but they have a decent amount of room for the animals and most are not chained up. The workers will help you get close to an elephant to pet and they will take lots of pictures for you but be prepared that they will expect a tip. It costs 200 LKR for a plate of fruit to feed an elephant but you can not share the plate or take turns feeding with your party. You can also buy a ticket to feed an elephant a bottle. The best experience of our day was bathing time which is scheduled at 10am-12pm and 2pm-4pm and this is included in your admission fee. They walk the elephants down a street full of shops to the nearby river which has a beautiful view - perfect for photo taking. If you have extra cash, I would recommend having a worker take you down to the water so you can help bathe an elephant. It was an amazing experience and they took many great photos for us with our camera. Just again be prepared to give a tip! I would recommend going early in the morning as it is a little less crowded and it can get very hot or rainy in the afternoon. The gates open at 8:30am and feeding time begins at 9:15.

We booked a day trip to Kandy during our recent hoilday at The Blue Water hotel. Our own travel company had not made any contact with us so we asked the hotel about trips on offer. They gave us prices and itineraries to various places but on talking to guests in the hotel it was clear that the best tours were offered by a company called Ruchitours which were based in an office just behind our hotel. We met Ruchi on the beach and he came to the hotel and spent time with us going through places we could visit. He offers bespoke trips and the beauty is there is just you Ruchi in a minibus with a great driver! Also competitively priced. We decided on the Kandy one day trip. After a very early start, our first  stop was the Elephant orphanage. Amazing! Ruchi had managed to secure tickets to feed the baby elephants - not everyone gets to do this so this was a real bonus. We were also first at the river to see the elephants have a bath. We could wash them too If we had wanted. They were beautiful creatures and the work they do there is fantastic. There were mother elephants who had obviously adopted babies and could be seen stroking the orphans with their trunks. We stroked them and fed them some bananas and then watched 2 baby elephants run playfully off into the water like naughty children. The elephants are well looked after and it feels as close to a normal habitat as possible for them. Feeding the baby elephant was the highlight. The huge bottle of formula didn't last long. We the went onto visit a herb and Spice farm, the Temple in Kandy and a tea plantation but the elephants were the highlight for me. A great day thank you Ruchi tours. Email address  if you want to prebook bespoke tours of Sri lanka is: rucitailoredtours@ hotmail.com

it is a must visit place in sri lanka when you are in sri lanka. the only elephant orphanage in the world. you could see how the jumbos eat,drink,bath and so many things about them. remember to take your camera with you to take memorable pictures. once in a life time visit

I'm not a fan of captive animals as a tourist attraction but as pinnewala is an orphanage we decided to visist. I think that it is certainly better for the orphaned and abandoned elephants here than other places where they are riden by tourists. It is a fairly big area and the elephants roam around in groups freely but are bought up for tourists to feed etc.They are taken to a nearby river daily for baths but as the river was too high they werent taken  while we were there. Tip there are two seperate entry gates one  for locals one for tourists(the tourist queue was heaps shorter than the local one)

Pinnawala elephant orphanage is surely a memorable experience. They are doing a pretty good job of rescuing elephants and have donation coming from all over the world. Giving elephant rides is a way of raising money for the elephants. Don't expect too much from the ride, the 10 minute ride barely lasts 10 minutes and I saw some people arguing over this. The way I see it, we spend a lot of money here n there then why not donate some for a good cause like this. I must warn you, my legs were numb when I got off! lol...

Considering an orphanage , its very well maintained and the elephants are given food at regular time. Now the sad part, if you properly observe the elephants, then you discover that one of the elephant has only one ear and one elephant is blind. This goes to the fact that these elephants were saved from pathetic situation like landmine blast or poachers. It was very depressing to hear the stories of few elephants and how they were tortured in the past before they were bought here. Also point to mention, the money hungry mahouts, who take money in return you can feed the elephants. I personally do not like such activities. The elephants are taken to bath twice everyday in the river nearby. As a SAARC citizen the entrance fees was 500 LKR. I would rather wish these elephants were sent into the wild as its there natural environment. The food is very expensive here.

The Orphanage is certainly cashing in on the tourist dollar with local and foreigner entrance fess being hugely different. But part of me says, "Good on them". Generally, we tourists are more cashed up than the average local Sri Lankan! What became tedious, however, was the constant request from staff for money - for photos taken, feeding fruit/milk to elephants, for answering questions. The management seriously need to take this habit in hand with their staff. I'm happy to pay generous admission prices but expect some of that to go towards decent wages so I'm not constantly hassled for more money during my visit. Apart from that, our visit was magical. You can get right up close and observing the elephants at play is so special. Feeding fruit/milk to the youngsters was worth the 200 rupee for our 6yr old daughter.

It was evident the elephant's at Pinnawala were being very well cared for, though I have to say the Orphanage felt a lttle more like a zoo than an orphanage - perhaps I'm splitting hairs. It was great to be able to get close to so many Indian elephants: there were approximately 80 elephants in the orphanage when we visited. Give it a go :-)

Hi, Pinnawela Elephant Orphanage is a cruel place- and is no orphanage. They send elephants to circuses and an elephant died last year at the hands of a staff member (who brutally attacked it). This is no place to promote or put your money towards. If you are looking for an elephant rescue centre in Sri Lanka- try Millenium Elephant Foundation- just not Pinnawala

Instead of spending the money to go inside the park, just wait out front to see the Elephants parading down the street to the lake and be up close to them at the lake. I've been to many elephant sanctuaries around Asia and this government run orphanage is a downer. The mahouts are very greedy and will try to squeeze any money out of you for any price. For foreigners who don't do the research on trip advisor, be aware that you do not need to pay any money for taking a picture with an elephant!! Feeding the elephant, or bathing the elephant at the park is also a major rip off. You'll spray the elephant for 5 seconds with water and take a picture, thats it! You'll also get to shove milk down the babys throat for 5 seconds as well. Instead ask your guide, driver, or someone in the neighborhood about local elephant owners in the neighborhood who offer these perks. For a cheaper price you'll get to feed, bathe, or ride their elephant for as long as you want for an up close and personal experience. From what our driver told us, it's about 10 US Dollars to bathe and feed them. Also be aware of beggers nearby that will hold your hand to do a fake palm reading and then ask for money!

We passed by there on our way from Kandy to the airport .. The place is very smelly! We chose the shortest experience, as we didn't have time .. There are 3 in general .. We had a little tour, watched the elephants taking a bath, we rode the elephants which was an AMAZING experience, & then we fed them fruits :) .. In general, it's a lovely interesting thing to do, especially if you have kids ..

I had a mixed trip here some good points some bad: I arrived early before the park opened and the guide suggested taking an elephant ride.  The ride was a little scary at first, its a LONG way down!! But the elephant walked incredibly slowly so felt safe.  I asked for a half hour ride in which we went up a lane, back again a very quick paddle in the water and then that was it (I'm sure it was more like 15-20 minutes but I was pretty happy to have both feet on the ground).  A half hour ride was 5,000 rupees and an hour ride would have been 10,000 - quite a lot in my opinion. But that was all fine my gripe here was with the staff.  As soon as I had paid for the ride the guide was harrassing me to give the person who looked after the elephant a tip of 500 rupees.  I really do not appreciate being harrassed in to doing something against my will, may be this is because I'm not from a 'tipping culture' but all the same I think it should be up to the individual on whether you give a tip or not.  Anyway this man would not go away and I parted with a 500 rupee note.  Then he held out his own hand repeatedly saying "tip" "tip" apart from a few 20 rupee notes I only had 2000 rupee notes and I'll be blown if I was giving him that.  I gave him a bunch of 20 rupee notes and got away as fast as I could.  I even wouldn't have minded so much had he been an informative guide but most of the time he was far ahead spitting on the ground.  But I have to be fair to him he did take a couple of nice pictures.... I then paid 2000 rupees for entry into the orphanage.  We went to see the elephants being fed this was lovely to see them interacting in a more wild way however again you were constantly harrassed by staff trying to get you to have your picture taken next to an elephant so they can have a tip.  This continued for the whole visit, I understand this is the way they operate and also how the make money but it made me feel uncomfortable and pressured.  I learnt not to make eyecontact and to ignore them if they talked to you. I got taken on a tour of a botanical garden where there were some coco trees and cinnamon trees.  I could tell this was the prelude to a sales pitch so I made it quite clear I wouldn't be buying anything to which he then just walked off. After this we got to see the elephants bathing in the river and for me this was the absolute highlight.  This is what I came here to see elephants playing and interacting with each other not the guides.  There were some adorable young elephants who obviously loved bathing time and enjoyed every second. I would love to see elephants again but would only go if it was a more wild environment, I love seeing them behave naturally not chained up.  The elephants looked healthy and happy (to my eyes) so I'm not insuiating that they are poorly treated at all, I would just prefer to see them at a distance in future where they can play normally and I am not harrassed every few minutes by staff. Just to add I do tip but where I feel the service warrants it but I hate doing it because I have been pressured into it.

The whole point of us going to Sri Lanka was the Pinnawalla Elephant Orphanage, before we got there our driver suggested we call in at a friends who had some disabled elephants, we agreed, it was a wonderful experience and just a few metres from the Orphanage, my girlfriend got to ride an Elephant down to the river and was absolutely soaked, we had lunch then moved on to the main attraction. There is a bit of a walk onto the site which for me was a struggle but it was really worth all the struggle, all the elephants being shepharded down to the river in all there must of been 50, what a great site, really recommended.

Not to be missed place specially when you have kids with you on the trip. We did not go inside the orphanage as all the elephants were on the river for bath. Just ensure that you visit this place only if you have kids/children with you.

Wonderful to see so many elephants bathing in the river, tramping through the streets and being fed in the Orphanage itself.  The mahouts/ handlers are a bit scary, asking for money for a photo or a touch of an elephant, but if you ignore them there's a whole load of wonderful sights & photo opportunities.

We arrived a little late, so missed the feeding. Highly recommend to come early enough to see the feeding before they walk the elephants to the river for bathing. They were beautiful and majestic to watch & we were able to get up to close with the elephants. Travelling with my Sri Lankan partner (I am Australian) they tried to charge him the 'foreigner' rate for entry, being 10x the local rate. After some discussion & with the assistance of a travel guide who was also queuing along with us, they relented & allowed my partner in on local rates. Agree with the other reviews about the money grabbing. We were expected to pay/tip for any photos with elephants & there are lots of people loitering around trying to sell their wares, otherwise would give the top rating. Would happily return.

Would not recommend feeding the elephants.  I had a bottle of milk shoved in my hands by the handler who actually fed the elephant.  It was crowded, noisy and smelly. I found the conditions, with the animals chained up, distressing.  I did enjoy watching the elephants roaming free in the paddocks.  Unfortunately the river was too high to see the elephants bathing.  Perhaps we should have scheduled in a quick visit to a national park to see wild elephants instead.

This elephant orphanage is one of the cutest places I've ever been to. So many elephants at such close range is hard to find, except maybe in Chobe National Park in Botswana. Anyway, there is an entrance fee to the orphanage and if you want to take your picture with an elephant then you have to pay a hefty extra fee again directly to the mahout. And you get asked all the time whether you want to have your picture taken... There is a separate building for baby elephants where they get fed and played with (picture no. 5). Also we were told that there were not so many orphan elephants coming in anymore but that most of the young elephants were actually born there. Whichever way it is, it seems to be a thriving business - but what a cute one! There are 3 elephant bathing time. The first one is around 11am. Then you can stroll around the open area where you can take pictures with the elephants. After that, you can proceed to the riverside for viewing the elephants to bath

I visited this Lovely Place several time and each visit giving your great Experience and each time it was highly enjoyable. There is lot of gift shops and you can visit, don’t miss to stroke the elephants and follow them down to the Mahavali Ganga to watch their bath. It’s Amazing...

It was lovely to see so many elephants at the Pinnewala Elephant Orphanage, however it was sad to see some of them chained up. Some of them were left to roam free and so I assume there was a valid reason to have some chained up, but it was sad watching some try and pull away from the chains. It was however lovely to see so many elephants in a natural environment, especially when it was bathing time down at the river. If you don't have the chance to see elephants in the wild during your stay, Pinnewala Elephant Orphanage is worth a visit and I'm sure the entrance fee helps the elephants somehow.

This is an awesome way to get to know elies and their habits. They spend around 4 hours a day bathing, playing and chilling out in the river. There are loads of places to view these creatures in a natural habitat and there seems to be no rush to get back to the orphange which I love. I was a little disappointed that I couldn't learn more about the elephants and their indivdual stories on how they got to the orphangae and personalities however they all seemed pretty happy. I would definately recommend getting there for midday and spending a couple of hours just watching and being entertained!

My wife and I went to Pinnawala Elephant sanctuary and had a really good time. We were guided around with our taxi driver who was very knowledgable. The actual site is good and you can really interact with the elephants (sometimes at a small charge). After you have been guided around you can go to were the elephants bathe. We done this relaxing from the Bar whilst taking some really good photos. My only gripe was that when we were there, there was a conference for the commonwealth ministers which took a bit of precedance over us. Certainly worth a visit

I visited the elephant orphanage in '99 and again this year. What I have noticed is that this time round it was all about the money. The orphange is great to rescue lame/orphaned elephants.  What is not great is the men working there who want money if you are taking photos. Or asking for money to feed the elephants. The entrance fee (2000rupees) for adults is itself quite high.  You walk in, see the elephants, watch two get fed and leave, this does not take so long, then you can walk down a street, lined with traders, to two restaurants at the end (slightly overpriced with not the greatest food) and watch the elephants bath in the river. It all seems fairly forced this time round.

Brilliant for elephant lovers - First see them all getting fed with truck loads of leaves etc - really close up. Bottle feeding of babies was a bit of a con - I saw this 25 years ago when they did exactly that - but this time it was a couple of elephants which had to be at least 4 or 5!! They were having a great time tho and loving the fuss! The highlight is when they all traipse down to the river - just seeing them come down the street is an experience! Then they play freely in the river - beautiful backdrop too. All the babies just mess about dunking each other and making a lot of noise just like a bunch of kids!! The mahoots all try and make a few rupees on the side by getting tourists close to elephants - we didnt get involved in any of this. All in all - yo must not go to Sri Lanka and not go here ........

Accompanied by a tourist office driver I enjoyed a visit to the "orphanage".  At 10.00 a.m. the herd proceed down the main village street to the river for their daily bath. It is worth while finding a comfortable seat in one of the riverside cafe's offering refreshments and a panoramic view and photo opportunity not to be missed. This can be followed up by going down the steps to the to rocky river bank for close up encounters! Be sure to have some smaller notes to tip the Mahout.

This is one of the most popular atttractions in Sri Lanka and I can see why. If you are an animal lover/lover of elephants then you will love this. We went with a guide which I think was helpful as he knew his way around and what time to be in certain areas for the best views. Initially when we entered we stood and watched a large group of elephants in a huge paddock. Lots of opportunity to take photos. The local men were encouraging people to enter the paddock, but then asked for money. I must admit I did fall for this and was then roughly pushed aside as one of the "bosses" approached. Next I was able to bottle feed one of the baby elephants (for a small fee). Then went down to the river and watched them bathe. This was probably the nicest part. Again the men looking after  the elephants were encouraging people closer and to wash the elephants, but always in exchange for some money. Despite this, I did still enjoy it as these are majestic creatures and it is so rare to see so many at such close quarters. After this we visited an "elephant safari" a little further down the road. This is where you get to have an elephant ride. I would not recommend this. It felt very unsafe. You were essentially riding "bare back" with very little to hang on to. I thought I was going to fall off and at one point the elephant seemed as though it was going to run. It was perhaps very naive of us to get on in the first place. They are wild animals at the end of the day and if the elephant had become upset we would have definitely ended up on the floor, probably injured. Thankfully, we got back in one piece, but best to admire from a distance I think.

On our Exodus tour we visited only the Mahavali Ganga (river) when the elephants come from the Orphanage down to the river for bath and play time. We didn't go to the actual orphanage. It was amazing to see the pachyderms coming down the street (two carrying pieces of wood-bath toys?) and then their enjoyment getting in the water and having fun. The mahouts there try to keep the people away from the elephants (for our safety) but some people won't listen/obey their orders and stay behind the marked line. They all want their photos of the elephants. If you have bananas you can feed them. You can also pay the mahouts and have your photo taken next to an elephant (if you've never gotten close before). We spent about 2 hours watching the elephants enjoying their time in the river.

A wonderful place to see feeding and bathing of probably the biggest captive elephant herd in the world You have to understand Sri Lanka problems with elephants and especially captive elephants and only then to say “It is disgraceful cruelty" or "Don't go there"

If you have never seen an Elephant before and are not going anywhere where Elephants may be in Sri Lanka and you do not like going to your local zoo then i can understand why this tourist trap might appeal.  For anyone else, just give some money to a charity and pass this by and carry on up to Dambulla.

The elephant orphanage is a great stop off between Colombo and Dambulla. But it's the twice daily river bathing sessions across the street that are a real treat! Make sure you catch this as we almost missed it!  10am-12pm and 2pm-4pm when we went.Check out a group of 30+ elephants free swimming and playing in the river while looking on from the shore or overhead restaurant. You can then follow them back to the orphanage for a visit. Very cool!

We went there as part of an organised tour to Kandy. What used to be an elephant orphanage for actual baby elephant orphans, is now a money making elephant circus for tourists. The ugly truth is that they are capturing wild elephants (who aren't real orphans) and put them into this place, chain them up and beat them into submission until they are obedient, and then use them to extort as much money out of tourists as possible. There was also an elephant who had one leg blown off by a landmine years ago - anyone with a grain of common sense will know that with the weight of an elephant, it is cruel to keep such an animal alive - it just stood there looking really miserable leaning against large posts as it struggle to stand upright, looking on whilst the other elephants were being fed and he just ignored. Its back was totally lobsided from overcompensating on having just 3 legs. The most merciful thing would be to put this animal down. Then there are the staff (zookeepers) who will offer to take a photograph of you with your camera, and then demand a minimum of €10 for their service before giving you your camera back. Take your own photograhs and don't fall into this trap. It was so dissapointing but sadly the authorities won't do anything about the cruelty of the situation as it makes so much money out of tourists. Unfortunately everyone there, apart from the poor elephants, gains benefit. The only thing that can help these beautiful, sad creatures is if tourists don't support this place.

We visited here on Saturday 15 September.  It took about 2 hours by car to get there from our hotel and we started out really early in the morning to reach in time for the feeding.  It was well worth it and we even got to bottle feed a baby elephant!!  The entrance fees are minimal (approx $15 per adult), but it is something you will never forget.  I would highly recommend a visit. The only downside is be prepared to tip constantly to the staff for photographs etc.  We spent more on this than anything else!

This was my third trip to Sri Lanka and 3rd visit here. I admit coming to Pinnewala Elephant Orphanage was on the top of my to do list, and was on the top of the best experiences in Sri Lanka at the end of the 5 week holiday.( an elephant safari was second so you know I am an elephant freak!) We started at the orphanage feeding fruit to a large female, then watched the other elephants , including the blind tusker Samul, before heading down to the river to watch them bathe. Seeing so many beautiful elephants up so close and getting incredible photos was really awesome. The elephants really do seem to love the water and getting scrubbed. A good vantage point was at the Elephant Hotel on the edge of the river, where the meals were good as well. Sure its touristy, but well worth it. Don't buy the recycled elephant poo paper though if you are returning through Australian customs; not allowed in!

The Pinnawala elephant orphanage has the biggest herd of captive elephants in the world. Many babies are born each year, and when we visited in January 2012, there were several baby elephants, including one very small, very pink and very cute creature. We missed the 9 am baby feeding time but managed to catch them going for their bath. Except for one elephant that was chained, the rest roamed free. Don't follow unscrupulous people who offer to let you feed the elephants. We did, we were asked to buy over ripe bananas at a ridiculously high price to feed one elephant. Give an official donation instead! Look forward to going back to catch the 9 am feeding session.

Visited the elephant orphanage en route to Kandy and it was well worth a visit. As is usual in Asia there are two prices for tickets-one price for local visitors and a more expensive price for foreign tourists. It was lovely to see so many elephants in spectacular surroundings although it is touristy and pretty busy. You can pay to feed a baby elephant with a bottle and the staff are quite pushy to get you to have photographs taken with the elephants (with your own camera) for a charge but it was nice to get so close to the elephants. We walked down to the river in time to see the elephants herded into the river to bathe and play. The elephants seemed to be enjoying their time in the water and the young elephants were a delight to see.  We enjoyed cold drinks in a restaurant overlooking the river and although there were lots of people about, we got a good view. The souvenir shops near to the river were very expensive and consequently we were not tempted to buy anything. A enjoyable visit which would appeal to all ages.

Having visited the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage on a previous visit some years ago, this visit was a great disappointment. Even more so when compared with our visit to the Millennium Sanctuary. The grounds at Pinnawala are dry and dusty (we visited in June 2012). Many of the elephants we saw were chained up and looked miserable. Several of the elephants are wounded either by poachers or war. Although they had plenty of food, they did not look at all happy. We waited for the afternoon elephant feeding. There aren’t any baby orphan elephants so the handlers bottle fed two adolescent elephants purely for the tourists. It was all rather sad and tacky. Only the souvenir shop was worth visiting. It was full of good quality elephant carvings and carved wooden furniture. We would not recommend Pinnawala elephant orphanage. If you want to experience elephants first hand, then go to Millennium Sanctuary.

This is an excellent option for a day trip from Colombo or Kandy. Conveniently connected by train and road, Rambukkana station (on the Colombo-Kandy route) is about 2km away from the Pinnawala Orphanage with plenty of tuk-tuks plying the route for Rs.150. The orphanage itself is  clean, organised and well maintained. The best part of it is that you get to see plenty of elephants of all sizes, shapes and tusks -roaming around in their natural habitat spread over hundreds of acres. Some are also kept chained.Visitors are allowed to feed, touch and take pictures with the elephants ( after paying un-authorised fees to the minders)- but were not allowed to bathe the elephants in the river. One can only watch the bathing from a distance. The routine of the elephants ( feeding and bathing) is repeated in the morning and afternoon - so you can plan your travel conveniently. I thought the manner in which  a whole herd of elephants is herded to and fro from the river Maha Oya , twice daily, across a highway and a narrow lane clogged with shops,restuarants and tourists - speaks volumes about the efficiency and care of the management in running the place. To see about 30-40 giant elephants marching peacefully across the orphanage grounds and onto the river is a fabulous sight!The elephants looked peaceful and calm and were very freindly.......one Mommy elephant and her baby came over to say hello to my friend and her child! :). The elephant minders or Mahouts do have sharp tipped spears to control the animals- but while we were there , we did not see a single animal being poked or ill treated. The mahouts just used the spears as deterrents without touching the animals to maintain a safe distance between the animals and visitors.  Also - there are plenty of hotels and restaurants around-outside the orphanage- for food, drink and stay- so all your needs are taken care of. Overall - a fantastic experience in SL!

Elephant orphanage at kandi road is a must go place where you have a chance to see more than 100 + elephants including baby elephants. If planning to visit this place you must reach the location by 09 Am local time. All elephants are marched to the river for bathing. See the attached photos. Offcourse its a great view.

En Route between Colombo and the cultural triangle, the orphanage is well worth a stop. Get there in time for when they take the elephants down to the river for a bath (just before lunch). There are several restaurants overlooking the river where you can have lunch and watch the elephants (there would be 50 or so elephants). After that, head back to the orphanage and walk through the compound. You can watch the elephants being fed, or for a small fee, you can feed some of the smaller elephants a bottle. Fun for the kids. With lunch, allow 1-2 hrs for the stop-over.

The elephant orphanage was a nice experience. When we went they were at the lake supposedly having bath. The ticket rates were rather steep. SLR (Sri Lankan Rupees) 1000 for foreigners with a discount of SLR 500 for visitors from SAARC Nations per adult. The best part was to watch the baby elephants enjoying by pushing each other into the water. It was interesting to note that while we were there, none of the elephants we saw had tusks. (only females and babies, perhaps!) Apparently, the elephants are herded to the lake twice (at fixed hours). This may have been the reason why many of the elephants didn't seem interested in staying in the water and were trying to move away! This place is very touristy, though. Though they say one mustn't go near the elephants, most people were actually taking photographs next to them.

We had already seen many wild elephants on safari but it was good to get up close and personal to the orphaned elephants at Pinnewala. We arrived in time for their morning visit to the river and it was a delight to see them washing, bathing and playing (especially the younger ones). Yes, this is a bit of a "tourist attraction" but these people are looking after elephants that would probably not have survived without help and they did seem happy. Well worth a visit if you are within a couple of hours.

It was great to see the elephants in as near their original habitat as possible. As everywhere in Sri Lanka tips are expected to show you are "Happy" but it was an unforgettable experience. To see all the elephants down in the river was magical. we stopped off just before the orphanage where we were able to get into the river to bathe the elephants (Additional cost) and ride them bare back, a free shower was thrown in thanks to the elephant. This made our holiday.

Open 8:30am-6pm. Daily features of interest displayed at entrance. Features include bottled milk feeding (separate charge), fruit feeding (unofficially charged by staff), leaf feeding (unofficially charged by staff), stroke an elephant (unofficially charged by staff) and pose for photo with an elephant (unofficially charged by staff). There is a small gift shop. If you're after elephant-related merchandise there's dozens of tourist shops on the path to the river, across the road from the Orphanage (see description below). I saw over 50 Orphanage elephants being herded across the road from the Orphanage to the river, entering the river, then herded back to the Orphanage. You can watch from the riverside or in one of the overlooking restaurants. Times: 10-12 and 2-4. I watched from the Hotel Elephant Park.

We drove from Colombo to Kandy  and en route stopped at Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage. The orphanage has around 30-40 elephants that have been orphaned at a young age.There are numerous baby elephants that make this place unique and a must visit. The elephants are fed 4 times in a day.They are then walked to a stream for bathing.  We reached at around 10 am and as we had missed the feeding routine, we walked down to the river. This is were we saw the herd. The scene was heart-warming to see the baby elephants jostle and play with each other in water. You are allowed to go down to the river and touch the elephants. There are mahouts(men who take care of elephants) who watch out for the safety of the visitors. To feed the elephant, you pay extra. There are a lot a souvenir shops on the way to the stream. A must see is the 'paper-making from elephant poo' demo. The number of articles made from elephant poo is amazing. Incase you are travelling from India or any of the SAARC countries, please show your passport at the ticket counter to avail of a discounted entrance fees  (for adults -Rs. 500 (Srilankan Rupees) & Kids below 12- Rs 250). For feeding the elephants the charges are extra. Photography is permitted and no extra charges are levied.

There are a couple of decent restaurants by the river that give you a pretty good opportunity to have food/sip beer and watch the elephants bathe. Tour Organizer - Kanota Tours

However, we felt that the  name of the place was misleading and animals were being exploited for entertainment purposes rather than being given refuge.  More focus could have been placed on educating the public about the conflict between wild elephants and humans, and on conservation measures.

It's a 1.5 hour journey from Kandy via a public bus and autorickshaw. I took the public bus from Kandy (heading in the direction of Kegalle) LKR 53 and I alighted at the Karandupuna junction (the bus conductor was kind enough to tell me where) and took an auto rickshaw in. It should cost about LKR200. Along the way, the auto rickshaw stopped at an elephant place for rides and asked me to take the ride which cost LKR2000 for 15minutes. I ignored him and told him to send me to Pinnewala instead. I come from Singapore - have seen the elephants in our zoo and maybe that's why I have high expectations of an elephant show or sorts. There are only two main areas to see - the elephants out in the open, and them in the sheds where they are bound by chains and all they were doing was eating leaves. It was very hot, so I spent a short an hour there. The elephants are seemingly "paraded" for tourist to touch them and take pictures with them. The mahouts seem to encourage that - they kept asking if I would like a photo but I rather admire them from afar. It's worth a trip if you have never seen elephants in their natural habitat, but if you do, perhaps you can give this a miss.

The elephant orphanage is well worth a visit, although be very aware that they want tipping for everything. If you walk closer to the elephants or want to touch them or feed them you will need to pay a tip and they are not worried about telling you the tip is not enough! Our guide had warned us that tips were expected before we went so we did not have any problems although we met others that felt uncomfortable with this and ended up spending a lot more than they had intended. In saying that the trip was well worth the while. We sat and watched the elephants play and wash in the river for a good hour. They go down to the river at 10AM after feeding time. If you get down to the river about 15 minutes early you can get a good seat in the cafe over looking the river. You will also see all the elephants walk straight past you down the street to the river. It's quite a scene! We went with Chamilla tours. Chamillatours.com We met Sarath and his son Chamilla while staying at jetwing sea in Nagombo. He took us out for the whole day. This included the 'Upalis elephant safari' which we visited first where we were able to ride and wash the elephants (Without the pressure and extra costs of the orphanage). We also fed the elephant bananas at the end of the ride as well as brought back loads of photos. The guide was happy to take our camera and snap away while we rode the elephant for a small tip - Well worth it. The safari is only a couple of miles from the orphanage. We continued on to Kandy to see the temple of the tooth and then on to a wood carving factory where you can buy wooden elephants at much better value than at Pinnawala itself.

On the one hand the experience is unmissable, on the other it is commercialisation of wild animals (to varying degrees across the different aspects of the trip which can leave a negative impression). Bathing in the river - mostly the elephants enjoy the water and the time to splash about - especially the boisterous younger elephants.  Largely the elephants were subdued so the 'keepers' seemed primarily money driven (photo's, feeding etc) - we didn't see mistreatment at all.  At the end of bathing the elephants have to walk past all of the visitors to get back across the road to the orphanage and this is a lot of movement with a lot of elephants done quickly - maybe there is risk of trampling of the littler ones here!  We hung back in the restaurant at the top by the river when all the other visitors moved over to the orphange and this was a nice opportunity to see a few (probably in ill health/pregnant) elephants enjoy bathing in a more peaceful less touristed feeling way. The Orphanage & Feeding Time - We kept this part of our trip at Pinnewala short.  Here you can see the elephants working in the field and you can attend feeding time, and even (if you pay extra) feed a baby milk and it is this part of the trip where we felt more uncomfortable.  There was a very large and old elephant chained under a covered area where you can pay for photo's, the chains had clearly been there a long time and this was saddening to see.  With the feeding, there was an element of teasing initially with the elephants chained at a distance where they had to really strech and pull against their chains to reach the food and this we found unnecessary (although it was clearly to delay to maximise visitor numbers viewing). Compared to other elephant haunts on this stretch, Pinnewala is clearly a more properly run tourist trip.  Our driver tried to convince us to stop at an earlier place that lets you "ride the elephants" which we declined.  On the way back we explained that they are wild animals not really meant to be ridden and we have seen with others that they don't like being ridden (at this point he admitted that in some of these establishments whilst the elephants may not like it they are made to do it to pay - almost pay for their keep) so please if you aren't getting to a National Park (likely Udawalawe) Pinnewala is the best bet for experiencing these awesome creatures in a more natural setting than a zoo back home.

Despite some reviews critical of this elephant orphanage, my family enjoyed seeing the elephants having their bath at the river while we enjoyed lunch as a nearby hotel restaurant.  It was a sight to behold.  We observed how some younger elephants played with a wet shirt and snatching it from one another.

The Orphanage is really a must see! The experience of having dozens of elephants walking around you in the backdrop of lush green mountain ranges is just priceless. There are also tickets available to feed the elephants which is just mind blowing and worth every Sri Lankan rupee! We were so close to the elephants and could touch them and see every detail of their faces. We loved every minute of it and wish we could have spend more time there.

It was a nice experience, got to touch and take snaps with Elephants. Yes the tickets look little high priced at $20. This is nothing when we consider attractions like the Sky Deck in Australia cost me about $20 just to go up the tower and come down. Make sure you take a good camera you can get good closeups with Elephants. Food is somewhat cheap can buy a pack of lunch for about $5 max. I met a cool tour guide named Sarath Kumara, he didn't take money from me but promoted lot of shops and elephant rides for me. Not sure the prices because i didn't do any of those. 3 hours is a good time or you will feel lousy going too much in the sun.

We actually watched the Elephants bathing in the river and had an early lunch while this was happening. We were able to get up very close to the elephants including some gorgeous babies.
