If you want to visit Sri Lanka as a tourist the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is a must. You can see elephant bathing, feeding baby elephants (even you can feed them) and you can also experience elephant rides. Please be there around 10.00 am so that you don't miss anything. This is the world largest elephant orphanage which does most successive captive breeding and you could see the biggest Asian elephant herd in the world. This will be your once in a lifetime experience for sure. If you love animals one of the best places on earth.

Pinnawela elephant Orphanage is the home for elephants, babies abandoned, orphaned or injured in the wild.  They are being taken care, fed and trained by the wild life authorities. The best time to visit is during the feeding times, when one will have the opportunity of seeing the baby elephants being bottle-fed. Pinnawela elephant orphanage is located northwest of the town Kegalla, 77 Kms from capital Colombo and about 13 Km. from Kegalle Town on the Kegalle. These 24 acres large elephant orphanage is also a breeding place for elephants. The orphanage was primarily designed to afford care and protection to the many baby elephants found in the jungle without their mothers. In most of these cases the mother had been either killed or dead. Over time this place has become a sanctuary for injured elephants as well.  It's quite an experience to see the elephants parade one after another to the river for their bath. There's a restaurant by the river whereby you can dine and at the same time enjoy site of the elephants frolicking by the river.

This was an experience not to be missed. I had read some no so good comments about PEO, but hopefully times have moved on. What I saw was well attended elephants who appeared to interact well with their mahouts and did not seem to be afraid of them, so I take comfort in that. What I kow is that the blind tusker of mre than 60 years was shot in the head by a 'human' which lead to Raja's blindness and the chain is for protection, rather than anything else. There was also a number of bull elephants chained against trees in the jungle close by, though this was as a result of the aggression around mating season. Overall I found the experience noth calming and a spiritual one. To seethe elephants taken down to the river and left to just enjoy their time was a delight. I now see that you can volunteer to stay there, so this is on my list of things to come back to do. I am sure if there was any poor treatment going on that volunteers would be blogging this I have not seen this as the case. I would encourage you to have some 'bills' on hand for closer photos and given the income of locals, I don'that've a problem with this. Overall fantastic must do experience - go when the sun is out to get the best

Seeing them walk the street and bath in the river is a unique experience. All and all, this was the best place I visited in Sri Lanka.

Massively disappointed with this place on many levels. Lots of tourists about having a lovely time - but just take a look and think about the ethical nature of this. The elephants are not well looked after and its clear to see if you just look deeper. its a shame not many people see this. I've been to other elephant sanctuaries (mainly one in Nairobi, Kenya) and this place is not a sanctuary. Its sad to see. Someone in our group decided to do an elephant ride too (I discouraged this). Personally I dont know why you would want to ride an elephant anyway - they are not designed to carry humans or any other large loads really. But each to their own! If you decide to do this, be aware that it is private companies that run this and not the sanctuary. They actually 'hire' the elephant for a fee. I didn't really like the sound of this and again, the elephant was in chains and didnt look well looked after. I asked the handlers some questions about how they look after the elephants etc etc but they really didn't care. i know its tempting to go to this place and see an elephant, feed a baby and ignore whats going on but please just think about it. You will have a life time of holidays and there are a whole heap of other sancturies and opportunities to see these animals but in a humane way. save it for that occasion.

I visited the orphanage as part of a tour package, so I can't comment on whether it was good value. However, seeing them bathing in the river and then being able to interact with them without any barriers was a great experience. Inevitably, the mahouts try to tap visitors up for a few hundred rupees to photograph them posing with the animals - which are very gentle & tame (usually). The bottle feeding is a bit of a rip-off - the elephants seem to be 'juveniles' rather than 'babies' - didn't do that one. Some reviewers say it's a cruel place - I didn't see any evidence of this, although some are chained. I realize it's better to see them in the wild, but these 'rescue' elephants would probably be dead if it wasn't for the orphanage. Although I wonder whether the one missing part of a leg (see other reviews) has much quality of life.

We found the elephant orphanage very enjoyable.We stopped off on the way to Kandy from Colombo and it was worth the detour.The sight of the elephants rushing to get to the river to bathe was awesome.For anyone going you may want to leave the place where they are fed and make your way down to one of the hotels by the river early and get a seat in the front where you can watch the elephants bathe

I realy enjoyed the location of the orphange; you have the chance to see elephant bottle feeding and their bathing in the river. The place is very nice and we enjoyed walking to the river. We had lunch at Pinnalanda restaurant and watched the elephants bath. I was impressed by the disabled and blind elephants at this orphanage. A very nice place to visit for families with children.

After reading some of the negativity about the orphanage I was in two minds if to go or not.  I am so glad that I went this was a trip to last a lifetime it was the most amazing experience I have ever encountered. We arrived at the river and after looking around the very small muesum we walked out to the river where the elephants were lying in the river being washed by the boys who looked after them. We were invited into the river to help wash the elephants.  (They are scrubbed with coconut shell halfs)  This was amazing, we were then asked if we wanted to climb on the elephant for a ride which we did with pleasure, as a thank you from the elephant for washing him he returned the pleasure by spraying us with water from his trunk.  After about a dozen sprays he walked out of the water and took us for a ride around the village they live in. After leaving this area we went for a short drive to another area where you got to see the baby elephants being bottle fed (The baby elepants were chained up whilst being fed ) but there was baby elephants walking around freely. We walked up an slight hill and when we got to the top there was the most amazing sight I have ever seen.  There was an heard of elephants just walking around. Wow what a sight. After I had taaken in enough of this fantastic sight we went walking down a hill through a market street and when we turned around the elephants were walking behind us down to the river. The elephants all seemed to be happy and enjoying themselves. I did NOT at any time see any elephant being mistreated or hit. Go and see for yourselves I am so glad I did.

The Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is a major tourist attraction in Sri Lanka. It was started in 1975 with 5 baby elephants. It is now home to around 84 elephants. Each day at 10am and 2pm the elephants are walked down to the Maha Oya river to bathe. It is a magnificent sight to behold.

After doing some research and reading some of the negative reviews about the elephant orphanage (on Trip Advisor and The Lonley Planet book) I was not 100% sure about a visit to the orphange with my family. However, our visit to see the elephants turned out to be one of the highlights of our trip. I can see how others may not like to see the elephants in captivity, but it was a wonderful experience to see the elephants go down to the river to bathe. This is something they seem to thoroughly enjoy and we were actually able to feed some of the elephants...for a price of course:) Well worth the time and money in our opinion.

After reading some of the negative reviews about the elephant orphanage I was apprehensive about a visit with two young boys. But a visit to see the elephants turned out to be one of the highlights of our trip, and it was a wonderful experience to see the elephants go down to the river to bathe - something they do twice a day and which they clearly enjoy. We didn't get too close, and it made for a fantastic photo opportunity as others have said. I'd like to respond to some of the comments that others have made. I did not observe cruel treatment or any elephants being mistreated. There is a large elephant population at the orphanage. One large, old elephant (65) which is blind after having been shot in the jungle is chained and kept under a shelter, but when we were there he was enjoyed a shower and plenty to eat. Visitors were discouraged for getting too close. About half a dozen others were chained also, but were otherwise able to walk around with the others. We were not pestered by people for money for photo opportunities,which frankly was amazing, as this was our experience almost everywhere else in Sri Lanka. The boys were able to feed baby elephants bottles of milk, and this was a wonderful experience. The only negative from our point of view was to see one elephant chained up in the enclosure where the baby elephants are kept. This particular elephant lost part of one leg as a result of a landmine. I wondered if it was humane to keep him alive, as he was clearly in discomfort. Otherwise, it was a wonderful experience for us and for the boys and I would definitely go again if I had the opportunity.

this is the second time to see the elephants, paying a little extra for the priviledge of my wife feeding a baby elephant is something I did not begrudge, she will remember the occassion for the rest of her life. Having a beer in the resturant on the left by the river was cheaper than I expected and walking down to the river by the side steps and giving a mahout the equivalent of a pound to stroke baby elephants and have him take a photo of us with them is also something I will treasure. I am going again and will do the same again, the entire day out cost less than visiting a zoo in Sussex.

My heart sunk and I felt sick when I saw that some of the elephants were chained.  They were led through the crowds which must have been quite scarey for them and also I thought was very dangerous as they are WILD animals.  I understand that they must be controlled but rather than put chains on them and prod them with spear ended sticks why not keep them away from the tourists? On entering the orphanage there was a huge elephant under a canopy and the chains had left marks on his legs at different points from scarring.  The men were taking 1000 rupee backhanders for photos with the elephants or to wash them in the river.  Even the pregnant elephants were used to make money being washed numerous times in the river.  How good is this for the unborn elephant to be squashed inside the uterus when the mother lays down?  Also the elephants are not re-released but kept in captivity.  We bought a ticket to feed the baby elephants but when we saw that even they were chained we were very upset. We were over the moon when our guide from Kanota Tours (who made our honeymoon absolutely amazing) took us to The Elephant Transit Centre in Udawalawe, where the public don't get close to the elephants but are kept approx 40ft away so there is no need to chain them.  Not a single chain in sight.  And the elephants are re-released to the wild when they become teenagers.  This is a much better set up and the elephants looked really happy wandering about the feeding enclosure, socially interacting with each other.  We would recommend this rather than the elephant orphanage.  Also you are nearly guaranteed to see an elephant stood at the road edge behind the electric fence at some point in Udawalawe, usually opposite a fruit stall!!!  We bought some sugar cane and fed the wild elephants through the fence, but were careful to stay at arms length.

Great attraction. On arrival the elephants were returning from the river, and it was quite the site to stand to the side as they pass. We later fed a baby, photographed many elephants eating, then returned to the river as the elephants returned for their second swim of the day. Fascinating to watch. Be mindful, the workers always have their hand out for a tip.

A very entertaining place I have now visited quite a few times which I would highly recommend. Amazing to see so many elephants and get so close them. The best view is whilst sipping a cold drink by the river as they make their way for the daily swim. Yes it’s a bit touristy now and the Mahout's try and earn a few rupees whilst staging photographs which is part of the course with such places. I have never seen the overt cruelty to these animals descibed in some of the reports here, which I would say would be unusual in Sri Lanka where elephants are in general valued above people! Chains are used on some but these are wild animals after all and many can be dangerous and the numerous stampedes that have occurred during festivals are testament to it. Despite some of the reservations a thoroughly enjoyable day and one not to miss if you are in the area.

We arrived at the orphanage on the way to Kandy from Negombo. At the time we arrived, the elephants had been taken to the river (which they do twice daily). You can stand on the bank or a rocky jetty to see them and photograph them. The yellow t shirted keepers are on hand and are easily recognisable by their long sticks with metal points on the end (!!) the elephants ranged in size from tiny babies to grand old ones. The odd thing is that the keepers charge to extra to stroke the elephants on top of the 2000rupee entrance fee. Now, I'm not an advocate of touching/riding animals but even so, this approach of the keepers did seem a little devious. On top of that, there didn't seem to be much rhyme or reason behind their random pokings and proddings (with those sticks) of the elephants. This didn't make me overly comfortable. That said, the animals seemed in good nick and they seemed to be enjoying themselves. There is the usual tourist trap shops dotted around but one which caught my eye was the elephant dung paper shop (which won and ecology award in 2006). Pop in for a gander if you do go.

Really amazing experience of a LOT of elephants in one place.   Make sure you are there when the elephants are taken to the river to bathe, there are a fantastic photo opportunities there.   The herd moves down to the river at 10am if I remember correctly.   Make sure to buy some things from one of the shops, the dung paper is a truly unique gift!

Spent time watching the elephants being fed in the field. They looked to be having lots of fun. Later went to the river to watch them bathing.  The elephants appeared to throughly enjoy their time in the river. Spent ages just watching them. Did not witness any cruelty others have mentioned.

It was obvious from the time we arrived this is nothing but a cruel circus and should not continue to be run in this way.   Elephants bore heavy chains around 3 of their legs and even after being taken to the river, were then chained to chains that had been fixed to rocks.  One blind, old elephant, takes ‘pride of place’ chained by his legs, just inside the entrance beneath a sun shade.  Further round there are baby elephants chained up beneath small shelter/sunshades.  All look so unhappy, it is very, very sad.  Some elephants have been chained for so long that the chains are eating into their flesh. With so many young elephants it looked pretty obvious they are being bred, a point which our Sri Lankan driver confirmed !  He also stated the ‘keepers’ are generally boys/young men with drink and drug problems who have no regard for the animals.  We watched them being herded to the river by way of ‘keepers’ using hand held, spear like contraptions with a metal hook and a sharp point on one end.  The hook being used against the elephant’s ear in order to pull it in the direction the ‘keeper’ wants it to go, the point being used to move an animal forward should it stop.  When I complained, the 'keeper' told me it doesn’t hurt them !  We then watched as an elephant picked up and ate three plastic bags from the river bank.  When this was pointed out, the remaining pieces were picked up by a staff member and thrown just out of the elephant’s reach !  No doubt by the time we’d left for the day they’d blown back to be picked up by another elephant. My Wife and Sister were in tears during a large part of this visit, I will be complaining to whoever I can but no doubt this will fall on deaf ears as it's all about the money.   The entrance system to the place was an absolute joke, with the ticket master/supervisor - or whatever he was -  getting in one big panic after another when trying to issue tickets.  We'd pre-paid and it was still a shables aswe didn't get inside the complex until some 20  minutes after arrival.  the place wa absolutely packed, so I would imagine it's a real money spinner. Ii just hope the money is being put to use to beneit the poor elephants within it's walls.

I have seen the mixed reviews on the Elephant Orphanage. Personally I have some sympathy for the views expressed that it is far better to see elephants in the theit natural environment. (see my review on the Mahoora camp at Yala for a truly unique experience). The orphanage is also not without its challenges by western standards. That said, the orphanage management has been successful in creating a supportive environment for this wonderful animals, in focussing attention on cottage industries such as paper from dung (yes dung!) and raising awareness in the wider local community. The highlight for us was sitting with a cold beer or two and a snack in their open air restaurant and watching the elephants playing in the nearby river. Well worth a visit in my view.

This place is definitely very touristy but we could not make it to the Born Free Foundation place.  I think the biggest problem is not the handlers but the tourists themselves.  I saw some tourists obnoxiously “harassing” a wild elephant to touch her ears … folks … really???  These are wild animals and human contact/interaction should be kept at a minimum.  There should be no feeding and no touching whatsoever.  These creatures can be unpredictable and you do not want them to get used to humans … how can they ever be released into the wild that way?  It was an amazing experience watching the elephants in the river but tourists should be kept at their distance.  I guess money gets whatever you want (as our Sri Lankan driver/guide told us) … everybody is afraid to say “no” to tourists as they bring money … but at what cost?  Something to think about …

We arrived @ Pinnawella during the mid-day heat since we got late to leave Colombo. (2 hour drive from Colombo) .. The tickets were priced moderately for locals (100/-) while the foreigners had to dish out 2000/-..  My cousin who came back from Aussie was charge the full 2000/- due to his lack of the local dialect.. The main orphanage is built on several dozen aches of land. A total of some 50+ elephants roam within the confines of the park under the watchful eyes of the rangers. Restaurants generally charge double for foreigners (Ex: Water 100/-).. Price discrimination runs rampant.. Do watch out for the Annoying Bystanders, who appear to be helpful, but in reality - All they want is your hard earned MONEY !! Avoid all forms of communication with loiterers and free loaders... Its best to ask information from the Security Guards stationed within the park.. The food is pricey compared with the Ambepussa Avanhala (Restaurant)..  Elephant rides are ~2000/- per/person.. Bottle feeding starts @ 1:15 pm... Bathing starts @ 2:00pm..  As the herds are too large, they are split into 2 groups prior to the river baths.. Parking is available at 2 locations (one is free)..

If you admire elephants, this is a place to see over 60 of them about as comfortably as you could get.  Three tour bus loads of us (some 70 passengers) arrived from the Regent Voyager in Colombo, and the facilities accommodated us easily without issue at the prime viewing spot for the elephants bathing.   A terraced dining spot overlooking the bathing spot meant that most could sit, sip a cool drink, and watch the elephants for over an hour, cavorting in the water.  The baby elephants in particular (at least four), were fascinating to watch as they played in the water.  On top of this eye candy, the food served at the restaurant was a delicious buffet, and the stores lining the walk back to the main road, were interesting, and fun shopping.  After lunch there was a second show on the other side of the road, with the elephants freely walking in a field, after first having the baby elephants (over 200 pounds of baby, each!) fed with milk bottles. As an extra bonus, a four foot long snake slithered across the dirt in front of us, as we headed towards the field; nobody screamed, just watched it with great interest.   If you bring small children, be prepared to watch them carefully, as the elephants ARE loose, and large.  All in all, this tour was a great delight, and we'd recommend it to all.

We reached Pinnawala when the elephant's were at the river for their bath and it was an amazing and amusing sight to see so many elephants in a playful mood , taking a dip in the water. A sight worth visiting . The sidewalks were full of souvenirs.

There is no doubt that making money is one of the main aims but at least a very significant amount of what they  if not all is ploughed back to care for the elephants. If the elephants were not there, they would be under much greater stress and in danger of being shot. It is an enormous lot better than a zoo apart from Raja, the blind elephant who sadly, is being exploited purely for the benefit of the tourists taking pictures. Also it is not really an orphanage, there are only two orphans there in about 100 elephants and they have all been domesticated.  Most of the babies have their natural mothers with them. There are no plans to return them to the wild. If you want to see a lot of elephants close up, then it is worth going but make sure you are there when they go to the river. If you want to see them in the wild, go to Uda Walawe or Yala and if you want to help save the elephants, go to the elephant transit home at Uda Walawe to see genuine orphans being prepared to return to the wild and make a donation there to help. However, don't be tempted to stop and feed the elephants waiting beside the road. Tourists are getting them into bad habits by doing this and it stops them foraging properly for their own food. And by the way, don't ride on elephants if it is in a howdah. It injures their backs and should be banned. Go bareback - its much more fun.

our score indicates that we expected a bit more. But to be fair, its an orphanage doing a lot of good things. since we have seen elephants in the wild, we were a bit disappointed. The workers there were forcing the calves to come to us if you pay them some money. it is a nice place to stop by, and we felt sad at the state of some of the elephants which were rescued. i guess the place would improve further to cater for more elephants. we should all encourage this idea by visiting, in our opinion

Don't like when animals is showing up for money. I hope that the money is going back to the elephants itself. The boys that took care of the animals was no nice, take other caring people to take care of this wonderful animals. We stayed overnight.

The orphanage is run by the government it is extremely expense for Sri Lankan standards,we were travelling independantly and on our visit approximately 600 other tourists were bussed in to gather round an enclosure to watch 2 adolescent elephants being bottle fed it was like being at a zoo. There were articles in the Sri Lankan press very condeming of the practices going on here particularly about orphaned elephants being sold on often to temples were there care was very poor. The government need to be made aware that this is not acceptable and I would advise anyone thinking of visiting to go 3 kms down the road to the Millenium elephant museum,small and independant where you will have a much more rewarding experience

We were very dissappointed at what we saw at the "Orphanage". It was more like a Circus for the elephants. We have seen elephants in the wild in Africa and did not expect to see  some of the elephants chained up, with the male elephants chained up in another area which we were not allowed to visit. There is a blind elephant chained up in a sheltered concrete area but at least they hosed him down to help cool him down in the heat. Elephants should be able to roam free. We were warned by our guide not to buy any of the bananas sold by locals to feed them and not to pose for a photo with elephants as you were badgered for payment by the 'minders'. This might well have started of as an orphanage a long time ago, but now it is just a breeding business, as once the elephants are used to people, they are unable to be released into the wild as they would not survive. It feels very much like a circus when you see them all being herded down to the river, across a busy road for a cool down, but the minders a busy prodding them with big poles and some were chained up to the rocks. Please don't go here if you are concerned about elephants and I wish our tour guide had not taken us here.

enjoyed the visit to the sanctuary you get up very close to the elephants and if your guide is able to obtain one of the tickets available you are able to bottle feed one of the baby elephants.disliked being asked for tips by the mahoots for photographs of you with the elephants did not see any abuse by the mahoots on the elephants did not mind paying the 2000 rupees entrance fee as this covers the  orphanage grounds as well as watching the elephants bathing in the nearby river

here is the Born Free review of Pinnawala & another article on a young female elephant showing signs of horrible injury from 'training' & treatment at this place - really sad that something that could do so much good is taking advantage of it's privileged situation and causing so much suffering and misery. http://www.bornfree.org.uk/campaigns/elephants/campaign-action/sri-lanka-elephants/responsible-tourism/pinnewala-elephant-orphanage/ http://www.bornfree.org.uk/campaigns/elephants/campaign-action/sri-lanka-elephants/captive-elelphant-welfare/mahasen-campaign/

I am a bit amazed by some of what people have written here as when we went all the elephants were roaming free, we didn't see any being mistreated in any way. Ok, it's not cheap to get in by Sri Lankan standards but elephants need a lot of care. The mahouts clearly love their elephants. They did grab my wife to get her to pose for photos but you don't have to give them any money to take any photos with the elephants. We loved it and would recommend anyone to go.

We bitterly regreted our visit to the elephant 'orphanage' and have avoided it had we known that it was cruel exploitation of captive elephants to make a lot of money from tourists. The visit was very distressing and left me with horrible memories. The elephants are prodded with sharp spikes and we saw one being whipped across its face. They are all chained and it looks like the bull elephant cannot move from its concrete platform. We were literally pushed by the 'guides' to stand near the elephants and then they demanded money for taking a photo and got angry when we did not want to pay. Pinnawala may have started off as an orphanage maybe but they now actively breed elephants and we were told they have no programme to release them. The place is the subject of a report by the Born Free Foundation because of the animal welfare issues. I found this out when I got back from Sri Lanka and was not surprised. It is very sad.

I am late in writing this review as my husband and I visited in December 2011. We had been to Pinnewala once before about 10 years ago and our experience then was different to what we saw this time. When we arrived the elephants were already in the water, many of them shackled.  There was a constant stream of mahouts beckoning you to go close enough to stroke the elephants, and only afterwards it was very obvious that the mahouts were after your one dollar and were not at all interested in the animals welfare.  I witnessed mahouts poking the tiny baby elephants aggressively with their spiked sticks, and the babies were terrified.  Is this how these magnificent creatures were to spend their lives with no chance of escape from this cruelty. We then witnessed the elephants line up to walk back up the hill to the so called sanctuary...they were clearly very scared of the mahouts. In reaching the orphanage there were many starving stray dogs around hoping, I guess that someone would take pity on them and feed them. One poor dog chased a baby elephant in play, but the mother did not see it that way and rushed very quickly towards the crowd of people, making an alarmed elephant noise.  The mahout had a stick in his hand and threw it violently at the dog, who yelped loudly in pain.  A friend of mine witnessed this with me and shouted at the mahout who just ignored her.  The whole episode was totally unsafe for the visitors, and seconds off a stampede.  The poor dogs should not be allowed in to the orphanage in the first place, but they should not be ill treated either. This place is not for the elephants, it is a money making exercise for the Sri lankan authorities and the mahouts. If you, like me are an animal lover and were saddened and shocked by what you saw, please may I ask that you contact international animal welfare charities like IFAW and the Humane Society in the USA.  I intend to do so as I can't bear to think of these animals suffering for the rest of their lives.  Can you?? In response to the previous comments about the blind elephant, I recall a blind elephant being there 10 years ago, but have no evidence that it is the same one. Visiting this facility only encourages the poor treatment of these elephants to be prolonged.  As in many cases like this, the best thing to do, in my opinion is to stay away and stop the elephants being exploited.  If I can help one elephant from me writing this and you reading it, I will be very pleased.

I visited the orphanage a few weeks ago in February 2012, with a group of friends.  We are all veterinarians and are in agreement that the orphanage is not that great. The elephants we saw were free roaming and well fed, but when not out roaming they were chained by one or both legs, with evident rub marks and scars from older wounds.  Several had health conditions and none of the mahouts or other workers there could or would tell us if they had been looked at and/or treated.  One old male was blind in one eye, with what looked like an untreated eye cancer, and a young half grown elephant had a nasty swollen open wound on one hind leg, from where it had tried to free itself from the shackle and chain; this was obviously paining it as it kept lifting it's leg and looking around at it. There were a large amount of 'workers' offering to take photos for tourists and then asking for huge sums of money (after paying the equivalent of $20AU entry), they were not safety conscious and pushed tourists and their children to stand very close to elephants, babies included.  Tourists from other parts of Sri Lanka and India in particular let their children run around unsupervised with the elephants, and while we were there we saw a 2 year old baby elephant accidentally push a child (maybe around 10 years old) into a metal rail.  Totally not the elephants fault, more the parents who were busy doing who knows what - but when the child started crying a worker came running up and repeatedly hit the baby elephant with a large stick, chasing it off.  He then proceeded to chain the baby to a tree by the shackle on it's back leg.  The baby had obviously never been chained up before, as it cried and struggled in obvious distress.  The baby's mother was chained up a few meters away out of reach and was also distressed, trumpeting loudly.  When I tried to explain what had happened the worker, who didn't speak English, waved his stick at me and stomped off. While it is nice to be able to see these animals up close, I do not think their welfare is a priority at this orphanage.  It seems more about making as much money as possible with little regard for visitor safety or the health of the elephants there.  I would recommend visiting the neighbouring smaller elephant orphanage that has much less publicity but a much better standard of care.

We visited today and was uncertain what to expect due to mixed reviews on here.  All I can say is GO!  It is well worth it.  The inside feeding bit is a bit touristy and like a zoo and the staff do try to milk all of the tourist photo opportunity money off of you, but when you go down to the river and see them bathe it is a fantastic experience and one of the top things I've seen during my holiday in Sri Lanka

I agree with other reviewers that the bottle feeding and washing are unnecessary but to see all those elephants running free was great as was feeding them fruit from a platform. To then see 50-60 elephants bathing in the river with almost no human intervention was the highlight of our tour of Sri Lanka.

Having read the 'terrible' reviews below, I was a bit worried. But all is fine. The elephants all looked happy and well-cared for. There was no listlessness, runny eyes, and no current or recent injuries. Not a scratch. And as a passionate advocate of animal welfare, I looked carefully. They seem to have more space and more companions than the average western zoo - not to mention regular playtime in the river. Animal body language speaks a lot, and these animals quite obviously had no ill- feelings towards their mahouts. There was no fear or shying away. The mahout's hook looks a bit scary, but these are elephants. If one decides to stand on a tourist, then hooking his ear is the best way to drag him off. But that is exceptional. These animals had no marks at all suggesting they had ever been prodded or hooked. Zero. And I saw no sign whatsoever of cruelty or even indifference. The mahouts seem genuinely to care for their charges. A chain on an elephant is like a leash on a dog. It needs to be strong. They're elephants! And they do need to be stopped from wandering off at times. The 'bad' chained elephants one reviewer mentioned probably had a case of the raging hormones and the mahout was embarrassed to say. In that state an elephant gets a bit crazy and will go over or through anything in the way of having sex. The old blind bull is chained up when tourists are around, but he does get regularly walked- although he is getting on a bit and does not seem to like it much. Yes, the mahouts will ask for money. But this is a poor country recovering from a civil war, not to mention a tsunami. Some of these guys and their families literally live in wooden packing crates. A few 'take your picture with the elephant's can mean supper that night or not. Most tourists live a life these guys can only dream about. It's a hard business if you can't spare them four or five dollars for their expertise. Most human-elephant interaction in Sri Lanka is a shotgun blast for stealing from a farm. You can see this on some of the rescued animals. If the orphanage is the alternative, then bring it on. If I was an elephant and my choices were to run wild and dodge armed farmers to steal crops, a lifetime hauling logs, or free food at the orphanage, several daily swims and lots of tourists feeding me fruit, I know what I would choose. If you are an animal lover deciding what to do, then as one to another I would say go there without guilt or hesitation. Your tourist dollars will help both Sri Lanka and the elephants.

We visited the orphanage based on the idea that we could really get a feel for the elephants and also be involved in feeding them. The feeding time transpired to be the worst part of the visit, the babies were in a fenced area and it felt uncaring and abit of a circus act, the crowd was very big also. Watching the elephants graze and bath in the river was a highlight they looked very happy at play and the photo opportunities are great. There are many places to view and have a drink whilst doing so but it all felt a little too much of a routine and a bit soul less.

People have posted a lot of negative reviews of this place, I seriously don't understand why. Being from a different country, I applaud the Sri Lankan Government which has taken this initiative to safeguard and take care of these elephants who have suffered in one way or the other in the jungle. I am a hard core animal lover and a naturalist and i think that this is a great place to promote. Yes, the entry charges have gone up in the past 1 year but why not .... hasn't the market prices gone up. And there is no time restrcition at all - I spent atleast 2 hours with all these lovely animals.  This place has about 90 elephants and it is just not easy to take care of such a big herd. Its easy to point out the negatives... but frankly speaking, i found none. Elephants have to be chained for our security else why would they be called wild. I fed the baby elephant some milk which i bought for just about 2 USD and then fed some fruits to the big ones.. and trust me it was an amazing feeling to feed these poor animals who need our support. These elephants are also given bath i think 2-3 times in a day in the near by rivery pond. It is an amazing sight to see all these elephants together.. Will definitely visit again whenever i visit Lanka and I suggest all to do so too.

This is a good place to visit, especially with kids. The entrance fee is very expensive, but I guess it takes a lot of money to feed these huge beasts. You will almost be able to walk up to them and for a tip you will be able toget your photo with the large pachiderms. No tip, no photo though, the mahouts will chase away any elephant that is curious enough to get close to you. Probably the best is that you get to see a lot of baby elephants, which are very cute.

The elephant orphanage is a couple hours away from Negombo and was a great place to start our travels.Kathy & I much enjoyed seeing the elephants bathing in the adjoining river. These elephants are either orphaned or have been injured & are treated at this reserve. Our guide & holiday organiser, Upil from srilankatailoredtours.co.uk,who arranged our complete 13 day holiday, was excellent and very knowledgeable about not only the orphanage but about most aspects of local culture and wildlife. I would highly recommend a visit.

Visiting the orphanage was probably the most disappointing part of my holiday in Sri Lanka. I felt the orphanage was more interested in making money out of the tourists instead of educating the visitors on the rehabilitation work they have done they encourage you to get a guide at steep prices. I am not an expert on elephant caretaking but it seemed like the caretakers were unnecessary hard on the beautiful animals. They chain the baby elephants so that the visitors can feed them and take pictures. It seemed so inhumane and like a circus! Had to move away from the area. The elephants are taken across the road for a bath. One can either sit at one of the adjoining cafes and sip of a drink while watching the elephants bathe (for about 10 – 15mins) or just stand near the banks of the river. I got to Pinnawala Elephant camp from Kandy using the local buses. It's a cheap but long way of getting there. If you are traveling in a group you can negotiate with cab or tuk-tuk drivers near the watch tower in Kandy. I would not recommend anyone to visit the orphanage and would rather encourage other to try and see elephants in the wild!

We went this morning despite the previous comments. We had already bOoked our tickets but it only took one look at a young cow's scarred hind legs to see that the shackles on her were the cause of her discomfort. I have been to many elephant tourist attractions but have never seen so much chaining before; it seemed even more pathetic that the elephants carried their own chains with them back to their pens. We spent no longer than 10 minutes there before getting our driver to take us back. We felt embarrassed as human beings that our kind mistreat these highly intelligent and beautiful creatures. Save your money and spend it carefully elsewhere.

We visited the orphanage with our Aitken & Spence guide over the public holiday weekend.  The place was packed out with people making a huge amount of noise and the elephants were being prodded, poked & whipped to get them to do what their trainers wanted. It was especially cruel to see the old blind elephant chained up in the heat of the midday sun surrounded by noisy crowds.  And the feeding of 2 young elephants in a pen as described in earlier reviews was just awful - we didn't stay to watch.  It was sufficiently bad to see them moving backwards & forwards in a distressed manner and being prodded by spears to ensure they were totally petrified.  I will be writing to the Born Free Foundation about their treatment as soon as I get home.  It was clearly a money making venture & it left me feeling very sad and concerned about the treatment of the elephants.

If you only have the time to go to one Elephant Sanctuary, pop up the road  and go to the Millennium Elephant Foundation instead (or Elephant Bath as many of the local guides call it). Initial good impressions formed by the entrance area, efficient entrance staff, with 2000 rupee charge and clean toilets quickly disintegrated into nothing more than a disorganised and slightly distressing event. I am not an over zealous animal lover but to I was truly disgusted. Whilst it was amazing to see the array of elephants, especially the babies, there was no explanation as to what was going on in the various parts of the orphanage, tips were constantly demanded by the handlers with other seemingly, non-staff members taking cameras from customers to take pictures of them with the elephants and they too also demanding money. The handlers were inconsistent with the elephants, with shouting  and use of ankhs /stick,  one minute encouraging them to get closer to people for the obligatory photo opp and then hurriedly moving the elephants away again, more shouting, more stick . Particularly distressing were elephants chained to a fence with no shade opportunities near them and  an old elephant chained up tightly, interestingly I didn't see him when they were all moved to the river. At the river we chose to stand at street level, to avoid the other tourist scam of getting you  into one of the hotels to pay for an overpriced drink and it was amazing to see them go past and watch them in the river but again it was disorganised.  There were signs everywhere saying “do not to feed the elephants”, whilst staff members seemingly encouraged people to do exactly that by buying bananas from the street hawkers. These elephants maybe in an orphanage but  I didn't feel that their care and treatment was a priority. An amazing opportunity to inform and educate a huge amount of people has been totally lost.

We were staying in Hotel Elephant Bay and after having breakfeast while watching elephants taking a bath and also feeding one of elephnats (for a tip of course) we continued to Elephant Orphanage, but I have to admitt that seeing them in river was more fun for us as adults and especially for kids (4y and 1,5y). We were late for baby elephant feeding with milk but our driver organized it only for us (for a tip of course). If I would go to Pinnawala once again with kids then I would choose option of staying in a hotel and money saved on Elephant Orphanage entry tickets would use for chance for kids to feed elephants with bananas. That's my opinion.

We have just returned from a trip to Sri Lanka and our first trip was to the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage.  The visit made me question my decision to spend a family holiday in Sri Lanka. We arrived in time for feeding to find two young elephants chained up inside a small pen, surrounded by tourists.  The elephants were visibly distressed and tourists were laughing at their cries of frustration as they struggled with the chains.  Our children were disturbed by what they saw and asked to leave rather than wait for the actual feeding.  They could not understand why the animals could be mistreated in such a way and were just as shocked by the factor that tourists found such behavior amusing. We had lunch by the river and watched the elephants bathe there a little later.  This was a much more pleasant experience.  What was concerning though was that the elephants, especially the younger ones, seemed unusually subdued.  We left with the impression that the orphanage may have started off with good intentions but that the tourist dollar rather than the wellbeing of the animals has sadly become the driving force. We sincerely regret paying money to this facility because we believe that by doing so, albeit with the best of intentions, we may have unwittingly facilitated the mistreatment of such wonderful animals.

We got back from Sirlanka on Sunday, on the Wednesday we attented the so called elephant "orphange" expecting it to be a caring environment with happy elephants. Unfortuneatly this was not the case, the baby elephants were chained in a barn, so that tourists could pay money to feed them and get there picture taken, they were very agitated and distressed. Following this we were brought to what could only be called a cage like box were a blind elephant was kept chained with little room to move. Opposite this was a field were lots of elephants were feeding many chained, 3 other elephants were kept away from the others chained from the neck and all feet chained together, when I asked why I was told, " they are bad elephants, dangerous". There were numerous men with sharp spears with a hook on the side so when the tourist wants there picture taken the man sticks the metal hook into the animals back of ear to drag it over, while the elephant screams out in pain! This was a horrific experience to see such beautiful animals so misserable being exploited and abused, to make matters worse its tourists money that is keeping them in business! Shameful also the elephant riding place next door to the orphange was worse 2 of the elephants were bleeding from wounds that appeared to be cane marks on its side, we did witness the staff assault the animals with a pole previously! I hope it gets shut down.

We visited some years ago and were looking forward to taking friends during our current trip. Firstly the charges have doubled and then doubled again. The elephants you used to be able to mix with are now closely tethered and segregated. The display was of one man hosing down one elephant for an eternity. Feeding involved 2 small tethered elephants. And the previous free facility of watching the elephants bathe in the river whilst enjoying a hugely overpriced drink is now charged for (and the drinks are still hugely overpriced! I'd recommend giving this a miss until clear evidence emerges that they have got their act togther and have started charging sensibly.

If you've been to a zoo, then save yourself the trip and don't bother going to the Elephant Orphanage. The orphanage is somewhat of a misnomer as they also breed elephants there. There was no educational aspect to the facility nor anything else for that matter that seemed like they were doing anything special for the elephants besides feeding them and giving them water.  It just seems like one big tourist scam and nothing I enjoyed in the least. Save your 2,000 rupees for something else.

It's really worth to be there, you'll never forget this nice and touching visit.  You may  even touch and caress elephants and their babies; observe them while eating also feed elephant babies with milk from the bottle. Then you may accompany whole herd on their way to the river and observe their bath. The funniest moment is when they make themselves a "shower" with sand on their way back. Orphanage is open from 8:30. Feeding of elephants 9:15,  13:15,  17:45.  Walk to river bath  10-12 and 14-16. Entrance fee 2000 Lkr (17 US dollars) per person.

Just go to the elephant orphanage and visit the elephants bathing in the river which is just happens until noon. You don't need a guide so don't let any of those people help you to get into the orphanage or get the ticket. if they claim to take you to the bathing place again this is something very easy. just take the street opposite the orphanage and that will end up by the river where all the elephants are taking a bath. these guide like people will take you to elephant Safari which is nothing but abusing a hurting animal. Normally, these elephants are very old and sick and they don't care about them at all! these elephant suffer a lot to give the people a ride! it's not a safari at all. they ask you 5000 Sri Lanka rupees per person an hour! you can bargain this until 5000 for two people or less but again this is a trick! whatever you gain you lose at the end. if it is one hour it takes only less than half an hour! and Safari is only a small lane of 30 meters max. At the end you see the poor animal suffering and how bad they behave them and lose your trust in Sri Lankan people! you can enjoy watching the elephants in the orphanage with the same ticket which you buy at official rates which is 2000 rupees. of course, everybody in the orphanage will ask you for a tip. the bad part is you don't have to get to the field but if you pay the tip you are allowed to go inside the field or they will bring the elephants for you!

Initially I'd decided not to visit Pinnawela Elephant orphanage.  I'm not really an animal person and feel uneasy with zoos and circuses.  Plus as a independent traveller hiring a car and driver was starting to add up. However, I found out about local buses to get there and back from Kandy for a total of 200 Rupee and the whole experience started sounding like an interesting excursion. The orphanage itself was pretty much as I imagined.  The views were amazing though.  I didn't experience any problems with keepers asking for money for photos or witness any direct crulety to the animals.  I did find it a little unpleasant seeing the blind elephant chained up moving in a rhythmic manor on the spot (reminding me of rocking behaviour adopted by individuals in long term mental health institutions) .Apparently there are good reasons why he needs to be chained up. For me the part that made it worth doing was watching the elephants walk down to the river and sitting in the cafe watching them bath for two hours before they returned.  Quite a surreal experience.  Like a previous reviewer I would also recommend skipping the orphanage and just go for the river experience, but they do check your ticket on route to the river so you still have to pay the fees and therefore might as well go in. If you are an independent traveller and want to take the bus from Kandy its bus No 1 heading to Colombo from the main bus station.  Ask to be dropped off at Pinnewala junction to go to the orphanage.  You'll find everyone who has overheard the conversation will make sure you get off at the right stop. This bit takes approx 1 hour.  From there cross over the road and either take another bus the remaining 6km down the turnoff or easier still take one of the passing Tuk Tuks (approx 300 Rupees).  To come back do the same in reverse.

Went with a big group of friends on Jan 7, 2012. The orphanage did not follow the schedule program to arrange the activities of the elephant. Staff told us only after we bought the ticket Rs2,000 per person. We saw around totally 30 elephants there. Workers there were just  pushing us to take photo with the elephant and then asking for tips. Nobody explained anything about the orphanage and how it operates. We paid Rs2,000 (US$18) for the ticket and spent just 25 minutes there.  Extremely disappointing about this place.

I visited Pinnewalla in January this year, what an amazing place. The elephants all appeared well cared for and I never saw any signs of ill treatment. The baby elephants were gorgeous and I was lucky enough to feed one of them with a bottle of milk, which he guzzled in seconds. There were plenty of photo opportunities and not once was I asked for money for the prviledge of taking photos. Bathing one of the elephants was amazing. A true experience and one I will always remember.

We went to Pinnawala as part of a nine day tour of Sri Lanka and I did have my doubts about visiting as I had read some mixed reports. Not all the elephants are in chains but they are taken down to the river and you sit and watch them (at one of the restaurants overlooking the river). It's all very staged and most of the elephants were very inanimate and looked very bored. We didn't learn anything about the work the orphanage does and we really wished we hadn't gone because it really did feel like a tourist rip off. Much better to go and see elephants in the wild (which we did at Yala NP!). Obviously this is just my personal opinion and I'm not saying don't go but just be aware of the set-up they have there.

Whilst its been a couple of years since I visited I did feel somewhat uncomfortable with some of the sights inside the ophanage. (prompted no doubt by a lack of understanding) It was nice however to 'walk amounst elephants' and especially nice to see the 'mini jumbo's' Having said that, I fully understand the concerns raised in many reviews here-zoo's and circus' are viewed as non pc these days by many. I was reassured though by the review from a former volunteer at the orphanage which helps explain/understanding. I would recommend perhaps that visitors skip the orphanage itself and head straight for the restaurant/bar riverside on the other side of the road. Find out 'bath times' (twice a day) -the elephants cross the road and march down to the river. This is always the highlight to the trip anyway.

We first met up with the Elephants across the road from the orphanage when they were in the river at the bottom of the road - what an amazing sight!!  About 50 Elephants just milling about, washing and just chilling out in the water.  So much time to take pictures and join in with the washing of the Elephants :-)  You can sit and have lunch or a drink over looking their playtime - personally i couldn't take my eyes off them long enough to eat anything!! Once they have trooped back across to the orphanage ( a real sight seeing them all marching up the street!!) there are more photo opportunities and chance to get up close and personal with them. There is a chance to feed some young ones but, whilst I understand the need for it, I wasn't keen on seeing them chained up and decided to give it a miss after about 5 mins. All in all, it was a worthwhile visit and thoroughly enjoyable, but don't think that is the only chance you will get to see elephants - they roam wild all over the place and we saw several a day for the rest of the week in Sri Lanka, just on the side of the road :-)

We have been in Sri Lanka for three weeks having a wonderful time and left this until the last day (today) as a treat.  Myself, my husband and our young adult children had to leave as we were so upset by the degradation of the animals . It was overcrowded and had the atmosphere of an old fashioned mean-spirited circus. The "Mahouts" were aggressive,  pushing people to touch the animals while having their photo taken and then demanding outrageous sums of money for taking a photo. We saw elephants beaten, several in chains and they are afraid of their handlers. This may have started with good intentions, but has degenerated into a sad tourist dollar extraction machine.   We were tempted to start a refuge to rescue the elephants from the rescuers!   After experiencing the peace and beauty of other parts of the island and seeing the elephants in the wild in the national parks, this place has left a nasty taste.

had a super day out at the elephant orphanage... a great chance to see the animals up close, and interacting with each other away from the crowds. there was feeding time in the afternoon, that encouraged tourists to have a go at feeding the younger animals, but it never felt like the animals were forced into it, didnt have the grimair of an english zoo. something to see, all the elephants trooping down to the water for their bath, and to watch them playing in the mud... definitely worth a visit.

The drive from Kandy to Colombo is about 3 hours by road. En route, is the famous elephant orphanage at Pinnawala. Ask the person arranging for your car to get you there before you get to Colombo, if you don’t have too much time. If you have the time, spend a couple of hours over there as well. For someone who loves elephants, it’s a sight to see so many of them completely unperturbed by so many humans in their presence. The mahuts even allow the tourists to oblige the elephants to pose with them. Obviously one needs to be a little cautious around them to make sure that they are not antagonized, but if that’s done well, it’s a treat to be there. Try to avoid going near calf’s which are wandering by themselves. You run the risk of an irtate mother charging you. Don’t miss the old tusker who is a sight to see and behold. Also, there are feeding times when people are given fruit baskets from which elephants can be fed and also slots when the calves are given bottles of milk which the people can also see. There’s also a bathing ritual for the elephants in the river, which we missed,  but we are told it is quite a lot of fun.

Watching the elephants bathing is amazing-we had never been so close before. It is great to see them in the river-but the rest of the experience felt very touristy and exploitative. I did not get a feeling that there was much conservation activity to protect these beautiful animals in the future-it really feels like a money making tourist trap. Especially when the keepers keep searching for the rich tourist to get close to the elephant for money and get upset when the fee given does not meet expectations. Enjoy being close to the elephants but know what yu are letting yourself in for.

We arrived at the car park across the road from the "orphanage" and were immediately accosted by some Sri Lankan opportunists that shepherded us down near the river and extracted 6,000 rupees for two of us. We assumed that this was the orphanage charging the price but soon became suspicious when asked if the money was going to the elephants they seemed to lose their knowledge of english. We were intimidated into elephant rides and I have to say I was petrified. No saddle of any kind just a piece of foam covered in vinyl over the elephant back. BEWARE! When you go to Pinnewala elephant orphange go straight to the real ticket booth and don't get caught by these opportunists who are using elephants to make money for themselves. The orphanage is not much better in that when the person at the ticket booth was asked if this money went back into the facility she said "No" it goes to the government. This was a money making venture no doubt and there was not much thought given to visitor safety in regard to the elephants. It is all very well to get up close and personal with them but after all they are wild animals and very big and heavy and there were children running around and people walking very close to them. This is a recipe for disaster. I would rather that they are actually rehabilitating the elephants and having them go back in the wild. It would be much better if they show you how they do that rather than try and extract a tip to allow you to feed the baby elephants. I have to say I was glad to get away from there. This attraction was a big disappointment.

I happened to be lucky that I arrived right before the feeding and the bathing time for the elephants so if you plan to go, it would be best to know the schedule ahead of time so that you don't miss it. After the feeding, the elephants are led to the river to bathe in groups. You get to watch the elephants herded and led to the river. We got a table at one of the restaurants by the river to watch them bathe. Just order drinks as the food is priced higher than an average restaurant because of the view of the river while the elephants are bathing. There are numerous gift shops along the road towards the river, they keep calling out to you to the point that it's almost annoying but all you need to do is decline if you aren't interested. I've never seen (well I don't remember as I was told I had visited this place when I was very young) so many elephants so close and the babies were very adorable playing in the dirt and bathing.

Before our holidays to Sri Lanka, I read many reviews on Tripadvisor.  I found them very helpful as I knew what to expect: quite expensive site, having to tip for any little extra like pictures or feeding elephants. Because I knew about all that, I choose not to be bother and just enjoyed being with elephants. My son (2) and I gave a bottle to a baby elephant... it was amazing to see the look on his face!

I visited Pinewala Elephant Orphanage in the month of November. i started from colombo in the morning but as i was bit late so missed the opportunity to see milk feeding of small elephants. when i reached there, it was time for elephanst to take both in nearby river. so i went straight to river and observed closely these huge but gentle human friendlyy creatures> most interesting scene for me is to see young elephnats taking bath and moving in between the legs of big ones. i recommend early morning arrival there so one can see the small elephants being feeded milk through bottles

We had a fantastic few hours here and it was the first time my girlfriend had got up close and personal with the elephants.  It's worth getting there early in time for the feed and then wondering over to see all the elephants waiting to head to the river.  We hung around right until the last moment before they headed down to the river and this was a treat as you get so close to them (great pictures!). Once you're down at the river, you can sit and watch the elephants for hours just playing in the river - such amazing creatures! Only downside is the elephant keepers.  They were the worst money grabbers I experienced in all of Sri Lanka.  They were forever asking for tips for this and that.  Any photo they were near, they seemed to want to be paid for.  And when you do tip them an amount easily acceptable elsewhere, they start moaning about "small tip" and demand more.  I'm sure they are poorly paid but the entrance fee isn't cheap so we shouldn't be hassled by them to supplement their wages the whole time. Luckily this didn't ruin our experience and we had a great few hours there!

My friends and I made a visit here thinking that it was an elephant 'sanctuary'. The road to the so-called orphanage should have given us our first clue that everything wasn't kosher...as there were elephants chained up along roadside for people to ride and feed. When we arrived we were just in time to see the bottle feeding of the baby elephants....which is where they tie up the younger elephants in a paddock, and charge tourists to feed them with a bottle. The chains on the elephants legs aren't taken off and one poor elephant couldn't walk on his chained leg....it appeared as though his foot was swollen and the circulation had been cutoff. As we followed the elephants to the field he kept holding his leg up to try to get the chain off. It was unbelievably sad. There are also several large bull elephants with chains around their necks and on each foot. When it was time for the elephants to head to the river for their bath, the handlers were very aggressive with them, and one of the elephants shirked(and even yelped) at the sight of a handler coming at him with a spear. After that, my friends and I decided to leave without going to the river to watch them bathe. It was too much. If you're picturing a large open pasture, where the elephants are free to roam and do what they please, don't go here. Don't give them any more money. I'm so upset that I contributed to such an awful place.

It is not as though this place goes out of it's way to misrepresent itself, it is just that it is way off what I expected. Maybe I was looking for some benevolent organisation that is using visitor money to fund animal welfare and my disappointment comes from finding little more than an exploitative circus. I am not a veterinarian and so cannot comment on the health of the elephants, but I do know that there is little if any effort to move the orphans back into the wild; in fact the opposite is happening as they are bearing very cute babies. The handlers use long spiked poles to marshal the elephants which for my tender European eyes looks cruel, but then I have not tried to control a huge elephant with a gentle word and a pat on the back; maybe I am naive to expect anything else. What is clear is that the elephants are there to make money. It is not possible to stand and admire these majestic animals without a 'handler' dragging an unsuspecting tourist to stand beside the elephant for a photo opportunity; the arguments that sometimes ensued over the inadequacy of the tip were an eye opener. Lastly, get used to the special tourist price and local's price difference. I would not recommend travellers to avoid this place, just to go in knowing what you are about to experience. I have never been so close to an elephant before, but I would gladly forego this pleasure if it meant that these animals would be introduced back into the wild as soon as was possible to live their days free rather than part of this circus.

We visited the orphanage in Nov 2011. The best part- the place is really punctual - thing start and end as per the scheduled time. It is hot and sunny - so please take a hat along and rub on some sunscreen. The elephant feeding (baby elephants with milk bottles) is a must have experience. It is fun to see the baby elephants play when they are in the river. On the way to the river, there are numerous souvenir shops- bargain hard before you buy anything. At the banks of the river are restaurants that are over priced, only because they offer a great view point for the elephant bathing activities. The food is not tasty, so, order a milk shake of coffee and sip on it until you are done with watching the elephants frolicking.

The most enchanting elephant orphanage ever.  The elephants roam freely all day.  They are taken to the Maha Oya river twice daily for cleaning themselves and playing and drinking in the water.  They are each fed twice daily and could want for nothing more than their incredible laid back life style.  Some of these elephants I remember from my first visit seven years earlier and all I have seen this time around is more improvements to their enclosures and environment.  I cannot speak highly enough of this tourist attraction.  The elephants are well cared for and still as cheeky as ever.  I highly recommend everyone who visits Sri Lanka, should go and visit this magical place in Kegalle (near Kandy).

This was my second visit to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage and I found that the grounds and enclosures had been improved dramatically since my initial visit seven years prior. The most serene part of my visits are walking the elephants across the road to the riverbank and enjoyed watching them frolic and play in the water and spray the mahouts in a cheeky manner. When the elephants were exiting the river area to return to the pathway to cross back over the road to their other enclosures, I had one particular elephant who took a liking to me and I wasn't coaxing him to come near, he decided to walk right up to me and cradle my ankle with his trunk whilst I took close up photos of his beautiful eyes, mouth and trunk. Walking them back to the feeding pens was also a treat and then just grazing in their vast grounds with a  jungle backdrop was breathtaking. Whenever I do travel back to Sri Lanka, I will always go and visit the PInnawala Elephant Orphanage. I highly recommend everyone visits this particular orphanage because even though it is a little pricey, its the most beautiful highlight of anyone's tour of the most magnificent island on the planet. I will endeavour to return in August though because the Perahera is on and the elephants are dressed in national costumes and lights, then take part in a parade through the streets of Kandy swaying to the music of drummers and fire twirling baton Kandian dancers.

Great to see so many elephants well cared for the kids got to wash them in the river, feed them mangos and milk to a baby, however everyone that looks for the elephants was after money, which when you pay to go in you don't expect (even in Sri Lanka) The paper products made from Elephant Pooh are wide ranging and certainly worth buying as a novel gift, just a pity it was so expensive, and the quantity of products in the shop reflected the high price.

Its a lovely place to be with your family and especially with young kids. The sight of so many elephants being together is lovely! The place has been well maintained and the wilderness of forest has been kept intact so that the elephants enjoy in their natural habitat
