I volunteer in the orphanage for 2 months and let me tell you it was amazing, I got to see the elephants all day and see them in the activities of the day.,. I am a veterinarian and let me tell you that these elephants are quite healthy considering the circustances that this is a country were human-elephant conflict exsists.  People like to see them up close and for that they need to be trained I did not witnes any abuse and they have chains for training as you can se the adult ones are unchained it is the young ones that have then and the male working ones for they are more agressive. They are dangerous and smart animals and well they have a good home at pinnawala. The fees to enter are not that high and well about the fee that was mentioned with a camara and that it is because they are using it for a documerntary or for tv.  I used my camara every day and my fee was as a regular tourist. And about the maiting of the elephants they are animals and by nature they need to mate and they are not back in the wild because there is no were to be taken,  Raja and Sama are 2 elephants that should of died long ago but by the help of pinnawala they are alive and taken care of.  Raja is blind and old and has nice baths every day, clean water, food every day, and a veterinarian on call, every day.  Sama is the elephant missing part of her leg and she is in a family environment and is loved by the herd. So not expect to see them in a natural habitat because they are not, they try to keep it as natural as posible by allowing interaction in the herd, mating and bathing in the river.  This is a good place to visist if you like to see elephants up close but as a tourist do not expect to ride them or to ineract with them because they try for them to have little human contact with outside staff.  ther is a schedule in the enterance for you to see the activities and not miss any of the elephant activities. I truly recomend this place and please do not write crap if you expect something without thinking of the great help that this place does for this animals.  I know that it is in human nature to see $$$ every were, but they are still doing a great job.

We have been to see this orphanage before in the 80's & 90's and it has changed alot and not for the better. Everytime a photo opportunity came along, someone was holding their hand out for a tip and when one was given I was told it wasn't enough! When the elephants were taken down to the river, we were already waiting in the cafe with a great vantage point.  5 of the larger elephants were chained up just under neath where we were sat and they began to wash and play.  For no reason what so ever on of the handlers started throwing stones at one of them whilst it was just lying in the water.  Then another took his pole and threw it and it stuck in the elephants ear, it let out such a scream all the other elephants began to call and get up.  It took him a while to release his pole and he then sat and smiled for the tourists. I understand that these animals need to be controlled but this was absolutely disgusting behavour. I would not recommend this trip again.

I've visited this place Couple of  years back and this is the best place to see the elephants up & close as the heard goes to bath, you can see the elephants really close here. Even the small ones when they pass you by .their is a time in the morning and in the evening where they put them to bath. (it's the closest I've been to a herd) their are good reputed hotels if you plan to stay over night

We visited the orphanage in the morning and saw the baby elephants being fed - they were so sweet and you can stroke them after they have been fed, great experience.  We saw the elephants in the park working, and feeding etc.  Visit the blind elephant, he is kept away from the others as they are too rough for him.  The best bit is watching the elephants bathing in the river. Don't be alarmed that the elephants and even the baby are chained up, as they are still wild animals and can be extremely dangerous.  The poles with spikes on the mahouts use are not to hurt the elephants they are to control them.  They touch pressure points behind there ears, so they respond to commands. I'm a big softie when it comes to animals and I felt quite privileged to get so close to wild animals.  Enjoy.  By the way the elephant poo paper and gifts are quite expensive!

The Pinnawela Elephant Orphanage is not an orphanage. It is not a sanctuary. It is a crime scene, where elephants are bred for the amusement of humans. A blind elephant is chained by a front and back foot, forced to stand in place day after day for people to look at. An elephant who lost part of its from leg from a land mine limps around the park. Every elephant is “trained” with a bull hook. In order to have tourists pay for photos the workers fetch each elephant in turn by catching them in a tender spot with the bull-hook and drawing them to the unsuspecting tourists. An elephant is persuaded to lie down in the water, and a bull-hook is laid across his neck to convince him to say in place. He lies there for hours. Two young elephants are chained under a roof, too far apart to offer comfort. They strain at their chains, trying to touch each other. An elephant is chained at river’s edge, the only one not allowed to enter the water, She spends the next two hours swaying, attempting over and over to immerse herself in the cool river along with all of the others. Tourists feed peanuts to the elephants, who are then chased away with bull-hooks by the workers. I don’t know much at all about elephants, but I know something about fear. These elephants are obviously terrified of the workers, and no doubt they should be. It is brutal existence and incredibly sad to watch.

Went on a overnight trip to see the elephants at Pinneewala. What a great day out never seen so many elephants in one place enjoyed the feeding of the baby elephants to seeing the elephants in the river enjoying their splash around. It is well worth going on this trip. I went a bit "snap happy" with the camera to ensure I had plenty of memories. It's a long way to go so overnight is better. We did other things along the way but for me this was the best part. Janis Oliver

I have visited the elephant orphanage more than 10 times by now. I was really surprised to see some reviews, because i think the place is really amazing. Pinnawala Elephant orphanage is the home for nearly 100 elephants. Some of these are born in the orphanage itself and some are taken from the outside because of the injuries. I have seen some injured elephants at the time of taking them to the orphanage and they are really lucky to have this kind of place, after injured that much badly. In the elephant orphanage these elephants have enough space to live freely.  But elephants are not domestic animals and if they got wild they may be highly dangerous. you can imagine if 10 elephants got wild, how dangerous it could be.   so I don't see anything wrong about chained elephants. I want to say that if some one think that the staff dragging elephants to the bath, they are badly mistaken, because elephants love to play in water very much. Once I saw an elephant (this one was not allowed to go for bath, because she gave a birth that morning) who struggled to go for bath. At the time of bath one of the staff member blow a horn and elephants are very sensitive to the sound, so they start moving towards the river immediately. Therefore it is not fair to say 'drag the elephants to the bath'. it is true that you have to pay a tip to feed a baby elephant, but you don't want to pay for watch it. And it is not true if you say "they are not going to feed until we give money". Since I have visited this place several times, i can simply recommend this place as a very good attraction.

At the front scene only one elephant was chained but at the back scene they were ALL chained to the ground. A baby elephant was forced to pose for pictures & another elephant (the mother I suppose) tried to protect the baby & lifted the mahout from the ground. This act resulted in a storm of mahouts poking the poor thing with their metal hood sticks. They were even chasing her after she let go of the mahout. I’ve seen them using their sticks more then once, just to get the elephants moved to pose for (tipping) tourists. Baby elephants were not allowed to natural nursing, can you imagine! The baby elephant’s needs to perform at a nursing show were they get milk from tourists who paid extra for this. Show must go on! If you like scared & chained elephants poked with metal hood sticks, this is definitely the place to be! If you’re an animal lover go on safari in one of the national parks & avoid this so called ‘orphanage’

I've never seen elephants wandering around except at a zoo, so I was excited to visit this place! Instantly, you could tell that this attraction is for tourists. The ticket prices are high, and there are two areas to see the elephants: 1) in the main eating area, 2) in the water bathing. The bathing part was pretty cool to see. However, I didn't like how some elephants had chains on their legs :( I'm sure the chains were scorching hot on the legs. In addition, some people fed the elephants bananas and the security yelled at the elephants and the people. Watching the elephants bathe can take around 10-15 minutes before it gets boring. When you cross the street to the eating area, it is also not that exciting. You could pose next to the elephants, but it is for a price. The security people pocketed the money. In addition, it seemed like the elephants didn't get to eat much. It was a good experience, but you could easily see everything with 20 minutes. Don't bother spending an entire day here.

Useful info: 2000 SLRp (foreigner), feeding times (9.15 am, an an afternoon one- sorry can't recall, but it is findable in guidebooks), toilets available. You need to arrive at least 30mins early to buy extra tickets (500Rp) to feed the elephants. However, the staff feeding the elephants were openly taking money/ bribes to allow people to feed. Around 1 hour drive from Kandy. When you arrive, you can watch the feeding of young elephants and then get herded over to see the elephants in pens and enclosures. After observing for around 30mins, the elephants are guided to a near by river where you can watch them being washed. Some staff were taking money to allow people to assist in the cleaning but we were told that this is not official practice. You again observe for 30-60mins. The elephants are then taking back and that marks the end of the experience. The walk back to the main road is the 'exit through the gift shop' part. It was a fun experience, but note that you will not be alone- there were around 100 others present. I have since read many concerns regarding the care of the elephants, I did not see any overt evidence of mistreatment. However, I am not an expert and would suggest that, as with any commercialised interaction with animals, you research and satisfy yourself regarding its integrity.

The elephant orphanage at Pinnawala is a must visit. To see the elephants bathing at a lake is very picturesque. You can also feed bananas to the elephants. Its a treat to watch The landscape near lake is also very beautiful. After bathing near the lake the elephant are taken to the orphange where they jus move in the mud. You will find elephants of all sizes. One can also take up an elephant safari but its pretty expensive. Overall a beautiful place and a must visit if travelling to sri lanka

Elephant orphanage was pretty nice. Like the rest of Sri Lanka, the tourist price is insanely high compared to the local price (2000LKR vs 50LKR), but that's to be expected with Sri Lankan tourism. There were lots of beautiful elephants, and despite what some of the other people reviewing here say, the conditions were completely reasonable compared to other Asian countries, and, really, better than the Canadian zoo in the city we come from. Seeing them bathe and play in the river was an absolutely fantastic experience, though the chained up bottle feeding was a little strange. I recommend seeing this on a day trip, the town surrounding (well, basically in between) the orphanage is a giant tourist trap. Hotels are expensive (we went with a Sri Lankan friend and they quoted him 500LKR/night and then found out the room was for tourists and changed the price to 2500LKR, Hotel Elephant View by the way, don't stay there), tuk tuk drivers and other touts are annoying beyond comprehension and it's probably in general the most expensive place we found in our month in Sri Lanka. Don't stay overnight, pack a lunch, and remember that any souvenirs are going to be about ten times more expensive than from a market in Galle, Kandy or Colombo. See the sight worth seeing, don't contribute to the flagrant price gouging.

The other less positive reviews sum it up - it's grossly overpriced for the region, and it's not much of an attraction, nor is it really an orphanage. It felt more like a zoo or circus where the animals are exploited. We had a better experience getting recommendations from our driver (who I will happily recommend) on great locations to spend time with animals and see them out in the wild. There were kids there on a field trip, though, and they seemed to really love it.

This place is good due to below points - You can see lots elephants all together, I think more than 120 in numbers. - You can see them very closing whether its baby or old elephants. - You can feed milk to baby elephants, that you can capture it in video or images. - You can see then bath enjoying, bathing etc. But its not very good because you may expect elephant show, some dance or something else rather than just seeing them doing normal stuff. If you will plan correctly then you will not feel bad, no need to spend full day over the, finish this in the early morning time and then jump into other place like exploring Colombo for rest of the. That’s why what we have done, while going to Colombo from kandy we have covered this place early morning and after that we had lunch and then rest of the day we have utilized for colombo sight seeing.

I'm lucky enough to have seen elephants in India, Nepal and Thailand and I truly believed this place was interested in the welfare of the elephants. I was wrong. It is a complete rip off and having to pay $20 to sit in a restaurant and have an overpriced cup of tea while watching scared chained elephants in a river is not my idea of fun. The tacky shops along the street that leads to the river sell the sort of stuff you could buy 20 years ago in Bali. A total disappointment. If you really want to help elephants donate your money to a decent charity. Or go to a zoo. Or a wildlife park.

The pinnawela elephant orphanage is located nortwest in the town of kegalle,srilanka. the aim of the orphanage is provide nurse,.feed, and home for abandon baby elephant in the jungle .which is .very popular among local and foreign tourists.main atraction is the opportunity to observe elephants from abroad river bank as the herd interacts,bathes and plays.vistors to the park can also observe  many differant  aspects of the orphange which include the daily routines of elephants such as bottle feeding calves  to peeding elephants as well as the close attention and care provided to them by the orphanage staff.

The sri Lankans are very fortunate to have Both the Largest living Animals theELEPHANT & the WHALE in the same country and as tourist attrctions both are doing an immense service to the trade. However I reserve my comments on the Elephant Orphanage at Pinnawela, Kegalle, Srilanka as a must as well as a should not be place as it collects wild orphan elephants in an open but restricted area disallowing them the chance of behaving as free wild animals. while the departement of Zoological Gardens should be praised for the gigantic effort they take to maintain the Kraaal (enclosed elephant center ) this tourist attrction I think that the authorities should try to give them more space and relocate the elephants in places like UdaWalawe so that the tourists could travel inside the area and watch them than at a single space observing a daily routine which makes the animals domesticated. i invite any enterprise or an animal lover to write to the Zoological Departement and assist in Funds to them so that this beautiful and valuable asset in srilanaka could be preserved for future generations to enjoy.

It is no longer an orphanage as most of the young are born there now and should be called a sanctuary.  As soon as you get there you have to go to the main entrance and pay the tourist price of 2,000 Sri Lankan Rupees (Approx. US$20).  Locals will pay a lot less, you also have to pay extra if you wish to take professional photo's.  It has become a money making scheme for the most of it. You will then have to cross the road again to see the elephants bathing in the river and you will then be approached by people trying to sell you DVD's of the elephant orphanage, try and sell you banana's to feed the elephants with.  Once they are finished bathing the elephants are led back to the 'sanctuary' where you can see them there. It isnt anything special unless you have never seen elephants up close and personal before.

I do not agree with most of the reviews.  Our family had a great time.  It is a safe environment to see a heard of elephants and to go back home with a lot of good memories. Also remember Sri Lankan there is always the case of people looking for money for the smallest thing.  That is because it is a poor country and when they see people from other countries they think they can get a little extra money, but no body is forced to give. Have a look at the pictures below, I did not see anyone poking elephants for no reason or chaining them. As you have probably seen from other reviews, there is a lot of controversy surrounding this attraction. You should be aware of this situation, and make up your mind. My friend and I did NOT like: -The staff, constantly looking for tips -Admission is ~$20 USD (overpriced!) -Feeding time was another opportunity for them to ask for more money. The elephants were clearly very hungry, and the staff wouldn't feed them until a tourist paid to feed the elephants. The excursion to this delightful elephant orphanage, located about one and a half hour drive away from Kandy, was a truly memorable experience for our family. We were overjoyed when we got a SAARC discount on the entrance ticket. We saw the elephants feeding, bathing and playing.We also witnessed their orderly parade. The Orphanage housed a rare  Tusker as well. There was a clean restaurant and  serviceable wash-rooms on the  grounds.There were elephant dung paper stores located all around the Orphanage.

you need to check the time schedule before visiting the orphanage as they have timing for each activity as baby elephant bottle feeding, river bath........... we were on time to see the elephants  in the river which was amazing and deserve stopping by  but since we had to wait for 1 to 2 hours for the next activity , we prefered to drop it,

This place is beautiful and a paradise for elephant lovers. You could treat yourself to an elephant bath to it being treated by a doctor. One can have the opportunity to milk feed a baby elephant too. Be ready to save yourself when it rains as it has got no sheds. Lots of place to shop for souvenirs outside the orphanage.

This is sold/advertised as an orphanage, it is the complete opposite it's a money pot for Sri Lanka. On arrival we had to que for fifty minutes with people constantly pushing and people were offering over the ticket price to be able to get to the front of the que which was happily accepted by the ticket men! Tickets are very expensive but we assumed it was all going to a good cause.....when we finally got into the venue we stood with thousands of people to watch CHAINED elephants get dragged to a river to have a bath. The elephants were really scared of their owners who kept pushing and poking them with sharp sticks. On the walk to the river you are bombarded with people trying to sell everything from elephant toilet paper to a special elephant hand massage?! If you want to film the elephants you have to pay extra, the whole thing is just ridiculous. Granted watching the elephants in the water is lovely. This is not an orphanage it is a zoo, they do not care about these elephants it is simply a money making scheme which is terribly sad.

We chose to do a daytrip from Colombo to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage which we were very excited about. The car journey from Colombo would be around 1.5 hours we were told, although ultimately it was closer to 3 hours each way. Highlights: - Bathing session in a beautiful stream. Quite a breathtaking sight to see almost a hundred elephants wading and bathing in a herd, against a backdrop of verdant Sri lankan forest. We ate lunch at a hotel which overlooked the elephants and the stream, this was quite unique. - Elephant Dung showroom & shop. This is a part-museum, part-shop; you are educated in the intricacies of elephant dung paper production, including a brief introduction in how its manufactured, and then a tour of the showroom in which you  can see a large volume of surprisingly varied products which are made from the stuff. Easy to miss as its on the road back from the bathing site, but very interesting and well worth taking a look inside. Lowlights: - Total lack of information about the park, its objectives, and elephants in general. There is no guide to explain the behaviour of the animals, their feeding patterns, bathing habits, and the reasons for them being in the "orphanage". Indeed, at times this felt more like a zoo than an orphanage. - Elephants being kept in order by mahuts with large, dangerous spears. This seemed quite inhumane and unnecessary. - Constant touting by park rangers. You are always being badgered by the mahuts to "touch the elephants" or take photos with them, for which they expect a tip. By all means take pictures with the elephants, but ignore their please for money. OVERALL: While this was an enjoyable experience, we would agree with reviewers who state that this is not worth the long journey from Colombo. Due to the lack of information and guidance provided by the park, there was not much more to this experience than merely watching the elephants, which gets boring after a while as they are not particularly active. With a bit of information, this could have been a much more enriching and fulfilling experience. Recommended if you are with children; or if you are visiting Kandy anyway. Not recommended if you are coming all the way from Colombo only for this.

How anyone could write a positive review of this horrific place is beyond me. This place is unbelievably cruel to the elephants, the mahouts are sadistic, the animals are kept chained and standing in their own waste 23 hours a day. The babies are prodded with sticks and bullhooks to "nurse" for tips. I literally threw up as I exited this concentration camp for elephants. The saddest thing I have ever witnessed.

This was a wonderfull experiance. The elephants are all taken down to the nearby river twice a day to bathe. We arrived just befor lunch and had a meal at a cafe over looking the river while the elephants all bathed and played. Yes they are in captivity but they seemed happy enough and were showing all the signs of acting like a wild heard.The older females were very protective of the younger ones.After lunch we went up to the orphanage and I paid a very small fee to feed an orphan baby elephant with a bottle of milk. This is a memory I will treasure for ever. Yes it would be better if the elephant were still in the wild but as with all natural habitats these days there is just not enough of it lleft. A lot of the animals have been badly injured and would not have survived if left to fend for them selves. A very large bull elephant had been attacked by poachers and left blind, a smaller female elephant had one of her frount legs very badly damaged by a land mine thanks to Pinnawala these animals still have a good life. I would recomend a visit to anyone, But remember it is not a wildlife reserve it is an orpanage and hospital for the unfortunate elephants that end up needing human help to survive, and thankfully Pinawala is there for them.

I wasn't sure about visiting this place after reading the mixed reviews on this site but figured it was best to judge for myself. I thought it was lovely & a real opportunity to see up close a big herd of elephants interacting together. The site is broken up into two parts - the main centre/feeding area & then the river.  We watched as approx 60 elephants grazed & mingled at the main centre & also watched the younger ones being bottle fed. Then the real highlight was bath time. The elephants make their way across the road & down a road lined with shops & into the river. Its quite a sight! You can sit at a local restaurant & have lunch while you watch the elephants wallow, play & enjoy themselves. The elephants all have different stories behind why they are there - victims of landmines & the long-running civil war, rescued from cruel work conditions & accidents. The centre opens 8.30 - 6pm daily with bottle feeding at 9.15am, 1.15pm & 5pm and bathing at 10am - 12noon & again 2-4pm. We drove from Kandy (approx 2 hours with some stops).

We stayed at the Kani Lanka hotel in Kalutara and went for a over night tour with Jambo a beach boy working outside the hotel. His tour was half the price of the travel rep. Let's get a few things straight about Pinnawala.  My husband and I go once or twice a year and would not miss it for the world.  Pinnawala is a great example of how animals and man can live and work together in harmony for the benefit of all concerned. Why shouldn't the Mahouts ask for a small contribution for the services they provide,  you'd tip a waiter wouldn't you?   Ok 100 rupees to feed, pat, wash, play with and bond with an animal is less than most people earn in an hour!  They earn perhaps 1000 rupees a week!.  As for the use of the goads,  if you care to look carefully you will see that the Mahouts with goads are mostly with the elephants that are chained.  The reason why they are changed is because they are working elephants.  They work within the reserve, tree felling, clearing shrubbery and generally keeping the place tidy.  It is a well known fact that Elephants love to work.  If they didn't like their treatment they are strong enough and big enough to make it known, jumbo style!    I have never seen a wound on an elephant in the five years I have been going. Before you make rash judgements on this place, take time out to go down to the river at about 8pm every morning.  Here you will see the sick, old, nursing mothers and baby elephants being washing and watched over by two Mahouts.  They are not chained or in fear and are free to roam the length and breadth of the beautiful river for two hours before the massive procession of the  healthy, robust and excited herd run down the street to the river. Please also remember the elephant who's foot was blown off by a mine and the beautiful tusker who's been blinded by a shot gun and the female's who regularly give birth at the sanctuary,  without year in, year out care by obviously caring staff, these animals would not have survived at all.

There is a entry fee for foreign visitors. Place is quite good and was told that there were 80 elephants here. We could see around 4 baby elephants and one of them was 3 days old. Elephants are taken to the river for bathing which is across the road, they are taken in batches. Elephants are pretty well looked after in this place.

The "elephant orphanage" is a refuge for old, maimed or otherwise unwanted elephants. It is extremely rare to see working elephants in Sri Lanka these days.  You can see some in the wild if you are lucky and go on safari (such as Yala). But these are rather artificial surroundings and the animals are not in the wild habitat, but I really I really can't understand the people who say "don't go there" or say the elephants are all chained up. It's just been the case when I have been there (more than once). It was the same in April 2011 as it was in January 2006 on my previous visit and I loved it. At 2,000 LKR per head it is not a bargain, but it is a great way to see elephants close up and get some fabulous photos. The only thing I didn't like before was the feeding milk to the baby elephants from bottles (it may have changed in 5 years but probably not). It's best to arrive so you get to see the elephants bathing. But before and after that they live across the road and most roam freely. Just a handful of elephants there have been chained up and they don't go down to the river either - that is for the safety of the public. The best time is when the siren sounds and the elephants all march en masse out of the river. You can sit in a cafe and watch them from afar if you don't want to go close. I think it is great experience for all ages. Not sure I would make a special trip from Colombo just for that - but combine it with other sights in the Kandy area. There was no free parking at Pinnawala so it also cost an additional 100 LKR on a piece of wasteland nearby. We didn't bother with the souvenir shops that also line the lane down to the river. Our driver/guide made sure we got to see the elephants bathing and thought we would not want to go inside as well. But it is worth it and taking the time to enjoy the unique experience.

I found our visit to pinnawala very disappointing. The elephants were eating and were all chained up at the time. Only the babies were allowed to roam free. The people working there are opportunists of the worst kind and ask for money for everything which definitely puts a damper on the visit. Some of the elephants are also clearly distressed and rock back and forth in their chains. It would be good to have someone around to tell you a little about the elephants but there was no one in sight when we were there. All around disappointing.

We have just come back from Shri Lanka, the people were good and the places we saw were good, except the elephant orphanage. If you have any emotions for elephants or animals please do not go and support this place. I found that the Shri Lankan people who worked here were consistently prodding an poking these poor animal with long pointed sticks and continually forcing these animals to perform for the public for a few tips. The whole experience disturbed me and from here I would not go near any other elephant attraction to see what I considered was animal cruelty. If this attraction were in England then this place would have been shut down for the way it treats its animals.

Pinnewala is a good place to be in, specially if you like elephants. The place offers various facilities like Feeding milk to baby elephants, bathing elephants, ride etc. We took the bathing one and it was very good. the mahaut actually made us give a bath to the elephant (and we also got drenched...) The elephant ride was unique. Unlike in other places, they dont use saddles here. Meaning, you sit on the animal directly (with just a cloth mat on it). So, be prepared for that! Elephant hair is long and pirckly though, so its not very comfortable and stable, but it gives a raw feeling! i liked it. There are quite a few folks there who want to rip you off, not very common in Sri Lanka, but  at this place yes - so do watch out for it.

This is NOT an orphinage, it is a zoo and a bad one at that. The baby's were being fed in a small enclosure surrounded on all sides by people flashing cameras, talking waving things. Remember these are wild animals, there were also a couple of adults to make up the numbers they were swaying about clearly distressed. Outside in the main enclosure, the mostly adult elephants, were hearded up in a dusty paddock to be viewed in the full sun in the heat of the day. There is no programme for releasing these money making animals and it was distressing to see them treated like that. We did not stay long. PLEASE if you want to see orphan elephants visit the Elephant Transit home at Udawallah. There the puplic are kept at a distance from the elephants and they have a programme to release them back into the wild. The Born Free charity backs that one.

Pinnawela Orphanage is wonderful and I would recommend it to all!!  I have to disagree with the bah humbug people who feel they had been scammed and paid money to see "performing"  "sad" elephants.  I asked why some were tied and when you looked it made sense.  The male was tethered because he was trying to get to any available female elephant which when you think about the power of him it was tie him up so he could be in the river with the others or he stayed at the shelter on his own! It was a truly wonderful experience to see them playing in the water and mud!

This was a very sad part of my trip to Sri Lanka. These elephants are underweight and this is very visible. They say this is an orphanage,but not all these elephants are or have been orphans. They are a money making spinner for tourists. I have seen elephants in the wild and when you see these chained  and performing elephants it breaks your heart. They actually look sad. they are poked with large sticks with metal hooks on the end, and recently a large bull elephant was killed by the keepers...look in the news. if you want to see elephants in Sri lanka go to the national park and see them wild and without there bones sticking through there skin.

Located 3 hours drive away from Colombo, Pinnawala is a must see place. You can bathe and feed baby elephants, but make sure to reach before 9am. Elephant ride is a bonus. Charges are 2000 SL Rupees for foreigners. You do get value for money. Avoid the spice gardens which line up on the way. They are just places for a costly spice massage, which is not great in any case. Hiring a Taxi from Colombo is advisable, though there are buses from the central bus stand in Colombo. The road is quite ok, once you move away from the city hustle and bustle. The scenery is super neat.

If you want drive for hours to get totally ripped off (70 bucks for a family of five) in this poo hole then be my guest.  While you're at it, you can watch a bunch of scum bags abuse some of the sadest looking elephants you could imagine. The staff are rude, unhelpful and just want your cash. After that you can get stuffed. This is no more an 'orphanage' than Changi gaol. I've never been so embarrassed to be a tourist in my whole life. If you do go, all I can say is I told you so

Went to see elephants as advised by a colleague who visited the orphanage several years ago. I found it not as I expected but then again we English are rather silly over animals, personally I found the mahouts rather over zealous using their canes on the animals to get them to move and pose for photos. I felt it was all a rather sorry spectacle.

I thoroughly enjoyed my time at the orphanage. It was a positive experience and seeing the elephants enjoy themselves, both in the park and in the river, I wondered how anyone could find fault with the place. It cost around $18 USD for an adult, which I thought was very reasonable given that you get to spend a few hours feeding, petting, and watching the elephants. I felt sorry for the baby elephant who had been injured by a train, but he is well looked after and seems to be healing. I highly encourage anyone visiting Sri Lanka to think about this as an option. I even got to see a guy with a cobra on the road down to the river.

I visited this place 13 years ago and don't remember much about it, just a lot of walking and rather smelly! They seem to have simplified the place more now, there really isn't a lot to see which is why people may complain about it, but me and my husband enjoyed it. They seemed to be quite freely roaming around, and hubby got to feed a baby elephant with a milk bottle. We then stood really closeby while they marched past us to the river to bathe- that was really an awesome experience. But if you want to get in the water and bathe them, and then ride one then millenium foundation is the place to go.

I had really been put off going to Pinnawela Elephant Orphanage by reading some of the reviews on TripAdvisor, but the entrance fees were already included as part of our Private Tour and having read a bit more about it I decided that surely a place that is looking after the elephants rather than having them being shot by farmers etc., must be worth a look and if I didn't like what I saw then we could always ask our driver to take us straight to the hotel...especially as we went there first thing in the morning straight from landing in Colombo. I don't really understand what people have seen regarding elephants being chained up.  When we were there just 2 weeks ago the elephants were happily wandering around, they'd even taken on an elephant that had a foot missing from stepping on a landmine and they had a blind elephant there.  The elephants were milling about and then it was time for the babies to be fed, they happily walked down to where they get fed and at that point they were chained, but realistically you can't have baby elephants running riot waiting for their milk surrounded by on-looking tourists, let's not forget that elephants can be dangerous.  The chains didn't look tight and they were munching away on the soft innards of trees and then wolfed down gallons of milk each.  We then went across the road to a restaurant for lunch which was right on the river and the elephants came across as well, went down to the river and some chose to have a lie down in the water, some had a good scrub from the keepers which they seemed to really enjoy, some of the elephants walked right across the river and onto the opposite bank and some walked into the jungle on the otherside of the river.  We didn't see anyone raise a hand to them, they weren't chained up.  From reading up about it the only time that they really chain some of the male ones up is when they are in season - basically when they are horny buggers - unless they were to build a big concrete enclosure like a zoo, then what other option do they have than to tether them - people in UK zoos have been killed accidentally by elephants crushing them.  I had a good luck at the ankles of the elephants and didn't see any with wounds or open sores and I honestly was really pleased that I had gone - I have some lovely photos of the elephants bathing and despite having not had more than about an hour's sleep on the flight over - watching the elephants was a real joy.

we went to the elephant orphanage in 2008 and again in 2009 we both found the experience very enjoyable, yes you pay a fee to get in just like you would to visit the zoo in england, so why are so many people moaning, we believe that the handlers do a good job of taking care of the elephants, the small fee you pay {when you convert it to sterling it is only pennies} is food money for them to take home to the family. money has been spent to buy the elephant who lost her lower leg from a mine a false leg, so money is being used to improve their lives, we will be going back in 2011, so if you are going to go to sri lanka visit the elephant orphanage.

My daughter went 2 months ago as she lives In Columbo, she had a good experience and during that visit the public were allowed much closer to the elephants. I am here on holiday and our visit today felt very sad. The elephants were very much more controlled possibly as there had been an incident but no one would really say what had happened. The 2 babies were chained in the compound and seemed agitated, and when feeding time with the bottles commenced only so many tickets were allowed, one couple got really cross as they were told no they couldnt use there ticket. The highlight of the visit was seeing all the elephants come down to the river and bath, you can sit and have lunch and they were there for quite a while. You can walk down onto the rocks within a certain area and have your pictures taken, you have to tip the keepers though. There wasnt a good atmosphere there today, something didnt feel right and it cost 2000 rupees to go in which was more expensive than my daughters visit 2 months ago. Would love to know what money is being channelled into theses elephants futures

We went to Elephant Orphanage as my parents went on there 1st trip to Sri Lanka and loved it well it was very expensive and the elephants were all chained up and in distress including one that was very ill.  I would say to anyone wanting to go please think twice as the orphanage is not what it used to be

unmissable when in Sri Lanka, try to get a baby bottle feeding token - not expensive but difficult to get hold of!!! We stayed at the BlueWater hotel in Wadduwa and had our trip organised by Ruchi. He managed to get us a ticket to feed the babies!!! Try and go to the Elephant Park Hotel to watch the elephants in the river, you get a better view and can buy a much needed cold drink !! Excellent

I have just been work at MEF (elephant bath) for 4 weeks and loved it went to visit pinnawala and cant believe how they treat the elephants its truly horrible and the area is very unsafe nearly got trampled on! If you want to see elephants in sri lanka and go for elephant rides MEF is the place to go. Its cheaper and you get so much out of it, you can rife them, feed them, wash them in the river its a truly magical experience .

I found my trip to Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage very uncomfortable and not at all enjoyable. It is an intensely contrived tourist trap. The 'feeding sessions' are very clearly put on for the benefit of the tourists and it does not look or feel at all genuine. It is also quite distressing to see how the elephants are treated by their handlers who pull, push, and drag them for photographs with tourists so that they can collect their 'tip'. Despite the high fee you pay to get into the orphanage, the handlers will try to force you to pay them another fee for any photographs you take of or with the elephants. It is simply outrageous and left a very bad taste in my mouth. When I finally refused to pay any more of this artificial tips, telling them that I had already paid a high entrance fee and didn't want to pay another fee simply for taking a photograph, I was publicly berated by the handlers and intimidated by them. Avoid this place at all costs. It is only there for unthinking tourists who cannot see through the sham.

The Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is more of a tourist spot than an orphanage.  I've seen my share of elephants at zoo's and such so wasn't really too excited about this visit.  But when I arrived to the bathing area, I have to admit, it was pretty darned cool.  There must have been over 50 elephants and they roamed free, walking right through the village. After the bath, they roamed to an open field where it was nice to see them wondering freely, except for a few adults and a few babies who were chained to a center ring and we cheesy tourists were just staring at them.  They didn't seem to be in distress, but it was a bit uncomfortable to watch. There is a disabled elephant wandering around that stepped on a landmine and is now being cared for by the orphanage. It's worth the visit, but just be prepared that it's a tourist attraction, not an animal rescue organization.

walked over the ridge and saw the elephants in the open which was amazing, and then got taken to the feeding pen and was absolutely heartbroken. Two baby elephants were chained in the centre of a pen surrounded by tourists all clamouring to get close.  At least half of the people there were looking bewildered at what they were seeing. These baby elephants were distressed, wide - eyed and trying to pull from their chains.  I refused to join in the feeding (using some lame large baby bottle) as did a few others who were there. I would never recommend this place, it is enough to see them out in the open without resorting to this shameless tourist attraction by distressing these lovely animals at such a young age.

I've had the opportunity to visit elephant sanctuaries and rescue centres in Chiang Mai and Malaysia, but this place is quite special. You enter the main compound and get to view the herd in a large open plantation, and for a 100 rupees to the mahout you get up close and personal with a young one, whose trunk will explore your pockets and rucksack for food. Then twice daily, at 10am and 2pm, the herd is led down a narrow road to the river for their baths. So you are standing in a shop entrance or hotel front area as 70 elephants come trundling past you. Then you go watch them in the river for 2 hours if you wish. You can get in and wash one if you want, or just sit in one of the hotels watching the amazing spectacle.

What we saw on a recent trip to the Pinawela Elephant 'Orphanage' was a disgrace. Rather than the orphanage we were expecting / had read and heard about, we found the whole operation geared to milking as much cash from tourists as possible, with little regard for the elephants welfare. Entry prices had been inflated from 200 to 2,000 rupees - plus another 500 if you wanted to bring in a camera. Does that cash go to helping the elephants or lining someone's pockets? Hmmm. Admittedly, we saw the vast majority of elephants roaming free and I'm sure that they are better treated than most other elephants in Sri Lanka, and particularly those that are put to work. However, this is just one clip (link below) to highlight the problems there - these baby elephants had been chained with about 2-3ft of movement for feeding time. Not the 10-15mins the guides would have you believe, but for several hours. Watching them in distress, trying to break free was heartbreaking. None of the workers there appeared to have any interest in the elephants themselves, more in making cash from taking pictures and hearding tourists into the nearby restaurant. There were other issues we saw at the 'washing in the river' bit, but I'll try to upload the video for that separately. http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UPu4_0K1fWE It was shameful, and not something I would recommend anyone to pay money for. And yes, we've reported them to the WWF. Hopefully things will revert back to the way they seemed to be not so long ago, soon...

This is a must if you are visiting Sri Lanka. Having seen the elephants in the orphanage we moved down to the rivers edge and waited a short while. The elephants were then brought down and it was as if they were in the wild. Approx. 89 elephants all in the river and some meandering to the other side of the river to throw soil over their backs. Others were drifting down stream and they were left to their own devices for nearly 2 hours. Fantastic to see and although a bit pricey it was well worth it.

The trip to Pinnawala Ranks high among my "Things to do" list in Colombo  – It’s where they take care of elephants who got injured in the civil war with LTTE. Some of the calves are real cute and you feel sad for them. But mind you – these are wild elephants – as you are reminded immediately when they trumpet real loud and wild! So those chains on their feet are mere ornaments! There are interesting sessions, like feeding the calves with a HUGE milk bottle. See the attached photo for a list of the programmes at Pinnawala and timings. The funniest part is when the calf tries to pull the bottle from it’s caretaker doctor and push him in it’s childishness…. And the doctor nearly falls off. Wow – are they strong or what! The elephants are very well taken care of. The unfortunate part is that most of them cannot be put back in the wild, since they have already lived some time away from the forest. See the attached photo for timings of the various programmes. A good thing is that this place does not feel crowded as it is so large, and people are extremely well behaved – including the visitors. It’s a long 3 hour drive from Colombo. But on the way, you can also see the beautiful and serene “Temple of the Buddha’s tooth”. Give at least 2 hours here for the temple – there is an audio guide available at the entrance.

its wasnt a very great experience as we missed the feeding time. however, we went to the river across the orphanage to see the elephants bathing.  it was fun to see them enjoyed so much.  i got to feed them with 'banana' only coz no one was selling something else.  i had a lot of photos and yeah, you really need to get a timing as other spectators will be there in the background too, not to mention the care taker. well, it was really a good experience.  i just wished we arrived on time for the feeding session!

I have just got back from 2 weeks in Sri Lanka, working at the Millenium Elephant Foundation.   I would advise people to ask their guides or drivers to take them to the 'elephant bath' as this is a much smaller but much more hands on place to visit. We had many families call in who had been to the orphanage and found the jostling to feed the elephants and the requests for money a little bit too much to deal with. At the elephant bath, the price to get in is over half the price of Pinnawala, you get to ride an elephant, have photos taken close up, talk to the mahut about your elephant, and most fun of all.... go down to the river and bath your elephant, or in many cases be showered yourself by it.  There is no time scale, no rushing you in or out, no requests for tips from the guides or the mahuts and its a quiet and peacefull place to be. I loved the place, and loved watching families enjoying themselves up close to the elephants without any hassle

i have visited this orphanage, and am about to visit again in march this year...What most people do not understand is that this orphanages income is donation based...the majority of the elephants there, are due to past injuries, the elephants that are chained are usually of an agressive nature...Wish people would not judge until they know the facts..

This is worth visiting just for the experience of being so close to so many of these magnificent animals.  Some of the rescued Elephants have injuries (blindness, missing leg) but they seem to be looked after and have plenty of space to roam.  This has certainly changed for the better since my last visit 12 years ago.  The price however is still a bit extortionate for tourists (1500 rupees)  and they also charge extra if you want to use a camcorder (500 rupees).  After all, there is only so much you can see inside the orphanage (about 1 hours worth).  What's more interesting is when they go for their bath to the nearby river.  This event is free to watch and quite entertaining as they cross the road and walk past all the shops to get there. Word of warning...try not to get conned by the nearby 'Spice Garden' people.  They take you on a trip around the garden, give you what is said to be a free head/shoulder/back massage with various spices, then try to make you buy natural (Ayurvedic) remedies which are very expensive and ask for a tip for the massage of which they suggest 500 rupees each.  My sister, unfortunately, felt obliged/intimidated to part with17000 (£100) rupees.  This is their business but try not to get too engrossed in the sales pitch.

Wasn't sure what to make of the place when we first went in - as first thing we saw were 5 elephants chained up, but soon came to realise that another 79 were roaming free around the park.  Those chained up were old, blind or particularly temperamental.  Wasn't sure about the feeding pen where they fed the baby elephants - though obviously was just for tourists.  Bit strange so many people crowded around, but baby elephants didn't seem to mind.  Highlight of our day and quite obviously the elephants day was when they went down to the river.  Amazing seeing them enjoy the water, bathing and playing.  They all looked so happy!  The staff washed the older elephants - which looked like pretty hard work!  Some people might find treatment of elephants harsh, but they were all healthy, happy and a lot better off than if they were in the wild. I'd definitely recommend going with a guide - Ramdulla found us a great place to view, and very close to the elephants, and you don't have to queue for tickets.  Plus they're able to fill you in regarding conditions elephants were saved from, though most of the younger ones are born at the Orphanage.  Opportunity to help wash the elephants as well. Small tip - washrooms are typically sri-lankan, make sure you go before you get there unless you keep tissues handy!

A large number of elephant of all ages, impressive to see at the time for the bath in the river, if you're lucky enough to be there at the right time. Apart from that, the orphanage itself has nothing special. Nice for kids. but be aware that if you want to take a picture of your kid/partner next to an elephant, you will not miss the sri lankan worker next to it, and it will cost you yet another tip... The feeding of baby elephants is only a show organized for the visitors.

The entry fee was LKR 250 per person since we were from SAARC country. When we reached there the elephants were bathing in the river. The handlers were rude and were not allowing tourists to get photos with elephants. Better place to spend time with elephants was a place on our way back from Pinnewala (about 5 KMs) which offered 30 mins elephant ride for LKR 2500. The elephant would also go to the river and sprinkle water on you as part of this 30 mins. Here the handlers were good and polite with the elephants.

If you don't want to see elephants ill-treated give this tourist trap a miss. I thought the days of hobbling, chained and beaten elephants were gone. If you do go make sure not to tip the aggressive "mahouts" who will happily bully baby elephants into posing nicely for a photo. Read the Born Free report for further detail.

The elephants have very limited space. The older male that is nearly blind is always chained to a tree and for photos. He even has a sign about him nailed to the tree. I think that is just wrong. Yes, you will see elephants chained, not just the elder, but also simply to a tree, during feeding and sometimes just chained under the "station." They have a sign, "explaining" that.  When the elephants are brought to the feeding/nursing spectacle, they are chained and food is just thrown to them. When the food was out of reach, none of the mahuts even got it for them. The eating station is a noisy spectacle, designed just so that people can be closer to them, just like at the river. They are chained to eat just for a show! Unlike someone commented, I did see them occassionally hit and hook them. I also noticed that natural nursing was discouraged. Then the baby would squeal...and it is probably done so that they can do their nursing show...Now that I think about it, it was the older ones I saw chained to trees and they were probably the lactating mothers. Overall, the workers did not even seem to enjoy their work, and were not affectionate with the elephants,  which  is such a shame. I would love to work with elephants! I thought well I guess it's better than logging, giving rides, circuses and zoo's....when I did research at home, I found out that they actually send them to zoo's and circuses....even more depressing! There are sanctuaries you can go to that ARE sanctuaries, FOR the elephants, not the exploitation of them. I know because I am volunteering at the Elephant Nature Park in Thailand in 2008. I have only found 4 true sanctuaries. There are 2 in America, but there you can not have contact with the elephants.

I've been fascinated with elephants ever since I got the chance to ride on one. A visit to Pinnawela Elephant Orphanage was on the top of my list when we decided to travel to Sri Lanka. And it was the highlight of our trip for me. We could touch the elephants, watch the feeding of the baby elephants and help wash them when they were being led to the river. Standing there knee deep in the river while washing a huge elephant was one of the most wonderful experiences of my life. It took me the rest of the day to get that huge grin off of my face. Of course you have to pay for a lot of stuff but this orphanage can't exist without gifts from tourists. So I don't mind spending a few bucks on these endangered animals. It was so worth it!

An absolute must-see. The mahouts really interact well with the elephants, and the elephants are of course gorgeous. You can get really close to the water, or enjoy a panoramic view from a very nice restaurant just above. When I was there, a newly-married couple were having some wedding photos done, so that was an added bonus! Recommended, Sunday morning is a good time to go. It's listed as Colombo but in reality is at least an hour's drive away. As it's a very beautiful drive, you shouldn't mind too much!

I last visited Pinnawela a few months ago on one of my many trips to Sri Lanka. The elephants, many of them babies line up at 9am for feeding. These tiny waiste high babies trumpet till they are fed using giant milk bottles. The get agitated if the carer takes time. They then cross a main road, down a narrow alley way of shops to the river for their bath (twice a day). Watching this group of over 60 elephants play in the water is incredible. I really miss the place and will go back in 2007 for sure. I go for breakfast, and sit their till lunch time. Don't try to rush through it.

Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is situated in the Sabaragamuwa province of Sri Lanka which is about 87 Kilometers away from Colombo. To reach Pinnawala you have to turn from the 82nd kilometer post of the Colombo – Kandy main road and come through Rambukkana road. If you travel by train the nearest railway station to reach Pinnawala is Rambukkana (2 Kilometers from this railway station). The orphanage has a bunch of 84 elephants at the moment which is also considered as the biggest bunch of elephants in the world that are living under the human supervision. The age groups of these elephants are from One week to 50 years of old. The orphanage starts at 8.30 am daily for the visitors. At about 10.00 am this bunch of elephants starts walking towards Ma-Oya where they refresh with their daily bathing. Ma-Oya provides the water for drinking bathing for these elephants. The Elephant bathing at Ma-Oya provides a picturesque scene every morning & evening. Most of the visitors enjoy this scene every day while 84 elephants having their bath in this picturesque river according to their own rhythm. At 13.15 pm the staff of the orphanage starts feeding baby elephants with milk. This is another eye catching event for which most of the visitors enjoys themselves. At 14.00 pm again these elephants are accompanied for bathing at Ma-Oya. They bring back to the orphanage at about 16.00 pm and they are sent to the respective cages where they stay the night. The elephant orphanage enriches with a restaurant to provide delicious foods & refreshments for the visitors who likes to have some refreshment. The daily routine of the Orphanage is • 08.30 AM - Open for visitors • 09.15 AM - Feeding the baby elephants with milk • 10.00 AM - Accompanying the elephants for bathing • 12.00    -  Return to the orphanage after bathing • 13.15 AM - Feeding the baby elephants with milk • 14.00 PM -  Accompanying the elephants for bathing • 16.00 PM -  Return to the orphanage after bathing • 17.00 PM -  Feeding the baby elephants with milk • 18.00 PM - Close the Orphanage Safety Tips • Please do not enter the restricted areas • Smoke only the allocated areas • Keep the distance with the elephants • Keep the ticket with you • Do not disturb the elephants • Do not bring the pets

Contrary to the other review, we visited Pinnawela this week and found it to be nothing but a large scam. Three young elephants were chained within a compound for "feeding time" plus the smallest was not chained, which was nothing but an excuse for the two handlers to demand money in return for letting us tourists hold bottles of milk to feed the elephants whilst being photographed by our chums. One elephant was chained with a pile of kitul palm leaves out of reach which it vainly tried to reach to no avail....I guess this made it more keen to perform for the milk. All but the one baby elephant was well past the age where they required milk feeding but clearly being under the size of a mature elephant qualified them to be trotted out for the requisite opportunity to empty tourist pockets. This "orphanage" may have begun with noble intentions but these have been rapidly dumped in the name of opportunism. It is a disgrace. The Millenium Elephant Foundation just down the road may only have 8 elephants but at least they are not chained, appear well cared for and will give an elephant lover a more realistic opportunity to interact with these magnificent, intelligent animals. For the more adventurous, if you are on a road trip there are places where you may find working elephants being washed after their working day has finished. You may well find the mahout is willing to let you have some time with their elephants...we helped scrub them down whilst in the river thus giving the elephants the scrub they love, the little village a good deal of entertainment as the mad English frolicked, the nearest stallholder a good deal on a hand of bananas...and the mahouts got a tip. Everyone went home happy and the English were bordering on euphoric.

Arrived at Pinnawela just in time for the Elephants 2nd bath of the day. Their handlers march them through what appears to be the main road in town, down to the lake. This narrow road consists mainly of shops and stalls on either side selling leather goods and woodcarvings. That is a sight in itself and rather nerve racking for the stall owners I imagine, as it is a rather cramped walk and its better to get high up and out of the way. My boyfriend and I thoroughly enjoyed this spectacle and took hundreds of photos. We were told there are approximately 60 elephants currently living there and we counted about 40. The oldest elephant was supposed to be about 100 (?) he was absolutely huge with menacing tusks. Unfortunately he was also blind, due to getting to close to a landmine, another reminder of Sri Lanka’s turbulent past. When they were finished with their bath, they were marched back up while we stayed for a meal in one of the restaurants over looking the lake. I can't remember the name of the restaurant, but you can't miss it...the doorway is shaped like an elephant. The buffet meal wasn’t half bad, shame about the flies (but what do you expect). After finishing our lunch it was back up to the orphanage to watch some of the residents getting fed. I was particularly impressed with the care that the keepers took and progress they are making ie with the building of elephants housing, I imagine this is mostly due to the tourist attention they get and I was glad of it. Go and enjoy, my BIGGEST REGRET IS THAT YOU CAN’T TAKE AN ELEPHANT HOME WITH YOU X

I was  fortunate enought to have the opportunity to spend a week working at the Orphange -Thanks to winning it on a TV show here in the UK (Richard and Judy) As you would expect  the TV camers offered me extra opportunities but for anyone visiting it is just wonderful. Almost 60 elephants of ALL ages are there, just wandering around.  They are VERY well looked after and I saw NO mishandeling. Get there early and have a wander around, then go to see the greedy cheeky babies getting fed.. 10 am  Hold on to your bag they are strong and naughty..  :~) Then take a walk up to the top and see the herd wandering around there is ample photo opportunities - Rajha is a must see, he is an enormous blind bull with hugh tusks. When you are at the top it looks barren but this like a waiting area  and dust bath are for them, If you look down you will see lush green pasture and a private pool for them. Sumanabanda is the chief mahout, he is tiny but you know he is the boss, he is one of the best mahouts in the world and to see him just shout a few commands and watch these enormous beasts do as he asks is amazing. He taught me so much, look at the eyes, different coloured toes, and different shaped ears...  I ended up taking almost 500 photos and I could not have a camera with me when I was being filmed !!  I was a little enthusiastic ..... Anyway you will hear a big horn and that is the sign for bath time, get down to the rivers edge quicky to get a good vantage spot.  All the hotels and resturants are excellent but if you go down to the bottom and go to the one on the left you can still see if the elephants are moved over to the pool on the left..  the resturant on the right has teired seating so you still get excellent views and good food..  Im allergic to garlic and spices and they cooked everything fresh for me in all the resturants.. Take a change of clothes or some water shoes and you can go into the river and wash them, you have to give the mahouts some money about 200 rps but it is well worth it, I think you have to be discreet.  You can go around all the mahouts if you want.  Just stay at the side of the elephant, if you go past the back you  may get pebbledashed ... poo style :~)  they just go for it...  :~)  all part of the experience .. The mahouts work hard to protect both the elephants and the tourists..  Remember these elephants are still wild unpredictable elephants - ALWAWS listen to the Mahout.. if they say move then DO IT.. It is incredible watch the babies and how they play and tickle each other, and how the herd protects them.  Bath time takes a couple of hours. then its back to the Orphange so they cam be fed.. Then then the whole thing starts again in the afternoon... Enjoy it ,cos you dont have to muck them out like I did ... now that is an adventure !!!!   :~( Yo must go if  visiting Sri Lanka..

We got to the elephant orphanage just in time to watch them go in the water for bathing.  It's a good thing to stand away from the water as they would spray not just each other.  I laughed and laughed at a baby elephant, who really didn't seem to want to be in the water, but was constantly being pushed down and under the water.  I guess you don't argue with a mother that big.
